<meta>This page concludes Johannes Kepler's defense against Robert Fludd (Robertus de Fluctibus). On the previous page, Kepler was likely discussing the epistemological foundations of geometry as a reflection of the divine mind, a central theme in his "Harmonice Mundi" (The Harmony of the World).</meta>

APPENDIX TO THE APOLOGY FOR THE HARMONIES.

...our mind's natural aptitude for perceiving geometric things, we rightly credit all innate knowledge received. Therefore, the geometric foundations of arguments are not weak or fictional because they are in the human mind; but firm, because they depend on a natural participation in the image of God: nor, if man reasons from the light of nature <note>The "light of nature" (lumen naturae) refers to the human capacity for reason and discovery, which Kepler believed was a gift from God to understand the universe.</note> about what fits the structure of the heavens, does the Architect of the heavens follow human rules because of it: but because He himself took such rules from within Himself for building the world, therefore His image <note>Referring to the concept of *Imago Dei*, where humans, created in God’s image, share a capacity for God's own geometric logic.</note> [man], by reasoning, finds no others.

### Regarding the Testimonies in Favor of the Harmonies of Robert Fludd.

<margin>Page 46 to 54.</margin>Even though in this final repetition of your philosophy, which you insert over nine full pages, I find my name or my "crimes" mentioned more than ten times: I did not think that reason enough to be more long-winded in examining it. For I believe that hardly any reader, whether they be a Mathematician or a Hermeticist <note>A follower of Hermeticism, a philosophical tradition that emphasizes mystical correspondences between the "microcosm" (man) and "macrocosm" (the universe). Fludd was a prominent Hermeticist.</note>, will endure this reading until the end: and so my name will easily remain hidden in this Chaos <note>Kepler suggests Fludd's writing is so disorganized that it resembles the primordial Chaos.</note>: but even if it is found, all the objections have been dissolved in the preceding sections. 

Truly, it was not my intention in this writing to sample more of your philosophy than what serves to explain to readers the difference between your Harmonics and mine. And you end, not without bitterness, crediting God's preceding grace for the fact that, spurred on by the stings of my envy, you successfully completed the work: I, however, strongly deny that envy; I appeal to the judgment of the skilled reader, whether he finds any enviable goods that support the opinion of the crime imputed to me. 

For the rest, I candidly excuse myself to you: I have confessed in almost every line that I sought nothing else: namely, I aimed for this one thing: that unskilled readers, who are easily deceived by titles, might know what they would find with each of us, and by what distinction. If that could not be done otherwise—whether you were lightly grazed or heavily offended—consider the former done by necessity, the latter against my will. And these things indeed regarding my Comparisons, from the Appendix to the Work on Harmony.

As for the present apology, although provoked by frequent injuries, I would have had cause to fly into a rage here and there; I hope, however, that nothing has been said too harshly against you, or against your honor or dignity, nothing that can be compared with your bitterness; for wit and jokes are the seasonings <term>embammata|A Greek term for savory sauces or dips used to flavor food, here used metaphorically for rhetorical wit.</term> of debaters. If you are softened by this equanimity of mine, nothing will prevent us in the future from cultivating a literary friendship; and whatever talent each has received from God, let him contribute it to the praise of the Creator and the education of his neighbor, without disparaging the other; and whatever well-written things one finds from the other, let him accept those with a grateful heart, venerating the Giver Spirit, and enjoy them. Farewell.

->The Calends [1st] of August, in the year 1621.<-

->**T H E  E N D.**<-

# Johannes Kepler’s
# THE HARMONY
## OF THE WORLD
### IN FIVE BOOKS, OF WHICH

The First is **GEOMETRICAL**, On the origin and proofs of the Regular Figures <note>The "Regular Figures" refer to polygons like squares and equilateral triangles, and the five Platonic solids, which Kepler believed were the building blocks of the universe.</note> which constitute Harmonic Proportions.
The Second is **ARCHITECTURAL**, or from **FIGURED GEOMETRY**, On the fitting together of Regular Figures in a plane or solid:
The Third is properly **HARMONIC**, On the origin of Harmonic Proportions from Figures; and on the Nature and Differences of things pertaining to song, against the Ancients:
The Fourth is **METAPHYSICAL, PSYCHOLOGICAL, & ASTROLOGICAL**, On the mental Essence of Harmonies and their types in the World; especially on the Harmony of rays descending from celestial bodies to the Earth, and its effect on Sublunary <note>The "sublunary" realm refers to the Earth and its atmosphere, traditionally thought to be subject to change and decay, unlike the "perfect" heavens.</note> and Human Nature or the Soul:
The Fifth is **ASTRONOMICAL & METAPHYSICAL**, On the most perfect Harmonies of celestial motions, and the origin of Eccentricities <note>In astronomy, eccentricity describes how much a planetary orbit deviates from a perfect circle. Kepler's discovery that orbits are ellipses was central to this book.</note> from Harmonic proportions.
The Appendix contains a comparison of this work with Book III of the *Harmonics* of the celebrated Ptolemy, and with the harmonic speculations of Robert Fludd (called Robert de Fluctibus), an Oxford Physician, included in his work on the Macrocosm and Microcosm <note>The "Macrocosm" is the great universe, while the "Microcosm" is the human being, viewed as a miniature reflection of that universe.</note>.

<meta>This page concludes Kepler’s "Apology," a defensive essay appended to his "Harmony of the World." Having laid out his mathematical laws for the universe, Kepler here offers a final rebuttal to his rival, Robert Fludd, and a philosophical justification for why human geometry can actually describe the divine mind of God.</meta>

<page-num>50</page-num>
<header>APPENDIX TO THE APOLOGY FOR THE HARMONIES</header>

We rightly attribute our mind's natural aptitude for perceiving Geometrical things to all our innate and accepted knowledge. Therefore, the Geometrical foundations of our arguments are not weak or invented simply because they exist within the human mind; rather, they are firm because they depend on a natural participation in the image of God. <note>Kepler refers here to the concept of *Imago Dei*—the belief that humans are created in God's image, allowing them to understand the mathematical "language" God used to design the universe.</note> Nor is it the case that the Architect of the heavens looks to human rules when a man reasons from the light of nature <note>The "light of nature" is a philosophical term for human reason and observation independent of divine revelation.</note> about what fits the structure of the heavens. Instead, because God Himself drew those rules from within Himself to build the world, His own image—the human mind—finds no other rules when it reasons.

### Regarding the Testimonies in favor of the Harmonies of Robert Fludd.

<margin>
Page 46.
Line 34.
</margin>
Even though in this last repetition of your philosophy, which you have stretched over nine full pages, I find my name or my "crimes" inserted more than ten times, I did not think that was reason enough to be more long-winded in examining it. For I believe that no reader, whether he be a mathematician or a Hermeticist, <note>A follower of Hermeticism, an esoteric tradition of philosophy based on writings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus. Fludd was a leading Hermeticist who used symbols and mysticism where Kepler used math.</note> will endure this reading until the end; thus, my name will easily remain hidden in this Chaos. But even if it is found, all the objections have already been washed away in the previous sections. Indeed, it was not my intention in this writing to sample anything more from your philosophy than what serves to explain to readers the difference between your Harmonics and mine.

And as for your ending—where you, not without gall, <note>original: "non sine felle." This phrase implies Fludd's writing was bitter or spiteful.</note> attribute it to the *preceding graces of God* that you successfully finished your work while being spurred on by "envy" toward me—I vigorously deny that envy. I appeal to the judgment of a skilled reader to see if he finds any enviable qualities in your work that would support the charge you've leveled against me. For the rest, I candidly excuse myself to you: except for the fact that I have admitted it in almost every line, I sought nothing else but this one goal: that unlearned readers, who are easily deceived by titles, should know what they can find with each of us, and what the difference is. If this could not be done without you being either lightly grazed or heavily offended, consider that the former was necessary, while the latter happened against my will. And so much for my Comparisons, from the Appendix to the *Harmonic Work*.

As far as this present apology <note>In this context, an "apology" is not an admission of guilt, but a formal defense of one's positions (from the Greek *apologia*).</note> is concerned, although I have had cause to flare up here and there, provoked by frequent insults, I hope that nothing has been said against you or your honor and dignity that is too grave, or anything that could be compared with your own bitterness. Indeed, wit and jokes are the seasonings of debates. If you are softened by this equanimity of mine, nothing shall prevent us from cultivating a literary friendship in the future; and let each man contribute the talent he has received from God to the praise of the Creator and the education of his neighbor, without disparaging the other. May each man receive and enjoy with a grateful heart, and with reverence for the Giver of the Spirit, the well-written things he finds in the other. Farewell.

->The Calends of August in the Year 1621.<- <note>August 1st, 1621.</note>

->T H E   E N D.<-

<meta>While the previous page concluded the "Apology" (a defensive rebuttal to Robert Fludd found at the end of the work), this page is the main Title Page of the entire volume. It establishes the grand structure of Kepler’s masterpiece, where he attempts to unify geometry, music, and astronomy into a single "Harmony of the World."</meta>

### Johannes Kepler's
# THE HARMONY
# OF THE WORLD
## FIVE BOOKS, IN WHICH:

The First is **GEOMETRICAL**, On the origin and proofs of the Regular Figures <note>The "Regular Figures" refer to the Platonic solids and regular polygons, which Kepler believed were the building blocks of the universe’s design.</note> which constitute Harmonic Proportions.
The Second is **ARCHITECTURAL**, or concerning **FIGURED GEOMETRY**, On the Congruence <note>In geometry, "congruence" refers to how shapes fit together perfectly to fill a space (tessellation).</note> of Regular Figures in the plane or the solid.
The Third is properly **HARMONIC**, On the origin of Harmonic Proportions from Figures; and on the Nature and Differences of things pertaining to song, against the Ancients. <note>Kepler argues against ancient Greek musical theories, proposing his own system based on geometry rather than simple arithmetic.</note>
The Fourth is **METAPHYSICAL**, **PSYCHOLOGICAL** & **ASTROLOGICAL**, On the mental Essence of harmonies and their types in the World; especially on the Harmony of rays descending from the celestial bodies to the Earth, and its effect on the sublunary <note>The "sublunary" realm refers to the Earth and its atmosphere, which in pre-modern science were thought to be subject to change and decay, unlike the eternal heavens.</note> and Human Nature or Soul.
The Fifth is **ASTRONOMICAL** & **METAPHYSICAL**, On the most perfect Harmonies of the celestial motions, and the origin of Eccentricities from Harmonic proportions. <note>This book contains Kepler's famous Third Law of Planetary Motion, relating orbital periods to distances from the sun.</note>
The Appendix contains a comparison of this Work with Book III of the *Harmonics* of the famous Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer whose theories Kepler sought to update.</note>, and with the Harmonic speculations of Robert Fludd (called Robert de Fluctibus), a Physician of Oxford, which were inserted into his work on the Macrocosm and Microcosm.

->TO THE<-
->Most Serene and Most Powerful<-
->Prince and Lord,<-
## LORD JAMES,
### King of Great Britain, France, and Ireland, Defender of the Faith, etc.
->*My Most Clement Lord.*<-

<image-desc>A large square ornamental initial letter 'C' decorated with dense floral and foliate patterns.</image-desc>
Why I should send these books on Harmony abroad across the sea—away from the court of the most August Emperor <note>Referring to Ferdinand II, the Holy Roman Emperor, Kepler’s primary employer.</note>, my Lord; away from his hereditary Austrian Kingdoms and Provinces; and finally, away from Germany itself—to present them to your most serene gaze, O Illustrious King: for this, I have reasons both immediate and long-standing.

First, I did not think this was out of keeping with my duty. Since I serve as the Emperor’s mathematician <note>original: "Cæsaris in re Mathematicâ stipendia mereo." Kepler held the prestigious title of Imperial Mathematician.</note>, I wished to demonstrate even to those abroad how much care this Prince of the Christian Commonwealth takes for the most divine studies. I wanted it to be understood, by the undisturbed pursuit of the "ornaments of Peace" throughout these provinces, that the sinister rumors of internal war <note>This refers to the beginning of the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), which was ravaging Central Europe at the time Kepler published this work.</note> will undoubtedly soon be extinguished along with the conflict itself. And this somewhat harsh dissonance—just as in a moving melody <note>original: "Patheticâ Melodiâ." Kepler uses musical theory as a metaphor for the political and religious turmoil of his time, suggesting that conflict is a temporary "clash" before a resolution.</note>—is even now in its...

<summary>In this dedication to King James I, Johannes Kepler explains his decision to send his work on universal harmony to England, framing the scientific patronage of the Holy Roman Emperor as a sign of enduring peace despite the looming Thirty Years' War.</summary>

# D E D I C A T I O N.

...which will resolve into a closing cadence. <note>original: "quam Clausulam desituram." Kepler continues his metaphor from the previous page, comparing the "harsh dissonance" of the Thirty Years' War to a musical phrase that must eventually find a harmonious resolution.</note> Indeed, whom could I judge a more worthy appraiser of Imperial goodness than a great King? Whom could I have chosen as a more suitable Patron for a work on the *Harmony of the Heavens*—a work echoing the spirit of Pythagoras and Plato—than that King who has testified to his study of Platonic wisdom in his own writings <note>King James I was a prolific author; Kepler likely refers here to works like *Basilikon Doron*, which presented the King as a learned and wise ruler.</note>, which we, through the veneration of his subjects, even hold in public esteem? Who, while still a boy, judged the Astronomy of Tycho Brahe <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601) was the greatest observational astronomer of the era; Kepler served as his assistant and used Tycho's data to discover the laws of planetary motion.</note> (upon which this work rests) as worthy of his own brilliant mind? Who, finally, having reached manhood and taking up the rudders of government, noted the vanity of Astrology with public censure? This vanity is clearly exposed in Book IV of this work, where the true foundations of the influence of the stars are revealed. Thus, no one can doubt that you will be the most discerning judge of this entire Work and all its parts.

But I have an even greater, more ancient reason for this dedication. Nearly twenty years ago, when I first conceived the subject of this work in my mind and chose its title—though the specific motions of the Planets were not yet known to me—an instinct of Nature told me that Harmonies must exist within them. Even then, I destined the support and protection of this work for Your Majesty, should it ever be successfully completed. I declared this vow to your Ambassadors at the Imperial court on several occasions. My reasons for seeking your protection for my *Harmonics* <note>term: Harmonics. To Kepler, this was the science of finding mathematical proportions (ratios) that appear in music, geometry, and the movements of the planets.</note> were provided by that manifold Dissonance in human affairs—so obvious it cannot help but cause offense. Yet, this discord is composed of well-proportioned and distinct intervals; it is their nature to soothe the ear in the middle of a discord with the promise of a sweet harmony to follow, sustaining the listener with that very expectation. Truly, it is a conviction worthy of a Christian that it is God who moderates the entire Melody of human life. It is a patience worthy of God’s greatness not to be offended by the long duration of these dissonances, nor to abandon hope; for we must remember that it is not God's...

# DEDICATION.

...providence acts slowly, but the span of our individual lives flies swiftly away. I was indeed taught by the sacred oracles <note>Kepler refers to the Holy Scriptures.</note> that all things are destined by God for certain and beneficial uses: even these dissonant things, to illuminate and recommend the sweetness of Harmony. Why my desires should bid me to expect some beginning of restored harmony especially from your **Davidic Harp**, O Illustrious King—although this is not the place to explain it at length, lest I seem to disregard the warnings of the wise—yet let no one forbid me to touch upon this part of your glory, long acknowledged by the whole world, concerning the deeds performed by You: that, having obtained the Kingdom of England by inheritance and the consent of the people, you shortly gave to it, in common with the Kingdom of Scotland, the name of **Great Britain**; you tempered together from both provinces one Kingdom and one Harmony (for what else is a kingdom but a Harmony?), and you most happily removed the hereditary discord of the most hostile Nations; you have utterly extinguished the memory of frequent and most bloody slaughters, which, like certain markers, had punctuated the series of ages. 

This domestic work of yours seemed to me to contain a faithful omen (among other weightier matters) that you would, even abroad—a King among Kings, a **Defender of the Faith** <note>original: "Fidei Defensor," a title held by English monarchs since Henry VIII.</note> among the faithful of Christ—complete some greater and more excellent, and also more durable work. Indeed, I pursued this both in my silent prayers and in a public prediction in my book on the **New Star** <note>original: "De Stella Nova," Kepler's 1606 work on the supernova of 1604.</note>, which "burned like a Carbuncle" <note>A carbuncle is a deep-red gemstone, often a garnet. Kepler quotes a "well-known Scottish verse" (notus Scotiæ versiculus) likely referring to a poem or heraldic motto associated with the King's lineage.</note>. Therefore, as if that which I hoped for and predicted were now accomplished, I proposed to myself all the more firmly to eventually sing my own **Harmonies of the World** <note>original: "Mundanas Harmonias," the title of the work currently being dedicated, *Harmonices Mundi*.</note> to so praiseworthy a **Harmonizer**. <note>original: "Harmostæ," from the Greek term for a regulator or governor who brings order.</note>

I could wish here that the public **Dissonance** of voices clamoring in three ways <note>Likely referring to the religious and political divisions between Catholics, Lutherans, and Calvinists that led to the Thirty Years' War.</note> were a little milder toward me, so that I might be heard publicly according to my heart’s desire; in what way has the outcome seemed to favor my prayers? What wounds of the head, which...

<summary>Kepler praises King James I for the unification of England and Scotland into Great Britain, framing this political union as a "Harmony" that mirrors the celestial order. He hopes the King's peacemaking will extend to the religious conflicts of Europe.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Johannes Kepler’s dedication of *The Harmony of the World* to King James I of England. In the preceding text, Kepler praised James for unifying England and Scotland into Great Britain, seeing this as a terrestrial "harmony." He now transitions into a medical and theological metaphor to describe the religious and political strife in Europe, contrasting his private intellectual work with the "public noise" of war.</meta>

# D E D I C A T I O N .

...by these new Harmonies <note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely continuing from "new harmonies" mentioned on the previous page.</note>, and by which Physician? And how I myself depicted this very thing in vivid colors long ago in my book on the **New Star**? <note>original: *De Stella Nova* (1606), Kepler’s work on the supernova of 1604, where he discussed the astrological and providential significance of celestial events.</note> But what reward will there be for the labor if, while striving for Harmony with my private noise, I do not overcome the public outcries due to the weakness of my lungs, and instead increase the annoyances of an absurd discord in my own ears? It must indeed be confessed, alas, that the **cross-shaped wound** <note>original: *vulnus decussatum*. The term "decussis" refers to the Roman numeral X or a cross-shape; Kepler is alluding to the religious wars tearing Europe apart, symbolized by the Cross.</note>—or if we prefer a more sacred and auspicious word, **cruciform**—is still swollen with many lips; and with none of them closing, the medicine has so far been ineffectual and mocked on all sides. This is because the Physician, in order to sneak medicine into a patient suffering from delirium, adds many things at once which seem to depart greatly from sound reason. 

I am nonetheless refreshed by this very thought: that the **Supreme Healer** <note>original: *Curator*. Kepler refers to God as the ultimate physician of the world's ills.</note> of our wounds is certain of His art, and applies nothing in vain. Therefore, He who has already begun the cure, who has already prepared and shown these healing agents to the world, meanwhile uses corrosive agents through public calamities, until—once the rotted and wild flesh of extinguished charity is consumed—some sense of pain descends to the depths of the living flesh. The same Healer will undoubtedly also use soothing remedies soon to reduce the swellings, so that there may finally be a place for those healing agents; and at last this long-lasting **Dissonance** (to return to the example proposed) may end in pure and lasting Harmony. 

In this hope, even against hope, I am confirmed not only by the success of my Harmonic speculations—whose success far exceeds my boldness in searching—but also by this very fact: that among the other things necessary for the perfection of the Work which have remained in their original place for so many years, I have seen Your **Royal Majesty**, to whom I had destined the patronage of this work before it was even begun, safe and flourishing until now; nor shall I cease to strive with devoted prayers to God, the author of Peace and Concord, that...

<summary>Kepler uses a medical metaphor to describe Europe's religious conflicts as a "cruciform wound" that God, the Supreme Physician, is treating through the "corrosive" pain of war to eventually bring about a lasting "Harmony." He expresses hope that King James I will serve as a patron for this cosmic harmony, noting that the King has remained a stable figure throughout the years of the book's long preparation.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Johannes Kepler’s dedication of *The Harmony of the World* to King James I of England. # D E D I C A T I O N .

...may He preserve both your life and your Royal Majesty in safety until that longed-for day.

In the meantime, I humbly ask Your Most Reverend <gloss>Most Reverend</gloss> Majesty to look upon this work of **Harmony** <note>Kepler refers here to his book, *Harmonice Mundi* (*The Harmony of the World*), which explores the mathematical order of the universe.</note>, dedicated to your Name, with a serene expression, and to judge this token of my most devoted affection toward you with kindness and favor. May you indeed delight your royal mind with the contemplation of the works of God, as far as the necessary duties of the Kingdom permit. By the examples of the Concord shining out from the visible works of God, may you strengthen and stir up within yourself a zeal for Concord and for Peace, both in the Church and in the State <note>Kepler frequently argues that if the stars and planets follow a geometric harmony established by God, humans should seek a similar harmony in religion and politics.</note>. Finally, may you deign to look upon me and my studies with your most merciful royal patronage.

Given at Linz <note>original: *Lentiis Noricis*, a Latin name for the city of Linz in the ancient province of Noricum.</note> on the banks of the Danube, on the Ides of February <note>February 13th</note>, in the year 1619 of the Western era.

# DEDICATION.

...attempted by these **Harmonies**, by what Physician? And how did I myself depict this very thing in my book on the **New Star**, <note>Kepler refers to his 1606 work *De Stella Nova*, which discussed the supernova of 1604 and its astrological and political implications.</note> long ago in vivid colors? But what will be the reward for the effort if, while striving for **Harmony** with a private sound, I fail to overcome the public clamor because of the weakness of my lungs, <note>original: "imbecillitate laterum," literally "weakness of the sides," a common idiom for a weak voice or physical frailty when speaking or singing.</note> and instead only increase the annoyances of an absurd discord in my own ears? 

It must indeed be confessed, alas, that the crossed wound—or should we prefer the more sacred and auspicious word, **cruciform**—is still swelling with many lips; <note>Kepler uses "cruciform" (cross-shaped) to describe the religious wars tearing Europe apart, implying the conflict is centered on the Cross of Christ itself.</note> and with none of them closing together, the medicine has so far been in vain and mocked on all sides. This is because the Physician, in order to administer a deceptive remedy to a delirious patient, adds many things at once that seem to depart greatly from sound reason. Yet I am refreshed by this very thought: that the supreme **Healer** of our wounds is certain of His art, and applies nothing in vain. 

Therefore, He who has already begun the cure, who has already prepared and shown to the world these healing remedies; <note>original: "consolidantia," referring to medicines that cause a wound to close and scar over.</note> meanwhile, however, He uses corrosive agents through public calamities, until—once the putrid and wild flesh of extinguished charity is consumed—some sense of pain descends to the depth of the living flesh. He will undoubtedly also use soothing remedies soon to reduce the swellings, so that there may finally be a place for those healing ones; and at last this long-lasting **Dissonance** (to return to the proposed example) may end in a pure and lasting **Harmony**. 

In this hope, even against hope, I am confirmed not only by the success of my **Harmonic** speculations—the success of which far exceeds my boldness in searching—but also by this very fact: that among the other things necessary for the completion of the Work, <note>His book, *Harmonices Mundi* (The Harmonies of the World).</note> which have remained in their original state for so many years, I have seen even Your **Royal Majesty**—to whom I had destined the patronage of this work before it was even begun—safe and flourishing up to this point. Nor shall I cease to strive with devoted prayers to God, the author of **Peace and Concord**, so that...

<meta>This page follows the title page and represents the beginning of the Preface to Book I. Kepler is establishing the philosophical and mathematical framework for his study of harmony, heavily drawing upon the work of the Neoplatonist philosopher Proclus.</meta>

DE FIGURARUM HARMON:
<note>original: "DE FIGURARUM HARMONIA" — On the Harmony of Figures</note>

## Preface.

<margin>
Proclus on the 
intellectual 
essence of 
Geometric 
things.
</margin>

Since we must seek the causes of Harmonic Proportions from the divisions of the circle into a certain number of equal parts, which are made geometrically and scientifically—that is, from demonstrable Regular plane figures—I thought it necessary to point out at the beginning that the mental <note>Kepler uses "mental" (mentales) here to refer to the conceptual or "ideal" existence of mathematical truths, as opposed to their physical representations.</note> differences of geometric things are today, as far as can be seen from published books, entirely ignored. Furthermore, among the ancients, hardly anyone occurs who indicated that they exactly understood these specific differences of geometric things, except for Euclid and his commentator Proclus. To be sure, the distribution of problems into Plane, Solid, and Linear by Pappus of Alexandria <note>A 4th-century Greek mathematician known for his "Collection" (Synagoge), which categorized geometry into these three types.</note> and the ancients whom he follows, is suitable enough for explaining the habits of the mind arising around each class of the geometric subject; however, that division is brief in words, and while applied to practice, no mention is made of theory. And indeed, unless we are occupied with our whole mind in the theory of this matter, we shall never be able to attain the reasons for harmony. Proclus Diadochus, in his four books published on the first book of Euclid, acted as a Theoretical Philosopher in a mathematical subject by profession; if he had also left us his commentaries on the tenth book of Euclid, he would have both freed our Geometers from ignorance (had he not been neglected) and relieved me of this labor of explaining the differences of geometric things in their entirety. For it is easily apparent from his very introduction that those distinctions of Mental Beings were well known to him, since he established the same principles for the entire Mathematical essence which also govern all Beings, and generate all things from themselves: namely, the Limit and the Infinite—or the Bound and the Unbounded—recognizing the Bound or circumscription as the Form, and the Unbounded as the Matter of geometric things.

For Shape and proportion are the properties of Quantities: shape of individual things, proportion of things joined together. Shape is perfected by boundaries; for a straight line is bounded by points, a plane surface by lines, and a body by surfaces; thus it is circumscribed and shaped. Therefore, those things which are finite, circumscribed, and shaped can also be grasped by the mind; but infinite and indeterminate things, insofar as they are such, are matched by no knowledge (which consists of definitions) and can be constrained by no barriers of demonstration. Moreover, figures exist in the Archetype <note>Kepler’s "Archetype" is the divine blueprint or pre-existent model in the mind of God according to which the universe was structured.</note> before they are in the Work; they are in the divine mind before they are in created things—different, indeed, in the manner of the subject, but yet with the same form of their essence. Therefore, for quantities, shaping becomes a certain Mental essence, or intellection: their essential difference. This is much more clear from proportions. For since shaping is perfected by many boundaries, it happens that because of this plurality, shaping makes use of proportions. But what Proportion might be without the action of the mind can in no way be understood. And for this reason also, he who gives boundaries to quantities as an essential principle posits that shaped quantities have an intellectual essence. But there is no need for argument; let the whole book of Proclus be read. It will sufficiently appear that the intellectual differences of geometric things were well known to him; even if he does not place this assertion separately and alone in the open and conspicuous as if to warn even a drowsy reader. For his speech flows like a full channel, spread on all sides with the most abundant opinions of the more abstruse Platonic philosophy, among which is this one, the singular argument of this book.

<meta>catchword: But</meta>

<summary>In this preface, Kepler argues that mathematical shapes and proportions have a "mental" or "intellectual" existence that precedes their physical reality. He identifies these geometric truths as divine archetypes and credits the philosopher Proclus with understanding this connection between geometry and the mind of God.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s preface to Book I. Having previously praised the ancient commentator Proclus, Kepler now defends Euclid against modern critics—specifically Petrus Ramus—who failed to see the deeper philosophical purpose behind Euclidean geometry.</meta>

# ON DEMONSTRATION. BOOK I.

<margin>Petrus Ramus’s unfair and ignorant judgment of Euclid</margin>
But our own age has not yet had the leisure to penetrate into such hidden depths. Petrus Ramus <note>A 16th-century French humanist and logician known for his aggressive critiques of Aristotle and Euclid.</note> read the book of Proclus, but as far as the core of philosophy is concerned, he despised and cast it aside, just as he did with the tenth book of Euclid. Ramus had also written a commentary on Euclid; however, as if he had written a defense of him, he was rejected and ordered to be silent. Thus provoked, the anger of this hostile Critic turned against Euclid as if he were the defendant. Euclid’s tenth book was condemned by a harsh sentence, so that it might not be read—even though, if read and understood, it could reveal the mysteries of philosophy. 

Read, I pray you, the words of Ramus, than which he never produced anything more unworthy of himself: *In the 21st book of his Mathematical Schools, he says: "The material proposed in the tenth book is delivered in such a way that I have never encountered similar obscurity in human literature or arts. I do not mean obscurity in understanding what Euclid prescribes (for that might be clear even to the unlearned and illiterate, who look only at what is immediately present), but rather in thoroughly seeing and exploring what end and use is proposed for the work, and what the genera, species, and differences of the subject matter are. For I have never read or heard of anything so confused or involved. Indeed, it seems as if Pythagorean superstition has been led into this cave, etc."* 

But by God, Ramus, if you had not believed this book to be too easy to understand, you would never have slandered it for such obscurity. There is a need for greater labor, a need for stillness, a need for care, and especially for focused attention of the mind until you grasp the intention of the writer. When a noble mind has exerted itself toward that goal, then at last, seeing itself moving in the light of truth, it is drenched and exultant with incredible pleasure; and from that vantage point, as if from a watchtower, it perceives the whole World and all the differences of its parts with the greatest exactness. But as for you, who here act as the patron of ignorance and of the common crowd of men who snatch profit from every thing—divine or human—I say to you: let those "prodigious sophisms" be yours; let it be you who consider Euclid to have immoderately wasted your leisure; let those "sharp points" of his have no place in your Geometry. Let it be your lot to carp at what you do not understand. For me, who investigates the causes of things, no paths have opened toward them except through the tenth book of Euclid.

<margin>Lazarus Schonerus</margin>
Lazarus Schonerus <note>A student of Ramus and a mathematician who later corresponded with Kepler.</note>, following Ramus in his *Geometry*, confessed that he could see absolutely no use for the five Regular bodies <note>The five Platonic solids: the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron.</note> in the World, until he read through my little book, which I titled *The Secret of the Universe* <note>original: "Mysterium Cosmographicum" — Kepler's first major work (1596), which proposed that the orbits of the planets were determined by the five Platonic solids.</note>. In that work, I prove that the number and intervals of the Planets are derived from the five Regular bodies. See how much Ramus the master harmed Schonerus the disciple. 

First, having read Aristotle—who had refuted the Pythagorean philosophy regarding the properties of the Elements being derived from the five bodies—Ramus immediately conceived a contempt for the whole of Pythagorean Philosophy. Then, since he knew Proclus had belonged to the Pythagorean sect, he did not believe Proclus when he affirmed what was most true: namely, that the ultimate goal of Euclid’s work, to which absolutely all the propositions of all the books refer (except those leading to the Perfect Number), is the five regular bodies. From this arose in Ramus the most confident persuasion that the five bodies were to be removed from the goal of Euclid’s *Elements*.

Once the goal of the work was taken away, as if the design of a building had been removed, there remained in Euclid a formless heap of propositions, which Ramus—throughout all twenty-eight books of his *Schools*—attacks as if it were some ghost, with great mockery <note>original: "dicca" — likely a shorthand or cutoff for "dicacitate" (mockery/sarcasm).</note>

<summary>Kepler defends Euclid’s tenth book and the five Platonic solids against the criticisms of Petrus Ramus, arguing that these mathematical concepts are the essential "watchtower" for understanding the physical structure of the universe.</summary>
<keywords>Petrus Ramus, Euclid, Proclus, Lazarus Schonerus, Mysterium Cosmographicum, Pythagorean philosophy, Regular solids, Platonic solids, Geometry, Tenth Book of Euclid</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s critique of those who dismiss the higher purpose of geometry. He specifically addresses Lazarus Schöner and Petrus Ramus, who rejected the utility of the five regular solids. Kepler transitions into a defense of the "mystical" Pythagorean view, which he believes aligned with his own planetary theories.</meta>

## ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES.

<margin>Lazarus Schöner’s opinion on the five solid figures</margin>
...with a bitterness of speech and a great rashness most unworthy of such a man. Having followed Ramus’s conviction, Schöner also believed that regular bodies are of no use; and not only this, but he also neglected or despised Proclus, following Ramus’s judgment. From Proclus, he could have learned the use of the five bodies both in Euclid’s *Elements* and in the fabric of the World. Indeed, the disciple [Schöner] was more fortunate than the Master [Ramus], because he joyfully accepted the use of the bodies revealed by me in *The Secret of the Universe* <note>Original: *Fabricâ Mundi*. Kepler refers to his 1596 work, *Mysterium Cosmographicum*, where he first proposed that the orbits of the planets are separated by the five Platonic solids.</note>, which Ramus had rejected even when urged by Proclus. For what does it matter if the Pythagoreans attributed these figures to the elements, and not, as I do, to the Spheres of the World? Ramus should have striven to remove this error of theirs regarding the genuine subject of the figures, as I have done, rather than abolishing this entire branch of Philosophy with a single tyrannical word.

<margin>The Mystical interpretation of the five figures by the Pythagoreans.</margin>
What if the Pythagoreans taught the very same thing that I do, but covered their meaning in a shroud of words? Does not the Copernican form of the World exist in Aristotle himself, though wrongly refuted by him under other names—while they [the Pythagoreans] called the Sun "Fire" and the Moon the "Counter-Earth"? <note>The Pythagoreans believed the Earth and a "Counter-Earth" revolved around a Central Fire, a precursor to the Sun-centered model.</note> For if the arrangement of the spheres was the same among the Pythagoreans as it is in Copernicus; if the five Bodies were known, along with the necessity of their five-fold number; if they all constantly taught that the five bodies are the Archetypes of the parts of the World; how much is left but to believe that their opinion, read by Aristotle as an enigma, was refuted as if the words held their literal sense? For instance, Aristotle read "Earth," to which they gave the Cube; when they perhaps meant Saturn, whose Sphere is removed from Jupiter by the interposition of a Cube. Indeed, the common people ascribe rest to the Earth, but Saturn has been allotted the slowest motion, closest to rest; for which reason it also obtained its name from "Rest" among the Hebrews. <note>The Hebrew name for Saturn is *Shabbatai*, which shares a root with *Shabbat* (Sabbath), meaning rest.</note> Thus Aristotle read that the Octahedron was given to Air, while they perhaps meant Mercury, whose sphere is enclosed by the Octahedron; nor is Mercury less swift (being indeed the swiftest of all) than Air is considered mobile. By the word "Fire," perhaps Mars was suggested, which elsewhere is named *Pyrois* <note>Greek: *Pyroeis*, meaning "fiery."</note> from fire, and to it the Tetrahedron was given, perhaps because its sphere is enclosed by this figure. And under the shroud of "Water," to which the Icosahedron was attributed, the star of Venus could lie hidden (as its course is contained by the Icosahedron), because moisture is subject to Venus, and she herself is said to have been born from the foam of the Sea, hence the name *Aphrodite* <note>From the Greek *aphros*, meaning "foam."</note>. Finally, the word "World" could have signified the Earth; and the Dodecahedron be ascribed to the World, because the Earth’s course is contained by this figure, distinguished by twelve parts of length <note>A reference to the twelve signs of the Zodiac.</note>; just as that figure is contained by twelve planes in its whole circuit. Therefore, the fact that in the Mysteries of the Pythagoreans the five figures were distributed in this way—not among the Elements, as Aristotle believed, but among the Planets themselves—is most strongly confirmed by Proclus, who among others hands down this goal of Geometry: that it teaches in what way the heavens received fitting figures for their specific parts.

<margin>Willebrord Snell’s opinion on Binomials:</margin>
Nor is there yet an end to the damage that Ramus has caused us. Behold Snell <note>Willebrord Snellius (1580–1626), the Dutch mathematician famous for Snell's Law.</note>, the most skillful of modern Geometers, clearly supporting Ramus in his preface to the Problems of Ludolph van Ceulen <note>Ludolph van Ceulen (1540–1610), known for his calculation of pi.</note>. First, he says that the division of incommensurables <note>Original: *ineffabilium*. This refers to the irrational lines discussed in Euclid's Book X.</note> into thirteen species is useless for practice. I grant this, if he recognizes no use except in common life, and if no one despises...

<summary>Kepler defends the regular solids (Platonic solids) by suggesting that the ancient Pythagoreans used them as a coded language for planetary orbits rather than physical elements. He also begins a rebuttal against Willebrord Snell’s dismissal of Euclid’s study of irrational numbers.</summary>
<keywords>Platonic solids, Pythagoras, Aristotle, Saturn, Mercury, Mars, Venus, Earth, Proclus, Petrus Ramus, Willebrord Snellius, planetary orbits, geometry, irrational numbers</keywords>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>This page continues Kepler’s critique of contemporaries who undervalue theoretical geometry. Having just discussed Lazarus Schöner and Petrus Ramus, Kepler now addresses Willebrord Snellius and further develops his argument that geometry's highest purpose is not mere utility, but the uncovering of divine Archetypes.</meta>

### ON DEMONSTRATION. BOOK I.

A 3

<meta>catchword: I would bring [ferrem]</meta>

...the use of physical trials for life. But why does Snellius not follow Proclus—whom he cites—who recognizes that there is some greater good in Geometry than the arts necessary for living? Had he followed him, the use of the tenth book <note>Euclid’s Book X, which deals with the classification of irrational magnitudes, often considered the most difficult and "useless" by practical-minded mathematicians of the era.</note> would have appeared in the assessment of the types of figures. Snellius cites geometric authors who do not use Euclid’s tenth book. Truly, all those authors treat either linear problems or solids, and deal with figures or quantities that do not have their end within themselves, but clearly tend toward other uses, and would not be sought out without them. But **regular Figures** are sought for their own sake as **Archetypes**; they possess their own perfection within themselves, and they are among the subjects of planar Problems, notwithstanding the fact that a solid is also enclosed by planar faces; similarly, the material of the tenth book primarily pertains to planes. Why then should heterogeneous things be cited? Or why should merchandise be judged of little value because a beggar like Codrus does not buy it to feed his belly, but a queen like Cleopatra buys it to adorn her ears? *Is this merely a cross fixed for geniuses?* <note>original: "Crux tantùm defixa est ingenijs?" This is a common early modern proverb for a problem that torments the mind.</note> Indeed, it is so for those who vex the **Inexpressible** <note>original: "Ineffabilia," referring to irrational numbers/surds which cannot be expressed as a simple ratio.</note> with numbers—that is, by speaking them. But I treat these types not with numbers, nor through Algebra, but by the reasoning of the Mind; clearly because I have no need for them to subtract accounts for the marketplace, but to explain the causes of things. Snellius thinks those subtle things should be segregated from the **Elements** <note>original: Στοιχειώσει (Stoicheiosei). Kepler refers to the foundational system of Euclid’s *Elements*.</note> and hidden away in libraries. In this, he acts as an entirely faithful disciple of Ramus, and employs no small effort: Ramus took away the form from the Euclidean Building and cast down the roof—the five bodies—without which the entire structure was dissolved, the walls stand cracked, and the arches threaten ruin. Snellius, therefore, even removes the Cement, as if it has no use except for the solidity of a house joined together under the five figures. O happy understanding of the disciple, how dexterously he learned to understand Euclid from Ramus! Namely, they think they are called "Elements" because one finds in Euclid an all-encompassing abundance of propositions, problems, and Theorems for every kind of Quantity and the arts occupied with them; whereas the book was called the **Foundational System** <note>original: Στοιχειώσις (Stoicheiosis)</note> because of its form, in that the following proposition always rests upon the preceding one, all the way to the last proposition of the last book (and partly of the ninth book), which cannot lack any of the prior ones. They turn an Architect into a woodsman or a supplier of materials, believing that Euclid wrote his book for the purpose of accommodating everyone else, while he alone would have no house of his own. But enough of these matters in this place; I must return to the main point of the discourse.

<margin>The reason for this Book I.</margin>
For when I perceived that the true and genuine differences of geometric things—from which I must summon the causes of **Harmonic Proportions**—are generally ignored entirely; that Euclid, who had handed them down with zeal, was exploded and hissed off stage, oppressed by the quibbles of Ramus; that he was heard by no one amidst the noise of the playful disturbers, or was telling the mysteries of Philosophy to the deaf; and that Proclus—who could have opened Euclid's mind, unearthed the hidden things, and rendered the difficult easy to grasp—was held in derision and had not continued his Commentaries as far as the tenth book: I saw that this must be done by me. Namely, that at the beginning, I should transcribe from Euclid’s tenth book those things which would especially serve my present purpose, and bring to light the series of matters in that book, with certain divisions inserted.

<summary>Kepler defends the "foundational" nature of Euclid's Elements, arguing against critics like Ramus and Snellius who view geometry only as a tool for practical utility rather than a pursuit of divine archetypes. He announces his intention to rehabilitate Euclid's Tenth Book as the basis for his study of harmony.</summary>
<keywords>Euclid, Book X, regular solids, Petrus Ramus, Willebrord Snellius, Archetypes, irrational numbers, Elements, geometric demonstration</keywords>

--- Page 19 ---
<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion regarding the classification of magnitudes. Kepler is explaining his editorial choices in organizing this book, specifically why he departs from Euclid’s traditional order to better serve his philosophical goal: the study of universal harmony.</meta>

...I would bring, and I would indicate the reasons why certain parts of the divisions were omitted by Euclid: only then was it necessary to deal with the figures themselves. In those cases which were most clearly demonstrated by Euclid, I was content with a simple citation of the propositions; many things that were demonstrated by Euclid in another way, because of the goal I set for myself—namely, because of the comparison of knowable and unknowable <note>original: "scibilium & inscibilium." In this context, Kepler refers to "knowable" figures as those that can be constructed with a straightedge and compass, and "unknowable" as those that cannot.</note> figures—had to be repeated here, or separated things joined together, or the order changed. I have embraced the series of Definitions, Propositions, and Theorems in a continuous numbering, as I did in the *Dioptrics* <note>Kepler’s 1611 work on optics and telescope lenses.</note>, for the convenience of citations. Even in the lemmas themselves, I was not meticulous, nor too concerned about vocabulary, being more intent on the things themselves: since I am acting not as a Geometer in Philosophy, but as a Philosopher in this part of Geometry. And would that I could have discussed Geometric matters even more popularly, provided it were both clearer and more palpable. But I hope that fair readers will judge my work well in both respects: both because I present Geometric matters in a popular way, and because I could not overcome the obscurity of the material through industry. To these readers, I give this final piece of advice: if they are entirely unskilled in Mathematical matters, they should skip my narrations and read only the propositions, from XXX until the end; and having placed faith in the propositions themselves without demonstration, let them proceed to the other books, especially to the last; lest, terrified by the difficulty of Geometric arguments, they deprive themselves of the most pleasant fruit of Harmonic contemplation. Now let us approach the matter with God’s help.

# I. Definitio.

A plane regular Figure is said to be that which has all sides and all angles, turned outward, equal.

# II. Definitio.

Of these, some are primary and radical, which do not exceed their own boundaries, to which the stated definition properly applies; some are augmented, which exceed their own sides, as it were, by continuing the non-adjacent sides of some radical [figure] until they meet: they are called **Stars** <note>Kepler is defining "Stellae" or star polygons (like the pentagram), which he was among the first to treat with geometric rigor.</note>.

# ON DEMONSTRATIONS. BOOK I.

Just as here A B C D E is a perfect pentagon <term>quinquangulum: literally a "five-angled" shape; we call this a regular pentagon</term>, and it is a primary figure, not requiring any other perfect figure from which it might be produced by extending its sides.

<image-desc>Two circular diagrams side-by-side. The left circular diagram contains a regular pentagon labeled A, B, C, D, E with a center point labeled L. The right circular diagram contains a five-pointed star (pentagram) inscribed within it, with the outer vertices labeled F, G, H, I, K.</image-desc>

But F G H I K is a five-pointed star <term>stella quinquangula: literally a "five-angled star"; known today as a pentagram</term>, and it is an augmented figure, created by extending pairs of non-adjacent sides—for example, AB and DC—until they meet at a point L.

### III. Definition.

Semiregular figures are those which have varying angles but four equal sides, such as the Rhombi NMPO and GEKD.

<image-desc>Two side-by-side diagrams of rhombi. The left rhombus is labeled with vertices N, M, P, O. The right rhombus is labeled with vertices G, E, K, D.</image-desc>

### IV. Proposition.

All Regular figures can have all their angles rest simultaneously upon the same circle.

*For by the 21st Proposition of the Third Book of Euclid <note>Euclid's Elements, Book III, Prop. 21 states that angles in the same segment of a circle are equal to one another.</note>, all equal angles can be inscribed in the same, and thus also in equal segments of the same circle. However, all angles of a Regular figure are equal; therefore, all angles of a single figure can be inscribed in equal segments of a single circle. But it is also necessary that they all be inscribed in practice once a single one is inscribed. For all sides are equal; wherefore the segments of the circle that are cut off by the two sides of a single angle are also equal, by the 24th Proposition of the Third Book of Euclid <note>Euclid's Elements, Book III, Prop. 24: Similar segments of circles on equal straight lines are equal to one another.</note>. Therefore, both the angle and the ends of the sides coincide with the same circle at once. The ends of the sides are, of course, the angles themselves. It would be otherwise if, although the angles were equal, the sides were not: for then the necessity of all parts being inscribed in the circle would be dissolved.*

### V. Definition.

To describe a Figure is to determine the proportion of the lines subtended <term>subtended: a line "subtends" an angle when it connects the two endpoints of that angle's sides, like the string of a bow</term> by the angles to the sides of the angle by a geometric act; from these determined elements, to construct the elementary triangles of the figure; and from these joined triangles, to complete the figure itself.

<image-desc>A diagram of a regular pentagon labeled with vertices A, B, C, D, E. Dotted lines are drawn from the top vertex (A) to the bottom-left vertex (D) and the bottom-right vertex (C), dividing the pentagon into three internal triangles: ABC, ACD, and ADE.</image-desc>

For given the proportion of DA to AE and ED, the triangles DAE, DAC, and CAB are formed; from these, the figure is established.

ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES.
<meta>catchword: As here</meta>

...I might bring forth and indicate the reasons why certain parts of the divisions were omitted by Euclid: then at last the figures themselves had to be dealt with. In those cases where Euclid provided very clear demonstrations, I have been content with a simple citation of the propositions. However, many things demonstrated by Euclid in another way had to be repeated here because of my stated purpose—namely, for the comparison of **knowable** and **unknowable** figures <note>original: "scibilium & inscibilium." In Kepler's system, "knowable" refers to shapes that can be precisely constructed using only a straightedge and compass, which he believes reflects the mind of God.</note>. In some cases, separated points had to be joined, or the order changed. I have organized the series of Definitions, Propositions, and Theorems with a continuous numbering system, as I did in my *Dioptrics* <note>Kepler's 1611 work *Dioptrice*, which revolutionized the study of lenses.</note>, for ease of reference. Even in the lemmas <term>lemma: a "helping" proposition used to prove a larger theorem</term> themselves, I have not been overly precise, nor too concerned with specific wording, being intent more on the things themselves. For I do not act here as a Geometer in Philosophy, but as a Philosopher in this part of Geometry. And I wish that I could have discussed these geometric matters even more popularly <note>meaning: in a way more accessible to the general public</note>, provided it was both clearer and more tangible. But I hope that fair-minded readers will value my effort in both respects: that I hand down geometric principles in a popular manner, and that I could not, through my own industry, overcome the inherent obscurity of the subject matter. To those readers I also give this final piece of advice: if they are entirely unskilled in mathematical matters, they should skip my narrations and read only the propositions, from the 30th to the end. Accepting the propositions themselves on faith without the proof, they may proceed to the remaining books, especially the last one; thus, they will not be frightened away by the difficulty of geometric arguments and deprive themselves of the most delightful fruit of Harmonic contemplation. Now let us approach the matter, with God's help.

## On the Demonstrations of Regular Figures.

### I. Definition.

A regular plane figure is said to be that which has all sides and all angles, facing outward, equal.

<image-desc>A circular diagram containing an inscribed square. The vertices of the square are labeled P (top), R (right), O (bottom), and Q (left). Inside the square, a central point is marked L, with points M and N on the horizontal diameter.</image-desc>

</insert>

### II. Definition.

Of these, some are primary and radical, which do not exceed their own boundaries; to these the given definition properly applies. Some are augmented, which exceed their own sides (so to speak) by continuing the non-adjacent sides of some radical figure until they meet: these are called **Stars**.

# ON DEMONSTRATION. BOOK I.

*Just as A B C D E here is a perfect pentagon <note>original: "quinquangulum"; a five-angled figure</note>, and is a primary figure, not requiring another perfect one from which it might be produced by the extension of its sides.*

[Two circular geometric diagrams. The left diagram shows a regular pentagon with vertices labeled A, B, C, D, E inscribed within a circle; the letter L is positioned in the center. The right diagram depicts a five-pointed star (pentagram) inscribed in a circle, with the outer vertices labeled F, G, H, I, K and the internal intersection points labeled A, B, C, D, E; the center is also marked with the letter L, showing the star formed by the intersection of extended lines.]

*But F G H I K is a five-angled star <note>often called a pentagram</note>, and an expanded figure, produced by continuing two non-adjacent sides—for example, AB and DC—until they meet at the point L.*

### III. Definition.

Semi-regular figures are those which, while having varying angles, have four equal sides, such as the Rhombuses <note>a diamond shape where all sides are the same length, but the angles are not 90 degrees</note> NMPO and GEKD.

[Two side-by-side rhombuses (parallelograms with equal sides). The left rhombus is labeled with vertices N, M, P, O. The right rhombus is labeled with vertices G, E, K, D.]

### IV. Proposition.

All Regular figures can have all their angles rest upon the same circle at the same time <note>meaning they can be "inscribed" so that every corner touches the curve of the circle</note>.

*For by the 21st Proposition of Euclid's Third Book, all equal angles can be inscribed in the same segment, and thus also in equal segments of the same circle. Since all angles of a Regular figure are equal, all the angles of one figure can therefore be inscribed in equal segments of a single circle. Furthermore, it is necessary that once one angle is inscribed, they all are. This is because all the sides are equal; therefore, the segments of the circle that are cut off by the two sides of a single angle are also equal, according to the 24th Proposition of Euclid's Third Book. Thus, both the angle and the ends of the sides fit into the same circle simultaneously. The ends of the sides are, of course, the angles themselves. It would be otherwise if the sides were not equal, even if the angles were; in that case, the necessity of inscribing all of them would be lost.*

### V. Definition.

To Describe a Figure is to determine, through a geometric act, the proportion of the lines stretched across the angles <note>original: "subtensarum"; lines connecting two non-adjacent corners</note> to the "legs" or sides of the angle. From these determined values, one constructs the elementary triangles of the figure, and from these joined triangles, the figure itself is completed.

[A geometric diagram of a pentagon with vertices labeled A, B, C, D, E. Dashed lines are drawn from vertex D to vertices A and C, illustrating how the polygon is composed of three internal triangles: DAE, DAC, and DCB.]

*For once the proportion of the line DA to the sides AE and ED is given, the triangles DAE, DAC, and CAB are formed; the figure is composed of these.*

## VI. Definition.

To **inscribe** a figure in a circle is to determine, through a geometric act, the proportion of the figure's side to the diameter of the circle in which it is to be inscribed. Once this proportion is established, the proposed figure is easily drawn within the circle.

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram showing a pentagon (vertices labeled A, B, C, D, E) inscribed within a circle. The center of the circle is labeled L. A solid radius line connects L to vertex D. Dotted lines connect the center L to vertices A and B, and mark the sides of the pentagon.</image-desc>

*For example, if the radius <note>original: "semidiameter"</note> LD is given, or its double, the diameter: if we know what to do with it so that we grant the side DE its correct length, we can then easily complete the figure by repeating that length DE around the circumference.*

## VII. Definition.

To **know** in matters of geometry is to measure by a known measure; in this business of inscribing figures into a circle, that known measure is the diameter of the circle.

## VIII. Definition.

A thing is called **knowable** <note>original: "scibile"</note> which is either immediately measurable by the diameter (if it is a line) or by its square (if it is a surface); or that which is formed at the very least from such quantities by a certain and geometric reasoning, which, however long the series of steps may be, ultimately depends upon the diameter or its square. In Greek, this is called *gnōmenon* <note>original: "γνώμενον"; that which is known or understood</note>.

## IX. Definition.

A **demonstration** is the deduction of a quantity—whether it is to be drawn or to be known—from the diameter through possible intermediate steps. In Greek, this is called a *porisma* <note>original: "Πόριμα"; a corollary or a finding</note>.

*Thus, a demonstration commonly gives birth to either a description <note>a physical drawing</note> or to knowledge. A description offers the bare quantity, while knowledge further declares its quality or its certain quantity. However, a certain line can be geometrically determined—in Greek called tachē <note>original: "ταχὴ"; fixed or set</note>—which is not yet "known" by an act of the mind as to what kind of line it is. Conversely, some quality of one or more lines can be known which does not yet determine or necessitate the lines themselves; this happens if that quality is common to many other things that differ in quantity. Furthermore, the description of certain lines is easy, but the knowledge of them is most difficult. Finally, many things can be described by some kind of geometric act, yet by their very nature they cannot be "known" in the way we defined "knowable" above.*

<vocab>inscribe (inscribere), circle (circulus), diameter (diameter), geometric (geometricus), knowable (scibile), that which is known (γνώμενον), demonstration (demonstration), deduction/finding (Πόριμα), determined (ταχὴ)</vocab>

<summary>Kepler defines the "knowability" of geometric shapes as their ability to be measured against a circle's diameter. He distinguishes between the physical act of drawing a shape (description) and the intellectual act of proving its proportions (knowledge).</summary>

## X. Definition.

A **proper demonstration** occurs when the number of angles of a figure (either the figure itself, or one related to it by having double or half the number of sides) serves as the "middle term" <note>In logic, the "middle term" is the bridge that connects two ideas in an argument.</note> to determine the proportion that the side has to the diameter.

*For every regular figure is either a triangle itself, or can be broken down into triangles by drawing diagonal lines. Since every such triangle has three angles equal to two right angles <note>180 degrees</note>; therefore, in the angle of a Triangle, there is a third part; in the smallest elementary angle of a Square, a fourth part; in a Pentagon, a fifth part; in a Heptagon <note>a seven-sided figure</note>, a seventh part, and so on, of two right angles. And from this quantity of the angle, the demonstration of each figure begins.*

---

## XI. Definition.

An **improper demonstration** occurs when the proportion of the side to the diameter cannot be determined geometrically directly from the number of angles used, unless the side of a different figure is used—one that does not have double or half the number of sides.

---

## XII. Definition.

There are different **degrees of knowledge**, some remote and others near. The first and closest degree is when I know a certain line and can demonstrate it to be equal to the diameter, or a plane (though shaped differently) to be equal to the square of the diameter.

*Here the known measure perfectly—namely by itself and in a single act—measures the object of knowledge.*

---

## XIII. Definition.

The **second degree** of knowledge is when the diameter is divided into a certain number of equal parts, or its square is similarly divided, and the proposed line or plane is equal to such a part or parts. Such a line is called in Greek *rhētē mēkei* <note>original: "ρητὴ μήκει"</note>, **Expressible in length**. Such a plane is simply called *rhēton* <note>original: "ρητὸν"</note>, **Expressible** <note>In traditional geometry, these are often called "Rational" lines or planes, meaning they can be expressed as a ratio of whole numbers.</note>. For number is the language of Geometers.

*We reach this degree of knowledge either through the act of describing and inscribing the shape; or otherwise, through its kinship with some other quantity that was reached by those means. Therefore, this quality does not define just one single quantity; for it is not enough for "knowing" that I understand something is compared in this way or that for the sake of shared measurement; one must also know how—that is, by what number—it is Expressible.*

<summary>Kepler distinguishes between "proper" proofs based on a figure's own internal angles and "improper" proofs that rely on unrelated shapes, while also defining the "degrees of knowledge" based on how directly a shape's dimensions relate to the diameter of a circle.</summary>
<keywords>proper demonstration, improper demonstration, degrees of knowledge, expressible length, rational lines, geometry, diameter, angles, circles</keywords>

### XIV. Definition.

The third degree is this: when a line is Inexpressible <note>original: *Ineffabilis*; a line that cannot be measured as a simple ratio of the diameter</note> in length, but its square is Expressible <note>original: *Effabile*; the area formed by squaring the line can be compared to the square of the diameter</note>, and belongs to the second degree. It is called **Expressible in power** <note>original Greek: ῥητὴ δυνάμει, *rhetē dynamei*</note>.

### XV. Definition.

<margin>
What "Irrational" means to Latin Geometers.
</margin>
<margin>
Deaf/Surd Numbers.
</margin>
The degrees that follow are all called **Inexpressible** <note>original Greek: Ἄλογοι, *Alogoi*, literally "without word" or "without reason"</note>. Latin translators have rendered this as **Irrational**, which carries a great risk of ambiguity and absurdity <note>Kepler dislikes the term "Irrational" because it implies these proportions lack logic or "reason," whereas he believes they are perfectly logical parts of God's geometric plan.</note>. Let us bury this use of the word, because there are many lines which, although Inexpressible, are nonetheless contained by the best of reasons <note>proportions</note>. Arithmeticians, using a similar metaphor, call them **Surd Numbers** <note>original: *Numeros surdos*, meaning "deaf numbers"</note>, that is, numbers that "speak" no more than a deaf person hears. But under this name, they include both quantities that are Expressible only in power, as well as those that are truly Inexpressible.

Therefore, the fourth degree in order—but the first of the inexpressibles—occurs when neither the line nor its square is Expressible; yet the square can be transformed into a rectangle whose sides are at least Expressible in power. This line is called the **MEDIAL** <note>original Greek: MESE, meaning "middle"</note>, because it is the mean proportional between two lines that are Expressible only in power and are commensurable <note>having a common measure</note> with one another: for instance, if one is Expressible in length and the other only in power; or if both are Expressible only in power, yet their powers do not have the same ratio as one square number to another.

Such a line is not known or measured by the length of certain equal parts of the diameter, nor is its square measured by the square of the diameter. Furthermore, the two lines between which the **MEDIAL** is the mean proportional are not both measured by the diameter at the same time; rather, it is the squares of those lines that are finally measured by the square of the diameter.

The square of a MEDIAL line is itself called a **MEDIAL area** <note>original: *MESON*</note>, whether it remains in a square shape or is transformed into a rectangle. This is the second kind of Plane after the Expressible plane. By these two planes—the Expressible and the Medial—the following species are distinguished from one another.

### XVI. Definition.

WE move toward other singular lines by the coupling of two lines, which themselves introduce new degrees of knowledge. For if the diameter, or something commensurable with the diameter at least in power (and thus Expressible), or even some Medial line, is cut—I say, let it be cut into two unequal parts; or let any two parts from the sections of two such lines be compared, whether they are composed of those parts, or have powers that are composed or diminished from them—two parts, I say, that are generally unequal: these will either be commensurable with each other in length, or they will be incommensurable in length but commensurable in power. Here, although the individual lines have clearly moved away from commensurability, when joined together, some of them still—either by their squares being combined into one sum, or by a rectangle formed between them—constitute planes that have so far been ex-

## XVII. Definition.

Let there be, therefore, a fifth degree of knowledge: When two lines, neither of which is **Expressible** <note>original: *Effabiles*; lines whose relationship to the diameter can be stated as a ratio</note> nor **Medial** <note>original: *Mesæ*; a line whose square is equal to a rectangle formed by two Expressible lines</note>, and which are moreover completely incommensurable with one another, produce something Expressible in both the sum of their squares and their common Rectangle. This is no less than what is produced by two lines that are Expressible in length (according to the 20th proposition of Euclid's tenth book), or even two lines expressible only in power <note>that is, their squares are expressible</note> but which are nonetheless commensurable with each other in length, by the same proposition. 

For example, the side of a square of 2 <note>$\sqrt{2}$</note> and the side of a square of 8 <note>$\sqrt{8}$</note> are in a double proportion to each other, because their squares are in a quadruple proportion <note>2 to 8 is a ratio of 1:4; the sides are therefore 1:2</note>. They are, therefore, Inexpressible in length, but commensurable with each other. Their squares, 2 and 8, joined together make 10, an Expressible plane. And when multiplied by each other (which is to form a Rectangle), they make a rectangle of 4 <note>$\sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{8} = \sqrt{16} = 4$</note>, which is also expressible. This same thing, I say, is also done by two lines that are neither Expressible nor Medial, and are moreover completely incommensurable with each other; and therefore they are not to be referred to the second or third degree of knowledge, like those former ones, but to the Fifth.

Note, therefore, that in this degree we do not measure the lines themselves, nor the squares of each individually, but we measure both their common Rectangle and the joined squares of both into one sum; so that what one square lacks in being expressible is exactly compensated for by the other associated square.

## XVIII. Definition.

The sixth and less noble <note>Kepler ranks geometric relationships by "nobility," meaning how close they are to the perfection of the circle's diameter</note> degree of knowledge is when two lines joined together—neither of which is Expressible nor Medial, and which are also incommensurable with each other—make at least one of the two Expressible, while the other is **Medial** <note>original: *Meson*</note>. This degree is twofold: either the sum of the squares is Expressible and the Rectangle is Medial; or the sum of the squares is Medial and the Rectangle is Expressible.

> *In the former effect, they are similar to two lines that are Expressible only in their squares* <note>original: *solâ potentiâ commensurabilibus*</note>*. For both squares, being Expressible, also make the sum of both Expressible. The Rectangle, however, is Medial, according to the 22nd proposition of Euclid's tenth book.*

> *In the latter effect, they are similar to two Medial lines commensurable only in their squares, which are related to each other as two Expressible lines, between which the first of the two Medials is the mean proportional; according to the 26th and 28th propositions of Euclid's tenth book. For because they are commensurable in their squares, the added squares produce a sum commensurable with the parts. But the parts are Medial, and what is commensurable with a Medial is itself also Medial, according to the 24th proposition of Euclid's tenth book.*
