### XIV. Definition.

The third degree of knowledge is this: when a line is **Inexpressible** <note>original: *Ineffabilis*; a line whose length cannot be stated as a simple numerical ratio to the diameter</note> in its length, but its square is **Expressible** <note>original: *Effabile*; the area of the square built upon this line can be stated as a ratio to the square of the diameter</note> and belongs to the second degree. Such a line is called <term>expressible in power</term> <note>original Greek: *ρητὴ δυνάμει* (rhētē dynamei)</note>.

### XV. Definition.

<margin>What "Irrational" means to Latin Geometers.</margin>
<margin>Surd Numbers.</margin>
The degrees that follow are all called <term>Inexpressible</term> <note>original Greek: *Ἄλογοι* (Alogoi)</note>. Latin translators have rendered this as "Irrational," which carries a great risk of ambiguity and absurdity. Let us bury that use of the word, for there are many lines which, although they are "Inexpressible," are nonetheless governed by the most excellent "rational" proportions. Arithmeticians, using a similar metaphor, call these **Surd Numbers** <note>from the Latin *surdus*, meaning "deaf" or "silent"</note>—that is, numbers that speak no more than a deaf man hears. However, under this name they include both quantities expressible only in power and those that are entirely inexpressible.

Therefore, the fourth degree in order—but the first of the inexpressible ones—is when neither the line nor its square is **Expressible**. Nevertheless, the square of such a line can be transformed into a rectangle whose sides are Expressible, at least in power. This line is called the <term>MEDIAL</term> <note>original: *MESE*</note>, because it is the "mean proportional" between two lines that are Expressible only in power and commensurable with each other: for instance, if one line is Expressible in length and the other only in power, or if both are Expressible only in power, yet their "powers" (their squares) are not in the ratio of a square number to another square number.

Such a line is not known or measured by the length of specific equal parts of a diameter, nor is its square measured by the square of the diameter. Furthermore, the two lines between which the **MEDIAL** is the mean proportional are not measured by the diameter when taken together; rather, it is only the squares of those lines that are finally measured by the square of the diameter.

The square of a **MEDIAL** line is itself called a <term>Medial area</term> <note>original: *MESON*</note>, whether it remains in the form of a square or is transformed into a rectangle. This is the second type of Plane <note>area</note> after the Expressible plane. By these two planes—the **Expressible** and the **Medial**—the species that follow are distinguished from one another.

### XVI. Definition.

We now transition to other singular lines by joining two lines together, which also introduces new degrees of knowledge. For let a diameter (or something commensurable to the diameter at least in power, and thus Expressible, or even a Medial line) be cut into two unequal parts. Or, let any two parts from the sections of two such lines be compared—whether they are composed of parts, or have "powers" that are composed or diminished from such parts—provided the two parts are generally unequal. These parts will either be commensurable to each other in length, or they will be incommensurable in length but commensurable in power. Here, although the individual lines have completely departed from commensurability, when joined together, some still constitute planes that have been, until now...

<meta>This page continues the classification of geometric lines based on their degree of "knowability" or "expressibility." ...fully explained, no less than those that are commensurable with one another. However, since the pairing of such plainly incommensurable lines is manifold—some more base <note>Kepler uses "noble" and "ignoble" to rank how close a geometric figure is to being perfectly "knowable" or "rational."</note> than others—we cannot assign all pairs to a single degree.

### XVII. Definition.

Let the fifth degree of knowledge be: When two lines—neither being **Expressible** nor **Medial** <note>original: *Mesæ*; lines whose square is a medial area</note> individually, and being plainly incommensurable with each other—nevertheless produce something **Expressible** <note>original: *Effabile*; a value that can be stated as a ratio to the diameter or the reference unit</note> in two ways: both in the sum of their squares and in their shared rectangle. This is just as two lines expressible in length do (according to Euclid, Book 10, Proposition 20), or even two lines expressible only in power <note>Lines whose lengths are irrational but whose squares are rational, like the square root of 2.</note> but commensurable in length with each other, such as the side of a square of 2 and the side of a square of 8. These are in a double proportion [1 to 2] because their squares [2 and 8] are in a quadruple proportion [1 to 4]. Therefore, they are indeed inexpressible in length, yet commensurable with each other. Their squares, 2 and 8, joined together make the expressible area 10; and when multiplied by each other (which is to form a rectangle), they produce the rectangle 4, which is also expressible. I say that two lines that are neither Expressible nor Medial, and are plainly incommensurable with each other, can do the same thing; and thus they should not be assigned to the second or third degree of knowledge like the former ones, but to the Fifth.

Note, therefore, that in this degree we measure neither the lines themselves, nor their individual squares, but we measure both their shared rectangle and the sum of their squares joined into one total. Thus, whatever one square lacks in being "expressible" is exactly compensated for by the other square joined to it.

### XVIII. Definition.

The sixth and more base degree of knowledge is when two lines are joined which are neither Expressible nor Medial, and are also incommensurable with each other; yet together they produce at least one **Expressible** result, while the other is **Medial** <note>original Greek: *Mέσον* (Meson); an area that is the square of a medial line</note>. This degree is twofold: either the sum of the squares is expressible and the rectangle is Medial; or the sum is Medial and the rectangle is expressible.

> *In the former case, they are similar to two Expressible lines commensurable only in power. For both powers—that is, the Expressible squares—also make the sum of both expressible; while the rectangle is Medial, according to Euclid, Book 10, Proposition 22.*

> *In the latter case, they are similar to two Medial lines commensurable only in power, which are related to each other as two Expressibles, between which the first of the two Medials is a mean proportional; according to Euclid, Book 10, Propositions 26 and 28. For because they are commensurable in power, the added powers produce a sum commensurable with the parts. But the parts are Medial, and what is commensurable with a Medial is itself Medial, according to Euclid, Book 10, Proposition 24.*

# ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES:

Here we measure the Rectangle of two lines indeed by the square area of the diameter, but not the sum of their squares: for we find only two lines for it, forming a rectangle equal to it, whose squares we measure by the square of the diameter.

### XIX. Definition.

The seventh degree of knowledge, even more base <note>Kepler uses "noble" and "ignoble" to describe how close a geometric value is to being "knowable" or rational; the more irrational a line, the more "ignoble" it is.</note>, is when neither result of two lines incommensurable with each other is expressible—neither the sum of their squares nor their shared rectangle; yet both results are still Medial <note>original: *Meson*; a "medial" area is the square of a medial line, essentially an irrational area that is the square root of a rational one.</note>.

*In their effect <note>original: *effectu*; referring to the areas they produce when squared or multiplied.</note>, these are similar to two Medial lines commensurable only in power <note>Lines are commensurable in "power" if their squares are commensurable.</note>, of which one is to the other as one of those between which the MEDIAL is truly the mean proportional (namely, those commensurable only in power) is to a third line, which is also commensurable only in power, according to Euclid, Book 10, Proposition 29.*

*Euclides teaches how to find these three pairs, distinguished by two kinds of areas, primarily because they contribute to the composition and constitution of the following species.*

### XX. Definition.

Therefore, the eighth degree of knowledge is derived from the preceding ones placed together, and it concerns single lines again, but those which are constituted by the composition of two "names" <note>original: *Nomina*; in geometry, this refers to the individual terms in a binomial expression, such as the 'a' and 'b' in 'a + b'.</note> (that is, two terms coupled from the previous pairs) or by the subtraction of one from its partner—called *Epharmozusae* <note>Greek term meaning 'fitting together' or 'adapted'; in this context, it refers to the line being subtracted in an apotome.</note>—making a new species. So that in these we may know or measure not whole lines, nor the squares of whole lines, nor the two "names" of each individually, but their joined squares and shared rectangle, as in the preceding degrees XVIII and XIX. And although we could count as many degrees of knowledge as there will be species (of which the earlier is always more noble than the later), since every composition or subtraction refers back to its own degree, and no difference is created by the act of composition or subtraction itself—as all stand equally in relation to their pairs of Names or Elements—we will therefore make only one degree for them; but let us recognize that its species are distinguished by their nobility.

### XXI. Proposition.

It must be known, however, that from two lines commensurable with each other in length, nothing arises that ought to be reckoned here: whether they were Expressible <note>original: *Effabiles*; lines whose ratio to the reference unit is a rational number.</note>, or Medial, or more base.

*For if they are commensurable in length, the whole line composed of them will also be commensurable with its parts. Moreover, that which is commensurable with an Expressible line is itself Expressible: through de-*

...by the definitions before [Proposition] 20 of Euclid's tenth [book]. That which is commensurable with a Medial line <note>original: *Mesae*; a medial line is the square root of a rational area</note> is itself Medial, according to [Proposition] 24 of the same. And whatever is commensurable with any of the following Inexpressible lines <note>original: *Ineffabilibus*; irrational lines that cannot be expressed as a ratio of whole numbers</note> after the Medials is of the same species as it, by [Propositions] 66, 67, 68, 69, 70, 103, 104, 105, 106, 107. And so it is also with other more remote species, not mentioned by Euclid, which make up more remote degrees. And even if it were not so with them, it does not concern us. For they either fall back into one of the species which we will now establish from the incommensurables, and thus do not increase the number; or they create less noble <note>Kepler ranks geometric values by "nobility"; the more complex or irrational a line is, the "ignobler" or less harmonious he considers it.</note> species of either their own or another genus, and so they do not belong here, where we are constructing degrees closest in nobility to the preceding ones.

## XXII. Definition.

Having passed over those which are commensurable in length, let us approach those which are commensurable only in power <note>Lines are "commensurable in power" if their squares have a rational ratio to each other, even if the lines themselves do not.</note>. Therefore, if two such Expressible lines <note>original: *Effabiles*; rational lines</note> are added together, a **BINOMIAL** <note>original: *Binominis*; a line made of two rational parts added together</note> is formed; if they are subtracted, an **Apotome** <note>A line formed by subtracting one rational part from another</note> is formed from what remains. Of each, there are six subordinate species, according to Proposition 48 and 85 of the tenth book.

But if two such Medial lines are joined, forming either an Expressible Rectangle or a Medial one, they become **BIMEDIALS** by addition, and **MEDIAL APOTOMES** by subtraction—named **FIRST** in the former case and **SECOND** in the latter.

Here it is not permitted to join an Expressible line with a **MEDIAL**: for two such lines are simply incommensurable, a genus we must now deal with in what follows.

## XXIII. Proposition.

There remain, then, lines clearly incommensurable with each other. Among these, however, are others which, in pairs, cannot produce the required effects; such as two Medial lines, or likewise one **MEDIAL** with one Expressible.

The former because of the unworthiness of the pair, the latter because of their clashing Natures. See [Propositions] 71, 108, 109 of Euclid's tenth [book]. No species of composition can therefore be summoned from here; there remain for us only those that are more Unworthy, with both the Expressible and Medial lines excluded.

## XXIV. Proposition.

From the first pair of such clearly incommensurables—specifically those which are knowable at the fifth degree in the preceding Proposition XVII—by adding or subtracting, an Expressible area is again born; and they are necessarily the **BINOMIAL** and the **APOTOME**. See [Propositions] 112, 113, 114 of Euclid's tenth [book]. So that if both the sum of the squares of the Binomial and Apotome, and their shared Rectangle, is Expressible, the individual Terms <note>original: *Nomina*; literally "names," referring to the two parts that make up an irrational line</note> of the one must be commensurable with the individual Terms of the other—which does not happen in all **BINOMIALS** and **APOTOMES**.

### XXV. Definition.

**T**herefore, from the second pair of the sixth degree (Number XVIII, previously mentioned), of lines that are completely incommensurable with each other, for which the sum of the squares is **EXPRESSIBLE** <note>original: *EFFABILIS*</note> and the Rectangle is **MEDIAL** <note>original: *MESON*</note>: by composition is born the **GREATER** <note>original: *MIZON*, or *MAIOR*</note> line; by abstraction, the **LESSER** <note>original: *ELASSON*, or *MINOR*</note>.
From the third pair, where the sum of squares is **Medial**, and the Rectangle is **Expressible**, the line produced by composition has the name **POWERFUL OVER THE EXPRESSIBLE AND THE MEDIAL** <note>original: *POTENS EFFABILE ET MESON*</note>; that produced by abstraction is **MAKING A MEDIAL WHOLE WITH AN EXPRESSIBLE** <note>original: *FACIENS CUM EFFABILI MESON TOTUM*</note>.
Finally, from the fourth pair of the seventh degree (Number XIX, previously mentioned), where both effects become **Medial**; by composition is made the **POWERFUL OVER TWO MEDIALS** <note>original: *POTENS BINA MEDIA*</note>, and by abstraction the **MAKING A MEDIAL WHOLE WITH A MEDIAL** <note>original: *FACIENS CUM MESO MESON TOTUM*</note>.

And behold the Origin of the twelve Euclidean species, and the reasons for their number. For Euclid did not think he should proceed to more remote types, which produce either the sum of squares, or the common Rectangle, or both, beyond Expressibles and Medials into more ignoble species.

## XXVI. Definition & Comparison.

These things could have been enough for us to establish the grades of Demonstrations by which the sides of figures, necessary for our **Harmonics**, are distinguished: were it not for the fact that other properties were added to those already reviewed; or rather, that the properties reviewed so far were preceded by other, more noble ones, which crown the grades of scientific Demonstrations.

We have come to composition and abstraction <note>In this context, "composition" refers to the addition of line segments, and "abstraction" refers to subtraction.</note>; where we have taken lines to be composed or subtracted freely, with no necessity of a fixed quantity imposed upon them. But if we now tighten the laws, imposing a certain proportion on the pairs—not indeed given in such a way that when joined they make one of the twelve species <note>The twelve types of irrational lines defined by Euclid in Book 10.</note>; but given in another way, namely, for one given straight line to find its "greater part," such that the smaller part is to the greater as the greater is to the whole composed of both; or conversely, the Greater is to the smaller, as the smaller is to the remainder. When this is done by the abstraction of two parts, a more remote grade is not always produced, but as the situation arises, we fall back into one of the explained species; and having made the return, we will compare the established line (which is of the eighth grade by itself) with lines of the fourth grade.

For just as in the fourth grade, Definition XV, two straight lines by their common labor formed a plane, from which—when reduced to a square—a line was born called the **Mese** <note>original: *Mese*; from the Greek *μέση*, meaning "mean" or "middle." In geometry, it refers to the mean proportional between two lines.</note>: so now two straight lines, the **Whole** and **one part**, form the other part itself by subtraction, or two parts form the whole by addition. In the former case, the lines forming it were commensurable to each other only in power <note>Lines whose squares have a common measure, but the lines themselves do not.</note>: here, setting aside commensuration, there follows an identity of proportion between the whole and the parts. In the former, there was a similarity of proportion between the smaller and the line to be made, and between the line to be made and the larger; here also there is a similarity of proportion between the two to be made, and between one of them and the proposed whole, in abstraction: but in composition, between one of those to be made and the proposed line, and between the proposed line and the other to be made. Therefore, in the former case, given two lines, a Rectangle was given equal to the square of the line to be made, and thus the plane came before the line: here, on the contrary, once the two lines to be made are produced, there finally follows an equality between the Rectangle of the extremes and the square of the Mean, through **Euclid**, Book 6 Proposition 17 and Book 2 Proposition 11.

In the former, the forming lines had squares commensurable to the square of the proposed line: here, **Euclid** teaches in Book 6, Proposition 30, to take a square commensurable to the square of the proposed line—namely, its **five-fourths** <note>original: *sesquintuplum*; though literally "one and one-fifth" (6/5), Kepler’s geometric description of subtracting "half the proposed line" from its root to find the Golden Ratio indicates he is referring to the ratio 5:4 (1.25), where the side is $\sqrt{1.25}$ or $\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}$.</note>—and from the side of this square to take away half of the proposed line, so that the part to be established in the proposed line remains; and when this part is taken away from the proposed line, the other required part is left (or when added to the whole, a third required part is also made). And for so many reasons, these parts seem to be reckoned in the fourth grade.

But at this point, the line is rendered more noble than the **Mese** itself, whatever position that proportion occupies: because the **Mese** depends on the proposed **Expressible** <note>original: *Effabili*; a rational line that can be stated as a number or a simple ratio.</note> line by a longer chain composed of four links: but the parts of this—

<note>original: DE FIGURARUM HARMON.</note>

...they rely on their own proportion, which they have immediately to the Expressible <note>original: *Effabilem*; in Euclidean geometry, a "rational" or "expressible" line segment used as a standard for measurement</note> line itself. Because of this, it happens that many Medial <note>original: *Mesôn*; lines whose squares are rational but whose lengths are not</note> lines can exist, all at the same distance in degree from the Expressible; but there is only one major part in this proportion of the Expressible itself, and indeed, for every line after the Expressible, there is one unique major part. For this reason, its demonstration is in some way equated to the first degree.

When, therefore, a proposed Straight line is ordered to be the "whole," and its two parts are sought, this is called by Geometers the **section according to Extreme and Mean**. This name implies that while a common section of a whole into two parts does not otherwise respect a proportion—or if one part is compared to the whole in the same proportion as the smaller part is to the larger, there would be four terms: two extremes and two means—here, by contrast, there are only three terms: the whole and the smaller part are the two extremes, while the major part is the single mean term.

For the same reason, it is also called the **proportional section**. Modern writers call both the section and its ratio **Divine**, because of its admirable nature and its many privileges <note>Kepler refers here to the unique mathematical properties of the Golden Ratio, which he viewed as a reflection of the Creator's mind</note>. The chief of these is that if the major part is always added to the whole, the resulting composite line is again cut in the same proportion; what was the major part now becomes the minor part, and what was the whole now becomes the major part of the new composite, according to Euclid, Book XIII, Proposition 5.

## XXVII. Proposition.

Although such a section can occur in all lines—in a line Rational in length, in a line Rational in power alone, in a Medial line, and in the twelve other species reviewed, and in all others—we only have need of two of its species in the present work, which coincide with the species explained so far, according to the two types of lines to be cut. For that length is either Rational <note>original: *Effabilis*</note> or Greater <note>original: *Mizon*; another of Euclid's irrational species</note>. If the line proposed for cutting is Rational in length, the major part of the section becomes an **Apotome of the fourth species** <note>An "Apotome" is a line formed by subtracting one rational line from another that is commensurable with it only in power</note>; and there is a corresponding **Binomial of the same fourth species** having the same terms <note>original: *nomina*; the two parts of the irrational line</note> as the Apotome. But take care not to be confused: it is called the "major part" in relation to the line being cut; but it is called an "Apotome" here not in relation to that line, but qualitatively <note>That is, it belongs to the mathematical category of an "Apotome" based on its internal properties</note>. If you ask what it is an Apotome *of*, the answer is that it is the Apotome of a line which is commensurable in power only to the proposed line—specifically, one whose square is five-fourths <note>original: *sesquiquartum*; the ratio 1.25 or 5:4</note> of the square of the proposed line.

### ON PROOF. Book I.
C
<meta>catchword: XXIX</meta>

which can do <note>original: *poteſt*; in geometry, this refers to the "power" or the area of the square formed by the line</note> as much as GA, as well as AM, which is its half: so that if the power of GA itself is 4, the power of AM will be 1. Consequently, the power of GM will be 5. Insofar as AO or AP is an Apotome <note>original: *Apotome*; a type of irrational line formed by subtracting a rational line from another rational line that is commensurable with it only in power</note>, the Binomial <note>original: *binominis*; a line composed of two rational parts commensurable only in power</note> AX corresponds to it; and the names <note>original: *nomina*; the two terms or parts of a binomial or apotome</note> of this line are MX, or MP, or MG, and AM.

That both the Apotome AP and the Binomial AX are of the fourth species is proved as follows: for each name, both MX and MA, is expressible <note>original: *effabile*; a line whose length or square can be expressed as a ratio to a standard unit</note>; however, they are commensurable only in power, because MX (that is, MG) has a power of 5, where MA has a power of 1. Yet the ratio of 1 to 5 is not as a square number to a square number. Finally, the difference between the powers 1 and 5 is 4, which is a square number, whose side is 2, and is Expressible in length—namely, equal to the proposed line GA. These are the characteristics of the fourth species of Binomials, found in the definitions before Proposition 74, and of Apotomes, before Proposition 85, of the tenth book of Euclid.

Finally, if the Expressible line GA is cut proportionally <note>i.e., in the Golden Ratio</note>, its greater part OA, and the line composed of both OA and AG, fall into the fifth degree of knowledge. For their squares joined together make an Expressible sum—namely, triple that of the expressible GA itself, according to the 4th proposition of the thirteenth book of Euclid. The rectangle formed by them is also Expressible, because it is equal to the square of the expressible GA, since GA is the mean proportional between the part OA and the composite line OA and AG, according to the preceding arguments.

## XXVIII. Proposition.

**Conversely, if any line Expressible in length is cut proportionally, its smaller part will be an Apotome of the first species.**

As if GA were Expressible, as before, and its major part when cut proportionally is AO, and the minor part is OG; then OG will also be an Apotome, according to the 6th proposition of the thirteenth book of Euclid.

Again, however, OG is called an Apotome qualitatively, not in relation to the line GA (which is expressible in length and of which OG is the smaller part), nor in relation to MG or MP (of which AO or AP is an Apotome); rather, GO has its own unique Names. For since, according to Proposition 97 of the tenth book of Euclid, the squaring of any Apotome—and thus also the square of PO—when extended to an Expressible line (as here to GT, which is equal to GA) produces a width GO that is an Apotome of the first species: conversely, AO itself was an Apotome of the fourth species. Therefore, the greater name of that GO is Expressible in length; but the greater name of this AO, which was MP, was expressible only in power. And conversely, because the names are commensurable only in power, the Lesser name, or the attachment <note>original: *Prosharmozuſan*; from the Greek *prosharmodzousa*, the line which, when "fitted" to the greater name, creates the irrational ratio</note> of GO itself, must be expressible only in power: since the lesser name of AO itself, AM, was expressible in length. Yet for both, this remains true: the difference of the squares described by the names is the square of some line expressible in length.

But as for what the Names of this first Apotome GO are, I leave that to others to seek. Indeed, the attachment for GO as a First Apotome is unique and solitary, according to Proposition 79 of the tenth book of Euclid. It must be such that its square is Expressible but not a square number; and it, together with GO, must make one line Expressible in length. And by the 30th proposition of the tenth book, if from this whole line a diameter of a circle is made—for example, PX—and the attachment, a little longer than PA (if indeed the whole were equal to PX), is applied to the circumference XG from one end of the Diameter X; then the line connecting the points GP must be commensurable in length to the whole PX.

-> ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES <-

They depend on their own proportion, which they have immediately to the proposed Expressible <note>original: *Effabilem*; in Euclidean geometry, an "expressible" or "rational" line is one whose relationship to a starting unit can be defined by a square area</note> line itself. Thus it happens that there can be many Medials <note>original: *Meſôn*; from the Greek for "middle" lines, whose squares are areas equal to a rectangle formed by two expressible lines</note>, all distant from the Expressible by the same degree; but the greater part in this proportion of the Expressible itself is only one, and altogether, for every line after the Expressible, there is one singular one. For this reason, its demonstration is equated, in a certain way, to the first degree.

Therefore, when a proposed straight line is ordered to be the "whole," and two such parts of it are sought, this is called by Geometers the **section according to Extreme and Mean**. This name implies that while an ordinary division of a whole into two parts does not consider a specific proportion—or if one part is compared to the whole in the same proportion as the smaller part is to the larger, four terms result (two extremes and two means)—here, by contrast, only three terms are formed: the whole and the smaller part are the two extremes, while the larger part is the single mean term.

For the same reason, it is also called the **proportional section**. Modern writers call both the section and its proportion **Divine**, because of its wonderful nature and its many privileges. The chief of these is that whenever the greater part is added to the whole, the resulting composite line is again similarly cut; and what was the greater part now becomes the smaller, while the previous whole now becomes the greater part of the composite, according to Euclid, Book 13, Proposition 5.

## XXVII. Proposition.

Since such a section occurs in all lines—in an Expressible length, in one Expressible only in power, in a Medial <note>original: *Meſe*</note>, in the twelve other species reviewed, and in all others—we have need in this present work of only two of its species, which coincide with the species explained so far, according to the two lines to be cut. For either that length is Expressible, or it is a Greater line <note>original: *Mizon*; a specific class of irrational line from Euclid's Book X</note>. If the line proposed for cutting is Expressible in length, the greater part of the section becomes an **Apotome of the fourth species**; and the **Binomial of the same fourth species** corresponds to it, having terms in common with it. But take care not to be confused: that part is called "greater" in relation to the proposed line, but it is called an **Apotome** here not in relation to the proposed line, but qualitatively. If you ask of what it is an apotome, the answer is that it is the apotome of something which is commensurable only in power to the proposed line—namely, one that can produce <note>original: *poteſt*; meaning the square of the line has this area</note> five-fourths of the square of the proposed line.

...which can be as much *GA* as *AM* its half: So that if the power <note>original: *potentia*; in geometry, this refers to the area of a square built upon a line</note> of this *GA* is 4, that of *AM* will be 1. Consequently, the power of *GM* will be 5. Insofar as *AO* or *AP* is an *Apotome* <note>An "Apotome" is a type of irrational line formed by subtracting one rational line from another when they are only "commensurable in power" (their squares have a whole-number ratio, but their lengths do not)</note>, the binomial *AX* corresponds to it: their common terms are *MX*, or *MP*, or *MG*, and *AM*.

The proof that *AP* is an *Apotome* and *AX* is a **Binomial**, both of the fourth species, is as follows: Each term, both *MX* and *MA*, is expressible <note>original: *effabile*; a line whose square can be compared to a standard unit area</note>; yet they are commensurable only in power, because *MX* (which is *MG*) has a power of 5 where *MA* has a power of 1. However, the ratio of 5 to 1 is not like that of a square number to another square number <note>since 5 is not a perfect square</note>. Finally, the difference between the powers 1 and 5 is 4, which is a square number, and its "side" <note>square root</note> is 2, which is expressible in length—specifically being equal to the proposed line *GA*. These are the recognized marks of the fourth species of Binomials, found in the definitions before Proposition 74, and of Apotomes, before Proposition 85, of the tenth book of Euclid.

Finally, if the expressible line *GA* is cut proportionally <note>referring to the Golden Ratio section</note>, its larger part *OA* and the composite line formed by *OA* and *AG* fall into the fifth degree of knowledge. For their squares joined together create an expressible sum—specifically triple that of the expressible line *GA*, according to Proposition 4 of Euclid’s thirteenth book. Furthermore, the rectangle they form is also expressible, because it is equal to the square of the expressible line *GA*, since *GA* is the mean proportional between the part *OA* and the combined line *OA* and *AG*, according to the preceding arguments.

## XXVIII. Proposition.

Conversely, if any line expressible in length is cut proportionally in this way, its smaller part becomes an Apotome of the first species.

For if *GA* is expressible, as before, and its larger part when cut proportionally is *AO* and its smaller part is *OG*; then *OG* will also be an **Apotome**, according to Proposition 6 of Euclid’s thirteenth book.

Again, <margin>a.</margin> *OG* is called an *Apotome* qualitatively, not in relation to the expressible length *G* <note>likely referring to the line segment GA</note>, of which it is the smaller part; nor in relation to *MG* or *MP*, of which *AO* or *AP* is the *Apotome*; rather, *GO* possesses its own unique terms. For since, by Proposition 97 of Euclid’s tenth book, the squaring of any Apotome—and thus the square of *PO* extended to an expressible line (as here to *GT*, which is equal to *GA*)—produces a width *GO* that is an Apotome of the first species: so in turn *AO* was an *Apotome* of the fourth species. Therefore, the greater term of that *GO* is expressible in length; whereas the greater term *MP* of this *AO* was expressible only in power. And conversely, because the terms are commensurable only in power, it is necessary that the smaller term, or the **Annex** <note>original: *Prosharmozusa*; the line segment added to an irrational line to "fit" it to a rational relationship</note> of *GO*, be expressible only in power: whereas the smaller term *AM* of *AO* was expressible in length. Yet for both, this remains true: the difference of the squares described by the terms is the square of some line expressible in length.

As for what the terms of this first-order Apotome *GO* are, I leave that for others to seek. The **Annex** for *GO* as a first-order Apotome is unique and solitary by Proposition 79 of Euclid’s tenth book. It must be such that its square is expressible but not a square number; however, together with *GO*, it must form a single line expressible in length. And by Proposition 30 of the Tenth Book, if the diameter of a circle is made from this one whole—for instance, *PX*—and the Annex, slightly longer than *PA* (if the whole were indeed equal to *PX*), is applied from one end of the diameter *X* to the circumference at *XG*; then the line connecting the points *GP* must be commensurable in length with the whole line *PX*.

## Proposition XXIX.

When a certain **Greater** line <note>original: *Mizon*; a specific type of irrational line defined in Euclid’s Elements, Book 10, Prop. 39</note> has been cut proportionally; if its square is equal to a rectangle formed by a length (composed of a proposed expressible line and one whose square is five-quarters of it) and a width whose square is five-quarters; then let the smaller part be a **Lesser** line <note>original: *Elasson*; a type of irrational line defined in Euclid’s Elements, Book 10, Prop. 76</note>—where **Lesser** is a name of its specific quality, not a simple comparison—and let the larger part be another **Greater** line, again understood qualitatively, whatever its constituent elements may be.

<margin>In the diagram on page 16.</margin>
As before, let the half-length of the proposed expressible <note>original: *effabilis*; a line is "expressible" if its square can be compared to a standard unit area using whole numbers</note> line be *GA*, and let *AM* be its half again; so that where the square of *GA* is 4, the square of *AM* is 1. Let the angle *GAM* be a right angle; therefore, the square <note>original: *potest*; literally "is powerful of," referring to the area of the square built on that line</note> of the hypotenuse *MG* will be 5. Let *MA* be extended on both sides, and with center *M* and the distance *MG*, let the semicircle *PGX* be drawn. Therefore, *PX* is double the length of *GM*; because of this, the square of *PX* will be five-quarters of the square of the proposed line (which is double *GA*). <note>If the proposed line is $2 \times GA$, its square is 16. If $MG^2 = 5$, then $PX^2 = 20$. 20 is $5/4$ of 16.</note> But the squares of *PG* and *GX* joined together are equal to the square of *PX*; therefore, they too are five-quarters of the square of the proposed expressible line. 

Furthermore, if you make one continuous line from *PG* and *GX*, its square will consist of the two squares of *PG* and *GX*, and of two rectangles formed by *PG* and *GX*. To these are equal two rectangles formed by *GA* and *PX*—that is, one rectangle formed by the proposed line (double *GA*) and by *PX*. These two are expressible lines, but commensurable only in power <note>This means their lengths cannot be expressed as a simple ratio, but the ratio of their squares is a rational number</note>; for this reason, this rectangle will be a **Medial** <note>original: *Meson*; a type of irrational area</note> according to Euclid, Book 10, Proposition 22. 

Since, therefore, the square of the whole line *PGX* consists of the expressible square of *PX* and a **Medial** rectangle of the same width *PX*: these two—the square of *PX* and the rectangle formed by double *GA* and *PX*—are equal to the rectangle contained by the expressible line *PX* and by the line composed of *PX* and double *GA*. These parts are commensurable only in power, and the square of the greater part *PX* exceeds the square of the lesser (double *GA*) by an amount that is incommensurable with *PX* in length (for *PX* has a power of 5 where the double of *GA* has a power of 4; the difference is 1, and since 1 to 5 is not a ratio of square numbers, the lengths are incommensurable). For these reasons, the said composite of *PX* and the doubled *GA* is a **Binomial** of the fourth species. Since, I say, the square of the whole *PGX* is equal to such a rectangle formed by a fourth species **Apotome** and an expressible line, the whole line *PGX* will therefore be a **Greater** line. 

The elements composing it are the parts *PG* and *GX*. For because *PA* is an **Apotome** and *AX* a **Binomial**, they are therefore incommensurable with each other in length. Now, as *PA* is to *AX*, so is the square of *PG* to the square of *GX*. Therefore, *PG* and *GX* are incommensurable with each other even in their squares. They make a sum of squares that is expressible (equal to the square of *PX*), while the rectangle formed by *PG* and *GX* is **Medial**. Therefore, by Euclid Book 10, Proposition 39, the line composed of *PG* and *GX* is a **Greater** line. And by Proposition 76 of the same book, if *PG* is taken from *GX*, what remains is a **Lesser** line. 

And yet the whole *PGX* is cut proportionally at point *G*. For as *PA* is to *AG*, so let *PG* be to *XG*. But *PA* is the greater part of the line *GA* when cut proportionally, because the square of *MP* is five times that of *MA*, and the **Apotome** *AP* is equal to *AO* by Euclid, Book 2, Proposition 11. Therefore, *PG* is also the greater part of *GX* cut proportionally; and by Euclid Book 13, Proposition 5, when the greater part *PG* is added to the whole *GX*, it creates a new whole *PGX* cut proportionally at *G*. Thus *PG* is the smaller part of this composite, and *GX* its greater part. And so *PGX*, being a **Greater** line, is cut at the same point *G* into its geometric elements and simultaneously into its parts of the **Divine Proportion** <note>The "Divine Proportion" is the Renaissance term for the Golden Ratio</note>.

Having previously established the construction of the line segments, he now uses Book 10 of Euclid’s Elements to classify these segments as specific types of irrational lines—specifically the "Greater" and "Lesser" lines—and explains why these names are both descriptive of their size and their mathematical category.</meta>

->ON THE DEMONSTRATION. BOOK I.<-

I say that these same parts of a proportionally cut line are simultaneously both the **Lesser** <note>original: *Elasson*</note> and the **Greater** <note>original: *Mizon*</note> lines. Since the segment *AP* is a fourth **Apotome** <note>An irrational line formed by subtracting one rational line from another that is commensurable only in square</note>, that which is contained under the Apotome *AP* and the **Expressible** line <note>original: *Effabilis*; a line whose square is rational</note> *PX* is the "power" of the **Lesser** line, according to Proposition 94 of the tenth book of Euclid. And because *AX* is a fourth **Binomial** <note>An irrational line formed by the addition of two rational lines</note>, that which is contained under this and the Expressible line *PX* is the "power" of the **Greater** line. But the squares of *PG* and *GX* are equal to the Rectangles *AP* by *PX* and *AX* by *PX*, each to each; therefore *PG* is a **Lesser** line, and *GX* is a **Greater** line.

Thus, in this instance, the names of qualities and the names of proportions meet in one. For *PG* is called the "minor part" with respect to the whole *PGX* which is proportionally cut at *G*; it is also called the "lesser line" or "lesser element" of the whole *PGX*, as the latter is qualitatively a **Greater** line. Finally, it is called in Greek *Elasson*, which in Latin sounds like "minor" <note>or "lesser"</note>, understood qualitatively with respect to two other lines (not expressed here) from which it is formed by the subtraction of one from the other.

In the same way, *GX* is first called the "major part" of the whole *PGX* cut proportionally; secondly, it is called the "greater line" or "greater element" of the whole line *PGX*, as this is qualitatively a **Greater** line in its own right, no less than the whole *PGX* is in its own. However, the lines that make up *GX* as a **Greater** line through their composition are not shown here.

Because of this meeting of the proportional section <note>the Golden Ratio</note> and the division of a **Greater** line into its elements, I believe these qualitative names—**Greater** and **Lesser**—were bestowed upon these species.

However, we must be carefully on guard here lest we confuse the distinctions between things. The proportional section is an absolute proportion, not tied to any one specific line that is first in our knowledge (which is called the proposed **Expressible** line). But those species of the **Greater** and **Lesser** are shaped by certain degrees of their departure from the first proposed Expressible line. And so, while the "Divine Section" proceeds into infinity, the qualitative state of being **Greater** or **Lesser** does not follow it. In that section, the part which was just now "major" becomes "minor" in the next step; but in this qualitative system, a **Lesser** line never, in any respect, becomes a **Greater** line, nor a **Greater** a **Lesser**. Thus, if the **Greater** line *GX* is divided again proportionally, its major part will be equal to *PG*, and therefore it will remain a **Lesser** line qualitatively; it will by no means become a **Greater** line in quality, even though it becomes the "major part" in quantity—at least as long as *GA* is the proposed Expressible line.

You may ask: if *PGX* is a **Greater** line by quality, and *GX* is also a **Greater** line by quality, why can the "greater element" of *GX* not also be some **Greater** line, just as the "greater element" of the **Greater** line *PGX* was *GX*, itself a **Greater** line? It is because even though both *PGX* and *GX* are **Greater** lines, the formation in the former case is different from the latter. For into the square of *PGX* comes the whole square of *PX* and the whole rectangle under double *GA* and under *PX*. But into the square of *GX*, there enters only half of the square of *PX* (namely, that under *MX* and *XP*), and from the rectangle under double *GA* and under *PX*, only a fourth part (namely, that under *AM* and *PX*). Therefore, the ratio of the **Medial** <note>original: *Mesi*; the geometric mean between two rational lines commensurable only in square</note> to the **Expressible** is one thing here, and another there. Our proposition strives to demonstrate this meeting of the "Divine Section" and qualitative composition in the same parts of a line only regarding the first line *PGX* and its own specific ratio of the Medial to the Expressible, and not likewise regarding the subsequent ones.

Note this also for the perfection of the analogy: just as the **Greater** line *GX*, by the composition of the divine proportion, becomes a certain larger **Greater** line, namely *PGX*, so too—

# XXX. Proposition.

Individual classes of Figures are created by individual Prime numbers of sides: and those figures which have a number of sides that is a continuous double of its Prime number are considered to belong to the same class.

*This follows from Definition X of this book. For if the specific form of demonstration is the same for all figures that have side-numbers which are continuous doubles of some single number, then the Class of all those figures is the same, due to the nature of the demonstration. Indeed, bisection <note>dividing an angle or side into two equal parts</note> does not change the genus or class when applied to each of them; this is because of its simplicity and the equality of the parts taken together: for from each individual arc of the previous figure, it creates only two parts, and those are equal. But with trisection <note>division into three</note> or quinquisection <note>division into five</note>, or those following, you cannot avoid either designating unequal parts (if there must be only two), or many parts (that is, more than two) if they are to be equal. As in the trisection of an arc, it is either cut into 2 and 1 (two unequal parts), or into 1, 1, and 1 (equal but many parts).*

*The preceding point is proved thus: The demonstration is sought from the number of sides, according to Definition X of this book. Now, Prime numbers do not share any numerical factor; for the "unit" <note>the number 1</note> which they share, since it does not admit division, is not a numerical part or a "number" in this sense. Therefore, the demonstrations made through them also do not share anything with each other. Thus, the Classes of individual Primes are distinct. The first of these is that in which the figures (or quasi-figures) have these numbers of sides: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, and so on to infinity. The second has 3, 6, 12, 24, 48, 96, and so on to infinity. The third has 5, 10, 20, 40, 80, 160, 320, and so on to infinity. Others are infinite.*

# XXXI. Proposition.

Individual classes of Figures are created by the smallest multiples of sides of two Prime numbers (excluding the number two).

*This follows from Definition XI of this book. For if such a figure does not use the number of its angles for the demonstration of its side, the form of its demonstration is therefore different from all the ones above, which is why it is also a different class. The number two <note>original: *binarius*</note> was excluded from the generation of a new class when multiplied into some Prime, because since the bisection of an angle is a Geometric property, it is that which extends the individual classes equally into infinity. If this were not so, there would be no classes, but only singular figures. The first of these [new classes] is 15, 30, 60, 120, 240, 480, etc., by multiplying 3 by 5. The second is 21, 42, 84, etc., by multiplying 3 by 7. Infinite classes follow, such as when 5 is multiplied by 7, hence 35, 70, 140, etc.*

<meta>catchword: XXXII</meta>

He argues that bisection (doubling the sides) preserves a figure's mathematical class, while multiplying different primes creates entirely new classes of figures.</summary>

# ON DEMONSTRATION. BOOK I.

### XXXII. Proposition.

But also the squares of Prime numbers <note>A prime number is a whole number greater than 1 that cannot be formed by multiplying two smaller whole numbers.</note>—except for the square of Two—and products formed from squares and another Prime, or the square of a Prime, produce individual classes that are distinct from those previously mentioned.

*The reason the square of a Prime number does not belong to the same class as the Prime itself is because the Prime number creates a new class of figures that divide the entire circle (according to Proposition XXX of this book). However, when that same Prime divides not the whole circle but only a part of it, it creates an entirely different demonstration—provided such a demonstration is even possible. A Part of the circle differs significantly from the Whole in terms of its specific type and absolute shape; and it is this shape we are concerned with now, as it is what forms the basis of the mathematical demonstration.*

*As for why the square of Two <note>original: "Binarij"</note> (which is four) is excepted: the reason is that a figure with twice two angles—that is, a Square <note>original: "Tetragonus"</note>—falls into the first class. Furthermore, four multiplied by a Prime falls into that Prime's class, because four is simply twice two. Every figure with double the number of sides is referred back to the same class as the figure with half that number of sides.*

*The first of these new classes includes figures with 9, 18, 36, 72, 144, 288 sides, and so on to infinity.*

*The second includes figures with 25, 50, 100, 200, 400 sides, and so on to infinity.*

*The third includes figures with 49, 98 sides, and so on to infinity.*

*There are infinite other classes derived from squares.*

*Thus: 27, 54, 108, 216, 432, and so on, from 3 and 9.*
*Thus: 75, 150, 300, and so on, from 3 and 25.*
*Thus: 147, 294, and so on, from 3 and 49.*
*Thus: 45, 90, 180, 360, and so on, from 5 and 9.*
*Thus: 125, 250, 500, 1000, and so on, from 5 and 25.*
*So also: 225, 450, 900, and so on, from 9 and 25 (two squares multiplied).*

*There are infinite other classes resulting from Primes multiplied by squares, or from the squares of Primes multiplied by each other.*

### XXXIII. Proposition.

If you subtract four from double the number of a Figure’s angles, you will produce the Numerator of the parts of a right angle <note>A 90-degree angle.</note> that the figure's angle is worth; the Denominator of those parts is the number of Angles itself.

*For example, in a Triangle <note>original: "Trigono"</note>, twice three is six; subtract 4, and 2 remain. Therefore, the angle of a Triangle is worth two-thirds of a Right angle. Similarly, in a twenty-sided figure <note>original: "Icosigono"</note>, twice 20 is 40; subtract 4. Therefore, the angle of a twenty-sided figure is worth 36 twentieths (or 9 fifths) of one Right angle. This is because the angles of any figure can be divided into as many triangles as it has sides, minus two. Since the angles of any single Triangle are equal to two Right angles, the total angles of any figure are equal to twice as many Right angles as the figure has angles, minus four. This total number of Right angles must then be distributed among the total number of the figure's angles; therefore, the angle count names the denominator, and the calculated number counts the numerator of the parts of one Right angle.*

## XXXIV. Proposition.

**A** Circle is cut into two equal parts by a geometric description; and the line bisecting it is known by knowledge of the first degree; for it is the Diameter itself.
*For the principle of shaping in a circle is to draw a straight line through a designated point as far as is necessary.*
*The straight line bisecting the circle is the diameter, that is, the line drawn through the center, because the semicircle is the largest of the equal parts of the circle; therefore, the line cutting it into two semicircles is itself the longest, by Euclid's Elements, Book 3, Proposition 14, and it is the diameter by Proposition 15 and by definition.*
*Furthermore, the diameter is that very same Expressible* <note>original: "Effabilis"</note> <term>Expressible|Kepler uses this term to describe "rational" magnitudes (from Euclid’s 'rhetos')—lengths or areas that can be expressed in relation to a given unit of measure.</term> *line proposed as the Measure of the others; it is equal to itself and is its own perfect Measure, the very principle of Geometric knowledge.*

## XXXV. Proposition.

**T**he side of a Square <note>original: "Tetragoni"</note> has a Geometric description from its angles, outside the circle; and if it is inscribed in a circle, the side itself is in the third degree of knowledge, while its square is in the second, as is the area of the figure.
*Let OQPR be a Square; its angle, according to Proposition XXXIII of this work, is a right angle; therefore, by Euclid, Book 1, Proposition 46, a Square is easily described once a side is given.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a circle with an inscribed square. The square's vertices are labeled Q and P at the top, and O and R at the bottom. A horizontal line passes through the center of the circle and square, with points labeled L, M, and N from left to right, where M is the central point. A diagonal connects O and P, serving as a diameter of the circle.</image-desc>

*And since it has four angles and just as many sides, two sides meeting together intercept two-fourths of the circle—that is, a half-circle. Therefore, by Proposition XXXIV of this work, the diameter of the circle connects the ends of the adjacent sides. For instance, QO and QP form a right angle OQP within the semicircle OQP, and their endpoints O and P are connected by the circle's diameter OLP. Therefore, by Euclid, Book 1, Proposition 47* <note>The Pythagorean Theorem.</note>*, the squares of the two sides OQ and QP equal the square of the diameter. And if half of the square of the diameter is reduced into a square form, by Euclid, Book 2, Proposition 14, its side will be the Square's side. Thus, the square of the side is Expressible.*
*And because the square of the diameter OP is to the square of the side OQ as 2 is to 1—which is not a ratio of a square number to a square number—and since OP is Expressible in length, it follows that the side OQ is Expressible only in power* <term>Expressible in power|A line that is "rational" only when squared; for example, if the diameter is 2, the side is the square root of 2. You cannot name the side as a simple whole number, but its area is a clear, whole value.</term>*, by Euclid, Book 10, Proposition 9. However, the area of the square is the same in this figure as the square of the side; therefore, the area of the Figure is also Expressible.*

## XXXVI. Proposition.

**T**he side of an Octagon has a Geometric description from its angles, and no less so the side of an Octagonal star (or the chord subtending three-eighths of the circle); these are in the eighth degree of knowledge,

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram containing a regular octagon and an inscribed eight-pointed star. The circumference is marked with points labeled u, P, S, R, X, T, O, and Q. Internally, points are labeled A, L, N, and M, with L being the central point of the circle.</image-desc>

Therefore, having described a Square (omitting other ways of describing an Octagon) in a circle, let a perpendicular be drawn to its side *O Q* from the center *L*, cutting the side at *M* and the arc at *T*, according to Euclid Book 1, Proposition 11. Having done this, by Euclid Book 3, Proposition 30, the two parts of the quarter-circle *O Q*—namely the arcs *O T* and *T Q*—will be equal. Thus, with points *O* and *T* connected, the straight line *O T* will be the side of the Octagon, and with *O* and *S* connected, *O S* will be the side of the star.

Connecting the center *L* with *Q*, because *Q M L* is a right angle, therefore *Q L* is Expressible <note>original: "Effabilis"</note> <term>Expressible|A rational line; one that can be measured or compared to a given standard length.</term> in length, and its square is equal to the squares of *Q M* and *M L*. Moreover, the square of the radius *Q L* is double the square of *Q M*, the half-side of the Square. Therefore, *Q M* and *M L* are equal, and both are Expressible only in power <note>original: "solâ potentiâ"</note> <term>Expressible in power|Lengths whose squares are rational, even if the lengths themselves are irrational (like the square root of 2).</term> according to Proposition XXXV of this work. Therefore, the square of *L Q* is greater than the square of *L M* by the square of *M Q*, which is incommensurable in length to *L Q*. But *L O*, *L S*, and *L T* are equal. Therefore, the composite line *S M* will be a fourth Binomial <term>Binomial|An irrational line formed by the sum of two terms.</term>, whose terms <note>original: "Nomina"</note> are *S L* and *L M*, according to the definition before Euclid Book 10, Proposition 48. Truly, the remainder *M T* will be a fourth Apotome <term>Apotome|A type of irrational line formed by subtracting a rational line from another rational line that is commensurable with it only in power.</term>, whose terms are *T L* and *L M*, according to the definition before Euclid Book 10, Proposition 85.

And because *M S* is a fourth binomial, and *S T* is expressible, therefore by Euclid Book 10, Proposition 57, the line *Q S*, whose square is equal to the Rectangle contained under them, is a Major; likewise, because *T M* is a fourth Apotome, and *T S* is expressible: therefore *T Q*, the side of the Octagon, whose square is equal to the rectangle under *M T* and *T S*, is a Minor, by Euclid Book 10, Proposition 94.

The Elements of those lines are in this drawing: *P A* the greater, and *A T* the lesser. For when *A T* is added to *P A*, it makes *P T*, the side of the star; conversely, when *T A* is taken away from *P A* or *T T*, it leaves *A T*, which is *Q V*, the side of the Octagon. That is, the Minor *T Q* has a square double that of the Attachment <note>original: "Prosharmozusæ"</note> *T A*; the side of the Square *Q P* has a square equal to both Elements *P A* and *A Q*, which is *A T*.

And just as the Major *P X* is to the greater Element *P A*, so is the Minor *T Q* to the lesser Element *T A*; and conversely, as the greater element *P A* is to the lesser *A T*, so is the Major *P X* to the Minor *T Q*: As the greater part is to the lesser, so is the whole to the difference.

Furthermore, these sides *S Q* and *Q T* are not only themselves Major and Minor; they are also such lines from which others of the same kind are made by adding or subtracting. For first, they are incommensurable with each other; second, the squares of *T Q* and *Q S* joined together are equal to the expressible square of *T S*. Third, the Rectangle under *T Q* and *Q S* is Medial, for it is equal to the Rectangle under *Q M* (the half-side of the Square, expressible only in power) and *T S* (expressible in length): for which reason they are also joined in the sixth degree of knowledge. Wherefore, by Euclid Book 10, Proposition 39, when combined into one, *T Q S* becomes a Major, and by Euclid Book 10, Proposition 76, *T Q* (that is *Q Z*) taken away from *Q S* leaves *Z S* a Minor. Thus, it can happen that the Minor and Major of one pair become the Elements of another...

Regarding the area of the Octagon, it consists of eight such triangles as is *L Q T*. But the Rectangle *Q T R S* consists of four such triangles: it is therefore half of the Area. ## Proposition XXXVII.

The side of the **Hexadecagon** <note>A sixteen-sided polygon.</note> has a geometric description based on its angles, but the knowledge of its side wanders further afield, into degrees more ignoble <note>In Kepler's hierarchy, "ignoble" means more complex or farther removed from the simple rationality of a square or circle.</note> than all those previously mentioned; and much more so for the sides of its stars, or the lines subtending three, five, or seven sixteenths of the circle.

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram containing inscribed polygons and star patterns. The outer circle has points labeled Q, P, N, R, X, M, T, S along its circumference. Interior intersection points are labeled A, L, Y, and Z. The diagram shows the construction of a 16-sided figure (hexadecagon) and related octagonal stars.</image-desc>

Because twice eight is sixteen, this figure is described by the side of the **Octagon** using the same foundations as the **Octagon** was previously described by the side of the **Square**.

Let *Q O* now be the side not of a **Square**, but of an **Octagon**, and let *Q T, T O* be sides of a sixteen-sided figure; and let *Q P* be the side of an **eight-pointed star**. That was previously a **Major** line <note>original: "Mizon"</note>: therefore *L M*, its half, was a **Major** line. Wherefore the rectangle formed by the **Expressible** <note>original: "Effabili"</note> <term>Expressible|A line whose square is commensurable with a given reference area; often called "Rational" in Euclid.</term> line *S T* and the **Major** line *L M* is of a completely new species, of which no mention is made among the degrees explained above as being more noble. Truly, such a new thing, taken away from that which is contained by the lines *L T* and *T S* (both **Expressible** in length), leaves behind again some even more remote species—namely the rectangle under *M T* and *T S*, which is equal to the square of *T O*, the side of the **Hexadecagon**. This is even more true for the many-angled figures of this class, such as those with 32, 64, 128 angles, etc.

Since this is the case with one side (or the line subtending one-sixteenth), now its power <note>The "power" of a line refers to its square.</note> subtracted from the power of the diameter leaves the line subtending seven-sixteenths; that line is therefore of an even more remote degree.

But the lines subtending three-sixteenths are derived from the line subtending three-eighths by bisection: they are therefore in a more remote degree than those. And the power of the line subtending three-sixteenths, subtracted from the power of the diameter, leaves the power of the line subtending five-sixteenths. This, therefore, is again of a more remote degree.

## Proposition XXXVIII.

The sides of the **Triangle** <note>original: "Trigoni"</note> and the **Hexagon** have a geometric description from the angles of the figures; and when inscribed in a circle, they are knowable—the former in the third degree, the latter in the second; but the planes, or areas of the figures, are **Medial** <note>original: "Mesa"</note>, and stand in a double proportion to one another.

# ON THE DEMONSTRATION. BOOK I.

The construction of a **triangle** <note>specifically an equilateral triangle</note> outside a circle is very easy through the first proposition of the first book of Euclid. Its inscription into a circle is most direct—to say nothing of other methods—by the benefit of the **hexagonal side**. This is because three is half of six. The description and inscription of the **Hexagon** are indeed found in Euclid’s Book 4, Proposition 15. However, the determination of the quantity of its side must be shown from the ratios of its angles.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram featuring a circle with an inscribed hexagon labeled BHCGDF. The vertices are arranged clockwise starting from B at the top. The center of the circle is marked A. Radii connect the center to each vertex. A vertical diameter connects B and G. A triangle is inscribed with vertices B, C, and D. A line segment BE is drawn from vertex B to point E on the chord CD, meeting it perpendicularly.</image-desc>

Let there be a Hexagon *BHCGDF*. Since, therefore, there are 6 angles, the plane of the Hexagon is also divided into six triangles meeting at their vertices in the center *A*; one of which is *CAG*. Therefore, the sum of the four **Right Angles** surrounding the center *A*, divided among the six vertices, gives to one vertical angle *CAG* four-sixths, or two-thirds, of one Right Angle <note>In modern terms, 360 degrees divided by 6 equals 60 degrees</note>. But all three angles of triangle *CAG* joined together are equal to two right angles, or six-thirds of one Right Angle. Therefore, having subtracted the angle at *A* (2 thirds) from the total sum of 6 thirds, there remain 4 thirds for the two angles at *C* and *G*. These are all equal; therefore, 2 thirds of a Right Angle remain for each at *C* and *G*, no less than for the vertical angle at *A*. But if three angles are equal, the sides in the triangle must also be equal. Therefore, the side *CG*—which is the side of both the Hexagon and the triangle, and is its sixth part—is equal to the radius <note>original: "semidiametro"</note> of the circle *CA* or *AG*. The side of the Hexagon is therefore <term>Expressible in length</term> <note>original: "Effabile longitudine." In Euclidean geometry, this means its length can be expressed as a rational number relative to the diameter</note>, being half of the diameter. This is indeed the **Second Degree** according to Proposition 13 of this book.

Now, for the **Triangle** <note>original: "Trigoni"</note> *BCD*, the side *BC* connects two sides of the Hexagon, *CH* and *HB*, which meet at *H*. Since, therefore, arc *BHC* is 2 thirds of a semicircle and *CG* is one third, the arc *BCG* is therefore a semicircle, and *BG* is the diameter passing through *A*. Therefore, the angle *BCG* within it is a **Right Angle**, by Euclid’s Book 3, Proposition 31. The squares of *BC* and *CG* are therefore equal to the square of *BG*, by Euclid’s Book 1, Proposition 47 <note>The Pythagorean Theorem</note>. But *CG* is the radius, and its square is a fourth part of the square of the diameter; thus, having subtracted a fourth part from the square of *BG*, the square of the **Trigonic** <note>triangular</note> side *BC* will remain. This square is therefore **Expressible**; but because it does not relate to the square of *BG* as a square number to a square number, but as 3 to 4, *BC* is therefore <term>Expressible only in power</term> <note>original: "sola potentia Effabilis." This means the side itself is an irrational number—like the square root of 3—even though its square is a rational number</note>. This is indeed the **Third Degree**, according to Proposition 14 of this book.

And because *BC* and *CD* are equal, and angles *BCD* and *BDC* are equal, the perpendicular *BE* dropped onto *CD* will cut it at *E* into equal parts *CE* and *ED*. The whole side *CD* was indeed **Expressible only in power**; therefore so is its half, *CE*. Therefore, the rectangle formed by *CE* and *AG*—which are commensurable only in power, and of which *AG* is **Expressible in length**—is <term>Medial</term> <note>original: "Meson." In Euclid's classification, a Medial area is the square root of a rational area; it is a step further into the realm of the irrational</note>. But this rectangle is equal to the area of two triangles equal to *CGA* itself (of which there are six in the Hexagon), and thus equal to a third part of the Area of the Hexagon. Therefore, the Area of the Hexagon is a **Medial** plane. And because triangles *BCA* and *BCH* have sides *BA* and *BH*, and *CA* and *CH* equal, with one common side *BC*, they therefore have equal areas. But *BCH*, *BDF*, and *CDG* are the parts of the Hexagonal area by which it exceeds the Triangular area *BCD*, [being] just as many equal triangles [as] *BAC*, *CAD*, and *DAB*. Therefore, the Hexagonal area is double the Triangular area; thus, the Triangular area is also **Medial**, because it is commensurable (namely, half) to the Hexagonal area, which was **Medial**.

### Proposition XXXIX.

->The sides of the **Dodecagon** <note>A twelve-sided polygon</note> and of the stars of the same name, or their chords <note>original: "subtensae"</note><-

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s systematic investigation of regular polygons. ### ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES:

...stretched across five-twelfths of a circle can be geometrically described, and when inscribed in the same circle, they are knowable—each in the eighth degree of the more noble knowledge, and joined in the fifth degree; the area of the Dodecagon, however, is **Expressible** <term>original: *Effabile*; in Euclidean geometry, this refers to a value that can be expressed as a rational number or its square root relative to a given standard</term>.

Let the Dodecagon be *BMHLCKGQDPFN*, and the Dodecagonal star be *BKFLDMGNCPHQB*.

Since twice six is twelve, the figure is described from the same foundations through the side of a Hexagon, just as the Octagon was previously described through the side of a Tetragon <note>a square</note>. This is done by drawing a perpendicular line from center *A* to *HC* (the side of the Hexagon), cutting the side at *O* and the circle at *L* and *P*. By connecting *LH*, we find the side of the Dodecagon, and *HP* for the side of the star.

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram demonstrating the construction of a dodecagon and a star dodecagon. A large circle contains an inscribed twelve-sided polygon with vertices labeled B, N, F, P, D, Q, G, K, C, L, H, M. A twelve-pointed star (stella dodecagonica) is also inscribed. The center point is A. A radial line from A passes through point O on the chord HC and ends at L on the circumference. Point P is also on the circumference. Internal points of intersection and construction are marked with letters R and S. The text explains the geometric relationships between these points and the resulting polygons.</image-desc>

Since the side of the hexagon *HC* is Expressible in length, half of it *HO* will be as well. But *AC* (which is equal to *HC*) has a square equal to the sum of the squares of its half *OC* and the line *AO*. Therefore, the square of *AO* relates to the square of *AC* (or *AP*) as 3 to 4, which is not a ratio of a square number to a square number <note>meaning the relationship involves the square root of 3, an irrational number</note>.

Therefore, *PA* and *AO* are commensurable with each other only in power <note>their lengths are irrational relative to each other, but their squares are rational</note>, as are *LA* and *AO*. And *CA*—that is *PA* or *AL*—being greater than the Expressible line, is greater than the smaller line *OA* by an amount equal to the square of *CO*, which is commensurable with it. Therefore, by the definition before Book 10, Proposition 48 of Euclid: the compound line *PO* is a **Binomial** <term>original: *Binominis*; a line formed by adding two quantities that are only commensurable in power</term>, and by the definition before Proposition 85, the remainder *OL* is an **Apotome** <term>original: *Apotome*; a line formed by the difference of two quantities only commensurable in power</term>, both of which are of the "First" type. The "names" <note>Euclid's term for the two parts of these irrational lines</note> are *AP*, which is Expressible simply, and *AO*, which is Expressible only in power. But by Euclid Book 10, Proposition 54, *HP*—being the side of a square equal to the rectangle formed by the First Binomial *OP* and the Expressible line *PL*—is itself a **Binomial**. And by Proposition 91 of the same book, *HL* (the side of the Dodecagon)—being the side of a square equal to the rectangle formed by the First Apotome *OL* and the Expressible line *LP*—is an **Apotome**. Thus, each falls into the eighth, more noble degree of knowledge.

The names of this compound *PH* and the reduced *HL* are *PS* and *SH*. Since *HB* is the side of a hexagon, *KP* of a Triangle, and *BP* of a Quadragon [Square], the first's square is equal to double the smaller name (that is *HS* and *SB*), the second's is double the greater name (*KS* and *SP*), and the third's is equal to both together, taken once (*BS* and *SP*).

The binomial *PH* is also composed of *PR*, the side of a square, and *RH*, the side of a Dodecagon: but it is not called a Binomial because of this composition; for by Euclid Book 10, Proposition 42, no other point except the one marked *S* can divide it into its "names."

Since *HO* and *LP* are Expressible in length, the rectangle formed by them (that is, by *LH* and *HP*) will be Expressible, and the sum of the squares of *LH* and *HP* is likewise Expressible, being equal to the square of *LP*. Therefore, by this name, the joined lines *LH* and *HP* are in the fifth degree of knowledge. These joined lines create nothing new, nor do they form a Binomial or Apotome again: for *LH* added to *HP* makes a line Expressible only in power—specifically, one whose square is one-and-a-half times the square of *LP*. But if *LH* (or *HR*) is subtracted from *HP*, it again constitutes a line Expressible in power, *PR*, the side of a square, whose square is half the square of *LP*.

And since the Area of the Dodecagon consists of 12 triangles (of which *LAC* is one), and the Expressible rectangle *LHPD* contains four of them (that is, one-third of the whole Area), therefore the entire area is Expressible, specifically as much as...

## XL. Proposition.

**A** Regular figure of twenty-four sides, and all those resulting from it by a continuous doubling of the number of sides, certainly have geometric inscriptions, but the knowledge of their sides wanders further off, into more remote degrees than those previously set down: as is also the case for its stars—or the chords of 5, 7, and 11 twenty-fourths of the circle.

*This is proved as before in Proposition XXXVII concerning the sixteen-sided figure; with this difference, however: that here the side of the Dodecagonal star and its half are first **Binomials** <term>original: *Binomines*; a Euclidean term for an irrational line composed of two parts</term>. Therefore, the rectangle formed by the half-side and the diameter, being from an **Expressible** <term>original: *Effabili*; a rational or square-root value</term> line, does not yet become a new species, because the line whose power <note>original: *potentiâ*; in geometry, this refers to the square of a line</note> it is, is again a Binomial according to the 4th theorem of the 10th book of Euclid. But now this rectangle, when subtracted from the Expressible rectangle formed by the whole and the half Diameter, leaves something new, which has not been mentioned thus far, and is "less noble" because it is more complex; and this is produced by the power of the side of the 24-sided figure.*

*This is much more true of the many-angled figures of this Class, such as the 48-sided figure, the 96-sided figure, and so on.*

*The chord of five twenty-fourths of the circle is revealed by the bisection of the arc containing five-twelfths; its power, subtracted from the power of the diameter, leaves the power of the chord of seven twenty-fourths. Similarly, from the power of the side (or the chord of one twenty-fourth) formed by the same method, the power of the chord of eleven such parts is produced. Therefore, all these are in a more remote degree of knowledge.*

Because OFG is indeed 2/5, and OGF (namely AGF) was 4/5, then FOG will also be 4/5. With the angles at O and G being equal, the sides FG and FO subtending them are also equal.

In the same way, in triangle AOF, because AFO is 2/5, just as FAO was: therefore both AO and FO (which is the side FG) will be equal. As AF is to FG, so is AO to OG, as has already been demonstrated; therefore also as AG is to the part AO, so is this part to the remainder OG. Therefore, the leg AG is cut <term>proportionally|original: *proportionaliter*; referring to the 'extreme and mean ratio' or Golden Ratio</term> at O. Thus, by Euclid Book 13, Proposition 5: with OA or OF continued to I, so that OI is equal to the whole of AG, then FI is also cut proportionally at O; and with the points AI connected, the triangle AIO will be congruent to the initial triangle FAG, and thus OAI is double FAO itself, and FAI is 6/5. Therefore, with center A and the interval of the radius AG, having drawn the circle FGI, FG will be the side of the decagon, the major part of the radius AG cut proportionally, and FI will be the side of the star subtended by three-tenths <note>the decagram or 10-pointed star</note>, composed of FO and OI, the side of the decagon and the radius.

For this reason, these sides, when joined to the radius, can be assigned to the fourth degree, according to Proposition XXVI of this book.

And since AG is cut as an <term>Expressible|original: *Effabilis*; a rational line or a line whose square is rational</term> length, and the side of the decagon is its major part; the side of the star is composed of the whole and the major part; therefore, by Proposition XXVII of this book, the former is an <term>Apotome|original: *Apotome*; a line formed by subtracting one rational line from another</term>, and the latter is a <term>Binomial|original: *Binominis*; a line composed of the sum of two rational parts</term>, both of the fourth species: in this respect, they are in the eighth degree of knowledge, immediately following the side of the Dodecagon and its star, and clearly in the same order as the side of the Octagon and its star.

And by Proposition XXVIII of this book, the remainder OG, and thus also its half NG, is an Apotome of the first species. But be careful not to think that its names <note>the two parts that make up the irrational line</note> are the greater AG and the lesser AN.

Finally, by the same Proposition XXVII of this book, the sides GF, or OF and FI—not joined with the radius, but with each other—because they have both the sum of their squares and their common rectangle as Expressible, are in the fifth degree of knowledge.

Therefore, the side of the Decagon joined with the side of its star makes a line <term>expressible only in power|original: *effabilem potentiâ solâ*; a line whose square is rational but which is not rational itself</term>, equal in power to five-fourths of the power of the radius, which in the preceding diagram from Proposition XXVII is PX, composed of PA (equal to OA) and AX: between which GA is the expressible mean proportional.

Conversely, the side of the Decagon OF subtracted from the side of the star FI leaves the Expressible OI, namely the radius. Thus, nothing new arises from those operations.
