## XLII. Proposition.

The sides of the Pentagon and the Pentagonal Star, or those subtended by two fifth parts of the Circle, have a geometric description based on angles, and they are knowable, each in the eighth degree; when joined, in both the sixth and fourth degrees of knowledge. <note>Kepler categorizes polygons into "degrees of knowability" based on how they can be constructed with a compass and straightedge. The "eighth degree" is less fundamental than the "fourth."</note>

<margin>
As here FB and BH are the legs, and FH is the base.

<margin>
As here FDB is upon FB and BKH is upon BH.

The description outside the circle is as follows: if the length of the intended side is given, we will divide it proportionally, through Euclid Book 2, Proposition 11 or Book 6, Proposition 30 <note>These propositions describe the Golden Ratio, or "divine section," where a line is divided so the ratio of the whole to the larger part is the same as the larger part to the smaller.</note>, and we shall add to it the larger part of that division. Having thus created two "legs" <note>original: "cruribus"</note>, each equal to the combined length of the side and its larger section, and using the original side as the Base, we shall establish the innermost triangle of the Pentagon. For since the combined leg consists of the whole proposed side and its larger part from the divine section, the combined leg itself will be divided in that same ratio; its larger part will be the proposed side. Therefore, the angle of this triangle at the base will be double the angle at the vertex, just as we saw above with the Decagon. Upon these two legs, acting as Bases, we shall add two outer triangles whose own legs are equal to the proposed side.

The inscription into a circle is very easy using the side of the Decagon. For since five is half of ten, we can take two contiguous sides of a decagon, FG and GH, meeting at point G. If we connect the endpoints F and H, the line FH will be the side of the Pentagon; likewise for HK. By connecting the endpoints F and K, the line FK will be the side of the star. Let the Pentagon therefore be BDFHK, and its star BFKDHB.

Euclid demonstrates in Book 13, Proposition 10 that the side of the Pentagon FH is "capable" <note>original: "posfit". In classical geometry, one line is "capable" of others if its square is equal to the sum of their squares. Here: (Pentagon side)² = (Hexagon side)² + (Decagon side)².</note> of the side of the Hexagon FA and the side of the Decagon FG—that is, the radius AG and the larger part of the divided radius AO together. This demonstration in Euclid is difficult to grasp; I will therefore attempt an easier one here.

From the endpoints of the Pentagonal side B and D, let straight lines BG and DI be drawn through the center A. Just as DB subtends two-tenths of the circle, let the next line DL subtend three, and DK four, intersecting BG at points S and R. Therefore, the angle <unclear>L</unclear> DSA (which is the same as SDA) consists of two-fifths of one Right angle; this is because arc LI is one-fifth part of the circle, just as FH is, and equal angles at the circumference stand upon equal arcs, according to Euclid Book 3, Propositions 21 or 27. However, the angle DAB (or DAS) is four-fifths of one right angle, because DB is a fifth part of the circle, and the total circle measures four right angles around the center A. Therefore, the angles SAD and ADS together are six-fifths of a right angle. Since all three angles of a triangle must total ten-fifths <note>Two right angles, or 180 degrees.</note>, the remaining angle DSA must also be four-fifths. Thus, angle DSA is equal to DAS; therefore, the side DS is equal to the side DA, which is the radius. Consequently, by the previous arguments, the larger part of the proportionally divided radius DA equals SA, and SA is equal to the side of the Decagon. Since DA is the radius (the side of a Hexagon), I say the side of the Pentagon DB is "capable" of both SA and AD.

Finally, because the side of the Pentagon and the side of the star are as the larger part and the whole of a "divine section," they are also in the fourth degree of knowledge when joined together: see Proposition 29 of this book. It follows from these properties that just as the side of the Pentagon is the Lesser and the star's side is the Greater, so also the line composed of both is again a Greater, and the side of the Pentagon is the smaller element of this composite Greater line; while the side of the star is its larger Element; and also that the difference between each side is some Lesser line, namely DQ or QF, by the same Proposition 29.

## Proposition XLIV.

The sides of the **Pentakaidecagon** <term>Pentakaidecagon</term><note>A fifteen-sided polygon.</note>, and of its stars—namely the lines subtending two, four, or seven fifteenths of the circle—do indeed have a geometric description, but not outside the circle; and within the circle they are not derived from the angles, and therefore they are improper, and constitute a heterogeneous knowledge of a more remote degree than all the preceding figures. The Triacontagon <term>Triacontagon</term><note>A thirty-sided polygon.</note> and the rest of this class are still more remote.

For it is described from figures prior to itself, which must have a number of sides other than half its own, because 15 is odd and does not have a numerical half: specifically, it is derived from the Triangle BCD and the Pentagon BIFHK, both starting from the same point B. For if you subtract the third part BC from two-fifths BIF—that is, 5 fifteenths from 6 fifteenths—there remains CF, which is 1 fifteenth. Therefore, when the angles C and F are connected, the line CF will be the side. Here, for the act of description, I do not summon the quantity of the angle, nor the number of angles of the proposed figure; nor do I form any triangle according to this number, as was done in the higher figures. But it cannot be described otherwise. Therefore, its knowledge is also remote and base. For since the side of the Pentagon FH is parallel to the side of the Triangle CD (because both odd-sided figures started from the same point B): let a perpendicular be drawn from F to L, and from B, a diameter through the center A, cutting the lines at E, N, and G. Therefore, the side CF is equal in power to CL and FL joined; but CL is the excess of CE (which is Expressible in Power) over FN, which is the Minor line <term>Minor line</term><note>original: "Elassona"; a specific type of Euclidean irrational line.</note> LE: therefore CL is of a plainly new species. Conversely, AN is the line which is equal in power to the remainder of an Expressible plane when the plane of a Minor line has been subtracted from it: it is therefore of a new species. But EN is the remainder of this [which belongs to] us...

## Proposition XLV.

The Heptagon and all figures derived from it, which have a number of sides that is one of the Primes (as they are called), and their stars, and even all the classes derived from them, lack a Geometric description outside the circle; and within the circle, although the quantity of their sides is necessary, it is equally necessary that it be unknown.

> *A great matter is being dealt with here; for by this effect it has come to pass that the Heptagon and other figures of this kind were not employed by God for the adornment of the World, as the knowable figures explained above certainly were.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a regular heptagon inscribed within a circle. The vertices are labeled clockwise starting from the top as B, H, G, F, P, D, and C. A vertical diameter line connects vertex B to point P at the bottom of the circle, passing through the center point labeled A. Internal lines connect all seven vertices to each other, creating a complex star-like pattern (a heptagram). Along the vertical diameter, two internal intersection points are marked with the letters I and K.</image-desc>

For let *I* and *K* be the points by which line *BF* is cut by *EH* and *EG*, which trisect the angle *BEF*. Therefore, in triangle *FEI*, because angle *FEI* has been bisected; just as in it *FE* is to *EI*, so is *FK* to *KI*. But *EF* is equal to the whole of *FI*. For angle *FEI* consists of 4 sevenths of one right angle, whereas *EFI* consists of 6 sevenths; therefore *EIF* is also 4 sevenths. Thus the sides <note>original: "crura", literally "legs" of a triangle.</note> *FE* and *FI*, being opposite to equal angles, are equal. Furthermore, in triangle *KEB*, because angle *KEB* is bisected by line *EIH*: as *KE* is to *EB*, so is *KI* to *IB*. But *KE* and *FE* are equal, because triangle *KEF* is isosceles and similar to *EBF* itself; and *EF* was equal to *IF*, and *EB* is equal to *FB*, wherefore also as *IF* is to *FB* so is *KI* to *IB*. Therefore, in the same line *BF* subtended by three-sevenths of the circle, two proportions of three parts have been found: first, as the greatest *KI* is to the smallest *KF*, so the greatest *KI* is to *IF* (which is composed of both smaller parts), that is, to the side *FE* of the heptagon <note>original: "septanguli"</note>; and again, as the greatest *IB* is to the middle *IK*, so is the whole *BF* to *FI* (composed of the 2 smallest parts). This proportion indeed bears the appearance

For no certain quantity follows for *EF* or *IF*; because that which we think we obtain anew in the second instance coincides with the first. For whenever there are four <term>Proportionals</term> <note>Four numbers or lines where the first is to the second as the third is to the fourth.</note> in which the first two equal the third, it also happens that just as the first is to the third, or the second to the fourth, so also the third is to the sum of the third and fourth, which sum becomes the fifth in the series. ### XLV. Proposition.

The Heptagon <note>A seven-sided polygon.</note> and all figures derived from it which have a number of sides that is one of the Prime numbers (so-called), and their stars, and thus all the classes derived from them, lack a geometric description outside of a circle: and within a circle, although the quantity of their sides is necessary, it is equally necessary that this quantity remains unknown.

> A great matter is at stake here; for it was because of this effect that the Heptagon and other figures of this kind were prevented from being used by God to adorn the world, whereas the knowable <note>original: "scibiles," meaning figures that can be constructed with a compass and straightedge.</note> figures explained above were indeed utilized.

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram showing a heptagon inscribed in a circle with vertices labeled B, C, D, E, F, G, H. A seven-pointed star is formed by connecting the vertices. The center of the circle is labeled A. A vertical diameter BAP is shown, with point P on the circumference opposite B. Lines connect the center A to various vertices and intersection points, including points labeled I and K.</image-desc>

Let there be, therefore, a Heptagon BCDEFGH, and let all the angles be connected with one another; let A be the center of the circle, and BAP be the Diameter, and let A be connected with E.

First, such figures obtain no "improper" demonstration as described above: for the number of their sides and angles is one of the Primes. But no pair of the preceding figures divides the whole circle into parts countable by any Prime number; instead, they happen upon a Number that is a Multiple of the numbers of both figures.

But neither do figures of this kind have a "proper" demonstration based on the number of angles: because whatever is elicited from this is vague, manifold, and least of all determined.

For let the Heptagon be cut into its five triangles: two outer isosceles <note>original: "æquicrura," literally "equal-legged."</note> obtuse-angled triangles BDC and BGH; one innermost isosceles acute-angled triangle BEF; and two scalene triangles BED and BFG placed between them. Since, therefore, the arc on which the legs of the angle stand (being made at the opposite part of the circumference) measures the quantity of the angle, the angle BEF stands upon three parts of the circumference: BH, HG, and GF. Angle BFE similarly stands upon three: BC, CD, and DE; but EBF stands upon only one: EF. Therefore, BEF is such a triangle that has each angle at the base triple that which is at the vertex. In the same way, it is proved that the Scalene triangle BED has angles...

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s argument that the heptagon (a seven-sided polygon) is "unknowable" to human reason because it cannot be constructed using the traditional tools of geometry (straightedge and compass). He compares the failure to find a fixed geometric proportion for the heptagon with the successful construction of the pentagon.</meta>

<header>OF THE HARMONY OF FIGURES:</header>

For as 15 is to 9, so 40 is to 24, which is composed of 15 and 9. And as 40 is to 15, so 64 (consisting of 40, 15, and 9) is to 24, composed of 15 and 9.

Behold a common property of many proportions, which necessarily follows from an established heptagon <note>original: "septangulum"</note>; but from this property alone, a heptagonal triangle cannot be constructed. The reason why in a Pentagon the proportion of the side depends certainly on the angles, even outside the circle, while in the Heptagon and others of that kind it does not, is easily apparent from what has been said. In the Pentagonal triangle *BFK*, by the bisection of the angle *BKF*, one immediately arrives at two of its elements—the isosceles <note>original: "æquicrura"; literally "equal-legged"</note> triangles *BKT* and *KTF*. It follows from their equal angles *BFK* and *BKT* that the sides *BK*, *KT*, and *TF* are equal. But in the Heptagonal triangle, by the trisection of the angle, three elements of the triangle are formed: two isosceles triangles *BEI* and *KEF*, and one scalene <note>A triangle with three unequal sides</note> triangle *IEK*. In this case, the proportion of the sides does not follow the proportion of the angles, as is well known in Geometry. Since, therefore, the angles of this figure do not teach us anything further outside the circle, the required triangle cannot be constructed outside the circle. Therefore, this figure is not inscribable in a circle by means of anything prior to itself in science or description. Rather, only through the act of inscription itself—however that is managed—is that wandering proportion forced into the narrow confines of a single case. Thus, the principle is "begged" <note>original: "principium petitur"; the logical fallacy of begging the question, or assuming what one is trying to prove</note>: for so that the thing by which the inscription is completed may be found, we are ordered to use the inscription itself, as if it were already possible beforehand.

<margin>In the diagram on page 32.</margin>
<image-desc>A geometric diagram inscribed in a circle. The circumference features labeled points B (top), L, K, H (right side), G (bottom), and F, E, D (left side). The center is marked A. Dashed and solid lines connect these points to form an internal star-like polygon (heptagram/heptagon) and various triangles. Internal intersection points are labeled R, S, T, and I. Dashed radial lines extend from the center A to several points on the circle.</image-desc>

Therefore, the proportion of the Side *EF* to the side of the star *FB* lies hidden; it lies hidden, I say, in quantitative matter. In terms of the material principle of quantities—which is indeterminate magnitude—it is indeed possible to establish the side of a heptagon in the proper proportion to the circle's diameter. This is because there is something within the Circle itself that is certainly greater than the side of the heptagon, and something smaller. Furthermore, as the process of dividing <note>sectioning</note> proceeds into infinity, one can always find something slightly greater than the side *EF*, or something slightly smaller. But in terms of that which is *formal* in quantities <note>the "formal cause" or the defining logic/rule</note>, it is simply impossible. This is because the figure of the heptagon and its like lack any means—whether demonstrated or discovered—by which a certain proportion of the side may be known. It utterly lacks a knowable formation or determination. Since this is so, a figure of 14 angles cannot be inscribed in a circle (whose semidiameter is *AP*) by the side *EP*, nor can its two contiguous sides be spanned by one straight line *EF* (which would be the side of the Heptagon in that circle). Nor can this side be compared with the diameter, since by its own Nature it is of an unknown comparison to the Diameter.

And so, no regular Heptagon was ever constructed by anyone knowingly, willingly, and acting with purpose; nor can it be constructed by purpose. It might well be constructed by chance, and yet it must necessarily remain unknown whether it has been truly constructed or not.

In the diagonal of the new quadrilateral, whose sides are chords of three parts, the rectangle formed by them is 9 $ij$ — 6 $iij$ + 1 $vj$ <note>Kepler is using early algebraic notation: $ij$ = $x^2$, $iij$ = $x^3$, $vj$ = $x^6$, and so on.</note>; which, when subtracted from the rectangle 16 $ij$ — 20 $iij$ + 8 $vj$ — 1 $viij$, leaves the rectangle of the remaining sides as 7 $ij$ — 14 $iij$ + 7 $vj$ — 1 $viij$. ->7 $j$ — 14 $iij$ + 7 $v$ — 1 $vij$ or 7 — 14 $ij$ + 7 $iiij$ — 1 $vj$.<-

From this equation, he obtains the value of the root, which he assists mechanically <note>Meaning by calculation or instrumental means rather than pure geometric construction.</note>; there is not just one root, but in a Pentagon there are two, in a Heptagon three, in a Nonagon four, and so on; for one value is the side *BC*, the second is *BD*, and the third is *BE*.

Therefore, so that it may be clear that this way of investigating the sides of a figure has absolutely nothing in common with our Definitions I, II, and III, set out earlier: you will first note what this algebraic <note>original: "cossica"</note> chord of Bürgi’s actually professes. It professes this: that if seven terms are established in a continued proportion <note>A sequence where the ratio between successive terms is constant.</note> in the same ratio that the side of the heptagon has to the radius of the circle, where the first of these proportionals is the side of the heptagon itself; then seven of the first terms together with seven of the fifth terms produce as much as fourteen of the third terms with one of the seventh.

This statement is indeed geometric and demonstrable, no less than in the earlier sections where it was demonstrated that the plane of an Octagon is *Meson* <note>original: "Meson"; a term from Euclid’s Book X referring to a "medial" area, a specific type of irrational quantity.</note>, or that the side of a Dodecagon is an *Apotome* <note>original: "Apotomen"; another Euclidean term for an irrational line formed by subtracting one rational line from another.</note> of some line. For there, something was stated about a plane or a line; here, something is stated about the proportion of lines.

But just as it is not enough for me, for the science and measurement of a plane, to know that it is *Meson*, nor for the measurement of a line to know that it is some *Apotome*—since there are many of this kind, and no construction arises from this general knowledge, nor is any certain and determined quantity of the plane or line drawn out, but these properties only follow after the quantities have been established and described beforehand—so also here: it is not enough for me to know what will happen once seven continued proportionals are made in the ratio I desire. Since I do not yet have that proportion described by any geometric act, I was therefore waiting for someone to teach me how to establish that proportion first. For in all the previously mentioned figures, the description, inscription, and determination of a certain quantity preceded everything, along with a certain geometric act by which this determination was perfected; only then did the knowledge of those properties follow, which served for the comparison of figures with one another.

To make the difference between the two things clearer, let us look at the side of the Pentagon, the method for describing which was this: that by joining two squares, one of the radius and the other of its half, into a square form, we should take away half of the radius from the side of this square. We would then reduce the square of the remaining line, combined again with the square of the radius, into a square form; for the side of this square will be the side of the Pentagon. All these things were feasible and possible, and easier to do than to say, as those who handle compasses know. For what is easier

# ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES.
<meta>catchword: simple</meta>

...be left behind: this reasoning, on the contrary—as stated in the second point—assumes no other aids besides numbers, but always divides the diameter in various ways into many myriads of myriads <note>original: "Myriadas Myriadum," meaning millions upon millions</note> so that the ratio might become more exact. Yet, in this way, it never becomes perfectly exact. Briefly put: this is not to "know" the thing itself, but at most to know something slightly larger or smaller than it. Any subsequent calculator can always get closer; but to arrive at the point itself is never granted to anyone. Such, indeed, are all things that lie hidden in the mere possibility of quantitative matter; they do not have a knowable formation by which they might eventually be established in an act of human knowledge.

Fifthly, to deal specifically with the heptagon <note>a seven-sided figure</note> and the figures of this kind that follow: since continuous proportionality is extended through them in their following order along with the number of sides, it follows that even if the last term—the seventh proportional in the heptagon—were perfectly known, the intermediate terms could not be obtained through it. For between two terms that do not have a ratio to each other like two numbers of a continuous proportion (such as cubes, fifth powers, etc.), any number of intermediate continuous proportionals cannot be established geometrically—only one, or three, or seven, or fifteen, etc. <note>Kepler is referring to the geometric construction of mean proportionals, which in a plane are limited to specific powers</note>. But two, four, five, six, eight, nine, and so on, cannot be established in a plane, since we are dealing here with plane figures.

Indeed, between the radius (1) and the seventh proportional (1 $v$ ij) of the heptagonal proportion, there are six mean proportionals. The ratio of 1 to 1 $v$ ij is not like a ratio of one number to another in a continuous proportion of equal length; that is, the ratio of the radius to the side of the heptagon does not consist of two numbers—it is not **Expressible** <note>original: "Effabilis," a technical term for a ratio that can be defined by rational numbers or square roots constructible by ruler and compass</note>. For if it were **Expressible**, it would fall into the categories explained earlier in the prior classes, and the seven angles would not be seven, but three or four, which involves a contradiction. For the ratio of the sides was derived from the angles of the primary figures. It would therefore be necessary to establish all six mean proportionals in a single act—namely, those between 1 and 1 $v$ ij. Conversely, if 1 $v$ j were given as a quantity, then five means would fall between 1 and 1 $v$ j. If the ratio of 1 to 1 $v$ j were then like a cubic number to a cubic number, then first 1 $v$ ij and 1 $v$ iij could be established in one act; then between 1, 1 $v$ ij, 1 $v$ iij, and 1 $v$ j, three mean proportionals could be established in three acts. But if 1 $v$ were given as a quantity, then once again all four intermediates would have to be established in a single act; which could not happen except in an **Expressible** ratio, as before. Let the rest be understood according to these points.

We conclude, therefore, that these **Algebraic Analyses** <term>original: "Analyses Cossicas," referring to the 'Cossic' art, an early name for algebra</term> are foreign to the present contemplation; nor do they constitute any degree of science comparable to those we have explained above.

<margin>Lest these things be thought spoken blasphemously, one of my friends, most skilled in mathematics, judged that they could be omitted. Yet nothing is more common...</margin>
Furthermore, in passing, Metaphysicians should be warned to consider, on the occasion of this algebraic consideration, whether they can take anything from here to explain that Axiom: *Of a Non-Entity, there are said to be no conditions and no properties.* <note>original: "Non Entis nullæ dicuntur esse conditiones, nullæ proprietates"</note> For here we are indeed occupied with "beings of knowledge" <note>intellectual or mathematical constructs</note>; and we correctly pronounce that the side of the Heptagon is made of **Non-Entities**—specifically, scientific ones. For since its formal description is impossible, it therefore cannot be known by the human mind, since the possibility of description precedes the possibility of knowledge; nor is it known by the **All-knowing Mind** simply...

### BOOK I: ON DEMONSTRATION.

<margin>
Nothing is more frequent among theologians than that those things are impossible which contain a contradiction in terms.
</margin>
...simple eternal thing: because by its own nature it is among the unknowables. And yet, there are some scientific properties of this non-existent scientific object; just as there are conditional beings. For IF there WERE a Septangle <note>a seven-sided figure or heptagon</note> described in a circle, the proportion of its sides would have such attributes. Let it suffice to have given this warning.

They maintain that God's knowledge does not extend to such impossibilities, especially since these formal reasons of geometric things are nothing other than the very Essence of God; because whatever is in God from eternity, that is one individual divine essence. It would, therefore, be in a way to know Himself as other than He is, if He were to know things that are incommunicable as if they were communicable. And what sort of flattery would it be, for the sake of the unlearned who will not read the book, to defraud the rest?

There are also other false propositions by geometers concerning the sides of figures of this kind, but which even more clever mechanical practice <note>referring to physical drafting and measurement</note> would refute; although they are thrust upon the youth for the sake of mechanics. For instance, when the side AC of a septangle is stated by **Albrecht Dürer** to be equal to the semi-side of a triangle AB of the same circle. But that this is too short, even mechanical practice itself teaches; yet, lest a too-crude manual experimentation deceive anyone, he will be able to detect the falsehood by this reasoning alone before setting his hands to work. The side of a triangle is proved from the number of its angles to be expressible in power <term>effabile potentia: a term from Euclidean geometry meaning the square of the line is commensurable with the square of the diameter, even if the line itself is not</term>; and therefore its half is also so. The side of a heptagon is not expressible in power, by that very fact that it is a heptagon; and because seven is neither six, nor five, nor three. For prime numbers produce species; but species are incommensurable among themselves, nor is one the same as another.

Regarding the false arguments <note>original: "paralogismis"</note> of **Carlo Mariano of Cremona** and **François de Foix-Candalle** concerning the heptagon, see **Christopher Clavius**, *Practical Geometry* Book VIII, proposition 30, and in the commentaries on Euclid Book IV, Prop. 16.

This wrestling-ground <note>original: "palaestra," a metaphor for intellectual competition</note> even stirred the Most Illustrious **Lord Marquis of Malaspina**, Ambassador of the Serene Duke of Parma to the Imperial Court in the year 1614; who surpassed all the descriptions of everyone else with a most ingenious diagram; thinking that a chord subtending three-fourteenths of a circle is equal to five-quarters of the semi-diameter, and thus expressible in length. The apparatus of his demonstration was of such skill that it escaped even Euclid himself that something unproved had been assumed.

Undecagon <note>an 11-sided figure</note>.

For the side of a Hendecagon <note>another name for an undecagon</note>, such a description is circulated: In a circle, from the same point A, let the side of a square AC be drawn to one part of the circumference, the side of a triangle AD to the opposite, the side of a hexagon AB', AF to both; and let the angle FAB of those two hexagonal sides be subtended by another triangular side BF, which will cut the previous triangular side AD at G. Let a diameter CE also be drawn from the end of the square side C through the center I, and from the other end of the diameter E, through the intersection of the triangle sides G, let a straight line EG be drawn, cutting the square side AC at H. The line GH between these two intersections is said to be the side of the undecagon. It is, however, too long, as even mechanical practice teaches. But the clever geometer...

->ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES<-

geometry considers the appearance of a line, which necessarily shares something from the sides of the <term>Trigonic and Tetragonic</term> <note>These terms refer to the triangle and the square, the primary "knowable" shapes from which others are derived.</note> figures, however remote the degree. Yet the number 11, being Prime, leads to these figures in no way at all, since as a Prime it has nothing in common with 3 or with 4. Therefore, the Geometer is certain that the description is false and can easily forgo the labor of calculating it.

It remains true, through all objections and through all the fruitless efforts of everyone, that the sides of figures of this kind are by their own Nature unknown and unknowable. Thus it is no wonder that what could not be found in the <term>Archetype of the World</term> <note>Kepler’s theory that God used geometric "blueprints" to create the universe.</note> was also not expressed in the physical formation of the parts of the World.

# XLVI. Proposition.

The division of any arc of a circle into three, five, seven, etc., equal parts—or into any ratio that is not the <term>continual double</term> <note>Ratios based on 2, 4, 8, 16, etc.</note> of those previously demonstrated—is not of such a Geometric possibility that it generates scientific knowledge.

*The division of an arc into two, four, eight, and so on—the continually double division—is indeed Geometric, and has been used until now. It happens that the whole Circle can be divided into three parts by a Triangle; a Semicircle can be so divided, as in the Hexagon; a quarter part, as in the Dodecagon; a fifth part, as in the Pentekædecagon <note>A 15-sided figure.</note>; an arc of 135 Degrees, as in the Octagon; and an arc of 108 degrees, as in the Decagon. Similarly, the whole circle happens to be divided into five by a Pentagon; a semicircle, as in the Decagon; a third part of the circle, as in the Pentekædecagon; and an arc of 150 degrees, as in the Dodecagon. The same is true of the halves, quarters, and other parts of these arcs in the proportion of continual halving. But this does not happen because of the nature of Trisection or Quinisection <note>The act of dividing something into three or five equal parts.</note>, but by accident, and because of other properties of the figures, which have been discussed until now.*

*But it is clear that miscellaneous trisection, or division in any other proposed ratio that is not continually double, is impossible, as seen by comparison with possible bisection. In bisection, the "medium" <note>The mathematical means or bridge.</note> for the arc and the angle to be bisected is a straight line—the <term>chord</term> subtending the arc—which can be divided into two equal parts Geometrically. Since the equality of these parts is followed by the equality of the parts of the arc, whether small or large, in respect to the whole circle: and it is from this same source that in a Triangle, from the equality of the sides, one may argue for the equality of the opposite angles. But this "medium" deserts us in other divisions. For even if a straight line subtending an arc can be divided into any number of parts Geometrically, it does not follow that any proportion of the parts of that line (after the proportion of equality) results in the same proportion of the parts of the arc; just as in a Triangle it is not permitted to argue from any proportion of the sides (except for the one of equality) to the same proportion of the opposite angles. For if the line subtending an arc is divided, for example, into three equal parts: if the dividers were perpendicular to that line, the middle part of the arc would be smaller than the side parts; if the dividing lines started from the center of the arc, the middle part of the arc would be larger than the side parts. Therefore, between the distance in—*

...finite length and the center of the circle is a point from which two <term>sectrices</term> <note>Lines that cut or divide a figure.</note> are drawn, which would cut both the <term>chord</term> <note>original: "subtensam"; the straight line connecting the two endpoints of an arc.</note> and its arc into three equal parts. Indeed, that point is always further removed from the arc of the circle the smaller the arc to be trisected is, yet the proportion is not constant. Since the arcs of a circle can be diminished toward infinity, the distance of this point will also run out toward infinity. Truly, of the infinite, or of infinite variety, there is no scientific knowledge. This difficulty holds for <term>Trisection</term>, which is even simpler and closer to equality. A much greater difficulty arises in the following divisions of any arc—for example, into 5, 7, 9, 11, etc., equal parts. For then, it is no longer possible even to find a single identical point from which straight lines could be drawn to cut the chord into the commanded equal parts and simultaneously cut the arc into equal parts.

<margin>*What the nature of the Byrgian method is for dividing an arc into several equal parts.*</margin>
Yet whatever aids we can bring to such arbitrary division derived from the number that names the section, it must necessarily be general and common to the chords of any arc—as much for a large one that differs greatly from its chord as for a small one that differs little. However, to leave the proportion of the chord to the parts of its arc vague is not to determine it scientifically. Let this be said especially regarding the <term>Byrgian Analysis</term> <note>Referring to the methods of Jost Bürgi (1552–1632), a Swiss clockmaker and mathematician who developed early logarithmic and algebraic methods for calculating sine tables.</note> for trisection or <term>quinquisection</term> <note>Division into five parts.</note>, which we dealt with copiously in the preceding Proposition. Although everything said there also applies here, certain things said there are more proper to this place, and they become more illustrious and admirable in the division of arcs than in the division of the whole circle. For I shall pass over those common points: that the <term>beginning is assumed</term> <note>original: "principium petatur"; a logical fallacy where the conclusion is assumed in the premises (begging the question).</note> by commanding us to do what we were seeking to know how to do; that the properties of continuous quantity are not scientifically produced through discrete quantities or Numbers; and that whatever number is elicited for the side determining the commanded part of the arc, it can teach nothing more than that it is either greater or less than what is required. Therefore, just as raw and undigested matter relates to something formed, or as an indeterminate and undefined quantity relates to a figure, so also does that *Analysis* relate to Geometric determinations. That which is especially excellent and noble in this semi-mechanical **Algebra** <note>original: "Cossâ"; from the Italian "cosa" (the thing), an early term for algebra where the unknown variable was called "the thing."</note> is, however, degenerate and abject in scientific **Geometry**. For since every chord smaller than the diameter is associated with two unequal arcs of the circle—one smaller than a semicircle, the other larger—the chord of the equal part of the smaller arc is smaller, and the chord of the equal part of the larger arc is larger. This *Byrgian Analysis* prescribes something general not only for these two unequal chords but also for several other chords of the circle, which is useful for expressing them all very closely in numbers. For example, in trisection the law is this: If an arc is given (let it be 48 degrees) along with its chord, and that arc is to be cut into three parts, each of 16 degrees—that is, the chord of this part must be found—take its proportion to the chord of the whole 48 degrees. Then I am ordered to make a proportion such that as the chord of the whole is to the sought chord of the part, so is this to a second, and the second to a **third proportional** <note>A term in a geometric progression (a:b = b:c, where c is the third proportional).</note>. Now I am ordered to triple the chord of the part and subtract from it the third proportional; what remains is said to equal the chord of the whole. That is: from the given chord, let the third part be multiplied cubically, like a fraction, and let the resulting number be added to the whole. One third of the part thus increased is a little less than the sought chord. For if this itself, multiplied cubically, is again added to the whole, the third part so increased comes closer to the truth; and this continues on to infinity. Indeed, by this process, one gradually comes very close to the chord of 16 degrees.

He demonstrates the iterative, "semi-mechanical" process of finding the chord of an arc through cubic calculations.</summary>

### ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES:

But if you establish a larger number to be cubed, and roughly as much as the compass indicates is owed to the third part of the remainder of the circle after 48 degrees are removed—namely 312 degrees, a third of which is 104—then you will also complete the <term>chord</term> <note>original: "subtensam"; the straight line connecting the two ends of an arc.</note> of the 104-degree arc and its complement of 256 degrees in this manner. Nor is this all; for if you also add a full circle of 360 degrees to 48 and 312, you will also find another chord for the thirds of those sums (namely 408 and 672, which are 136 and 224), by the same <term>Cossic Name</term> <note>original: "Nomen Cossicum." The term "cossic" comes from the Italian "cosa" (thing) and refers to early algebraic notation where variables and their powers were given specific names rather than modern symbols like x² or x³.</note>. And in general, for as many units as remain in the number of the section once two are removed, that is how many times one may add a full circle or an arc according to the proposal, so that the chords of the new arcs may be tracked down by the same cossic name. From this, the huge difference between these cossic names and the <term>scientific degrees</term> <note>Kepler's term for divisions that can be achieved through rigorous, step-by-step geometric construction.</note> which I explained above becomes apparent.

But can some more noble art not be found by which the sections of arcs can be completed in every way? I respond: if all chords of arcs to be divided are considered under a common notion, and if we only have those aids which are common to all sought-after chords—such as any number of continued proportionals in the sought proportion—then no one will ever devise anything more noble. Anyone who strives in this direction is merely repeating what has been done and, in their confusion, establishes a contradiction. For from common principles, nothing specific to any individual case can be concluded.

However, if we begin a discussion about the specific differences of the lines that <term>subtend</term> <note>Stretch across or connect the endpoints of an arc.</note> the arcs to be divided, the state of the question changes. Instead of a universal sectioning of an arc, we substitute a sectioning of the whole circle through a <term>Regular Figure</term> <note>A polygon with equal sides and angles, such as a square or pentagon.</note>, which grants its own specific property to the proposed chord. We have already dealt with these Regular Figures above and will deal with them more fully in what follows. Indeed, in this very question, we were seeking a means by which we could describe some of those figures. Since such a means ought by nature to exist before the thing itself is produced by that means, we would certainly be "begging the principle" <note>A logical fallacy where the premise assumes the conclusion is true.</note> if we sought help from Regular Figures to explain our Means.

<margin>The universal arc sections of Pappus and Clavius.</margin>
But here some adversary might object to me: that **Pappus of Alexandria**, in the fourth book of his *Mathematical Collections*, Proposition 31, provides the trisection of an angle by means of a **Hyperbola**; and in Proposition 35, the cutting of an angle in any given ratio by means of the **Quadratrix** and the **Helix**; and **Clavius**, in the 13th book of his *Practical Geometry*, Proposition 25, performs the same by the **Conchoid of Nicomedes**.

Yet the inventions of those authors establish no possibility for a universal, "scientific" geometric section. To make this clear, I will first explain Pappus’s mechanisms regarding trisection; then, I will bring to light the difference between those and scientific descriptions.

<margin>Pappus's trisection of an angle.</margin>
First, Pappus himself, in the preamble before Proposition 31, divides problems (which he calls "Geometric" in the more general sense of the word, whereas for us, "Geometric" has a specific meaning) into **Plane**, **Solid**, and **Linear**. He admits that the trisection of an angle cannot be performed by "Plane" means (which, in my specific sense, are the "scientific" geometric degrees explained earlier), and for that reason, he rebukes the ancient geometers for their ill-advised efforts, who sweated over this in vain.

He himself, therefore, performs his trisection through **Solids** <note>Problems requiring conic sections, like parabolas or hyperbolas.</note>, and the universal section through "figured lines" <note>Complex curves that are not simple circles or straight lines.</note>.

# BOOK I OF THE DEMONSTRATION.

<margin>

He refers to this mode of philosophizing elsewhere.
</margin>

The method of trisection is as follows. With an angle proposed to be trisected, let a perpendicular be dropped from a point on one leg to the other leg, which is understood to determine the length of the legs; then, for that other leg made shorter by the perpendicular, let parallels be drawn—one from the first point, the other from the proposed angle—so that when they meet they form a straight line and an angle themselves. Now, through that point where the perpendicular was dropped, he makes the surface of a **Cone** (a solid figure) pass; then he tilts the Cone so applied, or makes it "nod," until it marks out with its surface the section called a **Hyperbola** in the plane of the drawn parallels, which serves as its own <term>asymptote</term> <note>original: "Asymptotôn"; the lines that a curve approaches but never meets.</note>. Then, from that point where the perpendicular was dropped, at an interval which is double the first leg, he describes an arc in the plane, cutting the line of the conic section. Having connected the center of the arc with this intersection, he draws a line parallel to it from the proposed angle; and having done this, he demonstrates that a third part has been cut off from the angle.

<margin>
Pappus considers this section from proposition 35 to 4[0] of the 4th book.
</margin>

Pappus indeed makes this a <term>Solid problem</term> <note>In classical geometry, "Solid" problems required conic sections (cones), whereas "Planar" problems used only ruler and compass.</note> in this manner, by the use of a Cone, a solid figure. But insofar as a Conic section, called a **Hyperbola**, can be traced in a plane even without a Cone—between given asymptotes (the drawn perpendiculars) forming a right angle and through a point given within them—the same problem seems also to be classified among the **Linear** problems. For such a line is produced by a **Geometric motion** and a continuous change of intervals; that is, it is represented by any number of points, an indeterminate number. This is no less true than for the <term>Quadratrix</term> <note>A curve used for squaring the circle and trisecting angles.</note> and the <term>Spiral</term> <note>original: "Helix."</note>, lines with which he completes both the Trisection and the Universal Sectioning in Proposition 35. Such is the mechanical device of Pappus.

What then shall we say? Is it not the case that between given asymptotes, through a given point, only one single Hyperbola is drawn, whether it is done by the "nodding" of a Cone or by the continuation of infinite points? Is there not only one single intersection of a circle with a Hyperbola from one side? Is there not only one single and certain inclination of the line connecting the points of the Hyperbola to the diameter of the figure?

<margin>
The mechanical is not understood.
</margin>

Indeed, I confess that all these things are necessary and certain, provided the Hyperbola is already drawn. For even previously, in the <term>analytic trisection</term> <note>Numerical or algebraic methods.</note> of **Bürgi** <note>Jost Bürgi (1552–1632), a Swiss clockmaker and mathematician who developed an early form of logarithms and algebraic methods for chord tables.</note>, there was a certain and necessary length or proportion of the <term>chord</term> <note>original: "subtensæ."</note> of the established third part to the chord of the whole arc. But because we are not asking what the thing *is* once it is already done, but rather *how* it is to be made in the first place, when it is not yet done; therefore, we gain nothing more from the **Solid** and **Linear** problems of the ancients regarding the sought-after science of lines than we previously did from the **Analytic** doctrine of the moderns. To be sure, there is only one single Hyperbola line capable of being drawn in their plane between the positioned asymptotes through the proposed point. But as it is not yet drawn, I am ordered to tilt the Cone over the point of application for as long as it takes until that line exists and is drawn. Or, without a Cone, I am ordered to change the lines that trace the Hyperbola through continuous points for as long as it takes until the Hyperbola is sufficiently prolonged. And those intermediate parts that fall between the points made, I am ordered to imagine as being made. I am ordered on both sides to pass through that which exists in the power of infinite division, either by act or motion, so that by this passage even that which lies hidden in that potential infinity might be reached, yet without the light of perfect knowledge—such as the problems named **Planar** by the ancients possess.

<margin>
Vieta and other modern Belgian Geometers.
</margin>

**François Viète** the Frenchman and modern **Belgian Geometers** <note>Likely referring to Adriaan van Roomen or Simon Stevin.</note> frequently use postulates of this kind in the solutions of those problems which by their own nature are not solvable except "inartificially"—either through numbers or through Geometric motions governed by a certain infinity of changes.

For when everything is ready that is thought to serve in making the mind certain: we will hold onto the determination of that which is either greater or less than the required value by the closest margin, and always closer still: *as we said previously regarding Analytical trisection.*

<margin>From plane figures to solid figures, there is no scientific transition.</margin>
What I say is true regarding this <term>solid problem</term> <note>In traditional geometry, a "solid" problem is one that requires conic sections or three-dimensional shapes to solve, rather than just a flat ruler and compass.</note> of Trisection, as the very word "solid" warns us. For unless the proportion of the solids is given such as exists between two cubic numbers, we cannot measure the proposed solid by another known solid to inform the mind: because two <term>intermediate proportionals</term> <note>These are specific values needed to solve problems like doubling a cube; they cannot be found using basic flat geometry.</note> cannot be exactly established in a plane. Although they can exist within cubes, no transition is given from planes to form those cubes, whatever they may be, without those same two means—as if across a broken bridge. <margin>It is impossible to find two mean proportionals scientifically.</margin> Others teach how to find two mean proportionals through "Geometric motion" <note>This refers to using mechanical instruments or moving parts, which mathematicians like Kepler felt lacked the pure certainty of static geometry.</note>, commanding what is impossible regarding the certainty of an adequate Geometric act. Pappus himself also teaches it through <term>Conic sections</term> <note>Curves like ellipses or parabolas created by slicing a cone.</note>, to be expedited by the benefit of two proportionals, since even a Cone is a kind of solid. Thus, the principle is always begged, and the bridge lies on the opposite bank.

## Proposition XLVII.

Figures with an odd number of sides greater than 5 (excepting the Pentadecagon <note>original: "Pentekædecagono"; a 15-sided figure</note>), along with the chords of several parts, and thus entire Classes, are in the same sense as the Heptagon <note>7-sided figure</note> and other figures with a Prime number of sides.

*For if the number of sides is odd and not one of the Primes: it is either the smallest multiple of two odd Primes; or the square of some Prime; or a multiple of one Prime and the square of another Prime, or a multiple of several squares separately or joined together.*

*Now, if these figures were describable, inscribable, and <term>knowable</term> <note>original: "scibiles"; in this context, "knowable" means a figure that can be precisely constructed using a compass and straightedge.</note>; then they would either have their own demonstration from angles, or an improper one from a comparison of the figures with which they share properties. But they do not have their own; because they do not have a Prime number of sides from which a demonstration could be formed. Nor do they have an improper one—neither the first type, for instance, the 21-gon <note>original: "Unetvigintangulum"</note>, because the figures sharing properties with them (either both or one or the other, as here the Heptagon—after the Triangle and Pentagon from which the 15-gon is formed) have no demonstration of their own, according to the preceding Proposition XLV; nor the second type, for instance, the Nonagon <note>9-sided figure</note>, because there is no way to divide a part of an arc—say, a third—into as many equal parts as the whole circle was divided into, according to the preceding Proposition XLVI; nor the third or fourth types, because the earlier figures sharing properties with them are undemonstrable.*

<margin>The side of a Nonagon is not knowable.</margin>
Concerning the Enneagon <note>original: "Enneagono"; another name for a 9-sided figure</note>, whose number 9 is the square of the first odd prime among Primes, namely *three*, Geometers have struggled until now, with many striving to demonstrate even the side of this figure. All, however, were in vain; nor would they have ever attacked this problem if they had paid attention to the distinction between *knowable* and *unknowable* things.

<margin>Campanus on the Nonagon.</margin>
Campanus <note>Campanus of Novara (c. 1220–1296), a famous commentator on Euclid.</note> wanted to demonstrate the Nonagon through the Trisection of an angle, which was shown to be *unknowable* <note>original: "inscibilem"; impossible to construct via standard geometric rules.</note> in the preceding Proposition XLVI. For even though the path of Pappus and Clavius <note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612), an influential Jesuit mathematician.</note> is necessarily trisected—assuming, of course, Geometric motion—*yet what does this have to do with plane figures, which we are dealing with here, since solid bodies are needed to make the lines for trisection—*

...lines, such as the Hyperbola, the Quadratrix, the Helix, or the Conchoid? Indeed, Campanus himself <note>Campanus of Novara, a 13th-century mathematician famous for his edition of Euclid's Elements.</note>, while attempting the trisection of an angle, did not notice that he was taking a third part of the angle as if it were already certain, which was the very thing that remained to be sought. This passage exists in my own copy at the end of Euclid's work on folio 586, pertaining to the end of Book IV.

<margin>Giordano Bruno's Nonagon.</margin>
Giordano Bruno of Nola <note>The famous philosopher and cosmologist (1548–1600), whom Kepler often criticized for lacking mathematical rigor.</note>—in a hexagon ABCDEF—extends the opposite sides BC and EF in both directions, drawing the perpendiculars GH and IK which touch the circle at points A and D. Then, by drawing the diagonal IH of the resulting parallelogram, he believed the circle would be cut in such a way that between the points of contact AD and the intersections M and N, there would exist the ninth parts of the circle <note>i.e., arcs of 40 degrees, which would form a 9-sided nonagon</note>, AN and DM. However, it is demonstrated from the diagram that since the square of that semi-diagonal LH is <term>expressible</term> <note>original: "effabile"; in this context, it means a value whose square is a rational proportion of the diameter.</note>—namely, 7/16ths of the square of the diameter (for if angle ABH is 60°, then BH is half of AB or AL; and its <term>power</term> <note>original: "potentia"; Kepler uses this to mean the square of a line segment.</note>, therefore, is one-fourth the power of AL;

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a circle and an inscribed hexagon ABCDEF within a rectangle GHKI. The circle touches the rectangle at points A and D. A diagonal line IH intersects the circle at points M and N. A central vertical axis AD passes through the center point L. Various line segments connect the vertices and the central axis.</image-desc>

Therefore the square of AH is three-fourths <note>original: "dodrans"</note> of the square of AL. Since the square of LH equals the sum of the squares of LA and AH), the <term>sine</term> of 40 degrees—that is, half the chord of two-ninths of the circle—would have been expressible by its square: specifically, the square root of 3/28ths of the square of the diameter. For by dropping a perpendicular AO from A onto LH, the ratio would be as the square of LH (7/10ths) is to the square of HA (3/10ths): just as the square of LA (4/10ths) is to the square of AO (12/7ths of 1/10th, which is 3/28ths). Thus, this chord of the nonagonal angle would be "nobler" than some of the previously mentioned figures, and share a relationship with them; yet, since it has an odd number of sides—specifically a number based on the prime 3 squared <note>3 x 3 = 9</note>—it shares nothing with the <term>Square</term> or the <term>Triangle</term> through the bisection of arcs, which are the figures to which this degree of "nobility" properly belongs.

# XLVIII. Corollary.

It follows, therefore, that the boundaries of Conception, Knowledge, Determination, Description, and Demonstration consist within the first orders of figures: so that there are no more than four classes of <term>knowable figures</term> <note>Figures that can be perfectly constructed using only a straightedge and compass.</note>. Three of these have their own proper demonstrations, in which the "heads of the families" are: in the first, the **Square** <note>original: "Tetragonus"</note>, following the diameter of the circle, whose character is the number 2; in the second, the **Triangle** <note>original: "Trigonus"</note>, whose character is 3; in the third, the **Pentagon**, with the character 5. There is, however, one class of "improper" demonstrations, whose number is a multiple of 3 and 5—namely, 15; for the first figure of that class is the **Pentekædecagon** <note>A 15-sided polygon.</note>.

# XLIX. Proposition.

Since, however, **bisection** (which the first class uses as its own property) is common to both the second and third classes: it is clear that the first class exists under one law, and the remaining two under another; so that the first has a "familiarity" with both of the others; but those others, in their configurations, are distinct from each—

<meta>This page concludes Book I of Kepler's treatise. He has been categorizing polygons based on their "knowability"—how their sides relate to the circle's diameter—which he views as the geometric foundation for musical intervals. He moves here from the construction of individual shapes to a hierarchical classification of their "nobility."</meta>

...are distinguished, so much so that among those which have their own proper demonstrations, there are in a certain way only two Classes.
For the Square and the Octagon immediately attach themselves, as if entirely, to the Triangular division: because the sixth and twelfth parts of a circle, when joined, make a fourth; and the twelfth and twenty-fourth parts, when combined, make an Eighth part. And the Square accommodates itself in a certain way to the Pentagonal division; because a fifth part of the circle, added to a twentieth, constitutes a fourth part. The cause is that the Numbers 3 and 5 can be divided into numbers of a continuous double proportion: for the parts of 3 are 1 and 2; the parts of 5 are 1 and 4. Truly, such a communion does not exist between the classes of the Threes and the Fives. For although a sixth part of the circle, added to a thirtieth, constitutes a fifth; yet the thirtieth belongs to the class of the 15-sided figure <note>original: "Pentekædecagonicæ"</note>, which does not have its own proper construction.
In the same way, a tenth of the circle, added to a fifteenth (behold the mixing of the fourth class), makes a sixth. Because of this quality of Classes, the characteristic numbers are: 12 in the first, and 20 (or its half, 10) in the second. These things, therefore, are to be referenced and ascribed below in Book III to the distinction of the genres of song <note>Kepler is preparing the reader to understand how these geometric ratios create the "Major" and "Minor" scales in music.</note>.

## 50. Comparison of Figures
->or of the divisions of the circle,<-

The diameter holds the first rank; for it is <term>expressible</term> <note>original: "effabilis"; a term from Euclid meaning a magnitude that can be compared rationally to the reference diameter.</note> in length. Second is the side of the Hexagon, being equal to the semi-diameter, and thus likewise Expressible in length. In the third place stand the Square and the Triangle, because they have sides that are Expressible only in <term>power</term> <note>original: "potentiâ"; meaning their squares (the "power" of the line) are rational proportions of the diameter's square, even if the lines themselves are not.</note>. The fourth order is held by the sides of the 12-sided figure, the 10-sided figure, and the sides of their associated stars; for they are of <term>inexpressible</term> power, and belong to the "Composites of the first species"—namely, they are <term>Binomials</term> and <term>Apotomes</term> <note>These are technical terms from Euclid's Book X for specific types of irrational numbers formed by adding or subtracting two incompatible magnitudes.</note>: those of the 12-sided figure being of the First type, and those of the 10-sided being of the Fourth. In the fifth place follow the sides of the Pentagon and its star, as well as the sides of the Octagon and its star; for they are from the fourth species of composites, called the <term>Greater</term> and the <term>Lesser</term> <note>original: "Mizon & Elaffon"; Greek terms for specific irrational lines.</note>.

But lest any good quality in the 10-sided figure should prejudice the 5-sided one, or lest the same species of the 8-sided side should equal its own figure to the 5-sided or 10-sided: a new virtue comes to the 5-sided figure at its very origin. Because through this Division, which communicates with the number Ten, the <term>Divine Proportion</term> <note>original: "proportio Divina"; today known as the Golden Ratio.</note> reigns everywhere. This proportion is immediately present in the sides of the 5-sided figure and its star; but it does not fit the 10-sided figure and its star except by the mediation of the side of the Hexagon; and it does not fit the 8-sided figure at all.

Beyond these properties of the sides, there is yet another assessment of nobility: that figures are distinguished by the suitability and perfection of the area which the figure encloses. Here, after the diameter (which encloses no area, and which alone cuts the area of the circle into two equal parts, as Ptolemy reminds us, no less than it cuts the circumference), the Square and the 12-sided figure obtain the primary place, for they have an Expressible area. The Square indeed has an exceptional prerogative; for its area is the same as the square of its side, since the species of the area is itself square: thus it encloses half of the square of the diameter. The 12-sided figure stands next after these principles, enclosing three-quarters <note>original: "dodrantem"</note> of the square of the diameter. In the next place follow the Triangle, the Hexagon, and the Octagon, whose areas are of the <term>Medial</term> <note>original: "Mesôn"; an irrational area whose side is the mean proportional between two rational lines.</note> species. The areas of the Pentagon and Decagon have as yet no names for their concepts.

->END of Book I.<-

I have so far explained the mental or <gloss>intelligible</gloss> <note>original Greek: νοητὴν (noetēn). Kepler distinguishes between the abstract idea of a shape and its physical representation.</note> essence of individual Regular Figures. Now follows the property of these figures when joined, and their "effect," so to speak, within the realm of Geometry—which is either Congruence <note>the ability of shapes to fit together perfectly without gaps, like floor tiles</note> or Incompatibility. For Demonstrability <note>the ability to prove or construct a shape</note> and Congruence do not cover the same ground: while the former belongs to individual shapes and extends to infinity through the continuous doubling of a single figure's sides, the latter is restricted by certain laws where multiple figures are called into a single fellowship. Congruence soon reaches an end because the increasing angles of the shapes eventually block further expansion. And although there is a choice of levels in knowledge and demonstration—and those shapes we have explained differ greatly in "nobility" from those we dismissed without a name—Congruence does not walk in perfect step even with this nobility of demonstration. Thus, one is not the cause of the other; rather, both depend on the same common cause (which is the fitness of the angles of the figure), though each follows its own laws.

However, how necessary this part of our contemplation is can be seen from the very purpose of this entire work. Since we have undertaken to explain the origin of Harmony and its most excellent effects in the whole World, how could we say nothing about the congruence of figures, which are the very fountainheads of Harmonic proportions? For the Latin words "to fit" and "Congruence" <note>original: "Congruere" and "Congruentia"</note> mean the same thing as the Greek "to join" and "Harmony" <note>original: ἁρμόττειν (harmottein) and ἁρμονία (harmonia)</note>. This effect of figures within Geometry, and within that part of Architecture that deals with Archetypes <note>the original master patterns used by God to create the universe</note>, is a kind of image and prelude to the effects found outside Geometry and outside the concepts of the mind—in natural and celestial things themselves. Indeed, this property of congruence, which results in some structure or physical body, is such that it invites even the contemplative Mind to do, create, and embody something externally. Hidden from eternity in the most-blessed divine mind through the orders of Ideas, as the Supreme Good, which shares itself, it could not be contained in its own abstraction

...are distinguished, so much so that among those which have their own geometric proofs, there are in a sense only two <term>Genera</term> <note>Classes or families of shapes</note>.

For the **Square** and the **Octagon** immediately attach themselves, as if entirely, to the **Triangle** class; this is because a sixth and a twelfth part of a circle joined together make a fourth part <note>1/6 + 1/12 = 1/4</note>, and a twelfth and a twenty-fourth part, combined, make an eighth part <note>1/12 + 1/24 = 1/8</note>. And the **Square** adapts itself to some extent to the **Pentagon** class: because a fifth part of the circle, with a twentieth added, constitutes a fourth part <note>1/5 + 1/20 = 1/4</note>. The reason is that the numbers 3 and 5 can be divided into numbers of a continuously double proportion <note>1, 2, 4, 8, etc.</note>: for the parts of 3 are 1 and 2, while the parts of 5 are 1 and 4. However, such a fellowship does not exist between the classes of Three <note>the Triangle family</note> and Five <note>the Pentagon family</note>. For although a sixth part of the circle, with a thirtieth added, constitutes a fifth <note>1/6 + 1/30 = 1/5</note>; yet the thirtieth belongs to the class of the **15-sided figure** <note>original Latin: Pentekædecagonicæ</note>, which does not have its own independent proof. In the same way, a tenth of the circle added to a fifteenth (note here the mixing of the fourth class) makes a sixth. Because of this duality of Genera, the characteristic numbers are 12 in the first and 20 (or its half, 10) in the second. These matters are therefore to be referred to and ascribed below in Book III to the distinction of the types of song <note>musical modes or scales</note>.

## L. Comparison of Figures
->or divisions of the circle.<-

The **diameter** holds first place; for it is <term>expressible in length</term> <note>original: effabilis longitudine; meaning its length can be stated as a rational number</note>. Second is the side of the **Hexagon**, which is equal to the radius and is thus also expressible in length. In third place stand the **Square** and **Triangle**, because they have sides expressible only in power <note>their lengths are irrational, like the square root of 2, but their squares are rational numbers</note>. The sides of the **12-sided figure** (Dodecagon) and the **10-sided figure** (Decagon), along with the sides of their related stars, hold the fourth rank; for they are among the lines "inexpressible in power" and the first species of compounds, namely <term>Binomials</term> and <term>Apotomes</term> <note>specific types of irrational lines defined in Euclid’s Elements, Book X</note>. Specifically, those of the Dodecagon are of the First type, and those of the Decagon are of the Fourth. In fifth place follow the sides of the **Pentagon** and its star, as well as the sides of the **Octagon** and its star; for they are from the fourth species of compounds, called **Greater** and **Lesser** <note>original Greek: Mizon & Elaßon</note>.

Lest any good quality in the Decagon should prejudice the Pentagon, or lest the same type of side in the Octagon should equate that figure to the Pentagon or Decagon: a new virtue comes to the Pentagon in its very origin. Through this division, which communicates with the number ten, the **Divine Proportion** <note>the Golden Ratio</note> reigns everywhere; this proportion is immediately present in the sides of the Pentagon and its star. Yet it does not belong to the Decagon and its star except by the mediation of the side of the Hexagon; and to the Octagon, it clearly does not apply at all.

Besides these properties of the sides, there is another assessment of nobility: figures are distinguished by the fitness and perfection of the **area** which the figure encloses. Here, after the diameter (which has no area, and which alone cuts the area of the circle into two equal parts, as Ptolemy reminds us, no less than it cuts the circumference), the chief place is held by the **Square** and the **Dodecagon**, as they have an "expressible" area. The Square indeed has an exceptional prerogative, because its area is the same as the square of its side—for its very species of area is square; thus it encloses half of the square of the diameter. The Dodecagon stands after the leaders, enclosing three-quarters <note>original: dodrantem</note> of the square of the diameter. In the next place follow the **Triangle**, **Hexagon**, and **Octagon**, whose area is of the **Medial** <note>original Greek: Mesôn</note> species. The areas of the **Pentagon** and **Decagon** have as yet no conceptual names.

### Preface.

I have thus far explained the Mental or <term>intellectual</term> <note>original Greek: νοερὰν (noeran), meaning pertaining to the mind or intellect</note> essence of individual Regular Figures: what follows is the property of them joined together, and as it were their *Effect* within *Geometry*, which is *Congruence* or *Incompatibility*. For *Provability* <note>The ability to construct a shape with a compass and straightedge</note> and *Congruence* are not of the same extent; since the former belongs to individual shapes and runs out to infinity with the continuous doubling of the sides of a single figure, while the latter is restricted by certain laws by which several figures are called into one society, and, hindering itself due to the increase of angles, it quickly comes to an end. 

And although there is a selection of degrees of knowledge and demonstration, and those shapes which we have explained differ greatly in nobility from those we have dismissed without a name <note>Kepler previously categorized "noble" shapes as those that are "knowable" or geometrically constructible</note>: nevertheless, *Congruence* does not walk plainly at an equal pace even with this nobility of demonstration; and so one is not the cause of the other, but both depend on the same common cause (which is the suitability of the angles of the figure), yet each according to its own laws. 

Indeed, how necessary this part of our speculation is for us can be seen from the very purpose of the whole work. For since we have undertaken to explain the origin of *Harmonics*, and its most excellent *Effects* in the whole World, how could we say nothing about the congruence of figures, which are the headwaters of *Harmonic* proportions? Especially since what the Latins call *to fit together* <note>original: Congruere</note> and *Fittingness* <note>original: Congruentia</note> sounds the same as what the Greeks call <term>to harmonize</term> <note>original Greek: ἁρμόττειν (harmottein)</note> and <term>harmony</term> <note>original Greek: ἁρμονία (harmonia)</note>? 

Since this effect of figures within *Geometry*, and within that part of *Architecture* which deals with *Archetypes* <note>The original divine blueprints of the universe</note>, is a certain image and prelude of *Effects* outside of *Geometry*, and outside the concepts of the mind, in natural and celestial things themselves? Since this property of congruence, which results in some structure and bodily form, is such that it even invites the speculating Mind to make, create, and embody something externally: so that, lying hidden from eternity in the most blessed divine mind, through the orders of Ideas—like the highest good, which communicates itself—it could not be contained in its own abstraction

...unless it should break forth into the work of Creation, and make God the Creator of bodies enclosed under these same figures. I will therefore deal briefly with this <term>Congruence</term> <note>The way geometric shapes fit together perfectly to fill a space or form a solid</note> of figures; since the demonstrations are by no means difficult, nor do they require almost any other apparatus than the very drawing of the figures themselves.

# On the Congruence of Regular Figures.

### I. DEFINITION.

Congruence is of one kind in a plane, and of another in a solid. In a **Plane**, **Congruence** occurs when the individual angles of several figures meet at a single point in such a way that no gap is left.

### II. DEFINITION.

This is called **perfect** when all the angles of every meeting figure meet in the same way, so that all the points of meeting are similar to one another, and the order of these meetings can be continued to infinity.

### III. DEFINITION.

It is **most perfect** when the meeting figures in the plane are also of the same <term>species</term> <note>In this context, "species" refers to the specific type of regular polygon, such as all squares or all equilateral triangles</note>.

### IV. DEFINITION.

It is **imperfect** when a larger figure is surrounded on all sides by similar meetings, yet a continuation to infinity is not possible; or if it is possible, it is not without a mixture of different types of meetings. A lower degree of imperfect congruence occurs when a larger figure is not suited to meet with a similar type at all its angles.

### V. DEFINITION.

**Solid congruence** exists, and creates a solid figure, when the individual angles of several plane figures constitute a **solid angle**; and once the regular or semi-regular figures are fitted together, no gap remains between the sides of the figures—which meet each other on the opposite part of the solid figure—that cannot be closed by a figure of one of the types already used, or at least by Regular figures. 

*Note that there is another kind of congruence: not of plane figures to form a solid figure, but of the solid figures themselves among one another, to fill a solid space around a single point. Of this kind of "corporeal" figure, there are only two.* <note>Kepler is likely referring to the cube and the rhombic dodecahedron, which are the only shapes that can fill three-dimensional space perfectly without gaps.</note>

<summary>Kepler defines the geometric concept of 'congruence'—how shapes fit together to fill space—distinguishing between plane and solid arrangements. These definitions establish the mathematical rules for what he considers "perfect" versus "imperfect" harmonies in the physical structure of the universe.</summary>

CONGRUENCE, BOOK II.

...two: the Cube and the Rhombic Dodecahedron <note>A 12-sided solid where each face is a rhombus; Kepler was one of the first to describe its role in space-filling</note>. For the eight angles of a Cube meet at one point and fill one space everywhere. But the Rhombus has two kinds of angles: eight obtuse <term>trilinear</term> <note>Formed by three lines or edges meeting at a point</note> ones, and six acute <term>quadrilinear</term> <note>Formed by four lines or edges meeting at a point</note> ones. Therefore, four obtuse angles fit together to fill the space, or six acute ones; just as bees build their structure with touching cells, so that three from the opposite base surround one at its bottom, and six at the sides; and three others could even surround it at the front to complete the figure, if it were not necessary for the doors to be open. But we are not dealing here with this congruence of solid figures.

<margin>The geometry of bees in hexagonal cells with rhombic bases.</margin>

### VI. DEFINITION.

The **most perfect** solid congruence and solid figure is when all the faces of the congruence are also of the same figure.

### VII. DEFINITION.

This is either **entirely regular**, when the faces are regular polygons; it has all its angles on the same spherical surface and they are similar to one another.

### VIII. DEFINITION.

Or it is **semiregular**, when the faces are semiregular (see Book I, Def. III); it has solid angles distinguished and dissimilar in the number of lines; yet of no more than two types; nor arranged in more than two spherical surfaces described from a single center; and it has as many angles of each type as one of the Regular figures possesses.

> *It does not stand in the way that this solid congruence is called "most perfect"; for whatever imperfection exists in its faces should not be ascribed to the solid formation itself, but occurs by accident to it. Yet this semiregular one is called "most perfect" in an <term>equivocal</term> <note>Using a term in a way that allows for multiple interpretations; here, meaning it's "perfect" as a solid even if its faces are not identical</note> sense.*

### IX. DEFINITION.

A **perfect** congruence of a **lower degree** is when the faces are regular, and all angles are on the same spherical surface and similar to one another; but the faces are nevertheless of different species, specifically as many of each as there are in one of the most perfect figures—that is, not fewer than four, which is the minimum number of faces by which a solid figure is bounded.

### X. DEFINITION.

An **imperfect** congruence or figure is when, with the other conditions remaining, the larger figure is found no more than once or twice.

<margin>A. B. on page 53 and following.</margin>
> *For in that case, the figure becomes more similar to a part than the whole, and here more similar to a plane than a solid; since every solid is bounded by at least four surfaces. As in the copperplate prints following at letters A and B, where the larger figure is a Heptagon <note>A seven-sided polygon</note>. These two classes, along with the number of sides of their larger figure, extend into infinity; starting from the triangle on both sides, which in class A is among the most perfect regular congruences; but having made a transition through the square; and then in class B, we fall again into one most perfect regular congruence; all others are imperfect.*
