<meta>This page begins Chapter 1 of Book III. On the previous page, Kepler established that the causes of musical harmony must be sought in geometry and the "knowable" proportions of the Mind, rather than in abstract numbers alone. He now moves into defining his technical terms to build his geometric theory of music.</meta>

<header>ON PROPORTIONS</header>

## CHAPTER I.
### On the causes of consonances.

->DEFINITION.<-

Since the ancients used these terms: *Single-sounding* <note>original: Μονόφωνον (*Monophonon*)</note>, *Counter-sounding* <note>original: Αντίφωνον (*Antiphonon*)</note>, *Same-sounding* <note>original: Ομόφωνον (*Homophonon*)</note>, *Dissonant* <note>original: Διάφωνον (*Diaphonon*)</note>, *Consonant* <note>original: Σύμφωνον (*Symphonon*)</note>, and *Inharmonious* <note>original: Ασύμφωνον (*Asymphonon*)</note>; for us, **Dissonant** shall mean the same as *Inharmonious*, and **Consonant** the same as *Consonant* <note>Kepler is equating the Latin *consonum* with the Greek *symphonon*.</note>. Of the latter, there are different types: **Identical**, which we shall use in place of *Same-sounding*; and **Non-Identical**, which we use for *Dissonant* <note>original: Διάφωνῳ (*Diaphono*). In this context, Kepler uses "Diaphonon" not as a harsh discord, but as a "differing" but still consonant sound.</note>. Of the Identical, there are two species: the unison, and the "identical from the opposite" <note>This refers to the Octave, which sounds so similar to the starting note that it is considered "identical" even though the pitch is higher.</note>.

->DEFINITION.<-

In Geometry, the words **Part** <note>original: *Pars*</note> and **Parts** <note>original: *Partes*</note> differ. A "Part" is said to be that by which the Whole is a **multiple** <term>multiple proportion: a relationship where the larger quantity contains the smaller one exactly a certain number of times (e.g., 2:1, 3:1).</term> according to a certain proportion, such as double, triple, or quadruple. However, "Parts" is used when not just one Whole, but some multitude of Wholes would be a multiple of them. For example, one-seventh is called a *Part*, because the whole circle is seven times this part; but three-sevenths are called not a *Part* but *Parts*, because the sum of three circles is seven times this arc.

Here, however, we shall not use this distinction. We shall call a **Part** both the one and the other of these portions; that is, every portion whose length is **knowable** <term>knowable: original *effabilis*. In Kepler's geometry, this describes a line or arc that can be expressed or constructed in relation to the whole using a compass and straightedge.</term> shall be called a "Part" by us; yet with this restriction: that it must not be greater than a semicircle.

*The **Remainder** <note>original: *Residuum*</note> shall be called that which remains from the Whole once the knowable portion is taken away, being itself not less than a semicircle.*

*The distinction between the Remainder and the Part is very necessary, because a Part can be consonant while its Remainder is dissonant, as we shall see.*

->DEFINITION.<-

**String** <note>original: *Chorda*</note> is taken here not to mean a line spanning an arc of a circle as it does in Geometry, but for any length that is suited for producing a sound. And because sound is drawn out through motion, in the abstract, a "string" is to be understood as the length of any motion whatever, or any other length, even one conceived only in the mind.

<meta>This page continues the introduction to Book III, moving from definitions of musical terms to the foundational geometric axioms that Kepler believes govern why certain sounds are harmonious (consonant) while others are not. He bridges the geometry of Book I and II with the musical theory of Book III.</meta>

<header>ON HARMONICS, BOOK III</header>

## AXIOM I.

The diameter of the circle, and the sides of the foundational figures <note>original: *figurarum Radicalium*. Kepler refers to the basic polygons like the triangle, square, and pentagon discussed in Book I.</note> explained in Book I, which possess their own geometric proof <note>original: *demonstrationem*. In this context, it refers to the ability to construct the figure using only a compass and a straightedge.</note>, determine a part of the circle that is consonant with the whole circle.

*How a circle might be stretched so as to produce a sound, and how it must be attached to a hollow body so that resonance exists—whether from a single point so that the whole sounds, or from two points so that the parts sound—would be a lengthy matter to explain here. Nevertheless, it was necessary to begin in this way, because we are not only dealing with song, which is harmony made concrete in sounds, but we must also understand the interval as an abstraction from sounds. As far as song is concerned, it is sufficient that a string stretched in a straight line can be divided in the same way as it would be if it were bent into a circle, by the side of an inscribable figure.*

## Corollary.

Consonances are infinite, because the number of figures capable of geometric proof is infinite. However, it is not yet time to speak of the selection of concords, which will not appear for some time. Here the Pythagoreans, using their numbers as causes, sought limits for the magnitude of consonant intervals; however, it is the human hearing alone that fixes these limits, for it is not of infinite power. Therefore, that restriction of the number of concords is only accidental to the abstract harmonic intervals, not truly causal. Even modern musicians go beyond the Pythagorean limits; *not to mention for now the celestial harmonies.* <note>Kepler is foreshadowing his later work on the "Music of the Spheres."</note>

## AXIOM II.

By whatever degree the geometric proof of a side is distant from the first <note>i.e., the most basic proof, like that of the diameter or the square.</note>; by that same degree the consonance of the part of the circle cut off by that side, in relation to the whole circle, recedes from the most perfect consonance of the unison. Or: whatever the rank of the figure to which the side belongs among the other figures, that same rank belongs to that consonance among the others.

*This axiom will be employed below for making the selection of concords based on their sweetness.*

## AXIOM III.

The sides of the Regular Figures and Star-polygons that are incapable of geometric proof <note>original: *indemonstrabilia*</note> determine a part of the circle that is dissonant from the whole circle. This is also true for the side of a figure that is indeed capable of proof, but not through its own merits nor its own specific proof. Alternatively, for the lack of its own proof, one may cite from Book II the lack of congruency <term>congruency: the ability of a shape to tile a surface perfectly without gaps.</term>: in both ways, the **Quindecagon** <note>a 15-sided figure</note> is excluded.

# AXIOM IV.

->Figures that have related proofs of their<-
->sides also produce related Harmonies.<-

*Through this axiom, the origin and cause of Harmonic Proportions from the remainder <note>original: *ex superfluo*. This refers to the part of the circle or string left over after a "knowable" part has been removed.</note> will be proved.*

# AXIOM V.

Strings or arcs of a circle, under equal tension, having between them—on account of their length—the same proportion that exists between a Part or Remainder of a circle and the Whole circle, also possess the same Consonance or dissonance, even if that relationship is contained between other terms or sounds.

*In an abstract sense, let it be understood thus: that the circle, together with its part, constitutes certain Harmonic proportions; wherever these are found in other terms—whether sounds, or even silent motions <note>A reference to the "Music of the Spheres," where the "sounds" are the mathematical ratios of planetary speeds.</note>—they are always harmonic.*

*This Axiom is added, however, because not all Harmonic Proportions arise immediately from the circle itself through its first division by a Regular figure, but some others are added, propagated from those prior to them, up to a certain Limit <note>original: *Metam*. In Kepler's system, there is a limit to how complex a harmony can be before the human ear can no longer perceive it as pleasing.</note>: as we shall see in the propositions.*

*The use of this Axiom is in Propositions VII and VIII.*

...third, if it is consonant with one of them, it will also be consonant with the other; if it is dissonant from one, it will also be dissonant from the other, regardless of any different consonances or dissonances involved.

*Note that the species "Identical-sounding" <note>original: *Identisoni*. This refers to notes that sound so similar they are almost the same, specifically the octave.</note> is placed in the Subject, and the Genus "Consonant" is in the Predicate: so that we may understand two things. First, it does not follow that if two notes are consonant in any way whatever, then a third note must be consonant to both or dissonant from both. This is false regarding the general category of "Consonants," but true regarding the specific category of "Identical-sounding" notes. Second, it does not follow that if a third note is consonant with one Identical-sounding note in a certain specific harmony, it will be consonant with the other in that same specific harmony. This is not always true, as I shall demonstrate by example, albeit prematurely: Let there be two voices making an octave <note>original: *diapason*</note> between G and g. Let the third voice be d. That third voice makes a fifth <note>original: *diapente*</note> with G; therefore, it also harmonizes with g, but not through a fifth, but through a fourth <note>original: *diatessaron*</note>.*

*The primary use of this axiom is in Proposition IV.*

## AXIOM VII.

**When two strings or voices produce Identical sounds, a third voice that is Identical-sounding with one of them will also be identically consonant with the other.**

*What could not be affirmed generally in the previous axiom is now true specifically regarding Identical-sounding harmony.*

<margin>The Metaphysical Cause of Harmonies.</margin>
Concerning these Axioms, then, especially the first five, the speculation is sublime, Platonic, and analogous to the Christian Faith, looking toward Metaphysics and the doctrine of the Soul. For Geometry—the part of which relevant here was contained in the first two books—is co-eternal with God and, shining forth in the divine Mind, supplied God with the patterns (as was said in the preamble of this book) for decorating the World, so that it might become the Best and Most Beautiful, and finally, most like the Creator. Indeed, all Spirits, Souls, and Minds are images of God the Creator, each set over their own bodies to govern, move, increase, preserve, and even propagate them.

Since, therefore, they have embraced a certain pattern of Creation in their own duties, they also observe the same laws of work as the Creator, laws drawn from geometry. They rejoice in those same proportions which God used, wherever they find them: whether by pure speculation, or by the intervention of the senses in things subject to the senses; or even without a discourse of the Mind, through a hidden and innate instinct. This is true whether God himself expressed these proportions invariably in bodies and motions, or whether, by a certain Geometric necessity of matter being infinitely divisible, these harmonies happened to occur among infinite non-harmonic proportions in their own time through the quantity of matter and motion. Thus, they consist not in BEING but in BECOMING. <note>original: *non in ESSE sed in FIERI*. Kepler distinguishes between eternal truths and things that happen through physical movement.</note> Nor do Minds only rejoice,

# ON PROPORTIONS

...images of God, by these proportions: but they also use them as laws for carrying out their duties and for expressing those same proportions in the movements of their bodies, insofar as it is possible. The following books will present two brilliant examples: one of the Creator God himself, who distributed the motions of the heavens <note>original: *motus cœlorum*</note> according to harmonic proportions; the other of that Soul which we are accustomed to call "Sublunary Nature," <term>Sublunary Nature: the vital force Kepler believed governed the Earth’s atmosphere and weather.</term> which stirs up meteors <note>original: *Meteora*. In the 17th century, this referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including wind, rain, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note> according to the prescription of the proportions that occur in the radiations of the stars. Let the third example, therefore, and the one proper to this book, be that of the human soul, and even to some extent that of the beasts. For they, having perceived the harmonic proportions of voices, rejoice; they are saddened by those that are not harmonic. From these affections of the Soul, the former are called Consonances, and the latter Dissonances. If another harmonic proportion—that of long and short voices and sounds—is added for the sake of time, then they move their bodies in dances and their tongues in speech according to those same laws. To this, the craftsmen coordinate the blows of their hammers; to this, soldiers coordinate their step. All things live while the Harmonies last, but grow numb when they are disturbed.

Whether these and similar things are a matter of Deliberation or Instinct—that is, the work of the Mind—or whether it happens by the Nature of the Elements and the necessity of Matter, such that no temperament can be pleasant to the senses unless it consists of the harmonic proportions of figures; this has been variously debated by philosophers. All of them seek the source of that sweetness which flows into the ears from the proportion of voices, by which sweetness we define Consonances. Those who lean toward the Matter and Motion of the Elements cite this example, which is truly wonderful in itself, that 

<margin>
A wonderful 
experiment 
in strings.
</margin>

a plucked string <note>original: *Chorda pulsata*</note> draws another unplucked string into sound with it, if it has been stretched in consonance with itself; but if stretched dissonantly, it leaves the other unmoved. Since this cannot happen through the ministry of any Mind (because the sound, which caused this, has no Mind or intellect), it follows that we must say it happens through the contemplation of movements. For the sound of a string has highness or lowness <note>pitch</note> from the speed or slowness of the vibration <note>original: *vibrationis*</note> by which the entire free length of the string vibrates. These differences of sounds are not present primarily and immediately in the length or shortness itself, but secondarily; because, naturally, as the length is diminished, the slowness of vibration is diminished, and the speed is increased. This is why, while the free length of the string remains the same, the tension itself raises the pitch of the sound, because by leaving the string less slack, it also diminishes the space through which it can vibrate in reciprocal motion.

Therefore, when the tension of two strings is the same, so that they can produce a unison, then the sound of one—that is, the immaterial species <term>species immateriata: a "form" or "image" of the physical vibration that travels through the air without carrying the matter of the string itself.</term> of the body of the string set in vibration—having glided from its own string, strikes the other string. It is just as if someone were to make a shout toward a lute <note>original: *Chelyn*</note> or another hollow space; by that shout, he strikes that hollow space and makes all its strings resonate. Moreover, that "species" of vibration strikes the second string with the same rhythm of speed with which it also moves, because it is equally stretched; so that the individual strikes (into which the vibration is understood to be divided) in individual perfections...

### ON HARMONICS, BOOK III.
<meta>catchword: of the ancients</meta>

...the strokes of a **struck** string perpetually fall into the tiny pauses <note>original: *cessiunculas*</note> of the other; thus it happens that the string which is stretched to a **unison** with the first is moved most of all. However, that string which is of **double** or **half** the speed <note>The octave (2:1 ratio).</note> is also moved, because two strokes of vibration are completed within one pause of the string, and thus every third stroke from the first string consistently coincides with the end of the other's pause. Finally, even that string which is of **one-and-a-half** speed <note>The musical fifth (3:2 ratio).</note> is moved somewhat, because three tiny strokes occur within two of its pauses. But at this point, those strokes and these pauses begin to encounter one another too frequently and impede each other; while two of its strokes stray from the end of this pause, only one coincides correctly. By this encounter, the motion of the other strings is halted, just as if someone had placed a finger upon a vibrating string. This seems to me the cause of this wonderful experiment; to whoever is more fortunate than I in the investigation of the mind, I shall grant the palm of victory.

<margin>What is the cause of pleasure from harmonies?</margin>
What then? If the speed of one string is enough to move another proportioned string—which, to the sight, remains untouched—will not these same relative speeds of two strings be enough to cause a sweet tickling of the hearing? Is it perhaps because the hearing is moved in a somewhat uniform way by both strings, and two strokes from two sounds or vibrations happen at the same moment? Not at all, I say; the matter is not settled so easily. I marvel that such an explanation for the cause of this thing could satisfy **Porphyry**, the commentator on **Ptolemy’s** *Harmonics*, since he is a philosopher of the profoundest investigation. Unless, as is likely, he was restrained by the difficulty of searching for the cause, preventing him from penetrating as far as he wished; and he thought it better to put something forward than to remain entirely silent, which they say is a disgrace for a Philosopher. For what, I ask, is the proportion of a "tickling of the hearing"—a physical thing—to that incredible pleasure which we perceive most deeply within the soul from harmonic **Consonances**?

Does not the primary place of pleasure belong to the limb that sustains the tickling, if there is any pleasure from such a thing? For I saw fit to define every sense in my 
<margin>What is sense?</margin>
*Dioptrics* <note>Kepler's 1611 work on optics and the physiology of vision.</note> in this way: that it is only an absolute sensation, producing pleasure or pain, when the "species" <note>In 17th-century science, "species" referred to the sensory image or information traveling from the organ to the brain.</note> of the limb destined for sensation (as it is affected by an external thing) comes inward to the tribunal of the **common sense** <note>original: *sensus communis*; the faculty that integrates all five senses.</note> by the passage of the spirits. Now, in the hearing of consonant voices or sounds, what parts of the pleasure actually remain in the ears? Do we not sometimes suffer pain in our ears while we are intent on this listening, even shielding them from excessive clanging? Yet we nevertheless continue to perceive the consonances, and our hearts leap within us. Add to this that this reasoning based on motion is strongest in a **unison**; yet the greatest sweetness is not found in a unison, but in the other Consonances and their composition.

<margin>The cause of the sweetness of Harmonies must be sought from the approval of the Mind.</margin>
Many arguments could be brought forward to destroy this cited reasoning of sweetness from Consonances, which for now I refrain from writing down too meticulously. I emphasize this one point, which I have already touched upon above, which can stand in place of all: that the works and movements of bodies, which emulate harmonic proportions, stand on the side of the parts of the **Soul** and **Mind**, assigning to them the cause of why Consonances delight. Nor does the authority of the **ancients** <note>original: *veterum*</note> shrink from this...

# ON PROPORTIONS

...of the ancients; who, defining the Soul now as **Motion**, now as **Harmony**, did not speak so much absurdly as they were poorly understood. Indeed, in difficult matters, **mystical senses** usually lie hidden, concealed beneath the husks of words. The philosophy of **Timaeus of Locri** <note>A Pythagorean philosopher and character in Plato’s dialogues.</note> concerning how the soul is composed of harmonic proportions (which I mentioned in the introduction) was refuted by **Aristotle** according to the literal meaning of the words. Yet, I would not dare to assert that nothing else lies hidden in those pages beyond the literal sound of the words. On the contrary, I think no one would deny that this author holds at least this much, which I here maintain: that it is the **Mind** and the **human Soul** by whose judgment or instinct the sense of hearing distinguishes pleasant (that is, consonant) proportions from unpleasant and dissonant ones. For one who considers this carefully will see that **Proportions** are **Beings of Reason** <note>original: *Rationis Entia*; abstract concepts that exist in the intellect rather than as physical objects</note>, perceptible by reason alone, not by sense, and that it is the work of the Mind to distinguish the proportion (as the **form**) from the thing proportioned (as the **matter**).

<margin>
From the
scientific
demonstration
of figures.
</margin>
Now, since we have explained two properties of **Regular Figures**—the scientific demonstration of the sides in each, and the **Congruence** <note>The ability of shapes to fit together perfectly without gaps, like floor tiles.</note> between them when joined together—they are not both of the same breadth. Regarding the **Demonstration**, our axioms speak most clearly, because this is more familiar to the proportions of motions, from which sounds also arise.

For **Congruence** belongs to figures as they are whole; but **motions** (to which harmonic proportions happen) extend the sides of the figure from which they are derived into a straight line (since almost all are considered as rectilinear). In doing so, they slay and destroy their figure, **as snakes destroy their Mother** <note>original: *ut serpentes Matrem*; referring to the ancient belief that baby vipers ate their way out of their mother’s womb.</note>. A figure, insofar as it is congruent, divides a whole circle into parts; harmonic proportions extend that divided circle into a straight line, erasing the act of division made by the figure. Thus, consonances associated with demonstrable figures run on into infinity; but **Congruent Figures** are limited to the number twelve. Finally, any figure makes only a single division of the circle; yet the parts established in the circle always create two **Consonances** with the Whole.

<margin>
And
congruence.
</margin>
Even though in this third book the account of the **scientific demonstration** of the sides will be more important than the **Congruence** of the whole figures, the latter should not be neglected because of its great kinship to the subject. First, the Latin meaning of the word *Congruentia* (Congruence), if you examine everything, sounds the same as the Greek word *Harmonia* (Harmony), which we shall treat in this book—except that usage has distinguished these words slightly based on their subjects. Secondly, the congruence of figures bestows a certain **Congruence** upon the motions (which we discuss in this and the fifth book). Thirdly, although we do not look at the whole figure so much as at one of its sides and the part it cuts off (which is consonant), it is simultaneously true that we do not consider merely how large a part of the circle is intercepted, but rather by **what kind of figure** it was made—whether demonstrable and congruent, or the opposite. For every figure, from its angles (by which it obtained **Congruence** in Book II), has also attained **Demonstration** in Book I. Therefore, the consideration of the **Congruence** of figures must not be removed from the study of Harmonies.

## PROPOSITION I.

->**The Consonance of the Half with the Whole <note>This refers to the Octave interval, where one string is exactly half the length of another.</note>, after the unison, is the only one in the first rank that is simple, perfect, and "Identical"—specifically, arising from Opposite points.**<-

For whatever possesses a "figure" <note>In this context, a geometric shape like a triangle or square.</note> is composed of diverse parts; therefore, it is neither simple nor "Identical" <note>original: *Identica*; Kepler uses this to describe the Octave because the two notes sound so similar they almost share an identity.</note>. A figure has an area, parts defined by that area, and angles located in different positions. However, that which is not "figured"—where the area lacks width and consists of a single, mere straight line equal to the proposed Measure—is, for these very reasons, both simple and the "same" as the Measure; that is, it is identical. Of the first kind are the Regular Figures inscribed in a circle; of the second kind is the **Diameter** of the circle.

1. In figures, all sides turn away equally from the center; the Diameter is drawn through the center itself.
2. A measure that divides the circle from one point using the side of a figure must proceed several times to return to the first point; the Diameter, however, passing through the center, returns to the starting point in the very first repetition <note>That is, going across and coming back completes the journey.</note>.
3. Other figures have both a length of sides and a surface area which they surround; the diameter surrounds or includes no part of the plane, and in its repeated iterations, it coincides with itself on the second pass.
4. Other figures dividing the circle create many parts; the Diameter creates the smallest number of all: only two. Indeed, to divide a whole, one could not possibly make fewer than two parts.
5. Since the Diameter is the measure to which the sides of figures must be compared for the sake of understanding and demonstration, the sides of other figures are described with much more labor and are brought into the state of scientific knowledge through a less perfect degree of demonstration. But the diameter of a circle is described by the simplest law: a path through the center from one point of the circle to the opposite; it equals itself and is the Measure of itself.
6. Furthermore, the sides of figures, in the division of a single circle (or the cutting away of a Part), create unequal portions, making the Part smaller than the Remainder. The diameter leaves the Part cut away equal to the Remainder. This proportion of equality is pure, simple, and perfect; because parts that are equal to each other are "the Same" for the purpose of measurement.
7. Finally, other figures may divide the circumference of the circle into several equal parts, but they divide the *area* of the circle into unequal parts, because one part—the area of the figure itself—is left in the middle, larger than any of the segments. The diameter divides not only the circumference but also the area into two equal halves simultaneously.

But according to **Axiom II**, the character of the side or line which divides the circle harmoniously passes into the consonance itself. Therefore, the Consonance of the Part which the diameter cuts from the circle (that is, the semicircle) with the whole circle is simple, perfect, and identical. And by **Axiom V**, all other lengths that are to each other as the whole circle is to its half create the same identical, perfect, and simple consonance. In numbers (not strictly abstract counting numbers, but lengths that have been numbered), the **Double Proportion** <note>original: *Proportio dupla*; the ratio of 2:1.</note>—between 1 and 2, as well as between their multiples—produces this Identical Consonance.

Note here that although the diameter, through all its simplicities and perfections, is still not as simple as a point; it remains a line, [stretched] between two [points of the] circ-

Hence this is called **Identical Consonance from the Opposite**.

You have, therefore, the genuine cause from the diameter of the circle why the sound of the whole string compared to the sound of half the string <note>the 2:1 ratio</note>—though they are different from each other—is nonetheless regarded by the hearing as somehow the same, compared to other harmonies.

In vain do others seek the cause of this **Identity of Sound** <note>original: *Identisonantiæ*</note> from the number of eight voices, since this Identity of Sound is prior by nature to the division of this interval into the seven fitting <note>original: *Concinnas*; notes that sound pleasing together</note> intervals by which the eight sounds are designated.

However, it is not yet time to give names to this consonance, nor to the others; for this must be deferred to Chapter V.

Note also this: that other parts also consonant identically, which are not constituted through the diameter; but not in the first degree, nor as if by primary shapes, but as if by propagation, which the following propositions address.

## PROPOSITION II.

**If the ratio of the smaller of two parts of a circle to the larger is the same as the ratio of the larger to the whole circle, in any continuous proportion other than the double <note>The "double proportion" is 1:2:4, etc. Kepler is testing other geometric progressions like 1:3:9 or 1:5:25 to see if they create harmony.</note>: then while the larger part is consonant with the whole circle, the smaller part will be dissonant from the whole.**

For after the double is the triple; indeed, a continuous triple proportion establishes in the third place a *ninth* part of the whole circle; the quintuple establishes a *twenty-fifth*; the sextuple implies the *ninth*, the decuple the *twenty-fifth*, because 6 times 6 is 36, which is four times nine, and 10 times 10 is 100, which is four times 25. And so also for the others. Yet the *ninth*, the *25th*, and similar parts are dissonant from the whole, by Axiom III. See Book I, Proposition *XLVII*.

## PROPOSITION III.

**Strings in a continuous double proportion are all identically consonant with each other, though the more distant they are, the more remote the degree of harmony.**

For three neighboring strings have the same relationship to each other as the whole circle, the half, and the quarter part have to each other. But since both the half and the quarter consonant with the whole circle (by Axiom I), and the quarter also consonants with the half (by Axiom V), therefore all three neighbors consonant with each other. Indeed, the consonance of the fourth part with the whole circle is also "Identical," because the Whole and its half consonant identically (by Prop. I). So also the fourth part with the half, by the same rule; wherefore by Axiom VII, even the **fourth** part consonants identically with the **Whole** circle; and by Axiom V, any quadruple consonants with the single.

Now truly, whatever the ratio is of the first, second, and third proportionals, the same

<summary>Kepler explains that the Octave's "identity of sound" arises from the diameter of a circle, rejecting the idea that it stems from the number of notes in a scale. He further proves that only the "double proportion" (1:2:4:8) maintains this identity across multiple intervals, while other proportions lead to dissonance.</summary>

the second, third, and fourth will also be [proportional]; and so on continuously for any three neighboring proportions. Therefore, all strings proportional in a **continuous double proportion** <note>ratios like 2:1, 4:1, 8:1, 16:1, which represent successive octaves</note> are identically consonant with one another.

Note, therefore, in such cases, the distinction between **Consonance** in general and **Identity of Sound** <note>original: *Identisonantia*; Kepler's term for the octave relationship where two notes sound like the same "type" of note</note> in particular. Parts like the Fourth, Eighth, Sixteenth, and similar ones consonant because of Axiom I and the geometric figures—the **Square**, the **Octagon**, etc. However, they consonant *identically* because of the way this class of figures is propagated from the **bisection of the circle** <note>the process of repeatedly cutting the circle in half</note>. If they had existed without this propagation, their consonances would not have been identical. For all other figures produce either many equal parts of the circle, or unequal ones (if there are only two); they encompass an area, yet they do not divide the circle’s area into equal halves, nor do their sides pass through the center, nor do they return upon themselves, nor are they equal to the diameter. Consonances arising from the **Square-based group** <note>original: *Tetragonica secta*; the family of shapes created by doubling the sides of a square</note> would have, in a sense, expanded themselves in the hearing and stretched the mind with a manifest variety and diversity of voices—just as consonances do that arise from other figures whose number of sides is not **even-even** <note>original: *pariter pari*; a number like 4, 8, or 16 that can be divided by 2 repeatedly until reaching 1</note>, according to Proposition I.

Nevertheless, this group of figures has not lost all power to vary consonances and to turn them away from the purity of Identity (just as the figures themselves have moved away from the simplicity of the Diameter). First, although the Consonance of the part of the circle cut off by the figure is transformed into mere Identity (because of the aforementioned propagation of parts from the first bisection), the **degrees of Identity** become more remote. For a smaller part, sounding identically from the opposite side with its nearest larger neighbor, becomes higher in pitch as the turns of opposition are multiplied; thus the intervals between voices are always increased. Second, Identity remains in the **Part** (as in the section through the diameter), but by no means in the **Remainder** <note>original: *Residuo*; the portion of the string or circle left over after the harmonic part is removed</note>. For this Remainder in subsequent figures is always "worse" than itself regarding its **Harmonic Nature** <note>meaning it becomes less consonant or more complex</note>. But specific Propositions regarding such Remainders follow.

And conversely, it is not only the Square-based group that produces identical consonances; other groups also do so, insofar as they participate in bisection. For the part of the circle cut off by a later figure always consonants identically with the part cut off by an earlier side, as the remaining propositions show. Thus the **Analogy** <note>the fundamental correspondence between geometry and music</note> holds firm in all its members.

<margin>The use of this Proposition is in the following.</margin>

## PROPOSITION IV.

->A string that is consonant with either member of a continuous<-
->double proportion is also consonant with the rest; and if it<-
->dissonates with one, it also dissonates with the other.<-

For according to Proposition III, the sounds of continuous doubles are identical to each other. That which consonants with one of the identical strings also consonants with the other, and so forth, according to Axiom VI.

Axiom VI was established for the sake of this proposition, and this proposition now serves to examine the Parts and Remainders of circles. Let the **sciolists** <note>original: *scioli*; people with superficial or "smattering" knowledge</note> beware of seeing a contradiction between the Propositions and Axioms: for there is no tautology here; anyone who wishes to settle the matter more briefly will find that all necessary truths involve themselves in one another.

<sig>C 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: PRO</meta>

<summary>Kepler explains why octaves (ratios of 2:1, 4:1, etc.) sound "identical" to the ear, attributing this to the geometric process of repeatedly bisecting a circle. He distinguishes this "Identity of Sound" from other types of harmony and introduces Proposition IV, which states that any note consonant with one octave of a sound is consonant with all its other octaves.</summary>

<header>ON PROPORTIONS</header>

## PROPOSITION V.

Even if the sides of **Star Polygons** are otherwise demonstrable <note>In geometry, "demonstrable" means a shape can be constructed using only a compass and an unmarked straightedge.</note>, they determine consonant parts in a Circle by the same right that their radical figures <note>The basic polygon from which a star is derived; for example, a pentagon is the radical figure of a five-pointed star.</note> do, as stated in the first Axiom. However, an exception is made for those which cut off a part of the circle consisting of a number (of the parts made by the radical figure) that is characteristic of an indemonstrable figure; this occurs when the numbers of the Part and the Whole are **Prime** to one another <note>Numbers are "prime to each other" (coprime) if they share no common factors other than 1, such as 9 and 20.</note>.

*The first part of this proposition is an axiom; so that it would not become too general, it had to be restricted by the second part of the proposition. It is demonstrated as follows: Let there be a circle divided by a demonstrable figure, for example, a 20-sided figure (**Icosigon**). Now let there be an Icosigonic star whose side spans nine of the twenty parts made by the Icosigon; such that 9 and 20 are Prime to each other. Since the Part cut off is from the circle, it will surely be smaller than the Whole. However, it can be larger than half, a quarter, or an eighth of the whole. By continuously dividing the whole by two, eventually a part will be reached that is smaller than half of the Part we are discussing. For example, in our case where the Whole is 20 and our Part is 9: take half of the whole (10), then half of that (5), and thirdly half of that (2$\frac{1}{2}$), which is an eighth of the Whole. This is now smaller than half of 9 itself. Therefore, our part (9) relates to the eighth of the circle (2$\frac{1}{2}$) as a circle divided by an indemonstrable figure relates to one of its parts—specifically, as 18 relates to 5. The Corollary to Axiom III declared that five-eighteenths is dissonant from the whole of 18. Therefore, by Axiom V, our division's part (9) will be dissonant from the Eighth of the circle (the 2$\frac{1}{2}$ parts of our division). Consequently, by Proposition IV, our part (9) will also be dissonant from the whole circle (20), even though its spanning line is demonstrable; it is at a most remote degree, and its star is among the "incongruous" ones.* <note>Kepler is arguing that even if a shape can be drawn, its musical ratio might be dissonant if it behaves like a shape that cannot be drawn (like an 18-sided figure).</note>

## PROPOSITION VI.

The remainders of circles or chords, after consonant Parts have been cut away, are also consonant with both the part cut off and with the whole circle or chord, provided they are continuous doubles of their consonant part.

->With the part cut off through Prop. I; with the whole through Prop. IV.<-

## PROPOSITION VII.

If such a **Remainder** has the same proportion to the half or quarter part of the circle or chord as the Whole circle has to some other consonant Part of itself, it will also be consonant with the Whole circle; if it relates as it would to a dissonant portion, it will be dissonant.

*For the whole circle, its half, and its Quarter part are in a continuous double proportion <note>A sequence of doubling or halving, like 1, 2, 4, 8...</note>: therefore (through Prop. IV) those remainders which are consonant with such a Part of the circle are also consonant with the whole; and those which are dissonant from that part will also be dissonant from this whole. But those Remainders are consonant with such a Part if they have the same proportion to it as the whole...*

---

*The Whole, in relation to any consonant part: stands in dissonance from such a Part if it holds the same proportion to it as the circle does to any dissonant part; and this is by Axiom V.* <note>Axiom V likely states that proportions derived from "indemonstrable" or non-constructible figures result in musical dissonance.</note>

*Therefore, such Remainders <term>Residua</term> <note>The "Remainder" is the portion of the circle left over after a specific part is removed; for example, if you cut away 1/3 of a circle, the remainder is 2/3.</note> are consonant with the Whole circle; conversely, others are dissonant from the whole circle.*

*This proposition exists for the sake of the following Proposition VIII.*

## PROPOSITION VIII.

Indeed, if the Remainder has the same proportion to the Cut-off Part as the Whole circle has to any consonant Part, it also harmonizes with that cut-off part, just as in the previous proposition it harmonized with the Whole. But if it holds that proportion which the Whole has to some dissonant Part, it will be dissonant from both the cut-off part and the Whole.

*The first part of this argument relies on Axiom V, as does one specific detail of the latter part—namely, that the Remainder is dissonant from the Cut-off Part. But that such a Remainder is also dissonant from the Whole is proved as follows:*

*For in the stated proportion, it takes the place of a whole circle divided by an indemonstrable figure <note>In Kepler's geometry, an "indemonstrable figure" is a polygon (like a 7-sided heptagon) that cannot be perfectly constructed with a compass and straightedge; he argues these figures create musical dissonance.</note>. Therefore, even if such a Remainder is smaller than the whole circle of which it is the remainder, it is nevertheless larger than a semicircle, according to the definition of a Remainder. But if it is larger than its own semicircle, then a quarter part of its circle—being half of a semicircle—is smaller than half of this Remainder. Therefore, just as the Remainder relates to a quarter of its circle, so will some circle divided by an indemonstrable figure relate to some part of that division. But such a whole circle is dissonant from such a part by Axiom III. Therefore, the said Remainder will also be dissonant from a quarter of its circle by Axiom V. It will therefore also be dissonant from its own whole circle, by Proposition VII.*

<header>ON PROPORTIONS</header>

# CHAPTER II.

## On the Harmonic Division of a String.

Thus far, we have explained the origin of harmonic proportions. We have shown this origin to be twofold: one is immediate, arising from demonstrable figures <note>In Kepler's geometry, these are "constructible" shapes like the square or pentagon that can be drawn using only a compass and straightedge.</note> that are congruent; the other is by means of the duple proportion <note>The 2:1 ratio, which creates the Octave.</note>, upon which the identity of consonances rests. However, since harmonic proportions are infinite in number—and to our current understanding, they remain raw, unpolished, unseen, and unnamed, piled up or rather scattered like a heap of rough stones and timber—it follows that we must proceed to polish them. We must assign them names and, finally, construct from them that most beautiful edifice: the Harmonic System, or the musical scale. The structure of this scale is not arbitrary, as some might think, nor is it a human invention that could be changed at will. Rather, it is most rational and natural—so much so that God the Creator himself expressed it in his contemplation of the celestial motions. These Harmonic Proportions are joined together into a single System through "harmonic sections" of the string; how many of these sections exist is what we must investigate in this chapter.

### DEFINITION.

<margin>
The Whole
1. Major Part.
2. Minor Part.
Middle:
Extremes
</margin>

**When a whole string is divided into parts such that they sound together harmoniously (consonate) both with each other and individually with the whole: that shall be called a Harmonic Section. The "Middle" of this section, proportioned musically (that is, harmoniously), is one of the two equal parts; or if they are unequal, it is the Major part. The "Extremes" of the harmonic proportion are the remaining (or Minor) part and the Whole string.**

> *The Geometer should observe here the analogy of the "Divine Proportion" <note>original: "proportionis divinæ"; also known as the Golden Ratio.</note>, or the ratio according to Extremes and Means: in which the Whole has the same proportion to the Major part as the Major has to the Minor. For what is the "same proportion" in that Geometric section is, in our Musical section, the "same quality"—which is called Consonance, Concord, Congruence, or Harmony. Beware, however, of assuming that the specific type of consonance is always the same, just as that specific proportion is unique in geometry.*

> *The Ancients did not mention this section in this sense, because they did not know the true causes of Consonances; we shall deal with their specific method of dividing the string later.*

### PROPOSITION IX.

The sectioning of a string into two equal parts is Harmonic.

<summary>Kepler defines the "Harmonic Section" of a musical string, explaining that a string must be divided so that the parts and the whole are all mutually consonant. He compares this musical division to the geometric "Divine Proportion" (Golden Ratio) and argues that the musical scale is a divine, natural law rather than a human invention.</summary>

For because equal parts emit the same sound under any given tension, by Axiom II. However, the Whole is the double of each individual part; therefore, it consonates "identically" <note>original: "identicè." Kepler uses this term for the octave (1:2 ratio) because the two notes sound like the same pitch at different registers.</note> with each of them, by Proposition I. There are therefore three consonances; wherefore, by the definition, the String has been divided harmonically.

## PROPOSITION X.

### The division of a String into two parts in a duple proportion is Harmonic.

*For the parts of this proportion <note>The 2:1 ratio, which creates an octave.</note> consonate identically, by Proposition I. And because the major part is double the minor, the whole is therefore triple the minor. The whole is therefore to the minor part as a circle is to the part cut off by the side of a triangle <note>original: "trigonico latere." This refers to a 1/3 division of a circle, which Kepler previously linked to the musical interval of a Twelfth.</note> and is consonant, by the last corollary of the previous chapter. Wherefore the Whole itself is consonant to the minor part, by Axiom V. It also consonates with its double, that is, with the Remainder <note>The major part.</note>, by Proposition IV. Therefore, three consonances are established by this division. Therefore [it is harmonic].*

<image-desc>A musical staff diagram placed to the right of the text. It contains four diamond-shaped notes arranged in a specific pattern. Beside the staff are numbers 3, 6, 2, and 3. To the right is a vertical line with markings 1, 2, 3.</image-desc>

## PROPOSITION XI.

### The division of a String into two parts in a triple proportion to each other is Harmonic.

*For because parts 1 and 3 are to each other as a consonant part of a Circle is to the whole, they will also consonate with each other, by Axiom V. And because 1 and 3 make 4, part 1 will consonate with the whole 4 by Axiom I and by Proposition III.*

*Finally, because the Remainder [the part of] 3 consonates with part 1, it will also consonate with its quadruple [which is] 4, that is, with the whole string. Wherefore here too there are three consonances.*

<image-desc>A musical staff diagram placed to the right of the text. It contains four diamond-shaped notes. Beside the staff are numbers 4, 12, 3, and 4. To the right is a vertical line with markings 1, 2, 3, 4.</image-desc>

## PROPOSITION XII.

### The division of a string into two parts in a quadruple proportion to each other is Harmonic.

*For because the parts are in a quadruple proportion <note>A 4:1 ratio, which in music is a double-octave.</note>, they therefore consonate identically with each other, by Proposition III. And because 1 and 4 make 5, therefore part 1 consonates with the whole 5, by Axiom I and the stated Corollary. Wherefore the whole 5 also consonates with the quadruple of part 1, which is 4, by Proposition IV. Thus three consonances are created. Therefore, etc.*

<image-desc>A musical staff diagram placed to the right of the text. It contains four diamond-shaped notes. Beside the staff are numbers 5, 20, 4, and 5. To the right is a vertical line with markings 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.</image-desc>

->The division of a string into two parts in a fivefold proportion <note>A 5:1 ratio, which corresponds to a Major Third plus two octaves.</note> to each other is Harmonic.<-

Therefore, they are also consonant with each other, by Axiom V. And because part 1 together with the Remainder 5 makes the whole 6: therefore (by Axiom I and the Corollary) part 1 consonates with the whole 6 <note>The ratio 6:1 is a Fifth plus two octaves.</note>. ## PROPOSITION XIV.

->The division of a string into two parts in a sesquialterate proportion <note term="sesquialtera">A 3:2 ratio, which produces the musical interval of a Perfect Fifth.</note> to each other is Harmonic.<-

<image-desc>A marginal diagram similar to the one above, featuring a vertical line with marks for the numbers 2, 3, and 5. Circular symbols are located at the levels of 2 and 3.</image-desc>

For because part 2 with the Remainder 3 constitutes a sesquialterate proportion, the Part is to the Remainder as some consonant Remainder 2 is to the circle 3, by the Corollary; therefore this part 2 will consonate with its Remainder 3, by Axiom V. And because part 2 with the remainder 3 makes the whole 5, and indeed part 1 and its remainder 4 consonate with the whole 5 by the Corollary: the whole 5 will therefore also consonate with the double of the consonant Part 1 (which is 2)—which in this case is our Part—or with half of the consonant Remainder 4 (which is 2), by Proposition IV. The same also follows simply from the first axiomatic part of Proposition V; because the chord subtending two-fifths of a circle is demonstrable, it is therefore Consonant. Finally, because the Remainder 3 of part 2 is to a fourth part of the whole 5 as the whole circle 12 is to the consonant part 5, by the Corollary: our Remainder 3 will therefore also consonate with the whole 5, by Proposition VII. Three consonances therefore exist. Therefore.

## PROPOSITION XVI.

If a string is divided into two expressible parts <term>expressible (effabiles): lengths that can be defined by rational numbers or ratios, rather than "irrational" geometric lengths</term>, and among those parts and the whole—that is, among the three terms—there is one dissonance; then there must also be a second dissonance among them.

*For the cause of the dissonance will be that either the whole or a part has a number of portions for that division which belongs to an indemonstrable figure <note>original: "figurae indemonstrabilis"; Kepler refers to polygons that cannot be constructed with a straightedge and compass, such as the 7-sided heptagon. He argues these shapes cannot produce harmonic music</note>. However, such a number is neither harmoniously associated with any larger number that belongs to a demonstrable figure, nor with any number smaller than itself, according to Axioms III and V and Propositions V and VII. Therefore, that term, which consists of such a number of portions, is dissonant with the two remaining terms of that division; and thus, there are two dissonances at once.*

In geometry, there is a similar principle to this proposition: if a straight line is cut into expressible parts, and one of them is incommensurable <term>incommensurable: having no common unit of measurement; an irrational relationship</term> with some third line (not the Whole composed of both, as in this case), then the other part must also be incommensurable with that same third line.

Or, if a straight line is cut into parts that are incommensurable with each other, then both will be incommensurable with the Whole.

## PROPOSITION XVII.

If a string is divided into two parts of expressible length, and there are two consonances among those and the whole—that is, among the three terms—the third must also be a consonance.

*For if there are two consonances, since there are no more than three proportions [among three terms]: it is therefore impossible for there to be two dissonances. If there are not two dissonances, then there is not even one, by the converse of Proposition XVI. Therefore, all three proportions will be consonant.*

So in Geometry, if a straight line is cut into parts that are commensurable with each other, the whole will be commensurable with both parts.

## PROPOSITION XVIII.

A division of a string into two parts of expressible length, in which either the Whole or one of the Parts acquires a number of portions belonging to an indemonstrable figure (provided the numbers of the Whole and the Parts are prime to each other <note>i.e., they share no common factors other than 1</note>) is not Harmonic.

*This is demonstrated as in Proposition XVI. For out of the three proportions of the three terms, at least two become dissonant, which is contrary to the previously established Definition.*

## PROPOSITION XV.

->The division of a string into two parts in a<-

*5. relates to half of the whole 8 (which is 4) as the whole circle 5 relates to the consonant remainder 4; or it relates to the fourth part of the whole 8 (which is 2) as the whole circle 5 relates to the consonant part 2, by the Corollary: therefore our Remainder will also be consonant with the Whole 8, by Proposition VII. Therefore, here too three consonances are produced. Done.*

## PROPOSITION XVI.

If a string is cut into two expressible parts <term>Effabiles: Kepler uses this to mean lengths that can be expressed as whole numbers or rational ratios</term>, and among those parts and the whole—that is, among the three terms—there is one dissonance; then there must also be another dissonance among them.

*For the cause of the dissonance will be that either the whole or a part has a number of portions from that division belonging to an indemonstrable figure <note>Kepler refers to "indemonstrable" shapes like the seven-sided heptagon, which cannot be constructed with a compass and straightedge and thus, in his theory, cannot produce harmonious sounds</note>. However, such a number is neither harmoniously associated with any larger number belonging to a demonstrable figure, nor with any number smaller than itself, according to Axioms III and V and Propositions V and VII. Therefore, that term which consists of such a number of portions is dissonant from the two remaining terms of that division; and thus two dissonances occur at the same time.*

In geometry, there is a similar proposition: if a straight line is cut into expressible parts, and one of them is incommensurable to some third line (not the Whole composed of both, as in this case), then the other part must also be incommensurable to that same third line.

Or, if a straight line is cut into parts that are incommensurable with each other, both will be incommensurable with the Whole.

## PROPOSITION XVII.

If a string is cut into two parts expressible in length, and there are two consonances among those and the whole (that is, among the three terms), then there must also be a third consonance.

*For if there are two consonances, since there are no more than three possible proportions between three terms, there cannot be two dissonances. If there are not two dissonances, then there cannot even be one, by the converse of Proposition XVI. Therefore, all three proportions will be consonant.*

So in Geometry, if a straight line is cut into parts that are commensurable with each other, the whole will be commensurable to each of the parts.

## PROPOSITION XVIII.

A division of a string into two parts expressible in length—in which either the Whole or one of the Parts acquires a number of portions belonging to an indemonstrable figure (provided the numbers of the Whole and the Parts are prime to each other)—is not Harmonic.

*This is demonstrated just like Proposition XVI. For out of the three proportions between the three terms, at least two become dissonant, which is contrary to the definition provided earlier.*

# PROPOSITION XIX.

After the Octagonal <note>A division based on the eight-sided figure, or the number 8.</note>, no harmonic section of a string is possible.

For the following sections are either created through indemonstrable figures <note>Kepler's "indemonstrable" shapes are those that cannot be constructed using only a compass and straightedge, such as a heptagon (7-sided). He believed only "knowable" geometry could produce "hearable" harmony.</note> and their stars; and then, although the parts might be consonant with each other, they are nevertheless dissonant with the whole, according to Axiom III. Or they are created through figures demonstrable by an "improper" demonstration, such as the Pentakaidecagon <term>A 15-sided polygon</term>; and then the proper parts of that section clash with the whole, according to the Corollary to Axiom III. Or they are created through figures demonstrable by a "proper" demonstration: all of which after the Pentagon <term>5-sided polygon</term> are equilateral <note>original: *parilatere*</note>, see Book I. Therefore, it is necessary to establish the proper parts of such sections by an odd number of portions; for if they were taken in an even number, the part would not be unique to this section, but would belong to a prior one. For instance, if a string is divided into 10 parts, and you take 4 or 6 portions, it is the same as if you had divided the string into 5 and taken 2 or 3 portions. Since, therefore, the Part consists of an odd number and the Whole an even number, the Part itself could be consonant with the Whole if it is not larger than five (according to Proposition V). However, one consonance is not enough to create a harmonic section, as is clear from the definition; then the Remainder <term>Residuum: the leftover length of the string after a part is cut away</term> will truly be dissonant. For the whole is set at more than 8 portions, and the definition of the Remainder is that it must be more than half, namely, greater than 4. Therefore, the minimum Remainder in an eight-fold division is 5; in divisions of higher numbers, it is greater than 5. In all sections of the string after the octonary <note>The division of the string into eight equal parts.</note>, the Remainders are odd numbers greater than 5. But odd numbers greater than 5 belong to indemonstrable figures, according to Propositions 45 and 47 of Book I. Therefore, by Proposition XVIII of this book, these Remainders cause the sections to be non-harmonic.

## Corollaries.

**1. The harmonic sections of a single string are seven in number, and no more.**
II. The propagation of the numbers which characterize these sections happens in this way. In the beginning, the Whole is placed in the form of a fraction—namely, unity above for...

### THE HARMONIES, BOOK III, CHAPTER II.

...above for the numerator, and one below for the denominator: then each number is placed separately above, and the sum of both is placed below on each side: so that from any one fraction two branches arise, continuing until the sum produces a number indicating an indemonstrable figure. <note>Kepler is describing a method for generating ratios, but stopping when the sum of the terms reaches 7, because a 7-sided figure cannot be constructed geometrically.</note>

<margin>The causes of this seven-fold division found successively.</margin>

I first found these seven sections of the string with my hearing as a guide—specifically, as many as there are Harmonies no larger than one Octave <note>original: Diapason</note>. Afterward, I extracted the causes of both the individual sections and the universal Number from the innermost springs of Geometry, though not without great effort. Let the curious reader look at what I wrote about these sections twenty-two years ago in *The Secret of the Universe* <note>original: Mysterio Cosmographico</note>, Chapter XII. Let him consider how I was deluded <note>original: hallucinatus</note> in that place regarding the causes of the sections and the Harmonies, wrongly striving to deduce their number and ratios from the number of the five Regular solid bodies <note>The Platonic solids</note>. The truth is rather this: both the five solid figures and the Musical harmonies and string sections share a common origin in the **plane Regular figures**.

<margin>Unknown to Ptolemy and Porphyry.</margin>
Indeed, I have recently obtained the *Harmonics* of Ptolemy along with the commentary of Porphyry <note>Two of the most important music theorists of antiquity</note> (whom I mentioned in the place cited above) in manuscript form, through the generosity of Johann Georg Herwart von Hohenburg, the Chancellor of Bavaria. I have translated the better part of their third book into the Appendix for Books IV and V of this work. However, I did not find the genuine causes of the Harmonies in them; thus, there is no mention of these sections or their seven-fold number.

Even though I realized early enough that the causes must be sought from plane figures—as you can see the seeds of this idea already scattered in the cited Chapter XII of the *Secret*—nevertheless, they tormented me for a very long time before every doubt in my mind was satisfied. First, the demonstrable figures <note>Shapes that can be drawn with a compass and straightedge</note> had to be separated from the indemonstrable ones. Next, a cause had to be found why, since these sections were derived from figures, the sections should stop at seven, while the figures run on to infinity. Third, a distinction had to be established between the Fifteen-sided figure <term>Pentekædecagonum</term> and the other demonstrable figures; for I saw that this figure was excluded from the creation of Harmonies, as the hearing testifies. Each of these points had its own difficult details, every one of which kept me occupied for a long time. Take Proposition V as an example: I saw it had to be added at the very last moment, while I was already writing the work, though I had been ignorant of it until then. For unless that proposition were also among the principles—if, for example, 7/20 were fit for establishing a harmony because they are demonstrable through 3/20 (with which they form a semicircle)—then 7/10, 5/7, and consequently 2/7 and 1/7 would be proven to create harmonies. Yet, the ears and our Axioms reject this in every way.

Therefore, by the testimony of my book *The Secret of the Universe* alone, the hearing is sufficiently fortified against the detractions of the Sophists...

This ensures that the things whose causes we labor to understand rest upon the most certain experience of the senses and are not—as the Pythagoreans were guilty of—fictitious things made up by me and thrust forward as truths.

## CHAPTER III.
### On Harmonic Means,
### and the Trinity of Concordant
### Sounds.

The definition of a harmonic proportion is empty <note>original: "vana"</note> if it is merely said to be that where, with three numbers placed in natural order, the differences between the two neighbors <note>the differences between the middle number and the two outer numbers</note> are in the same ratio <note>original: "proportione"</note> as the outer numbers <note>original: "Extremorum"</note>. For example, in the numbers 3, 4, and 6: the largest (6) is double the smallest (3); and thus also the difference (2) between the two larger neighbors (4 and 6) is double the difference (1) between the two smaller neighbors (4 and 3).

-><image-desc>A proportional diagram with numbers connected by lines. Row 1: 3, 3, 6. Row 2: 2, 2, 4. Row 3: 3, 6, 6. The numbers are connected by a grid of lines to illustrate mathematical ratios.</image-desc><-

<margin>The method for establishing any Musical Mean according to the opinion of the ancients.</margin>
I will, however, introduce the method for finding numbers containing such a proportion—called "Musical" by authors—because it is frequently transferred from harmonic doctrine into Ethics and Politics. The method is as follows: *Take two numbers that are prime to each other <note>meaning they share no common factors other than 1</note>, which contain the ratio of the outer terms (from the three to be considered musically, according to the opinion of the ancients) and the ratio of the differences from the Mean <note>middle term</note>. Multiply each number by itself, and multiply both together. Of the three products, add the two smaller ones to find the Minimum number, add the two larger ones for the Maximum, and double the middle product to find the ancient Musical Mean.* For example, if we are to find three numbers in the ancient musical proportion such that the outer numbers have the same ratio as 3 to 5:
- 3 times 3 is 9.
- 3 times 5 is 15.
- 5 times 5 is 25.
The products are therefore 9, 15, and 25.
- Add 9 and 15 to get 24 (the Minimum).
- Add 15 and 25 to get 40 (the Maximum).
- Double 15 to get 30 (the Musical Mean).
The three numbers sought are 24, 30, and 40, whose differences from the middle are 6 and 10. Just as 3 is to 5, so 24 is to 40, and so also 6 is to 10. In their simplest prime form, these are 12, 15, and 20.

<margin>A refutation of this kind.</margin>
This is indeed a harmonic proportion even to me, because not only is the proposed ratio between 3 and 5 harmonic (by Proposition VIII, Corollary), but the middle number found (15) also makes concordant ratios with the outer numbers 12 and 20. But this does not always happen. For whenever the arithmetic mean between two proposed numbers determines a dissonant ratio with the outer numbers...

<vocab><term>harmonic proportion</term>: a sequence of three numbers where the ratio of the two extremes equals the ratio of the differences between the middle and the extremes; <term>mean</term> (medietas): the middle value in a set of three; <term>prime numbers</term> (numerus Primis): numbers divisible only by 1 and themselves; <term>concordance</term>: a harmonious sounding of notes.</vocab>

<summary>Kepler critiques the traditional Pythagorean definition of "harmonic proportion" as purely mathematical, arguing it must also be validated by the sensory experience of concordant sounds. He provides a specific geometric/algebraic method for calculating musical means between two numbers.</summary>

### HARMONICS BOOK III.

<margin>CHAPTER III.</margin>
Often, three numbers arise from this operation in a proportion that is not truly harmonic, even though the two numbers initially proposed contain a solitary harmonic proportion <note>Kepler means that just because the outer numbers form a concord, it doesn't mean the mathematical "middle" will also be concordant</note>. This occurs in the ratios 1:6, 1:8, 3:4, 4:5, 5:6, 2:5, 3:8, and 5:8. For example, between 2 and 5 (which is the same as 4 and 10), the **Arithmetic mean** is 7. This is not harmonic because 7 sounds concordant with neither 4 nor 10, according to Proposition V. Therefore, if you work according to the Rule, the numbers 14, 20, and 35 will be produced, with differences of 6 and 15. In this case, 20 would be called the "harmonic mean" according to the ancients, because as 14 is to 35 (which is 2:5), so 6 is to 15. Yet the ears completely reject the intervals 20:35 (which is 4:7) and 14:20 (which is 7:10) <note>Kepler rejects these because ratios involving the number 7 were considered dissonant in his system</note>.

In the harmonic sections discussed in Chapter II, as many means present themselves as there are sections, minus one. In those sections, "Mean" is taken in a stricter sense: it is the larger part of a string harmonically cut into unequal parts, or the number expressing it. Thus, 2 is the **harmonic mean** between 1 and 3; 3 is the mean between 1 and 4, and also between 2 and 5; 4 is the mean between 1 and 5; and 5 is the mean between 1 and 6, as well as between 3 and 8.

Besides these, however, there are also other Means, freed from this law of dividing a single string into two parts, yet encompassed by our general definition. These do not divide just one string, as in the previous chapter, but rather divide a **proportion** of strings into smaller concordant proportions.

First, all proportions greater than the <term>dupla|the 2:1 ratio or octave</term> are resolved into their principles by removing the double proportion. For example, the ratio 1:24 consists of four doubles (that is, from a <term>sedecupla|sixteen-fold ratio</term>) and a <term>sesquialtera|the 3:2 ratio or perfect fifth</term>. Therefore, the Harmonic Means falling between 1 and 24 under this name are 2, 4, 8, and 16, with the sixteen-fold ratio placed above; or those of 12, 6, 3, and 2. One double can be placed above and three below; it can be done in various ways.

Next, the **double proportion** <note>the octave</note> is resolved into these concords: 3:4 and 2:3; or into 3:4, 4:5, and 5:6; or into 4:5 and 5:8; or into 5:6 and 3:5. Finally, the **sesquialtera** (2:3) <note>perfect fifth</note> is resolved into 4:5 and 5:6.

<image-desc>The musical notation illustrates these mathematical divisions. The first staff shows an interval spanning 1 to 24, divided by notes at 2, 4, 8, and 16. The lower staves show how larger intervals like the octave (1:2) or fifth (2:3) are subdivided into smaller musical steps like the fourth (3:4), major third (4:5), and minor third (5:6).</image-desc>

Thus, 5:8 <note>the minor sixth</note> is divided into 5:6 and 3:4; and 3:5 <note>the major sixth</note> is divided into 3:4 and 4:5.

Therefore, these three proportions—3:4, 4:5, and 5:6—are the smallest among the concords. That is, they are "immediate," or lacking a Harmonic mean. They are, of course, the **Concordant Elements** of all the others.

<margin>Two Harmonic Means.</margin>
From these it follows that there can be two means within a single double proportion <note>the octave</note> that are also concordant with each other, and this can happen in six different ways. Because the "double" consists of three smallest concordant elements <note>the 3:4, 4:5, and 5:6 ratios</note>, their order can be varied six times. For 3:4 is either in the first place from the smaller string, in the middle, or in the last; and in each case, of the remaining elements, either the larger (4:5) is toward the smaller string, or the smaller (5:6) is.

First, all proportions larger than a <term>double</term> <note>original: "dupla," referring to the 2:1 ratio or octave.</note> are resolved into their principles by removing the double proportion. For example, the ratio 1:24 consists of four doubles (that is, a sixteen-fold proportion) and a <term>sesquialtera</term> <note>original: "sesquialtera," the 3:2 ratio which produces the interval of a perfect fifth.</note>. Therefore, the harmonic means that fall between 1 and 24 are 2, 4, 8, and 16, with the sixteen-fold placed above; or they are 12, 6, 3, and 2, with one double placed above and three below; for this can be done in various ways.

Next, the <term>double proportion</term> (the octave) is resolved into these concords: 3:4 and 2:3; or into 3:4, 4:5, and 5:6; or into 4:5 and 5:8; or into 5:6 and 3:5. Finally, the <term>sesquialtera</term> (3:2 ratio) is resolved into 4:5 and 5:6; likewise 5:8 is resolved into 5:6 and 3:4; and 3:5 is resolved into 3:4 and 4:5.

[Four small musical staves illustrating harmonic divisions with numerical ratios. The first shows the division 3, 4, 6; the second shows 4, 5, 8; the third shows 6, 8, 10, 12; the fourth shows a resolution of the number 24 into tiered ratios including 8, 10, 12; 5, 6; and 3, 4.]

Therefore, these three proportions—3:4, 4:5, and 5:6—are the smallest of the concords. This means they are immediate, or lacking a harmonic mean; they are, in fact, the concordant elements of all the others.

<margin>Pairs of Harmonic Means.</margin>
From this it follows that for a single double proportion (octave), there can be two means that are also concordant with each other, and this can happen in six different ways. Because the double has three minimal concordant elements, the order of those elements can be varied six times. For instance, the 3:4 ratio is either in the first place from the smaller string, or in the middle, or in the last; and in each case, of the remaining elements, either the larger (4:5) is toward the smaller string, or the smaller (5:6) is.

Of these six pairs of harmonic means, only one, in the numbers 10, 12, 15, and 20, allows for the definition used by the Ancients. For 12 is the musical mean (in their sense) between 10 and 15; likewise, 15 is the musical mean between 12 and 20. For the differences <note>original: "excessus"</note> are in the ratio 2 to 3. Yet, as the extremes of one group of three <note>original: "trigæ"</note>, 10 to 15, are in the ratio 2 to 3; so the extremes of the other group of three, 12 to 20, are in the ratio 3 to 5.

<margin>Concerning the Trinity of concords.</margin>
->Since, therefore, the strings of a double proportion<-
sound identically <note>When notes are an octave apart, they sound like the same note at different pitches.</note>, and between them there cannot be more than two means at once that are consonant both with each other and with the "doubles" <note>the octaves</note> themselves: from this has arisen that famous observation of musicians, who marvel that all harmonies are completed by three voices.

<image-desc>A vertical musical staff with eleven diamond-shaped notes. Next to the notes are the numbers: 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 15, 16, 20, 24. Brackets connect numeric pairs representing octaves: 3-6, 4-8, 5-10, 6-12, 8-16, 10-20, and 12-24.</image-desc>

For no matter how many voices are added besides, each one returns to one of the original three through the identical resonance <note>original: "identisonum"</note> of the double proportion.
For although a single consonance exists from all these string lengths—3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16, 20, 24—whatever follows after the strings 3, 4, and 5 returns to one of these through identical sound: just as 6 relates to 3, 8 relates to 4, and 10 relates to 5; likewise 12 relates to 6 and 3; 16 to 8 and 4; 20 to 10 and 5; and 24 to 12, 6, and 3.

Others seek the cause of this matter elsewhere in vain: some from the triple dimension of a perfect quantity or body (that which is evident in length, breadth, and depth); others from the perfection of the number three; others from the adorable Trinity itself in the Godhead.

In vain, I say, all of them: for "solid quantity" <note>Three-dimensional geometry</note> does not enter into this business, since we have shown that the origin of harmonic proportions comes from plane figures <note>Two-dimensional shapes like the circle or triangle</note>; and the cause of knowledge for solid quantity is far different from that of plane figures, since the former requires two mean proportionals, which [cannot] be known...
