# ON THE HARMONICS, BOOK III.

<margin>CHAPTER III.</margin>
...it is impossible for this to be known indiscriminately. Nor can the power of number have any influence, insofar as it is considered as a counting tool; nor is the origin of this Trinity <note>Kepler is referring to the "triad" or the three-part nature of harmony.</note> derived immediately from the divine essence through exemplary causation. As appeared above, the cause of a thing is composed of the principles already explained, which by no means intend any specific number of voices for their own sake. Instead, these principles harmonically fit the individual voices to one another; and thus, while acting as if on something else, they produce by accident something similar to divine things because of that same number—a phenomenon that frequently occurs in many other things as well.

In short, this ternary number <note>The number three.</note> is not the efficient cause of Harmonies, but their effect, or rather a companion to the harmony already produced. It does not give form to harmonies but is the reflection of that form. It is not the material substance of harmonic voices but is the offspring procreated from material necessity. It is not the "end for the sake of which" <note>original Greek: "οὗ ἕνεκα" (hou heneka). In Aristotelian philosophy, this refers to the "final cause" or the ultimate purpose for which a thing exists.</note>, but the extremity of the work. Finally, it is nothing of the harmonic thing itself, but is a secondary "being of reason" <note>An "Ens rationis" is a concept that exists in the mind to help us understand reality, rather than a physical object.</note> and a concept of the mind—a "second intention." For we should no more ask why only three voices sound harmonically together (while the fourth and all others return, in a way, to the same sound through the double proportion of the octave), than why there are only six pairs in any Octave, or six forms of triple consonances. For just as that number six does not come from the six days of creation, so that Trinity is not because of the Trinity of persons in the Godhead. Rather, since the number three is common to both divine and worldly things, wherever it occurs, the human mind—ignorant of the true causes—marvels at it as if it were a divine conspiracy.

# CHAPTER IV.
## On the origin of the melodic
->intervals which are smaller than Consonances.<-

---

<margin>
What is Low?
What is High?
What is Deep?
What is Up?
</margin>
Since the senses testify that, among strings stretched with equal tension, the sounds of those that are longer are lower (*Grave*), and those that are shorter are higher (*Acutum*), these paired terms, *High* and *Low*, are the proper distinctions of Harmony. Individually, these terms belong to other separate sciences where they are paired with different opposites: *Acute* with *Obtuse* in Geometry; *Heavy* (*Grave*) with *Light* in Physics. In other contexts, *Acute* in mechanics sounds like something sharp and penetrating; *Heavy* (*Grave*) in the sensory world is used for smells which, like heavy weights, are less tolerable due to their "magnitude." But when paired as *High* and *Low* and placed in opposition to each other, they are understood only in reference to voices. Yet they retain something of their original meaning. For just as in Geometry an "acute" angle is smaller than an "obtuse" one, so too in Harmony a "high" (*acuta*) voice sounds small, and therefore penetrating and high—in the German idiom <note>original: "idiotismo Teutonico." Kepler is likely referring to the German word "hoch," which describes both physical height and musical pitch.</note>—flying as if in the heights because of a certain lightness. And just as in Physics "heavy" (*Grave*) things have great weight and "light" things have little, so here a "low" (*Gravis*) voice sounds "large." Just as heavy things seek the bottom and lower parts on a scale while light things leap upward, so also in Harmony: a low voice, because of its "magnitude," is regarded as ponderous and therefore inferior or deep (*bassa* <note>original: "bassa," an early term for the bass register.</note>), while a high voice, as has been said, is regarded as being "up" or "high."

<summary>Kepler argues that the "Trinity" in music is a mathematical byproduct rather than a mystical imposition, then defines the physical and linguistic origins of musical pitch terms like "high" and "low."</summary>

# ON PROPORTIONS

For the reason that on the Lute <note>original: *Testudine*, literally "tortoise shell," referring to the lyre or lute</note> the *Hypate* <note>The "highest" string in physical position on ancient instruments.</note>, that is the Topmost, produced a deep sound, it was called that only because of its position on the instrument (as is still the case today), and not because of any vocal similarity with light and "flying" things <note>A reference to high-pitched sounds being associated with birds or lightness.</note>. However, its position on the instrument has a mechanical reason: the *Nete* <note>The "lowest" string in physical position.</note>, that is the Last and Lowest, because it sounds most shrilly <note>The highest pitch.</note>, had to be struck most frequently; since a rapid motion is suited to small things. Indeed, we pluck downward more easily than upward because of the shape of the thumb. Added among the causes is the experience of the human throat. For men are generally taller than women, and adults taller than boys, and they emit a deeper voice, as if it were sought from further down. Individual humans, taught by the very sense of touch, draw out a deeper voice from lower down and a higher voice from further up; and those who sing most deeply extend their bodies so that the voice may exit from as deep as possible. To be sure, those who sing shrilly also stretch their necks, but not to make the neck long, but rather to more tightly constrict the topmost circles of the throat.

<margin>What a Diastema or Interval is.</margin>
For these reasons, therefore, the concept of the "High" and the "Deep" was born in Harmonics <note>The study of musical ratios and sounds.</note>, for which we frequently use the terms "Acute" and "Grave" <note>Sharps and flats, or high and low pitches.</note>. Since High and Deep are otherwise words describing location, the custom of speech, following these principles, also accommodates to voices that which is proper to locations—namely, **Intervals**, or in Greek *diastemata* <note>original: διαστήματα</note>. For locations are said to "stand apart" <note>original: διΐστασθαι (diistasthai)</note>. Finally, the discipline of Harmonics transferred this word even into its paintings or Diagrams (of which more below), which consist of high and deep lines; in this way, its Geometric sense was restored to it.

Therefore, what have until now been called "Proportions" of strings will henceforth almost always be called **Intervals** of voices, which are emitted by strings of unequal length. For voices sounding the same, to which correspond strings of equal length and equal tension, do not create an Interval, since they are of the same height.

However, in Book V, we must refrain from this sense of the word "Interval"; because there, by frequent use, that word must be repeated in an astronomical sense, regarding the straight line between the Body of a Planet and the Sun, and likewise concerning that space which lies between different orbits.

<margin>What is a higher and what is a lower interval.</margin>
Furthermore, just as in the preceding chapter proportions were considered in two ways—namely, either individually by themselves, or compared to one another for the sake of order, which extended from the term or shorter string of some composite proportion to the greater or longer one, and vice versa—so now also **Intervals** are considered either individually or compared to one another for the sake of harmonic "location." In a continuous ordering of several intervals (such that two adjacent ones always have the same common boundary, which is the higher boundary for one and the lower boundary for the other as it tends toward deeper voices), that interval is always called *lower* which is between deeper voices, and *upper* which is between sharper voices.

<margin>Which Intervals are equal.</margin>
And in Geometry indeed, proportions are recognized as equal even if the terms of one are unequal to the terms of the other, and the difference between the terms of one is unequal to the difference of the terms of the other: As, for example, if there are three strings in the proportion of the numbers 4, 6, 9; the proportion is considered the same...

<summary>Kepler explains the transition from physical string ratios to the musical concept of "intervals," justifying the use of spatial language (high/low) through the mechanics of instruments and human anatomy. He also distinguishes between musical intervals and the astronomical distances he will discuss later in the work.</summary>

# ON HARMONICS, BOOK III.

<margin>Chapter IV.</margin>

4 to 6 is the same as 6 to 9, notwithstanding the fact that both the terms themselves and the differences—2 and 3—are unequal. <note>Original: *excessus*. Here Kepler points out that while the difference between 4 and 6 is 2, and 6 and 9 is 3, the ratio (2:3, a Perfect Fifth) remains the same.</note>

<image-desc>A small vertical diagram showing three numbers (4, 6, and 9) each preceded by a square-shaped musical symbol, likely indicating proportions on a monochord or musical staff.</image-desc>

In the study of Harmonics, all intervals of voices coming from strings of the same proportion are similarly judged to be equal and are written with the same numerical sign; they are even depicted with equal line-intervals in a diagram. We do this so thoroughly that we completely forget the inequality that exists between the physical differences of the various strings.

It follows, therefore, that we call a smaller proportion a "smaller interval," and a larger proportion a "larger interval," without regard for the actual size or smallness of the corresponding terms on either side.

<margin>What are consonant and dissonant intervals? What are Concinnous and Inconcinnous, and the origin of the names?</margin>
With these definitions established, we must now look further into the differences between intervals. Thus far, all proportions that we have demonstrated to be consonant (with the exception of the one of equality <note>The unison (1:1).</note>) are likewise to be considered consonant intervals. Those proportions we called dissonant are likewise dissonant intervals. However, because there is a great difference among dissonant intervals—such that some are not only taught by Nature as consonant and approved by the ear through instinct, but other smaller intervals are also established by that same sense—these, though they be dissonant, are nevertheless suitable for a melody to be carried through. Harmonics, following Nature, gives them the name <term>Concinnous (from the Latin *concinnus*, meaning "well-joined" or "neat")</term>, and distinguishes them from <term>Inconcinnous</term> intervals, which do not enter into the flow of any orderly song. In Greek, these are called *emmele* <note>original: ἐμμελῆ — meaning "in tune" or "melodic."</note> and *ekmele* <note>original: ἐκμελῆ — meaning "out of tune" or "unsuitable for melody."</note>.

When the Ancients saw this natural talent for discriminating between the Concinnous and the Inconcinnous, they thought they should seek out some common "smallest element" shared by all Concinnous and Consonant intervals. They believed that by taking this element in a certain number, any Consonant or Concinnous interval could be composed. It seemed necessary that such a minimum interval should exist as a "simple" unit, appearing earlier than the Consonances themselves, which appeared to be composed of such a minimum, seeing as some intervals are larger than others.

Yet the reality is far different, as can be shown by many examples. For if individuals of all species that differ in size consisted of one common "Minimum," there would then be some single minimum quantity for the human species; any man would be composed of a certain number of such "tiny-man-units" as if from elements—the tall man from many, the short man from few. But this quality, Consonance, informs the proportion of strings (or the interval of voices) no less than the "form of a man" informs that mass of matter enclosed by a human skin. And why have they forgotten Geometry? In geometry, there are many examples of all kinds of <term>incommensurable quantities</term> <note>Quantities that cannot be measured by the same whole-number unit, such as the relationship between the side and the diagonal of a square.</note>. The definition of these is that they share absolutely no common measure from the same class of quantities that could act as a fixed element of composition.

<margin>Most musical intervals are incommensurable.</margin>
Thus, it must be held that consonant intervals (except for those where one is a multiple of the other) are, like those very proportions, incommensurable—

<summary>Kepler argues that musical intervals are defined by ratios rather than physical distances, introducing the distinction between "Concinnous" (melodic) and "Inconcinnous" (unmelodic) intervals. He challenges the ancient idea that all musical intervals can be built from a single "smallest" unit, comparing music to geometry where many quantities are incommensurable.</summary>
<keywords>proportions, musical intervals, consonance, dissonance, concinnous, emmele, geometry, incommensurability, Kepler, ancient music theory</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the mathematical investigation into musical proportions, moving from the physical measurements of strings to the abstract nature of how these ratios relate to one another. The previous page established that the "size" of a musical interval is determined by its ratio rather than physical length; this page explores why certain intervals cannot be simply added or subtracted like whole numbers.</meta>

# ON PROPORTIONS

<margin>
VI. Question 8
Chapter IV.
</margin>
...remarkable things, so that although their differences are expressed in numbers—which in simple numbers is a sign of <term>commensuration</term> <note>The ability for two quantities to be measured by the same standard unit.</note>—these differences, because they are not simple numbers but fractions, are not <term>aliquot parts</term> <note>A part of a number that divides the whole number exactly, such as 2 being an aliquot part of 6.</note> or portions of the things they differ from according to any whole number. For example, two proportions—1:2 <note>An octave.</note> and 1:4 <note>Two octaves.</note>—are related to each other as the number 1 is to the number 2. They are therefore commensurable, for 1:4 is the double of 1:2. This occurs only in the series of continuous doubles. For in the series of triples and other <term>multiples</term>, there are no two consonant proportions: while 1:9 is indeed the triple of 1:3, only 1:3 is among the <term>consonants</term> <note>Pleasing, stable sounds.</note>, whereas 1:9 is among the <term>dissonants</term> <note>Clashing or unstable sounds.</note>, according to Axiom III. The same can be seen in non-multiples, such as the <term>sesquialter</term> 2:3 <note>A Perfect Fifth.</note> which is consonant; it certainly has its multiple and is thus commensurable—for 4:9 is to 2:3 as the number 2 is to 1—yet 4:9 is not among the consonants. Conversely, take two other consonants outside the series of doubles, such as 1:4 and 2:3; these two proportions are not commensurable with each other—that is, they do not relate as whole number to whole number. For the remainder <note>Original: *excessus*.</note> of 3:8 <note>A Perfect Eleventh.</note> between 1:4 and 2:3 measures neither 1:4 nor 2:3.

<margin><unclear>Logic of intervals</unclear></margin>
Consonant intervals, therefore, are by nature prior to the smaller intervals which we call <term>concinnous</term> <note>From the Latin *concinnus* meaning "well-arranged." These are melodic intervals like whole tones or semitones that are not primary consonances but "fit" within a musical scale.</note>. The former are not composed of the latter as if from elements or from some smaller quantity; on the contrary, the latter arise from the former as if from their causes.

Here we must note the ambiguity of the word "composition." Sometimes it denotes the natural origin of a thing; at other times, it denotes the quantitative division of a thing, which is not an origin but rather a destruction. For instance, when we say a circle "consists" of three thirds, we are first dividing the circle in our minds into three; or when we say the human body is "composed" of limbs, it is not because the limbs existed before the body and the body was collected and constructed from them (like a house from stones and wood), but because the body, by reason of its mass, is divisible into these limbs—which, taken individually, are no longer an organic body.

In the first sense, it must be denied that consonant intervals are composed of either other consonants or concinnous intervals. In the second sense, they certainly "consist" of them, and thus are "composed" (as we ourselves used the term above): larger consonant intervals are made of smaller ones, and the smallest consonants are made of concinnous intervals, etc., because they can be dissolved into these as if into elements. But they do not all consist of some number of a single, common, smallest species of interval, nor can they be dissolved into such a thing.

<margin><unclear>Logic of proportions</unclear></margin>
Although consonant intervals are related, they do not all share the same cause; rather, each has its own peculiar cause, distinct from the causes of the others, as explained above. For <term>consonance</term> belongs to the intervals themselves, not simply because of their size, nor simply because they are relationships, but because they are qualitative (that is, in a certain way, "shaped") relationships. Therefore, wishing to establish a "common minimum interval" for them is irrelevant. Minimums and maximums are considered in bare quantities and their proportions, not in qualities. To divide a consonant as a consonant is to abolish the "species" of the sound, and to establish in its place either other species of consonants, or concinnous dissonances, or even plainly <term>inconcinnous</term> <note>Intervals that are neither consonant nor melodic, sounding "out of tune" or "unfit" for music.</note> intervals.

<summary>This page argues that musical consonances (like the octave or fifth) are primary "qualitative" units that cannot be reduced to a single common denominator or "smallest" unit. Kepler explains that while we can mathematically divide large intervals into smaller ones, the musical identity of a consonance is destroyed when it is treated merely as a sum of parts.</summary>
<keywords>commensurability, aliquot parts, consonant intervals, concinnous intervals, musical composition, qualitative relations, proportions, mathematical harmonics</keywords>

### BOOK III OF HARMONICS

<margin>CHAPTER IV.</margin>
An interval, therefore, possesses the causes or elements of its own consonance from its parts, as if from principles; just as commensurable quantities grow by the multiplication of a common measure, and exist with this measure under one and the same genus. But on the contrary, those things which the ancients <note>Kepler refers to Greek theorists like Aristoxenus or the Pythagoreans.</note> held to be the principles of consonances (namely **Tones**, **semitones**, and **dieses** <note>A 'diesis' is a very small interval, often a quarter-tone or the difference between a major and minor semitone.</note>) actually arise from consonances as their own genuine principles.

<margin>Consonance as such does not arise from numbers as parts.</margin>
For although these Consonances consist of those <term>Concinnous</term> <note>Kepler uses 'concinnus' (fitting/elegant) to describe intervals that are not consonances themselves but are suitable for melody, like the steps of a scale.</note> intervals which are not themselves consonances—if not from one common interval, then at least from several combined with each other in different ways—this should not be attributed to the consonance of the interval itself. For if concinnous intervals provided their own consonance to a larger interval composed of them, this would always happen in any multiplication of concinnous steps, and a consonance would be better the more concinnous steps it contained. But that is false; for as we shall hear below, two combined tones make a consonance <note>A Major Third (81:64 in Pythagorean tuning, or 5:4 in Kepler's preferred tuning).</note>, but three combined tones constitute a dissonant interval <note>The Tritone or 'Augmented Fourth,' famously known as the 'Devil in Music.'</note>.

However, the fact that a consonance can be dissolved into concinnous steps (as follows) is plainly accidental to that consonance considered by itself; and it happens only insofar as several consonances are compared with one another, each having arisen from its own principles.

<margin>Definition of a Concinnous Interval.</margin>
Therefore, **Concinnous intervals** are defined as all the differences of consonances that are smaller than a double interval <note>A 'double interval' refers to the Octave (ratio 2:1).</note>; nor does the natural faculty of hearing receive any other concinnous intervals than those which arise from this subtraction. Thus, consonant intervals have their origin in Geometry and demonstrable figures, while concinnous intervals arise from the consonances themselves. They are "concinnous" in relation to consonances, just as in Geometry the <term>Apotomes</term> <note>An 'Apotome' in Euclidean geometry is an irrational line formed by subtracting one rational line from another; Kepler uses this as a mathematical analogy for melodic steps.</note> (ineffable lines) are related to those that are effable in power; because those too are defined by the subtraction of an Effable line from another Effable line.

<margin>The origin of Concinnous intervals from consonances.</margin>
Furthermore, there is one method of comparison or abstraction that is general or arithmetic, and another that is special and proper to Harmonics. Arithmetically, those consonances smaller than an octave are chosen where one is not such a part of the other as designated by any harmonic mean <note>original: "Medietas harmonica"</note> in the previous chapter.

The following are therefore the differences:

| Between these consonances: | These Concinnous intervals: |
| :--- | :--- |

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Chapter IV of Book III, where Kepler is explaining that musical consonances are primary and whole, rather than being built up from smaller melodic building blocks like the tone or semitone. He uses mathematical and organic analogies to prove that harmony precedes melody.</meta>

# ON PROPORTIONS

<margin>
Chapter IV.
</margin>
...remarkable things happen; even though we can express the differences between these intervals as numbers—which in simple whole numbers is a sign of <term>commensurability</term> <note>Commensurability refers to the ability for two quantities to be measured by the same unit, like two lengths being measured in inches.</note>—these differences are actually fractions, not simple numbers. Therefore, they are not an aliquot part or parts <note>An "aliquot part" is a factor that divides a whole number exactly, like 2 is to 6.</note> of the intervals being compared.

For example, the two proportions 1:2 <note>The Octave</note> and 1:4 <note>The Double Octave</note> relate to each other as the number 1 relates to the number 2. They are therefore commensurable, because 1:4 is exactly double the 1:2 ratio. However, this only happens in a series of "continuous doubles" <note>The sequence 1:2, 1:4, 1:8, etc.</note>. In a series of triples or other multiples, you do not find two matching consonances. For instance, 1:9 <note>The Octave plus a Major Twelfth</note> is indeed triple 1:3 <note>The Twelfth</note>, but while 1:3 is a consonance, 1:9 is a dissonance according to Axiom III. We see the same thing in non-multiples: in the <term>sesquialtera</term> <note>The ratio 3:2, which forms a Perfect Fifth.</note>, which is a consonance, we can find a multiple of it that is commensurable—specifically 4:9, which is to 2:3 as the number 2 is to 1—yet 4:9 is not a consonance. On the other hand, take two other consonances outside the "doubles" series, like 1:4 and 2:3; these two proportions are not commensurable with each other as number to number. The "excess" of 1:4 over 2:3 (which is 3:8) does not evenly measure either 1:4 or 2:3.

->Consonant Intervals are naturally prior to the smaller intervals which we call concinnous; they are not composed of those smaller intervals as if they were built from elements or some smaller quantity. On the contrary, the smaller intervals arise from the consonances as if from their own causes.<-

On this point, we must note the ambiguity of the word "composition." Sometimes it denotes the natural origin of a thing, but other times it refers to the quantitative division of a thing—which is not its origin, but rather its destruction. It is like when we say a circle "consists" of three thirds, because we first divide the circle in our minds into three parts; or when we say the human body is "composed" of members. We do not mean the limbs existed before the body and that the body was collected and constructed from them (like a house from stones and wood); rather, the body is divisible into these members because of its mass—members which, once separated, are no longer an organic body.

In the first sense of the word, we must deny that consonant intervals are "composed" of other consonances or melodic <term>concinnous</term> <note>Kepler uses 'concinnous' to describe intervals that are not harmonious on their own but are "fitting" for use in melody, like a whole tone.</note> steps. In the second sense, they certainly do "consist" of them, and thus are "composed" (as I have used the term previously): larger consonant intervals consist of smaller ones, and the smallest consonances consist of concinnous steps, etc., because they can be dissolved into these as if into elements. But different consonances do not consist of a specific number of one single common "smallest" interval, nor can they be dissolved into such a thing.

<margin>
Pitch
Division
</margin>
Even though consonant intervals have related causes, they do not all share the same cause. Instead, each has its own peculiar cause, distinct from the causes of others, as explained above. For consonance belongs to these intervals not simply because of how "large" they are, nor simply because they are "relations," but because they are "qualitative" relations (that is, in a sense, "shaped" relations). Therefore, wanting to establish a single "minimum common interval" for them is irrelevant. Concepts like "minimum" and "maximum" are considered in bare quantities and their proportions, not in qualities. To divide a "consonance as a consonance" is to destroy the very essence of the harmony, and to substitute for it either other types of harmony, or melodic steps, or even completely unmelodic intervals. It does not—

<summary>Kepler argues that musical harmonies (consonances) are primary geometric wholes rather than being constructed from smaller units like tones. He explains that while we can divide a Fifth or an Octave into smaller parts, the harmony itself is the "parent" of those parts, much like a body is the parent of its limbs.</summary>

...harmonics. Therefore, from all the numbers of the greater terms of the seven harmonic sections—namely 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 5 <note>The repetition of 5 in the transcription likely refers to the terms of the ratios 5:6 and 5:8.</note>, and 8—the <term>least common multiple</term> <note>original: "communis minimus dividuus." The smallest number that can be divided by all these factors without a remainder.</note> of 120 must be sought. The entire string is to be divided into that many equal parts, so that the sound of the whole string is established as the common greater term for all the consonances created through the sections. The smaller terms are then to be adjusted so that, when compared among themselves, they constitute the <term>melodic intervals</term> <note>original: "intervalla concinna." These are the functional steps of a musical scale that sound "fit" or "well-arranged" even if they are not primary consonances like the Fifth.</note> which are being investigated in this chapter. Indeed, these turn out to be the same as those produced earlier by the arithmetic method.

## Arithmetic Corollary
-> quite beautiful in the numbers and the layout <-
-> below. <-

<image-desc>A numeric diagram arranged in three levels showing mathematical relationships between integers and their neighbors. 
Top level: The numbers 3, 15, 35, and 63 are placed above brackets.
Middle level: Integers 1 through 10 are laid out in a horizontal row.
Bottom level: Squares of certain integers (9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81) are written directly below their respective roots in the middle row.
Brackets connect the levels: 
- On top, brackets connect pairs of odd numbers (1 & 3 to 3; 3 & 5 to 15; 5 & 7 to 35; 7 & 9 to 63). 
- On the bottom, brackets connect pairs of even numbers (2 & 4 to 8; 4 & 6 to 24; 6 & 8 to 48; 8 & 10 to 80), representing the product of the neighbors of the squared number in between them.</image-desc>

That is to say, for every number below ten, its square—along with the rectangle <note>Kepler uses "rectangle" to mean the product of two numbers, a term derived from Greek geometry where multiplication was visualized as an area.</note> formed by its two nearest neighboring numbers—constitutes an interval that is either consonant, melodic <note>original: "concinnum"</note>, or a Third, with the exception of the square of seven (49) and its two rectangles (35 and 63). But here the melodic interval 9:10 is excluded, as are most of the consonances, except for 3:4. Therefore, this occurrence is accidental with respect to the general order of numbers and the construction of this diagram.

The arithmetician will seek causes here in vain; in vain will Pythagoras be preoccupied with the superstition of the seven <note>original: "septenarij." The Pythagoreans held the number seven in mystical awe.</note>, as if it were a "number that counts" <note>original: "numeris numerantis." A technical distinction in scholastic logic between abstract numbers used for counting and the actual things being counted ("numeris numeratis").</note>. The matter must be traced deeper from geometry and from "counted" and figured numbers—that is, from the indemonstrable figures themselves, the first of which is the heptagon <note>original: "septangulum." A seven-sided polygon. Kepler argues that because a heptagon cannot be constructed using only a compass and straightedge, it cannot produce harmonic ratios.</note>. For as to why this diagram cannot be continued beyond ten with a subsequent melodic fitting: it is no longer the number seven that hinders it, but other numbers of indemonstrable figures, 9 and 11, which produce the rectangle 99; this, compared with the square of ten (100), constitutes an interval entirely foreign to the nature of Song <note>original: "Cantus." Referring to melodic music or the art of singing.</note>. So great is the difference between <term>doxastic axioms</term> <note>original: "Axiomata doxastica." Axioms based merely on opinion or belief.</note> and <term>epistemic axioms</term> <note>original: "epistemonica." Axioms based on true scientific knowledge and demonstration.</note>.

## The order of melodic intervals in
## perfection, and their names.

We have spoken so far of the origin and order of intervals which are smaller than consonances; we must now also speak of their differences and their names, which we cannot keep exactly the same as the ancients, since we have had to learn from them regarding both the things themselves and their causes.

It is therefore consistent with what was said above, especially with Axiom II, that any of these intervals belonging to the nature of a melodic interval <note>original: "concinni"</note> should retain the nature of those consonances from which it is formed. Since, therefore, among the consonances smaller than a doubled interval <note>referring to the octave, 1:2</note>, the most perfect are 2:3 <note>the Fifth</note> and 3:4 <note>the Fourth</note>...

CHAPTER IV.
What is a Major Tone?
</margin>
<image-desc>A musical staff with two notes on adjacent lines and spaces, labeled below with the numbers 8 and 9.</image-desc> Because of the nobility of the shapes from which they derive their origin, their common offspring among the <term>melodic intervals<gloss>concinna: intervals suitable for melody rather than just harmony</gloss></term>, namely 8:9, will be preferred above the others. Let us therefore call this interval, by the name common among the ancients, a TONE; and because of this excellence, we call it a Perfect Tone, but because of the magnitude of its proportion, a Major Tone.

Conversely, if you compare the major perfect <note>Kepler refers to the Perfect Fifth (2:3) as a "perfect" interval.</note> 2:3 with the major imperfect <note>The Major Sixth (3:5), which Kepler considers "imperfect" because it derives from the pentagon rather than the primary shapes like the square.</note> 3:5 above, or if you compare the minor of the perfects (the Fourth, 3:4) with the minor of the imperfects (the Minor Third, 5:6) below, there will be born from this marriage a melodic interval of a more imperfect nature, 9:10. This is smaller than 8:9. Since this interval was almost never

<margin>Minor Tone.</margin>
<image-desc>A musical staff showing a series of four notes with various accidentals (flats, sharps, and naturals), labeled below with the numbers 9 and 10.</image-desc> noticed in ancient music before Ptolemy—for the theorists used to demonstrate everything through the "full tones" defined previously—we shall give it the name of the Minor or Small Tone, so that this may be a mark of its imperfection. Here, the reader should be warned in a word: some others have given this name to a different interval; let the reader not be disturbed by carelessness if he should happen to come across their writings.

But if you have associated the major perfect (2:3) with the minor imperfect (the Minor Sixth, 5:8) above, or the minor perfect (3:4) with the major imperfect (the Major Third, 4:5) below, the melodic interval arising from the comparison, namely 15:16, again draws something of imperfection from this origin of its own. It shall be called a "semitone," using the same 

<margin>Semitone.</margin>
<image-desc>A musical staff with five notes in a sequence moving between adjacent lines and spaces, labeled below with the numbers 15 and 16.</image-desc> word that this very interval has in the common music of today, because it is a little larger than half <note>original: "semisse"</note> of a Major Tone. Some have repeatedly called this a "Minor Tone," against whom the reader should be on guard, lest he be confused.

These three, then, arising from the perfect intervals compared either among themselves or with the imperfect ones, have obtained this property: that they are melodic <note>original: "concinna"</note> in their own right and always.

On the other hand, if you have compared the imperfect intervals among themselves—those arising from the Pentagon or Decagon—either 3:5 with 5:8 above, or 4:5 with 5:6 below, the interval arising from this, namely 24:25, is of such great 

<margin>Diesis.</margin>
<image-desc>A musical staff with three notes in close chromatic succession, labeled below with the numbers 24 and 25.</image-desc> imperfection that it almost ceases to be among the melodic intervals. We shall call this interval a "Diesis," using the ancient word <note>original: "voce veteri"</note>, as if you were to say, a "slackening" of the string. Nor do I labor to propose the same quantity of interval under this word as the ancients did; let it suffice to have warned of this again. The causes of its imperfection are three: its origin, its smallness (since it does not even equal a third part of a perfect tone), and because it is also counted above among the "Thirds"—namely among those intervals which serve to harmonize the <term>genera of song<gloss>The ancient Greek systems of tuning: Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic</gloss></term>. For it also arises from the comparison of a minor tone and a semitone. For this interval is not melodic <note>original: "concinnum"</note> in its own right, nor always; for the human voice is not accustomed to move through this interval in one and the same <term>melodic flow<gloss>original: ἀγωγή (agoge)</gloss></term> as it does through other intervals. Instead, the voice neglects and leaps over it, except only in the variation of a song for the sake of "seasoning." Then it becomes extraordinarily melodic, but in such a way that a new "genus" of song seems to begin; and it is a task of no small labor to achieve this with the human voice without an organ. Therefore, this interval only distinguishes the types of melodic intervals, and in that way, it serves them.

# BOOK III ON THE HARMONIES

<margin>Chapter IV.</margin>
We began to speak of the third class of intervals; for the first among them, 24:25, or the <term>diesis<gloss>a very small musical interval, the difference between a major and minor third</gloss></term>, was also the last of the <term>melodic intervals<gloss>concinna: intervals Kepler considers mathematically "fitting" or harmonious enough for song</gloss></term>. Now follow the names of the remaining ones. For the ratio 128:135,

<margin>Major Diesis or Remainder</margin>
<image-desc>A small musical diagram containing sharp symbols (♯) arranged in a grid-like pattern on staff lines, next to the numbers 2025 and 2048.</image-desc>
which arises from the ratio of 15:16 <note>the major semitone</note> and 8:9 <note>the major tone</note>, can be called the *major and irregular diesis*. As was stated just a little while ago, this is smaller than the melodic interval of the semitone by a quantity of 2025:2048, and can scarcely be distinguished from it. It is included among the melodic intervals by this name because it takes the place of a legitimate diesis, especially in the changing of a song <note>modulation</note>. Indeed, its origin is not so much natural as it is necessary for use, so that semitones and dieses may be available everywhere for the various "seasonings" of a song. For this reason, since the legitimate semitone is cut away from a Major Tone, leaving this interval remaining, we can also call it by the Greek word <term>Limma<gloss>original: "Limma", meaning "Remainder"</gloss></term>.

<margin>Comma</margin>
Finally, the difference of 80:81 coming between the melodic intervals 8:9 and 9:10 can be called by us a <term>Comma<gloss>from the Latin "segmentum" or "conciſio", meaning a segment or a cutting</gloss></term>. For the ancients used to cut their Diesis into four parts, and for that reason called them "Commas," believing this to be the common element of all consonants. This interval, however, is a little larger than a fourth part of our diesis, and smaller than a third part. For 24:25 is the same as 72:75 or 96:100. Therefore, a third part would be 74:75, and a fourth part approximately 96:97; but 80:81 <note>The Syntonic Comma</note> falls between the two. We could define it by a closer number as the eighth part of a major tone (8:9). This is also evident as follows: here the Major Tone 8:9 is divided into a diesis 72:75, a semitone 75:80, and a comma 80:81. A comma was just now about a third part of a diesis; therefore, approximately four commas are equivalent to half a Tone; eight to a whole Tone—at least approximately, if not perfectly. This interval, therefore, is clearly not among those melodic intervals that are sung in succession, because its smallness is scarcely perceptible to the ear, let alone expressible by the human voice on its own in two successive notes. Yet it does not on that account cease to be "melodic" like 11:12 and similar ratios, because we also compare those things which are separated by place and time. A double semitone must be established for this reason: in the division of Tones arranged in succession, two semitones are sometimes placed one after another; and when these are fused into one, they are sometimes used instead of a tone by those who affect variety and the unusual to express deep emotions of the soul.

# CHAPTER V.
## On the natural division of Consonant intervals
### into Melodic ones, and the names arising
### from this.

What the Melodic intervals <note>original: "Concinna"</note> were—that is, those intervals observable by human ears in the performance of song and imitable by the voice of the singer—was discussed in the preceding chapter. Now we must examine with special care into which Melodic intervals each of the Consonants is naturally divided, with Nature as our guide.

Taking up again the same numbers through which all the natural harmonic divisions of a single string were gathered into one view: it will appear to us that the interval between the numbers 75 and 100, with 80 and 90 placed in between, has been divided into these three melodic intervals: the semitone 75:80 (or 15:16), the **Major Tone** 80:90 (that is 8:9), and the **Minor Tone** 90:100 (that is 9:10).

<image-desc>A musical/mathematical diagram illustrating the division of the interval 75-100. A horizontal line contains the numbers 75, 80, 90, and 100. Curved arcs above indicate the ratios 15/16, 8/9, and 9/10 respectively between these points. Brackets indicate larger composite ratios, including the 3/4 interval across the whole set.</image-desc>

<margin>The Fourth or Diatessaron</margin>
The same thing also happened with the interval between the numbers 72 and 96, with the same 80 and 90 intervening. For 72:80 is the 9:10 **Minor Tone**; and 80:90, as above, is the **Major Tone**; finally, 90:96 is the 15:16 **Semitone**. On both sides, however, between the extremes—both 75 to 100 and 72 to 96—the interval of 3:4 is found. Therefore, since Nature has taught us to fit these numbers together because of the division of a circle through demonstrable figures: Nature, therefore, through the very act of division, divided two <term>sesquitertial<gloss>a ratio of 4:3, where the larger number contains the smaller plus its third part</gloss></term> intervals into three perfect Melodic intervals: the Major Tone, the Minor Tone, and the Semitone. And yet, for three contiguous intervals, there must be four locations, or voices, or strings. Hence, the sesquitertial interval began to be called a "Fourth"—implying the fourth voice from the first, whether counting from the one above or the one below. For the same reason the Greeks call this interval *Diatessaron* <note>original: "Διατεσσαρων"</note>, which we also express with Latin letters, writing it in the customary way as <term>Diatessaron<gloss>from the Greek for "through four notes"</gloss></term>.

<image-desc>A second diagram similar to the first, showing the interval 72-96. The horizontal line is marked 72, 80, 90, and 96. Arcs show ratios of 9/10, 8/9, and 15/16. A bracket highlights the overall 3/4 ratio between 72 and 96.</image-desc>

<margin>The Fifth or Diapente.</margin>
It follows, therefore, that because the <term>sesquialterate<gloss>a ratio of 3:2, where the larger number contains the smaller plus its half</gloss></term> interval adds one perfect tone (since the difference between 2:3 and 3:4 was 8:9), for this very reason it is called a "Fifth," or, in imitation of the Greek pronunciation, <term>Diapente<gloss>from the Greek for "through five notes"</gloss></term>. This is despite the fact that, by our harmonic divisions, sesquialterate intervals are not actually divided into that many melodic intervals; for that reason, one number necessary for this full division is still missing for us. This is a defect which God the Creator Himself expressed even in the motions of the planets, as we shall hear in Book Five.

Furthermore, because in this way both 5:8 and 3:5 add to the sesquialterate...

From this, they are called Sixths: the former the major, the latter the minor.

<margin>What the major & minor third are.</margin>
Conversely, because both the 4:5 and 5:6 ratios take away one of the aforementioned Elements from the <term>sesquitertia</term> <note>The ratio 4:3, which defines the musical interval of a Fourth.</note>—namely, that semitone 15:16 or that minor tone 9:10, as was shown in the preceding chapter—there remain for them only two of the melodic elements: for the former, a Major and Minor Tone; for the latter, a Major Tone and a semitone. Because of this, some call these intervals by the Greek word <term>Ditonos</term> <note>Ditone: literally "two tones."</note>, the major and minor (or "semiditone"). Since two intervals require three terms or pitches, they are therefore called the **Major and Minor Thirds**. Of these intervals, which are established by the natural divisions of the string, the others are indeed actually divided in this way, but the highest and lowest are not yet actually divided.

<margin>Galileo <note>Referring to Vincenzo Galilei, the music theorist and father of the astronomer.</note> uses the word "Ditone" to signify something else from the most ancient music, which differs from the major third consonance. See Chapter XII.</margin>

<margin>The origin of the names "Major" or "Minor" Third and Sixth, or "Hard" and "Soft."</margin>
And since the harmonies 3:5 and 4:5 arise from the <term>Pentagon</term>, whose side is <term>ineffable</term> <note>In geometry, "ineffable" or "irrational" means the side cannot be expressed as a simple fraction of the diameter.</note>, and since 5:8 and 5:6 also share something of the nature of the Pentagon, it follows that both pairs are of a more "imperfect" consonance. The smaller the interval, the more "soft" and pleasing it falls upon the ears. Indeed, the interval is "minor" in 5:6 and 5:8 because they divide the whole circle—either by a more perfect figure (such as the Hexagon, whose side is <term>effable</term> <note>Rational/expressible in length.</note>) or into parts of a continually doubled proportion (which is identical to itself)—namely, into 6 and 8. Therefore, 5:8 and 5:6 are considered the **soft sixth and third**; whereas 3:5 and 4:5 are considered the **hard or harsh sixth and third**; and they are so named.

<margin>What the eighth or Diapason is.</margin>
It follows, therefore, that the last note in the counting of the sequence is the eighth. From this, the interval obtained the name **Octave**. The Greeks, looking at how the sound is identical to the first, call it *Dia pason* <note>original: "Διὰ πασῶν", meaning "through all [the notes]"</note>, which is written in Latin letters as **Diapason**. It is named as if, once all the differently sounding notes have been used up, the singer's voice returns to itself at the eighth sound. From there, a new beginning and a new series of Melodic intervals arises, similar in every way to the first: see Proposition I.

<image-desc>A musical staff with five horizontal lines and eight notes in an ascending scale. Three brackets above the staff identify specific intervals: 'Diapente' (the Fifth) spans the first five notes; 'Diateffaron' (the Fourth) spans the fourth through seventh notes; 'Systemadiapafon' (the Octave System) spans the entire eight-note octave scale.</image-desc>

Philosophers wonder in vain about this Number: why, for instance, does the eighth voice consume all others and return to the same starting point? The true answer must be given by "begging the question" <note>The author suggests the answer is inherent in the definition itself.</note>: namely, because it is an act of nature that the interval of the double ratio (the 2:1 proportion), which according to Chapter I is an **Identical-sounding** interval, is divided into seven melodic intervals determined by eight sounds, as has been proven in this chapter. These philosophers <margin>What is a System?</margin> think this happens because the Number 8 is the First Cube and the first "Tessera" <note>A solid or die; in geometry, 8 is the first cubic number (2x2x2).</note>. But what does the dividing of a string have to do with solid shapes? And why then would the twenty-seventh voice (which is the second cube, 3x3x3) not also return to the same sound?

Consequently, the name **System** properly and primarily applies to the interval of the double ratio (the octave), when it is divided into its seven Melodic parts, described by its eight voices or strings, and expressed on musical instruments. We will discuss this further in Chapter IX.

<margin>The Double Octave.</margin>
For those intervals that exceed the octave or Diapason, we use multiples. A double Octave is usually called in Greek *Dis dia pason* <note>original: "Δὶς διὰ πασῶν", meaning "twice through all"</note>, a triple is a *Trisdiapason*, and so on. In other cases, we name the Diapason (or its multiple) and add the remainder, in this way: a "Fifth above the octave," or an "Octave above the Fifth," or *Diapason-plus-diapente* <note>original: "Διά πεντε επι δια πασῶν"</note>. Sometimes we also continue by number, calling them the Ninth, Tenth, Twelfth, etc.

This division of consonant intervals into melodic ones is natural. This quantity and the number of melodic elements—being no greater than three <note>referring to the major tone, minor tone, and semitone</note>—is not based solely on the ears becoming accustomed to them. Rather, the sense of hearing possesses this by natural instinct. No other intervals, nor any other number of intervals, can be accepted as melodic divisions for any of the consonances. For if you wanted, for example, to add a **Diesis** <note>A very small musical interval, even smaller than a semitone.</note>, first of all, that interval is the offspring of dissonant elements. Secondly, even if you specifically wanted to add it because it originates from Consonances, you could not do so alone; it would drag with it the **Limma** or **minor Semitone**, which arises only from dissonances. It is only fitting that the sense of hearing distinguishes that from the offspring of consonances; while admitting the latter during singing and as secondary intervals, it rejects the former as spurious.

->Therefore, the Diesis shall not be counted among the principal intervals of the Octave.<-

# CHAPTER VI.

## On the types of song: Hard and Soft.

The types of figures were discussed in Book I, Proposition XLIX. Since the sections of the string itself imitate these figures (according to Axiom II of this book), it follows that because the section of the continuously double proportion <note>The 2:1 ratio of the Octave</note>, the Triangular section, and its continuously double proportions are derived from the primary figures with expressible sides <note>Kepler uses "expressible" (effabilium) to mean rational—lengths that can be measured as simple whole numbers or fractions</note> (namely the Triangle and the Square); while the Pentagonal section is created from an in-expressible side <note>The side of a regular pentagon is irrational in relation to the radius of its circle</note>; then, by Axiom IV, those first sections produce one type of song, and the latter produce another. To this second type, the bisection <note>the 1:2 ratio</note> is also mixed—not because of the four-sided figure, but solely because of the identity of the bisection's consonance.

Hence, two types of sections are born. One possesses these sections:

<margin>CHAPTER VI.</margin>
These are those two commonly celebrated types of Song; the former is called the **soft song** <note>Latin: *cantus mollis*, corresponding to the modern minor scale</note>, because within it are found the intervals of the **Third** and **Sixth** arranged from the lowest note as "soft" <note>minor</note> intervals. The latter is called the **hard song** <note>Latin: *cantus durus*, corresponding to the modern major scale</note>, named after the intervals of the same denomination <note>the Third and Sixth</note> arranged in the same place in the system of the octave, the reasoning for which names was stated in the preceding Chapter V.

For just as in that instance, in the lowest position, the ratio 5:6 did not allow for 3:5, so here 4:5 does not allow for 5:8. This is because the nature of a harmonious song requires that the third combined with the sixth must create a <term>perfect fourth</term> <note>Latin: *diatessaron*, the interval of a fourth (4:3)</note>.

From this, the natural boundary of each genus becomes apparent. For since in the soft song the 5:6 ratio <note>minor third</note> is in the lowest position, and in the hard song the 4:5 ratio <note>major third</note> is there, the difference between them—namely the <term>diesis</term> <note>A small interval with the ratio 24:25</note>—does not arise from the ordinary harmonious intervals according to Chapter IV. Therefore, the 4:5 and 5:6 ratios cannot stand together in the lowest position within the same series of natural song. Instead, when the 4:5 <note>major third</note> is assumed, the 5:6 must be exiled from that position for that turn; or, if the 5:6 is accepted, the other is pushed out. Where the 4:5 ratio draws the 3:5 <note>major sixth</note> along with it, the 5:6 ratio draws the 5:8 <note>minor sixth</note> with it.

Furthermore, God himself expressed this distinction between both types of harmony in the motions of the planets, as we shall hear in Book V.

Regarding those three Genera of the Ancients, which bear the names **Diatonic**, **Chromatic**, and **Enharmonic**, I deliberately refrain from speaking of them here, lest I confuse the reader. However, you might interpret the **Diatonic** as the Hard Song, and the **Chromatic** as the Soft Song—or perhaps the Diatonics as the individual types, while the Chromatic is a mixture of the hard and soft. As for the **Enharmonic**, it has nothing corresponding to it in natural song; yet in the music commonly practiced, the vibrations of the human voice, the "tremor" of Organs, the <term>mordents</term> <note>rapid melodic ornaments</note> on the strings of the lute, and similar effects correspond to it to some extent.

See what we discuss regarding these Genera below in the Appendix to the text of Ptolemy.

# CHAPTER VII.
## On the full division of one Octave
## in both types of song, and on the natural order of all concordant intervals.

Thus far, Nature herself has shown that in the **soft song**, the third concordant interval from the bottom is the **minor Tone** (9:10), the fourth is the **major Tone** (8:9), and the fifth is the **semitone** (15:16). In the **hard song**, however, the third from the bottom is the **semitone** (15:16), the fourth is the **major Tone** (8:9), and the fifth is the **minor Tone** (9:10).

There remain in both types of Song two thirds—one minor and one major—which have not yet been actually divided into their minimal concordant elements by the natural sections of the string.

First, let us see into which concordant intervals those thirds can be divided, and then in what order each should be placed.

Nature teaches us well enough if we can divide them into the same elements of which we have seen them to consist so far; Nature showing that the Diatessa- <note>original: "Diatessa-" is the start of "Diatessaron"</note>

<margin>CHAPTER VI.</margin>
...the <term>perfect fourth</term> <note>Latin: *diatessaron* (4:3)</note> consonances; we ought not to use others whose examples nature does not show. Arithmetic therefore teaches that the ratio 4:5 <note>the Major Third</note> consists of 8:9 and 9:10; likewise 5:6 <note>the Minor Third</note> consists of 8:9 and 15:16. Behold the same elegant arrangement <note>Latin: *concinna*</note> as we have seen thus far.

Unless you arrange the **Major Tone** <note>the interval 8:9</note> in the lowest position of each lower Third, there cannot be a single string shared by both types of song. For if in the **soft song** <note>minor key</note> you were unable to place the major tone in the lowest position, you would necessarily have to place the semitone 15:16 there, because these two alone are contained within the undivided 5:6 interval. In the **hard song** <note>major key</note>, on the other hand, the **Minor Tone** <note>9:10</note> would have to be placed in the lowest position, because that undivided consonance—namely the Major Third—does not contain the semitone which previously would have been placed in the lowest position for the soft song; thus two strings would be created, the longer of which would form a semitone with the lowest note for the soft song, and the other a minor tone for the hard song.

Secondly, it is added that it seems agreeable to nature that, wherever we have a free choice of section, the larger intervals should incline toward the lower sounds, because the lower sounds themselves are <note>vibrationally</note> lesser than the higher ones.

By this same primary reasoning we shall also prove that the upper third, which has remained undivided until now, must be divided such that the major tone is in the highest position, so that the seventh string does not become doubled. For in the soft song the upper interval is 4:5, and in the hard it is 5:6, according to the natural method delivered in the previous sections. If, therefore, we were to arrange the perfect tone (the other element of the Third) in the lower position of this upper Third, then the same interval rising from pitches of different heights would also reach pitches of different heights, which would make two strings instead of one. These reasons are demonstrative and plainly necessary; they suffice against the authorities of **Ptolemy**, **Zarlino**, and **Galilei** <note>Vincenzo Galilei, father of Galileo</note>, who place the minor tone in the lowest position of the octave.

Therefore, the eight strings are explained by these numbers, reduced to the same common lowest denominator.

<margin>CHAPTER VI.</margin> These are those two commonly celebrated types of song; the former is called **soft song** <note>Latin: *cantus mollis*; essentially the minor mode</note>, because there are found in it, ordered from the lowest note, soft intervals—the **Minor Third** and **Minor Sixth**. But the latter is **hard song** <note>Latin: *cantus durus*; essentially the major mode</note>, named from the intervals of the same name <note>the Major Third and Major Sixth</note> ordered in the same place in the octave system. The reasoning for these names was given in the preceding Chapter V.

For just as in that case the ratio 5:6 <note>Minor Third</note> in the lowest position did not tolerate the 3:5 <note>Major Sixth</note>, so now here the ratio 4:5 <note>Major Third</note> does not tolerate 5:8 <note>the Minor Sixth</note>; for the nature of a harmonious song requires this: that the **Third** together with the **Sixth** should form a <term>perfect fourth</term> <note>Latin: *diatessaron*; the ratio 4:3</note>.

From this, therefore, the natural boundary of each genus appears. For since in soft song the 5:6 ratio is in the lowest place, and in hard song the 4:5 ratio is there, the difference between the two—namely the <term>diesis</term> <note>the ratio 24:25, a small melodic interval</note>—is not among the ordinary harmonious intervals according to Chapter IV. Therefore, the 4:5 (Major Third) and 5:6 (Minor Third) cannot stand together in the lowest position in the same sequence of natural song. But once the 4:5 Major Third is adopted, it must for that turn exile the 5:6 from the lowest place; or if the latter is received, the former is extruded. In this arrangement, the 4:5 Major Third draws with it the 3:5 Major Sixth, and the 5:6 Minor Third draws with it the 5:8 Minor Sixth.

Furthermore, God himself has expressed this distinction between both types of harmony in the **motions of the planets**, as we shall hear in Book V.

Concerning those three Genera of the Ancients, whose names are **Diatonic**, **Chromatic**, and **Enharmonic**, I deliberately refrain from speaking here, lest I confuse the reader. You could, however, interpret the **Diatonic** as Hard Song, and the **Chromatic** as Soft Song; or perhaps the Diatonic refers to each individually, while the Chromatic is a mixture of hard and soft. But the **Enharmonic** has nothing corresponding to it in natural song; in common music, however, the vibrations of the human voice, the "tremolo" of organs, <term>mordents</term> <note>rapid alternations between notes</note> on the strings of the <term>lute</term> <note>Latin: *pandurae*</note>, and similar ornaments respond to it to some extent.

See what we dispute concerning these Genera below in the Appendix to the text of <note>the ancient astronomer and music theorist</note> Ptolemy.

# ON THE HARMONICS, BOOK III.

<margin>CHAPTER VI.</margin>
The <term>perfect fourth</term> <note>original: *tessaron*; the ratio 4:3</note> consonances; we ought not to use others whose examples nature does not show. Arithmetic therefore teaches that the ratio 4:5 <note>the Major Third</note> consists of 8:9 <note>a Major Tone</note> and 9:10 <note>a Minor Tone</note>; likewise, 5:6 <note>the Minor Third</note> consists of 8:9 and 15:16 <note>a Semitone</note>. Behold the same elegance that we have seen so far.

Unless you arrange the **Major Tone** in the lowest position of each lower Third, it would be impossible to have a single string shared by both types of song. For if, in **soft song** <note>minor mode</note>, you could not place the major tone in the lowest position, you would necessarily have to place the semitone (15:16) there, because these two alone are contained within the undivided 5:6 interval. In **hard song** <note>major mode</note>, on the other hand, a **Minor Tone** would have to be placed in the lowest position, because that undivided consonance—namely the Major Third (4:5)—does not contain the semitone that would have previously been placed at the bottom in the soft song. Thus, two separate strings would be created: the longer one forming a semitone with the lowest note for soft song, and the other a minor tone for hard song.

Secondly, it is added that it seems consistent with nature that, wherever we have a free choice in dividing a scale, the **larger intervals** should gravitate toward the **grave** <note>lower-pitched</note> sounds, because the grave sounds themselves are physically larger than the acute <note>higher-pitched</note> ones.

By this same primary reasoning, we shall also prove that the upper third—hitherto undivided—must be divided so that the major tone is in the highest position, lest the seventh string become doubled. For in soft song the upper interval is 4:5, and in hard song it is 5:6, according to the natural method handed down for the upper parts. If, therefore, we were to arrange the perfect tone (the other element of the Third) in the lower position of this upper Third, then the same interval rising from voices of different pitches would reach voices of different pitches again, making two strings where there should be one. These demonstrative and plainly necessary reasons are sufficient against the authorities of **Ptolemy**, **Zarlino**, and **Galilei**, who place the minor tone in the lowest position of the octave.

Therefore, the eight strings are explained by these numbers, reduced to the same lowest common denominator.

You see expressed in the smallest numbers not only the <term>proportions</term> <note>the mathematical ratios between notes</note> of all eight string lengths, but also the four highest and the four lowest in even smaller numbers. This is especially true of the three highest and the three lowest notes, concerning whose middle notes and their numerical values I have a dispute with other authors in this chapter. For the 7th position in both types of song is 405, and the 2nd position is 640 in both.

Remember, however, that only the eight principal strings of each type are placed in this chapter. Concerning the accessory strings—one of which **hard song** adopts in the position of the "almost-highest" note—we shall examine those in the following chapter. For here our goal is to see how the "almost-highest" and "almost-lowest" notes must be established so that they can be the same in both types of song.

And because, in the joining of these eight principal strings of each song, it happens that two of them are doubled on musical instruments, there are therefore ten principal strings for one <term>octave</term> <note>original: *diapason*</note> in the common system. Nevertheless, no more than eight "Positions" are recognized (and thus also named). See the origin of this term in Chapter IV. **

# CHAPTER VIII.
## On the number and order of the small-
## est intervals of one octave.

The lowest and highest intervals, as well as the fourth, are by nature **Major Tones** <note>the ratio 9:8</note>; the others are made Major Tones by the imitation of nature. From these, again by the imitation of nature (which cuts the **Minor Tone** <note>the ratio 10:9</note> into a semitone and a <term>diesis</term>), the 15:16 semitones are likewise cut off for the sake of greater variety, especially in the bends or turns of the song; and that occurs in the upper part of the interval. There remain, therefore, in the lower part, <term>Limmas</term> <note>the Greek term for the "remainder" or small semitone</note>, or major <term>dieses</term> of 128:135, which exceeds the 24:25 diesis by one <term>comma</term>. <meta>This sentence continues onto the next page.</meta>

The necessity of this <term>division</term> <note>original: *abscissio*; refers to the mathematical "cutting" or dividing of the string length</note> is especially important in the highest interval, which we defined as a <term>major tone</term> <note>a ratio of 9:8</note> in the previous chapter. This is because <term>hard song</term> <note>original: *cantus durus*; the musical system that uses B-natural, often sounding like a major key to modern ears</note> uses either a semitone at the top or a major tone interchangeably as the situation requires. However, it uses the semitone more frequently and almost as a rule. This is because just as the seventh note makes a perfect fourth <note>original: *Epitriton* or *Diatessaron*, a 4:3 ratio</note> with the fourth note (namely, the value 405 with 540 from the previous chapter), so too does this extraordinary seventh note love to form a perfect fifth <note>original: *diapente perfectum*, a 3:2 ratio</note> with the third note. This is because the third note is characteristic of the "hard" genus (specifically, the value 576), so that the melody might be made more brilliant in this way. And indeed, a 2:3 ratio of 576 is 384, which, when compared with the eighth note (360), creates a ratio of 16:15 <note>a standard semitone</note>.

The Lack of Art

among

You see that in two places, two semitones occur below the <term>diesis</term> <note>The small interval that remains when subtracting a minor semitone from a major one</note>, just as I said would happen. Musical craftsmen seize upon this on their organs, using two semitones to make a whole tone whenever they introduce some unusually bold modulation. Although, according to the rules of their craft, they "temper" <note>Kepler is describing "Equal Temperament," where intervals are adjusted away from perfect mathematical ratios so that all keys sound acceptable</note> all the intervals so that none are left pure; they do this so that the intervals which ought to be perfect are slightly diminished—with very little loss of perfection—to support and soften the imperfection of the others. By this reasoning, it happens that all whole tones are equal for organists, and the <term>limma</term> <note>The "remainder" or minor semitone in Pythagorean tuning</note> is equal to the semitone; thus, for them, two semitones make a whole tone by a perfect bisection. So that this might succeed more easily, even the <term>diesis</term> does not retain its own demonstrable perfection among them.

## A Quick Division of the Monochord
## for the Lute, and its Rejection by the
### *Sense of Hearing.*

This place demands that I fulfill what I promised toward the end of the second chapter: namely, that I compare my own discoveries with the "Testudinary" <note>Relating to the lute or "tortoise-shell" (testudo) family of instruments</note> division of the <term>Monochord</term> <note>A single-stringed instrument used to measure musical ratios</note> brought forward by *Vincenzo Galilei* <note>Father of the famous astronomer Galileo Galilei; a prominent music theorist who advocated for equal temperament</note>, if I am not mistaken, following *Aristoxenus*. I shall also question the ears on this matter, yet in such a way that Reason may speak what it is appropriate for the ears themselves to say.

Since the <term>Diapason</term> <note>The Greek term for an Octave</note> consists of seven harmonious intervals (from which it takes the name "Octave," as said in the previous chapter), and among these intervals are five whole tones and two semitones; and since any of the whole tones can be bisected into parts close to a semitone, so that there become twelve intervals—defined in this chapter by the letters *G, G#, A, Bb, C, C#, D, D#, E, F, F#, g*—from this, the makers of instruments have also established twelve intervals within one Octave. They did this by a way that is not at all laborious, but entirely easy and expedient, as is fitting for most mechanical tasks; it is as follows: 

The total length of the neck of the lute—between the two "saddles" or <term>magadia</term> <note>The nut and the bridge which support the string and define its vibrating length</note> upon which the string rests and vibrates freely—is divided into 18 equal parts. They place the first ligature or <term>Tactus</term> <note>A fret, usually made of tied gut on a Renaissance lute</note> near the tuning pegs so that 1 part is above and 17 parts are below. Then, ignoring the previous division points, they divide the remaining 17 parts into 18 new parts, and cut off one part for the second fret as before. They repeat this twelve times. They claim that with the twelfth "cut," the part of the string remaining is such that the ratio between it and the whole string is the **consonance of the octave**. 

Let the length of the string be 100,000 units. If 18 parts make 100,000, what do 17 make? The result is 94,444. Again, if 18 parts are worth 94,444, what are 17? The result is 89,198. And if 18 parts are worth 89,198, what are 17? The result is 84,242, and so on. In this way, twelve numbers are produced for the twelve intervals. Next to them are placed the numbers that True Reason, as demonstrated thus far, requires for the total string length.

If this calculation were exact, then surely the ratio repeated twelve times would be equal to the double ratio of *1 to 2* <note>The mathematical ratio of an octave</note>. However, any good mathematician knows this is false, since *1 to 2* and *17 to 18* are <term>incommensurable</term> <note>Meaning they cannot be expressed as a simple whole-number ratio of each other; the "Rule of 18" never perfectly reaches a 2:1 octave</note>. This...

<margin>CHAPTER VIII.</margin>
Nevertheless, the mechanical sectioning of the string satisfies the hearing well enough; this is because the individual numbers closely approach the true ones placed beside them, and because the strings of lutes <note>original: *chelyum*, referring to instruments of the lute or lyre family</note> are flexible and their sounds are, in a certain way, varied—sharper <note>higher in pitch</note> at the beginning when their motion is still large, having just been released from the finger; and flatter <note>original: *graviores*, lower in pitch</note> and more relaxed when the width of the vibration is contracted into a narrow space as the string returns to itself. Indeed, there is even a difference in a lighter or stronger touch, and in the widening or reduction [of the vibration], according to the skill of the Musician. But if you examine the judgment of the hearing with the skillful investigation of *Reason*, the disagreement will immediately appear. I prove it thus: the ears certainly recognize the harmony between 100,000 and 50,363, as the *Craftsman* <note>Kepler refers to Vincenzo Galilei as "the Mechanic" or "Craftsman" because he prioritized practical instrument construction over pure mathematical theory.</note> affirms; they also recognize the same between 100,000 and 50,000, as I affirm. The question is whether the ears notice no difference, and whether this harmony occupies so great a width? I respond from my harmonic sections in *Chapter II* that it does not. For just as they discern nothing between two Consonances of strings 100,000 to 50,000 and strings 100,000 to 50,363, in the same way they would not discern between two Consonances of strings 100,000 to 50,000 and strings 100,000 to 49,637, because the difference between the two consonances is equal on both sides.

But if this part or that is not plucked against the whole 100,000, but rather the parts themselves—50,363 on one side and 49,637 on the other—are plucked next to each other: then it is absolutely necessary that the shorter part emit a sharper sound and the longer part a flatter sound. This difference of sounds is easily detected by the ears in an examination of unison parts. It is clear, therefore, that the ears judge the same consonance to exist between 50,363 and 100,000 as between 49,637 and 100,000 only insofar as 50,363 and 49,637 appear to be equal; that is, insofar as neither one differs sensibly from 50,000. Therefore, if the ears respond according to the questions of *Reason*, they will say that the exact *Harmony* exists between 100,000 and 50,000—that is, between 2 and 1 <note>the ratio of an Octave</note>. For this reason, it is false that there is an exact *Consonance* between 100,000 and 50,363.

The same judgment applies to the *Harmony* between 100,000 and 67,025 <note>an approximation of a Perfect Fifth</note>; for even if the ears do not at first discern it from 66,667, the just length of a truly consonant Part, yet the remainder of that (32,975) is not half of the 67,025 itself. Therefore, the double of that (65,950) will sound one way, and the 67,025 itself will sound another, since these strings, when compared to each other, make a different sound. The reason the ears do not discern these in *Harmony* is because they approve of the middle number—if the sense is sharpened—namely 66,667, so that its complement may be 33,333, which is exactly half of it.

Now that the sharpness of the sense has been established in the judging of the Harmony of 2 to 3, and likewise...

Likewise, from 1 to 3, it follows that we may judge similarly concerning 2 and 3 with 5, and concerning 1 and 3 with 4. For if 59,785 <note>This number refers to the ratio for the note 'e' in Galilei’s system from the table on the previous page.</note> were to harmonize with 100,000, and thus also the remaining 40,215, this is certainly not a two-thirds ratio <note>original: *bes*, a Latin term for the ratio 2:3, which in this context refers to the interval of a Major Sixth</note> of the former; even though the consonance of the Two-Thirds has already been justified as perfect, namely 60,000 with 40,000. In this way, the hearing is guided—if it is sharpened by reason—from one division to another, beginning from the unison, the recognition and judgment of which is easiest, until it traverses all of them, approving the parts which my numbers designate and rejecting the "mechanical" divisions of the first order.

Look at another very clever temperament of this kind in the work of Vincenzo Galilei, <note>Vincenzo Galilei (c. 1520–1591), father of the astronomer Galileo, was a famous music theorist who advocated for equal temperament on fretted instruments.</note> made not from ignorance of the demonstrable quantity of sounds, but with singular zeal. And indeed, I acknowledge its mechanical use, so that we may use organs with almost the same freedom of tension found in the human voice; but for theoretical contemplation—indeed, for discerning the very nature of song—I deem it pernicious. It causes the organ to never truly attain the purity of human singing.

## CHAPTER IX.

The matter is not without dispute; but I follow the necessary reasons. Musicians of our age draw the strings differently in lute diagrams <note>original: *diagrammatis Testudinarijs*, referring to lute tablature, as "testudo" means tortoise-shell, the traditional material for lutes</note> than in singing diagrams <note>The modern musical staff</note>. For in the former, the individual lines of the diagram denote individual strings, any of which produce different sounds for different fingerings if they are plucked. In singing types, not only do the individual lines signify individual voices or strings, but even the intervals <note>spaces</note> between two lines signify an intermediate string.

In this way, 4 horizontal lines with three spaces denote 7 strings, and 5 lines with 4 spaces denote nine strings. Next, they express the voices of the singing system either by specific notes in their proper place on the diagram (which notes simultaneously suggest the measure of time), or by the first seven letters of the alphabet, or finally by six syllables: *ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la*; or as the Belgians do today, with these seven: *Bo, ce, di, ga, lo, ma, ni*. <note>This seven-syllable system is known as "Bocedization," an alternative to the traditional six-syllable hexachord system.</note>

For because there are two kinds of song, *hard* <note>original: *durum*, associated with B-natural and major-sounding scales</note> and *soft* <note>original: *molle*, associated with B-flat and minor-sounding scales</note>, which begin from one common lowest voice, the difference is this: the third and the sixth are one *diesis* <note>A small musical interval or semi-tone</note> higher in "hard" song than in "soft." Therefore, the third and sixth strings cannot remain stable in both kinds of song; it is necessary either to make them double in instruments and organs (as was done in the numbers in Chapter VII) or to vary them by touch, as I believe was done of old on the lyre and the pan-pipes. The same must be said of the Diagram and the human voice. Since only one diagram is made for the octaves of both kinds rising from the same root, and in it there are only eight places for the eight sounds
