### ON HARMONICS, BOOK III.

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>
...indicators; from both types of song <note>Kepler refers to *cantus durus* (hard song, using B-natural) and *cantus mollis* (soft song, using B-flat), the ancestors of our major and minor modes.</note> ten principal strings are gathered into one octave, according to Chapter VII; however, there are thirteen of all kinds, according to Chapter VIII: thus it happens that two sounds, separated by a <term>Diesis</term> <note>A very small interval, often the difference between a major and minor semitone.</note> or a <term>Limma</term> <note>A "remainder" interval in Pythagorean tuning, slightly smaller than a semitone.</note>, are drawn in the same place on the diagram <note>The musical staff.</note>, whether that be on a line or in the space between lines. This is because diesis and limma intervals are not sung one after another like Tones and semitones; for this reason, I have also refused to call them "minor semitones," as some do. For this reason, then, certain **Signs** <note>original: *Notæ*</note> had to be placed before the lines and spaces—the images of the strings—by which "hard" song could be distinguished from "soft," and the location of the semitone would be clear, whether it be the ordinary one or the others cut off from the major tones. There is also another more hidden necessity, arising not from the diversity of types of song, but within any song itself, from the inequality of the Major and Minor Tones; so that they may be distinguished against one another in the diagrams. For it is necessary that the syllables **Ut**, **Re**, **Mi** <note>The early "solfège" system used to name notes of the scale.</note> be general and applicable to both the Major and Minor Tone. Therefore, however much these names may satisfy those learning to sing and practical organists, they by no means satisfy the theoreticians. Because of this function, these letters, when they are placed at the beginning of the diagrams, are usually called **Clefs** <note>original: *Claves*, meaning "keys."</note>, because without them, the entrance to the diagram is not open to the singer.

In fact, these same letters are also used on musical organs; for they are inscribed on the handles of the plectrums <note>The keys of a stringed keyboard.</note> in stringed instruments, or on the stops in wind instruments. By virtue of this inscription, those handles are called **Keys** <note>original: *Claves*</note> in their own right, and the arrangement itself, or the system of all the handles, is called the keyboard, *the Clavier*, and the type of instrument is called the **Clavichord**; this is because the strings are struck by "keys"—that is, by handles depressed from the outside—and by plectrums jumping up from the inside.

<margin>Tablature, or diagrams.</margin>
Furthermore, there are diagrams usually written for organists in which, instead of black lines, there are series of letters indicating which Keys ought to be touched: here letters stand in place of the Notes which the singing-diagrams used to employ, placed on lines or in spaces.

Concerning these letters, several things come to our observation which are quite pleasing. First, not all letters are placed on their own lines and spaces, but only these: *F, G, C*, whenever one of their places is upon a line; and *B* as well, even when it occupies a space.

<margin>Source of the sign <note>The C-clef symbol.</note></margin>
Next, the letter *C* has a sign far different from the letter itself, such as the one drawn here at the side. I believe this sign was born from a distortion of the old handwriting of the letter *C*. For because writers used broad-tipped pens <note>original: *calamorum mucronibus*</note>, most notes were made square by a shorthand style of writing; a round *C* could not be drawn with those pens. Therefore, they made a *C* out of three small lines: one thin one in place of the hollow, and two thick ones in place of the horns, with the pen drawn sideways like this: <note>three horizontal strokes, the middle one thinner than the outer two</note>. Now, as the pen hurried, the thin line was for the most part made longer, standing out on both sides beyond the horns, like this: <note>three horizontal strokes, the middle one elongated</note>. However, so that the horns would be finished, they drew lines parallel to the first one, like this: <note>the two thick horizontal strokes capped with vertical bars</note>. And so finally, from two such lines, one was made similar and parallel to the first, and the whole sign became like this: <note>C-clef symbol</note>, which, like the notes themselves on the lines, is made hollow by the gap of the pen, like this: <note>C-clef symbol centered on a staff line</note>.

Yet this also occurs to me: whether this sign might have been born from the use of the term "Musical Scale" <note>original: *Scala Musica*</note>, since it presents the figure of a ladder <note>Kepler notes the visual similarity between the C-clef and a ladder, *scala* in Latin.</note>: as if it were the beginning of the Scale...

<margin>
On the letter f.

But when there is no place for the letter *C.* on a line (because formerly there were mostly only four lines), then there is a place for the letter *F.* on one of the lines: which is written in other higher voices with its own natural mark, but in the Bass as a curved semicircle with two dots beside it <note>The modern F-clef or bass clef.</note>: which sign I think was, in the beginning before it was distorted, the Greek lowercase $\gamma$ (*gamma*), such that the two dots added signify a **Digamma** <note>An archaic Greek letter ($\digamma$) that represented a sound similar to /w/ or /f/. Kepler suggests our "F" comes from this 'double-gamma'.</note>, because our *F.* is the Greeks' double $\Gamma$. For that this method of signifying the sounds of the System through the letters of the Alphabet flowed down from the Greeks is attested to by **Vincenzo Galilei** <note>Vincenzo Galilei (1520–1591), father of Galileo, was a famous music theorist whom Kepler frequently cites.</note>, by producing very ancient examples of Greek songs. And it is admitted that even the simple Greek $\Gamma$ has found a place in our Latin Music, as will now be said.

<margin>
On the letter g.
</margin>
This *F*, therefore, is the second signed <term>clef</term> <note>original: *clavis*, literally "key". In early music, the "key" or clef unlocked the identity of the notes on the staff.</note>; moreover, both are marked near each other where a convenient place for both occurs. The third is *G*, which is expressed in higher voices when there is a place for it on a line. It is also marked, according to ancient custom, on the bottom line of the diagram. For the musical scale today begins from the sound $\Gamma$ ut, or **Gammut** <note>The lowest note of the medieval "Guidonian Hand" system; the origin of the word "gamut" meaning a full range.</note>, which indicates the lowest *G* sound <note>original: *phthongum gravissimum*</note>; so that Digamma and Gamma are the same as *F* and *G*.

<margin>
On the letter b.
</margin>
But *b* is also painted on the diagram in softer melodies <note>original: *molliusculis*, referring to the 'soft' hexachord which used B-flat.</note> additionally, to distinguish the genus of song, whether it falls on a line or in a space: its presence signifies "soft" song <note>original: *cantum mollem*, using B-flat</note>, its absence "hard" song <note>original: *durum*, using B-natural</note>. But not only this, but also in other lines or intervals which are not assigned to the Clef *b*, the letter *b* is nonetheless found and, by a certain misuse, repeated as a sign of a semitone or the syllable **FA**.

<margin>
On the letter $\natural$.
</margin>
On the contrary, when a semitone is extraordinarily established in place of a whole tone, and the syllable **MI** in place of the syllable **FA**, then the letter $\natural$ <note>The precursor to the natural ($\natural$) and sharp ($\sharp$) signs.</note> or a sign derived from it is placed before the note. For the ancients undoubtedly drew it as $\natural$; but in its place we use $\sharp$ or $\natural$: which **Galilei** thinks wishes to say the same thing to the reader as the ancient Greek word **Diaschisma** <note>An interval meaning a "splitting" or "fissure".</note>; for it expresses a fissure clearly enough and indicates to us the cutting-off of semitones, which we discussed in the preceding Chapter VIII.

In the manuals <note>original: *Manubrijs*</note> of Organ Tenors, we do not allow this ambiguity with the letter *b* in a place not its own. For first, all the Clefs or keys of those sounds which are formed by cutting off semitones from a whole tone, and which increase the eight-fold number of the Octave System <note>Kepler is describing the black keys on a keyboard that expand the basic 8-note scale into 12 or 13 tones.</note>; and are elevated, or standing out above the flat principal keys; and are black in color; then, upon each black key is inscribed the letter of the neighboring key, but with a tail, for distinction; (except for $\natural$, in whose place a simple black *b* is placed on the key) and the tail signifies a higher pitch, such as *f, g, g, b, ♮, c, c, d, d*; but between *f* and *e*, *g* and *g-sharp*, *c* and *c-sharp*, there is a <term>limma</term> <note>A small interval, specifically the Pythagorean minor semitone.</note>, and between *b* and $\natural$ a <term>diesis</term> <note>The smallest interval in Kepler's system, here the difference between a B-flat and B-natural.</note>, between the same letters, just as their two pitches [are found] in a single place of the dia-

<margin>
CHAPTER IX.
</margin>
...are expressed by letters. But between $d$ and $d_\sharp$ <note>Kepler uses a specific notation for sharps/flats which varies in the text; here he is discussing the semitone or half-step.</note> there is a semitone; so that these two letters, although they appear the same, are not assigned to the same place on the staff, but to successive ones. However, a **diesis** <note>In ancient theory, a diesis is an interval smaller than a semitone; in Kepler’s context, it refers to the small tuning difference between certain notes.</note> exists between $d_\sharp$ and $e$, and these different letters occupy the same place: this diversity must be granted to ancient custom and softened by practical use. Finally, between $f_\sharp$ and $g$, $g_\sharp$ and $a$, $a$ and $b\flat$, $b$ and $c$, $d_\sharp$ and $e$, and $e$ and $f$, there are semitones. Therefore, caution must be applied here, so that we do not presume anything about the identity of an interval based on an analogy from the same way of writing it.

It is also particularly strange—and similarly to be forgiven as an ancient custom—that in some *Clavichords* and organs (in which the octaves are continuous), although the same letters are rightly and deservedly repeated because of the identity of the **Diapason** <term>Diapason: The Greek term for an octave.</term> consonance, this does not start from the first *A*, but from the second *b*. For this is the order of the characters:

*C. D. E. F. G. A. b. c. d. e. f. g. a. bb. cc. dd. ee. ff. gg. aa. bbb. ccc. ddd. eee. fff. ggg. aaaa. etc.*

<margin>
System.
</margin>
Furthermore, what a diagram is on paper, a *System* is on the organ—namely, the series of all the strings that divide a single consonant interval. As was said in Chapter V, this primarily applies to the interval of the octave; and from that, to all larger intervals, however many a particular instrument encompasses.

<margin>
Ancient names of the strings.
</margin>
Even though it is not my purpose to dwell long on the Music of the ancients, since it is full of obscurity, I did not think I should skip the names by which they designated the eight sounds in a single octave System; for that naming system has a kinship with the letters we have discussed so far.

Therefore, the ancients in the time of **Aristotle** <note>The famous Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE) who wrote extensively on music theory and acoustics.</note> numbered the strings thus: *Hypate*, *Parhypate*, *Lichanos*, *Mese*, *Paramese*, *Trite*, *Paranete*, *Nete*. The voice of the *Hypate* was the lowest, and it seems to have been named so from its position on the instrument when it is held for playing: for it still holds that same position today on the *Chelys* <note>original: "Chely" - a type of lyre, literally "tortoise shell."</note>, the *Pandura* <note>A long-necked lute.</note>, and the *Cithara*.

And since Aristotle affirms that between the *Hypate* and the *Parhypate* there was a **diesis** (that is, the Platonic semitone, which remained when two major tones were subtracted from a **Diatessaron** <term>Diatessaron: An interval of a perfect fourth.</term>, leaving the ratio 243:256, which he called a Diesis): Therefore, the *Hypate* was the same as what we mark with the letter *A*. The *Parhypate* is what the letter *b* marks. Thus the *Lichanos* (named so from the index finger) is *c*. The *Mese*, however, is *d*: it was called by this name because it was the middle among seven, at the time when there were only seven strings on the Psaltery, and the first was struck to serve as the eighth. The *Paramese* holds the letter $d_\sharp$ or $e$; the older musicians used to omit this one. The *Trite* is the letter *f*; it was named so because it was the third in order from the high end, just as we call it the sixth from the low *A*. The *Paranete* is marked by the letter *g*. And the *Nete*, as if it were the last string touched by the plectrum drawn downward, returns to the letter *a*. This distribution is also confirmed by the fact that the interval between the *Nete* and the *Mese* is said to be a **Diapente** <term>Diapente: An interval of a perfect fifth.</term>.

However, such a System of eight strings could not serve both types of singing <note>Likely referring to the hard and soft hexachords or the different Greek genera.</note> unless the *Parhypate* (*b*) and the *Pa-*...

<margin>
CHAPTER IX.
Which notes were stable for the ancients, and which were mobile?
</margin>
...the $b$ and the *paramese* <note>original: "paramese." In ancient Greek music, the note just above the middle note of the scale.</note> $de$, so that they might become $B$-natural and $e$, or so they could be tightened by the tuning pegs in "hard" song <note>Hard song or *cantus durus* refers to music using B-natural, the ancestor of major keys.</note>, or loosened in "soft" song <note>Soft song or *cantus mollis* refers to music using B-flat, the ancestor of minor keys.</note>. On this occasion, the distinction was born between **stable** and **mobile** notes <note>original: "phthongi." In the Greek tetrachord system, the outer notes were fixed (stable), while the inner notes could be tuned differently (mobile) to change the "genus" of the music.</note>, and the very name **diesis** <note>original: "$\delta\iota\acute{\epsilon}\sigma\epsilon\omega\varsigma$."</note> comes from the "loosening" of the mobile strings.

<margin>
The Added Note.
</margin>
In the composition of larger systems of the **octave** <term>Diapason: The Greek term for an octave, literally "through all [the notes]."</term>, the method of the ancients was more intricate; however, it should be observed that they added one note deeper than the *Hypate* <note>The "lowest" note of the ancient tetrachord, though physically it was the highest string on the lyre.</note>, which for this reason was called the **Proslambanomenos** <term>Proslambanomenos: Greek for "the note taken in addition," the lowest pitch in the ancient Great Perfect System.</term>. A trace of this remains in the Musical Scale which our boys learn, which adds a note below the Latin letter $A$ to signify a deeper sound; it marks this note outside the usual order with the Greek letter $\Gamma$ (Gamma). For thus the scale begins: *Gamma-ut, A-re, etc.*

Let it suffice to have touched upon these ancient names of strings in this place. For below in Chapter XI, all fifteen strings of the composite system will be explained using ancient terms, but those of the later musicians.

Now at last, let us approach our **natural system** of a single octave, and apply to it the letters used in music.

<margin>
The natural system begins from G.
</margin>
I therefore establish that the deepest voice of this natural and demonstrative system is that which the ancients called the *Proslambanomenos*, and which the musical scale usually calls *Gamma-ut*; the letter $G$ is certainly to be assigned to it. The reasons are these: because the voices established through harmonic sections <note>Kepler refers to the mathematical division of a string to create intervals.</note> determine such intervals below the octave—with the voice of the whole string—as musicians ordinarily establish between $G$ and $A, B\text{-natural}, c, d, d\sharp, e$.

Someone might say that these same intervals could be understood between $D$ and $F, F\sharp, G, A, B\flat, B\text{-natural}$, or likewise between $c$ and $d\sharp, e, f, g, g\sharp, a$. I do not deny that instrumental musicians use these letters generally, and do not distinguish between **major** and **minor tones** in them <note>In "just intonation," which Kepler favors, there are two different sizes of whole steps (9:8 and 10:9). In modern tuning (equal temperament), these are averaged out.</note>. For what would prevent them from transposing a song from $G$ to $d$? Those who, on their organs, take two tones—the Major (8:9) and the Minor (9:10)—and fuse them into a single interval (4:5) <note>This ratio 4:5 is a Major Third.</note>, and then precisely bisect it into two "usual" tones that are equal to each other? Even if **Galilei** <note>Vincenzo Galilei (c. 1520–1591), a music theorist who advocated for equal temperament; Kepler disagrees with his sacrifice of mathematical purity for practical ease.</note> is more accurate in this tempering. But we are not looking here at the **unskilled practice** <note>original: "$\dot{\alpha}\tau\epsilon\chi\nu\acute{\iota}\alpha\nu$" (atechnian).</note> of the empiricists, but at the **precision** <note>original: "$\dot{\alpha}\kappa\rho\acute{\iota}\beta\epsilon\iota\alpha\nu$" (akribeian).</note> of Nature; therefore, we cannot imitate them. Indeed, they themselves would reject starting the natural octave system from the letter $c$ by this argument: for between their $g\sharp$ and $a$ there is a semitone; and this interval is in the fifth place, because $a$ is a sixth from $c$. But in the Natural System, we need a **diesis** before the sixth. Moreover, musicians themselves place the diesis only between $B\text{-natural}$ and $c$, and between $d\sharp$ and $e$. Therefore, with even the instrumentalists agreeing, our system must arise either from $D$ or from $G$, so that the pure Natural System may be expressed.

But the natural system cannot begin from $D$ either. For it is their custom to place a semitone between $d$ and $d\sharp$; but in my Natural System, there is a **limma** <term>Limma: A "leftover" interval in Pythagorean tuning, slightly smaller than a modern semitone.</term> in the lowest place, which is less than a semitone.

## CHAPTER X.
### On Tetrachords and the use of the syllables: Ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la.

It was the custom of the ancients to divide the system of the **octave** <term>Diapason: The interval of an octave.</term> into two **Tetrachords** <term>Tetrachord: A scale of four notes spanning the interval of a perfect fourth.</term>, and they did so in different ways according to the different intentions of the musicians. For they were either **conjoined** <note>original: "Synemmena." In Greek music, two tetrachords that share a common middle note.</note>, with one sound placed in the middle, which formed a **fourth** <term>Diatessaron: The interval of a perfect fourth (ratio 4:3).</term> both with the lowest note below and the highest note above. Thus, the extremes formed a dissonant interval, a **seventh** <note>original: "Dihepta." An interval of seven notes.</note>, and one whole tone was understood to be added above. For whenever the order required them to strike the octave **a**, they would strike the first **A**, as if it were an identical sound produced from the opposite side, an **antiphon** <note>original: "ἀντίφωνον" (antiphonon). A sound that responds to or mirrors another.</note>. In this way, there were not truly two tetrachords, but rather two intervals of a fourth forming a **heptachord** <note>A seven-note system.</note>. 

Alternatively, the tetrachords were **disjoined** <note>original: "Diezeugmena." In Greek music, two tetrachords separated by the interval of a whole tone.</note> by the interval of one **Major Tone**, which is what the Nature of things suggests even in our own division of the system. In our system, the lower tetrachord contains **G. A. B♭. c.** and the upper contains **d. e. f. g.**, where a major tone lies between **c** and **d**. Perhaps even by their physical position, the four lowest strings were separated from the four higher ones, leaving a larger gap between the two boundary strings.

<image-desc>Two musical examples on five-line staves with C-clefs and diamond-shaped notes. The left staff is labeled "Conjoined Tetrachords" and shows four ascending notes. The right staff is labeled "Disjoined Tetrachords" and shows two groups of four notes separated by a bar line.</image-desc>

The reason they thought in terms of a Tetrachord system was this: they saw that in one **fourth** <note>Diatessaron</note> there are two and a half tones. We also have a Major Tone, a Minor Tone, and a Semitone in a perfect fourth—all the elements arranged harmoniously in a "minor concordance" (for they did not even consider the ratios 4:5 and 5:6 to be concordances). The semitone could be placed in the lowest, middle, or highest position. Thus, all melody seemed to them to be comprised of these three forms of tetrachords.

<image-desc>A single musical staff with diamond-shaped notes divided into three groups of four. Below the first group are the labels "Tone, Tone, Semit."; below the second "Tone, Semit., Tone."; and below the third "Semit., Tone, Tone.".</image-desc>

<margin>A short little line marks a semitone; a medium one a minor tone; a somewhat longer one a major tone.</margin>

For me, the forms of the tetrachords are multiplied because of the distinction between the **Minor Tone** and the **Major Tone**. Instead of three, there become six, and in a single **octave** <note>Diapason</note> most of these appear in pairs. Thus, we also have a certain testimony from Nature for distinguishing the tetrachords, for the upper is [different] from the lower by some—

<image-desc>Six small musical staves arranged in two rows of three, numbered I through VI. Each displays a four-note tetrachord. Beneath the notes are horizontal lines of three varying lengths (short, medium, and long) to indicate semitones, minor tones, and major tones respectively, as described in the marginal note.</image-desc>

And these are only the forms of the perfect fourth <term>Diatessaron: An interval of a perfect fourth, spanning four notes.</term>; we shall deal with the imperfect ones in Chapter XII.

But if we ignore the difference between the major and minor tone, as the organists <note>original: "Organici." This refers to keyboard players and instrument builders who used temperament to simplify the math of tuning.</note> do, then these subsequent disjoined tetrachords are completely similar:

| G A B C | & D E F G |
| :--- | :--- |
| G A B C | & D E F G |
| **This is the bottom** | **& this is the top.** |

In both, the semitone is in the same place, either at the top or in the middle; the only difference is that the semitone is one comma <term>Comma: A very small interval—specifically the "syntonic comma"—which is the tiny mathematical difference between a major whole tone (9:8) and a minor whole tone (10:9).</term> higher in the lower tetrachord than in the upper one; a difference that is not strongly felt while singing.

<margin>Transposition.</margin>
On this similarity of tetrachords, therefore, is based the transposition of a song from one key <note>original: "clave" (clef or key).</note> to another, as used by musicians; it is made all the more convenient because organists have removed the distinction between major and minor tones, and other such things.

<margin>Use of the syllables Ut, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La.</margin>
Again, this similarity and threefold variety of tetrachords gave birth in more recent music to those six syllables *ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la*: by which the memory of learners is aided. If only one octave were sung, composed of two similar tetrachords, we could be content with only four syllables, *ut, re, mi, fa, ut, re, mi, fa*, ignoring the difference between major and minor tones.

But because there are three locations for the semitone in a tetrachord; so that these syllables would not be too general, but rather so that the semitone would always be denoted by *Mi Fa* or *Fa Mi*: it was necessary to add two other syllables; so that in these [*Ut, re, mi, fa*] the semitone would be in the highest place; in these [*Re, mi, fa, sol*] the semitone would be in the middle place; and finally in these [*Mi, fa, sol, la*] the semitone would be in the lowest place. And this is the reason why they used six syllables
<meta>catchword: discovered-</meta>

<summary>Kepler defines six varieties of the tetrachord based on the internal arrangement of major tones, minor tones, and semitones. He explains that the solmization system (Ut-Re-Mi-Fa-Sol-La) was designed to help singers identify the semitone's position across these different structures.</summary>
<keywords>tetrachord, solmization, major tone, minor tone, semitone, temperament, transposition, Guidonian syllables, music theory, tuning</keywords>

<margin>CHAPTER X.</margin>
...the inventors of Music, not eight. Therefore, let that Belgian <note>Kepler refers to Hubert Waelrant (c. 1517–1595), who introduced "Bocedization," a seven-syllable system intended to replace the traditional six-syllable Guidonian solmization.</note> see, who made seven syllables out of six: *Bo, ce, di, ga, lo, ma, ni*, what profit he gains from this increase. For he thought that syllables should be used in a number equal to the strings of one octave, minus one; so that the octave, because of its identity <note>The "identity" refers to the fact that an octave sounds like the same note at a higher pitch.</note> with the first note, would be represented by the first syllable *Bo*. What, I ask, does he find lacking in the letters a, b, c, d, e, f, g, which have long since been accepted for this use?

<margin>The change of song.</margin>
Since, therefore, six syllables <note>Ut, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La.</note> were born in this way on account of the triple form of the Tetrachord, from this was born the doctrine of Mutations through the modern musical scale. This doctrine is concerned only with these syllables being fitted to the letters explained above. It shows that the extra syllables *Sol, la* are sometimes equivalent to the first *ut, re*, and sometimes to the succeeding *Re, mi*, so that sometimes, out of order and without mutation, *fa* can be introduced after *sol, la*.

| 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. 6. |
| :--- |
| Ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la, fa, la, |
| Ut, re, mi, ut, re, mi, fa, mi |

<image-desc>A musical staff with eight notes using a C-clef. Underneath the notes, the syllables "ut re mi fa mi" and "ut re mi fa sol la fa la" are printed, demonstrating how a singer "mutates" or shifts between different sets of six syllables (hexachords) to cover a wider range or reach a specific semitone (fa).</image-desc>

There is indeed also a certain "dissimilar similarity" of Tetrachords, which is the foundation for the coordination of different melodies harmonizing among themselves—what they are accustomed to call Fugues and Fantasias <note>In Kepler’s time, a "Fugue" involved one voice "fleeing" and another "chasing" it by repeating the same melody starting on a different note.</note>. For if you take contiguous Tetrachords, separated by no interval from one another—just as a major tone was left over to complete the octave above or below—there will occur in certain systems of the octave, on both sides, the same series of elementary intervals. That is to say, the series of Semitones, Diesis, and Limmas <note>Kepler uses "Diesis" and "Limma" to describe specific types of semitones or small tuning increments.</note>. A major tone is added to one so that instead of a fourth, a fifth is produced—a fifth that is in some way similar to the other fourth. Thus, two melodies—one earlier in time traversing a fifth <term>Diapente: A perfect fifth, the interval between the 1st and 5th notes of a scale.</term> above, the other later in time traversing a fourth <term>Diatessaron: A perfect fourth, the interval between the 1st and 4th notes.</term> below—run their course; the later one follows the earlier, imitating its pattern as if it were a kind of rival.

<image-desc>A diagram showing "Similar Tetrachords" (Tetrachorda similia). On a musical staff, intervals are labeled: "Added Tone" (Tonus adjunctus), then a sequence of "Semitone/Limma," "Semitone/Diesis," "Minor Tone," etc. Braces on the right group these into an "Upper" (Superius) and "Lower" (Inferius) section, showing how the mathematical structure of the bottom half of an octave mirrors the top half.</image-desc>

# CHAPTER XI.
# On the composition of Systems.

Although the voice of a single human usually moves within the system of a single octave, the harmony of several melodies together teaches us to arrange several contiguous octaves. The Ancients, therefore, defining everything by the properties of numbers, defined the "octave-plus-fifth" <note>original: "Diapason epidiapente." This is an interval of a 12th.</note> by the numbers 1, 2, 3 as the perfect system. For us, the individual harmonic sections mentioned above have each yielded individual systems, of which the largest was the "double-octave-plus-fifth" <note>original: "Disdiapason epidiapente." This is an interval of a 19th.</note>, in the numbers 1 and 6. Although for our Composers, as they are called, the limit...

Divide G into 3, and any of those into 2, 4, 8, 16, so that 48 parts are made; of these, 12 are gg, 15 are d-d-sharp <note>dde</note>, 16 are dd, 18 are cc, 20 are bb, 24 are g, 27 are f, 30 are d-sharp <note>de</note>, and 32 are d.

---

Again, divide G into 5. Of these, 3 will be e, and 4 will be b-natural <note>h</note>. Finally, divide b-natural <note>h</note> into 3, and any of those into 3, so that they become 9; of these, 8 give c-sharp <note>cç</note> and 10 give A. Lastly, trisect c-sharp <note>cç</note>, and take 4 of these for g-sharp <note>ge</note>.

H 2 <note>This is a signature mark, used by early printers to help binders assemble the book's pages in the correct order.</note>

<header>ON PROPORTIONS</header>

# CHAPTER XII.
## On Adulterated Consonances.

From the continuation of two octaves <note>original: "diapason"</note>, imperfect consonances <note>intervals that sound slightly out of tune compared to pure mathematical ratios</note> result. For at the junction of both, two major whole tones (8:9) follow in succession between *f* and *g*, and *g* and *a*. Therefore, in the interval *f* to *a*, the ratio is 64:81. This is exactly one comma (80:81) larger than a just Major Third (4:5, or 64:80). Following Galileo, let us call this a ditone.

<margin>Ditone.</margin>
<image-desc>A hand-drawn musical staff showing notes e, f, g, and a with mathematical ratios 64, 81, and 80. Connecting lines indicate the intervals between these notes.</image-desc>
The same interval exists between *e* and *g-sharp* <note>original: "ge"</note>, because between *e* and *f*, and between *g-sharp* and *a*, there is the same interval of a semitone on both sides.

<image-desc>A musical staff with notes f and b-flat (bb), annotated with ratios 20, 27, and 40.</image-desc>
Thus, between *f* and *b-flat* <note>original: "bb"</note>, if a semitone is added to the excessive ditone *f* to *a*, it creates an interval of 60:81 (or 20:27). This is one comma (80:81) larger than a pure Fourth (3:4, or 60:80).

Judge the same for the interval *e* to *a*, because just as *e* is a semitone lower than *f*, so also is *a* lower than *b-flat*.

If these imperfect or "excessive" consonances are subtracted from the interval of an Octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note>, they leave behind residues that are imperfect and deficient by one comma. For instance, between *a* and the higher *f* <note>original: "ff"</note> of a single octave, the ratio will be 81:128, which is a deficient minor sixth <note>original: "sexta mollis"</note>.

The same occurs between *g* and the higher *e* <note>original: "ee"</note> if you subtract the interval *e* to *g* from the octave.

Likewise, between *b-flat* <note>original: "bb"</note> and the higher *f* <note>original: "ff"</note> of an octave, after subtracting the imperfect fourth *f* to *b-flat* (20:27) from the octave, there remains a diminished Fifth (27:40, which is 81:120).

The same happens between *a* and the higher *e* <note>original: "ee"</note>, when *e* to *a* is subtracted from the octave.

However, if the excessive ditone *f* to *a* is added to the minor Third *a* to *c* (5:6), an excessive Fifth <note>original: "diapente"</note> is produced between *f* and the higher *c* <note>original: "cc"</note>, with a ratio of 160:243. This exceeds a pure fifth by one comma. For 160:240 is 2:3 <note>the pure fifth</note>, and 240:243 is the comma ratio 80:81.

<image-desc>A musical staff displaying the interval between f and c (diapente) with ratios 160 and 243.</image-desc>
And when this excessive fifth *f* to *cc* is removed from the interval of an octave, there remains a fourth *c* to *f* (243:320), which is deficient by one comma.

### Table of the six imperfect Consonances.

| | |
|---|---|
| Instead of 4:5 <note>Major Third</note>, it is 64:81 (excessive) | |
| Instead of 3:4 <note>Fourth</note>, it is 60:81 (excessive) or 20:27 | and 243:320 (deficient). |
| Instead of 5:8 <note>Minor Sixth</note>, it is 81:128 (deficient) | |
| Instead of 2:3 <note>Fifth</note>, it is 81:120 (deficient) or 27:40 | and 160:243 (excessive). |

Nevertheless, there is no need here for the Platonic Semitone or *Limma* (243:256), which Plato called a *Limma* for a different reason than I do. For him, after subtracting two major tones (the ditone 64:81) from the interval of a fourth (3:4), this *Limma* 243:256 remained in place of a semitone. But I have no need for this subtraction; rather, in my system, the 3:4 interval is increased and becomes 20:27.

# CHAPTER XIII.

## On What Constitutes a Naturally Har-
## monious and Fitting Song.

We shall say nothing of that shrill manner of singing which the **Turks** and **Hungarians** are accustomed to use for their war-calls <note>original: "classico suo"</note>; they imitate the unformed voices of brute animals rather than human Nature.

It seems entirely likely that the first author of such unformed melody derived it from an instrument that was poorly constructed; then, through long-standing habit along with the manufacture of that same instrument, he transmitted it to posterity and the entire nation. I was present in **Prague** during the prayers which the priest of the Turkish Ambassador used to chant at set hours, kneeling and frequently striking the ground with his forehead. It was easily apparent that he sang according to a discipline, and had acquired his skill and readiness through labor, for he never hesitated. Yet he used intervals that were strange, unusual, truncated, and abhorrent—so much so that it seems no one, led by their own natural instinct and of their own accord, could ever consistently devise anything similar. I shall attempt to express something close to it using our musical notes.

<image-desc>A single musical staff with square and diamond-shaped notes in an F-clef (bass clef). The melody includes various accidentals (sharps) and irregular rhythmic groupings, representing the "stridulous" music mentioned in the text.</image-desc>

A harmonious <note>original: "concinnus," meaning well-proportioned or elegant</note> song, fitting for the judgment of human ears, is therefore one which, having begun from a certain sound, tends from there through harmonious intervals toward consonant sounds—both those consonant with the first sound and, for the most part, consonant among themselves. It flies swiftly through dissonant intervals but lingers on the consonant ones, whether by the measure of time, the length of the syllables, or by frequent return to them. It is as if it affects the harmony of two voices between one another, but through the movement of a single voice from one place in the system <note>original: "Systematis," referring to the musical scale</note> to another. For example:

<image-desc>A musical staff containing a plainchant melody in square notation. Below the staff is the corresponding liturgical text.</image-desc>

*To the Paschal victim let Christians offer praises. The Lamb has redeemed the sheep: Christ, the innocent one, has reconciled sinners to the Father.* <note>original: "Victimæ paschali laudes immolent Christiani Agnus redemit oves Cristus innocens patri reconciliavit peccatores." This is a famous 11th-century Gregorian sequence for Easter.</note>

<margin>
<image-desc>A small musical diagram showing four notes on a staff, illustrating the G-scale described in the text.</image-desc>
</margin>

This initial sound is in the key of *G*, with which *b*, *c*, *d*, and *g* agree in the "soft" song <note>original: "cantu molli," likely referring to the hexachord system</note>. The song therefore runs out (first making a downward turn) to the key of *c*, which is consonant, and skips right over the dissonant place *A*. It would have been the same if it had touched it, but only with a brief delay. However, the rest of the entire series sounds most especially in the places *b*, *d*, and *g*, expressing such a scale of an octave. It returns most frequently to *d*, then to *b*, and sometimes raises itself to the higher *g*, landing significantly on all these places. It does not do so on *a* or *f*, which are places dissonant to the first note; and finally, it returns to *G* and finishes there.

Regarding the definition of song handed down to us, many things come to our attention to be noted.

I. **Euclid** names these four as the parts of a Song, from all or some of which every song consists: *Conduct* <note>original: "Αγώγήν" (Agoge), referring to the melodic motion</note>, *Tension* <note>original: "Τονήν" (Tonos), the pitch or tone</note>, *Placement* <note>original: "Πεττείαν" (Petteia), the art of choosing which notes to use and which to avoid</note>,

<sig>H 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: Interweaving <note>original: "Πλο-" (Ploke)</note></meta>

<summary>Kepler defines a "natural" melody as one that centers on consonant intervals and avoids lingering on dissonant ones, contrasting European liturgical chant with the "unformed" microtonal singing of the Turks.</summary>

<meta>The previous page introduced the concept of harmonious versus "unformed" melody, ending with a partial definition of what constitutes a "fitting" song for the human ear. This page continues that definition by categorizing the specific types of melodic movement using terms from ancient Greek music theory.</meta>

<header>ON PROPORTIONS</header>

<margin>CHAPTER XIII.</margin> **Interweaving**, and what these terms signify, is indicated by the words themselves. For <term>Leading<note>original: "Αγωγὴ" (Agoge); a Greek term for the melodic "leading" or progression of the voice.</note></term> is the carrying of the voice from a proposed root all the way to a place consonant with that root, or from one consonant to another that is consonant either with it or the first root. <term>Dwelling<note>original: "Τονὴ" (Tone); meaning the lingering or "stretching" of a note in one place.</note></term> is staying in a place, either the first or one consonant to it—or even a place consonant to a previous note, though it might not be consonant to the first. **Interweaving** <note>original: "Πλοκὴ" (Ploke); meaning an "implication" or "folding" of melodic lines.</note> is a certain species or "color" of **Leading**, just as <term>Selection<note>original: "πεττεία" (Petteia); literally "game of draughts," referring to the artful choice and placement of notes.</note></term> is a variation of **Dwelling**. As **Leading** relates to **Dwelling**, so **Interweaving** relates to **Selection**; because **Leading** passes through as if in a straight line, while **Interweaving** wanders about during its passage around the **Leading**, like a dog around a traveler.

Therefore, **Leading** is a movement that is, as it were, direct; **Interweaving** is a varied movement. **Dwelling**, however, is like the boundary of movement, or a rest in a desired place in the <term>System<note>original: "Systematis"; here referring to the structured scale or octave.</note></term>. **Selection** consists of many boundaries of smaller movements, like mini-rests. In our example, the syllables [*Christ takes away the sheep in* <note>original: "demit Oves Christus in"</note>] are a certain perpetual **Dwelling**, with only two syllables excepted. But the syllables [*innocent, reconciled, sinners* <note>original: "cens rec li peccat," fragments from the Victimae Paschali Laudes sequence</note>] express **Selection**. If you look at the **ligatures** <note>notes tied together over a single syllable</note> of the syllables in this song—[*praises, to the, father, sinner* <note>original: "laud an patr tor"</note>]—and consider them as two-toned, then in that song there would be no pure and unmixed **Leading**. But if you consider that it was done in a rustic manner—where a sound that was meant to be sung longer became two-toned by rising at the end—and if you restore to these syllables the simple long sound (which is the first note of the ligature), you will find pure **Leading** in these: [*Paschal praises* <note>original: "Paschali laudes"</note>], likewise in [*they sacrifice* <note>original: "immolent"</note>], likewise [*Christians* <note>original: "Christiani"</note>], likewise [*Innocent for the father* <note>original: "Innocens patri"</note>], and a short one in [*sinners* <note>original: "catores"</note>]. Pure **Interweaving**, however, though not natural, is found in the Turkish example <note>referring to the musical notation on the previous page</note>.

Just as the skeleton is to the body in the study of anatomy, so the octaves—consonant sounds both with themselves and with the root or base of the octave—are to the melody or song within a System. For just as flesh fills the cavities of the bones and clothes them for beauty, so these parts we have reviewed fill the skeleton of the octave—especially **Leading** and **Selection**. By wandering through the dissonant places cast between the consonant sounds, they shape and, as it were, give a body to the **Melody**.

II. Since a song is defined as starting from a certain specific sound which acts as the basis of the octave system, this is not always to be understood as what is happening in the moment. Because variety delights and serves to emphasize, a melody very often begins abruptly from a different key or place. Nevertheless, a certain fixed principle is understood by its power, which shines out from the entire stretch of the melody; as in this very ancient German song, it is easily understood that even if it begins in **D**, the root is nonetheless **G**.

<image-desc>A musical staff showing a melody in mensural notation. The notes move primarily in steps and small leaps, illustrating the "German song" mentioned. It is written in a C-clef on the second line.</image-desc>

III. A similar exception exists for the rule that a regular song is said to aim its **Dwelling** or **Selection** at places consonant with the root of the Octave. For frequently these parts, in the middle of a longer stretch of melody, are occupied around—

<meta>catchword: around-</meta>

<summary>Kepler defines the four elements of melodic movement (Leading, Dwelling, Interweaving, and Selection) using an anatomical metaphor: the mathematical octaves are the skeleton, while the melodic movement is the "flesh" that provides beauty. He also notes that while a melody may not start on the tonic note, its "root" is still perceived by the ear throughout the composition.</summary>

<margin>CHAPTER XIII.</margin>
...those places dissonant from the first root; but let this be for the sake of variety. It is just as if a new melody were mixed with the previous one, where a new beginning is fixed on that dissonant note, or a new <term>octave skeleton<note>Kepler uses the word "skeleton" to describe the basic framework or essential notes that define the structure of an octave's scale.</note></term> is marked. It is like an excursion or a digression in a speech: therefore, we do not linger on such things, but quickly return as if to the principal skeleton. And as long as the <term>dwelling<note>original: "τονή" (tonē); the act of holding or emphasizing a specific pitch.</note></term> and <term>selection<note>original: "πεττεία" (petteia); the artful choice of which notes to use from a scale.</note></term> revolve around dissonances, we understand that the song is not yet finished. For at the very end, one must return not only to the consonant notes—regularly, indeed—but also to the root of the proper octave itself. Because of this articulation of song and this aiming for consonances, the ancients seem to have called even a simple song "Harmony"; just as a decent and fitting correspondence of the limbs, which is the form of the soul, might be called harmony, as if it were beauty itself. Indeed, "Harmony" was even the name of a woman.

<margin>Jumps.</margin>
IV. Regarding <term>leading<note>original: "Αγωγήν" (Agōgēn); the melodic progression or "path" the voice takes.</note></term>, it is again varied; for it does not always actually pass through all the intervening places, but often leaps over some, and a jump is carried from one note to another consonant with it. In that case, the "leading" exists only in potential, and it is almost pure "selection" or "dwelling." This is the custom most frequent among our <term>trumpeters<note>original: "Tubicinum." Kepler refers to players of natural trumpets, which were limited to specific notes (the harmonic series) and often played military signals.</note></term> when they play a signal or a cavalry call; for then almost nothing is heard except the skeleton of the octave. Consider whether the <term>High Strain<note>original: "Νόμος ὄρθιος" (Nomos orthios); an ancient Greek melodic style, often described as high-pitched, vigorous, and rhythmic.</note></term> of the ancients was of this kind.

V. Since a fitting song consists of its own elements, which are fitting intervals, these must first be defined more accurately.

<margin>
The various
types of
unfitting
intervals.
</margin>
For intervals are called "fitting" or "unfitting" in a double sense. First, individual intervals are called fitting or unfitting in respect to their origin: those are fitting which nature admits in the divisions of consonant intervals; while those are unfitting which do not result from the comparisons of consonances, being entirely alien to Harmonics, as explained in Chapter IV. Second, in respect to the song or melody itself, there is this distinction even among musical intervals—those that are fitting in the first sense—that some of them, when considered together, although they are fitting by nature (that is, born from the comparison and abstraction of harmonies), are nevertheless rejected as unfitting by melodies in a certain respect. The <term>dwelling</term> and <term>selection</term> presuppose and look toward the first sense; but <term>leading</term>, whether actual or leaping, looks toward this second sense most of all. These become "unfitting," then, under two headings: either in respect to the <term>Genus</term> or the octave skeleton, because they are clearly not used in it, nor do they form it; or if they are arranged in an order other than what nature taught in Chapter VII. For example, if someone wanted to arrange three <term>semitones<note>A semitone is the smallest interval in common music, such as the step from E to F.</note></term> in a row: a semitone is indeed fitting in the first sense, but this arrangement of semitones is not fitting in this second sense. Likewise, a <term>Diesis<note>original: "Diesis"; a very small interval, smaller than a semitone, common in ancient Greek "Enharmonic" music.</note></term> is fitting by nature, yet it is separately unfitting whether in the "hard" <term>Genus<note>original: "duro Genere"; likely referring to the Diatonic scale or major mode.</note></term> of song or the "soft" <term>Genus<note>original: "Molli"; likely referring to the Chromatic/Enharmonic scales or minor mode.</note></term>. Or finally, they are not sung in succession, nor are they allowed for a jump of the melodic voice, nor are they suitable for "leading."

# ON PROPORTIONS

<margin>CHAPTER XIII.</margin> There are, therefore, in this second sense, unharmonious and forbidden intervals, governed by these principal laws:

I. A <term>diesis<note>A very small interval, smaller than a semitone, often associated with a sharp.</note></term> is not regularly sung before or after a <term>semitone<note>A half-step, the smallest interval in most Western scales.</note></term>.
<image-desc>Musical notation on a five-line staff showing a sequence of five notes, with a sharp (diesis) symbol on the second note and a natural symbol on the fourth note.</image-desc>

II. Although two semitones may be arranged sequentially in the order of the smallest intervals (as discussed in Chapter VII), they cannot be sung as three consecutive notes; instead, they must merge with two other elements to form two <term>whole tones<note>An interval composed of two semitones.</note></term>.
<image-desc>Musical notation on a five-line staff showing a sequence of six notes, with a sharp symbol on the fifth note.</image-desc>

III. Two semitones are not ordinarily sung within the span of a single <term>fourth<note>A perfect fourth.</note></term> or <term>fifth<note>A perfect fifth.</note></term> located at the bottom of the <term>octave skeleton<note>The basic structural framework of a scale.</note></term>. For if they were, the fourth or fifth note in the sequence would not harmonize with the first—neither perfectly nor imperfectly—and thus it would not truly be a fourth or fifth.
<image-desc>Three short musical examples arranged side-by-side. The first staff has four notes with a sharp; the second has four notes with a flat; the third has five notes with a sharp.</image-desc>

IV. Four <term>whole tones<note>Steps of a full tone.</note></term> are not sung in succession, except in the highest part of the octave, when the skeleton is changed for the sake of "color" and variety; therefore, this is not done ordinarily.
<image-desc>Musical notation on a five-line staff showing five notes. Below the staff are the labels: T. T. To. To. <note>These abbreviations stand for Tone, Tone, Whole Tone, Whole Tone.</note></image-desc>

V. The <term>seventh<note>An interval spanning seven scale degrees.</note></term> and all dissonant intervals larger than an octave are not ordinarily sung as notes arranged sequentially after the root; unless the preceding note acts as a sort of conclusion, and the following note as a new beginning.
<image-desc>Musical notation on a five-line staff showing various notes illustrating wide intervals, including a seventh and a ninth.</image-desc>

VI. We rarely admit <term>sixths<note>Intervals spanning six scale degrees.</note></term>, even though they are consonant, and then only <term>minor sixths<note>A slightly smaller version of the sixth interval.</note></term>.
<image-desc>Musical notation on a five-line staff showing two notes. Below the staff is the phrase: <note>original: "In me transierunt" (They have passed over me; a liturgical reference often used in mournful music).</note></image-desc>

VII. Two <term>tetrachords<note>A series of four notes spanning a perfect fourth.</note></term> within a single octave are rarely sung without the semitone being in the same relative position in both; this is done for the sake of "color" or <term>syncopation<note>Shifting the rhythmic stress to a typically weak beat.</note></term> (discussed in Chapter XVI). However, there is no absolute freedom in placing the semitone; it is restricted to the place allowed by the <term>Type of Song<note>original: "Genus Cantus"; referring to the specific musical mode or scale type.</note></term>.
<image-desc>Musical notation on a five-line staff showing two distinct melodic segments separated by a bar line. The first segment includes a flat; the second includes two notes with sharps.</image-desc>

VIII. Related to this is the fact that three <term>whole tones<note>original: "Toni"</note></term> are not sung in succession at the bottom of the octave, though they are allowed higher up according to the rules already mentioned.
<image-desc>Musical notation on a five-line staff with two melodic segments. The first has a flat on the second note; the second has sharps on the second and fourth notes.</image-desc>

IX. Two semitones do not naturally merge into a single whole tone, even if the difference is small to the ear. For example, if the octave begins from E, between C and D there would be an interval of 225:256 through composition, which is naturally unharmonious; see Chapter IV.
<image-desc>Musical notation on a five-line staff with two melodic segments comparing semitone and tone steps using sharps and flats.</image-desc>

### ON THE BOOK OF HARMONICS, III.

X. In general, every <term>Octave<note>The interval of an eighth.</note></term> system is unharmonious if it does not establish both a <term>Fourth<note>original: Diatessaron</note></term> and a <term>Fifth<note>original: Diapente</note></term> below.
<image-desc>A small musical staff with five lines. A C-clef is positioned on the third line (alto clef). Most of these laws will now serve us in establishing the number of Tones in the following chapter.

<margin>Concerning Rhythm.</margin>
VI. As for that part of the definition, *skimming quickly through dissonances, lingering on consonances*: although it is not my intention in this work to argue about rhythm and measurement, I nevertheless advise in general that the primary grace of a harmonious song lies in its measurement. For what has been said most generally—*Skimming over dissonances, etc.*—is made true in a specific way as follows. First, the Latins have a distinction between long and short syllables, of which they make the latter one "time" and the former two "times," and thus double the length. <margin>In Prose.</margin> Although today not only poems but even prose is sung, modern musicians completely neglect the distinction between long and short syllables; instead, they look solely to the custom of pronunciation, however corrupt it may be today. Any syllable that is usually uttered with a sharp accent is considered long, and any with a grave accent is considered short.

It is no wonder this happens in the Latin language, since the later Greeks did the same thing. Although they wrote purely, they embraced a most faulty pronunciation in which there is no longer any distinction between a sharp accent and the length of a syllable, or a grave accent and its shortness—even though they have an abundance of signs for this purpose, which are not in such frequent use among the Latins. And so the Greeks, having abolished the old custom of composing verse, began several centuries ago <margin>Greek "Political" verses.</margin> to write what are called <term>Political verses<note>A form of accentual poetry common in Medieval Greek, where the rhythm is based on stress rather than the length of syllables.</note></term>. In these, syllables are counted but not measured by length, and the verse favors the second-to-last syllable—not because it is long by nature, but because it is sharpened by accent in popular speech. Our musicians imitate this even in Latin, so much so that they do not spare even poems, <margin>In Meters.</margin> except very rarely, nor ever entirely. I believe this is because a constant double or triple proportion is accepted in songs, while poems mix these unequally—with the exception of the <term>Hexameter<note>A line of verse consisting of six metrical feet.</note></term>, which is content with a proportion of equality in the <term>spondee<note>A foot consisting of two long syllables.</note></term> and a perfect double proportion in the <term>dactyl<note>A foot consisting of one long syllable followed by two short ones.</note></term>. Therefore, musicians assign a dissonant sound to a short syllable (or one that stands in place of a short, as when a spondee follows an iamb), if it must be passed through; they assign consonances, or something like them, to long syllables.

<margin>In modern Meters.</margin>
Second, the Ionian languages <note>Kepler likely refers to the "Japhetic" or European language family here.</note> that use rhythm—German, French, Spanish, Italian—make either the last or the second-to-last syllable of a poem sharp. They utter the whole verse as if sharp or grave syllables follow one another alternately, whether this is done in a proper German verse or not (as is frequent in French). Thus, every one of their verses is either like a <term>Trochaic<note>A rhythm of "stressed-unstressed."</note></term> or an <term>Iambic<note>A rhythm of "unstressed-stressed."</note></term>, and these are either <term>Acatalectic<note>A verse with a complete number of syllables.</note></term>—*Creator of Heaven and Earth. Now we pray to the Holy Spirit.* <note>original: "Schöpffer Himmels vnd der Erden. Nun bitten wir den Heylgen Geist."</note>—or <term>catalectic<note>A verse missing a syllable at the end.</note></term>—*At which all the world wonders. He is the morning star.* <note>original: "Deß sich wundert alle Welt. Er ist der Morgensterne."</note> Therefore, musicians fix the place for dissonant sounds on the grave or shortened syllables, and consonances on the sharp ones.

<margin>In the beat.</margin>
Third, when a song receives its measure not from the syllables of the text but from the <term>Tactus<note>The steady beat or pulse, usually indicated by a hand motion.</note></term>, and it follows either a double or triple proportion: they reserve the first part of the beat for consonances, and the latter part—which in triple time is shorter and indicated by the raising of the hand—for dissonances especially.

## CHAPTER XIV.
->Concerning the Modes of Melodies, which<-
->they call Tones.<-

**A**bout to speak of modes, I first advise modern Musicians that regarding those things they are accustomed to call "Modes"—namely: the double and triple proportions of the beat, and the like (such as the "Modes" perhaps used long ago for flutes in Roman comedies)—there will be no further discussion from me beyond what has already been said. I call "Modes" those which they themselves, along with the ancients, are accustomed to call <term>Tones<note>original: Tonos. In this context, these are the structural frameworks for melody, similar to what we call "scales" or "modes" today.</note></term>, as when one asks which Tone a song belongs to. For there are certain qualities or species of harmonious song, divided against each other by the two greatest differences of <term>Genera<note>Classes or types of scales.</note></term>: the <term>Hard<note>original: Duri. Referring to scales using B-natural.</note></term> and the <term>Soft<note>original: Mollis. Referring to scales using B-flat.</note></term>.

The Greeks called them <term>Ways<note>original: Τρόπους (Tropoi)</note></term> and <term>Characters<note>original: ἤθη (Ethoi)</note></term>; the former from the form of the System, the latter from the Effect of the song upon a person, because most legislators judged that the Modes of songs serve to shape Morals.

Regarding the number and the distinctions of these Tones, there are great controversies among musicians not only today, but there were even long ago; some of these can be seen in the works of <term>Ptolemy<note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), an astronomer and music theorist who systematized the Greek modes.</note></term>, and most in <term>Vincenzo Galilei<note>An Italian musician and theorist (1520–1591), father of Galileo, who advocated for a return to ancient Greek musical ideals.</note></term>. Indeed, it is not my purpose to examine every person's opinions, nor to refute them; therefore, the Musician should expect nothing else from me on this question except that unique conclusion to which my principles, explained thus far, lead me. For although Tones seem to be named from the fact that one Mode begins either higher or lower than another by the interval of one <term>Whole Tone<note>original: Tonus</note></term> (or Semitone), I do not distinguish Tones by the highness or lowness of the song itself (which Vincenzo Galilei testifies some have observed exclusively). Instead, following Ptolemy, I require their number to match the number of species of a single <term>Octave<note>original: Diapason</note></term>. I say there are as many Tones as there can be legitimate and harmonious <term>frameworks<note>original: sceleta (skeletons)</note></term> of the Octave System, differing among themselves in their Genera, the sequence of harmonious intervals, the placement of the <term>Tetrachords<note>Groups of four notes that formed the basis of ancient scales.</note></term>, or the selection of two <term>harmonic medians<note>Internal notes that divide the octave into smaller consonant intervals.</note></term>. There are, to be sure, three things that vary Tones and distinguish them from one another: the Genus, the sequence of harmonious notes, and the articulation of the framework from smaller consonances.

First, the two Genera established in Chapter VI for the division of the Octave System provide us with two principal Tones that are first by Nature, arising with the system of a single Octave itself. Then, in both the hard and soft genera of the system, from the combination of two Octaves into one larger and perfect System (as we described in Chapter XI), the systems of individual Octaves are given, differing by their roots or the boundaries by which they are enclosed; however, those boundaries are the places of the natural system...

# ON THE HARMONICS, BOOK III.

<margin>CHAPTER XIV.</margin>
...[disti]nction is various, or in modern terminology, different Keys, which necessarily result in a different pitch height relative to the natural system that begins from G; and through this also a different position of the semitone, which is placed either in the third, the penultimate, or the lowest position of the Octave. For as concerns the pitch itself, considered absolutely, it changes nothing in the species of the song by itself, since the same species can be intoned either high or low. Nor are we bound to this: that we must take half of the remaining Tones lower than the principal and Natural System of G, and half higher, as Ptolemy did. For we can take either all of them higher or all lower, since the same Order of Concordances follows from both sides, provided that the System of the double octave, naturally composed, begins from the key G. But if we make some lower and some higher as Ptolemy did, the natural System must be so composed that we add a <term>Fifth<note>original: Diapente</note></term> below and a <term>Fourth<note>original: Diatessaron</note></term> above; and thus the composed System of the double Octave will begin from C.

<image-desc>A short musical staff showing four notes. This illustrates a melodic fragment or the positioning of notes within a specific system or key.</image-desc>

Thirdly and finally, in Systems thus constituted, there is a choice of two Harmonic Medians, toward which the <term>division<note>original: τομὴ (tomē)</note></term> and the <term>completion<note>original: τελεία (teleia)</note></term>—parts of the song—aim; or what amounts to the same thing, the position of the <term>Tetrachord<note>A scale of four notes spanning a perfect fourth, the building block of ancient Greek musical systems.</note></term> is given either at the top or at the bottom of the Octave, or in the middle of two Thirds.

Therefore, because of this diversity, there must be subjoined here before all else a Squared Grid, refined from Chapter XI, consisting of twelve Orders of the twelve smallest Natural intervals: not indeed so that we might make just as many Tones according to their number as Aristoxenus did (beginning each one a single such smallest interval higher); but so that, with these smallest intervals contracted into the usual concordances, it may appear whether any new species of Octave can begin from any one of the smallest intervals.

CHAPTER XIV.
The origin of the 14 Systems of the octave of differing species.
</margin>
Let us now see how many species of the Systems of the Octave exist if the first difference of the Octaves, which is that of Gender <note>Kepler uses "Genus" (Gender) to distinguish between types of scales, particularly those using the "Hard" B-natural or "Soft" B-flat.</note>, is added; that is, whether the intervals of all 12 Orders can be harmoniously <note>Kepler uses the word *concinnè*, meaning elegant, fitting, or musically pleasing according to mathematical laws.</note> contracted into the seven usual intervals of a single Octave, marked by eight positions, and in how many ways each can be done.

Note here that LS or SL stands for the Major Tone <note>The "Large-Small" ratio</note>, DS or SD stands for the Minor Tone <note>The "Different-Small" ratio</note>, and S stands for the semitone; and our descriptions will proceed from Low to High, or from below to above.

It is certain, therefore, in the Octave of G, that two species exist based on the double position of the semitone in either the second or third place from the bottom.

But in G-sharp, as well as in C-sharp, since two semitones do not form one harmonious whole, nor can they be sung melodiously <note>original: εμμελῶς (emmeleōs)</note> one after the other; therefore, the lowest semitone stands alone, according to laws 9 and 2 of the previous Chapter. The distribution would therefore be
either like this: $S. SD. SL. S. SD. SL. SL$, which is inharmonious according to law 3.

Or in G-sharp, it would be such: $S. SD. SL. SS. DS. \&c.$ and this is inharmonious according to law 9. Therefore, no harmonious species of the Octave begins from G-sharp.

<margin>XIV.</margin>
Finally, in the Octave of F <note>Original: "ſe". In context, this refers to the note F.</note> there are two locations for the semitone: either in the penultimate seat or in the last. If, therefore, you order them thus—**SL. S. SD. SL. S. SD. SL.**—it will be the first species, as appears from comparison. If otherwise, it will be the fourteenth: **S. LS. SD. SL. S. SD. SL.** <note>Kepler uses abbreviations for intervals: SL and LS represent Major Tones (9:8), SD and DS represent Minor Tones (10:9), and S represents a Semitone (16:15).</note>

It appears, therefore, the reason why in Orders II, IV, V, VII, and IX—namely, in the Octaves of G, B, C, and D—no peculiar species begins.

It appears secondly, that no genuine transposition can be made so that the same species of the Octave remains, except for these: I. from F to G. II. from G to A, but these are rejected forms. III. from A to B. IV. from B to C. V. from C to D. VI. from D to D <note>Likely a typo in the original for D to E.</note>, but these are rejected forms. VII. from E to F.

But if we comply with the common practice of instrumental musicians <note>Original: "Musicorum Organicorum", referring to organists or those playing keyboard instruments.</note>, who neglect the Comma <note>The "Comma" is a tiny mathematical difference between two types of whole tones. Keyboard players of Kepler's time often used "mean-tone temperament" to hide this difference.</note>, and do not distinguish between the major and minor Tones; then all our fourteen species of Octaves will constitute no more than three Modes, based on the triple position of the semitone (just as [Vincenzo] Galilei says was the case in his time, when no more than three Tones were recognized: Dorian, Phrygian, and Lydian). They are, however, multiplied into many more through pitch alone.

For as it concerns the third cause—the articulation of the "skeleton" of the Octave—that is still common to us and them; because of this, even more than fourteen species will be born for us.

Therefore, according to the common opinion regarding the Major and Minor Tone <note>Kepler distinguishes between two types of whole steps: the Major Tone (9:8 ratio, marked here as LS) and the Minor Tone (10:9 ratio, marked as SD). Modern tuning usually ignores this difference.</note>, many transpositions of Melodies from one letter [note] to another can be made by means of the signs ♭ and <term>♯</term> <note>Sharp sign.</note>.

It remains for us to examine which of our fourteen species of the Octave can be made multiple through the articulation of harmonious elements. For a fivefold distinction of species arises from the proximity of the Tones; for either three tones follow one another in succession, or only two. If there are three, they must either stand in the middle of the octave unnaturally, having single tones and single semitones on either side: or they must incline toward one end of the System <note>The "System" refers to the full scale or range being discussed.</note>, and then necessarily there is a semitone at that end, according to laws 8 and 3. But if only two Tones follow each other, with semitones intervening, then there is no place for the semitone at the extremities; and two pairs of tones stand either above or below, with a third "soft" [minor] one at the opposite end—the lower one being direct, having a semitone above it; the upper one being inverted, having a semitone below it.

2. Notes with sharps. Labels: Semitone. Three Tones. Semitone. Major third.

in the middle; finally, if they are occupied around the third and the fifth, the Fourth is in the highest position.

In short, Tones distinguished by real boundaries and differences—not just regarding the pitch of the voice on the Organ, but even in the human voice itself (which can begin the natural System from any voice, high or deep)—are either only 3, or 14, or 24, or 72.

What, then, you will ask, about the remaining ten species, since all the used Tones are reduced to four? Surely they serve this purpose: so that musicians may know that if we temper the systems of the principal Octave described from *G* as nature suggests, then a song cannot be transposed so easily and variedly without losing its purity, as they are accustomed to doing. It is therefore free for them either to reject all the remaining ten species—and with them their transpositions—or to admit that many more forms of melody (namely, more Modes or Tones) can exist, and that these differ from the ones established here, some more...

Pitch is threefold. 
1. Absolute and material, so to speak, as in the human voice and even in Organs if the root of the system ascends from G, where the form of the System is not changed: I shall say nothing of this now. 
2. The formal pitch of each root of a Tone in a natural System composed of two octaves. Nor is this intended here: for it implies a change of the Tone by changing the root Key of the system.

# ON PROPORTIONS

<margin>CHAPTER XIV.</margin> ...more [of one], others less; according as you see the equivalences noted in the margin above. For if we take no account of the ratios of the intervals of one <term>Octave</term> <note>The interval between one musical pitch and another with double its frequency.</note> among the higher notes, there are certainly several transpositions possible from *G* to *c* and from *A* to *d*, and others.

Finally, you might ask: what prevents those transpositions which I have already rejected so many times? For it seems that the ears do not prevent them, since it is admitted that the excess of a <term>Comma</term> <note>original: "Comma." In music theory, a tiny interval (ratio 81:80) representing the difference between different tuning systems, like the Pythagorean third and the just major third.</note> in intervals that are separated in different positions of the <term>System</term> <note>The "System" refers to the complete scale or range of notes available in a musical framework.</note> is not distinguished by the ears. Suppose the system were tuned as well as possible according to the laws of nature explained thus far; if the notes *G–a* and *a–b* were struck, and all people who heard them were asked which of these intervals was larger, they would say they did not know. They would not distinguish it until the intervals were joined in the same place in the Octave; that is, where the space of the string is marked out by a compass, the eighty-first part of the string is partitioned off, and thus two lengths of 80 and 81, struck in the closest moments, were compared with each other.

I respond that although the sense of hearing does not distinguish when only three strings of the Octave are struck (the boundaries of two intervals), yet when all the strings of one Octave are struck, it finally distinguishes the "first-born" and natural Octave of *G* from the Octaves of other keys. For in all species of the Octave, the same seven <term>Concinnous</term> <note>original: "Concinna." Pleasing or harmonious intervals that fit well within a scale.</note> intervals are present, which, once expressed by the striking of the strings, immediately stick in the memory through their proximity. Thus, it is easily apparent to the hearing at what place in the natural Octave any <term>Tone</term> <note>original: "Tonus." Here meaning a specific musical mode or key center.</note> begins. In this way, the perception of the Comma will be implicit in the distinction of the Octaves. For just as the Hearing approves the <term>Consonances</term> themselves and all the Concinnous intervals by their effect—even if it does not count the lengths of the strings that provide the cause of the concords—so the same hearing also notices the effect of the 80:81 comma, even if it does not count it, and thus does not grasp it separately by an actual, discrete sensation.

# CHAPTER XV.
## Which Modes or Tones serve
## which Affects.

Thus far we have discussed the principles from which the Tones consist and are distinguished from one another; now I shall say a few things about their effect, consistent with my principles.

First, the reader must be warned that we are not dealing here with the difference in the dispositions of the soul which cause a person to sing rather than to use plain and calm speech; nor of those things which follow upon singing on the one hand, or simple speech on the other, in the listener. For as it is the alacrity of the soul which precedes all singing in the singer and dictates the <term>Melody</term> to him, as it were; so also a pleasure in the listeners follows every kind of harmonious song.

We must separate this general disposition of the soul, or rather,
