# ON HARMONICS. BOOK III.

...must be subjected as matter to that diversity of affects <note>original: "affectuum." In the 17th century, "affects" referred to specific, categorized emotional states (like joy, sorrow, or boldness) that music was thought to be able to trigger reliably.</note> which we are seeking here. <margin>CHAPTER XV.</margin> Since all the parts of a harmonious and natural song are designed to stir the affects by imitating the sounds that animals produce to testify to their desires, it is clear that this discussion is varied and complex, even bordering on the infinite. Because this task exceeds my own "muscles" <note>Kepler uses "lacertos" (muscles/strength) to admit his limitations in practical musical composition compared to theory.</note>, it would be more rightly handed over entirely to the "Empirics"—that is, the practicing musicians. Without formal rules, and guided by nature alone, they constantly act as the authors of wonderful melodies. This is far easier for them to do than it is for them to explain in a long and eloquent speech what a song is, what it consists of, or how it is made.

For just as prose is represented by poetry, so the voices and gestures of living beings are represented and, as it were, "painted" by song. Certainly, just like the poetic art, the faculty for composing music must be learned through use and practice alone, provided that one’s genius has been fashioned by Nature for this purpose.

However, because it is one of the most honorable recreations of the Mind to track down the causes of things—or to look upon those discovered by others—so much so that even Aristotle devoted a significant portion of his *Problems* to harmonic contemplations, we must also attempt something here. We shall try to extend the boundaries of philosophy and, by applying the laws of method, restrain that infinite nature of the discussion, recalling it to general headings so that, through individual examples, the same judgment can later be applied to similar cases.

I. The elements of the song itself and of the affects that follow the types of song are proportional, and are nearly equal in number on both sides. For even the very terms for the parts of a song—*agōgē*, *tonē*, *petteia*, and *plokē* <note>original: "αγωγή, τονή, πετεία, πλοκή." These are ancient Greek music theory terms: *Agōgē* (rhythmic movement/tempo), *Tonē* (pitch or tension), *Petteia* (the "game" or selection of notes), and *Plokē* (the "weaving" or interlacing of melodic lines).</note>—allude to certain affects. The first serves simplicity, the last luxury; the former is like the body, the latter like colors. Equality of *Tone* <note>original: "Tones."</note> moves the attention; *Pettia*, or "playing about," is designed for delight and recreation. These are general principles across all musical Modes.

II. Regarding *Agōgē* <note>The "lead" or tempo of the melody.</note>, Galilei <note>Kepler refers here to Vincenzo Galilei (c. 1520–1591), a music theorist and the father of the astronomer Galileo Galilei.</note> notes this peculiarity: it has two variations, one upward and the other downward; the former serves joy, the latter sadness and weeping. The cause is natural: for below, a deep voice is produced by slow movement; above, a sharp voice is produced by rapid movement. Therefore, when the voice descends, it approaches rest; when it ascends, it advances in motion. For this reason, in choral singing, we usually finish at the bottom. Thus, in the lower range, the voice languishes; in the higher, it thrives. And so it is in life: in sorrow, the mind and all its functions languish; in cheerfulness, it is alive and active.

III. There is also great power in a "leap" <note>An interval where the melody jumps several notes rather than moving step-by-step.</note>, which is like a "potential" *Agoge*. It possesses rashness, movement, and audacity; it is military, masculine, and—if frequent—impudent. This is especially true through the *Diapente* <note>The interval of a Perfect Fifth.</note>, whose shape, the Triangle <note>original: "Trigonus." Kepler relates the musical fifth to the geometric triangle.</note>, consists of acute angles and consumes the whole circle in three lines. Conversely, a single ascending leap of a minor sixth, followed by an *Agoge* downward, expresses the greatness of grief; it is suited to wailing because of its similarity to the [human] voice, as heard in the *Me transierunt* <note>A sacred motet by the famous Renaissance composer Orlande de Lassus (Orlando di Lasso). The title means "My [sorrows] have passed over me."</note> of Orlando.

IV. It also matters greatly how much "height" within the system of the Octave the most important part of the song occupies from its lowest root. For if it runs through the entire Octave, or exceeds it, the song is spirited; if only a *Diatessaron* <note>The interval of a Perfect Fourth.</note>, it is modest and pleasant; the *Diapente* <note>The interval of a Perfect Fifth.</note> holds the middle ground; the minor Third is hum... <note>The text cuts off here at the bottom of the page.</note>

# ON PROPORTIONS
<note>While the header says "On Proportions," the content continues the discussion of musical modes and emotional expression.</note>

<margin>CHAPTER XV.</margin>
...dejection and faint-heartedness. Some attribute this to a descent below the root by a fourth <note>original: "diatessaron"</note>; they call the tones of this form "plagal" <note>original: "plagios," referring to the secondary church modes that sit lower in range than the "Authentic" modes.</note>, or the side-tones of their Authentic modes.

V. Among the general elements, one must especially consider the speed and slowness of the rhythm, or beat <note>original: "tactus"</note>; the former is suited to anger, movement, fighting, and joy; the latter to those affects which we enjoy in stillness: sorrow, love, longing, and the pleasure of possession.

VI. Add to this the meter—that is, the Rhythm itself. For the "triple" meter has one power, while the "duple" has another. This power is perhaps largely drawn from the imitation of dancing troupes; since the alternating variety of movements in them is known to everyone, it immediately warns the listeners, bringing them, as it were, into the presence of the activity. Therefore, the Triple meter is turbulent and active, while the Duple is quieter, more peaceful, and more modest. But concerning Rhythms and their signs, I shall say nothing in this book; therefore, I will let them pass.

<margin>Aristotle writes concerning the **Enharmonic** <note>One of the three ancient Greek genera of music, involving quarter-tones.</note> that it fills minds with a divine frenzy; on the other hand, the Spartan magistrates, because this genus of song was considered effeminate and artificial, drove its author out of the city, marked with ignominy.</margin>

VII. We must now come to those things by which we said the Tones are properly distinguished; the chief of these is the diversity of the **Genera** <term>Genera: The classification of scales. In ancient Greece, these were Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic. Kepler redefines them into "Hard" (Major) and "Soft" (Minor).</term> of Song. And here a most abundant harvest of disputes springs up: which of the three ancient genera was assigned to which affect? This is a topic we shall pass over untouched, since the distribution of song into three genera is not natural, nor are the ancients consistent with themselves on this matter. I shall speak of the two *natural* genera of song, namely the **Hard** and the **Soft** <note>original: "Duri" and "Mollis," which correspond roughly to the modern Major and Minor tonalities.</note>; the very names reveal which affects they stir. For just as the female is made chiefly for passive endurance and the male for action (especially in the business of procreation), so the **Soft** genus is accommodated to the feminine passions of the soul, and the **Hard** genus to masculine actions. The distinctions between these things will become clearer from what follows.

VIII. For it was not only the Genera of song, but also the Tones in general that differed by the placement of the semitone. This position of the semitone animates and affects both the Genus and the Mode or Tone. However, this placement must be discussed in one way regarding the genera, and in another way regarding all the tones. For we said that the Genera arise first of all in the principal Octave which begins from G; in this, the position of the semitone in the next-to-last place forms the **Soft genus**, and in the third-to-last place, the **Hard genus**. In the former, there is a minor <note>original: "mollis" (soft/minor)</note> third at the bottom; in the latter, a major <note>original: "dura" (hard/major)</note> third. What, then, is the connection of this placement with the affects? Or what does the minor third have in common with women, with passions, and with softness? Likewise, what does the major third have in common with masculinity, hardness, actions, and efficacy?

First, therefore, remember that the **Major Third** <note>original: "Tertia dura"</note> arises from the **Pentagon**. The pentagon uses a division according to the "Extreme and Mean Ratio" <note>The Golden Ratio.</note>, which forms the "Divine Proportion." In this proportion, there resides a beautiful idea of **Generation** <note>Procreation or reproduction.</note>. For just as a father begets a son, and the son another, each similar to himself, so also in that geometric division: when the larger part is added to the whole, the proportion continues; the composite takes the place of the "Whole," and that which was previously the "Whole" takes the place of the "Larger Part." Although this ratio cannot be expressed in [whole] numbers, a certain series of numbers <note>Kepler is describing the Fibonacci Sequence (1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8...).</note> is given which continually approaches the truth. In this series, the very difference between the numbers and their true terms (which are not countable but "ineffable" <note>Irrational numbers.</note>) produces "males" and "females" in an admirable alternation, distinguished by members that indicate their sex. For example, if the larger part is first 2, the minor 1, the total is 3. Here, 1 is not to 2 exactly as 2 is to 3; for the difference is a unit, preventing the rectangle of the extremes (1 and 3) from equaling the square of the mean (2).

<meta>The catchword at the bottom is "medij 2." (the mean 2). Kepler is illustrating the property of Fibonacci numbers where the product of the neighbors of a number differs from the square of that number by 1.</meta>

...of the middle 2. Then, by adding 2 to 3, a new total of 5 is made; and by adding 3 to 5, the total becomes 8, and so on. A rectangle formed from 1 and 3 creates a **female**, for it falls short of the square of 2 by one unit <note>Kepler is describing the Fibonacci property where the product of two numbers flanking a middle number is always one more or one less than the square of that middle number ($1 \times 3 = 3$, which is $2^2 - 1$).</note>; a rectangle from 2 and 5 creates a **male**, for it exceeds the square of 3 by one unit ($2 \times 5 = 10$, which is $3^2 + 1$). <margin>CHAPTER XV.</margin>
Since this is the nature of this "section" <note>The "Golden Ratio" or Divine Proportion, which governs the geometry of the pentagon.</note>—which coincides with the demonstration of the pentagon—and since God the Creator shaped the laws of generation according to it, He directed the seminal patterns of plants (which were each commanded to have their seed within themselves) toward the genuine proportion of "ineffable" terms <note>Irrational numbers/ratios that cannot be expressed as simple whole numbers, like the Golden Ratio.</note>, which is perfect in itself. However, for the conjunction of male and female, He directed them toward the proportions of two joined numbers (where the deficiency of one unit in one is compensated by the excess in the other). What wonder is it, then, if the offspring of the pentagon—the "Hard" Third (the ratio 4:5) and the "Soft" Third (5:6)—move human souls, which are the images of God, to emotions comparable to the business of generation? Here we must recall from Chapter III that although the ratio 1:6 arises from the hexagon, its remainder, the 5:6 ratio, does not harmonize because of the hexagon, but because of its derivation from the three-tenths of a circle through the doubling and halving of terms. Thus, even this "Remainder" and its offspring, the Minor Third, belong to the class of pentagonal figures.

Therefore, having established that the partnership of the two Thirds represents the partnership of male and female, it is now no trouble to assign each sex its own Third. For the **Major Third** will turn out to be virile, and the **Minor Third** feminine; since the same proportion exists in their very bodies and in the strength of both body and mind. And since the Major arises from an odd-sided figure (namely, the pentagon), while the Minor originally arises from an even-sided figure (the decagon), this is also consistent with the teachings of Pythagoras, who called odd numbers male and even numbers female. (This is confirmed by that observation of excesses and defects, since it is the odd number that exceeds), so that the former is considered of the masculine sex, and the latter of the feminine.

Let there be added to these reasons also the contemplation of the "concinnous" <note>musically pleasing or fitting</note> intervals, the smallest of which is the Semitone. For a succeeding Semitone always invites the voice to overcome it because of its smallness; it is like a ridge on a softening slope. Whenever a Semitone occurs in the higher parts of a melody, it is held as a kind of goal for the song toward which it strives; and from there, as if the ridge has been crested and the effort finished, the voice frequently tends to return to the lower notes. Certainly, if we sing *RE, MI*, the hearing is not satisfied, but expects *FA* to be added as well. Since, therefore, the **Hard Third**—which occupies the lowest place in the Eighth Tone <note>The Mixolydian mode</note>—lacks a semitone (which is only added later to complete the Fourth <note>original: "diatessaron"</note>), it is rightly considered active and full of effort. Its power is "generative" <note>original: γόνιμος</note> and an "unrestrained peak" <note>original: ἀκμὴ ἄσχετος</note>, seeking its own end—namely the Fourth—whose semitone is for it like an "outpouring" <note>original: ἔκχυσις</note>, sought with all its might. But the **Minor Third**, standing in the lowest place of the First Tone <note>The Dorian mode</note>, has already embraced the semitone, after the overcoming of which a return is usually made. It is as if it were content with itself, and made by its very nature for submission and passion; it always spreads itself on the ground, like a hen, ready for the treading rooster. And behold the causes of the affects in the Genera, and in the Tones of the primary system rising from G.

Speed is suited to anger, movement, fighting, and cheerfulness; slowness is suited to those affections which we enjoy in stillness: grief, love, desire, and the pleasure of possession.

VI. Add to this the meter, that is, the Rhythm itself: for the force of the so-called triple meter is one thing, and that of the duple is another. This force is perhaps drawn largely from the imitation of dancing choruses; since the alternating variety of movements in them is known to everyone, it immediately alerts the listeners, bringing them as if into the presence of the event itself. Thus, triple meter is turbulent and active, while duple is quieter, more peaceful, and more modest. This we shall pass over untouched, since the distribution of song into three genera is not a natural one, nor are the ancients consistent with themselves on this subject. What, then, is the connection of this position with the emotions? Or what does the Minor Third have in common with women, with passions, and with softness; and likewise, what does the Major Third have in common with masculinity, hardness, actions, and efficacy?

Indeed, in this proportion there is a beautiful idea of **Generation**. For just as a father begets a son, and the son another, each similar to himself, so also in that division: when the larger part is added to the whole, the proportion is continued. The composite takes the place of the Whole, and what was previously the whole takes the place of the larger part. Although this ratio cannot be expressed in whole numbers, a certain series of numbers is given <note>The Fibonacci sequence: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13...</note> which continually approaches closer to the truth. In this series, the very difference of the numbers from the genuine terms (which are not countable but "ineffable" <note>irrational</note>) produces males and females by an admirable alternation, distinguished by members that indicate their sex. For instance, if the major part is first 2, the minor 1, the total is 3. Here, 1 is not to 2 exactly as 2 is to 3; for the difference is one unit, by which the rectangle of the extremes (1 × 3) fails to equal the square of the mean (2 × 2).

(This is confirmed by that observation of excesses and deficiencies, since the male is odd and exceeding.) Therefore, the Major is considered of the masculine sex, and the Minor of the feminine.

To these reasons, let us add the contemplation of the melodic intervals, the smallest of which is the **semitone** <note>the smallest step in a standard scale</note>. For a succeeding semitone always invites the voice to overcome it because of its smallness; it is like a ridge on a hill that is becoming gentler. By its nature, it is made for submission and passion; it always spreads itself, like a hen on the ground, ready for the treading rooster. # BOOK III: ON PROPORTIONS

<margin>CHAPTER XV.</margin>

Now let us consider the same placement of the semitone with respect to all the Tones <note>original: *Tonorum*, referring to the musical modes or scales</note> indiscriminately: where I will adapt my discourse, as I have done so far, to the common Tones, as I have distinguished them according to my own principles. For regarding the remaining ten species of the Octave, which I added for the sake of comparison, it will be for the judgment of musicians whether they deserve the name of Tones.

It has often been said that by nature, among the concordant intervals, the larger ones demand the lowest position for themselves, so that great things are associated with great things. For low sounds, which are likewise below, are determined by a certain magnitude—that is, by long strings—and high sounds by short ones; or, what is the same thing, a low sound is produced by a large and slow motion, and a high one by a small and fast motion. The natural sequence, therefore, is when in a perfect Tetrachord <term>Tetrachord: A scale of four notes spanning a perfect fourth, the building block of ancient Greek and medieval scales.</term>, the Major Tone <note>original: *Tonus major*, a whole step with the ratio 9:8</note> is in the first place, the Minor <note>original: *Tonus minor*, a whole step with the ratio 10:9</note> in the second, and the Semitone <note>original: *Semitonium*, the half-step</note> in the third and highest place. Indeed, when all things are according to nature, we are joyful: therefore, those Tones are Joyful which have the lower Tetrachord divided in this way. The Seventh and Eighth Tones possess this; which they think were called by the ancients now *Phrygian*, now *Mixolydian*, with wonderful inconsistency; although I am more inclined to believe they were called *Lydian* by the Ancients; because they testify of their *Lydian* mode that it fills minds with divine frenzy—that is, with alacrity and military spirits—of which kind are our Seventh and Eighth Tones.

When, therefore, the order is overturned, so that the Semitone is in the lowest place—which happens in the Third and Fourth ecclesiastical modes, which were the *Phrygian* to the ancients—the natural order being reversed, it is consistent that a certain plaintive, broken, and lamentable sound is produced. But when the Semitone is in the middle position, the effect is a middle state of tranquility, humanity, and pleasantness arising from conversation and storytelling: for which the First and Second Tones are suited, being of the soft and feminine genus; these they think were once called *Dorian*. Indeed, *Vincenzo Galilei* <note>Vincenzo Galilei (1520–1591), an influential Italian lutenist and theorist, and father of the astronomer Galileo Galilei.</note> describes the *Dorian* as naturally stable, quiet, without violence, suited for gravity and severity: which is true of these two in greater or lesser degrees. For it is necessary that the Tones named by even numbers always be softer; because they are the plagal <term>Plagal: A secondary mode that shares the same final note as its "authentic" parent mode but has a lower range.</term> to their authentic counterparts <note>The "authentic" modes are the odd-numbered ones (1, 3, 5, 7); "plagal" modes are the even ones (2, 4, 6, 8).</note>, which are named from the odd numbers, for the reason that was brought forward a little earlier in Number IV. Thus *Galilei* also makes the Plagal of the First <note>The Second Tone</note> languid, mournful, and fearful; for he says motion toward the low notes belongs to languor, and motion toward the high notes belongs to vigor. And yet I would prefer both to temper those epithets and to distinguish the cause. For languor, weeping, and fear are not properties unique to the Dorian modes, but result generally from excursions into the low notes and frequent descents below the root note.

IX. So far we have spoken concerning the placement of the semitone; yet we have not yet assigned their specific properties to all the Tones. It follows, therefore, that we should also speak of the imperfect and "adulterated" <note>original: *adulterinis*, referring to intervals that deviate slightly from pure mathematical ratios</note> consonances, by which the skeletons of the octaves are articulated. And first, their essence, as it were, must be inspected, and afterwards their location in the System.

When, therefore, the disposition of the Octave system is natural and primal, in which the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth resonate perfectly with the lowest string: such a Tone stirs all those things in the soul that are according to nature—passions in the case of the soft <note>original: *mollis*, similar to the minor key</note>, and actions in the case of the hard <note>original: *durus*, similar to the major key</note>, or the affections suited to them. This property belongs to the First and Eighth Tones rising from G: by which name *Galilei* asserted, not without justice, that the Eighth coincides with the First; understand, however, that the property of each specific type or genus is preserved. Thus, for a double reason, the Seventh and Eighth stand out above the others, both because of the placement of the semitone, and also because of the perfection...

### ON HARMONICS, BOOK III.

<margin>CHAPTER XV.</margin> Conversely, the Fifth and Sixth, and the Third and Fourth [Modes] use adulterated and augmented consonances in their lower parts—the former a Fourth, the latter a Fifth—a circumstance which gives them a power of sadness and of emotions that depart from human moderation.

For in the Fifth and Sixth, the Fourth <note>original: *Diatessaron*, the interval of a perfect fourth</note> is indeed **high-pitched** <term>ὀρθίον: meaning "upright" or "high-pitched," referring to a scale structure where the intervals are stretched or placed higher.</term>, with the natural position of the semitone at the top, no less than in the Seventh and Eighth; but there are two major tones in the lowest position, followed by a semitone; from these is fashioned a Fourth that is "abundant by a comma" <note>Kepler refers to a mathematically imperfect fourth that is slightly wider than the pure 4:3 ratio due to the stacking of two "major" whole steps (9:8).</note>.

Therefore, these modes also promote emotions of magnitude, such as **Devotion**, **Admiration**, **Amplification**, and **Grief**; and again **Hope** and **Confidence**, acting as a kind of elevation of the mind above one's present lot.

But in the Third and Fourth, besides the inverted form of the Fourth itself, there is also an added "fermentation" of the consonances, which increases the sadness and the languors of the soul.

Namely, if one follows the analogy beyond the usual tones to a third species from my system—a **soft song** <note>original: *cantus mollis*, often referring to music using B-flat or the "soft" hexachord</note> described from the letter <insert>Δ</insert> <note>Delta, likely referring to the note D</note>—because that species has a semitone below it, but a perfect Fourth above. I would therefore adapt this to a **pleasant sadness**, such as when we take pleasure in a softness of spirit, in **Love** and **Desires**, or when joy expresses itself through tears.

These things concern the consonances by their own nature; now let us see what they effect by reason of their place in the system.

When, therefore, **pitching** <term>τόνη: the act of tuning or tensioning strings to a specific pitch.</term> and **compositional design** <term>πεττεία: an ancient Greek term for the art of musical composition, literally "playing the board," referring to how a composer chooses and uses notes.</term> are occupied chiefly around the fourth and sixth strings, it appears that the Fourth is placed in the lowest position by them. Because this is the interval of the Tetrachord <note>A four-note scale segment</note> which encompasses all three species of melodic intervals, it is the most important element in this "animation" of the Tones. At such times, this form invites the song toward **humility**, for the same reason I used above in No. IV. But if these parts of the song are occupied around the third and fifth strings, placing the Fourth higher up, the song is excited and elevated, especially if it runs up to the octave. This seems to have been the nature of the **High-pitched Song** <term>Νόμῳ ὀρθίῳ: the "Orthian Nomos," an ancient, high-pitched and vigorous Greek melodic style used for stirring emotions.</term> of the ancients. If, finally, it centers around the third and sixth, so that the Fourth is reduced to the middle—which happens more frequently in the First and Second Modes than in the Seventh and Eighth—then a **moderate emotion** will be promoted. Often, however, these "articulations of the skeleton" <note>original: *sceletôn articulationes*, Kepler's metaphor for the structural intervals of a scale</note> are mixed among themselves, so that there are different characters in different parts of the song, according to the variety of the text and the skill of the artist who paints the text with music.

X. If it is true, as some say, that the odd-numbered Tones (I, III, V, VII) are higher, and the even-numbered (II, IV, VI, VIII) are lower, even with respect to the root of the Octave: then certainly height corresponds to the excitation of the Soul, and depth to its lowering. We can then surely distribute the four classes of emotions into eight classes, according to these same eight tones:

*   The **Seventh** holds anger, violence, and fortitude.
*   The **Eighth** holds cheerfulness, alacrity, and sharp pleasure.
*   The **Third** holds sharp pain and desire.
*   The **Fourth** holds weeping and love.
*   The **First** holds festivity, weddings, and banquets.
*   The **Second** holds modest cheerfulness, conversation, and storytelling.
*   The **Fifth** holds public assemblies, exclamations, confidence, and hope.
*   The **Sixth** holds devotion, great pain, and so on.

->ON PROPORTIONS<-

And now it is time for the discourse to return to its beginning. For the philosophical reader must be reminded that our musicians express all emotions indiscriminately in all Tones <note>Kepler uses "Tones" here to refer to the ecclesiastical modes (Dorian, Phrygian, etc.).</note>; they do so because every song, without distinction, produces pleasure in the listener and requires a sense of spiritedness in the composer; and they are able to do so because the instruments for stirring the emotions are many (some of which were reviewed at the start), which can be applied everywhere through all Tones indiscriminately. If, however, they strive to use all the aids making for the same purpose, they will not easily neglect the choice of Tones suitable for the specific emotional premise <note>original: *hypothesin*</note>. But let them look to what is permitted in their own practice; for me, it is enough to have proceeded thus far theoretically.

# CHAPTER XVI.

## What Harmonic Song is, or Figured Song.

Although the word "Harmony" <note>original: *Harmonia*</note> was used by the ancients to mean "Song" [melody], it must not be understood under this name as a melody through several voices sounding harmonically together. For it requires little proof to show that the "Concert" <note>original: *Concentus*, a singing together</note> of several voices in a perpetual succession of harmonies is a recent invention, plainly unknown to the ancients. On this matter, one may consult Vincenzo Galilei in his Italian work on music <note>Kepler refers to Galilei's *Dialogo della musica antica et della moderna* (1581), which argued that ancient Greek music was monophonic.</note>. It is often objected that "harmonic song" was banished from Plato’s *Republic*, as if it were already in use then; but the passage is understood to refer to the Organ, the Pan-pipes <term>Syringe: a set of pipes of graduated lengths</term>, the Bagpipes <term>Utriculo: a bladder-pipe or early bagpipe</term>, and the Lute <term>Testudine: literally "tortoise," referring to the lyre or lute made from a shell</term>, where one voice either sounds perpetually <note>a drone</note> or pauses, giving way to an approaching dissonance. In that ancient custom, there was no greater skill than what is found among our own bagpipers.

In these recent centuries, this method of singing began to be called **Figured** <note>original: *Figurata*</note> because the first authors did not make their notations <note>original: *diagrammata*</note> as simple as they are in Plainchant <note>original: *Chorali cantu*, the traditional unison chant of the church</note>; instead, they used various figures and dots. Some of these signs command silence, some sound; some are long, others short; some are used for distinguishing the Tones, some for rhythmic modes <term>Modos mensurales: the medieval system of defining rhythmic duration by the shape of the notes</term>, and others for Fugues, Repetitions, and similar devices.

Let us, therefore, define a **Harmonic Concert** thus: that there be two, three, four, or more voices or suitable Melodies (such as we described in Chapter XIII), all of the same Genus, and of the same or related Modes, proceeding together in such a way that they create concords <note>original: *concordantias*</note>, either pure or "fermented" with a very brief punctuation of suitable dissonances; yet these are not identical in a perpetual tone, nor are they the same in succession, but are varied for delight by the very alternation of the successions. For just as the Consonance of two voices is to a Unison in terms of proportion, so is Harmonic Song to the simple song of a single

...the melody of the voice; from this principle depend all the components of the definition, which I shall explain in order.

<margin>CHAPTER XVI.</margin>
I. First, therefore, regarding the plurality of voices, we must note what musical craftsmen <note>original: *Artifices*</note> have established as being most in harmony with Nature: that although many voices often sing together, they are all nonetheless

called by only four names. This corresponds to the number of the perfect harmonic mediation <note>The mathematical division of an interval into smaller consonant parts.</note> within one perfect system of the octave <note>original: *diapason*</note>. For they name the highest voice the **Discant** <note>Today commonly called the Soprano.</note>; the **Alto** is the one closest to it; the **Tenor** is the higher of the deep voices; and the **Bass** is the lowest. For between two voices sounding an octave apart, there are only two 
<image-desc>A small musical staff showing two diamond-shaped notes an octave apart, connected by a bracket to indicate they form the outer boundaries of a harmonic system.</image-desc>
middle voices that are harmonically consonant at the same time with the outer voices (which sound as the same note), as was explained in Chapter III.

Although the origin of these terms is Italian, they seem to refer more to a composite system, so that the Alto and Bass hold opposite parts within it—not that the Alto is necessarily the highest, but because these two often (though not at the end) create 
<image-desc>A schematic musical diagram showing four voice ranges on a staff: Disc: (highest), Alt: (second), Ten: (third), and Bass: (lowest), each marked with a clef and a diamond-shaped note to show their relative positions.</image-desc>
an octave, the former being the higher and sharper, the latter being the lower and deeper. Likewise, the origin of the word **Tenor** <note>From the Latin *tenere*, "to hold."</note> gives us the idea of the simple melody or "carrying" of the song. The name **Discant** <note>meaning "apart-song" or "singing away"</note> seems to have been given because of its constant movement and wandering away from the path of the Tenor, which sits an octave away. Therefore, if we compare the parts of Song cited from Euclid in Chapter XIII, even though those parts belong to all voices, the **Tenor** is chiefly occupied in <term>Agoge</term> <note>original: *Ἀγωγῇ*; the "conduct" or directional flow of the melody</note>, the **Discant** in <term>Ploke</term> <note>original: *Πλοκῇ*; "weaving" or the intertwining of notes</note>, the **Alto** in <term>Tonne</term> <note>original: *Τονῇ*; "stretching" or sustaining a pitch</note>, and the **Bass** in leaping through harmonic intervals. However, <term>Petteia</term> <note>original: *Πεττείᾳ*; the art of choosing which notes to use and where to place them, like moves in a board game</note> is common to all four, though it is more distinguished in the Alto.

These properties of the four voices are taken from the very Nature of things. For because, according to our provided definition, the harmony must perpetually change from one state to another, it was necessary for this to happen in such a way that one of the middle voices, compared to the others, moves within a narrow space of the system. For if an equal, loose freedom were given to all, the result would inevitably be that the lower voice would frequently wander into the space of the higher and vice-versa; there would be a chaotic confusion, and the distinction between the four voices would be rendered useless. This narrowness of the middle voices ought to be occupied by one of them (either the Alto or the Tenor) rather than the outer voices, the Discant or Bass.

For if such a restriction were placed on the outer voices, every variation of intervals would tend toward only one direction—either toward the high or the low. It was better, therefore, for the Harmony to be fixed or tied to a narrow place by one of the intermediate voices, acting as a sort of boundary for the parts; the variation of the intervals could then stretch from it partly upward and partly downward. Yet, it was not right for the lower of the middle voices to be so constricted; because the "Idea" of the song is ascribed to the Tenor (the lower of the middle voices), it must be free and proceed through the middle quantity of the entire system, so that the surrounding voices are nothing other than its colors, ornaments, or emblems. Furthermore, the lower intervals are always larger than their higher counterparts. Thus, for the Tenor to hold the middle place of the total range, it was necessary for it to be the lower of the middle voices; and thus the Alto...

<margin>CHAPTER XVI.</margin>
...it was necessary to restrict the range, but not that of the Tenor. There remain, therefore, the ranges of movement for the **Discant** and the **Bass**, but with this distinction: the **Bass**, which sounds deep and is expressed by a great motion and long strings, wanders through slow and large measures and wide harmonic intervals. The **Discant**, which sounds shrill and "flies over" the others, is elicited from short strings and a swift motion within a narrow space; it wanders through everything with short and therefore more frequent measures, and the smallest fitting <note>original: *concinnis*</note> intervals. This, then, is the specific nature of the voices. Now I shall declare the remaining parts of the definition.

<margin>Dissonances.</margin>
II. Regarding that primary and chief seasoning of Melodic Song, **Dissonance**: First, it is necessary that these be drawn not from just any unmusical <note>original: *ἀναρμόσῳ* (anarmosō), meaning out of tune or non-harmonic</note> interval, but from fitting intervals. For because individual voices, meeting in a common harmony, admit no intervals between successive sounds unless they are fitting—and they are of the same genus and Tone, as stated in the definition—it is easily seen that if a harmony is established among such voices (since all harmony is dissolved into fitting elements), no wandering of a single voice from the root of its Octave <note>original: *Octavae*</note> can ever cause two voices together to make anything other than a fitting interval, even if it is not always a consonant one.

<margin>See book II of Giovanni Maria Artusi of Bologna on the art of composition, which is entirely about dissonances.</margin>
Secondly, although excellent craftsmen sometimes use larger dissonances—where the dissonant voice is a whole tone away from the one that would make a consonance—this does not happen except to express and draw out the deepest emotions of the soul. However, the ordinary dissonance, joined with pleasantness and thus in a certain way "natural," is created by the **semitone** <note>The smallest interval in traditional Western music, the distance between two adjacent keys on a piano.</note>.

<margin>The power of the Fifteen-sided figure in the choice of dissonances.</margin>
The cause of this matter, so that the last things may respond to the first, must be sought again from the innermost foundations of Geometry (from Chapter I, Axioms II and III, and from Book I) and the contemplation of the **Fifteen-sided figure** <note>original: *Quindecanguli* or *Pentekædecagoni*</note>. For since the semitone is contained in the numbers 15:16, and not only does the sixteen-sided figure have a geometric demonstration <note>A "demonstration" in this context refers to whether the shape can be constructed using only a straightedge and compass.</note>, but so does the fifteen-sided figure, it was very nearly the case that 15:16 defined a harmonic proportion for us. No less fitting were its derivatives: 15:8, 15:4, 15:2, 15:32, 15:64, and especially 15:1—those proportions which composite music very frequently admits to form legitimate dissonances. 

There was no other reason for us to exclude it from the primary consonances except this: the demonstration of the Fifteen-sided figure was not shaped by the number of the figure's angles immediately, like the others, and thus it is not "proper" to itself. Instead, it is transferred from different figures—the Triangle and the Pentagon—and is thus "borrowed" and of a most remote degree. Likewise, although an angle of a Fifteen-sided figure can work with others to fill a flat surface, the whole figure does not admit "congruence" <note>Kepler’s term for "tiling," or the ability of shapes to fit together perfectly to fill a space.</note> with all its angles. 

Therefore, since 15:16 and its associates come so close to Consonances by the nature of their forming cause, it is no wonder they are frequently mixed among the consonances in practice. On the other hand, the whole Tones (8:9 and 9:10) share in the **Nine-sided figure** <note>original: *Nonangulo*</note> via their other terms; this figure is entirely indemonstrable <note>A regular nine-sided polygon cannot be constructed with a straightedge and compass.</note>. Therefore, dissonances admitted through these and their associated proportions (4:9, 2:9, 1:9, 9:16, 9:32, as well as 9:5, 18:5, 36:5, 9:20, 9:40, etc.) are not sweet, but altogether harsh. Much harsher still are those consisting of the **Tritone** <note>The "Devil's Interval," an augmented fourth.</note>, the mutilated Fifth <note>original: *diapente*, referring here to the diminished fifth</note>, and similar intervals; regarding these, see Artu-

<margin>CHAPTER XVI.</margin>
<margin>Artusi:</margin>
...for they <note>dissonances</note> arise after the Tones—the Major and Minor—and the Semitone; namely, from the non-natural composition of these as if they were elements. However, the further one departs from Nature, the further one departs from sweetness.

<margin>Syncopation</margin>
Thirdly, another name for dissonances suggests their remaining laws when they are called **Syncopations** <note>In the 17th century, "syncopation" often referred to what we now call a "suspension"—holding a note over from a previous chord so that it becomes dissonant before resolving.</note>; although this is a common occurrence for both dissonances and imperfect consonances, we are now dealing with dissonances. For they generally hold to this rule: that they use dissonance like leaven, or salt, or vinegar in relishes <note>original: *opsonijs*, meaning side-dishes or seasonings</note>. That is to say, just as full courses are not made from these alone, so here entire songs do not abound in dissonances—unless for the sake of great emphasis. Nor does any voice, beginning at the very start of the beat, run into the other consonants while being dissonant itself. Instead, it admits dissonance stealthily and, as if by stalling, while occupying a place in the system when the beat is lifted <note>on the upbeat</note>. Thus, starting a specific sound in the later and less principal part of the beat while the others agree, it lingers longer and beyond the start of the next beat after those have finished. In this way, all the other voices—usually deeper than itself (so that it, being high-pitched, causes less noise due to its smallness, weakness, and speed)—occupy a place dissonant from its position at the start of the next beat by their common harmony, before it has left its own place. Then they drive it out as if it were slow, and usually push it down to a lower position. 
<margin>Cadences</margin>
On this occasion, the name **Cadences** <note>original: *Cadentiarum*, from *cadere*, to fall</note> seems to have been born for the concords and concluding phrases <note>original: *clausulis*</note> that resolve these dissonances.

Moreover, they observe this: that the battle of Dissonants is usually engaged not so often from a nearby interval, such as between seconds, as between sevenths. Thus the higher voice, driven from its place in this way, flows down by a Semitone or Tone to a sixth, or flies up to mark an Octave with the preceding voices.

<margin>Common Dissonances</margin>
There are also other very frequent dissonances, less artificial, when the deep voice continues its sound, staying on a unison, while the high voice runs out from the octave <note>original: *diapason*</note> of that deep sound with swift tones toward some note consonant with it through a fifth <note>original: *diapente*</note> or a fourth <note>original: *diatesaron*</note>, flying through all the fitting <note>original: *concinna*</note> intermediate places. Thus it is alternately consonant and dissonant. However, the one that is first in order always consonates; the dissonance is both brief, because it is in passing, and in a sound that is later in order. For example, if a beat of double proportion joins five sounds of the **Discant** with one of the **Bass**, the first, third, and fifth notes of the Discant will be consonant, while the second and fourth will be dissonant. Behold:

For just as in a simple melody, the leading of a single individual voice from the root of the system through dissonant but fitting intervals tends toward places harmonically tempered to the Root, and dwells in them; so melodic harmony, beginning almost from a unison, tends toward major <note>The text cuts off here to the next page.</note>

major and perfect consonances, and mostly (especially at the end) toward **Unison** <note>original: *Identisonantiam*, literally "identity of sound." Kepler refers to the voices resolving to the same note or its octave.</note>.

<margin>CHAPTER XVI</margin>
<margin>Imperfect consonances.</margin>
IV. Furthermore, just as in the simple melodies of those languages which consist of **Rhythm** and the length or shortness of syllables, not much account is taken of the short ones; but we direct the long syllables and the ends of verses toward places that are consonant with the primary sound: so also in a harmony, there are consonances, called minor and imperfect, which we fly through quickly; and there are perfect ones, toward which we tend, which are therefore called **Cadences** <note>original: *Clausulæ*, referring to the concluding points of a musical phrase.</note>.
<margin>Perfect ones not to be placed consecutively.</margin>
V. Moreover, just as the individual consonances considered separately are pleasing for the reason that they do not sound exactly identical, but are in a way shaped and "diverse-sounding," occupying a certain qualitative breadth in the hearing—drawing their nature from the regular plane figures from which they also arise: so now a **Harmonic Song**, or a perpetual sequence of several harmonies, loses all its grace without variety.

<margin>Why two fifths etc. [are not used] consecutively.</margin>
From this explanation of the definition, the causes can be given for the laws which composers observe in fitting together concords. For it can be asked: What is the natural cause why they think it permitted for themselves to arrange several natural Thirds and Sixths in a row; but do not admit several Fourths, Fifths, Octaves, and the like from a single species in a row?

->I respond,<- that this cause is that Thirds or Sixths following each other in pitch are usually, in truth, different—one major, the other minor. And although sometimes two minor Thirds might closely follow one another, they are nevertheless the smallest and most imperfect consonances. For let the first [voice] sing *Ut Re Mi Fa* <note>The syllables of the hexachord, roughly C-D-E-F</note>, and the second at those same moments of time sing *Mi Fa Sol La* <note>E-F-G-A</note>.
<image-desc>Musical notation on a staff showing four ascending notes, Ut Re Mi Fa.</image-desc>
Four Thirds follow each other; of which the first, *Ut Mi* <note>C-E</note>, is a **Major Third**; the second, *Re Fa* <note>D-F</note>, and the third, *Mi Sol* <note>E-G</note>, are **Minor Thirds**; the fourth, *Fa La* <note>F-A</note>, is again a **Major Third**.
<image-desc>Musical notation on a staff showing four ascending notes, Mi Fa Sol La.</image-desc>
On the contrary, all Fourths are commonly held to be intervals of the same magnitude; as are Fifths, and much more so Octaves. Therefore, if several of these perfect concords of the same species were arranged in a row, differing in pitch, the song would not be varied in its consonances.

But another principal cause prevents several Fifths being sung in order going upward, which does not prevent Octaves from being sung: about which **Aristotle** thought he should inquire in his *Problems*: "Why do they sing in Octaves (for example, men with women, or men with boys) but do not sing in Fifths and Fourths?" This, therefore, is the cause: that while two Thirds make the consonance of a **Fifth** <note>original: *Diapente*</note>, and two Octaves make the consonance of a **Double Octave** <note>original: *Disdiapason*</note>, on the other hand, two Fifths make a **Ninth**, and two Fourths make a **Seventh**, which are dissonant intervals. Therefore, a voice running through Octave and Third consonances stays equally within the **Tone** or **Mode**, observing the same species of Octave; here, if it runs through equal [fifths], it significantly changes the mode or Tone, which is against the definition.

VI. Concerning the choice of concords, some things should also be noted; first, that in general, large intervals express great emotions of the soul (as in those works of **Orlando** [di Lasso], *Where is Abel?* and *My Soul is Sorrowful*); small and high intervals express joy; low and small ones express sadness.

<meta>The catchword "Deinde" (Then) indicates the continuation of the list of expressive qualities of intervals on the next page.</meta>

<summary>Kepler explains why composers allow consecutive Thirds and Sixths but forbid consecutive Fifths and Octaves, arguing that Thirds provide natural variety in size (major/minor) whereas consecutive perfect intervals lead to dissonance or a loss of musical mode. He also begins to categorize the emotional "affects" of different musical intervals.</summary>

# BOOK III OF THE HARMONIES

<margin>CHAPTER XVI</margin>
Furthermore, since a harmonic song usually ends in **Unison** <note>original: *Identisonantiam*, literally "identity of sound." In this context, it refers to voices resolving to the same note or an octave.</note>: so that we may encompass a large interval at the end, as the text requires, it is necessary not only for the Bass to descend, but also for the Treble to ascend—contrary to the usual nature of finishing a song—in imitation of the pipes and the strings of the **Pandura** <note>A long-necked stringed instrument of the lute family.</note>. And it is then that the power of the **semitone** <term>half-step</term>, explained in the previous chapter, shines forth most clearly; for the natural and ordinary conclusion of a song through an ascent loves to overcome a semitone at the end, at least in those **Tones** <term>musical modes</term> which do not already have a semitone immediately above the root of their Octave.

<margin>Why large intervals are more pleasing</margin>
Thirdly, **Galilei** <note>Vincenzo Galilei (c. 1520–1591), a music theorist and father of the astronomer Galileo Galilei.</note> judged it a question worthy of study: why a **Fifth above an Octave** <note>original: *Diapente epi diapason*; a compound interval of a twelfth.</note> sounds more pleasing than a simple **Fifth** <note>original: *Diapente*.</note>, and so on, such that one harmony is always more pleasing than another. It is not worth the effort to examine the causes he himself brought forward, as they are obscure and uncertain. However, from my own principles, the causes of this matter appear most clearly. For because, by Axiom II of the first chapter, the degrees of knowledge by which the sides of figures differ from one another are also transplanted into the proportions themselves (the "offspring" of the figures), it is surely consistent that those degrees by which the demonstration of the **Part of the circle** and the **Remainder** differ also distinguish the sweetness of the Part and the Remainder. Therefore, those harmonies which exist immediately through the sectioning of the circle itself—namely, those between the **Whole** and the **Part cut away**—are more perfect and pleasing than those between the **Remainder** and the **Whole**, which are ultimately derived from the former through the admixture of Unisons from the halving or doubling of strings. Thus, the ratio 1:3 holds the primary place and is therefore more pleasing than 2:3; and 1:6 more than 5:6; and 1:5 more than 4:5; and 1:4 more than 3:4; and 2:5 more than 3:5; and 3:8 more than 5:8. For in the first case, the Part is consonant in itself, not because of the Remainder; in the latter case, and thus more imperfectly, the Remainder is demonstrated to be consonant only because of its partner or an outside Part.

<margin>The aim of this entire work.</margin>
The remaining rules of the composer’s art I leave to the craftsmen themselves to prove or to explain their reasoning. For me, what I have discussed up to this point is abundantly sufficient, both for illustrating the nature of Song (having shown at least its first and general foundations in Nature) and especially for the speculations of the following Book V. The subject matter of that book is the sole end I have proposed for this entire work. For I am an **Astronomer**; just as I discuss regular figures not so much geometrically (except where geometry seemed incomplete) as astronomically and metaphysically, so also I write about the proportions of song not so much musically as geometrically, physically, and finally—as before—astronomically and metaphysically. For just as I have need of the **five regular solids** from Geometry, so also I need the Proportions and the whole harmonic apparatus from Music to explain the causes of the proportions of the **celestial spheres**, the **eccentricities**, and the motions at the **apsides** <note>The points in an orbit where a planet is closest to or farthest from the sun.</note>. Truly, I do not profess the art of composing song, which is the practice of Music; whoever wishes for that will more rightly seek it from the books on the art of composition published by the aforementioned **Artusi** <note>Giovanni Maria Artusi (c. 1540–1613), an Italian composer and theorist.</note> and by **Sethus Calvisius** <note>Sethus Calvisius (1556–1615), a German astronomer and music theorist who was a friend of Kepler.</note>, formerly my friend. I name these men not because I think they are the best, but because I have not seen others.

ON PROPORTIONS

# On the Three Means
## A Political Digression.

<margin>See the most beautiful passage in Bodin's *On the Commonwealth*;</margin>
On Page 29, line 9, the following paragraph was excluded from its proper place because the printer's staff had carelessly distributed the leaves of the manuscript (specifically, pages 7 and 10).

Nevertheless, authors should not be criticized for this reason—namely, for adopting proportions of this kind into the **Commonwealth** <note>original: *Rempublicam*; referring to the state or organized civil society.</note> under the title of **Harmonics**. For although few proportions formed in this way define pure musical Harmonies, and the rest are all foreign to Harmonies, they all share this definition: they are tempered from both types of proportion, the **Arithmetic** and the **Geometric**. It is from this tempering that they possess their suitability for the Commonwealth. Conversely, if there is any power of Harmonics *as Harmonics* in the Commonwealth, then our harmonic means cannot be scorned, which I provide here under a broader definition:

<margin>What a Harmonic Mean truly is.</margin>
> It is everything that comes between two consonant voices, being itself consonant with both of them. Therefore, in the sections, etc.

*Thus far, the omitted material.* Now, since I mentioned Bodin in the margin, and since I have finished Book III and added the above paragraph, I judged that enough work has been done on mathematical speculations. Having finished this thorny matter, I decided to transcribe the principal points of this political discussion from Bodin himself, with the words and order mostly shaped by my own understanding of that passage. I do this both to bring some light to a place that is obscure in itself—for Bodin did not bring enough support from mathematical disciplines to this speculation—and to soothe the boredom of those peevish mathematical demonstrations (of which this whole work is composed) by interspersing pleasant, popular material, and to show a taste of its usefulness in understanding the Commonwealth. I shall begin, however, with a more detailed explanation of the mathematical subject, accommodated to the understanding of a non-mathematician.

When equal amounts are added to some numbers, without regard to their size, then it is an **Arithmetic proportion**. For example:

<note>For just as 6 is greater than 3, so (by just as many units) 12 is greater than 9.</note>

| 3. | 9. | 5. | 10. | 17. | 38. |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Add 3. | 3. | 3. | 3. | 3. | 3. |
| 6. | 12. | 8. | 13. | 20. | 41. |

This proportion in this example is **disjunct** <term>separate or non-continuous</term>. Therefore, a **conjunct proportion** or **arithmetic progression** occurs when, starting from any number, equal amounts are added to it continuously.

<note>Since, therefore, there is a continuous arithmetic progression between 3, 6, 9, 12, as well as between 38, 41, 44, 47; it follows that the middle of three such numbers placed in succession is called the **Arithmetic Mean**; just as 9 is the Mean between 6 and 12, and 41 is the Arithmetic Mean between 38 and 44.</note>

| As 3 | or 38 |
| :--- | :--- |
| 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 41 |
| 3 | 3 |
| 9 | 44 |
| 3 | 3 |
| 12 | 47 |

But when similar amounts are added to some numbers, taking their size into account, then it is a **Geometric proportion**.

<header>ON HARMONICS, BOOK III.</header>

<margin>**POLITICS**,</margin>

| 3. | 9. | 5. | 10. | 17. | 38. |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 9. | 27. | 15. | 30. | 51. | 114. |
| 12. | 36. | 20. | 40. | 68. | 152. |

For just as the triple of 3 (which is 9) is added to 3, so to 9 is added its own triple 27; this latter sum is as much greater than 9 as 9 is greater than 3, and as 15 is greater than 5, and so on. Therefore, as 3 is to 12, so 9 is to 36. And as 3 is to 9, so 12 is to 36. <note>Kepler is demonstrating a "disjunct" or discrete geometric proportion where the relationship between the numbers remains constant across different sets.</note>

Furthermore, the proportion in this example is discrete. Therefore, a **Geometric proportion** (or progression) that is "joined" occurs when, having started from any number, either a similar part or a similar multiple is always added to it.

| For example | 3 | 10 | 8 |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| | 9 | 30 | 4 |
| | 12 | 40 | 12 |
| | 36 | 120 | 6 |
| | 48 | 160 | 18 |
| | 144 | 480 | 9 |
| | 192 | 640 | 27 |

In the first two examples, the triple is added to the initial number; in the third, a half is added. Then, to the number that is produced from this, the same multiple or part is added again. Thus, as 8 is to 12, so this same 12 is further related to 18, and 18 likewise to 27. In this case, 12 is the **geometric mean** <note>original: *medietas Geometrica*; a value where the ratio between the first and second number is the same as between the second and third.</note> between 8 and 18. Similarly, 18 is the geometric mean or proportional middle between 12 and 27, and so on.

These things must first be understood so that one may grasp what a **Harmonic proportion** is. For it is defined by Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and political philosopher who argued that a "well-ordered" state should mirror mathematical harmonies.</note> in such a way that *within it, the ratios of equals and similars are moderately blended* <note>original: *modicè confuse*; Bodin used this to describe a mixture of Arithmetic and Geometric justice.</note>—that is, the earlier ratios are **Arithmetic** and the later ones are **Geometric**.

Furthermore, this definition is not entirely true. **1.** For there are many ways, even among non-harmonic numbers, in which the ratios of equals and similars can be "moderately blended"; yet this does not suffice to make a proportion harmonic. Indeed, it is necessary to include other relationships of numbers, which must be sought from Chapters I, II, and III. **2.** Conversely, there are many harmonic pairings of numbers in which the ratios of neither "equals" nor "similars" are contained. **3.** Nay, there are even harmonic proportions in which there is a simple Geometric proportion, such as 1, 2, 4; although these are identical in ratio and do not by themselves produce any special beauty. Indeed, Bodin goes so far as to deny that these produce any **harmony** <note>original: *concentum*; referring to a musical concord or "sounding together."</note> on their own—meaning a "figured" or complex harmony. Conversely, there are other harmonic proportions in which there is a simple Arithmetic proportion, such as 1, 2, 3, or 2, 3, 4; Bodin, forgetting his own rule, recognizes these as harmonic, even though they have no mixture of Geometric analogy. The same applies to 3, 4, 5; to 4, 5, 6; to 1, 3, 5; to 2, 5, 8, etc. Bodin wrongly denies that these latter sets produce harmonic concords, rising up on the authority of the ancients against the very evidence of the sense of hearing.

<summary>Kepler defines geometric progressions and means as a mathematical foundation to critique Jean Bodin's definition of harmonic proportion, arguing that Bodin relies too much on ancient authority rather than the actual experience of musical hearing.</summary>

# ON PROPORTIONS

<margin>DIGRESSION.</margin>
However, the assertion is true to some extent regarding that proportion which the ancients, through a false persuasion, called **Harmonic**. I say "to some extent" if, indeed, for the *Ratios of equals*, you understand **Arithmetic Means** <note>original: *Mediationes Arithmeticas*; an arithmetic mean is the "average" where the step between numbers is the same, like 2, 4, 6.</note> transformed into other numbers, in which the actual equality of the differences—which existed in the first three numbers—is no longer expressed. For the **Harmonic Mean** of the ancients is most properly defined in this way: *that the ratio of the differences between three numbers is the same as the ratio of the outer numbers (the extremes), as in 3, 4, 6.* <note>In the set 3, 4, 6: the difference between 3 and 4 is 1. The difference between 4 and 6 is 2. The ratio of these differences (1 to 2) is the same as the ratio of the outer numbers (3 to 6).</note> Whichever three such numbers they are, whether they are truly harmonic or not, it is always true of them that the *ratios of equals* (or rather, *arithmetic ratios*) and the *ratios of likenesses* (or *Geometric ratios*) are confused in one certain way. 

The method is this: given the outer numbers, such as 2 and 5, an arithmetic mean is given. So that it does not result in a fraction, let the doubles of the outer numbers be taken here: 4 and 10. The arithmetic mean of these is 7. Now, in such an arithmetic mediation—4, 7, 10—with equal differences of 3 and 3, two proportions are always established: one larger, between the smaller terms 4 and 7; the other smaller, between the larger terms 7 and 10.

<margin>
* 7. 10.
4. 7.
</margin>
Now, whoever wishes to create a **Harmonic mediation** from this **Arithmetic mediation**, and mix into it something of a **Geometric mediation**, let him place the smaller proportion in the first position and the larger proportion in the second position, like so: <note>referring to the marginal diagram swapping the ratios 4:7 and 7:10</note> and let him seek a number that relates to 10 just as 4 relates to 7. These three numbers will then be 7, 10, and 17 1/2; or in whole numbers that are prime to each other, 14, 20, and 35. Into this trio, something of an **Arithmetic progression** is mixed, though its expressed equality does not remain. For both proportions of the Arithmetic mediation between 4, 7, and 10 have been brought here, only with the order changed: for just as the earlier terms there (4 to 7) were, so are the later terms here (20 to 35). And just as the later terms there (7 to 10) were, so are the earlier terms here (14 to 20). Conversely, something of a **Geometric mediation** is also mixed in. For the smaller proportion, 7 to 10, is placed with the smaller terms 14 and 20; the larger proportion, 4 to 7, with the larger terms 20 and 35. Finally, it results that just as the smallest term 14 is to the largest term 35, so the smaller difference 6 is to the larger difference 15. All these things, in truth, savor of a certain similarity familiar to **Geometric proportion**, because in that, as the smallest term is to the middle, so the middle is to the largest.

These mathematical principles must be held firmly; Jean Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596) was a French jurist and political philosopher who argued that a "Harmonic" state combined elements of Monarchy, Aristocracy, and Democracy.</note> does not seem to have perceived them sufficiently when he proposes a **Harmonic proportion** in five numbers—3, 4, 6, 8, 12—and affirms of them *that equal and similar spaces exist in a certain tempered way*. For when he saw the differences to be 1, 2, 2, 4, he recognized an expressed equality in 2 and 2, and a similarity in 1, 2, 2, 4. But in the definition of the ancients, three numbers are sufficient; furthermore, no tempering of expressed equality with similarity is contained within that definition. For in 3, 4, 6, there is no expressed equality of differences.

Now it is worth the effort to see how Bodin, who is most prolific on this subject, applies these things to **Morals and Politics** in various ways. It often happens to him that, instead of the harmonic mediations—whether those of the ancients or the true ones—he seizes upon mere compositions of Arithmetic and Geometric proportions, relying on his own faulty definition. Just as this had to be stated as a preface at the beginning, so it will have to be repeated more often in what follows.

I. Since there are three forms of **Polities** <note>Polity refers to the form or process of civil government.</note>: the **Popular**, the **Aristocratic**, and the **Royal**;

Kepler sets the stage for applying these mathematical "means" to the three types of political government: Democracy, Aristocracy, and Monarchy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s analysis of Jean Bodin’s political theories, specifically how Bodin maps the three types of mathematical proportions (arithmetic, geometric, and harmonic) onto three types of government (democracy, aristocracy, and monarchy).</meta>

# ON HARMONICS. BOOK III.

<margin>POLITICS.</margin>
...the popular <note>original: *popularem*; referring to a democratic state</note> [state] he compares to **Arithmetic** proportion, that of the Aristocrats <note>original: *Optimatum*</note> to **Geometric**, and the Royal state to **Harmonic**. For just as in Arithmetic, the increments of all numbers are equal, whether they are large or small, so in a Republic, the people want the burdens, benefits, honors, and magistracies to be equal for everyone. They do not wish to tolerate any respect for persons; they want, for example, the right of hunting to belong to everyone, whether they are noble or ignoble, rich or poor. But if there is something that does not allow for division among many, the people want it decided by lot; for chance is blind, not distinguishing the noble from the ignoble, the rich from the poor, the well-deserving from the undeserving, the virtuous from the vicious, or the clever from the stupid. For a person only thinks himself equal to others if he draws lots with them for such things, whether he happens to receive good or bad fortune. In place of a lot, there can also be other means of acquisition; for instance, if the choice is permitted to someone who has no personal interest or who is believed not to favor specific persons. Thus at Rome, the Consulship was common to everyone of a certain rank; and it was permitted to seek it from the people, but not through bribery, lest the people be corrupted and the wealthy be preferred to the poorer. Even if in this case virtue is respected by a silent consensus, the judgment concerning those who have served well is ultimately left to the people.

Conversely, just as in Geometry, the **excesses** <note>the differences between numbers</note> of numbers are likened to the numbers themselves—so that a large number has a large excess and a small one a small excess—so in an Aristocratic Republic, persons are distinguished, and so too are burdens, rewards, magistracies, and duties. The most excellent things are reserved for the Aristocrats <note>original: *Optimatibus*</note>, and the remainder is left to the people. In this case, it is necessary that an arithmetic proportion also be admitted separately within each faction: for among those things which belong to the people, everyone among the people will draw lots; and among those which belong to the Aristocrats, all the Aristocrats will do the same. Unless this is done, there would be continuous ranks of "Aristocrats" even among the people, down to the very dregs of the populace, and continuous ranks among the Aristocrats up to the Prince of the State; in which case it would not be a Republic, but a Royal type of city.

The Royal state, however, is most of all likened to **Geometric** proportion because all the rights of Majesty are reserved for the King, just as he himself surpasses all others either by noble lineage, by arms, or by virtues. Nevertheless, the method of governing in this state can most correctly be tempered by both kinds of proportion. For one King is the arbiter of all—not by blind impulse, like a lot, but by the reasoning of virtue, merit, order, and rank; where permitted, he dispenses everything between the Aristocrats and the people. He carries out all the parts of <term>distributive and commutative justice</term> <note>Distributive justice gives rewards based on merit (geometric); commutative justice treats individuals as equals in exchanges (arithmetic).</note>. This conjunction of both proportions is sufficient for *Bodin* to constitute a **Harmonic proportion**. Yet, he refers all counsels not so much to individuals, or to specific ranks or men, but to the whole body of the City, and to its safety, mutual charity, and concord. This is just as if, in numbers, proportions were deflected somewhat from equality and from likeness (even so far as to destroy those qualities if necessary) so that they might be directed toward the common harmony of all: which is how he shall use my Harmonic means.

II. From the *Cyropaedia* <note>original: *Cyri pædia*; Xenophon's "The Education of Cyrus," a semi-fictional biography of Cyrus the Great.</note>, *Bodin* proposes an example by which all three types of proportion can be explained. When *Cyrus* was a boy, when a man pro-

<summary>Kepler explains Jean Bodin’s theory that different government types reflect mathematical proportions: Democracy is Arithmetic (absolute equality), Aristocracy is Geometric (proportional to status), and Monarchy is Harmonic (a balanced blend of both).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Jean Bodin’s political application of mathematical proportions. The text opens mid-sentence, completing the word "tall" (procerum) from the previous page's discussion of social and geometric fitting.</meta>

### ON PROPORTIONS

<margin>
DIGRESSION.
The judgment of the boy Cyrus.
</margin>
...[a tall boy] <note>original: *procerum*</note> dressed in a short tunic, and a small boy in a loose one, he judged that the tunics should be swapped so that each would have what was suitable for him. The teacher, however, declared that each should keep his own. If the tall boy had been ordered to pay some money to the small boy, and only then the exchange were made, the teacher would have been perfectly reconciled with the student. Here, Cyrus insisted on **Geometric** proportion, measuring the clothes to the bodies; the teacher insisted on **Arithmetic**, protecting the possessions of each. But a third person would have looked at both at once: both the physical need and the safety of each person’s property. Thus, he would have established **Harmonic** proportion in the sense used by Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596) was a French jurist and political philosopher whose work Kepler is analyzing</note>, as it is a mixture of the previous two. It is also harmonic in my own sense; for such a person would not hesitate to take the excess cloth from one and money from the other so that both are provided for, because the mutual benefit of both is compared to the sweetness of a musical harmony. I have said, moreover, that it happens sometimes that a Geometric proportion is also harmonic (such as 1, 2, 4), just as it is suitable here for the tall boy to have the long garment; but sometimes an Arithmetic proportion is also Harmonic (such as 2, 3, 4), just as it is suitable here for the small boy who owns the long garment to keep what is his, but exchanged for money, which he can use better than the extra cloth.

<margin>Types of Justice.</margin>
III. Since justice encompasses all methods of governing, [Bodin] cites two parts of it from Aristotle: **commutative** justice <note>justice concerning private transactions and trade</note>, which deals with arithmetic equality, and **distributive** justice <note>justice concerning the distribution of honors or goods based on merit</note>, based on geometric similarity. He himself proposes a third type of justice composed of both the former ones, which wishes both that a wealth of goods be sold to certain people at a lower price than to others, and that great things are not always distributed to the great; and thus, both types of justice are violated to some extent if the safety of the whole requires it, or if a public benefit emerges from it. A proportion is not well-composed from two other types if it destroys them both. Therefore, this application is better suited to my **Harmonic** medians <note>mathematical means</note>. Just as in the numbers 2, 3, 5, there is neither an arithmetic equality of differences nor a geometric progression, yet there is a Harmonic relationship between them.

To this, at the end of the book, he adapts the Poets, who imagine three daughters of **Themis** (who is Justice): **Eunomia, Epieikeia, and Eirene** <note>Law, Equity, and Peace; original Greek: Εὐνομίαν, ἐπιείκειαν, εἰρήνην</note> as the guardians of the three proportions: Arithmetic, Geometric, and Harmonic.

<margin>Marriage laws.</margin>
IV. The laws of marriage, the primary bond of the state, provide a clear example of the three proportions. If Patricians <note>the noble class</note> are ordered to marry Patricians, and plebeians <note>commoners</note> to marry plebeians, this is a **Geometric** similarity. But if the law allows everyone to seek marriage indiscriminately, either by lot or by striving as much as possible for beauty, wealth, or virtue without regard for lineage, and no condition is forbidden: this will be **Arithmetic** equality. However, in the former case, the minds of the citizens are torn into factions; in the latter, the social orders are confused. Both are ruinous to the Republic. Therefore, Bodin suggests sometimes permitting marriages between poorer Patricians and wealthy plebeians, or between rich plebeians and impoverished Patrician women.
