<margin>CHAPTER I.</margin>
...partly by acting, and partly by being acted upon <note>original: "patiendo," a philosophical term meaning to receive an action or be the subject of a change.</note>; by acting, while they emit their "species" <note>In the science of Kepler's time, "species" were immaterial forms or images emitted by objects that travel through the air to reach our sense organs.</note>: struck objects emit the species of their own motion, which are sounds; bright objects emit the species of their light and color, which are rays. As we say when we claim that objects "move" the senses—and to move is indeed to act. However, by being acted upon, it is not the things themselves through their own nature, but through their species—which, while being sensed, remembered, and compared, must always "suffer" something according to common usage. And altogether, this very union of two terms in the Soul, through which the Essence of sensible Harmony results—namely, the act of being related and compared—is for things taken together just such a kind of thing as is for single things the act of being seen or heard, or even less than that. For all these are certainly certain "passions" <note>Here "passions" refers to the state of being affected by an external force.</note>, though the term is used in various ways with a wide range of meanings.

<margin>Degrees of the various meanings of "Passions"</margin>
But I shall establish degrees of these passions. First, for the sake of example, water "suffers" when, being cold, it grows warm from applied fires. A second meaning says that moisture "suffers" when it acts on something else, namely by moistening dry things; for part of it is drawn into the parched channels and mixed with them, which is a form of suffering. In this way, water also "suffers" when it is tasted; for a thirsty person swallows and digests part of it. But in a third meaning, water "suffers" in the act of tasting when it is at least touched by the tongue—not only because it is warmed by the tongue’s heat while it cools the tongue with its own cold, nor only because some water sticks to the tongue, but simply because it is touched by the tongue, which is like being very lightly struck or pulsed, causing local motion of the parts within the whole. To be moved is indeed to be acted upon. Let the fourth meaning be that by which water is said to suffer when its emitted vapor strikes the nostrils and is perceived by smell. To be perceived, however, is to be acted upon; and here indeed it is not the water itself that suffers, but its bodily outflow, and by this "passion" some part of it is consumed. The fifth degree is that by which water is understood to suffer when the noise of it is heard. For first the water itself is in motion, then the immaterial species of the water, as it moves, is spread from it in every direction and received into the channels of the ears. This reception is a "passion," not of the water itself, but of its species, or its immaterial outflow; and in this reception, something is lost over time and through the multiplicity of receptions. For sound is duller when it falls upon the ears or clothing of a great multitude, or when it is emitted amidst falling snow.

Sixthly, even when water is seen, it suffers something. For it emits rays to the eye from its surface or as if from its surface—namely from its colors, insofar as it is colored—which rays are touched, reflected, refracted, and forced to a point, being received by the co-acted "net-like tunic" <note>original: "retiformi tunica," referring to the retina.</note>. All these are passions, not of the water itself, but of the immaterial species, or the rays. And these rays, already in this reception, lose nothing, neither in space nor in time; for once the thing that touches them is removed, they proceed further, entirely unharmed, which sound does not do.

Seventhly, after these species—and indeed the body of the water itself—have first acted upon the bodily instruments of the senses (that is, they have affected them to match themselves and made them like themselves, so that the membranes of the tongue and skin have perceived cold and flavor, the spirits of the hearing have resounded with its noise, and those of the sight have shone with its light), thus its sensory "type" <note>A mental impression or image.</note> and species have been formed. The eyes certainly carry this around, even after the object is removed, often against a person's will. Now, these sensible species [move] from the thresholds of the senses or o-

It is understood that all these things are "suffered" <note>Kepler uses "suffer" or "passion" in the classical philosophical sense of being the recipient of an action or a change, rather than feeling pain.</note> by the water, not in itself, but in its sensible and mental species <note>In the science of this era, "species" were the immaterial forms or images emitted by objects that travel to the eyes or ears.</note>. Then, therefore, even the supreme faculty of the soul, which presides over number and comparisons, fashions and forms for itself—from several mental species of things—a single species of relation, order, and comparison. It compares things existing outside among themselves. This comparison, as we were saying above, since it occurs regarding the things themselves but without their own effort, is understood to be a certain "passion" of theirs—in almost the same sense as when a judgment is made concerning the reputation of someone who is absent and unaware, or when someone is condemned to death or outlawed in their absence. 

This is altogether a fitting likeness; for just as such a person, even if he feels nothing bad within himself at that moment and thus suffers nothing, yet a little later experiences in reality the force of what he has "suffered." So too voices, and whatever is part of a proportion <note>original: "congruentiæ"</note>, are either continued, or rejected, fled from, prohibited, hindered, suppressed, or ended, according as it pleases the mind in this comparison. Although I do not say that sounds "suffer" in respect to this consequent outcome, but in that very act when the mind compares them among themselves; it is enough to have explained at length in what degree of ambiguous meaning I call this mental comparison a "passion." But I was not lengthy in listing these meanings without reason: for by this path we shall henceforth be wonderfully helped in recognizing the **Nature of the Harmonic Faculty** and in completing this part of **Metaphysics**, which Aristotle did not look at even through a lattice <note>original: "ne per transennam quidem aspexit," a Latin idiom meaning to not even catch a glimpse of something or to treat it only superficially.</note>.

<margin>Are sensible harmonies concrete or abstract?</margin>
From these things it is also clear what I was contending before: namely, that the "formal" aspect <note>The "form" or essential nature of a thing as opposed to its raw material.</note> of sensible Harmony, insofar as it is harmony, happens to sensible things, just as it happens to them to be seen, heard, and so forth. Secondly, it is evident that sensible Harmonies are things abstracted in a certain way from the objects themselves, insofar as it is not the objects outside, but the species of things entered through the senses and led to the tribunal of the soul, which become the terms of the sensible harmonic proportion. But in turn, these harmonies are still **concrete** for a twofold reason: first, because these species of sensible things are not species of their bare quantity, but also of a sensible quality, such as sound or light, etc. Secondly, because these sensible species, as sensible, cannot shine back within the soul unless the objects themselves—of which they are the species—are also present and remain outside. For if those are taken away, their species inside also cease: those of light, as far as their radiation is concerned, in that very instant; those of sound, however, within a very brief moment of time. 

To be sure, some impression is left in the sensory organs, as light in the eye; but that is not of the external thing, but rather another "species of a species," impressed into the body, having now become a momentary quality of the body. Just as in optics, colors—from the pure and least-colored light of the sun—conceive a power of radiating color in every direction. And this is what we were also contending at the beginning: that the sensible terms and the Soul must be present and exchange mutual works—by acting and by suffering—the former by moving the senses, the latter by comparing; so that the essence of sensible Harmony may be established.

Someone might object here that the Soul, by comparing, does not make, but finds—

<margin>
CHAPTER I. 
To what extent the Soul makes Harmonies and to what extent it finds them.
</margin>
...to arrive at a suitable proportion: because this was the fourth and formal principle of sensible harmony mentioned above; therefore, it might seem that the soul could be absent while the Essence of Harmony remains intact.

I respond by inversion: to find a suitable proportion in sensible things is to detect, acknowledge, and bring to light the similarity of that proportion in sensible things with a certain **Archetype** <term>Archetype: An original model or ideal pattern, which Kepler believes is pre-installed in the human soul by God.</term> of truest Harmony which is within the **Soul**. Therefore, just as the **Athenians** found some virtue in **Zeno** <note>Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism. Kepler is using a legal/social analogy here.</note>, they did not find the right of their **Prytaneum** <term>Prytaneum: A public hall in ancient Greece where distinguished citizens and guests were honored and fed at the state's expense.</term> within him, but they conferred it upon him—a status which Zeno could not have achieved without the Athenians. In the same way, the **Soul** finds order and proportion in sounds and in rays (even though it does not find this harmony itself outside, but at least the "terms" or boundaries, as was said); so that this proportion may be called harmonic, the soul makes it so by the comparison with its own **Archetype**. It could not be called harmonic, nor would it obtain any power to move souls, if this Archetype were not present. So much, then, for sensible Harmonies.

<margin>
What is insensible Harmony?
</margin>
For now we must pass to the pure and secret Harmonies, which is the other part of our division: namely, those which we have just now established as the **Archetypes** or **Paradigms** <note>original: "Paradigmata"</note> of sensible harmonies. If these Archetypes had their own existence outside the **Soul**, I admit we would be deprived of a great argument for asserting the necessity of the **Soul** in constituting the essence of **Harmony**. But to place them outside the **Soul** is a contradiction in terms <note>original: "oppositum in adjecto"</note>, as we shall hear.

<margin>
Its terms.
</margin>
For the principles of true and archetypal Harmony, which exists without being confused with any sensible species, are nonetheless divided and many in number. Since that too is a proportion, it also requires its own two terms. These terms, as we used in the previous books, are the whole Circle and its Part or parts (whether a single aliquot part or several), with the arc being demonstrably cut away. This is the specific difference of harmonic proportion, by which not only is harmonic proportion distinguished from other proportions located under the same genus, but also the pure and archetypal is distinguished from the sensible—except insofar as, by very common usage, the mere Concordance of sounds is called Harmony. For in this very thing the clearest distinction appears between pure Harmony and sensible or concrete Harmony: in pure harmony, the terms are from mathematical genera, the **Circle** and the **Arc**, formed in a certain way. For the circle has its own formation or configuration from itself; the arc has its terms from the **Chord** <term>Chord: A straight line segment whose endpoints both lie on a circular arc.</term> <note>original: "Subtensa"</note> and its shape from the circle. In sensible **Harmonies**, however, there is no need for this special formation; for they can be straight lines or other shaped sensible quantities, provided they are faithful examples of this archetypal Harmony in whatever their quantity may be—at least as far as faithful imitation is possible in sensible things. This is because in such things, whatever is close to the truth is received as the truth itself, according to the degree of more or less. These, therefore, are the terms of archetypal Harmony.

<margin>
That the Mind is required for the BEING of abstract Harmony.
</margin>
Furthermore, besides the terms, as was said before regarding sensible things, the **Mind** is also required, comparing the terms and judging whether those **arcs** <note>original: "arc9" (shorthand for arcus)</note> of the circle are such that some **side** <note>original: "lat9" (shorthand for latus), referring to the side of a geometric polygon.</note> of a demonstrable figure would cut them from the whole circle. # Book IV on Harmonics

<margin>
CHAPTER I.
</margin>
...of Archetypal Harmony, there are two components on the side of the boundaries—the **Material**, to speak by way of analogy, which are the **Circle** and its part; and the **Formal**, which is the cutting off of that part by a demonstrative figure; and there is one component on the side of the relationship between the boundaries, namely the **Efficient** cause, which is (in a sense) the **Mind**.

<margin>
Harmony is a qualitative relationship.
</margin>
Since every proportion—including this one of the part of a circle to the whole—falls into the category of **Relation**, this specific and defined form of proportion behaves like a "quality of the fourth species" <note>In Aristotelian logic, the "fourth species of quality" refers to the form or stable shape of a thing.</note>. For **Harmony** is, in a way, a qualitative or figured **Relation**, specifically one formed by regular geometric figures.

If it previously belonged to the Essence of sensible Harmony that physical things should flow into the soul through their appearance, how much more necessary is it here that those boundaries of "secret harmony" we mentioned—the **Circle** and its **Arc**—should be within the mind itself? Whether one says this happens through "species" <term>Species: In this context, the mental image or "form" of an object as perceived by the mind.</term> received from the outside, or whether they have endured along with the Mind itself, being present inside before any perception took place; this is a question we must now examine with all our intellectual strength.

<margin>
How the Genera and Species of mathematical things exist in the Soul.
</margin>
Having reached this point, I cannot hide the opinions of the **Ancients** who explored this part of philosophy before us without doing a great injustice both to the reader who is eager for philosophy and to those ancestors themselves—at least as far as their views are known to us. I believe only one thing must be established first: a distinction must be made between the mathematical species themselves—the **Circle** and its **Arc**—and the comparison between them. This is because if the species themselves, as the boundaries, are to be placed within the soul without being "received" from outside, then much more so must the **Harmony** (which exists between those parts) be placed in the mind. Thus, Harmony does not have its essence outside the mind, since its essence consists in a certain action of the mind regarding those species. While the circle and its arcs are in the Soul in such a way that they are also, beyond controversy, in physical things, **Harmony** (the relationship between the circle and its part) is, in its formal aspect, in no way outside the soul; this was shown earlier by the example of **Number** <note>Kepler argues that "three-ness" doesn't exist in three stones, but in the mind counting them.</note>. Now, the arguments of the ancients are primarily about the species themselves, which are simpler things; whereas Harmony is a more composite thing.

This is the point of difference between **Aristotle**, **Plato**, and **Proclus** on one side, and **Ptolemy** on the other. For the former dispute over the *Being* of the species, while Ptolemy disputes over the *Being* of Harmony. However, we shall move Ptolemy’s text to the Appendix of the entire work, lest it stir up the confusion we feared at the start of this chapter. Instead, we shall now listen to those who speak most appropriately to the present speculation.

<margin>
Plato's doctrine on the existence of mathematical things.
</margin>
**Plato's** opinion regarding mathematical things was this: the human mind is self-taught in all species or figures, as well as in axioms and conclusions about things. When the mind seems to be taught, it is actually nothing other than being "reminded" <term>Anamnesis: Plato’s theory that the soul is immortal and previously knew all things, and that "learning" is actually the recovery of forgotten knowledge.</term> through physical diagrams of those things which it knows within itself. He represents this with singular skill in his dialogues by introducing a boy who, when questioned by a teacher, answers everything exactly as desired <note>This refers to the *Meno*, where Socrates guides a slave boy to solve a geometry problem to prove the soul's innate knowledge.</note>.

<margin>
Aristotle's contrary doctrine.
</margin>
**Aristotle**, on the other hand, in his *Metaphysics*, calls this invention "a fictitious account, forced to suit the hypothesis" <note>original: "λόγον πλασματώδη, πρὸς τὴν ὑπόθεσιν βεβιασμένον"</note>. He argues that these mathematical things never exist separately from physical objects; nor...

CHAPTER I.
Aristotle's shortcoming.
</margin>
...that their existence is nothing else, not even in the Mind, except in the way that other universals are in the Mind, when the species <term>Species: In this context, the mental image or "form" of an object as perceived by the mind.</term> of the essence of individual sensible things is formed by definition in the Mind. Thus, he believes they are indeed prior to sensible things and are abstracted from them, but not in reality—only as a mental concept. 

Here it should be noted that whenever Aristotle happens to name a mathematical genus as an example, he always names a Point, a Line, a Surface, a Body, or a Number. These are the highest categories in the classification of Quantity. However, regarding quantities insofar as they are **figures** (which belong to the "fourth species of quality" <note>In Aristotelian logic, the "fourth species of quality" refers to the stable form or shape of an object, where the "material" is quantity but the "form" is the figure.</note>), mention is very rare in these disputes. As for **Relations**, there is absolutely no mention at all. Indeed, he goes so far as to claim that the science of Harmonics investigates nothing but sounds; and even those, only insofar as they are lines, exactly like Optics. 

But as for the intervals between lines, which constitute **proportion** (which is a relation, and specifically one of quality and figure), Aristotle does not even dream of it. There is no doubt that he would have progressed further in this investigation if he had been steeped in deeper mathematics—specifically the intellectual difference between possible and impossible figures, which we discussed in Book I. 

Therefore, insofar as he debates the highest categories of quantity, he easily wins without

However, when he * concludes universally and finds Plato guilty of this "folly" which he himself imagined; and finally, when he opposes the Platonic picture of the **self-taught boy** <note>original: "αὐτοδιδάκτῳ" — a reference to Plato's *Meno*, where a boy proves mathematical truths he was never taught, suggesting innate knowledge.</note> with a contrary picture, asserting that the Mind is empty of itself—void not only of other knowledge and mathematical categories, but even of species—and is plainly a **blank slate** <note>original: "Tabula rasa"</note> on which nothing is written, not even mathematics, though all things may be written upon it: in this part, I say, he is not to be tolerated in the Christian religion. After several centuries, he encountered many **accountings** <note>original: "εὐθύνας" — criticisms or demands for justification.</note> (as Proclus says), and specifically Proclus himself as an adversary. Although Proclus does not cite Aristotle by name here, he openly professes Plato (whom he defends by name) to be his leader.

<margin>CHAPTER I.</margin>
...from where does that great certainty and that great accuracy come in these ratios (or definitions)? For it must come either from sensory things or from the soul itself. But it is impossible for it to come from sensory things, for there is a much greater subtlety and exactness in these Ratios <note>Latin: *Rationibus*. Kepler uses this term to mean both mathematical proportions and the underlying "reason" or "definition" of a thing.</note> than in physical objects. It must come from the soul, therefore, which bestows perfection upon the imperfect, and grants that accurate subtlety to things that are not accurate at all.

For tell me, where among sensory things is there found a nature that is indivisible (like a point), or lacking width (like a line), or lacking depth (like a surface)? Or where is the equality of lines drawn from a Center <note>Kepler is referring to the radii of a circle, which are perfectly equal in geometry but never perfectly equal in a physical drawing.</note>, or where are the always constant Proportions of sides (the subject of my Book I), or where are the perpendicularities of angles? I certainly do not see them, since all divisible things are mixed and confused with each other; nothing is pure, nothing is free from its opposite. All things are divisible, both those separated in space and those joined together. How then shall we provide an enduring essence for immobile things from things that are mobile and constantly changing? For whatever has its existence from moving essences, they must admit that its existence is changeable. And how shall we obtain accuracy for accurate and certain species from things that are not accurate? For everything that is the cause of an ever-changing notion is itself much more so. It must therefore be assumed that the Soul itself is the mother of Mathematical species and Ratios. 

<margin>The true essence of mathematical things is in the Soul.</margin>
And yet, if the soul, containing within itself these things as first examples or Paradigms, makes them exist according to their essence, then generations (the Christian understands this as the creation of sensory things) are nothing other than the propagation of species <term>Species: In Kepler’s thought, these are the "blueprints" or archetypal forms that exist in the mind.</term> which were previously in it. (Christians know that the mathematical reasons for creating bodies were co-eternal with God, and that God is Soul and Mind in a pre-eminent way; and that human souls are images of God the creator, even in essential matters in their own way.) If we say this, then we shall agree with Plato, and the true Essence of Mathematics will have been found by us. 

But if the Soul—despite not possessing them, and not having previously received Mathematical Ratios from elsewhere (as if they had not been created within it)—nevertheless wove this marvelous immaterial ornament and labored at this most beautiful contemplation, how then will the things so born discern whether they are stable and constant (<note>original: *mónima* ($\mu\acute{o}\nu\iota\mu\alpha$), "stable"</note>—I read "stable" here, not <note>original: *gónima* ($\gamma\acute{o}\nu\iota\mu\alpha$), "productive"</note>), or whether they vanish into the winds as phantoms rather than truths? By what standards would the soul measure their truth? Indeed, how, when it did not possess their essence, does it produce such a variety of ratios? For in this way we would make their existence accidental, tending toward no goal or limit. Therefore, Mathematical species are the offspring of the Soul itself; it does not receive the Ratios it establishes from sensory things. Rather, the sensory things are propagated from the mental ones. These mathematical thoughts are the soul's own efforts, the birth-pangs of permanent and perennial species.

<margin>Mathematical species are not collected into one from individual quantities.</margin>
Secondly, if we gather the Ratios of Mathematics (or definitions) from below—that is, from sensory things—why would the demonstrations established by sensory things not be better than the demonstrations of more universal and simpler species? For we say that in the investigation of a sought-after thing, the principles and propositions are everywhere related to the demonstrations or conclusions.

And how could we prove that the essence of intellectual things is more related to demonstrations than the essence of sensory things? For they speak thus: "Not if someone demonstrates that an Isosceles <note>A triangle with two equal sides.</note> triangle has..."

Since Plato understood this, he composed the Soul out of all things, and divided it according to numbers, and bound it back together with Analogies and **Harmonic Ratios**; and into it he brought the first Principles, the producers of Figures—namely, the Straight and the curved—and he moves the circles, which are in the soul intellectually. Therefore, all Mathematical things are first in the Soul: before Numbers there are self-moving Numbers, and before visible figures, there are vital figures, and before Concordant or harmonious things, there are the very Ratios of concordances, or Harmonics; and before the bodies which move in a circle, the invisible cycles themselves were established; and the Soul is the Perfection of all things: and this is a certain other adornment (besides the sensible one) which also brings itself to things and is brought by a familiar and related principle: and it both fills itself with life and is filled by the Creator, in an incorporeal and non-spatial way. The Soul is therefore substantialized in these forms; and it must not be thought that Number, which is in it, is a multitude of units; nor should the form and idea of those things which are <unclear>distinguishable</unclear> in space be understood as bodily: but all things must be assumed vitally and intellectually, as the first examples of visible Numbers and Figures and Ratios and motions: and this Timaeus should be followed, who completes and perfects the whole origin and fabric of the World from Mathematical Genera, and places in it the causes of all things. For those seven terms of all Numbers pre-existed in it according to their cause. Again, the principles of Figures were placed in it in an architectural or craftsman-like way; and the first and most principal of all motions, which surrounds and incites all the remaining motions, existed together with it; for the circle and circular motion is the principle of all things that move. There are therefore essential and self-moving Ratios of Mathematical things which complete the Souls: which the Soul, by bringing forth, propagating, and evolving, makes every variety of the Mathematical sciences to exist. Nor will it ever cease to produce and draw out always one thing after another, as long as it strips its indivisible Ratios of their simplicity. For it received all things beforehand, like the principles of species and primeval things; and according to its infinite faculty, from these anticipated principles, it builds the progressions of every kind of speculation. Thus far Proclus.

But as it pertains to continuous quantities, I agree entirely with Proclus; although his speech flows like a torrent, overflowing its banks, and hiding blind shallows and whirlpools of doubt, while a mind full of the majesty of such great things struggles in the constraints of language, and the conclusion, never satisfying itself with the abundance of words, exceeds the simplicity of the propositions. Therefore, I believe that if I now subjoin my own reasons for why I establish an intellectual Circle and its parts as the basis for insensible Harmonies (conceived before I had read Proclus), I shall not only say things consistent with Proclus, but also produce a kind of summary of the described passage, insofar as it serves my purpose.

<margin>
The terms of insensible harmonies are abstract quantities.
</margin>
I will not say among these reasons that these things being compared were first outside, then in the senses, and finally abstracted from both things and the sensible species of things—which is the sense properly produced by the word "abstracting": for as said above, this method of abstracting pertains to the sensible Harmonies of Sounds and Rays, and takes place only when—just as the good or bad deeds of citizens are judged by laws passed of old—the Sounds and Rays are judged by an Archetypal Harmony <note>original: "Archetypica Harmonia"</note> already present within.

But this is the reason why the quantity is said to be intellectual, providing the terms for Harmonic proportions: because it is necessary for that quantity to be capable of a most subtle demonstration. Indeed, that demonstration is never obtained from sensible diagrams, even if it is assisted by them; nor does it arise from collections of many sensible particulars into one Axiom, but is obtained from first principles <note>original: "à priori"</note>. Since Proclus truly objected to Aristotle <note>Aristotle argued that the mind is a "blank slate" and knowledge comes from experience; Proclus and Kepler argue that geometric knowledge is innate.</note> regarding the intellect in general, I can, with very clear arguments drawn from the first book, render it most secure in this specific case. For the specific difference of the Figures which cut off the Harmonic arc of the circle—by which their essence is explained as part of a definition—is that they must be knowable <note>original: "scibiles"</note>. Now, what knowability is there without a Mind capable of knowledge? And you should not say that a thing can exist without there being knowledge of the thing itself: For knowledge consists in comparison, as when the side of a figure is equal to the Radius. Now, an equality that exists without a mind, especially in things separated by space, cannot be understood: and we are rolled back to the argument already brought forward above even for sensible Harmonies.

Nor is it enough that they be knowable; they must also be *known*: so that the Archetypal Harmony may shine in action within the soul. For the mere possibility of knowing is not enough for us as a criterion for sensible harmonies. Therefore, that whose part of essence is within the soul, and thus in its Operation or Activity <note>original: "Energiâ"</note>, that very thing must be established within: namely the terms of the Harmonies, the Circle, and its Part.

<header>ON THE HARMONICS, BOOK IV.</header>

<margin>
CHAPTER I.
The Soul possesses knowledge of Mathematics by instinct.
</margin>

You might ask how there can be knowledge of a thing that the mind has never learned, and perhaps cannot learn, if it were deprived of the sensation of external things? To this, Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher whose commentary on Euclid deeply influenced Kepler’s view that geometry is innate to the mind.</note> replied above in words common to his philosophy: today, if I am not mistaken, we shall most correctly use the term **Instinct**. Indeed, quantity is known to the human mind and to other Souls by instinct, even if it were deprived of every sense for this purpose. The mind understands the straight line by its own nature; it understands an equal interval from a single point; and through these, it imagines a circle for itself. If it can do this, it can much more easily find a demonstration within it, and thus supply the function of the eye in looking at a diagram (should it even have need of one). In fact, if the mind itself had never possessed an eye, it would demand an eye for itself to comprehend things placed outside of it, and it would prescribe the laws for forming that eye based on itself (provided the mind were pure and healthy and without impediments—that is, if it were only what it truly is). For the very recognition of quantities, which is innate to the mind, dictates what kind of eye there ought to be; and therefore the Eye was made as it is because the Mind is as it is, not the other way around. Why say more? Geometry, co-eternal with the Divine Mind before the birth of things, is God Himself <note>original: "Deus ipse"; Kepler argues that geometry is not just a tool God uses, but is part of God’s very essence.</note> (for what is in God that is not God Himself?). It supplied God with the patterns for creating the world, and it passed into man along with the image of God; it was not eventually received into the interior through the eyes.

<margin>
Proclus says nearly the same thing a little after the passage previously cited: that Mathematical Essences are likened in truth to the gods, and that the Architect of the entire universe used mathematical archetypes <term>archetypes: original patterns or models</term>, co-eternal with himself, in the conformation of the World.
</margin>

Since, therefore, the capacity for demonstration is inherent in quantities—not insofar as figures are placed before the eyes, but insofar as they are open to the eyes of the mind (that is, insofar as they are not so much "abstracted" from sensible things as they were never "concrete" within them)—we rightly establish abstract quantity as the terms for Archetypal harmonic proportions, since these arise from the demonstrable divisions of a circle.

There is another reason why I choose abstract quantities: because the circle, which is a figure—namely a species of the "fourth quality" <note>In Aristotelian physics, "quality" was a broad category; Kepler is categorizing the circle as a specific type of formal quality.</note>—is considered in this business purely as a figure, even though it is a quantity. It is considered without distinction of large or small, to the point that it is somehow abstracted even from quantity itself, as if from its own subject; its nature can be recognized even in the tiny space of a point. This, I believe, is what Proclus meant when he said that mathematical things exist in the Soul in an incorporeal and non-extended <note>original: "indistanti modo"; meaning without physical dimensions or distance.</note> manner.

<margin>
The Symbolism of divine and human things in quantities.
</margin>

Finally, there is also this supreme and extraordinary <note>original: "decumana"; literally referring to the 'tenth wave,' used idiomatically to mean the greatest or most significant.</note> reason: that there is a certain wonderful and plainly divine order <note>original: "politia"; suggesting a structured community or citizenship of mathematical laws.</note> of quantities, and a common symbolism in them of things divine and human. I have written elsewhere about the foreshadowing of the Most Holy Trinity in the sphere—in the *Optics*, in the *Commentaries on Mars* <note>Kepler refers to his *Astronomia Nova* (1609).</note>, and in the *Spherical Doctrine*—which I wish to be repeated here. It follows, then, that the straight line, which arises from the flow of a point in the center to a single point on the surface, outlines the first rudiments of creation. It emulates the eternal generation of the Son (depicted and figured by the departure from the center toward the infinite points of the entire surface, through infinite lines, under a most perfect equality for all), which straight line is, of course, the element of corporeal form. This line, extended in width, now foreshadows Corporeal Form itself, creating the Plane; but the sphere, cut by a plane, represents the Circle by that section—a genuine image of the created mind, which is set in charge of ruling the body. This circle is in that same proportion to the sphere as the human mind is to the Di-

...to the divine, namely as a line to a surface, yet both are circular. Toward the plane in which it exists, however, it relates as the curved to the straight, which are <term>incommunicable and incommensurable</term> <note>Kepler refers to the mathematical fact that a straight line cannot perfectly measure a curve (like the "squaring of the circle"), symbolizing the gap between the material body and the spiritual soul.</note>. The circle exists beautifully both in the cutting plane, circumscribing it, and in the sliced Sphere, through the mutual intersection of both; just as the soul exists in the body, giving it form and connected to the bodily shape, yet is sustained in God, like a certain <insert>irradiation</insert> derived into the body from the divine countenance, drawing from there a more noble nature. This cause, just as it establishes the Circle as the subject and source of terms for harmonic proportions, so it most especially commends abstraction. For the reflection of the soul's divinity is found neither in a circle of a fixed size, nor in an imperfect one (such as material and sensible circles are); and what is most important, it is fitting for the circle to be as abstracted from bodily and sensible things as the proportions of the curved—the symbol of the Soul—are distinct and, as it were, abstracted from the straight, which is the shadow of bodies. We are therefore sufficiently armed so that we may seek the terms of Harmonic proportions (which are objects of the soul alone) primarily from abstract quantities.

To conclude this section, therefore, we shall gather the main points into a bundle. Sensory Harmonies have this in common with Archetypal ones: they require terms, the comparison of those terms, and the energy of the Soul itself; in this comparison, the essence of both consists. But the terms of sensory harmonies are themselves sensory and must be present outside the Soul; the terms of Archetypal harmonies are already present within the Soul beforehand. Sensory harmonies, therefore, additionally require reception through a "species" <note>In 17th-century science, a "species" was an image or emanation emitted by an object so it could be perceived by the senses.</note> emitted from themselves, which reception is performed by the senses, the servants of the Soul. There is also a need for another comparison: of the individual sensory terms with individual Archetypal ones—for instance, a physical circle with the soul's inner knowledge of a circle. But the Archetypal Harmony needs neither of these, since the terms are already present in the soul, born with it, and are indeed the Soul itself. They are not an image of their true <term>Paradigm</term> <note>original: "Paradigma" - the ultimate original model or blueprint.</note>, but are, as it were, their own Paradigm. Thus, the simple comparison which the soul establishes between its own parts, as it were, completes the entire essence of Archetypal Harmony. Finally, the Soul itself, engaged in this energy, is the Harmony we are proposing; just as, without regard to this energy, the circle and its parts are the terms of Harmony. At last, the Harmony is thoroughly "souled" <note>original: "animificatur" - to be endowed with a soul or life-force.</note>, and even "deified."

# CHAPTER II.

## How many and of what sort the faculties of the Soul are according to the Harmonies.

We have spoken so far about harmonic proportions, what they are, and where they consist; yet we do not seem to have reached the question best suited to our purpose, which is concerned not so much with the harmonic proportions themselves as with the **harmonic faculty** of the Soul—namely, the power of acting according to proportions. Thus far, concerning...

We have dealt with proportions for the sake of their Essence; now we must deal with them for the sake of the Soul itself.

<margin>How many faculties of the Soul are occupied with Harmonies?</margin>
There is a double faculty regarding harmonic proportions: one is mental, or nearly so, operating through <term>discourse</term> <note>Latin: *discursum*. This refers to the step-by-step process of rational, logical reasoning, moving from one premise to another.</note>; the other is operative. The mental faculty is again twofold: it is either *inventive*, finding proportions within abstract quantities, or *cognitive*, recognizing and noticing selected proportions within sensible things. Therefore, the faculty that investigates harmonic ratios is the same one that embraces the rest of the sciences and arts—namely, the higher part of the human Soul. For we say nothing of God here, who does not investigate anything through discourse and study, but knows all things from eternity.

That faculty which notices and recognizes noble proportions in sensible things, or even in other things established outside itself, is a lower faculty of the soul. It is either the one that immediately informs the senses, or an even lower one: namely, the faculty of the vital soul. This faculty does not reason as Philosophers do, nor does it use a specific method; nor is it found only in humans, but also in wild beasts and cattle, and even in the "sublunary Soul" <note>Kepler believed the Earth itself had a kind of soul that responded to the movements of the planets.</note>. You may ask: if that faculty is not capable of reasoning, and therefore cannot grasp the science of Harmonic proportions, how then is it able to recognize those offered to it from the outside? <margin>Harmonic ratios are born with souls.</margin> For to "recognize" is to compare an external sensation with internal <term>Ideas</term> <note>Kepler follows the Platonic tradition, where "Ideas" are innate archetypes or patterns already present in the mind at birth.</note> and to judge the two to be congruent. Proclus expresses this beautifully with the word "awakening," as if from a sleep.

> Just as sensible things occurring outside make us remember those things which we knew before: so sensible mathematical things, if they are recognized, elicit intellectual ones, previously present within; so that they now shine forth in act in the Soul, which before lay hidden in it like under a veil of potentiality.

How, then, did they break inside? I answer that the Ideas or formal ratios of harmonies—as we discussed above—are entirely present in those things that possess this faculty of recognition. They are not received into the interior through reasoning; rather, they depend on natural instinct and are born with the soul, just as the number of leaves in a flower or cells in an apple (an intellectual matter) is born with the forms of plants. This occurrence in plants—which is similar to harmonic ratios (since number and proportion are kindred things, as shown above)—makes it so that I cannot confidently deny even to the vegetative soul of plants the faculty of recognizing the harmonic proportions of sidereal rays <note>Kepler is suggesting that plants might respond to the "harmonies" of light from the stars and planets, a concept central to his astrological theories.</note>; although I decide nothing without my own experiments. Thus it happens that children, the uneducated, farmers, barbarians, and even wild beasts perceive the harmonies of voices, even though they know nothing of the science of harmony. If you ask whence they get this instinct? Either I shall fly to God—who forms these shapes in bodies as images of Himself, yet in varying degrees, and makes them carry harmonic ratios with them just as He Himself embraced them from eternity and expressed them in creation—or, what comes to the same thing, I shall cite the kinship mentioned in Chapter I <margin>The Soul is in a certain way a circle. The foundation of birth-horoscope influences.</margin> between these souls (even the lower ones) and the Circle. They are composed and shaped according to the Circle as a norm and law; and along with the circle itself and its mathematical demonstrability, they took on the Idea of the harmonic proportions that depend upon it. For <term>horoscopes</term> <note>Latin: *Geneses*. In this context, it refers to the planetary configurations at a person's birth.</note> strongly confirm this philosophy, since we see the character of the flowing radia-

The means by which the Soul perceives Harmonies

Furthermore, the means used by these lower faculties of the Soul to perceive external harmonies are the same ones by which they receive the external objects themselves inwardly. If they are sensible things <note>Things that can be perceived by the five senses.</note>, they are also perceived by the senses—namely, by the faculties of the soul informing the senses. These lower faculties, no less than the higher one, are engaged in the comparison of certain things, but they do so by instinct, not by <term>discourse</term> <note>Latin: *discursu*. Step-by-step rational reasoning.</note>. Thus, by the sense of hearing and the power presiding over it, consonant sounds are discerned from dissonant ones. Thus, architectonic proportions are perceived by the eyes, and by that faculty which presides over sight, the beautiful and congruent are discerned from the incongruous. But if the things themselves in which the harmonic ratio exists are not sensible, but perhaps perceptible by another faculty, those same proportions of things reflect in the soul: as is the case with the proportions of sidereal rays <note>The angles formed between planets, often called "aspects" in astrology.</note>. How these are perceived by the <term>sublunary soul</term> <note>The "soul of the Earth," which Kepler believed animated the planet and responded to cosmic movements.</note> we shall investigate below in Chapter VII.

<margin>
What kind of perception?
</margin>
Yet this perception of Harmonies in the lower faculties of the Soul is obtuse and obscure, and in a way material, and as if under a cloud of ignorance. For they do not know that they are perceiving; just as when we see something, we nonetheless do not always notice that we see it. Such are those movements and terrors celebrated by the <term>Stoics</term> <note>An ancient Greek school of philosophy; Kepler refers to their ideas on "pre-emotions" or natural reactions that happen before reason kicks in.</note>, which are natural and without counsel, and beyond the will. Such also is the affection of natural Hate or Love—a truly wondrous thing—which, by the agreement of the limbs and the qualities of voice and temperament, estimates the goodness or similarity of another's Soul to its own, and miraculously flares up toward it.

<margin>
The instinct of Love.
</margin>
Thus a mad youth loves a girl, yet he does not know why, or what he loves most in her, which any common prostitute could not provide if it were a dishonorable love, or any marriageable girl if it were legitimate. 

<margin>
The physiognomic instinct.
</margin>
But a <term>Physiognomist</term> <note>One who practices the art of judging character from physical features, especially the face.</note> arriving finds in each person some similarity of character: which, if vicious, provides occasion for perpetual strife in marriage; if good, for tranquility of life. And thus to this must be referred the entire physiognomic instinct; which, though mute and in a way brute—and by no means acquired by art, though it can be refined by it—is nonetheless the unique interpreter and arbiter of human affairs. For each person obtains as much prosperity (speaking naturally) as their face, the agreement of their body, and the gait and movement of their limbs appeals to those in power, and as much as it creeps into them,

<margin>
The Fascination of the Gaze.
</margin>
even with no deliberation used on that matter, as if latent; so that they often testify that they love or hate someone, not knowing for what cause. Such, I say, is the sense of proportions in the lower faculties of the Soul: a sense without conscious awareness. Thus they do not distinguish the proportion from its "Terms" or its subject—as when, having heard a pleasant melody, we think of nothing regarding the art itself besides the sounds themselves—nor do they clearly distinguish different Harmonies from one another; they only notice that they *are*, but they do not know what or how varied they are. For even the **Ideas of Harmonies** themselves, which these lower faculties of the Soul have within them, are not instilled in them in a purely clear way, but with the "coverings" of the subject—namely, that which is the object of each faculty. Undoubtedly the faculty of hearing (to use the example of concordant sounds in place of all others), standing closest to the body, was too coarse, and thus also unsuited to receive the purest Idea of proportion; as I will now explain immediately in more detail.

<meta>This page continues from the discussion of how the soul receives external harmonies through its lower faculties. Kepler now shifts from the "passive" reception of harmony (how we feel it) to the "energetic" or active faculties (how the soul acts upon and creates harmony).</meta>

<header>BOOK IV OF THE HARMONIES.</header>

<margin>CHAPTER II</margin>
For now I come to the active faculties <note>Latin: *energeticas Facultates*. These are the powers of the soul that do work or create movement, rather than just receiving impressions.</note>, which are occupied with Harmonic proportions. This category is also twofold: for a faculty is either active within itself, or upon things outside of itself; in both cases, it either models its works after these proportions or introduces proportions into those works. The former is similar to a passive state, while the latter is indisputably exercised in action. The former is a product of the lower faculties of the Soul, the latter of the higher faculties. The former is subject to the forces of Nature; the latter to the human will. Indeed, the former possesses a power of "alteration" <note>A technical term in Aristotelian physics meaning a change in quality rather than position.</note> which it exerts upon its own body, so that it is entirely subject to the <term>vital faculty</term> <note>The basic biological power that keeps an organism alive and growing.</note>.

<margin>What the Soul undergoes according to Harmonies.</margin>
The fact that we are delighted by the Harmonies of sounds has the appearance of a "passion" <note>In this context, a "passion" is something that happens *to* you, rather than something you *do*.</note>, specifically a kind of soothing or smoothing. For this reason, philosophers call the "Sympathy" <note>original: *Sympathia*. Kepler uses this to mean a resonance or shared feeling between the soul and the music.</note> of souls with Song a "suffering" or "undergoing." However, it is in truth an operation of the soul, acting upon itself by a natural motion and arousing itself. The soul is drawn to this not by deliberate choice or will, but by natural instinct. From its very birth, the soul has certain "Ideas" linked together and, as it were, fused into one: these are the Ideas of the Harmonies incorporated into sounds and the corresponding emotions of the soul. Thus, the Idea of Harmony is implanted in the soul in no other way than as a source of joy; it is something delightful because it is an intricate movement conforming to that Idea. I believe this is what <term>Proclus</term> <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who greatly influenced Kepler's mathematical mysticism.</note> meant above when he affirmed that the Patterns <note>original: *Paradigmata*.</note> of mathematical things (and thus even more so of Harmonies) exist in the Mind **intellectually** <margin>intellectually <note>Greek: *νοερῶς*</note>,</margin> but in the Soul **vitally** <margin>vitally <note>Greek: *ζωικῶς*</note></margin>. In this way, these patterns exist in the sense of hearing as sounds, and in the vital faculty of the <term>sublunary world</term> <note>The Earth and its atmosphere, which Kepler believed responded "vitally" to the movements of the planets.</note> as radiations and operations. That is to say, these are not the pure internal Patterns themselves, but their "Images" <note>original: *Icones*.</note> derived and sent outward.

<margin>How Souls act according to harmonic ratios.</margin>
The fact that we do not merely delight in the Harmony of a song, but also adapt the movements of our fingers, mouth, feet, and body to it, is something we perform through the <term>animal faculty</term> <note>The faculty responsible for movement and sensation.</note> joined with the will. But when we even adapt the voice to intelligible Harmonies—composing a melodic song never heard before—here we use all faculties, from the highest to the lowest. We use the highest because we exercise will and purpose; we use the lower because we are able to express only the Ideas of intervals implanted by nature, even without a theoretical understanding of proportions. We shut out all dissonances and wander only through the consonant intervals.

<margin>Whence the Harmonic faculties are in the Soul.</margin>
Therefore, the faculties of harmony explained thus far were "breathed out" during creation by that essential Harmony, GOD Himself, who is **Being in action** <note>Greek: *οὐσία ἐνεργείᾳ*. A concept from Aristotle meaning something that exists not just as a possibility, but as a fully realized activity.</note>. He inspired this small portion of His own image into all souls without exception, though in varying degrees. With this final point, I bring this chapter to a close.

# CHAPTER III.
## What are the Categories of **harmonized things** <note>Greek: *τῶν ἡρμοσμένων* (the tuned/harmonized things).</note>, that is, of things whether sensible or immaterial, in which Harmonies are expressed, whether by God or by man, and in what way?

It is easily seen that these are distinct questions: 1. In whom do Harmonies exist as the Agent, Former, or Craftsman? 2. In what do they exist as the work formed? We have dealt with the former up to this point; we must now deal more accurately with the latter.

Those proportions which previously existed in the Soul as the Craftsman <note>original: *Opifici*. This refers to Kepler's first major work (1596), where he proposed that the distances between the six known planets were determined by the five Platonic solids.</note>. Shape follows quantity, as its own individual property; why a spherical shape should be owed to the stars, and indeed to the World itself—namely, from the Archetype of the Sphere—is a topic usually explained elsewhere in many places. A certain proportion immediately follows the shapes of different bodies, and this is threefold: one of diameters, another of surfaces, and a third of space or volumes. Therefore,

<margin>3. Whether in the movements of bodies.</margin>
if other causes for these Proportions were not available, we could probably assert that they were drawn from the Harmonies. However, whatever those proportions are, the celestial Globes maintain them without any change; for they do not become larger or smaller by any motion or through the passage of time. It is different with those Proportions which exist in bodies because of their position, and because of their local motions: for these retain the character of Motion itself. Just as motion is always in a state of "continual becoming" <note>original: *continuo FIERI*. <margin>4. Whether in intervals.</margin>
being different at different times. It is true, of course, that if the motion of the celestial bodies did not vary their intervals from the common center or Base of the world—that is, if there were no motion of theirs into the height and the depth <note>Kepler is referring to the "altitude" of a planet: its varying distance from the Sun due to its elliptical orbit.</note>, but all motion was in a mere concentric circle—then not only would the proportion of the intervals be constant, but it would also have been purely Harmonic, if other causes had not intervened. The same must be said of motion by reason of its own essence,

<margin>5. Whether in the speed of motions constantly.</margin>
that is, by reason of its true speed through the ether. If this speed were constant and perpetual for each planet, there is no doubt that these various speeds and slownesses would have been tuned to Harmonic laws. The boundaries or markers of harmonic ratios are not found at every point on a circle or a straight line, but only at certain specific ones. Likewise, harmonies cannot exist throughout the entire duration of a motion—neither in the intervals, nor in the speed of the movements, nor in the spaces of the Zodiac intercepted between the planets. They can, however, exist at specific moments of time, and this occurs without further intervention from God once the initial motion was given. For He who prescribed the extremes <note>original: *extrema*. These are the minimum and maximum speeds of a planet's orbit (aphelion and perihelion).</note> for the motions and allowed for the change from one extreme to the other also granted all the intermediates: both the incongruous ones, which are infinite, and the congruent or harmonic ones, which are interspersed in a certain number <margin>8. In the speeds of journeys.</margin> among the incongruous ones. For God did not leave these mutable things without any care for harmonic ornament; rather, in some (such as the planets' own motions), He reduced them to a harmonic order by prescribing the extremes themselves—which will be the subject of Book V. In others, where <margin>7. In the lengths of journeys through the Zodiac.</margin> extremes are not given but the quantity of motion is connected to itself in a circle, the Creator considered it sufficient to conform the souls presiding over mundane creatures so that they would expect, observe, and notice the harmonies arising at their proper moments throughout the whole circle, and would accommodate their operations to that prescription. This is what happens with the motions of the planets as they appear from Earth under the Zodiac—the proper subject of this fourth book.

<margin>
10. In Song
The difference between celestial harmonies and human singing.
</margin>
Therefore, regarding the works of God known to us, the matter stands as follows: if we compare these to things that men arrange according to harmonic laws, we must say they are partly the same and partly different. First, in Songs, although there is no less a continuous increase and decrease of quantity than in the heavens, this change is necessary in the motions of the heavens according to certain laws of nature, whereas in the human voice it is neither necessary nor even easy. For the throat <margin>Why the human voice cannot be tensioned by continuous increases, like an instrument or a string? Why are there not merely harmonic configurations, as in song there are only pleasant ones?</margin> was made for articulated voices by the distinction of circles <note>Kepler likely refers to the cartilaginous rings of the trachea and the structure of the larynx.</note>. We reach a destination from high to low (and vice versa) more easily through intervals, as if by leaps, and through discrete sounds, than if we were commanded to use continuous <term>intension</term> <note>original: *intensione*. The process of stretching or tightening the vocal cords or a string to change pitch.</note>. It is no wonder, then, that in celestial motions, because of that continuous increase and decrease which could not be avoided, there remained incongruous intervals mixed with congruent and consonant ones; while in human song, all incongruous sounds are eliminated, and only congruent and consonant ones are observed. Yet Song has no reason to boast over celestial motions on this account; for those motions are assigned a different duty to perform, and harmonic contemplation is only accessory to them. Song has nothing to look toward except the Harmonies; it requires nothing outside itself, being intent on the single end of delight.

The "beat" or "stroke" used to keep time in music, traditionally a down-up motion of the hand.</note>, participating in the double and triple proportion. The Ionians and their composites are related, such as the ratio of 3 to 2; to these same belong the Spondee, the Dactyl, and those which have the same number of beats, in a ratio of 2 to 3; and these same relate to the Pæons <note>Types of rhythmic "feet" in classical poetry.</note>, as 4 to 5. Indeed, Poets and Grammarians even delight in the names of proportions using a peculiar terminology, calling four-syllable feet with one short syllable "Epitrites" <note>original: *Epitritos*, from the Greek for a 4:3 ratio</note>, that is, Sesquitertials. This is because, just as in the proportion of 4 to 3 expressed by parallel lines, the first three units are represented by a double line while only the fourth exceeds them with a single line; so in the poetic foot, three syllables are of two beats <note>original: *temporum*, referring to the duration of a long syllable</note>, and the fourth is of only one. And since the very word for "Feet" <term>Pedum</term> <note>Kepler notes that "metrical feet" share a name with biological feet used in dance.</note> alludes to the Choruses, <margin>Theatrical harmonies.</margin> a part of Comedies and Tragedies; it seems that actors also expressed all these proportions through the motion of their feet, no less than "double" and "triple" time is expressed today. <margin>Architectural [harmonies].</margin> In Architecture, whatever proportions of length to width or thickness are most highly approved—even by non-mathematical spectators—are found to be those closest to the harmonic ratios. <margin>Why, among human things, are the harmonies of song the most exact?</margin> The reason why the proportions of sounds are more exact than all these others, and why human Nature delights more intensely in expressing them, is because every living creature has the greatest power over sounds. For sounds are formed within the self, sent forth from the very depths of the chest <note>original: *praecordiis*, the area around the heart/diaphragm</note>, and are most ready to follow every nod of the mind and every movement of the heart. Furthermore, as said before, man has obtained a most suitable instrument: the Throat, stretched out in length like a string or rather a pipe <term>fistula</term>, in which the voice wanders up and down most freely along a straight-line length.

<margin>
Why harmonies are not clearly present in the quantities of resting objects.
</margin>
Generally, however, in all things in which quantity exists and where harmonies can be sought according to that quantity, they are far more evident through motion than without motion. For although a half, a third, a fourth, a fifth, a sixth, and their multiples exist within any single straight line, they nevertheless lie hidden among other parts that are incommensurable to the whole. They are so concealed in one and the same confusion with the whole that even if a second line, equal to one of those fractional parts, stands next to the whole—for example, a lintel beam of three feet next to a doorpost of five—its proportion to the whole is not so easily recognized as it would be if some motion were to discern, establish, and determine the comparable lengths. The cause of this is that where quantity exists without motion, everything contained within that quantity exists simultaneously at the same time—namely, all the proportions of all the parts to the whole. <margin>Why proportions shine forth most through motion.</margin> But if some quantity is traversed by a certain motion, then (as is the essence of motion) the proportions that have been traversed no longer exist, and those not yet traversed do not yet exist; and any single proportion exists alone at the moment when the motion reaches its mark. Thus, by the succession of motions, harmonic proportions are thrashed out from the incongruous ones and separated from the mixture of them, as if they were placed in pure light and held out for the senses to grasp. Indeed, not even the mind itself discerns harmonic proportions from the infinite incongruous ones standing before and after them in a given quantity without some *image* of motion. Instead, it traverses them (for example, in a circle) among infinite chords; it is a laborious task to find the chord of a third or fourth part of a circle and similar parts, and the mind seeks a demonstration of it. The mind performs in thought what the hand performs by drawing a line: it separates that proportion from the infinite others by this act of...

<margin>
CHAPTER III.

Why do proportions shine forth most especially through motion?

However, this will serve us below as an example for sketching out Harmonies to some extent.
</margin>

Indeed, the mind is capable of this because it possesses will, and by its own judgment it "dances" within that infinite division of quantities which is entirely present for the mind to contemplate. However, the sensations and other natural perceptions—and finally the motions of bodies by which perceptions are aided—are not in the power of a living being in the same way. For instance, if infinite sounds, or the infinite "angular positions" <note>Kepler refers here to the geometric angles formed between planets.</note> of two planets throughout the whole circuit of the heavens, were confused together at the same time, the senses could not withdraw themselves from the discordant ones to find refuge in the pleasing ones alone. Therefore, they have need of **motion**, through which all things that were confused by reason of their quantity are unfolded through successive moments of time, so that each one falls upon the senses individually. And if the eyes are able to do something similar to the mind—selecting the more excellent parts from an infinite confusion of things present without motion (as when, using the service of the hands, they select and draw a chord <note>original: *subtensam*, a line connecting two points on a curve</note> of a third part of a circle, namely the side of a triangle)—this is not so much the work of the eyes as it is the mind itself acting through the eyes; and even this is not done entirely without motion, as I said, the motion of the hands.

<margin>
How sensible things must be arranged so that harmonies may be within them.

How sounding things become the subject of harmonies.
</margin>

To apply this observation to our previous statements: if any thing is to be a genuine "subject" <note>In the philosophical sense, the physical matter that "hosts" a quality.</note> of harmonic proportion, it is necessary that both quantity and length be present in that thing. There must also be "signs" <note>Kepler means points of reference or markers.</note>—at least two if the length is a circle, or three if it is a straight line—of which one or all traverse the length of the thing through some motion, becoming the boundaries of the parts of that length between which the proportion exists. This is the minimum requirement. This happens, in part, in "configurations" <term>configurations</term> <note>In astrology, "configurations" or "aspects" are the significant angles between planets, like the square or trine.</note>, which are the proper subject of this Fourth Book. For as will be said in the following chapter, Harmonies are indeed considered in the angles measured by the Zodiac without motion; yet those very angles are established, one after another, by the **motion** of the radiating bodies <note>The planets.</note> through the Zodiac. There are, however, more excellent ways tending toward the same end: such as when the bodies themselves that have length are determined by such signs—wandering up and down— and the segments intercepted at any turn are moved simultaneously. In this way, it is no longer the bodies, but the **motions** of the bodies themselves that are compared to one another, based on a physical length and shortness rather than a temporal one (since we are dealing with incorporeal motions, or bodies set in motion). This is exactly how it is with sounds: for sound is an "image" <term>species</term> <note>Kepler uses "species" to mean the formal influence or sensory image emitted by an object.</note> emitted from a body, both as it is a quantity, as it is shaped to some extent, and as it is set in motion; for both the motion and the sound depend on the suitability of the shape.

<margin>What the windpipe contributes to sounds for expressing Harmonies.</margin>

And this is now the second and more evident reason why human nature is devoted most especially to the harmonic proportions of sounds. This happens, again, because of the conformation of the human body. For in the body, that throat is the vessel which is now long, now short, depending on the constriction of the upper or lower cartilaginous ring in the windpipe <term>aspera arteria</term> <note>original: *aspera arteria*, the "rough artery," an old anatomical term for the trachea or windpipe.</note>. When it is struck by the breath squeezed from the "bellows" of the lungs, its cavity (that is, its shape) produces a motion; the "image" of this motion falls upon the ears, and the sensation of the windpipe itself (as it is set in motion) is present to the perceiving soul. Indeed, to perceive this through the "common sense" <note>The internal faculty that integrates data from all five senses.</note> is to enjoy the forms of the limbs of the body as they are affected and, as it were, shaped by various motions. These images, as I explained in my *Dioptrics*, are carried from the limbs of the body by the continuity of the spirits...

# CHAPTER IV.
## What difference there is between the Harmonies in the fourth book and those considered in the third book.

It is of no use to preface with a long speech how important it is for sound philosophizing to distinguish the boundaries of things; to compare related things so they are not mistaken for the same; and to contrast opposites so they may be clarified. Therefore, it will be worthwhile to bring under a single view everything useful for this purpose that has been said so far—whether scattered, obscurely, or in passing—and to illustrate them more fully where necessary, adapting them explicitly to the stated topic of the chapter. There is, therefore, a fivefold difference between the harmonic contemplations of this book and the previous one: First, in the Harmonic matter itself, because of its scope; Second, in its sensible **Terms** <note>The physical components or objects being compared, such as two notes or two angles.</note>; Third, in the cause that grants Harmony its essence; Fourth, in the manner of being present; and Fifth, in the order of causes that form the terms of the harmonic proportion.

<margin>Harmonies are narrower in this book.</margin>
I. Regarding the thing itself, which is called a Harmonic proportion: those in Book III first arose from the sections of a circle through demonstrable regular plane figures, were soon transferred to straight lines, and being combined and joined among themselves, they produced a considerable abundance of harmonic parts (such as harmonic sections, tones, genera, modes, systems, and the like), and a certain wonderful order among them. Almost that entire apparatus, however great it is, will also have to be examined and applied below in Book V. But now in this fourth book, although we start from the same sections of the circle, we have not progressed to straight lines; instead, we shall remain within the boundaries of the circle throughout the entire scope of the discussion. The reason was given in the preceding chapter and will be explained further below in Chapter VI, where we will deal more extensively with both the relationship and the effect of this distinction.

<margin>These harmonies are of angles.</margin>
II. As for the Terms of these harmonies or their sensible subject: in Book III, these were sounds differing in **pitch** <note>original: *acumine & gravitate*, literally "sharpness and heaviness"</note>; thus they were referred to the category of motion and were, in a sense, shaped motions. In this fourth book, however, they are not voices (as stated in the preamble), nor any motions among which one might recognize harmonies; but they reside in the **angles** which two planets, by emitting rays of light, form at the Earth, insofar as such an angle [is part of] the four right angles <note>Kepler refers to the 360 degrees of the circle surrounding the Earth.</note> meeting at a single point of concur-

...compared to those standing around. And here the reader needs a clear warning. For I can indeed explain these terms more clearly for understanding, but I cannot do so without the danger of confusion in sound philosophizing, unless I diligently prepare the philosophizing reader. For while the terms of a proportion must differ in quantity—and the quantity <margin>In what way the arcs of the Zodiac [are involved].</margin> of angles, which is to say their measure, is formed by the arc of a circle described from the point where the angles meet, as we are taught in **Geometry** <note>Kepler refers to the Euclidean principle that an angle is measured by the arc of a circle centered at the vertex.</note>—yet in the whole space of the world, which extends from here at the Earth to the ends of things, we cannot anywhere describe or perceive with our senses a circle suitable for measuring the angles of rays, except for that very sensible circle in the highest **ether** <note>The "ether" was thought to be the subtle substance filling the upper heavens.</note>, expressed by the very numerous fixed stars. From those stars, organized into certain shapes of animals, that circle has acquired the name **Zodiac** <note>original: *Zodiaci*; from the Greek *zōdiakos*, meaning "circle of little animals."</note>. Indeed, the Planets always move beneath this circle, and each one appears to us to cover one part of it by the positioning of its body; and in its center, the Earth—our dwelling place—seems to be hidden, not only by its own center, which is a point, but by the mass of its whole body, upon whose surface we humans are arranged. Nothing, therefore, is easier to perceive than if we say (as in the preceding chapter) that the harmonic proportions we are dealing with in this book exist between the whole Zodiac circle and its arc, which two planets seem to designate, limit, or cut away by that visible positioning of their bodies.

<margin>Not truly celestial.</margin>
Although this is how it is arranged, and is very well stated according to Geometric and Astronomic Reasons, the philosophizing reader must nevertheless be extremely careful not to assume in their mind that this matter (the subject of Book IV) exists in the heaven itself, in the Zodiac circle, or even in the planets. Not in the least! For this harmony exists in the parts of the Zodiac not for their own sake—since the radiating planets stand at an immense distance below this circle—but because those parts measure the angles of the rays meeting on Earth. Or rather, it is because the parts do not actually measure them themselves, but in their place, an exact **Image** <note>original: *Icon*</note> of the celestial Zodiac in the **sublunary Soul** <note>Kepler’s concept of a "soul" or formative faculty within the Earth and its inhabitants that responds to the geometric patterns of the heavens.</note> undergoes this duty of measuring. The harmony exists in the rays of the planets, not insofar as they each descend from their own planet or are the offspring of light (though not without this), but insofar as the pairs of rays from two planets, joined here on Earth, form a certain harmonic angle. On both counts, the subject of this harmony is **Terrestrial** <margin>But Terrestrial.</margin> (formally, and insofar as the rays become the Terms of the harmonic Proportion); it is not celestial at all, except materially and with respect to its own Being, without consideration of the Harmonies. That is, the rays of light—things originating in heaven but now fallen to earth—conform to the angles made on earth, which are the proper subject of this harmony. Regarding truly **celestial harmonies**, we shall deal with them as our main subject in Book V. In short, the Terms of the harmonies in Book III were the work of Man or Art; in this Book IV, they will be the work of Nature; and finally, in Book V, they will be the work of God the Creator.
