<margin>CHAPTER IV.</margin>
...of its own material subject (sounds) into the senses, harmonies were received and judged by reason of their formal essence—insofar as they are harmonies (that is, they were shaped)—by an instinct created within the Mind, which shares in reason without the need for verbal argument. And up to this point, Harmonies were considered only in themselves.

Then, however, through a hidden but acknowledged exchange between the powers of the soul, the harmonies received within were poured into the various emotions of the heart through certain likenesses or "Images." They were also poured into the power of movement, so that a human might express the harmonic form conceived in the mind not just with the voice, but also by imitating it with the movement of the body. In this way, Harmonies took on the role of a cause.

Similarly here, it is necessary to assume a Soul into which this <term>criterion</term> <note>original: *κριτήριον*; a standard or rule for judging. Kepler argues that the ability to recognize harmony is an innate "ruler" built into the soul by God.</note> of Harmonic proportions has been instilled since the creation of things. This Soul evaluates the angle of two radiating stars, however it is received within (whether that happens through something similar to the senses, or through a property of its own essence, as a soul; about which more was said in the preceding chapter and more will be said in the following ones). It compares the angle to four right angles <note>A full circle of 360 degrees.</note>, distinguishes the harmonic from the non-harmonic, and thus grants these harmonies their intellectual **Being** <note>original: *Esse*</note>, which these angles did not yet possess while they were still outside the boundaries of the mind.

<margin>These harmonies are reflected, 1. in the human Soul.</margin>
If one asks what kind of soul this is, or where or in what body it is located: I answer, first, that the souls of all humans are of this kind. But in Book Three, the faculty involved was the one presiding over hearing, and thus over the senses; here, it is not a sensory faculty. For the eyes, whose objects are Light and bright rays, make no suitable judgment of the harmonic radiation of two planets. Nor is it the Reasoning faculty: for although reason—using Astronomical Observations managed by the eyes—finds and calculates which aspects exist at any given time, it does not do so naturally (since it is not done by all people indiscriminately, but voluntarily, by a few specifically devoted to astronomy). Rather, human souls are the subject of those harmonies, first by reason of natural instinct, insofar as souls are patterns of the Creator (as stated in CHAPTER IV); and second, by reason of the Vital and Natural faculties and their movements—or in the Platonic style, the "Desiring" and "Spirited" parts <note>Kepler refers to the *Concupiscibilis* and *Irascibilis*, terms from Platonic and Scholastic psychology describing the emotional and impulsive parts of the soul.</note>. The harmonies exist in the former as forms, while in the latter, the patterns of the Harmonies are imprinted upon these faculties and become the driving forces and stimuli for the works of Nature, in both the mind and the body.

<margin>2. In sublunary Nature or the soul of the Earth.</margin>
Furthermore, the primary soul into which these Harmonies of radiation flow is that which philosophers call "Sublunary Nature." It is spread through the entire body of the Earth, our foster-mother, and is rooted in a certain specific part of it, just as the human soul is rooted in the heart. From this center—like a hearth, a fountain, or an inner Sanctuary—it goes out through its own form into the Ocean surrounding the Earth and the Air poured over both.

Just as someone listening to a singer performing a sweet melody testifies through a joyful expression, voice, and the clapping of hands or feet (timed to the measure of the melody) that they perceive and approve of what is harmonic in the music; in the same way, Sublunary Nature, with significant and evident commotion...

This causes them to exhale a great abundance of vapors and mists, from which, through the <term>Antiperistasis</term> <note>original: *Antiperistasies*; a philosophical concept where a quality is intensified when surrounded by its opposite, such as heat being compressed and strengthened by surrounding cold.</note> of the cold above, all kinds of <term>meteors</term> <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, snow, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note> are formed.

For this soul must be placed in the body of the Earth: because the harmonic angles of the rays do not exist in any other part of the world except on Earth; and the works of Nature, which follow from the configurations of the rays, draw their origin from the bowels of the Earth and the caverns of the mountains.

IV. The fourth distinction consists in the ways in which various Harmonies exist within their subjects.

<margin>
The difference between these harmonies and Musical ones, in their continuity.
</margin>
For in Book III, when harmonies were in Song, they were in it entirely—that is, during the whole time the Song lasted. And although the intervals of voices, like all things participating in quantity, allow for continuous division, there was nevertheless no transition in song from a lower sound through infinite intermediates to that which was first consonant or agreeable; instead, all the intermediates were passed over with a jump and with silence, and indeed every vocal dwelling was on sounds agreeable to one another. In the same way in Harmony, although infinite intervals exist between the <term>Diapason</term> <note>The interval of an octave.</note> and the <term>Dihex</term> <note>The interval of a major sixth.</note>, no continuous stretching of voices occurred through all the intermediates until the sixth was made from the octave; instead, the voices were carried by a jump from a pure Octave to a pure Sixth, with all the intermediates passed over in silence. And in organs, indeed, one jumped from one pipe to another; in stringed instruments, such as the Lute and the Harp, from one string to another; or if multi-sounding strings were used, as in the <term>Clavichord</term>, <term>Pandura</term> <note>An ancient long-necked lute.</note>, <term>Lyre</term>, or <term>Cittern</term>, from one fret to another; or in flutes, from one hole to another; and in the human throat from one ring of the windpipe to another.

It is not so in Book IV. For the harmonies we shall consider in it (as we began to say in the preceding chapter) do not always exist between the angle of two planetary rays and four right angles <note>A full 360-degree circle.</note>; instead, there is a continuous separation of the planets—to which this motion is given beneath the circle of the <term>Zodiac</term>—through all <term>proportional</term> <note>original: *ἀνάλογα*; meaning the planets move through every possible mathematical ratio.</note> intervals into the harmonic ones. The extremes of these are two right angles (a semicircle or Opposition), and from there in reverse order through all intervals that are unharmonious and dissonant, back to the Conjunction. No jump is made here from one harmonic angle to another—for example, from a <term>Trine</term> <note>An aspect of 120 degrees.</note> to a <term>Square</term> <note>An aspect of 90 degrees.</note>—but the transition from that one to this one is continuous, through all intermediates.

Therefore, unharmonious configurations of rays occupy the entire time of celestial motions; however, they mark off harmonic configurations of two, or sometimes three, or even four planets at least at specific moments, while the others continue in incongruity. # ON CONFIGURATIONS

<margin>
CHAPTER IV.
</margin>
...two or three [planets] would harmonize while the others remain dissonant. Thus, speaking truly and properly, the harmonic configurations themselves do not exist across a span of time, but are perfected in indivisible moments. Yet it is equally true that the disturbances created in Souls by these harmonies are not momentary. For harmonic configurations move things in so far as they are in the process of forming; 
<margin>
However, their effect is not momentary.
</margin>
at the very moment they become perfect, their stimulus relaxes again. But the works of Nature, which are stirred up by these stimuli, take the measure of their own time from the condition of the matter itself, and they often last far beyond the moment in which the radiation is completed. In this way, when a bronze machine <note>Kepler is likely referring to a cannon.</note> is discharged, it catches fire by the force of ignited gunpowder; the heat does not diminish immediately once the fire's material is consumed. Similarly, to use a more fitting example, the body of an animal tossed by a fit of fever remains hot; even though the faculty of the vital soul (the author of the inflammation) may relax its effort once its task is done—the feverish matter having been either dissolved or ejected from the innermost parts toward the exterior—the body is not immediately freed from all heat. That heat clings to the matter of the body, the flesh, bones, and nerves for a long time, until it too expires in the course of time.

<margin>
Fol. 124. They are mixed with ineffective discords.
</margin>
Therefore, these Harmonies are among those which we said above in Chapter II are not subject to free providence, but by the necessity of movements are mixed with infinite discords of their own kind. God ordained minds to recognize these harmonies when they occur. Indeed, sublunary Nature is far more successful at distinguishing these than the ears are at distinguishing song. For the sense of hearing is not greatly delighted by a harmony of two voices if five other dissonant voices are making a racket. Sublunary Nature, being accustomed to constant discordant configurations, treats them as nothing because it notices nothing new; but it is so intent on a harmonic angle as if that angle were the only one present. Just so, when a prophecy fails a thousand times, it is ignored; but if it hits the mark even once, it is deemed worthy of memory and is celebrated in the talk of all people.

<margin>
They are necessary, not staged.
</margin>
From these things, then, we are given to understand that while harmonies in voices are established by the choice and plan of the singer, harmonies in the angles of radiation occur by no plan of sublunary nature, but by the mere geometric necessity of the movements. Because two planets must be separated by the length of an entire semicircle (or 180 degrees), it necessarily happens that at certain moments they are also distant by its harmonic parts—namely 30, 60, 90, 120 degrees, and so on. Therefore, the harmonies of song are sought from within by the singer, but the harmonies of the rays are expected from without by sublunary Nature. They are observed when they happen, distinguished from non-harmonic ones (and thus receive their <term>Being</term> <note>original: *Esse*; a philosophical term referring to the essential nature or existence of a thing.</note> from the soul's perception), and are welcomed and applied. In short, the configurations lead the song, and sublunary Nature dances to the laws of this melody.

<margin>
Dissimilarity in the order of causes.
</margin>
V. The fifth distinction must be linked in some way to the first. For the Harmonies of this book and the previous one differ not only in their scope, but also in the order of the different respects by which Geometric Figures produce both kinds of Harmonic proportions. In the third book, the primary consideration was <term>Knowability</term> <note>original: *Scibilitas*; the quality of being able to be understood or known by the mind.</note>; in this fourth book, the primary consideration will be <term>Congruence</term> <note>original: *Congruentia*; the geometric fitting together of shapes.</note>. But regarding this fifth distinction, we shall now deal with it specifically in Chapter V, in the explanation of the Axioms.

ON THE HARMONICS, BOOK IV.
R 3
<meta>catchword: DEFINITION</meta>

<margin>CHAPTER V.</margin>
## CHAPTER V.
### On the causes of effective Configu-
### rations; and their Number and
### the order of their degrees.

### DEFINITION I.

The term **configuration** is used for that angle formed by two rays, each descending from its own planet, where those rays meet here on Earth (which is considered as a point). Or, what amounts to the same thing, it is used for the arc of a great circle described in the Zodiac, which serves as the measure of said angle—the arc which the two planets, by the positioning of their bodies, appear to us inhabitants of Earth to mark out and, as it were, cut off.

Regarding the name, it should first be noted that Ptolemy, in his *Quadripartitum* <note>Also known as the *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's foundational work on astrology.</note>, in his *Great Work* <note>The *Almagest*.</note>, and in his *Harmonics*, calls these "Schematisms" <note>original: Σχηματισμȣς, meaning patterns or configurations</note>, which the Arabs translated as "Aspects." It is as if "Pattern" (*Schema*) were the same thing as "countenance" or "face." This is also reflected in our German tongue, which is accustomed to calling the face *das Angesicht* (Aspect), and calls the patterns of actors—the coverings of the face—*Gesichter* (faces/masks), which the Italians call *Mascaras*. One also finds the word "Prosblepseis" <note>original: προσβλέψεις, meaning "looks" or "regards"</note>, which we translate from the Arabic not only as "Aspects," but which good Latin authors are also accustomed to call "Intuitions" or "Looking signs." However, in this sense, the term applies not so much to the planets as to the signs or <term>Dodecatemories</term> <note>The twelve 30-degree divisions of the zodiac.</note> of the Zodiac; since these have length, they can be turned toward one another in their hollows to a greater or lesser degree. For adjacent signs cannot "look" at each other, as their faces are not turned toward one another, but are positioned side-by-side facing the same direction.

Secondly, note that at the same time two planets form an angle at the Earth, they also form different angles in other locations in the universe. Yet nowhere is the angle so great as it is on the arc of the circle passing through their bodies and the Earth, or around the line that connects their bodies, like a rotation around an axis. Outside of these locations, their radiations meet at far different angles—whether those be Harmonic or discordant—as they do throughout almost all the rest of the universe. Most importantly, note that no angle is formed within either of the planetary bodies themselves. For an angle requires two rays, but every ray is outside the body; none exists within the body itself. This is worth noting because the effect on Earth follows the "angulation" <note>The forming of the angle.</note> on Earth. From the Earth, around the time of these Aspects, the matter of rain and other <term>meteors</term> <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and snow, not just falling stars.</note> is exhaled. Thus we can argue concerning the seat of the cause that moves these meteors: that cause is not in one planet or the other, nor in some other empty place in the universe, but in the Earth itself.

Thirdly, the mention that the Earth is considered as a point was not added in vain. From this it follows that even though there are countless living beings on Earth, and the rays from any planet onto them and other points on the Earth are infinite, the angle of the rays coming from two planets at the same time is, for all practical purposes, the same through all points of the Earth—whether at the center, on the surface, or in the caverns of mountains. All those aspects, though infinite in number, are considered as one single Aspect, because they are all essentially equal to one another.

<summary>Kepler defines a "configuration" (or aspect) as the angle formed by rays from two planets meeting at Earth. He argues that the astrological and meteorological effects of these angles occur because the Earth's own soul perceives and responds to this geometry.</summary>
<keywords>configuration, aspect, Ptolemy, geometry, Earth's soul, meteorology, zodiac signs, planetary rays, optics</keywords>

ON CONFIGURATIONS

<margin>CHAPTER V.</margin>
## Definition II.

An **effective configuration** is said to occur when the rays of two planets form such an angle that it is fit to stimulate the sublunary Nature and the lower faculties of living beings, so that each becomes more industrious in its own work around the time of that configuration.

*Effectiveness is attributed to a configuration—which is formally a "being of reason" <note>original: "Ens rationis"; a concept that exists in the mind rather than as a physical object</note>—but it is not an immediate effectiveness upon the physical thing itself. It is not as if rain and similar things fall from the sky itself, or from the configured planets, as is the foolish belief of the common people. Rather, the effect is mediated and objective. For just as objects move the senses—sound moves the hearing, not the eyes; and color moves the sight, not the hearing—so too here, the specific quality of this Relation, which is called a "configuration," moves not the senses of the body, but the animal faculty, which is capable of Reason by instinct without needing to deliberate. Therefore, the Configuration performs this not by its own power, but by the power of the Soul, which is said to be "acted upon" when in truth it is rather the soul itself acting upon itself. Afterward, the soul (or sublunary Nature), thus moved or stimulated by the aspect and reminded of its own nature, rouses itself to draw out from the bowels of the earth the material for all kinds of weather. If there were no Soul in the Earth—which we call the sublunary Nature—the planets themselves could do nothing to the Earth, neither through themselves nor through a favorable aspect. For it is an absurd thought, more like a poet’s joke or play, to imagine that from the harmonic coupling of two rays, as if from the intercourse of a male and female, a vapor is conceived as the matter of wind or rain. It is as if moisture and the other things that breathe out from the earth were made of the same substance as the Harmony (which is a relation), or the Angle (which is a qualitative quantity), or even the Light itself (which is a quality, not a substance), just as a seed is made of the substance of the parents. But just as we say nothing can be made from nothing, so too nothing material can be naturally drawn out of something immaterial. See more on this in Chapter VII.*

## Axiom I.

The arc of the circle of the Zodiac, which is cut off by the side of a fitting and knowable figure <note>A geometric shape, such as a triangle or square, that can be inscribed in a circle.</note> or star, measures the angle of an effective Configuration.

## Axiom II.

The angle of a knowable and fitting figure or star is the measure <note>original: "modulus"</note> of the angle of an effective Configuration.

*The whole business rests upon these two Axioms; I have made them two for this reason: because there are two probable ways by which the Soul and sublunary Nature can come to the knowledge of the Configurations that exist at any given time.*

*For they perceive either that figure whose side cuts off the arc from the Zodiac circle (the measure of the Configuration or radiant angle), or they perceive that figure of which the configuration angle itself becomes an element. What the difference is between these figures, and what their mutual relationship is, will be shown in order from these diagrams following one after another*

He argues that the planets do not physically cause rain, but rather act as a stimulus that the Earth's soul recognizes and responds to through internal geometric instincts.</summary>

For there are two figures that are **reciprocally proportional** <note>original: "ἀντιπεπονθότα" (antipeponthota); a term from Euclidean geometry describing a relationship where the parts of one figure correspond to the parts of another</note>. First, the diameter is reciprocal to itself, whether it bisects the circle by being drawn through the center, or touches it, when two rays forming an angle make two right angles or rather no angle at all, arranged in a single straight line.

The same should be considered regarding the **Conjunction** (☌) or **Opposition** (☍) of the planets, which is called a "configuration" only loosely <note>original: "impropriè"</note>. For if two planets were under the same point of the Zodiac, then the angle at the center is zero, while in the circumference there are infinite angles, and the sides of the figure are mere points; the circle is, as it were, a figure of infinite angles. This configuration did not require a visual representation.

<image-desc>Figure II: A circular diagram showing a square inscribed within a circle. Radii are drawn from the center to two adjacent vertices of the square, and a chord connects those two vertices. A star symbol and a cross symbol are positioned outside the circle as in Figure I, with lines indicating a geometric relationship between the external points and the inscribed figure.</image-desc>

<margin>Figure II.</margin>
Next, the **Square** <note>original: "Tetragonus"</note> is also reciprocally proportional to itself, because the angle formed by two sides on the circumference is equal to the angle at the center which one side subtends. Following this, the **Triangle** <note>original: "Trigonus"</note> is reciprocal to the **Hexagon**, the **Pentagon** to the **Five-pointed Star**, the **Octagon** to the **Eight-pointed Star**, the **Decagon** to the **Ten-pointed Star**, and the **Dodecagon** to the **Twelve-pointed Star**. This is such that if all the inscribed angles of one figure's vertices are on the circumference, one of its sides subtends a single angle of the other figure located at the center.

The centers of all these circles represent the **Earth**, as if situated in the middle. The circles themselves represent either the **Zodiac**, as perceived from the Earth, or any other circle subordinate to the Zodiac, imagined for the sake of measuring angles. Such circles are, in potential, the **souls** themselves, which are moved by passions—circles, that is, abstracted from their own quantity and reduced to the narrow confines of a qualitative point capable of receiving directions.

I have placed two radiating stars outside this circle, one higher than the other, so that I might demonstrate through this visual representation that it makes no difference to the Configuration on Earth whether a planet is high or low in the sky; one planet can be many times higher than the other while the same Configuration remains on Earth.

Furthermore, the fact that in the first axiom the word **fitting** <note>original: "congrua"</note> precedes, and in the second axiom the word **knowable** <note>original: "scibilis"</note> precedes, was not done by chance but by design. For the fact that a certain Aspect is effective is caused by both figures: both the one inscribed in the circumference and the one whose single angle is formed by the rays at the center. Each is effective both because of its **Knowability** and because of its **Fittingness**, though not equally so. All these matters require a slightly more lengthy explanation; there is only one reason why it is so thorny: so that the number of Aspects may be reduced by philosophical reasoning, or at least confined to certain degrees...

He emphasizes that the soul acts as a qualitative point that "knows" these geometric proportions regardless of the planets' physical distance from Earth.</summary>

# Proposition I.

The kinship of Radiations <note>Kepler uses "Radiations" to refer to the rays of light sent from planets to the Earth, which form astrological aspects</note> with the Circle and its arcs is greater than was the kinship of the Consonances.

The foundations for this were laid down in Book III and should now be rightfully carried over into Book IV as an Axiom; nevertheless, it is proven as follows:

1. Consonances belong to sounds, and sounds consist of motions; their high and low pitches, by which Consonances are expressed, arise from the speed and slowness of motions, as demonstrated in Book III. However, fast and slow sounds are elicited from stretched strings when they are struck—not only if the tension is circular, but also, and much more commonly, if the tension is rectilinear <note>in a straight line, like a lute or lyre string</note>. Therefore, consonances do not regard the circle and its arcs immediately because of their circular shape, but because of the length of the parts—specifically, their mutual proportion. Whatever they take from the circle, they retain even if the circle is broken and stretched out into a straight line. By contrast, Aspects, by Definition I, are angles measured by the circle and its arcs; they cannot exist unless the circle remains as it is, retaining its circular shape in its entirety.

2. Not all Consonances are propagated from the circle and its parts with equal closeness. For some traced their origin to parts of the circle not as *circular* parts, but as straight lines—specifically, the same division that happened to the whole circle, as shown in Book III. It is the opposite with Aspects: for the measurement of that which corresponds only to a circle can in no way have a relationship to straightness.

It is proven first from the circumferential figure. For where the circle is whole, there also the regular figure <note>A regular polygon, like a triangle or square, where all sides and angles are equal</note> is whole: but the circle is more "whole" in measuring the angles of radiations, according to Proposition I; therefore, the figure can be considered more as a whole figure <note>original: "Figura V."</note> in respect to radiations. On the contrary, in Consonances, just as the circle and its parts could be extended into a straight line without losing the consonances, so too could all the sides of a figure be extended into one and the same straight line, making a Consonance with one straight side of the figure. In this way, however, just as the circle loses its shape, so too the rectilinear figure loses its configuration, so that it is no longer a figure.

It is proven secondly from the central figure. Angles are the elements of figures; now two rays make an angle at the center, which, when repeated several times, completes the figure, as appears from these diagrams. <margin>Figure VI</margin> However, that did not occur in the origin of Consonances; for there, no respect was paid to the angle at the center. Therefore, figures are more closely related to Aspects <note>The specific angular relationships between planets in astrology</note> than to Consonances.

## Proposition III.

**T**he congruence of figures <note>term: <term>Congruence</term> refers to the property of geometric shapes to fit together perfectly without gaps, like floor tiles</note> is more powerful in establishing effective Configurations than in Consonances.

Many arguments for this fact are available. 1. *Congruence is a property of a figure insofar as the figure is a whole and possesses a specific form. But a figure, insofar as it possesses this whole form, is first of all more inherently related to configurations than to Consonances (by Proposition II). Secondly, it divides the circle harmonically as a whole, and the circle itself is also more related to configurations than to consonances (by Proposition I). Therefore, on both counts—by the specific nature of the figure and by the shared nature of the figure and the circle—the power of the congruence of figures is greater in configurations than in consonances.*

2. *From the number of figures. For we have made use of this principle, through the preceding Axioms, that figures are effective through their properties. Where, therefore, the Number more closely corresponds to the efficient...*

...to be made <note>original: "faciendorum," completing the word from the previous page</note>, there the kinship of the cause with the effect is greater, at least probably. And just as there are few congruent <note>fitting together perfectly, like tiles on a floor</note> figures, so also there are few Aspects, as experience testifies: for unless they were few, there would be great confusion among them and a great frequency; so that individuals could not be observed separately on their own days: but they can be observed, therefore they are not infinite in number. On the contrary, consonances can be infinite through the increasing of intervals by the Diapason <term>the octave; Kepler notes that music can theoretically stack octaves forever, whereas geometry is bound by the 360 degrees of a circle</term>: just as the number of knowable figures is infinite.

3. From the Essence of the Terms, in which the proportions on both sides consist. Motions, the affection of which is Sound, are considered in the state of BECOMING <note>original: "FIERI"</note>, and insofar as they occupy time; Radiations are more in a momentary state of BEING <note>original: "ESSE"</note>. For just as this body exists at this moment, so also at this moment there is some radiation: but of Motion, that which has passed no longer exists, and that which follows does not yet exist; in the moment, there is nothing. Truly, congruence seems rather to belong to those things which ARE, than those which ARE BECOMING: for the sides or walls of a house fit together <note>congruunt</note> so that there is a house; not so that it might finally and perpetually be built.

For the efficacy of configurations, the Congruence of figures is more powerful than Knowability.

## Proposition V.

**Congruence** is more a property of a **Circumferential** figure than a **Central** one.
   *For it holds a more important place in that figure which can become whole, by reason of the place from which it takes its name; because congruence belongs to whole figures, as is clear from Book II. But of a Central figure, no more than one angle can stand at the center, according to Definition 1. However, in the circumference, the whole can be Circumferential: therefore.*

## Proposition VI.

Of the two figures which each Aspect claims for itself, the **Circumferential** is more powerful than the **Central**.

<header>ON CONFIGURATIONS</header>

<margin>CHAPTER V.</margin>In turn, the point has a region around itself for the drawing of a circle; thus in the **Soul** also, there is no operation without an **image-forming impression** <note>original: "impressione imaginatitâ"; the process by which the soul forms internal mental images of external things</note>. Conversely, every internal reception or meditation exists for the sake of external motion; every interior faculty of the soul exists for the sake of those that are more exterior. What is the leading and supreme faculty of the Soul, called the **Mind**, if not the **Center**? What is the **Reasoning faculty**, if not the **Circle**? For just as the center is within and the circle is without, so the Mind remains within itself, while reasoning weaves a certain outer web. And just as the center is the basis of the circle, so the Mind is the basis, fount, and origin of reasonings. Again, every such faculty of the Soul—the **Intellect** as well as

<margin>Figure XI.</margin><image-desc>A geometric diagram consisting of a pentagram inscribed within a circle. Lines connect the five vertices to a central small circle. Various points are marked with asterisks or star symbols on the circumference and near the center.</image-desc> **Discourse** <note>the step-by-step process of logical reasoning</note>, and finally even the **Sensitive** faculty—acts as a certain **Center**; but the motive faculties of the Soul act as the **Circle**. This is because, just as the external circle is placed around the center, so operation is directed toward the outside, while cognition and meditation are perfected within. As the circle is to the point, so in a certain way is external **Action** to internal **Contemplation**, and animal motion to sensation. For the point, because it is opposite to the circumference on every side, is naturally suited for representing the **Patient** <note>the thing being acted upon</note>; and what else does the sensitive Soul (or here, the faculty perceptive of **Radiations**) do in sensing and perceiving, other than undergo an experience? That is, because it is moved by objects.

<margin>Figure XII.</margin><image-desc>A geometric diagram featuring a seven-pointed star-like figure (heptagram) or complex polygon inscribed within a circle. Neither, insofar as it is such, employs discourse within itself, but rather knows without it. Thus, this **sublunary Nature** <note>the "soul" of the Earth or the lower vital force that governs nature</note>, or even the sensitive nature, is a certain thin image of the leading **human Mind**. Just as that discourse of reason is an image of these actions or operations of the soul, so each is a circle.

Therefore, insofar as Souls perceive celestial radiations, and are thus moved within themselves by them, let them be **points** to us. But insofar as they in turn initiate motion—that is, insofar as they transfer the perceived harmonies of the radiations into their own works and are stimulated by them to act—they ought to be considered as a **circle**.

It follows, then, that in the degree to which the Soul knows the **Harmonies** of the rays, it is occupied chiefly with the **central figure**; but in the degree to which it operates, stirring up **meteors** <note>in the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and lightning</note> (and similar things in man), it accommodates itself to the **circumferential figure**. Indeed, in an **Aspect** <note>the geometric angle between two planets</note>, our first concern is for its efficacy <note>its power to produce an effect</note> rather than the manner in which it is perceived by the operating Soul. Therefore, the consideration of the circumferential figure is prior to, and more important than, the central figure.

<summary>Kepler uses the geometry of a circle to map the soul's functions, equating the Mind to a central point of perception and Reasoning/Action to the surrounding circumference. He concludes that the Earth's "sublunary nature" perceives planetary aspects like a soul, and we should judge these aspects by their external effects (weather and human action) rather than just their internal perception.</summary>

*In this section, the shape of a figure was compared within one and the same aspect; in the following twin comparison, assuming the same figure, its **Congruity** <note>original: "Congruitas"; the ability of shapes to fit together without gaps, like floor tiles</note> will be contrasted with its **Knowability** <note>original: "Scibilitas"; the degree to which a side can be mathematically defined or expressed in relation to the diameter of a circle</note>,*
<margin>CHAPTER V.</margin>

# Proposition VII.

**In a figure defined by its circumference, Congruity takes precedence over the Knowability of the side; conversely, in a figure defined by its center, the Knowability of the side takes precedence over the Congruity of the figure.**

*This proposition pertains to the completion of the matter begun in Proposition III. For although Congruity is more powerful in Book IV than in Book III, and demonstrability <note>the ability to prove a mathematical truth</note> was more important in Book III, this quality is nevertheless not entirely separated from the formation of the Aspects <note>the specific angles between planets, such as a square or trine</note>. Indeed, no Congruity lacks a scientific determination, and thus it depends upon it—both regarding the side and especially the area enclosed by the figure’s sides. For the demonstration is drawn from the angles, in which the aptitude for fitting together resides.*

*Regarding this specific proposition, it seems that its opposite might be true in both cases. For as far as a central figure is concerned, one of its angles is expressed by the rays themselves in actual fact. In a circumferential figure, no angle is expressed, but only a side, to a certain extent. Since Congruity is a matter of angles, it seems it should be looked for primarily in the central figure. For if sublunary nature <note>the soul of the Earth or the life-force residing below the moon, which Kepler believed responded to celestial geometry</note> perceives the size of the angle that the rays of two planets form at the Earth, it also seems able to perceive the aptitude of that angle for fitting together with others.*

*Conversely, it seems clear that in a circumferential figure, the Knowability of the side should be looked for rather than the Congruity of the figure. For the knowledge by which a figure is known—as demonstrated in the first book—consists in equality: either of the side with an expressible <note>original: "effabili"; a rational part of the diameter that can be named or measured</note> part of the diameter; or of the square of the side with an expressible part of the square of the diameter; or of the area of the figure with the same; or in some other connection and determination of either the side, its square, or its area, to the diameter or its square. Therefore, if we assume that sublunary Nature has a sense of the Zodiac circle—that is, the sensible circle standing outside, which it examines according to the idea of the abstract, intellectual circle that it has within itself, either innate or created with it—then it surely follows that by the order of nature, it first senses how great an arc of the Zodiac is marked off by two planets. It also senses how great a straight line is stretched under that arc <note>a chord</note>, and of what quality it is: whether it is expressible in length, or only in the power of its square; or whether it makes an expressible sum of squares and an expressible rectangle with some other part—the property upon which the Expressibility of the area is founded. These things, I say, seem to become known to sublunary Nature first by the order of nature, because the side exists before the figure which is described by the multiplication of the side. Only afterwards, when the whole figure has been described in the Zodiac circle, do its angles become apparent, along with their size, whether they are of the kind that fit together, whether the figure meets at all angles for that same type of congruity, and whether that congruity can be continued. In short, congruity is a property of angles, and knowability is a property of sides. Therefore, where the angle of a figure becomes known before the side, the roles of Congruity seem prior and more powerful than those of Knowability; where it becomes known later, they are secondary. But in a figure pertaining to the center, the angle becomes known first; whereas in a figure described on the surface (formed, for instance, by only two planets), the side becomes known first. Therefore, it seems right if, in a central figure, a greater account is held of Congruity, and in a superficial one, a greater account of Knowability.*

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s investigation into the hierarchy of geometric properties. Having proposed in the previous page that "Knowability" (the constructability of a shape) and "Congruity" (the ability of shapes to fit together) take different precedence depending on whether a figure is viewed from the center of the circle or the circumference, he now begins to dismantle counter-arguments to strengthen his own theory.</meta>

<header>ON CONFIGURATIONS</header>

<margin>CHAPTER V.</margin>
Therefore, these objections brought against our proposition must be dissolved by us; and by the same effort, the order of properties—**Congruity** <note>original: "Congruentia"; the property of regular polygons to fit together perfectly around a point without gaps</note> and **Knowability** <note>original: "Scibilitas"; the degree to which a geometric side can be defined or measured against the diameter</note>—must be strengthened with true arguments.

First, although it is true that in a **central figure** <term>central figure; an astrological aspect where the vertex of the angle is the Earth at the center of the universe</term> a single angle is formed by the rays of two planets, it does not follow that the mind perceiving the size of the angle perceives, by its nature and in prior order, the Congruity of the figure to which that angle will belong. The reason is clear: because Congruity—insofar as it belongs to a single angle and several of its equals meeting in one plane—is too general. For there are infinite forms of angles that "fit" in this way; they are always greater in number as the individual angles are smaller. This is not, therefore, that Congruity about which we disputed in Book II, which does not happen to angles in isolation, but to whole figures because of their angles, nor to single figures, but to several joined together.

Thus, the objection is not only dissolved but even turned back: for what that objection had claimed for the **circumferential figure** <term>circumferential figure; a geometric shape where the vertices lie on the circle's edge, such as the zodiac</term>, we can by equal right claim for the central figure. Namely, that the Congruity proposed here is posterior to Knowability; therefore, the parts of the latter ought to be more powerful than those of the former, by the opponent’s own admission. For a figure must first be made before it can "fit" as a whole. Now, unless the side of the figure is "knowable," the figure cannot be made. For even if it were true that given one angle of a figure (formed by the rays of two planets at the center), the number of all angles is given, and through them, the aptitude of the whole figure for fitting together—and that the nature of the side does not enter into this demonstration—nevertheless, that one angle of the figure is not "given," that is, it is not recognized as the angle of a congruous figure, except through a knowable side. Therefore, in the order of nature, the **Soul** <note>Kepler believed the Soul possessed an innate geometric instinct that allowed it to recognize cosmic harmonies</note> knows the side before it recognizes that a congruous angle is given to it.

<margin>Fol. 136. Figure IV. Figure III.</margin>
But if we compare both types of figures here, the side or area of a central figure is actually "given" less by the act of radiation itself than the side of a circumferential figure. For the rays themselves always determine the latter; they do not always determine the former, but only in certain figures, such as in the **Trine** <note>original: "Trigono"; a 120-degree aspect forming an equilateral triangle</note>, because the individual sides of the circumferential angle subtend an arc equal to the intercepted arc. Therefore, the central figure is remoter from the act of knowing than the circumferential one; thus, the notification of Congruity is also remoter. Yet the objection relied on the opposite, as if central Congruity were a more immediate form of knowledge than circumferential Congruity.

Furthermore, if the size of an angle is perceived, by what means shall it be perceived except by its measure? That is, by the arc of that circle which is described from the point of the proposed angle, which is the Earth. It is not perceived primarily by the arc of that circle which circumscribes the central figure and passes through the Earth. Wherefore, in perceiving the size of an angle in a central figure, the Soul must exert that power by which it is a circle, not that by which it is a tiny point reached by the angle. And yet, by that same pattern of its circular essence, it also perceives the side of the circumferential figure and its arc, and does so first. Only afterwards, by doubling this arc, does the arc of the smaller circle emerge, which circumscribes the central figure and is drawn through the center of the first; this arc serves the inscription of the central figure into a circle. For the order that exists in reasoning is the same as that in instinct. Thus, it is demonstrated again that the path to the perception of the central figure is longer, and likewise for its Congruity. Therefore, the objection—which placed the greater power in the prior perception—overturns itself.

To the reasons for the other side, we must respond thus: it is indeed true even in a circumferential figure that the Knowability of the side is prior to the Congruity of the whole figure, due to the stated arguments which also apply here. But it does not follow that from two things...

<summary>Kepler argues that "Knowability" (mathematical definition) must precede "Congruity" (the fitting of shapes) in the soul's perception of planetary aspects, refuting objections by showing that central figures are more cognitively distant than circumferential ones.</summary>

Having established that the soul perceives the relationships between planets through geometric figures, he is now weighing two specific properties: "Knowability" (the ability to construct a shape with a compass and straightedge) and "Congruity" (the ability of a shape to tile a plane without gaps). He argues that while "Knowability" matters for how the soul perceives an angle at the center of the Earth, "Congruity" is more important for how the soul translates those perceptions into physical action.</meta>

<header>ON THE HARMONICS, BOOK IV.</header>

...of these things, where one is the cause of the other, that which is the cause also moves a third thing even more strongly. *For according to the capacity of the Soul which must be moved, the cause often has less power over it than the effect: just as here, the **Sublunary Soul** <note>The "anima sublunaris" or world-soul of the Earth, which Kepler believed was a living entity that responded to planetary harmonies</note>, insofar as it is perceptive, is moved more by the **knowability** <note>original: "scibilitas"; the degree to which a geometric side can be defined or measured against the diameter</note> of the central figure; yet insofar as it is operative [active], it is moved more by the **congruity** <note>original: "congruentia"; the property of regular polygons to fit together perfectly around a point without gaps</note> of the circumferential figure.*

<margin>See Proposition VI above.</margin>
*Indeed, my own arguments for proving this proposition are these: for we have used the principle that the center is a certain idea of the Theoretical mind, or the intellect; whereas the circumference is an idea of the Practical or operative faculty. For just as the center of a circle is the base and origin, so is meditation the base of action. Therefore, a figure which extends its angle to the center (that is, to the Earth, where the Soul resides)—this perceptive figure—extends itself as if for the purpose of knowing and judging, since the center represents the tribunal of knowledge. Thus, in a central figure, knowledge should rather be observed; notwithstanding that it appears through the circle as an instrument, as was said a little earlier.*

*On the other hand, a figure which arranges its angles on the circumference applies itself more to imitating and expressing things in the work of the Soul, as if concurring with the "Idea" of works. Now, congruity rather than knowability possesses the "Idea" of sensible works and constructions, because congruity follows whole figures, whereas the side—by which a figure is "known"—is merely its element. For this reason, in a circumferential figure, one must look to congruity rather than knowability.*

*Another argument for this second part rests on the same consideration of the Soul. That which exists for the sake of other things is superior. But for the sake of the work of Sublunary Nature—and thus also of the human soul and its lower faculties—the configurations [of the planets] are perceived; that is, they are perceived so that they may be expressed through work. Therefore, the dignity of the **motor faculty** <term>motor faculty; the power of the soul that produces physical movement or biological changes</term> is greater in this business. But the knowability of the Circumferential figure serves perception, while Congruity serves operation, as stated hitherto: therefore, the congruity of the circumferential figure also excels its own knowability.*

## Proposition VIII.

The arc of a circle which is constituted by an **incongruous** figure grants no **Efficacy** to the radiations of the two planets determining that arc.

*For if congruity is the most powerful cause of Efficacy <note>The "Efficacy" refers to the astrological power of an aspect to influence the Earthly realm</note>, according to Propositions III, IV, and VII, then if this is lacking, the "meaner" cause—knowability—will not be sufficient in this place. For even if knowability prevails over congruity in the Central figure (by the other part of Prop. VII), conversely, the circumferential figure is more powerful than the central one (by Prop. VI). And in the circumferential figure, congruity is more powerful (by the first part of Prop. VII). Thus, the congruity of the circumferential figure still prevails over the knowability of the central figure.*

*Observe the cause why, though knowable figures are infinite (and of various degrees), the "Aspects" [in astrology] are nevertheless few.*

## Axiom III.

Arcs of a circle whose figures possess more and more powerful degrees of congruity and knowability also receive more effective configurations.

If the first two axioms are in agreement with the truth, this one will be as well: because of that by which each thing is such, when that thing is intensified, it will be even more such. Understand it this way: that in a circumferential figure <note>A geometric figure defined by its perimeter or the way it fits with other shapes, related to practical action</note>, the comparison of the degrees of **Congruity** <note>original: "congruentia"; the property of shapes to tile a plane without gaps</note> is prior; in a central figure, the degrees of **Knowability** <note>original: "scibilitas"; the capacity for a shape to be constructed and understood by the mind</note> are prior; and finally, the parts of the circumferential figure are more powerful.

## Proposition IX.

The effective configurations <note>Astrological aspects or angles between planets</note> are those which intercept these arcs of the Zodiac circle:
180 Degrees. **Opposition** ☍, from the Diameter of the circle: as in Figure I.
90 Degrees. **Square** □, from the Tetragon <note>A four-sided polygon</note>: as in Figure II.
120 Degrees. **Trine** △, and 60. **Sextile** ✳, from the Triangle and Hexagon, as in Figures III and IV.
45 Degrees. **Octile** <note>Also known as a semi-square</note> or **Sesquadrate**, and 135. **Trioctile** or **Sesquadrate** <unclear>⚼</unclear> from the Octagon and its star-shape: as in Figures V and VI.
30 Degrees. **Semi-sextile** ✳, and 150. **Quincunx**, from the Dodecagon <note>A twelve-sided polygon</note> and its star-shape: as in Figures VII and VIII.
72 Degrees. **Quintile** <unclear>☩</unclear>, and 108. **Tridecile** or **Sesquiquintile**: from the Pentagon and the Decagon-star: as in Figures IX and X.
144 Degrees. **Biquintile** <unclear>⚝</unclear>, and 36. **Semi-quintile** or **Decile**: from the Pentagonal star and the Decagon, as in Figures XI and XII.

*That these figures are **Knowable** and demonstrable was shown in Book I; that they are also **Congruent** was shown in Book II. That the configurations of the arcs expressed by such shapes are indeed effective is held by the two preceding axioms.*

## Proposition X.

The first and strongest degree of effectiveness among the Aspects is that of **Conjunction** ☌ and **Opposition** ☍.

For in a Conjunction, two rays coincide into the same line and descend from the same region; in an Opposition ☍, although they descend from different regions, they nevertheless become parts of a single continuous line. This is indeed the most perfect **Congruity** and a kind of principle of all congruity. Thus, while a marked point on the circumference of a circle represents a conjunction, the Diameter represents an opposition; these are certainly the principles, and that [diameter] is the measure of all knowledge in this branch of science. For all knowledge of a straight line within a circle is contained by a demonstrative determination through either the length or the power <note>original: "potentiam"; likely referring to the square of the line's length, common in Euclidean geometry</note> of the Diameter: *as shown in Book I.*

## Proposition XI.

The second degree in the Efficacy of Aspects is that of the **Square** □.

In the Square, many privileges meet. The first is that the central figure <note>The shape formed at the center of the soul’s perception</note> is similar to the circumferential figure <note>The shape inscribed within the circle of the Zodiac</note>. Therefore, whatever degrees of **Congruity** <note>The ability of a shape to tile a plane or form a solid</note> and **Knowability** <note>The mathematical capacity for a shape to be constructed and understood</note> it possesses, they are understood to be somehow doubled in comparison to the other Aspects. For just as the Square is the first aspect after the Opposition to unfold from the thinness of a line into a certain width or superficial extent of a tetragonal <note>four-sided</note> area, so the other Aspects depart from the "sameness" of the Square's figures into some degree of "otherness" or diversity of shape. Since, therefore, in physics a united power is generally stronger, there will also be a greater degree of strength in this ideal and objective impression where the figures in distinct places—namely, the central and the circumferential—are of the same species.

<margin>
$\Delta$
</margin>

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a circle with a large square inscribed within it. Inside this large square, there is a smaller central square oriented at a 45-degree angle relative to the outer square. Lines extend from the center to the vertices and sides of the squares, with various points marked by lines and small symbols like a star and a vertical dash.</image-desc>

<margin>
□
</margin>

Secondly, regarding **Congruity**, it is most perfect and all-encompassing in the Tetragon. For this figure fits with itself in three dimensions to form the cube—which is the measure of all solidity—and it fits most simply, with only three angles joined at a corner. It also fits with itself in a plane, with four angles meeting. Furthermore, it fits in three dimensions with the Triangle, Pentagon, Hexagon, Octagon, and Decagon <note>10-sided figure</note> in various ways to form solid figures <note>the Platonic and Archimedean solids</note>. It also fits with all of these, and additionally with the Dodecagon <note>12-sided</note> and Icosagon <note>20-sided</note> to some extent, in paving a flat surface. In this property of fitting together, the square is surpassed by no other shape.

Thirdly, the area of the Tetragon is *effable* <note>original: "effabilis"; meaning the area can be expressed as a rational ratio</note>, which is a principle of a unique and excellent Congruity in the plane. This means that a certain number of this figure's areas equals a certain number of the squares of the circle's diameter; thus, the figures do not only fit together by their angles and sides, but also, through certain lines, they fit with the squares of the diameter. In this property, the Square aspect has only the Semi-sextile as a partial partner. See Book II.

Fourthly, the degree of knowledge of its side is not insignificant, as it is *expressible in power* <note>original: "effabile potentiâ"; meaning its square is a rational number relative to the circle</note>. In this degree, it excels all other figures except the Hexagon. Yet it does not yield its place to the Hexagon for that reason, since Knowability is not to be compared to Congruity, as explained above; and indeed, the accumulation of privileges serves to increase Efficacy, according to Axiom III of this book.

The third Degree of Efficacy is that of the **Trine** $\Delta$, the **Sextile** $*$, and the **Semi-sextile** ⚺.

*So also the Triangle excels the Hexagon again in that the Triangular species fits with itself in a solid in various ways, and generates three regular bodies <note>The Tetrahedron, Octahedron, and Icosahedron</note>: the Hexagon only fits with other figures. Thus, having weighed the relative importance of these diverse properties, **Congruity**—which is the first and foremost element of efficacy—is brought almost to an equilibrium among these three. In **knowability** <note>original: "scibilitate," the ease with which a shape can be constructed using only a compass and straightedge</note>, the **Sexangle** <note>Hexagon</note> holds first place, as its side is expressible; the Triangle holds second, for it occupies the same rank as the Tetragon <note>Square</note>, having a side that is expressible in power <note>Meaning the square of the side is a rational number</note>, though in a lesser proportion. Last here is the Dodecagon, which has an inexpressible side. However, knowability is neither the primary argument for Efficacy, nor is it considered in the primary figure—that is, the circular one;*

*rather, it is considered only in the less primary central figure. If this has any power, it makes the **Trine** <note>120° aspect</note> slightly more effective than the **Sextile** <note>60° aspect</note>, because the Trine forms the angle of a Hexagon at the center; and it makes the **Semisextile** <note>30° aspect</note>, which is measured by the angle of a Dodecagon-star at the center, slightly less effective than both. Nevertheless, the knowledge of the Semisextile is nobler than the others that follow it, because the side of its central figure is of the most noble species among the **Inexpressibles**, namely the **Binomial** <note>A line composed of two parts that are mathematically "incommensurable" or cannot be measured by the same unit</note>; and in their twofold subdivision, it always holds the higher rank. This is so much the case that, together with its partner (the side of the circumferential figure), it forms an expressible rectangle, which is a mark of almost absolute perfection. Thus, this figure even contends with the Triangle and Hexagon in knowability, because this compensation for its inexpressibility carries a great deal of weight.*

## Proposition XLIII.

The Fourth Degree in the Efficacy of Configurations consists of the **Quintile**, **Biquintile**, and **Quincunx**. <note>The Quintile is 72° (1/5 of a circle); the Biquintile is 144° (2/5); the Quincunx here likely refers to the 150° aspect (5/12).</note>

For these have in common the tiling <note>original: "congruentia"; refers to the ability of shapes to fit together to fill a flat surface without gaps</note> of the primary figures as wholes in a plane, yet not of each individual species with itself; rather, the first two <note>The Pentagon and Pentagram</note> tile with each other, and the last <note>The twelve-pointed star</note> with others related to it. The first two aspects excel because their figures—the **Pentagon** and its **star**—also tile in three dimensions <note>original: "in solido"</note>, and they form two regular solid figures <note>Kepler is referring to the "Kepler-Poinsot" solids he discovered: the small stellated dodecahedron and the great stellated dodecahedron</note>; by this nobility, they almost associate their aspects with the **Trine** <note>120°</note> and the **Square** <note>90°</note>; whereas the **Dodecagonal star** does not tile in three dimensions. But in turn, the Dodecagonal star excels in plane tiling, which it can continue to infinity; while those others <note>the Pentagon shapes</note> cannot be continued far without an irregular mixture <note>Kepler notes that you cannot tile a flat floor using only pentagons; they require other shapes or they create gaps</note>. See all of this in Book II.

Regarding the **knowability** <note>original: "scibilitatem"; refers to how the side of the shape can be mathematically expressed or constructed using a compass and straightedge</note> of the sides in central figures: here also the sides of the **Decagon**, the **Tredecile**, and the **Dodecagon** <note>original: "Decagoni & Tridecilis & Dodecagoni". In Kepler’s system, the Tredecile is 108° (3/10) and the Decile is 36° (1/10)</note> hold a middle position. In this class, they are central between the side of the preceding **Triangle** and the sides of the **Pentagon** and the **Pentagonal star**, which are central figures in the following class. For in Book I, it was demonstrated that the side of the Decagon is prior in knowledge to that of the Pentagon, and the side of the **Tredecile** prior to that of the **Pentagonal star**. Therefore, Knowability leads to the same conclusion as Tiling, according to Proposition VII: which had to be put forward primarily for the sake of this demonstration, lest the **Decile** or Tredecile be preferred over the **Quintile** and **Biquintile**. If, however, anyone should wish to seek Knowability in the circumference rather than in the central figure—no less than Tiling—even if it must be admitted that in this way the Decile would be preferred to the Quintile, and the Tredecile to the Biquintile; yet let him remember that the principal roles belong to Tiling, as...

*As we have shown in Proposition IV, it is therefore a greater thing, and contributes more to efficacy, to create a solid figure (which is like a certain mathematical "Idea" of physical efficacy) than to have a side that is "knowable" <note>original: "scibile"; in geometry, this refers to a length that can be precisely constructed or expressed as a ratio</note> at a more perfect degree. Indeed, the side of the Dodecagon <note>a 12-sided polygon</note> brings its aspect into the same class as the lines spanning a tenth part of the circle, and three-tenths: because they compete with each other in the excellence of their knowability. For just as those two spanning lines are associated with each other—the smaller being a part of the larger—in the Divine Proportion <note>The Golden Ratio (section according to extremes and mean)</note>: so too the side of the Dodecagon and the side of its star are associated, and this also in respect to a certain section and composition, though not a proportional one. And indeed, this latter pair falls into the first species of "Ineffables" <note>original: "Ineffabilium"; irrational numbers as defined in Euclid's Book X</note>, which includes Binomials and Apotomes; yet, in turn, that former pair acquires a new property of the section according to extremes and mean, as can be seen in Book I. Therefore, not only are these degrees weighed against each other, but the side of the Decagon <note>10-sided polygon</note> actually excels slightly. It was therefore rightly done that I placed the **Quincunx** aspect (150°) in the same degree as the **Quintile** (72°) and **Biquintile** (144°), though the first rank among them was given to these latter two.*

### Proposition XIV.

**The fifth, last, and weakest degree of aspects consists of the Decile, Tridecile, Octile, and Trioctile.** <note>Decile = 36° (1/10 circle); Tridecile = 108° (3/10); Octile = 45° (1/8); Trioctile = 135° (3/8)</note>

*I have assigned the fifth place to the Decile and Tridecile (Maestlin <note>Michael Maestlin, Kepler's teacher</note> calls them the Semiquintile and Sesquiquintile), which I have hitherto omitted in my Ephemerides <note>astronomical tables</note>. With these I have associated the Octile and Trioctile (or Sesquadrate), which calendar-makers—at my own suggestion and with some authority from Ptolemy—have seized upon too hotly and thoughtlessly. Both must therefore be tested: first, that these four are weaker than the Quintile and Biquintile; and second, that the Decile and Tridecile are only slightly stronger than the Octile and Trioctile.*

*I have examined all these possibilities so that I might establish the truth with suitable arguments, lest the number of aspects <note>astrological "aspects" are specific angles between planets that were believed to influence the Earth</note> become too numerous and produce confusion in practical observation. Therefore, one must stop at the Square <note>90°</note>, the Quintile <note>72°</note>, and the Biquintile <note>144°</note>, and not proceed to the four derived from them of the lowest rank, however weak they may be, even though the first proposition might admit them. ### Proposition XV.

There are some configurations that are ambiguous, wavering between being effective and non-effective: namely the Arc of 24 degrees from the Fifteen-sided polygon <note>original: *Pentekædecagono*</note>, and the Arc of 18 degrees from the Twenty-sided polygon <note>original: *Icosigono*</note>.

*For these figures are "knowable" <term>scibiles; in geometry, this means they can be constructed using only a straightedge and compass</term>, but the former is so in an improper sense, and the latter at a remote degree, as demonstrated in Book I. They are also congruent <note>capable of tiling a surface without gaps</note>, but the former does not fit with all its angles equally in the same form of congruence. The latter fits with all its angles, but in a tiling that clearly cannot be continued indefinitely, as shown in Book II. Therefore, there is a certain rudiment of efficacy, a kind of striving <note>original: *conatus*</note>; but the effect is either non-existent or imperfect.*

These figures contain many stars: the former has five, whose sides subtend these arcs of the circle: 48°, 96°, 112°, 156°, and 168°. The latter has four, whose sides subtend arcs of 54°, 126°, 162°, and 171°. But since these stars have "hollow" angles <note>re-entrant or concave angles</note> into which other congruent angles are not received—just as the hollow angles of the Pentagonal and Decagonal figures receive Pentagonal angles, or the Octagonal receives the Square, and the Dodecagonal <note>12-sided</note> receives the Triangle <note>Trine</note>—there remains for them only the congruence of the sharp points, which we call Rays. They are, therefore, more base <note>original: *viliores*</note> than their own primary figures.

# BOOK IV OF THE HARMONICS

<margin>CHAPTER V.</margin>...fictions, truly astrological vanities; but even the philosophical arguments of Count Giovanni Pico della Mirandola <note>original: "Joh. Pici Mirandulae"; Pico (1463–1494) was a famous Italian Renaissance philosopher who wrote a massive critique of astrology</note> opposed to this part of astrology have been, in my opinion, solidly dissolved—at least those parts which needed to be dissolved and refuted. And when, nine years ago, Helisaeus Röslin <note>A physician and astrologer who disagreed with Kepler's rejection of traditional methods</note>—a Doctor of Medicine and a philosopher of no small renown—published a book in the German language attacking this new philosophy because he was himself devoted to the old astrology; and likewise another physician, Philipp Feselius, from the opposite side, attacked almost every chapter of astrology indiscriminately, including the doctrine of configurations <note>planetary aspects</note>; I resisted them both by publishing two small books in German. One was titled *Response to Röslin's Objections*; the other, *The Third Intervener* <note>original: "Tertius interveniens"; Kepler famously positioned himself as a "third man" between the superstitious astrologer and the total skeptic</note>. In the latter, I defended the truth of the Aspects, while in the former, I asserted the manner of the cause by which the Aspects are effective. Thus, learned men have testified in letters written to me that, finally, astrologers are being taught a purer philosophy by me.

In all these pamphlets, I mentioned the knowledge that links musical consonances with the Aspects. However, in the first one, I still hesitated regarding the number of Aspects, observing some as "spurious" or certainly weak among the principal ones, while entirely neglecting others that were stronger. But in the German works, I began to uncover these defects in my speculation; I decided that this must be repeated with a slightly fuller declaration, as the situation demands, recently in the *Prolegomena* to the *Ephemerides* <note>Kepler's published tables of predicted planetary positions</note>, pages 33, 34, 35, and 36. Those things which could not be explained more fully there due to the intended brevity, I shall now supply here, as the order of this work requires.

The Axiom which I used in the year 1606, and which I took up for examination and refutation in the cited place of the *Ephemerides*, was this: *That God the Creator either took the laws for ordering the Aspects from the Harmonies of Song within the Octave <note>original: "infra Octavam"</note>, described in Book III; or, He tempered the ears of man, the judges of those Concordances, to the celestial Aspects.* If this Axiom were true in every respect, there would have to be exactly as many Aspects as there are Concordances up to the Octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note>. 

For the mapping is as follows:
*   The **Sextile** <note>60°</note> corresponds to the **Minor Third** <note>ratio 5:6</note>.
*   The **Quintile** <note>72°</note> corresponds to the **Major Third** <note>ratio 4:5</note>.
*   The **Square** <note>90°</note> corresponds to the **Fourth** <note>original: "Diatessaron"; ratio 3:4</note>.
*   The **Trine** <note>120°</note> corresponds to the **Fifth** <note>original: "Diapente"; ratio 2:3</note>.
*   The **Sesquiquadrate** <note>135°; original: "Sesquadrus"</note> corresponds to the **Minor Sixth** <note>ratio 5:8</note>.
*   The **Biquintile** <note>144°</note> corresponds to the **Major Sixth** <note>ratio 3:5</note>.
*   The **Opposition** <note>180°</note> corresponds to the **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason"; ratio 1:2</note>.

This is because if you take away from the whole string <note>on a monochord</note> a portion equal to the portion of the circle that any aspect takes away, the remainder of the string forms with the whole that Consonance which is ascribed here to each Aspect. Since, therefore, this Seven-fold number of Concordances—or rather of harmonic Sections, which each Concordance follows below the Octave—is certain and demonstrative (no less than the five-fold number of Regular Solids in Geometry, as was shown in Book III, Chapter II), the method for demonstrating the number of Aspects would be easy and ready through this accepted Axiom. Nor would there have been any need for that laborious apparatus of new Axioms in Book IV.

And truly, if meteorological observations <note>the study of weather patterns as influenced by planets</note> had fully supported this seven-fold set of Aspects, I would have rested content with the axiom stated above; I would not have been very anxious about the objections that could be raised from the origin of Harmonic ratios or from the consideration of metaphysical causes. But because it has been frequently discovered that sublunary Nature <note>The Earthly realm</note> is also stimulated by the **Semisextile** <note>30°</note>, which intercepts a twelfth part of the circle, even though—when a twelfth portion is taken away from the string—the remainder, consisting of eleven... <note>original: "undecim..."</note>

And because the stimulations of weather <note>original: "Tempestatum"</note> through the Sesquadrum <term>Sesquadrum</term><note>A 135-degree aspect, representing three-eighths of a circle</note>—which marks off three-eighths of the circle—have been found to be unreliable, even though the remainder of five-eighths is entirely consonant with the whole eight when three-eighths are taken away from a string, I was forced by necessity to search more deeply for the causes of this disagreement and diversity in this Fourth Book. *The cause, therefore, why there are not as many Aspects as there are Harmonic sections in Music—as I had believed up until the year 1608—is this: because Music draws some of its principles of the number seven from the very straightness of the string; while the circle, in which we mark the Aspects, returns into itself, nor can another circle be made from the Remainder of the Zodiac, as can be done from a string.* These are the words of the aforementioned Prolegomena <note>Introductory remarks</note> on page 35, which are to be explained thus: for as was said in Chapter IV of this book, Harmonic sections arise in one way, and Aspects in another, even though both arise from the same circle. For in Book III, the Axioms were so arranged that any string and part of a string, whether long or short, could again be compared to the whole circle, just as the whole or longest string was compared to that same circle. But in this Fourth Book, an arc of a circle, whether larger or smaller than a semicircle, could not be compared to the whole. I will speak more clearly: in whatever ways a circle is divided demonstratively <note>proven by geometric construction</note>, all those ways can be transferred to a straight line—that is, a string—and any part of it. But it is not the case that a demonstrative division of the whole circle (for instance, into three or five parts) can therefore also be transferred into any of its arcs; this was sufficiently demonstrated in the final propositions of the first book. The cause lies in the shape; for a straight line remains straight whether it is cut short or lengthened, but a truncated circle does not remain a circle. Thus, a proportional section is possible for any two straight lines, and for any two circles, but it is not possible for any two arcs of a single circle. These points are applied to the proposal as follows: If a string is divided into eight parts by the demonstrative division of a circle, one-eighth is consonant with the whole, and three-eighths are also consonant, because one-eighth of a circle can be geometrically cut off, as can three-eighths. The same demonstrative determination is also among the reasons why the Octile <note>45 degrees</note> and the Trioctile <note>135 degrees</note> are effective. But here is the difference: in that case, a harmonic <term>SECTION</term> <note>A division of a string that produces a musical interval</note> is not yet established unless the Remainder—seven-eighths and five-eighths—also harmonizes both with the whole of eight parts, and with the parts cut off (seven with one, and five with three). Yet, the demonstrative determination of part 1 and part 3 does not grant their remainders, 7 and 5, the quality of being consonant themselves; for 5 is indeed consonant, but 7 is dissonant. Therefore, the section of the whole 8 into 5 and 3 is harmonic, but in 7 and 1 it is not harmonic. From where, then, does the Remainder of 5 get its consonance with the whole 8, and the Remainder 7 its dissonance from it? Surely from this: because a circle divided into 5 has a side subtending two-fifths <note>a chord connecting two points of a pentagon</note> that is demonstrative; hence it is that a string divided into five (as in this proposed part of string 8) is consonant with the part that is 2 portions long; wherefore also with...

4 and 8, which are in a continuous double proportion with 2. In contrast, a circle divided into 7 parts does not produce a line <term>chorda</term><note>original: "chordam"; here referring to a musical string or a geometric chord</note> that demonstrably shows a one-seventh portion; therefore, that Remainder of the string which has 7 is dissonant from 1, and likewise from 2, 4, and 8. Behold how the harmonic section of the whole 8 into 3 and 5 has only one consonance derived from the Octagon, while the other is from the Pentagon. Indeed, it even has a third consonance from another figure, namely the Decagon. For Part 3 would not harmonize with the Remainder 5, unless it first harmonized with its double, 10; and this is because, in a circle divided into 10, the line subtended by three-tenths is "knowable" <term>demonstrativa</term><note>Meaning it can be constructed using a compass and straightedge</note>. This coupling of multiple figures, however, has no place in the circle and its parts. For if you first inscribed a regular Octagon in the whole circle, and assuming you could divide the arc that contains three-eighths into five (though it is impossible to do so demonstrably), certainly a Pentagon could not be inscribed according to the divisions made; for it would become highly irregular, and more like a hexagon, since the arc has two endpoints before its division. Since, therefore, there is a vast difference between the Remainders of the string on one hand and the circle on the other, it is clear that unless we proceed from the circle even to the straight line, no account of the Remainder can be taken. But an Aspect is an angle, the measure of which is not any straight line, but an arc of a circle described from the point where the rays meet: therefore, the circle does not measure the Aspect, nor does it form it or make it effective by reason of the Remainder, but only by reason of the arc intercepted by the aspect. If it is not by reason of the Remainder, it is therefore not by reason of the harmonic section of the string arising from that division of the circle—because a harmonic section cannot be defined without a Remainder. And thus that axiom is destroyed: that the harmonic proportions of song are the causes of the Aspects. Nor does it follow that because the Trioctile or Sesquadrate <term>Sesquadrus</term><note>A 135-degree aspect</note> corresponds to the harmonic section which produces the minor third and is effective, its effectiveness therefore comes from the harmonic section of the circle as such. But it is true, as the Introduction <note>original: "Prolegomena"</note> states, that *a great kinship exists between Harmonies and Aspects*, both types having the same origin,

I speak, however, on the hypothesis that the mere knowability of a figure suffices for effectiveness, just as it suffices for the simple Consonance of a Part with the Whole. What is it then that sets a limit on the number of Aspects? And why is no Semisquare (or <term>Octile</term>), no Decile or Tridecile introduced, except after the primary ones?
