It is because Music does not form the Aspect; rather, Geometry forms both types, though by different laws for the one and the other. For whatever comes from a "noble figure" (which possesses certain unique privileges in Geometry) is both <term>Harmonic</term> in Music and <term>effective</term> in weather patterns <term>Meteoris</term>. But Meteorology and Music are like different nations born from the same homeland, Geometry. One of these—that is, the Harmonic proportions in Book III—acknowledged the circle as its homeland and credited its origin to it, no less than these Aspects do. Nevertheless, the harmonies, having departed as if from the circle, led out their own colony and propagated themselves by living under their own laws. The Aspects, remaining within the circle of their homeland, use no other laws than those which the roundness of the circle prescribes for them, taken from the Regular <term>Congruent</term><note>Figures that can tile a surface around a point</note> plane figures inscribed in the circle.

For in Music, that "seven-member council" <term>septemviratus</term> of sections is constituted from certain "marriages," even including the "females." For example, the line subtending three-eighths [of a circle], or the Eight-pointed Star, is indeed among the citizens of Geometry and the class of regular figures, but it is not of the highest nobility. In Music, however, its arc (three-eighths of the circle) has found a place because it was born from a marriage in which a common woman named the <term>Remainder</term> (namely, three-quarters of the circle) was joined to a Patrician (namely, the fourth part of the circle). ...fourths) through musical generation (by the addition of one <term>Octave</term><note>original: *Diapason*</note>) there is born a Part, the three octaves; to which, with all due respect to its senatorial rank, it is now permitted to lead another plebeian part named the five octaves. The condition of its birth is the same; for its mother is also a Remainder—specifically, four-fifths—while the patrician father is a single fifth, whose geometric nobility arises from the <term>Pentangle</term><note>A five-sided figure; original: *Quinquangulo*</note>.

However, as for the twelfth part of the circle, although it holds the right of citizenship in Music—since its <term>chord</term><note>The straight line connecting two points on a circle; original: *subtensa*</note> possesses a primary nobility in Geometry, earned both by its own merit (on account of its <term>Congruence</term><note>Kepler’s theory of how shapes fit together to fill a space</note>) and inherited from its parents (for the <term>Hexagon</term> and <term>Triangle</term> are noble figures, and from the doubling of their sides the <term>Dodecagon</term> is formed, which is more excellent than they are because its area can be expressed in rational terms)—yet, because this twelfth part has a wife, the Remainder of eleven-twelfths, who is of foreign origin in Music as well as in Geometry (tracing her lineage to the <term>Hendecagon</term><note>An eleven-sided figure; original: *Undecangulum*</note>, a figure that cannot be demonstrated or constructed), she cannot obtain the right of citizenship. Therefore, the husband holds no right of the "council of seven" in Music to establish the number of divisions of the <term>monochord</term><note>A single-stringed instrument used to measure musical intervals</note>.

On the contrary, in <term>Meteorology</term><note>The study of how planetary aspects affect the Earth’s atmosphere</note>, the custom is different. For just as each figure is noble in itself, whether by birth or by merit (namely, by its <term>Constructibility</term><note>original: *Scibilitate*</note> or Congruence), so it prevails greatly in authority; the rest flit about like shadows, and no account is taken of the "females" <note>Kepler’s metaphor for the "Remainders" or the unused parts of the circle</note>.

Thus here, the <term>Octile</term><note>An aspect of 45 degrees; 1/8th of a circle</note> or <term>Sesquiquadrate</term><note>An aspect of 135 degrees</note>, having set aside their rights in Music because they have ignoble chords, belong to the common people. They have no power except in the absence of the magistrates, when the weight of business is pressing. That is to say, if for a long time there were no primary <term>Aspects</term><note>Major planetary angles like the Square or Trine</note>, these minor Aspects might perhaps accomplish something, especially if the Earth is full of moisture, in which case she sometimes relieves herself without any stimulus from planetary configurations. But because the primary aspects are usually at hand, the <term>sublunary Nature</term><note>The "soul" of the Earth or its atmosphere</note>, exhausted by them, does not feel these lesser stimuli.

The <term>Decile</term><note>An aspect of 36 degrees; 1/10th of a circle</note> and <term>Tridecile</term><note>An aspect of 108 degrees</note> are indeed from an illustrious family—the ten-fold division of the circle which employs the <term>Divine Proportion</term><note>The Golden Ratio</note>—yet they have not made their lineage famous by their deeds (because they do not fit together perfectly in three-dimensional solids). Nor are they the heads of the family. And even if they have some power (being congruent to some extent in a plane, and even with others in a solid), all of that is snatched away from them by the aristocrats of other families; or rather, their glory is obscured by a greater splendor. For if Nature has been sufficiently exercised by an Aspect of 30 degrees, and the Earth sufficiently drained by it, very little is left for a neighboring, weaker aspect of 36 degrees to act upon.

Finally, for the <term>Semisextile</term><note>An aspect of 30 degrees; 1/12th of a circle</note> of 30 degrees, there is an exceeding nobility from the Dodecagon, which is remarkably both constructible and congruent. Nor does the "foreign marriage" <note>The 11/12ths remainder</note>, which had blocked its path to honors in Music, stand in its way at all in Meteorology. After this Dodecagon, the figures that follow—whether in the three secret families (the <term>Tetragonal</term>, <term>Trigonal</term>, and <term>Pentagonal</term>) or in the fifteen-fold mixture—besides the fact that they are all now of inferior nobility, also possess no distinct merits of their own regarding Congruence. Therefore, by the inviolable law of the state, they are barred from the honors and the power of establishing Aspects.

# ON CONFIGURATIONS #

<margin>
CHAPTER VI.
</margin>
From these things, it appears that what I stated in the *Introduction to the Ephemeris*<note>original: "Prolegomenis Ephemer:"</note> holds true: that in the establishment of <term>Aspects</term><note>The specific angular distances between planets—such as 60°, 90°, or 120°—that were believed to influence weather and human affairs.</note>, various causes are at work, and they often converge. **Nature** possesses a preference for those aspects equipped with more "prerogatives." For example, the **Semi-sextile**<note>An angle of 30°</note> shares certain rights with the **Square**<note>An angle of 90°</note>; specifically, the <term>Effability</term><note>original: "Effabilitatem"; the capacity for a figure's area to be expressed in rational terms relative to the whole circle.</note> of the area within the figure. It also shares certain rights with the **Sextile**<note>An angle of 60°</note>, namely a varied <term>Congruence</term><note>original: "congruentiam"; the way shapes fit together to perfectly fill a flat plane.</note> in a plane. When these strengths are combined, the semi-sextile becomes, in a certain way, more powerful than the sextile itself, insofar as the effability of the **Dodecagonal**<note>12-sided</note> area is superior to the effability of the **Hexagonal**<note>6-sided</note> side, because the former is followed by a more perfect congruence in the plane. And yet, in this Fourth Book, I have ordered the **Semi-sextile** to follow the **Sextile**, though placed on the same rank.

The **Trine**<note>An angle of 120°</note>, the **Square**, the **Quintile**<note>An angle of 72°</note>, and the **Biquintile**<note>An angle of 144°</note> are also made equal by the *Introduction to the Ephemeris* regarding the first and most powerful cause: that is, pure **Congruence** in a solid, which is required to form the Regular Solid figures<note>The five "Platonic Solids": the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron.</note>. I have said that the **Trine** and the **Square** add a second cause, which is not much lighter: namely, the pure **Congruence** of the figures in a plane. This is indeed also common to the **Sextile**; however, the sextile does not add this to the first cause, but possesses it separately. Just as the **Square** is held to add a third cause—namely, the **Effability** of the plane—not because the **Semi-sextile** does not also participate in it, but because those qualities which exist individually in the others are accumulated in the **Square**, so that it becomes the most powerful of all.

Thus, in weighing the votes in favor of the **sextile**, I said it shared a certain nobility with the **Opposition**<note>An angle of 180°</note>, hinting at the **Effability** of the side of the figure, because it is half the diameter of the circle. Again, it shares some nobility with the **Trine** and the **Square**, namely the pure **Congruence** in a plane mentioned before. Only a small portion of this—that is, the **Congruence** with figures of other species—belongs to the **Semi-sextile** and the other less noble aspects. In this particular category of **Congruence**, the first rank is held by the **Semi-sextile** and the **Octile**<note>An angle of 45°</note> figures. The star-form of the **Semi-sextile** could also be associated with this, because the congruence they begin can be continued without mixing different types of shapes. The **Quintile** and **Biquintile** hold the second rank, except that they have a nobler congruence in the solid. Likewise, the **Tri-octile**<note>135°</note>, **Decile**<note>36°</note>, and **Tri-decile**<note>108°</note> are in this rank because their figures continue by **Congruence**, but not without a mixture of different shapes; and all of these agree to some extent even in the solid, to a greater or lesser degree. The exception is the **Quincunx**<note>150°</note> star of the **Dodecagon**, which is therefore referred to the **Third** rank; the **Sesquadrate**<note>135°</note>, or the star of the Octagon, can also be joined to this, due to the obscurity of the science.

I have indeed extended these ranks even further, to the **Vigintile**<note>18°</note> and **Quindecile**<note>24°</note>—that is, to figures of fifteen and twenty angles—to which I gave the **Fourth** rank (in that single category of congruence alone); the reason is contained in our third proposition of this Book. To their star-forms, a **Fifth** rank was assigned, because they are equal to their primary figures in their <term>Knowability</term><note>original: "Scibilitate"; the ability to be constructed or understood geometrically.</note>, but far inferior in **Congruence**, as they only touch at their individual angles. But it was not necessary for me to do this, since not even as far as the third rank are clearly indubitable aspects produced. We could gracefully set a limit to these sprouting **Aspects** at the point of **Congruence** in the solid, and in the perfect **Effability** of the side or plane. Therefore, let the ranks of nobility for the Figures be sought instead from the ends of Books I and II; from those, the ranks of the **Aspects** in this book have been distinguished.

# CHAPTER VII.

## Epilogue: On Sublunary Nature and the Lower Faculties of the Soul, Especially Those Upon Which Astrology Is Based.

Much has been said concerning this contemplation in Chapter Two, and indeed throughout this whole Fourth Book; some things were even mentioned in Book III. I have also discussed this previously: a year ago in the *Introduction to the Ephemeris*<note>Kepler's annual astronomical tables and predictions.</note>, in Book I of the *Epitome of Copernican Astronomy* (page 125), and again in 1610 in the *Third Intervener*<note>original: "Tertio interveniente"; a work where Kepler acted as a "third party" mediator between those who totally accepted or totally rejected astrology.</note> (numbers 40 to 43, 59 to 72, 113, etc.), in my *Response to the Objections of Röslin*<note>Helisaeus Röslin, a physician and astrologer who disagreed with Kepler's physical explanations for astrology.</note>, and in 1606 in the book *On the New Star* (chapters 8, 9, 10, 24, and 28, especially from pages 171 to 175), and in 1604 in *The Optical Part of Astronomy* (pages 26, 27, and 224). As for the specific prognostications where I have occasionally discussed or mentioned the more certain foundations of astrology, I shall deliberately pass over them here, as they are not widely scattered.

However, since I have appeared to some most celebrated professors of Philosophy and Medicine to be establishing a new philosophy—and a most true one at that—this tender little plant (as all new things are) must be nurtured and raised with every care. It must be encouraged to take root in the minds of those who practice philosophy; it must not be smothered by the excessive moisture of vain sophistry, nor washed away by the torrents of common opinion, nor allowed to grow stiff in the cold of public neglect. If I happen to be successful in guarding it, I fear nothing from the winds of calumny that might break it, nor from the Sun of solid censure that might wither it.

Therefore, since in Chapter I, I touched upon the essence of the Soul, though only for the sake of the Harmonies; and since the Second Chapter was not specifically about the Soul, but about Harmonies for the sake of the Soul; it is now pleasing in this chapter to discourse upon the Soul for its own sake, and in a slightly more general manner. I wish to make a collection—a syllabus—of all things pertaining to the present matter from this Epilogue. Those things which were said scatteredly, or in passing, or hiddenly, I shall bring here under a single view, explaining the whole nature of the subject with a continuous thread of discourse.

That there is some **Soul of the whole universe**<note>The "Anima Mundi," a concept suggesting the world itself is a living organism.</note>—presiding over the movements of the stars, the generation of the elements, the preservation of living creatures and plants, and finally the mutual sympathy between higher and lower things—was defended by Timaeus of Locri (following Pythagorean doctrines) in the works of Plato. Proclus established this further, both elsewhere and especially in the words transcribed in Chapter I of this Fourth Book. They made this Soul distinct from the **Mind**<note>original: "Mente"</note>; for while the Mind was simple, this Soul was multiple in its faculties. Furthermore, the Ideas of all sensible things existed in the Mind primarily and of themselves, pure and identical; but they existed in the Soul secondarily, for the sake of the Mind and received from it, leaning more toward matter. Thus, they used a distinction of names: they called the Intellectual or Mental forms <term>Paradigms</term><note>original: "PARADIGMATA"; patterns or blueprints.</note>, while they called the Soul-based forms <term>Icons</term><note>original: "ICONES"; images or reflections.</note> of those Paradigms. The sum of it comes to this: a Christian might most easily understand **God the Creator** in place of the Platonic Mind, and the **Nature of things** in place of the Soul.

<margin>CHAPTER VI.</margin>
From these points, it appears that what I stated in the *Introduction to the Ephemeris* holds true: that in the constitution of the Aspects, different causes are at work, and they concur together. Furthermore, Nature has a preference for those aspects which are endowed with more "prerogatives" <note>Prerogatives: Kepler treats geometric properties as "legal rights" or privileges that give an aspect more power.</note>. The *Semi-sextile* <note>30 degrees</note> shares certain rights with the *Square* <note>90 degrees</note>; namely, the <term>Expressibility</term> <note>original: "Effabilitas"; the property of a geometric magnitude being rational or representable by square roots</note> of the area within the figure. It also shares certain rights with the *Sextile* <note>60 degrees</note>, specifically a manifold congruence in the plane. When these forces are joined together, the *Semi-sextile* becomes in a certain way more powerful than the *Sextile* itself, insofar as the expressibility of the twelve-sided (dodecagonal) area is superior to the expressibility of the hexagonal side; this is because a more perfect Congruence in the plane follows from it. Although in this Fourth Book, I have ranked the *Semi-sextile* after the *Sextile*, they are effectively in the same grade of importance.

The *Introduction to the Ephemeris* also makes the *Trine* <note>120 degrees</note> and the *Square*, as well as the *Quintile* <note>72 degrees</note> and the *Biquintile* <note>144 degrees</note>, equal in the first and strongest cause; namely, pure <term>Congruence</term> <note>original: "Congruentia"; the ability of shapes to fit together perfectly without gaps, like floor tiles</note> in the solid, for the purpose of forming the Regular Solid figures <note>The five Platonic Solids</note>. I have said that the **Trine** and the **Square** add a second cause, which is not much less significant: understand this as the pure congruence of the figures in the plane. This is indeed also common to the *Sextile*; however, the *Sextile* does not add this to the first cause, but possesses it separately from it. Just as the **Square** is also said to add a third cause—namely the Expressibility of the plane—not because the *Semi-sextile* does not also participate in that property, but because those qualities which exist individually in the other aspects are all accumulated in the *Square*, so that it becomes the most powerful of all.

Thus, in weighing the arguments in favor of the *Sextile*, I said it has a certain nobility in common with the *Opposition* <note>180 degrees</note>, hinting at the Expressibility of the side of the figure, because it is half of the circle's diameter. Again, the same *Sextile* has some nobility in common with the *Trine* and the *Square*: namely, the pure Congruence in the plane mentioned earlier. For only a small part of that—that is, the Congruence with figures of other types—belongs to the *Semi-sextile* and the other more ignoble <note>Lower-ranked or less geometrically perfect</note> aspects. In this particular category of Congruence, the *Semi-sextile* and the *Octile* <note>45 degrees</note> figures hold the first rank. The star <note>The astrological configuration</note> of the *Semi-sextile* could also be associated with this rank, because the Congruence they begin can be continued without mixing different shapes. The *Quintile* and *Biquintile* hold the second rank, except that they possess a more noble congruence in the solid. Likewise, the *Tri-octile* <note>135 degrees</note>, the *Decile* <note>36 degrees</note>, and the *Tri-decile* <note>108 degrees</note> hold this rank because their figures do indeed continue the Congruence, but not without a mixture of different shapes; and all of these agree to some extent even in the solid, to a greater or lesser degree. An exception is the *Quincunx* <note>150 degrees</note>, the dodecagonal star, which is therefore relegated to the Third rank. To this third rank, the *Sesquiquadrate* <note>135 degrees</note>, or the octagonal star, can also be added, due to the obscurity of our knowledge concerning it.

I have indeed extended these ranks even further, to the *Vigintile* <note>18 degrees</note> and the *Quindecile* <note>24 degrees</note>—that is, to figures with fifteen and twenty angles. I gave them the Fourth rank (in the category of congruence alone); the reason for this is contained in our third proposition of this Book. To their "stars," a Fifth rank was assigned, because while they are equal to their primary figures in terms of "Knowability" <note>original: "Scibilitate"; the degree to which they can be understood through geometry</note>, they are by far the lowest in terms of Congruence, as they only touch upon individual angles. However, it was not strictly necessary for me to do that; since not even up to the third rank are aspects produced that are entirely beyond doubt. We can beautifully set a boundary to this proliferation of Aspects at the point where solid Congruence and perfect Expressibility of the side or plane end. Therefore, the ranks of the "nobility" of the Figures should be sought rather from the conclusions of Books I and II, from which the ranks of the Aspects have been distinguished in this book.

<summary>Kepler provides a technical hierarchy of astrological aspects (Sextile, Trine, Square, etc.) based on their geometric properties of congruence and expressibility. He argues that the Square is the most powerful because it combines multiple geometric "privileges" that other aspects only possess individually.</summary>

ON THE HARMONIES, BOOK IV.

## CHAPTER VII.

### Epilogue: On Sublunary Nature, and the Lower Faculties of the Soul, especially those on which Astrology is based.

Much has been said regarding this contemplation in the second chapter, and much throughout this fourth book; some things were also mentioned in Book III, and a year ago in the *Introduction to the Ephemerides*, as well as in Book I of the *Epitome of Copernican Astronomy* on page 125. Again, in the year 1610, in *The Third Intervening* <note>original: "Tertio interveniente"; Kepler's work defending a middle ground in the dispute over astrology</note>, in numbers 40 to 43, and 59 to 72, and 113, etc.; and in the *Response to Röslin’s Objections*; and in 1606 in the book on the *New Star*, chapters VIII, IX, X, and XXIV, XXVIII, especially from page 171 to 175; and in 1604 in the *Optical Part of Astronomy*, pages 26, 27, and 224. For I deliberately pass over those prognostications in which I have, from time to time, either introduced or remarked upon the more certain foundations of *Astrology*, as they are not widely scattered.

Since, however, I have seemed to some very celebrated *Professors of Philosophy and Medicine* to be establishing a new philosophy—and a most true one at that—this tender little plant (as all new things are) must be nurtured and raised with every care, so that it may take root in the minds of those who practice philosophy. It must not be suffocated by the excessive moisture of vain sophistries, nor washed away by the torrents of common opinions, nor stiffen in the cold of public neglect. If I happen to be wary of these things, I do not fear anything for it from the winds of calumny, lest it be broken; nor from the Sun of solid <note>or "severe"</note> criticism, lest it be scorched.

Therefore, since in Chapter I, I touched upon the essence of the *Soul*, but only for the sake of the *Harmonies*; and since the Second Chapter was not explicitly about the *Soul*, but about *Harmonies* for the sake of the *Soul*; it is now pleasing in this chapter to discourse upon the *Soul* for its own sake, a little more generally. It is pleasing to make a Summary <note>original: "Syllogum"</note> in this Epilogue of everything that pertains to the present matter; those things which were said scatteringly, or in passing, or hiddenly, I shall here bring under a single view, and explain the whole nature of the matter with a continuous thread of discourse.

That there is some *Soul* of the whole universe, presiding over the movements of the stars, the generation of the elements, the conservation of living creatures and plants, and finally the mutual sympathy of higher and lower things, was defended by *Timaeus of Locri* <note>A Pythagorean philosopher featured in Plato's dialogues</note> based on Pythagorean teachings in the works of *Plato*; and *Proclus* established it, both elsewhere and especially in the words transcribed in Chapter I of this fourth book. They made this Soul distinct from the *Mind* <note>original: "Mens"</note>; both because the *Mind* was simple, while that *Soul* was manifold in its faculties; and because the Ideas of all sensible things existed in the *Mind* primarily through itself, pure and identical; but in the *Soul* secondarily, because of the *Mind* and received from it, inclining more toward matter. From this they also used a distinction of names: they called the Intellectual or Mental ones **PARADIGMS** <note>original: "PARADIGMATA"</note>, but the Soul-based ones **ICONES** <note>original: "ICONES", meaning "Images"</note> of those Paradigms. The sum of it comes to this: a Christian might very easily understand the creator *God* in place of the *Platonic Mind*, and the *Nature* of things in place of the *Soul*.

# ON CONFIGURATIONS

<margin>CHAPTER VI.</margin>

From these points, it is clear—as I stated in the Introduction to my *Ephemerides* <note>original: "Prolegomenis Ephemer:"; referring to Kepler's published astronomical tables</note>—that diverse causes and their convergence are at work in the establishment of the Aspects. Nature possesses a choice among those that are equipped with more "prerogatives" <note>advantages or higher geometric rankings</note>. The Semi-sextile <note>an aspect of 30 degrees</note> shares certain rights in common with the Square <note>90 degrees</note>; namely, the <term>expressibility</term> <note>original: "effabilitatem"; the property of a magnitude being rational or geometrically constructible</note> of the area within the figure. It also shares certain rights with the Sextile <note>60 degrees</note>, specifically a manifold congruence in a plane. When these forces are joined, the Semi-sextile becomes in a way more powerful than the Sextile itself, insofar as the expressibility of the dodecagonal <note>twelve-sided</note> area is superior to the expressibility of the hexagonal <note>six-sided</note> side; for a more perfect congruence in the plane follows from the former. And yet, in this fourth book, I have directed the Semi-sextile to follow the Sextile, but in the same rank.

The Trine <note>120 degrees</note>, the Square, the Quintile <note>72 degrees</note>, and the Biquintile <note>144 degrees</note> are made equal by the Introduction to the *Ephemerides* regarding the first and strongest cause: that is, pure congruence in a solid <note>original: "congruentiæ puræ in solido"; the ability of shapes to fit together to form the five regular Platonic solids</note>, for the purpose of establishing regular solid figures. I have said that the Trine and Square add a second cause, which is not much lighter: understand this as the pure congruence of figures in a plane <note>tessellation</note>. This is also common to the Sextile; however, the Sextile does not add this to the first cause, but possesses it separately from it. In the same way, the Square is said to add a third cause, namely the expressibility of the plane; not because the Semi-sextile does not also participate in it, but because those qualities which are individual in the others are accumulated in the Square, so that it becomes the most powerful of all.

Thus, in weighing the votes in favor of the Sextile, I said it possesses a certain nobility in common with the Opposition <note>180 degrees</note>, hinting at the expressibility of the side of the figure, because it is half of the circle's diameter. Again, it has some nobility in common with the Trine and Square; namely, the pure congruence in a plane mentioned before. Only a small portion of this—that is, congruence with figures of other species—belongs to the Semi-sextile and the other less noble aspects. In this particular category of congruence, the first rank is held by the Semi-sextile and the Octile <note>45 degrees, or Semi-square</note> figures: to which the star-shaped Semi-sextile <note>original: "Semisexti stella"; a star-polygon aspect</note> could also be associated, because the congruence they begin can be continued without a mixture of different forms. The second rank is held by the Quintile and Biquintile, except that they also possess a nobler congruence in the solid. Likewise the Trioctile <note>135 degrees</note>, Decile <note>36 degrees</note>, and Tridecile <note>108 degrees</note>, because their figures do indeed continue a congruence, but not without a mixture of diverse forms; and all of these agree to some extent even in the solid, according to a greater or lesser degree. The Quincunx <note>150 degrees</note> dodecagonal star is excepted; it is therefore referred to the third rank: to which the Sesquadrate <note>135 degrees, or "Sesquiquadrate"</note>, or the star of the Octagon, can be added on account of the obscurity of the science.

I have indeed extended the ranks even further, to the Vigintile <note>18 degrees</note> and the Quindecile <note>24 degrees</note>—that is, to figures of fifteen and twenty angles—to which I gave the fourth rank (in the aforementioned category of congruence alone); the reason for this is contained in our third proposition of this Book. To their "stars," the fifth rank was assigned, because they are equal to their primary figures in "knowability" <note>original: "scibilitate"; the ability to be theoretically understood</note>, but are far behind in congruence, as they only touch their individual angles. But it was not necessary for me to do this; since even up to the third rank, clearly indubitable aspects are not produced. We may gracefully set the boundary for these burgeoning Aspects at congruence in the solid and in the perfect expressibility of the side or plane. Therefore, let the ranks of the nobility of Figures be sought rather from the ends of Books I and II, from which the ranks of the Aspects have been distinguished in this book.

# ON THE HARMONIES, BOOK IV

## CHAPTER VII.

### *Epilogue: On the Sublunary Nature and the lower faculties of the Soul, especially those upon which Astrology rests.*

Many things regarding this contemplation were said in the second chapter, many throughout this entire fourth book, and some even in Book III. I also wrote of this a year ago in the *Introduction to the Ephemerides* <note>original: "Prolegomenis Ephemeridum"; Kepler’s published astronomical tables</note>, and in the first book of the *Epitome of Copernican Astronomy* <note>original: "Epitomes Astronomiæ Copernicæ"</note> on page 125; again in 1610 in *The Third Man Intervening* <note>original: "Tertio interveniente"; a work where Kepler sought a middle ground between fatalistic astrology and total rejection of it</note>, in sections 40 to 43, 59 to 72, and 113, etc.; and in the *Response to the Objections of Röslin*; and in 1606 in the book on the *New Star* <note>original: "stella nova"; concerning the supernova of 1604</note>, chapters 8, 9, 10, 24, and 28, especially from pages 171 to 175; and in 1604 in *The Optical Part of Astronomy* <note>original: "Astronomiæ parte Opticâ"</note> pages 26, 27, and 224. As for the prognostications, where I have occasionally spoken of the more certain foundations of astrology in the preface or in passing, I deliberately omit them here, as they are not widely scattered.

Since I have seemed to some very celebrated professors of Philosophy and Medicine to be establishing a new philosophy—and a most true one at that—this "tender little plant" (as all new things are) must be nurtured and raised with every care, so that it may take root in the minds of those who practice philosophy. It must not be suffocated by the excessive moisture of vain sophistries, nor washed away by the torrents of common opinions, nor frozen by the "cold" of public neglect. If I happen to be successful in guarding against these things, I do not fear the winds of calumny breaking it, nor the Sun of solid censure burning it.

In Chapter I, I touched upon the essence of the Soul, but only for the sake of the Harmonies. In the second Chapter, I did not speak of the Soul directly, but of the Harmonies for the sake of the Soul. It is now my pleasure in this chapter to discuss the Soul for its own sake, somewhat more generally. It is my pleasure to make this Epilogue a <term>compendium</term> <note>original: "Syllogum"; a gathering or collection</note> of everything pertaining to the present matter; things which have been said here and there, in passing, or hiddenly, I bring here under a single view, to explain the entire nature of the matter in a continuous thread of discourse.

Timaeus of Locri <note>a Pythagorean philosopher appearing in Plato's dialogues</note>, following Pythagorean doctrines in the works of **Plato**, defended the idea that there is a certain Soul of the entire universe, presiding over the motions of the stars, the generation of the elements, the preservation of living things and plants, and finally the mutual sympathy of higher and lower things. **Proclus** established this further, both elsewhere and especially in the words transcribed in Chapter I of this fourth book. They made this Soul distinct from the Mind; for the Mind was simple, while this Soul was multiple in its faculties. In the Mind, the Ideas of all sensible things existed primarily through themselves, pure and identical; in the Soul, they existed secondarily, because of the Mind and received from it, but leaning more toward matter. From this, they used a distinction of names: they called the Intellectual or Mental ideas **PARADIGMS** <note>original: "PARADIGMATA"; patterns or models</note>, but the Animal <note>related to the "anima" or soul</note> ideas they called **ICONS** <note>original: "ICONES"; images or reflections</note> of those Paradigms. The sum of it is this: a Christian might very easily understand the Platonic "Mind" as **God the Creator**, and the "Soul" as the **Nature of things**.

<margin>
CHAPTER VII.
See the Epilogue of Book V.
</margin>
What winds of contemplation specifically drove those ancient thinkers to arrive at these dogmas is for others to examine; I shall speak for myself. And first, regarding the **Soul of the entire universe**, although I do not reject the idea, I will say nothing of it in this fourth book. It seems (if such a thing exists) to reside in the center of the World—which for me is the **Sun**—and from there it propagates into its entire vastness through the communication of light rays, which serve as "spirits" do in an animal body.

Concerning **Nature**, however—which presides over the elements and which I call by the usual epithet **sublunary** <note>Refers to the region of the Earth and its atmosphere, literally "beneath the moon."</note>—I began to establish similar views twenty years ago. I was moved to this not by reading or admiring the Platonists, but by the sole and unique observation of the weather and the contemplation of the **Aspects** <term>Aspects: specific geometric angles (like 90° or 120°) between planets as seen from Earth, which Kepler believed created harmonic resonances.</term> by which the weather is stirred.

<margin>
See above, folios 123, 125, 130, 131, 132, 140, 143.
</margin>
For I saw, with great consistency, that the state of the air was disturbed whenever the planets were either in conjunction or configured by those aspects commonly celebrated by Astrologers; I saw that there was usually tranquility in the air if no aspects, or only a few, occurred, or if they were completed and passed quickly.

<margin>
The Laziness of Astrologers. From the Philosophers.
</margin>
Now, I judged that this matter should not be considered as lightly as the common crowd of **Prognosticators** <note>original: "Prognostarum"; those who make weather or fate predictions based on stars.</note> is accustomed to doing. They describe the "effects" <term>apotelesmata: the completed results or influences of the stars.</term> of the stars as if the stars were certain Gods, powerful over heaven and earth, doing all things by their own will. They are utterly unconcerned about the means by which the stars accomplish each thing here on earth, since the stars themselves remain in the heavens and send down nothing to us that is open to the senses except for glowing rays. This is the primary source of the most foul astrological superstitions. 

But I do not wonder much at the Prognosticators, a class of people mostly popular, childish, and prone to dreaming. Rather, the celebrated professors of **Philosophy** deserve more of a rebuke. While they accept from their master *Aristotle* that the life of animals and plants is nourished by the power of the Sun, they do not weigh the fact that the power of the Sun is therefore *perceived* by those creatures. All philosophy is sluggish and drowsy which allows the Sun to act upon these lower things as a sculptor acts upon lifeless material; for the Sun lacks a chisel, a graver, an axe, and all physical instruments. How much more vigilant than these philosophers was the poet *Virgil*, and how much wiser? He does not attribute everything even to the rains—which are themselves a part of matter—but compares the depths of the Earth to the **lap of a Spouse**, and a **joyful** one at that <note>original: "gremio Conjugis... lætæ"; a reference to Virgil's Georgics, depicting Earth as a living participant in fertility.</note>. That is, she perceives what is happening to her with pleasure, and aids her husband with a fitting movement. All these things are signs of **LIFE**, and they imply a **Soul** in the body that receives the action. For it would not be easy for the Sun, lacking suitable soldiers, to invade this fortress of the earth's innards, unless some kind of soul, sitting within, conspired with the "enemy" and opened the gates for him.

<margin>
The primary influence of the heavens belongs to the sublunary Soul. The material of rain comes from the Earth.
</margin>
You may see most people who attribute even the slightest bit to Astrology suffering from a neglect of this consideration, as if from some lethargy. Indeed, when I came forward to demonstrate the manner in which a change in the weather followed from an Aspect, a celebrated man arose who, in order to refute me, contended with great assertiveness that the material of rain was celestial (a notion we laughed at among the common folk back on folio 134). Yet even so, he did not teach how it happens that, although planetary rays are always meeting on the Earth, the rains fall only when the rays of two planets...

<summary>Kepler argues that the Earth possesses a "sublunary soul" that perceives planetary aspects and reacts to them, much like a living being. He criticizes traditional astrologers and philosophers for failing to explain the mechanism of celestial influence, suggesting that the Earth itself must be an active, sentient participant in meteorological changes.</summary>

<margin>
CHAPTER VII.
</margin>
Indeed, before all else, I decided that I must read the fourteen books of **Giovanni Pico della Mirandola** <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494) was a famous Italian Renaissance philosopher who wrote a massive critique of "divinatory" astrology.</note> written against Astrology, and I felt I must examine the reasons he opposed to every chapter of the art. Through this exercise, I was not only confirmed in my condemnation of many superstitions, but a new light also arose for me in certain matters. While I was shattering the force of his objections through an intense struggle of the mind, I began to see the matter itself more deeply. Ultimately, that book, by refuting some things, actually led me to place faith in others—things which I had previously distrusted because of the way other astrologers defended them.

<margin>
*Beware ambiguity: Aspects concur as causes for **Meteorological Effects** <note>original: "Effectus Meteoros"</note> in a general way; yet for some, such as the quality of a long part of the year, daily Aspects are not the cause, but instead act only on the specific days upon which they fall. See below.
</margin>
This was the case with the **Aspects**. For on one hand, I looked toward very consistent experience—not focusing specifically on snow, or winds, or thunder, and other such things that astrologers are accustomed to predict, but observing *generally* that the state of the air was stirred in whatever way if there were aspects (for instance, if **Mars** and **Jupiter** were in conjunction), and that it was quiet if there were none. 

On the other hand, I heard the man of Mirandola asking: why should one believe that Jupiter and Mars do more when they are seen together than when they are separate? For their lights are not increased by a conjunction; they bring just as much light to the meeting as they possessed when separate. Indeed, if planets of different qualities were to meet, it would seem that one would rather be hindered by the other. 

In this situation, I sought a response so that I might defend the **Aspects**, which I saw were followed by **Weather** <note>original: "Meteora," referring to all atmospheric phenomena.</note>. First, I began to consider the aspects more diligently as the cause, and then the weather as the effect. For the "form" of an aspect, which creates the configuration from a mixed arrangement of angles, was a qualitative quantity—or rather, it was a **Relation** of such quantities, a "being of reason" <note>original: "ens rationis," a philosophical term for something that exists only in the mind or through the perception of a rational being.</note>.

<margin>
Consideration of the cause of Storms.
</margin>
Therefore, in order for it to move the air, it was first necessary that it move some **Reason** (or Soul) which has power over either the air or that by which the air is disturbed. At the same time, I kept before my eyes the comparison of Aspects with **Musical Concords**, as handed down by **Ptolemy**, explained by **Cardano**, but too rashly exploded by the man of Mirandola. I was greatly helped by this analogy in the investigation of causes. For I saw that most of the things Pico objected against the aspects could also be objected against the blending of two voices. 

Truly, even the triple proportion (3:1) or the sesquialter (3:2) <note>These are mathematical ratios for musical intervals like the Octave-plus-Fifth or the Perfect Fifth.</note> of two sounds effects nothing purely by the cause of their pitch; and yet the sounds are pleasing if they are in these ratios, while they are conversely abhorred if they are in a septuple (7:1) or sesquisextal (7:6) ratio. 

Since, therefore, there must be a **Rational thing** <note>Kepler is arguing that the Earth itself possesses a "soul" or "nature" capable of perceiving geometry.</note> which distinguishes between the chords of 60 degrees and those of 59 or 61—whether it uses logic for this purpose like a human who understands **Geometry**, or holds it from a single "concreate instinct" <note>An innate, built-in ability.</note> (just as the forms of plants maintain a certain number of leaves entrusted to them from the origin of things, and always build themselves according to that architecture). There is no force of physical "mixing" here, like that measured for medical prescriptions, nor any physical body of instruments. Sounds do not delight, nor do rays animate, because they are "tempered" like hot water is mixed with cold until a quality results that is suitable for a person bathing. For in such physical mixtures, there is usually only one optimal temperature, and all others approach it by "more or less." But among configurations...

# ON CONFIGURATIONS

<margin>
CHAPTER VI. They are not physical. <note>original: "Non sunt naturales." In this context, Kepler uses "natural" to mean purely mechanical or material processes, distinguishing them from "animal" or "vital" responses.</note>
</margin>

Just as there are specific points between the intervals of sounds, it is only at these precise points that the logic of **Harmonies** <note>original: "Consonantiarum"</note> on one hand, and **Planetary Aspects** <note>original: "Aspectuum"</note> on the other, exists. If you deviate even slightly from these boundaries, the logic immediately perishes entirely. For as soon as the **Sun**, for example, has passed the **square** aspect <note>A 90-degree angle.</note> of **Saturn**, all stimulation of Nature cools down. It ceases for thirty whole days (at least regarding the rays of Saturn and the Sun) until the Sun reaches the **trine** <note>A 120-degree angle.</note> of Saturn. Then, once again, the storms are incited for a single day, and they cease again once that point is passed. Such are not the alterations of physical bodies; physical changes occupy the whole time from beginning to end, never intermittent, but increasing as the cause increases and growing with time, then slackening again as the cause diminishes. In a word, just as a line relates to a Number, so do common physical movements relate to these stimuli of the planetary configurations.

<margin>
But Vital. <note>original: "Animales," referring to the *anima* or soul.</note>
</margin>

If anyone considers this diligently, he will be able to conclude with no difficulty that, like Number, these momentary commotions—proceeding from an **Aspect**, which is a "Being of Reason"—belong not to the body but to **Vital faculties**. Therefore, it must be that there is a **Soul** <note>original: "Anima"</note> which, warned and as if excited by the Aspect, stirs up meteors and storms.

<margin>
The Soul in the earth. See pages 134, 143, 133, 131. The material of storms rises from the Earth. Page 133. The Earth is a living being.
</margin>

What kind of Soul this might be, or what its nature is, I have been able to gather chiefly from its seat in the world. For the aspects that trigger storms are angles formed by two rays—not the angles formed at one or the other of the mutually looking planets, nor those formed at the Sun (where the proportions would be vastly different), but the angles formed **here on Earth**. Since the planets themselves have no knowledge of the angles their rays form here on earth—unless we make them into astronomers—it follows that the Soul, which stirs the air according to the rule of the Aspects, must be here on Earth. And since that power accompanying the Aspects is felt throughout the entire globe, that soul must be equally widely diffused. 

Furthermore, the material of rains, winds, clouds, thunder, and atmospheric openings <note>original: "chasmatum," likely referring to rifts in clouds or auroras.</note> which are drawn out at the time of the Aspects, consists of moist vapor or spirit—some dry and fiery—boiling up and exhaling from the earth. (For why should a philosopher listen only to **Aristotle** here, while scorning **Rodolphus Agricola** <note>A Dutch humanist (1444–1485) who wrote on nature and logic.</note>, or indeed all farmers and his own senses? For every day he can see, as rains approach, the peaks of mountains vomiting out a great force of clouds). Therefore, this soul will be not only on the surface of the earth, but also deep within the subterranean caverns and the passages of the mountains. In short, the globe of the **Earth** will be a body like that of some animal; and what its own Soul is to an animal, this **Sublunary Nature** <note>The guiding spirit or "Earth-Soul" that Kepler believed translated celestial geometry into earthly weather.</note>—which moves the storms at the presence of the aspects—will be to the Earth.

<margin>
Page 155. Aspects are often ineffective.
</margin>

In this I was greatly confirmed by the very thing that might have deterred someone else: namely, that the commotions of the storms do not always respond exactly to the Aspects like a rule. Instead, the earth sometimes seems sluggish and stubborn. At other times (specifically after heavy and long-lasting configurations), having been exacerbated, it indulges in evaporations even without the continuation of aspects. Indeed, the Earth is not an animal like a Dog, ready at every nod, but rather like an **Ox** or an **Elephant**, slow to anger, but all the more violent once it has been inflamed.

Since this analogy was successful, it brought it about that I should pursue the same thing further...

<summary>Kepler argues that because weather responds to precise planetary angles felt only on Earth, the Earth itself must possess a soul (an "Earth-Soul" or Sublunary Nature) that perceives these geometric harmonies and reacts by exhaling vapors to create storms.</summary>
<keywords>Earth-Soul, Anima Mundi, Sublunary Nature, planetary aspects, meteorology, Aristotle, Rodolphus Agricola, geometric harmony, vital faculties</keywords>

<margin>
CHAPTER VII.
The works of the Earthly Soul.
</margin>
...I would inquire, also comparing the bodies of living creatures with the body of the Earth: I saw that almost everything that, arising from the body of a living being, testifies to a soul being within it, also arises from the body of the Earth. For just as the body produces hair on the surface of the skin, so the Earth brings forth plants and trees; and as in the former, lice are born, so here caterpillars, cicadas, and various insects and sea monsters are produced. And as the body produces tears, mucus <note>original: "blennam"</note>, and the waste of the ears—and sometimes even resinous gum from pustules on the face—so the Earth produces amber and bitumen. As the bladder pours out urine, so the mountains pour out rivers; and as the body produces excrement of a sulfurous odor and <term>flatulence</term> <note>original: "crepitus"</note> which can even be set on fire, so the Earth produces sulfur, subterranean fires, thunder, and lightning. And as blood is generated in the veins of a living being, and with it sweat, which is ejected outside the body; so in the veins of the Earth are generated metals, fossils, and rainy vapor.

<margin>
The Earth's nourishment.
</margin>
It is necessary, therefore, just as other living creatures draw in food and drink, that the Earth also draws in some material through certain channels from which it may cook up so many diverse things—for **nothing comes from nothing**. It draws in and swallows seawater; this is the reason why the sea never overflows despite the eternal pouring in of so many rivers. From the aforementioned points, you can gather how absurd those people are who attribute <term>metals</term> <note>Kepler argues that minerals are "grown" by the Earth's internal soul, rather than just being "baked" by the Sun's heat.</note> to the operation of the Sun alone, without the labor of the Earth.

<margin>
What species of Soul the Earth has.
</margin>
I also replied in my book on the **New Star** <note>*De Stella Nova* (1606), where Kepler discussed the 1604 supernova.</note> to that common objection: that if the Earth had a soul, it would also seem that it ought to grow and have limbs fit for movement. For as the body is, so the soul and its faculties correspond to it; since this soul exists for the sake of the Earth's body—but this body is not for the sake of the soul in the same way that a human body exists for the sake of the **Mind**, the primary faculty of the Soul. If, therefore, the Earth had needed growth, or a different kind of feeding (as if from hunting), then those duties would have been committed to this Soul, and suitable instruments would have been given. This was the philosophy of the dying **Socrates** in the *Phaedo* <note>A dialogue by Plato concerning the soul and the nature of the Earth.</note>, attributing everything to the governing Mind and to deliberation about what is best. Therefore, if anyone should argue that there are only four faculties of the Soul, none of which fit this Earthly Soul, and that there is therefore no soul in the Earth, I will bid him to add this fifth one to the number, by the same example and the same laws of reasoning by which those four were found in man.

<margin>
The Earthly Soul's imagination.

Geometry in gems.

The movement of its own body.
</margin>
But so that I might attribute a Soul to the Earth even more confidently, I was also moved by other things which are pressed here and there through my other books, and which I collected in a bundle in the *Epitome of Copernican Astronomy* (page 125): especially this, that there is a **formative faculty** in the bowels of the Earth. This faculty, in the manner of a pregnant woman, expresses the human things it encounters outside (as if it saw them) into fissile stones—such as the figures of **Soldiers**, **Monks**, **Popes**, **Kings**, and whatever new and unusual fashions are on the lips of men. This happens rather rarely; but this other thing happens perpetually: that in gems and fossils it expresses the **five regular geometric solids** <note>The Platonic Solids: tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron. Kepler believed these were the blueprint of the universe.</note>. For the work testifies to the craftsman. To these, let him who follows **Copernicus** add the diurnal rotation of the Earth’s globe, which is perpetual and most uniform; he will most correctly count this among the duties of this Soul.

# ON THE CONFIGURATIONS

<margin>Chapter VII. The sense of Touch in the Earth</margin>
What if a certain sense, either of touch or of hearing, seems to reside in the globe of the Earth? This is supported by the evidence of a constant tradition in many provinces: it is said that if someone climbs to the peaks of the highest mountains and throws a small stone into those very deep chasms they possess, a sound is usually stirred up; or if a stone is thrown into a mountain lake (which undoubtedly also lacks a bottom), storms are immediately excited. For in this same way, if one inserts something tickling into the tender passages of an animal's ears or nostrils, the animal—seized by a shudder—shakes its head or rushes into a run.

<margin>Diseases of the Earth.</margin>
There are also ailments peculiar to certain regions of the Earth, and internal changes of its "viscera" <note>Kepler uses "viscera" to refer to the Earth's internal layers or "guts."</note>. For sometimes they abound with too much moisture; at other times they suffer from indigestion or imperfect <term>concoction</term> <note>Original: "concoctionis." In early modern science, this referred to the "cooking" or ripening of materials through heat, like digestion in the stomach or the ripening of ores in the Earth.</note>, such as when mere winds come forth instead of timely rains. Sometimes, as if seized by a burning fever, the regions exude no moisture, but instead breathe out sulfurous vapors or pestilential damps. Therefore, not without reason in my book *On the New Star* <note>Kepler's *De Stella Nova* (1606).</note>, on page 173, I advised that all the faculties of digestion—the **Attractive**, the **Retentive**, and the **Expulsive**—should be sought in the Earth, for those diseases are simply afflictions of these faculties.

<margin>The Earth's respiration.</margin>
<margin>From where come the ebb and flow of the Ocean?</margin>
Indeed, what is more like the respiration of land animals—and especially that intake and output of fish, who suck in water with their mouths and squeeze it out in turn through their gills—than that marvelous twice-daily ebb and flow of the Ocean? Although it adapts itself to the motions of the Moon, such that it seemed probable to me (in the Preface to the *Commentaries on Mars* <note>Kepler's *Astronomia Nova* (1609).</note>) that the waves are pulled by the Moon as iron is by a magnet, through a bodily power of the union of bodies; and although I recently repeated this in the introduction to the *Ephemerides* where I examined the opinion of David Fabricius: nevertheless, if someone were to argue that the Earth adapts its own "breathing" to the motion of the Sun and Moon—just as animals have the same cycles of sleep and waking as the day and night—I judge that such a person should be heard with an open mind in philosophy. This is especially true if some evidence were added of flexible parts of the Earth in the deep, which might take the place of lungs or gills. For if those parts have a nature like that of our air—compressible and extensible—then there would no longer be a need for the movement of the Earth's surface to achieve this respiration (which would be analogous to the movement of the diaphragm muscles in a breathing human body).

Indeed, what more suitable reason could there be for the receiving of sea waters inward, as if into the "kitchen" of the metals, than this very process through those perpetual twice-daily channels <note>original: "Euripos," referring to the Euripus Strait, famous in antiquity for its erratic and powerful currents.</note>? What else does that marvelous event make us suspect: when, a few years before the crowds of merchants brought the news to Antwerp, the Ebb and Flow deserted the Ocean on a certain day (terrifying the city no small amount), even though the Moon did not desert its course? Surely the Earth itself, being the master of this reciprocation, although it participates by a natural motion, held back one respiration of that day; just as living creatures sometimes hold their breath, even though the motion of the Diaphragm itself is also mixed with natural <note>involuntary</note> movement.

Although perhaps we might more correctly prove that some respiration is necessary for the Earth from the presence of a Soul, rather than proving a Soul from the respiration.

Now, since we may proceed as if it were a settled matter that there is a soul in the Earth, let us come to the contemplation of its essence. Indeed, that soul is not merely some kind of light, such as that of fires or glow-worms <note>Original: "cincindularum." Kepler is comparing the Earth's internal "light" to bioluminescence.</note>, depending upon itself and not upon illumination from the sun. The proof of this is that it somehow perceives the bright rays of the planets. Rather, it clearly seems to be a kind of flame (to be nourished, of course, by breathing or "drinking" in), as evidenced by the perpetual and sensible subterranean heat. No such heat persists in naked matter in an active state without a soul; nor is it present even potentially in things proceeding from the substance of animals and plants, unless it is produced by the Soul and by the Forms, which are something of a fiery nature. See my *Optics*, pages 25, 26, 27.

The principle of the Soul's individuation.

We shall assign this "fire" as the matter, so to speak, of the Soul of the Earth; upon this, in the place of a "form," the image of the divine countenance has been impressed. This includes the Ideas of the Circle and all its ratios, as well as the Ideas of its own sensible body, over which it has been appointed to rule, and even of the whole World in which its body was to exist. For God possesses within Himself not only geometric models <note>Original: "exemplaria." Kepler refers to the blueprints or archetypes used by God in creation.</note>, but also the concepts of all sensible things to be created. All of these pass simultaneously into Souls—which are models of God—according to each soul's capacity or use. Therefore, there shines within the Soul of the Earth a certain image of the sensible Zodiac circle, and indeed of the entire firmament, which is the bond of sympathy between celestial and terrestrial things. Within that soul, most of all, shine the archetypes of all its duties and all the motions by which it moves its body in any sense. While others might call this <term>potentiality</term> <note>Original Greek: "δύναμιν" (dynamin).</note>, I would more gladly call it <term>activity</term> <note>Original Greek: "ἐνέργεια" (energeia).</note>. For this is the essence of souls; this is, as it were, the <term>nature</term> <note>Original Greek: "φύσις" (physis).</note> of this flame: that souls themselves are always so arranged within as if they were performing that for which they were made to perform, whether they actually possess the instruments of the body or are hindered from using them. For God is substantial Activity, and He exists by this very activity (if I may stammer about divine things in a human way). Therefore, the essence of the divine image consists **in acting** <note>Original Greek: "ἐν τῷ ἐνεργεῖν" (en tō energein).</note>, just as the essence of a flame consists **in growing** <note>Original Greek: "ἐν τῷ φύειν" (en tō phyein).</note>. Thus, unless God eternally sustained it by irradiating its "matter," it would suddenly cease and be extinguished. Nevertheless, for the principle of its individual identity <note>Original: "individuationis." The philosophical concept of what makes one thing distinct from another.</note>, it requires not only the body over which it is placed to rule, but also this very material particle of itself (which I described before), which distinguishes it from all other Souls.

<margin>
The perpetual duties of the Soul of the Earth.

Indeed, it never ceases from "cooking" <note>Kepler uses the metaphor of "coctio" (cooking/digestion) to describe the Earth's internal heat processes.</note>, nor is this cooking ever without smoke and vapor. In fact, <term>minerals<note>Original: "fossilia." From that same vapor exhaling outside above the surface of the Earth, the breathable air—which had fallen during the night by gathering into dews—is daily renewed.

<margin>

</margin>

<margin>
Why excesses occur through Aspects.
</margin>
This work of the Soul of the Earth, although it is perpetual, nevertheless required certain "excesses" in its evaporation. These were not meant to be continuous for all time, but reduced to certain specific days, so that from a bounty of vapors sent outside, timely rains might be supplied. Yet, with periods of Sunlight intervening, this is done for the sake of refreshing and moistening the surface of the Earth, from which crops and fodder might grow for Living Creatures.

<margin>
The Sun also stirs up vapors around the Aspects.
</margin>
Someone might object to me concerning the innermost parts of Africa and Peru, which lie beneath the equinoctial line <note>The Equator.</note>, where continuous rains fall through the whole summer. Where, then, is this distinction of "Aspects" from "ineffective configurations"? Where are the alternations of Suns and showers? And does not the course of the Sun—a solitary planet—alone do everything, without respect to its configuration with others? And does it not do so as a natural cause, rather than a <term>conceptual entity<note>Original: "Ens rationis." Kepler is distinguishing between a physical cause (the Sun's heat) and a mathematical/perceptual cause (the geometry of the Aspects).</note></term>, insofar as it intensifies heat and warmth in those parts, so that thinned moisture exhales from the bowels of the earth toward those scorched regions? 

I respond that this natural action must not be denied to the Sun; but it is not unique to the Torrid Zone alone, but can also be observed among us. For when the Sun remains in our Hemisphere through the summer, more abundant rains usually fall than there is usually any snow during the winter when the sun is absent. 

<margin>
How rivers are increased.
</margin>
However, as for the fact that our rivers are increased by melting snows—which do not seem to be increased so much by falling rains, or certainly not by such long-lasting increments—that happens partly because the individual layers of snow falling bit by bit are piled up and preserved in a "storehouse" for many months by the force of the cold. Meanwhile, the earth, parched by the Sun, immediately drinks up the greatest part of summer rains, even the largest ones. Partly, however, it happens because the snow in the Alps cannot be dissolved unless very abundant summer rains fall; thus those continuous increases of the rivers are not from the snows alone, but also from the joined rains. 

Therefore, if you weigh everything, a greater bounty of moisture mostly "sweats out" even among us through the summer than through the winter. This objection, therefore, achieves this much: it shows there is a concurrence of celestial causes, of which one is natural (the heat of the Sun) and the other rational (the Aspect). There is also a concurrence of sublunary causes, so that not only does one Zone have more moisture than another, but even in the same climate, one region has more than another for its own reasons. Meanwhile, even in the Torrid Zone, it can rain more around the time of the Aspects than on days void of aspects.

As for this "characterization" of the Earthly soul which I mentioned in the second place—made by the sensible Zodiac and the whole sphere of the fixed stars—that also...

<margin>Chapter VII.</margin>
<margin>Whence the effects of Comets and Eclipses arise.</margin>
Experience also confirms this: it is established by the great consensus of all times that if anything new appears in the heavens—whether according to the ordinary course of the sky, such as the rarer meetings of several stars or the more significant <term>Eclipses of the Luminaries<note>The "Luminaries" refer to the Sun and the Moon.</note></term>, or whether beyond common nature, such as Comets or new fixed stars—simultaneously, <term>sublunary nature<note>The "sublunary" realm refers to the Earth and its atmosphere, everything "below the moon," which was thought to be subject to change and decay unlike the "perfect" heavens.</note></term> is disturbed by unusual affections. These include an immense and continuous force of rains beyond the measure of the <term>Aspects<note>Geometric angles between planets that Kepler believed triggered physical responses on Earth.</note></term>, or contrary droughts and parched conditions, accompanied by earthquakes; and finally, unusual dampness in the air, which brings about pestilential catarrhs and other epidemic plagues, especially in those places from which they exhale with greater force, or toward which they are carried by more frequent winds.

<margin>Pages 110. 111.</margin>
<margin>A stone ignited by the day.</margin>
<margin>Whence the locations of conjunctions gain their efficacy.</margin>
<margin>Memory of the Soul of the Earth. 12.</margin>
Furthermore, I pointed out in my book on the New Star (Chapter X, page 44) that something similar to the **Memory of Animals** exists in this Soul. For this is the nature of all things related to light: when excited by the light of the Sun, or at least by the day, they conceive a certain affection that lasts for a definite time. Thus, in our eyes, the visual spirits (the offspring of light), when imbued by a sudden sight of the Sun, bear and carry that image around with them wherever they turn their eyes, even against their will. So too, among the secrets of the <term>Chemists<note>In Kepler's time, "Chymistae" referred to both chemists and alchemists, who studied the properties of matter and light.</note></term>, there is this wonderful and especially noteworthy experiment: they prepare certain gems (as I recently learned from a certain <note>original: "αὐτόπτῃ" (autoptē), meaning an eyewitness</note> eyewitness) which, while they remain hidden in the dark like other things deprived of light, if someone exposes them to the light of day alone, they are ignited by it like candles. They carry that splendor with them even into the darkness, glowing like the eyes of cats; however, this light is extinguished again after a short time. 

Something similar happens to this Soul—which I have said is related to light and fire—so that in that region (for the Soul is a single point, distinguished by regions, or a potential <term>Zodiac circle<note>Kepler imagines the Earth's soul containing an internal map of the Zodiac to track planetary movements.</note></term>) in which the superior planets met or an Eclipse appeared, it conceives a "character" or mark of that conjunction that lasts for some time. Therefore, as often as any of the planets, especially the Sun or the Moon, passes over that place, the Soul exerts its power in the same way it would at the initial stimulation of the conjunction. This whole business, I say, is similar to the memory of animals. For I carry the image of a man once seen in my mind, yet I do not always have him present in my thoughts; but when he or someone similar appears again, that old image is drawn out anew and placed into the act of thinking through <term>reminiscence<note>The act of recovering a memory or "remembering."</note></term>. Although human memory is nobler in this regard—because I am not only reminded of the remembered thing by an external encounter, but I can also remind myself whenever I wish—this is because the faculty of discourse <note>Reasoning or logical progression of thought.</note> is present in man, which is absent in this Soul. Truly, these things will be more evident in the contemplation of the human Soul.

<margin>How the soul of the Earth perceives an aspect.</margin>
Now, one difficulty, touched upon slightly above, must be resolved concerning the mode and means of reception. For the fact that we humans receive the "species" (images) of sensible things inwardly into the Soul seems an easy and plain matter; for the openings of the pupils are out in the open, through which they enter; there is the eye, the former of the image; there is the <term>crystalline humor<note>The lens of the eye.</note></term>, the temperer of the radiant pencil of light; there is the <term>retiform tunic<note>The retina.</note></term> of the optic nerve, the receiver of the picture of external things. Nothing of the sort appears in the body of the earth: no eye is here, by which the Soul of the Earth might see the radiations of the Planets and their angles. How then shall it sense the light without vision? How shall it perceive—

CHAPTER VII.
The true mode of seeing.
</margin>
<margin>
François d’Aguilon.

[Who] will receive or take up the angles without an instrument? There is some difficulty, I confess; and if you look into the matter more deeply, it is common to both this case and that. Refer to my <term>Astronomical Part of Optics<note>original: "Optices Astr. partis"; Kepler refers to his 1604 work *Ad Vitellionem paralipomena*, where he revolutionized the understanding of how the eye works.</note></term>, page 169; you will see an ancient complaint, even concerning human vision. For even if the more diligent Opticians and Anatomical Physicians confess that the mode of seeing was at last most solidly demonstrated by me in that place, after so many fruitless attempts by others—although <term>François d’Aguilon<note>A Jesuit mathematician whose work *Opticorum Libri Sex* (1613) was a standard text, though Kepler notes he missed Kepler’s own discoveries.</note></term>, whose great work on Optics appeared four years ago, did not see my book, and therefore, in the ancient error concerning the mode of vision, built a new and surely quite beautiful, but useless structure—nevertheless, that mode of seeing does not extend itself beyond the <term>retiform tunic<note>The retina. Kepler was the first to realize the retina, not the lens, is the primary organ of light reception.</note></term>, into which the humors of the eye look. There remains still a question, not yet discussed by the Physicists to whom I have appealed: how the picture of the thing to be seen, formed by me on the retiform tunic, is then passed through the opaque parts of the body inward to the secret chambers of the Soul? Does the soul go out to meet it? and other questions adhering to these. And I, to confess frankly, am more stuck on vision than on this perception of the angle of the rays; concerning the latter, I seem to be able to stammer something not ineptly, while in the former I am altogether mute.

I could indeed, without damaging the core of the matter, escape the labor of speculation, and to one asking "with what eyes does the Soul of the Earth see the rays of the stars?" respond: with the same eyes by which it saw the soldier with the ragged boots, whose image it planted in a <term>fissile stone<note>original: "lapide fissili"; Kepler refers to "figured stones" or fossils, which he believed the Earth's soul created as a kind of artistic expression or "imitation" of things it perceived on the surface.</note></term>. But truly, idleness is the death of philosophy: let us live and exercise ourselves.

<margin>
fol. 135. 139. 
140. 143.

How the Soul of the Earth governs its own body.
</margin>
First, the soul has obtained the character of a point in actuality (at least by reason of its bond to its body), but the shape of a circle in potentiality. Since it is an <term>Energia<note>Activity or vital force.</note></term>, it spreads itself from that seat of the point into a circle. For whether it must sense external things, they surround it in a spherical manner; or whether it must rule the body, it also has the body surrounding it. The soul itself lies hidden within, rooted in a certain point of the body, from where it goes out through an image of itself into the rest of the body. But how should it go out, except through straight lines? For this is truly to "go out." What other way of going out could it have—being itself both existing light and flame—than the way other lights go out from their sources, namely, in straight lines? Therefore, it goes out toward the exterior parts of the body by the same laws as the lights of the firmament surrounding it enter toward that soul residing in a point. Now, since the whole surface of the terrestrial hemisphere, and even all the points of the surface of the air with which it is clothed, are irradiated by one and the same Planet with infinite rays; out of all of these, only one single ray tends toward that point which is the seat of the soul. And in turn, since the Soul goes out into all points of the surface of its body in infinite lines (like the rays of the Sun, because it too is a kind of light, and the "spirits" so celebrated by the common people seem to be nothing else than these rectilinear rays and these species of the soul): yet there is only one line among them all which tends from the center to that point of the surface which is struck by that unique ray of the Planet tending toward the seat of the Soul. Let us suppose, therefore, that the perception of the rays of one planet consists in this: when the inward rush of the planet and the outward meeting of the soul coincide in one geometric straight line. This is very similar to the example of vision, which is perfect and accurate only in the single and unique perpendicular ray in the middle of the whole eye. Let us also suppose this, which I emphasized in my <term>Dioptrics<note>Kepler's *Dioptrice* (1611), a foundational text on telescope optics and refraction.</note></term> proposition XLV as the singular secret of all sensations: that no sensation of an external...
