### BOOK IV OF THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD 167

<margin>
CHAPTER VII.
What perception is, and how it occurs.
</margin>

...external things, except insofar as the sensory instrument is affected by that thing. For the **Soul**, through those outpourings of its own <term>representations<note>original: "specierum"; in Kepler's physics, "species" are the immaterial forms or images emitted by objects that allow them to be perceived by a soul.</note></term>, possesses a faithful knowledge of all the members of its own body, and of those things which occur anew in each of them at any time. Given these facts, it follows that if such an impression is made by a **Planet** upon some point of the air which does not tend toward the seat of the soul, but passes by it to the side, the soul may receive the representation of that point so affected through the return of its own representation, but it would disregard it as a thing of no value. 

However, if such an impression is made on a point of the surface of the air that *does* tend toward the seat of the **Soul**, this point so affected is also announced to the **Soul**, and this perception is valued as pertaining to the **Soul** and is distinguished from the others. Therefore, in that single point alone, the **Soul** imagines the star to be, and not at all in the others just mentioned. For the ray of the **Soul** is activated and, as it were, illuminated by the ray of the star when they coincide on the same straight line; just as the color of visible things is activated by the arrival of light, and as vision is activated when we gather ourselves and realize that we see. 

Since this is the case not only for one planet, but for two, the soul will also find two signs in two parts of its body. Whether its body is round, or unequal and rough, the **Soul** holds it surrounding itself in the manner of a sphere, sitting in a single point. By its rays, or the representations of its immaterial self—or, as others say, by its "secondary acts" emitted around itself—it breathes out a perfect sphere, as far as its body extends. Therefore, it examines that body according to the idea of a circle, and specifically the **Zodiac circle**, described around its own seat as a center, and it measures the parts and intervals of it. Thus, there is no need to grant that the earth is transparent all the way to the center, nor that the soul must go out all the way to the stars; nevertheless, the manner in which the angles of the <term>configurations<note>The angular relationships (aspects) between planets, such as a conjunction or square, which Kepler believed created harmonic resonances.</note></term> are perceived by the **Soul** is clear.

<margin>
Optical illusions apply to the Soul of the Earth and its works.
</margin>

By this supposition, all the arguments are dissolved which **Pico della Mirandola** <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494) was a famous Renaissance philosopher who wrote a massive critique of astrology, "Disputationes adversus astrologiam divinatricem."</note> brought forward to overturn the doctrine of Great Conjunctions and aspects. For because the **Soul** disposes all the bodies of the world around the point of its seat (by imagining them) into the form of a sphere, and all the planets into the form of a circle—and this by the law of straight lines drawn from a single point—it therefore makes no difference whether a star be large or small, whether it completes a long or short journey in the heavens, or whether it be high or near to the Earth. 

For all these things move the **Soul** exactly as they are perceived; and they are perceived by the same laws by which they are seen by us: namely, all as if they were at the same height, and as if they lacked <term>secondary motion<note>The actual orbital movement of the planets.</note></term>, but were equally swift in their <term>primary diurnal motion<note>The apparent daily rotation of the sky caused by the Earth's spin.</note></term>, and without any great difference in their visible size. For other things that can be answered to Pico’s arguments, look in the often-cited place in my book <term>On the New Star<note>original: "De stella nova"; Kepler's 1606 book about the supernova of 1604, where he first addressed Pico's criticisms.</note></term>. Enough for now regarding the **Soul of the Earth**, which they call **sublunary Nature**.

<margin>
On the human Soul.
</margin>

Whatever has been said so far regarding the **Soul of the Earth** can similarly be applied to the faculties of the **human Soul** as well. However, most of these things are more evident in humans, and are so much more manifold as these faculties are set over more duties than that of the Earth.

<margin>
On the Mind (pages 140, 143, 139, 120, 121, 135, 124, 115, 117).
</margin>

Regarding the sovereign faculty of the soul, which is called the **Mind**, beyond those things which I brought forward above in Chapter I from **Proclus**, the business of Radiations suggests nothing more that I should say. That Mind is a point, as **Mind**; it is a circle, as **Reasoning**; it is an image of the divine face; it is **Harmony**, insofar as it is a single energy; in it are the **Ideas** and mathematical species, by means of the circle; it gives...

### ON CONFIGURATIONS

<margin>
CHAPTER VII.

Mathematical Genera are in the mind in a different way.
</margin>
...to these, and to the Harmonies, it gives their own intellectual Being. The reader should seek all these matters from the preceding sections; there is no need for more words here. I give this one warning regarding the argumentation of Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who argued that mathematical objects exist in the soul as innate ideas.</note>: he does not seem to rely on good examples when he insists that lines, surfaces, and points must be established in the soul because no pure and separate surfaces, lines, or points exist in sensible things <note>Physical objects perceived by the senses.</note>. And yet, even in the Soul, a line is not pure or self-subsisting; rather, it exists within a mental surface of which it is the boundary, no less than in sensible, corporeal quantities. A mere surface exists at the extremity of a body, a mere line at the extremity of a surface, and a mere point at the end of a line; for the **BEING** of imperfect quantities is to **BE WITHIN** perfect ones.

<margin>
Specific Forms and the Circle.

Logarithmic Sines of Lord Baron Napier.
</margin>
To be sure, mathematical **GENERA** <note>General categories or classes of mathematical objects.</note> are not in the Soul in any way other than all other universals and various concepts abstracted from sensible things. But that one of the mathematical **SPECIES** <note>Specific forms or types; here, Kepler distinguishes the Circle as a primary, innate archetype.</note> which is called the Circle exists in the Soul by a far different reason—not only as an **Idea** of external things, but also as a certain form of the Soul itself. Finally, it serves as the unique storehouse of all Geometric and Arithmetic science. The former is most evident in the teaching of Sines, and the latter in the wonderful business of **Logarithms** <note>Kepler was an early adopter of John Napier’s logarithms, which revolutionized calculation in astronomy.</note>; in these things, having arisen from the circle, there exists a kind of abacus of all multiplications and divisions that can ever be made, as if they were already completed. But enough concerning the Primary faculty of the Soul; let us come now to the lower ones.

<margin>
Concerning the Vital faculty.

Scaliger on Ideas.
</margin>
The vital faculty in Man, therefore, possesses within itself not only Harmonies wrapped in rays of light, but also Harmonies encrusted with the <term>representations<note>original: "speciebus"; the formal images or patterns of things perceived.</note></term> of sounds. Indeed, it drinks in sounds with the ears as its own proper object; but it admits the rays of the stars not as with eyes, but in that same darker manner of perception explained a little earlier, and it examines them against the innate **Ideas** of Harmony. For those things which are seen with the eyes serve the process of reasoning <note>original: "discursui"; the step-by-step logical movement of the mind.</note>; but the recognition of Harmonies is without reasoning. Thus J. C. Scaliger <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a scholar who wrote on the nature of the soul and biological instincts.</note> writes that the idea of the hawk is innate to the young chick—not indeed as a simple idea, but with the mark of a destruction to be avoided.

<margin>
What the stars can do to the vital faculty.

How the tumults of war come from heaven.

How the plague [spreads].
</margin>
From this, therefore, human Souls have the property that near the time of celestial **aspects** <note>The specific geometric angles between planets.</note>, they take up their chief impulses to carry out the business they have on hand. For what a goad is to the ox, a spur or a rhythmic shout to the horse, a drum and a bugle-call to the soldier, an inspiring speech to listeners, or the melody of a pipe, bagpipe, and lute to a crowd of peasants—this is what a celestial configuration of suitable Planets is to all people, and especially to those gathered into one. Thus, each individual is incited in their meditations and works, and everyone becomes more ready to conspire together and join their right hands in alliance. Accordingly, in military affairs, you may see battles, fights, invasions, assaults, conquests, tumults, and Panic terrors generally exist near the times of the Aspects of Mars and Mercury, Jupiter and Mars, the Sun and Mars, Saturn and Mars, etc. In epidemic diseases, more people take to their beds at the time of strong Aspects, or are more severely tormented, or even die. This happens because Nature fails in the struggle with the disease—to which struggle (but not to death) it is incited by the Aspect. All these things are not done by heaven itself without an intermediary; rather, the vital faculty of the Soul, associating its own works with celestial Harmonies, holds the mastery in this—vulgarly called—**influence** of heaven. To be sure, this word "Influence" has bewitched some philosophers, so that...

<margin>CHAPTER VII.</margin>
...they would rather be insane with the foolish crowd than be wise with me. Their chain of reasoning is indeed weak: that the Stars act upon the air, the air upon the temperament of the body, and this in turn upon the Soul. Let this be so in some cases, but what has this to do with an **Aspect** <note>original: "Aspectum"; in astrology, the specific geometric angle between planets, such as 90 or 120 degrees</note>, which is a thing of reason? How shall the element of air capture this, or how shall the body? It cannot, unless each is perceived by its own soul, which perceives the aspect first through itself, in the manner I have just described.

<margin>The vital faculty is a flame.</margin>
I proved in the *Optical Part of Astronomy* <note>Kepler refers to his 1604 work, *Ad Vitellionem paralipomena*, folio 26</note>—by a brilliant comparison of the heart and its reciprocal movements, **Systole** and **Diastole** <note>The contraction and expansion of the heart</note>, with a closed lamp in which the flame must be fostered by oil, ventilation, and the exhaustion of smoke—that this vital faculty is a certain flame, ignited in the heart (and for that reason it dies when its fuel is consumed, while the Mind remains eternal).

<margin>How the birth-chart governs its own affairs, and on what foundation.</margin>
Therefore, that admirable business of **genethlialogy** <note>original: "genethliacum"; the practice of casting birth charts or horoscopes</note> rests primarily upon this property of its essence. For since the vital faculty, ignited in the heart and burning as long as life remains, is a kind of Zodiacal circle; and since its essence consists in energy and a sort of flame-like flux: it follows that the figure of the entire sensible Zodiac flows into that faculty, just then ignited at birth, and becomes deeply ingrained within it (even though the heavens, after the moment of birth, move on to entirely different configurations). In this **animal idea** <note>The "idea" or blueprint belonging to the 'anima' (soul)</note> of the Zodiacal circle, the faculty marks all the positions which the Planets held among the fixed stars, and which the rising, setting, or mid-heaven occupied.

<margin>folios 120, 124</margin>
<margin>Why it is the theme of birth, rather than of conception.</margin>
Beyond all other Astronomical matters, a much greater necessity exists between the radiant Harmonies <note>The geometric relationships of light rays from planets</note> and the first rising and formation of this vital faculty in man. For we have said that every faculty of the Soul is a circle by reason of its essence; but when it acts upon itself by instinct—namely, when it compares its circle with its parts—these are the **archetypal Harmonies**. Now, the vital faculty begins to act and is brought into reality when it is ignited within the lamp of the heart through birth, so that henceforth it has need of respiration to foster the flame of life. Therefore, when it begins to be what it is at that moment, it "architects" the Harmonies for itself; it is then that the sensible radiant Harmony of the Planets flows most strongly into it.

<margin>What Aspects can do in a Birth-chart.</margin>
This is the reason why those who are born at a time of many **Aspects** between the planets usually turn out to be both industrious and hardworking, whether they are accustomed to accumulating wealth from childhood, or are born or chosen as governors of public affairs, or finally, whether they devote themselves to studies. If I seem to anyone to be an example of this kind of life, I have not begrudged him the knowledge of my own birth-chart <note>original: "genesis"</note> in my book *On the New Star* <note>*De Stella Nova* (1606), folio 43</note>, which it is convenient to explain on this occasion as well. I do not care about the charge of boasting; let those people bring charges who condemn this entire genre of writing as folly—whether they be common people in speech or lifestyle, the half-learned, the vendors of titles and trappings intended to deceive the public, or even the "plebeian theologians," as **Pico** <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), who wrote a famous critique of "divinatory" astrology while supporting "mathematical" astrology</note> calls them. Among true lovers of wisdom of any rank, I easily wash away this charge by the utility it offers my reader; for I have explored no one's birth-chart, nor the internal disposition of their mind, as certainly as my own. <margin>CHAPTER VII.</margin>
...the trine <term>Trine: a harmonious astrological aspect where planets are 120 degrees apart</term> of Saturn had passed, while the Sun and Venus joined were flowing away from it and applying to it from both sides; in Sextiles <term>Sextile: an aspect where planets are 60 degrees apart</term>, they were flowing away from the square <term>Square: a challenging aspect where planets are 90 degrees apart</term> of Mars, to which Mercury was closely applying; the Moon was going toward a trine of the same, very near to the Eye of the Bull <note>The star Aldebaran in the constellation Taurus</note>, even in latitude: moreover, 25 degrees of Gemini was rising, and 22 degrees of Aquarius was culminating <note>The highest point in the sky at that moment</note>. The triple partial configuration of that day—the Sextile of Saturn and the Sun, the Sextile of Jupiter and Venus, and the Square of Mercury and Mars—was revealed by a change in the air; for after several days of frost, on that very day a warmth arose, melting the ice and bringing rain.

<margin>An objection against Astrology.</margin>
Nor, however, do I wish to defend and confirm all the aphorisms of Astrologers by this one example; nor do I transcribe the governance of human affairs to the heavens—this philosophical observation is immensely far removed from that folly, or I might say, madness. For to follow the tracks of this very example: I know a woman born with almost the same aspects, certainly of a most restless disposition, but by which she not only makes no progress in letters (this is no wonder in a woman <note>Kepler reflects the social prejudices of his time regarding female education</note>); but she even disturbs her whole town and is the author of her own lamentable misery. First, therefore, in addition to the aspects of the Planets, there was the long-lasting imagination of the pregnant mother, for whom the hearth, my grandmother—studious of popular medicine, which was also practiced by my father—was an object of admiration. Second, there is the fact that I was born a man and not a woman; a distinction of sex which Astrologers seek in the heavens in vain. Third, I derive a temperament of the body from my mother, more suited to studies than to other ways of life. Fourth, my parents' circumstances were not grand; that is, there was no plot of land to which I might be born or to which I might cling. Fifth, there were Schools present, and examples of the generosity of the Magistrates toward boys suited for studies.

<margin>The qualities of the soul agree most with the qualities of the planets.</margin>
Here, interfere again from the Nativity <note>original: "Genesi"; the birth chart</note>, the distinctions of the Planets in their qualities. For if the Soul is a certain light, it will also distinguish by the redness of Mars from the brightness of Jupiter, and the lividness of Saturn. Therefore, it must be confessed that there is great help from Mars, not only, as before, toward industry, but even toward the sharpness of the mind, which consists in fiery force. And you may see the foremost experts in natural Philosophy and Medicine born under suitable aspects of Mars with the Sun and Mercury: because, clearly, greater sharpness and greater skill are required to unearth the secrets of Nature than for the remaining business of life and the studies serving them. I would even grant something more: that it is from Jupiter being elevated in the Midheaven <note>The "Medium Coeli," the highest point of the zodiac at birth</note> that I am more delighted by Geometry expressed in Physical things than by that abstract kind which bears the dryness of Saturn; more, I say, by Physics than by Geometry. And that the gibbous Moon in the bright constellation of the Bull's forehead <note>Taurus</note> fills the imaginative faculty of the Soul with images—many of which I have actually found to be in agreement with the nature of things, as if descending from the Paradigms of Proclus <note>Proclus was a 5th-century Neoplatonist whose works on geometry and philosophy deeply influenced Kepler’s view of the soul</note>. But if I speak now of the outcome of my studies, what further do I find in the heavens, I ask, that alludes even slightly to it? Experts admit that parts of Philosophy, not to be looked down upon, have been either unearthed anew by me, or corrected, or clearly perfected. But here my stars were not Mercury oriental in the angle of the seventh house, in square to Mars: but Copernicus, but Tycho Brahe, without whose books of Observations all things which have now been placed in the clearest light by me would lie buried in darkness. My Lord of Mercury was not Saturn, but the August Caesars, Rudolf and Matthias, my Lords; not the house of the Planets, the Capricorn of Saturn, but Upper Austria, the house of Caesar and his...

<margin>CHAPTER VII.</margin>
Here is that Corner—not the "Occidental Angle" of a Horoscope <term>Angle: in astrology, one of the four cardinal points of a chart; the Occidental Angle is the 7th house, associated with the sunset</term>, but a corner of the Lands—into which I have retired by the grant of the Emperor my Lord, away from a too restless court. In this place, during these years now verging toward the sunset of my life, <margin>No one experiences an individual effect from the stars</margin> I strive to bring forth these *Harmonics* and the other works I have on hand. In vain will an Astrologer seek in my Birth Theme <term>Birth Theme: a horoscope or natal chart</term> the causes for the proportions between the celestial spheres discovered by me in the year 1596; or in the year 1604, the way of seeing <note>Refers to Kepler’s work on optics, *Astronomiae Pars Optica*</note>; or in this year 1618, the causes for why such a degree of Eccentricity fell to each Planet, neither smaller nor larger; or in the intervening years, the demonstration of celestial physics, the ways in which the planets move, and their true motions themselves; or finally, the metaphysical foundations of celestial influence upon these lower things. These things did not flow in with the "character of the heavens" into that little flame of the vital faculty recently ignited and brought into action at my birth. Instead, they partly lay hidden within the innermost essence of the Soul, according to the Platonic doctrine cited above from Proclus <note>Kepler follows the Platonic idea that knowledge is "recollection" of innate geometric truths</note>; <margin>Page 117. General effect of the stars.</margin> partly they were received inward by another way, namely through the eyes. The sole and unique work of the Birth Theme was that it both brightened those little sparks of talent and judgment and incited the mind to tireless labor, and increased the desire for knowledge; in short, it did not inspire the mind, nor any of the faculties mentioned here, but it stirred them up.

<margin>Vain chapters of Astrology.</margin>
From this example, it is easily clear to anyone how far Astrology is from being able to respond exactly—as is commonly proposed in those "chapters"—to questions regarding Parents, Sex, Wealth, Children, the number of Wives, Religion, Profession, Friends, Enemies, Inheritances, Family, Regions, and infinite other things, based on a single Birth Theme alone.

Regarding the length of life, insofar as an Astrologer can pronounce upon it—that is, the power of "directions" <term>Directions: a technique in astrology used to predict the timing of life events</term>—I shall speak a little later. But concerning the Fortune of the one born, I see that something must now be said separately, consistent with what was said above.

<margin>Through what mediating things does human fortune depend to some extent on the stars?</margin>
There are three things on which a man’s fortune seems to rest, as far as natural things go: the Soul, the Physiognomy <note>The physical appearance of the body, believed to reflect character</note> of the body, and the Guardian Spirit. Regarding the first, no one doubts it; the second is more hidden and not so well known to the common people; regarding the third, I can offer nothing but conjectures. We have dealt with the first until now, namely the Soul, from which Character depends; about which the common proverb is well-worn: *Each man is the architect of his own fortune*. In this saying, the sum of this whole part of philosophy is contained. <margin>Character is the architect of fortune.</margin> Come then, let us set before our eyes one type of action and character—previously touched upon by the example of the woman—in place of all others. For human affairs are so arranged that there is always a great abundance of thick-headed and "popularly wise" men, not only among the common people but also among Magistrates and in the sacred order. To these men, the discerning, the critics, and the reformers are annoying and are considered meddlers. Thus, so that one may enjoy a prosperous fortune—I mean that which comes from human society—even if there is an absolute need for right judgment in moral matters and for labor and industry in one's own affairs (which are kept separate from the common crowd), it is nevertheless necessary for some bit of "fatness" <note>Kepler uses "fatness" to mean a lack of intellectual refinement or a common, easy-going nature</note> to be mixed into the soul; it is necessary that his popularity and way of acting be such as to please the thick-headed populace. Souls that are too subtle and restless, unless they betake themselves to some retreat of studies (being despised and held in contempt for this very reason), usually create misfortunes for themselves.

<summary>Kepler argues that his scientific discoveries stem from innate Platonic knowledge and hard work rather than specific astrological influences. He critiques popular astrology's attempt to predict specific life details, asserting instead that character and social temperament are the true "architects" of a person's fortune.</summary>

Therefore, if someone possesses sufficient conjectures from the natal configuration of the heavens regarding the qualities of the Soul, they might also make a not-altogether foolish conjecture regarding the general fortune of a man. Yet, it remains a conjecture alone and nothing more; for indeed, that person can be deceived due to the intervention of many causes, both supernatural and natural. For, to summon another foundation of human fortune from higher things—namely, the dignity of the face—the imagination of mothers contributes much to this in the fetus throughout the entire time of gestation. Thus, the face, the character, and the fortune resting on those foundations of unhappy parents (and likewise of other humans or animals frequently and emphatically encountered by pregnant women) are often transferred to the fetus. 

But nevertheless—as I mentioned above regarding the mental paradigms of Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who argued that mathematical and geometric truths are innate to the soul</note>, which were multiplied into living, moving, and complex things through the ideas of life and motion—so also here this natal character of the heavens is immersed into the appearance of the face through a hidden power of the formative faculty. It is recognized from the face of the newborn by an even more hidden instinct in those who look upon it. You may see that for those born under the conjunctions of several planets before the Sun—which Astrologers call <term>idioprosōpeias: from the Greek for "personal countenances," referring to planets appearing in their own special "faces" or sectors of the zodiac</term>—crowds of common people are drawn to them as if by some charm or fascination. An example of this matter, commended to the memory of all posterity, can be seen in Girolamo Cardano's <note>An influential 16th-century Italian polymath and astrologer</note> nativity of Martin Luther, although many other causes of public upheaval coincided there. Those who are born thus (though no single certain form can be prescribed) are most powerful in authority among the people, in votes in council, and in favor among the Princes of the Republic; their nature indeed corresponds to this. Thus, fortune often stands on the side of the undeserving, even those not endowed with other suitable virtues of the soul. Refer here to the rest of what I said above regarding <term>Physiognomy: the practice of judging a person's character or fortune from their outward appearance, especially the face</term>, and more that could be said.

<margin>
The guardianship of Spirits.
Job 33.

</margin>

Divine oracles <note>Referring here to the Holy Scriptures</note> testify concerning the tutelary Genius <term>Genius: a "tutelary spirit" or guardian angel assigned to a person at birth</term> that a guard is attributed to each individual person, and that they are given both admonition and intercession at the tribunal of God's providence. Here, the nature of sensible things has no possession. If, however, astrologers can predict clearly fortuitous cases (speaking naturally)—that is, such events which happen neither from a man's bad habits, nor from rashness, nor from intemperance of anger or lust, nor depend on the dignity of the face (the two foundations of fortune explained thus far)—then we must look elsewhere. 

Consider a ruler falling from a roof and hitting a passerby; or a stray bullet or arrow hitting someone crawling in the woods; or a sunken ship exposing wretched travelers to the middle of the waves; or one person being extinguished by flames while another is crushed by the ruin of a house or a mountain; and conversely, one person coming into an unexpected inheritance while another finds treasure by chance. If, I say, the natal theme contains signs of these occurrences—which beyond controversy pertain to the duties of the Guardian Angel—it must be that obstacles to this guardianship, as well as opposite promotions, also arise from the natal star. 

<margin>
Whether the evils of fortune depend entirely on the stars?
</margin>

Whether this contains an impious sentiment within it, let the Theologians decide, especially those who write a great number of nativities and prognostications. I have an experience—of what kind, I know not—of two men who, although they were born under the most violent constellations and followed similar habits, so much so that for one of them it was a game...

<summary>Kepler discusses the "foundation of fortune," arguing that a person's life is shaped by their facial appearance (influenced by maternal imagination and the stars) and the interventions of a guardian spirit or "Genius." He questions how much accidental events, like falling objects or sudden wealth, can be attributed to one's astrological birth chart without bordering on impiety.</summary>

# ON THE HARMONICS, BOOK IV #

<sig>* 3</sig>

<margin>CHAPTER VII.</margin>
...it would be like being carried by a leap through precipices and seizing a rope in mid-flight; if he had missed it, his life would already have been over. Yet, they did not seem to have summoned destruction upon themselves by their own rashness: for one of them was struck by lightning, and the other by a lead bullet from a hunter who, lying in wait for wild beasts, had erred in his sight and hearing. 

<margin>
Sins are often the cause of accidental events.
</margin>
Nor do I see how the heavens could do such things to a man—setting aside guardian spirits <note>Kepler uses the term *genios*, referring to the classical idea of a personal guiding spirit or "genius" assigned to a person at birth.</note>—when everything else it is capable of is found to be done through a person's Soul or body (in which there is no inherent power for such accidents). It has happened to me more than once that, after having tormented myself for a long time with pity for certain people who perished by chance and who seemed to me most innocent, I finally learned from trustworthy sources that their lives, compared to others, were such that a good angel might easily be driven away (just as bees are driven off by smoke). In such cases, a man is usually left to blind chance, like a chariot without a driver, as if emancipated from the paternal power of God his Creator and left to his own judgment—or rather, to the tyranny of Satan. Whether something of this sort should also be concluded regarding the examples previously mentioned, and whether those accidents should be attributed to Divine Nemesis <note>original: "Nemesi divinæ," referring to the Greek goddess of retribution or divine justice.</note>, He alone knows who searches hearts: He who visits the iniquity of the fathers upon the sons unto the third and fourth generation. 

<margin>
The deeds of men are not from the sky.
</margin>
Yet, far be it from me to pass the same judgment on all who perish by chance. But such impiety of life cannot be seen by those who divine from the stars; for divine help against the wicked inclinations of souls is not described in the figure of the heavens. After the Fall, the influence of the heavens degenerates into these inclinations—not by corrupting the soul, but by inciting a soul that is already corrupt. Much less are the types of punishment owed for individual sins inscribed in the lividness of Saturn or the redness of Mars as if in the Pandects <note>original: "Pandectis." The Pandects (or Digest) were a massive compendium of Roman law. Kepler is saying the laws of punishment aren't literally written in the colors of the planets.</note>. 

<margin>
Is there some business of the guardian spirit with the client's spirit?
</margin>
Therefore, since there is no immediate natural connection between these things and the heavens, I have publicly offered this for consideration once or twice over these past 20 years: Whether, just as those spiritual overseers of provinces and peoples complain in the ninth chapter of Daniel <note>Kepler likely refers to Daniel 10:13, where the "prince of the kingdom of Persia" resisted the angel.</note> that they are hindered by lurking spirits, so too the guardian spirits of individual men are naturally hindered by the stars. This would prevent them from conveniently resisting the powers of the air—the wicked ones <note>original: "πονηροῖς" (ponērois), Greek for "evil ones" or "wicked spirits."</note> lying in wait for us—and these hindrances might be foreseen from the nativity of the one born. Perhaps this influence affects the Guardian Spirit no less than the soul of the newborn, resulting in some general misfortune for the person. From this comes the proverb: *No calamity comes alone.* Truly, God does not frequently hinder this course of the nature of invisible things, because He knows how to procure some good even from that hindrance of protection—which may result in good for the one in danger if he is pleasing to God, or if he is displeasing, it may fulfill the measure of just vengeance. 

<margin>
Warnings of guardian spirits.
</margin>
Certainly, if the guardian Angel cannot prevent an imminent evil, he at least warns in hidden ways, so that he does not allow his client to perish unprepared. Such omens and warnings even preceded that recent ruin of the mountain among the Rhaetians <note>Kepler refers to the catastrophic landslide of Mount Conto in 1618, which buried the town of Piuro in the Rhaetian Alps.</note>.

***

Let this, then, be the third foundation of a man's fortune, at least by way of 
<margin>
What is the beginning of a man's life in the womb, and of what kind?
</margin>
conjecture, for I affirm nothing. We must now return to the consideration of the Essence of the Vital Faculty of the Soul. For it can be asked: if the character of the heavens only flows in at the exact point of Birth, does the fetus then only conceive the vital faculty of the soul at the moment of birth? And should I say it was soulless before birth? It altogether conceives its own energetic vital faculty only then, in actual fact, when it is separated from the mother. Before that, it was illuminated by the rays of the mother’s vital flame through the umbilical vein and artery...

<margin>
CHAPTER VII.
How does the fetus live before birth?
</margin>
...the artery is inserted into the heart of the fetus, separated from those two passages through which it later—once it is nourishing its own flame of life within—draws blood from one side and air from the lungs on the other. This separate passage of the heart collapses on the first day of life and vanishes entirely, as was shown to me in Prague in a newborn piglet by George Horst <note>Georgius Horstius (1578–1636) was a prominent German physician and researcher.</note>, the Physician to the Landgrave of Hesse and a man most learned in all of nature. From this, I draw the argument that the heart of the fetus, while in the womb, lacks that movement of contraction and expansion <note>original: "systoles & diastoles"</note> just as much as it lacks respiration; consequently, the flame of its own life is not yet lit within it. To lean more firmly on a most faithful analogy: just as the smoke of a wooden roof, toasted by a fire, relates to the flame that suddenly seizes it, so does that which precedes in the fetus relate to the <term>vital faculty<note>Kepler’s term for the animating force that governs biological life and responds to the harmonies of the heavens.</note></term>, which is ignited at birth itself, or shortly before.

<margin>
From where does the power of planetary transits through the places of the Nativity come?
</margin>
In this vital faculty of Man, thus ignited at birth, there shines forth especially that "likeness of Memory" which I also showed above to exist in the Soul of the Earth. So great is the constancy of the celestial character and all parts of the <term>Genethliac Theme<note>The birth chart or horoscope calculated for the exact moment of birth.</note></term>, and so great is its durability in the Soul, that it is not laid down before the end of life. For this faculty is stirred by all the transits of the planets through the primary places of the birth chart, just as if those places were not mere empty images surviving in the soul of things that passed away long ago, but were true stars. Thus, for example, it is as if there were not one Sun in the sky, but two, coming together into one; and by that union, the nature of the vital faculty is stirred in the manner described above.

<margin>
Why are the horoscopes of parents and children related?
</margin>
The clearest evidence of this matter, beyond all exception, is found in the kinship of the horoscopes under which parents are born and those under which their children are born. For when the fetus is mature, the "formative faculty" of the soul, which is in charge of generation, then especially prepares itself to expel the fetus—igniting a new vital faculty of the soul by that expulsion—when the stars have returned to the positions of the mother’s or father’s birth chart, or into the same configurations, reminding the Soul of itself and its own celestial character. See my book *On the New Star*, page 43.

<margin>
Note the natural foundation of Directions.
</margin>
What of the fact that this faculty observes not only the true transits of the planets through the places of the birth chart, but also the successions of the parts of the heaven? It holds the planets that were present at birth in the primary places of the charts that are established once whole days have passed from the birth, observing a proportion of a day to a year (since both revolutions of the Earth are attributed to it by Copernicus). By this proportion, the soul dispenses its works throughout the whole life of the Man: as much as the Year is longer than the Day, so much later does the Effect follow its sign in the <term>direction<note>An astrological technique of "progressing" the birth chart to predict future events; Kepler here attempts to give it a physical/harmonic basis.</note></term>, just as the sign in the direction follows the birth. Thus, this celestial impression does not merely endure while resting, but by enduring, it propagates itself through a motion of extension into the longer periods of life. To be sure, this faculty is not just a circle, but an ideal circular motion, and a double one at that; finally, through motion, it is also an ideal Time. See the words of Proclus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who influenced Kepler's views on mathematics and the soul.</note> above on page 117. We can seek an example of this matter again from Memory, which is a faculty slightly superior to this one. For in a painting, things are depicted only with the circumstance of place; but in memory, past deeds are preserved even with the character of time. Finally, in this business of Directions, the character of positions and movements in time...

<summary>Kepler argues that the "vital faculty" of a human soul is ignited at the moment of birth, creating a permanent internal "memory" of the planetary positions that dictates how the person responds to astrological transits and "directions" throughout their life.</summary>

<margin>
CHAPTER VII.
Whether the length of life or the year of death can be predicted from the stars.
What a "direction" is physically.
The genuine cause of death.
</margin>
Whatever, therefore, Astrologers presume to predict from a <term>theme<note>An astrological chart or horoscope.</note></term> regarding the length of life, it is all condensed into this chapter: with the preludes of <term>Directions<note>A technique in astrology where the positions of planets at birth are "moved" or projected forward in time—often a degree for a year—to predict future events.</note></term> informing the vital faculty as if from the pulpit of the natal theme, showing in which year of life one or another redundant humor ought to be expelled from or stirred up within the body. This is the stimulus of Nature to perform its extraordinary work, which leads to the prolongation of life. There is no death in the stars, in the theme, or in the Direction, while there are various forms of Death: the cause is the matter of the body, which either overwhelms the flame of life by flooding it or deserts it by failing, which hinders the efforts of nature and twists them toward destruction. It is sin that once deprived the human race of the granted remedy of immortality; it is sin that even now drives away, hinders, and repels the Guardian Angel from the protection of life against the attacks of demons, men, and the elements. But this matter would need to be treated at greater length in astrology, and I have discussed it quite thoroughly in the book *On the New Star* <note>original: "de stellâ," referring to Kepler's 1606 work *De Stella Nova in Pede Serpentarii*.</note> ch. 43, and in *The Third Intervenor* <note>original: "Tertio inveniente," referring to his 1610 work *Tertius Interveniens*, where he sought a middle ground between fatalistic astrology and total rejection of the stars.</note> No. 65 and following. And perhaps it will come to pass that I shall publish the books of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola <note>Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494) was a famous Renaissance philosopher who wrote a major critique of astrology.</note> with a commentary, if I understand that I would be doing something pleasing to students of Philosophy, and if I am not destitute of the necessary means.

<margin>
Of the Horoscope or degree of the ascendant in a Nativity.
The Nativity of the World.
</margin>
Now, because I hasten toward the end, I shall subjoin a comparison of the <term>vital faculty<note>Kepler’s term for the animating force that governs biological life and responds to the harmonies of the heavens.</note></term> in man with the Soul of the Earth <note>original: "Anima Telluris"</note>, on account of the influx of the heavens. This seems to be the case: that the Soul of the Earth is a circle such that it has no beginning or end, nor is it knotted at any part of itself; but the vital faculty of man is compared to a circle knotted, as it were, at several points. The reason is that the Soul of the Earth has no natal character, since it always remains the same and is never born or ignited; but the birth of man is recent and close to death, and receives the character of its origin, which punctuates the Zodiac with certain points of beginning and end. And even if you assign a natal character to the Earth from the first day of Creation; nevertheless, the entire expanse of the sky is always open to it; nothing in it has the quality of a beginning or end, of rising or setting. For Man, the surface of the Earth hides half the sky and distinguishes the signs of rising and setting. The reason for the comparison is therefore clear.

<margin>
The foundation of Crises.
What disease is.
</margin>
Indeed, this comparison is so true—of the vital faculty constituted in action being like a circle knotted from certain points—that even at the beginning of a disease (which is like a new life, namely a new energy of the vital faculty or its extraordinary action, natural yet beyond the nature of the usual constitution, striving to expel noxious humor from the body), the place which the Moon possessed flows into the Soul and conceives a force like that of some true Moon, immobile in this its degree. If the true Moon in the sky reaches the square and opposite places of this degree, the Nature of the man is stimulated to struggle with the disease. On this matter rests the <term>doctrine of Crises<note>A medical theory, dating back to Galen and Hippocrates, suggesting that diseases have "critical days" where they reach a turning point, often influenced by the Moon.</note></term>, about which I have written accurately enough in *The Third Intervenor*, No. 70 and following.

<margin>CHAPTER VII.</margin>
Let enough have been said for the present concerning the lower faculty of the human Soul as well, and concerning this entire subject.

Furthermore, I have discussed these things regarding the Soul thus far, certainly not with the intention of drawing students of divine philosophy completely away from the reading of Metaphysical authors. Nor was it my aim to challenge the views <note>original: "oculos configerem" / literally 'to transfix the eyes,' meaning to defy or criticize sharply</note> of so many interpreters of Plato and Aristotle—men of the deepest investigation, whether Greek, Arabic, or Latin; such as Plotinus, Themistius, Simplicius, Porphyry, Alexander, Averroes (and the many of his own nation <note>Kepler refers here to other Islamic/Arabic philosophers cited by Averroes.</note> whom he cites), as well as Boethius, and the most recent and subtle **J. C. Scaliger**, when they dispute about the Soul and about Intelligences. Rather, my goal was to add these observations—drawn from my own profession and from the inner storehouse <note>original: "penu" / a larder or store of provisions</note> of this Harmonic work, and not yet touched upon by them, as far as I know—as a kind of supplement to their considerations. 

My hope is that those who, after me, will devote themselves to this Metaphysical contemplation and read the aforementioned authors, may compare these observations of ours (treating them as experiments) with the reasonings of those masters. By testing both against the file <note>original: "limam" / a tool for polishing or refining an argument</note> of the other through the most free judgment of reason (a task I confess I have by no means performed on this occasion), this part of the science of Metaphysics might finally be established more illustriously, more richly, and more complete in every respect. 

That this may yield to the glory of the Most Blessed Name, God the Creator of things Visible and Invisible, and to the increase of holiness and innocence in the lives of those who contemplate Him, and finally to the eternal salvation of many Souls, I, a suppliant, pray to that very
->Triune God,<-

## THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
### BOOK V.

# CONCERNING THE MOST PERFECT HARMONY
## OF THE CELESTIAL MOTIONS,
and the origin from these of the Eccentricities <note>In astronomy, eccentricity describes how much a planetary orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note>, the Semi-diameters, and the Periodic Times.

I begin a sacred discourse, a most true hymn to God the Creator <note>original: "τῷ δημιουργήσαντι" / the Demiurge or Craftsman</note>, thinking this to be true piety: not that I should sacrifice to him many hecatombs <note>A massive public sacrifice, traditionally of 100 oxen.</note> of bulls, or burn countless scents, perfumes, and cassia; but that first I myself should learn, and afterwards teach others, how great He is in wisdom, how great in power, and of what sort in goodness. For to wish to adorn everything with all possible order, and to begrudge no one His benefits, I establish as a proof of the most perfect goodness; and in this regard let Him be praised by us as Good. But to have discovered how everything might be most beautifully adorned is the height of Wisdom; and finally, to bring into work all that He had determined is the mark of invincible Power.

> I begin a sacred discourse, a most true hymn to God the Creator <note>Kepler provides a Latin translation of the preceding Greek passage by Galen, the famous 2nd-century Greek physician and philosopher.</note>, thinking this to be true piety: not that I should sacrifice to Him many hecatombs of bulls, or burn countless scents and cassia; but that first I myself should learn, and afterwards teach others, how great He is in wisdom, how great in power, and of what sort in goodness. For to wish to adorn all things with as much beauty as possible, and to not begrudge His own goods to any; I establish that as the evidence of the most perfected Goodness; and thus far I celebrate Him as Good. But to discover all things by which they might be most greatly adorned belongs to the most eminent Wisdom; and finally, to bring into actual work all that He had established belongs to Power unsurpassed.

DE MOTIBUS PLANETARUM <note>ON THE MOTIONS OF THE PLANETS</note>

# Preface.

What I first guessed twenty-two years ago, as soon as I had discovered the five regular solids among the celestial spheres <note>Kepler refers to his 1596 work, *Mysterium Cosmographicum*, where he proposed that the distances between planets were determined by the five Platonic solids nested within one another.</note>; what I firmly persuaded myself of in my mind even before I had seen *Ptolemy’s* *Harmonics*; what I promised to my friends in the very title of this fifth book before I was certain of the matter itself; what sixteen years ago I urged should be sought in a published writing; for the sake of which I spent the best part of my life in astronomical contemplations, met with *Tycho Brahe* <note>The preeminent Danish observational astronomer whose data Kepler used to derive his laws.</note>, and chose *Prague* as my seat; this, at last, I have brought to light.

By the grace of God the Best and Greatest—who inspired my mind, excited this great desire, and even prolonged my life and the strength of my intellect, while providing other means through the liberality of two Emperors and the Nobles of this province of *Upper Austria* <note>original: "Austriæ Supr-Anisanæ" / Austria above the river Enns.</note>—I have finally achieved it. Having completed my astronomical duties as much as was sufficient, I have found it to be truer than I ever could have hoped. I have discovered that the entire nature of *Harmony*, in all its magnitude and with all its parts as explained in Book III, is found among the celestial motions—not indeed in the manner I had first conceived in my mind (this being a significant part of my joy), but in another very different, and at the same time most excellent and perfect way.

In this intervening time, while the most laborious restoration of the motions <note>A reference to the years of intense calculation required to determine the orbits of the planets, particularly Mars.</note> held me in suspense, a chief increase in my desire and an incentive for my purpose occurred: the reading of the *Harmonics* of *Ptolemy*. This manuscript was sent to me by that extraordinary man, born to promote philosophy and every kind of erudition, *John George Herwart, Chancellor of Bavaria*. There, beyond expectation and with the greatest admiration, I found that almost his entire third book was spent on this same contemplation of celestial harmony fifteen hundred years ago.

Truly, at that age, much was still lacking in Astronomy; and *Ptolemy*, having attempted the matter unsuccessfully, might have caused others to despair, appearing like *Cicero’s Scipio* <note>A reference to the "Dream of Scipio" in Cicero’s *De Republica*, which describes the music of the spheres as a beautiful but unreachable poetic ideal.</note> to have recited a certain sweet *Pythagorean* dream rather than to have aided philosophy. But I was vehemently confirmed in pursuing my purpose both by that crudeness of ancient Astronomy and by this very agreement of our meditations, exactly aligned across an interval of fifteen centuries. For why use many words? Nature herself intended to reveal herself to men through different interpreters across distant ages. It was the "finger of God"—to speak with the *Hebrews* <note>A biblical idiom (Exodus 8:19) referring to divine intervention or manifest truth.</note>—this identical concept of the conformation of the world in the minds of two men who had devoted themselves entirely to the contemplation of Nature, even though neither had been the other's guide in entering upon this path.

Now, eighteen months after the first light, three months after the true day, and indeed only a few days after the pure Sun of this most wonderful contemplation has shone forth: nothing holds me back. I am free to indulge in sacred frenzy; I am free to taunt mortals with the honest confession that I [am stealing] the vessels <note>original: "vasa" / Part of a metaphor referring to "spoiling the Egyptians," meaning using ancient or secular knowledge for a sacred scientific purpose.</note>

<meta>catchword: vasa (vessels)</meta>

<summary>In this preface, Kepler triumphantly announces that he has finally proven the harmonic structure of the heavens after decades of labor. He notes with wonder that his findings align with the ancient theories of Ptolemy, suggesting a divine hand in the shared discovery across centuries.</summary>

<keywords>Johannes Kepler, Tycho Brahe, Ptolemy, Harmonices Mundi, planetary motion, five regular solids, John George Herwart, celestial harmony, history of astronomy</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: Following the conclusion of his personal narrative in the Preface, Kepler now makes his famous declaration of scientific triumph and provides an overview of the chapters to follow in Book V.</meta>

...stealing the golden vessels of the Egyptians, so that I may construct from them a Tabernacle for my God, far away from the borders of Egypt. If you forgive me, I shall rejoice; if you are angry, I shall endure it. Look, I cast the die, and I write a book to be read either by my contemporaries or by posterity—it matters not. Let it wait a hundred years for its reader, if God Himself has waited six thousand years for someone to contemplate His work. <note>Kepler compares his use of ancient knowledge to the Israelites taking Egyptian gold to build the Tabernacle. He also references the then-common belief that the universe was approximately 6,000 years old, suggesting he is the first to truly understand God's geometric plan.</note>

## The chapters of this book are these:

*I. On the five regular solid figures.* <note>These are the Platonic solids: tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron.</note>
*II. On their kinship with Harmonic proportions.*
*III. A summary of astronomical doctrine, necessary for the contemplation of the celestial harmonies.*
*IV. In which things pertaining to the motions of the Planets the simple Harmonies are expressed, and that all those which are in Song are found in the Heavens.*
*V. That the keys of the Musical Scale, or the locations of the System, and the Genera of Harmonies, the Major and the Minor, are expressed by certain motions.* <note>original: "Durum & Molle" / Hard and Soft. In the musical terminology of Kepler's time, these terms referred to the "hard" B-natural and "soft" B-flat, eventually evolving into our concepts of Major and Minor.</note>
*VI. That the musical Tones or Modes are each expressed in some way by individual planets.*
*VII. That universal Harmonies of all the Planets—and these being diverse, one following another—can exist.*
*VIII. That the natures of the four voices—Soprano, Alto, Tenor, and Bass—are expressed in the Planets.*
*IX. A demonstration that, to obtain this harmonic arrangement, the eccentricities of the Planets must have been established as they are, and not otherwise.*
*X. An epilogue concerning the Sun, from most pregnant conjectures.*

*The Appendix contains: I. A version of the third book of Ptolemy’s Harmonics, starting from chapter III, which treats the same subject.*
*II. A supplement to Ptolemy’s text, in the three final chapters of Ptolemy; for which Ptolemy provided only the titles.*
*III. Notes to this part of the Harmonics, in which I explain and refute the author, and compare either his discoveries or his attempts with my own.*

As I am about to discuss these matters, I am pleased to impress upon my readers the most sacred exhortation of *Timaeus*, the pagan philosopher, as he begins the same subject—an exhortation that Christians ought to acknowledge with the greatest admiration and even shame if they do not imitate it. It is as follows: *“But, O Socrates, all those who possess even a small amount of wisdom always call upon God at the beginning of every undertaking, whether small or great; and for us, who are about to make arguments concerning the UNIVERSE...”* <note>original Greek: "’Αλλ’ ὦ Σώκρατες... ΠΑΝΤΟΣ λόγους ποιεῖσθαι" / Kepler quotes from Plato's Timaeus (27c), emphasizing that scientific study is a form of worship that requires divine guidance.</note>

# CHAPTER I.
## On the five regular solid figures.

<margin>
The circles circumscribed around the angles represent the Spheres, but these must be conceived as slightly larger than those circles—except in figure 5—so that truly all figures may touch the angles. The ratio of magnitude in this diagram was observed so that the sphere of figure 5 can be inscribed in figure 4; the sphere of that one in figure 3; the sphere of that one in 2; and finally the sphere of that one in 1: the Cube, touching all six of its planes at their centers.
</margin>

In the second book, it was stated how regular plane figures might fit together to form solids; specifically, the group of five was demonstrated there. It was also added why they were called "Worldly" <note>or "Cosmic"</note> by the Platonists, and to which Element each one was compared, and because of what property.

<image-desc>A large cube labeled "1." with dashed lines indicating its internal geometry. Below it is a tetrahedron labeled "2." Now, in the entryway of this book, we must again treat these figures for their own sake, and not merely as extensions of plane geometry; at least as much as suffices for the <term>Harmony of the Heavens</term> <note>The idea that the proportions of planetary orbits correspond to musical intervals and geometric perfections.</note>. The reader will find the rest in the second part of the *Epitome of Astronomy*, book four.

Therefore, from the *Secret of the Universe* <note>original: *Mysterium Cosmographicum*, Kepler’s first major work published in 1596.</note>, I briefly reiterate here the Order of the five figures in the World, of which three are primary and two are secondary. For the Cube (1) is the outermost and largest, because it is "first-born" and contains the logic of the Whole by the very form of its generation. The Tetrahedron (2) follows, as if it were a Part established by a section of the Cube, yet it is also primary, having a three-lined solid angle just like the Cube. Inside the Tetrahedron is the Dodecahedron (3), the last of the primary ones, being similar to a figure composed of parts of a Cube that are themselves like Tetrahedrons—that is, from Tetra-

There are, however, two notable "marriages," as it were, of these figures, combined from different classes: The **Males** are the **Cube** and **Dodecahedron** from the primary class; the **Females** are the **Octahedron** and **Icosahedron** from the secondary class; to which is added one that is, as it were, celibate or **Androgynous**, the **Tetrahedron**; because it is inscribed in itself, just as those females are inscribed in and, as it were, subjected to the males, and possess female signs of sex opposite to the male ones—namely, they have angles where the males have planes.

Furthermore, just as the Tetrahedron is the element, the entrails, and as it were the "rib" of the Male Cube; so the Female Octahedron is an element and part of the Tetrahedron, though by another logic: thus the Tetrahedron acts as a mediator in this marriage.

The principal difference between these marriages or families consists in this: that in the Cubic marriage, the proportion is *Expressible* <note>original: *Effabilis*; in geometry, this refers to a ratio that can be stated in rational numbers</note>; for the Tetrahedron is one-third of the Cubic body, and the Octahedron is half of the Tetrahedric body, and a sixth part of the Cube. But the proportion of the Dodecahedric marriage is indeed *Inexpressible* <note>original: *Ineffabilis*; a mathematical term for irrational ratios, specifically the "Golden Ratio" which cannot be expressed as a simple fraction</note>, yet it is *Divine*.

The coupling of these two words warns the reader to be careful regarding their meaning. For the word *Inexpressible* here does not denote some nobility in itself, as it does elsewhere in Theology and divine matters; but it denotes the condition...

# CHAPTER II.

## On the kinship of Harmonic Proportions

->with the five Regular<-
->Figures.<-

This kinship is varied and manifold: there are, however, four primary degrees. For a sign of kinship is either taken from the external appearance alone which the figures have; or the same proportions that are harmonic are born with the very construction of the side; or they result from figures already constructed, either individually or joined; or finally, the proportions of the figures are either equal to or near the proportions of the planetary spheres.

In the first degree, Proportions whose character or greater term is 3 have a familiarity with the Triangular plane of the Tetrahedron, Octahedron, and Icosahedron; those whose greater term is 4 have a familiarity with the Square plane of the Cube; and those with 5 have a familiarity with the Pentagonal plane of the Dodecahedron.

This similarity of the plane can even be extended to the smaller term of the proportion; so that wherever the number three is found next to one of the numbers in a continuous doubling <note>i.e., powers of 2, such as 2, 4, 8</note>, that proportion is considered familiar to the three figures first named...

Likewise 3:5, 3:10, 6:5, 12:5, and 24:5. A relationship will be less probable if the sum of the terms expresses this similarity—as in the ratio 2:3, where the joined terms make 5—as if 2:3 were therefore familiar to the Dodecahedron.

<margin>CHAPTER II.</margin>

There is a similar relationship based on the external appearance of the **solid angle** <note>a vertex where multiple faces meet</note>, which in the primary solids <note>the Cube and Tetrahedron</note> is **three-lined** <note>three edges meet at each vertex</note>, in the Octahedron **four-lined**, and in the Icosahedron **five-lined**. Thus, if one term of a proportion shares a relationship with the number three, the proportion will be related to the primary bodies; if with four, to the Octahedron; and finally, if with five, to the Icosahedron. But in the **female solids** <note>original: "foemellis"; Kepler characterizes the octahedron and icosahedron as "female" because they are contained within the "male" cube and dodecahedron</note> this relationship is more striking, because the shape of the angle is followed by a characteristic figure hidden within: in the Octahedron it is a **Tetragon** <note>a square</note>, and in the Icosahedron a **Pentagon**. Therefore, 3:5, on account of both, would belong to the Icosahedral sect.

The second degree of relationship, which consists in the origin <note>of the figures</note>, is to be understood as follows. First, there are certain **Harmonic** proportions of numbers familiar to one marriage or family—namely, the individual perfect proportions belong to the **Cubic** family. Conversely, there is a proportion that is never expressed in whole numbers, nor demonstrated through numbers in any other way except by a long series of them gradually approaching it. This is called the **Divine proportion** <note>the Golden Ratio</note> when it is perfect; it reigns in various ways through the **Dodecahedral** marriage. Therefore, those harmonies—1:2, 2:3, 3:5, and 5:8—begin to foreshadow <note>original: "adumbrare"</note> that proportion. For it is most imperfectly present in 1:2, and most perfectly in 5:8; it would be even more perfect if we placed 8 over the sum of 5 and 8 (which is 13), were it not that this would cease to be Harmonic.

Furthermore, to establish the side of a figure, the diameter of the Globe <note>the circumscribed sphere</note> must be divided. The Octahedron requires its **bisection**, the Cube and Tetrahedron **trisection**, and the Dodecahedral marriage **quinquisection** <note>division into five parts</note>. The Proportions are therefore distributed among the figures according to these numbers which express them. Truly, the square of the diameter is also divided—or rather, the square of the figure’s side is formed from a certain part of it. And when the squares of the sides are compared with the square of the diameter, they constitute these proportions: the Cubic 1:3, the Tetrahedral 2:3, and the Octahedral 1:2. Wherefore, when joined in pairs, the Cubic and Tetrahedral make 1:2, the Cubic and Octahedral 2:3, and the Octahedral and Tetrahedral 3:4. The sides of the Dodecahedral marriage are **inexpressible** <note>original: "ineffabilia"; irrational magnitudes that cannot be written as a simple fraction</note>.

Thirdly, Harmonic proportions follow the already established figures in various ways. For either the **Number of sides of a face** <note>original: "plani"</note> is compared with the **number of sides of the whole figure** <note>total edges</note>, and these proportions arise: Cubic 4:12 or 1:3; Tetrahedral 3:6 or 1:2; Octahedral 3:12 or 1:4; Dodecahedral 5:30 or 1:6; Icosahedral 3:30 or 1:10. Or the number of sides of a face is compared with the **number of faces**: then the Cube gives 4:6 or 2:3; the Tetrahedron 3:4; the Octahedron 3:8; the Dodecahedron 5:12; and the Icosahedron 3:20. Or the Number of sides or angles of a face is compared with the **number of solid angles** <note>vertices</note>: and the Cube gives 4:8 or 1:2; the Tetrahedron 3:4; the Octahedron 3:6 or 1:2; the Dodecahedron with its Spouse 5:20 and 3:12, which is 1:4. Or the number of Faces is compared with the Number of solid angles: and it gives the Cubic marriage 6:8 or 3:4, and the Tetrahedron...

The bodies are also compared among themselves if a Tetrahedron is hidden within a Cube, or an Octahedron within a Tetrahedron and a Cube, by means of geometric inscription <note>nesting one shape perfectly inside another so their vertices touch the other's faces</note>: the Tetrahedron is a third of the Cube, and the Octahedron is half of the Tetrahedron—a sixth part of the Cube—just as that Octahedron which is inscribed in a globe [sphere] is a sixth part of the Cube that circumscribes that same globe. For the diameter of the Inscribed Orbit is to the diameter of the Circumscribed Orbit in a semitriple proportion <note>the ratio 1 to the square root of 3</note>. And if you compare the proportions themselves, the proportion of the Tetrahedral Orbits is double the proportion of the Cubic orbits <note>meaning the ratio is squared</note>. In the Dodecahedral marriage, the proportion of the orbits is again unique but inexpressible, slightly larger than 4:5. Therefore, let these Harmonics approximate the **Cuboctahedric** <note>related to the Cube and Octahedron</note> proportion of orbits: 1:2 as the nearest larger, and 3:5 as the nearest smaller. To the Dodecahedral proportion of orbits, however, let the Harmonies 4:5 and 5:6 approximate as the nearest smaller, and 3:4 and 5:8 as the nearest larger.

But if, for certain reasons, 1:2 and 1:3 are claimed for the Cube, then the relationship will be as follows: just as the proportion of Cubic orbits is to the proportion of Tetrahedral orbits, so will these Harmonies 1:2 and 1:3 (assigned to the Cube) be to 1:4 and 1:9 (to be assigned to the Tetrahedron), if indeed this analogy must be used. For these proportions are also the doubles of those Harmonies <note>squaring the ratios</note>. And because 1:9 is not harmonic, the nearest Harmony, 1:8, will take its place for the Tetrahedron. For the Dodecahedral marriage, through this analogy, there will come approximately 4:5 and 3:4. For just as the proportion of Cubic orbits is almost the triple of the Dodecahedral ones <note>the ratio cubed</note>, so also the Cubic Harmonies 1:2 and 1:3 are almost the triple of the Harmonies 4:5 and 3:4. For 4:5 tripled [cubed] becomes 64:125, and 1:2 is 64:128. Likewise, 3:4 tripled becomes 27:64, and 1:3 is 27:81.

This is because that author [Brahe] shares in common with Copernicus all other things that pertain to the arrangement of the bodies and the coordination of motions; he only transfers the Copernican annual motion of the Earth into the whole system of planetary spheres and into the Sun, which occupies the center of it, by the consensus of both authors. <margin>Comparison of both.</margin> For from this translation of motion, it nevertheless happens that the Earth—if not in that vast and immense space of the sphere of the fixed stars, then at least in the planetary system of the world—occupies the same place at any given time in Brahe’s system as Copernicus gives to it. Thus, just as one who draws a circle on paper moves the writing foot of the compass around, while one who fastens the paper or tablet to a spinning lathe <note>original: "torno volubili"; Kepler uses this mechanical analogy to show that relative motion produces the same geometric result</note> describes the same circle with an unmoved compass-foot or stylus as the tablet runs beneath it; so also here: for Copernicus, the **Earth measures out a circle** by the real motion of its body, walking in the middle between the circles of Mars on the outside and Venus on the inside. But for Tycho Brahe, the whole planetary system (in which, among others, are also the circles of Mars and Venus) is turned like a tablet on a lathe, applying to the immobile Earth—as if to the stylus of the woodturner—the gap between the circles of Mars and Venus. And it happens by this motion of the system that the Earth marks out in it the same circle around the Sun, intermediate between Mars and Venus, while remaining immobile itself, which it marks out in Copernicus’s system by the true motion of its body while the system rests. Since, therefore, **Harmonic contemplation** considers the <margin>Harmonic contemplation is valid in Brahe's Hypotheses.</margin> eccentric motions of the planets as if seen from the Sun: it is easily understood that if any observer were in the Sun (however mobile it might be), the Earth—however much at rest (if this is now granted to Brahe)—would nevertheless be seen by him to run through its annual circle, intermediate between the planets, and in an intermediate space of time. Therefore, even if there is a man of weak faith who cannot grasp the motion of the Earth among the stars, he may nevertheless enjoy the most excellent contemplation of this most divine mechanism; if, whatever he hears concerning the daily motions of the Earth in its **Eccentric** <note>an orbital path that is not a perfect circle centered on the Sun</note>, he applies that to their appearance from the Sun, which is the same appearance Tycho Brahe displays with the Earth at rest.
    Yet the true cultivators of the **Samian philosophy** <note>original: "Samiæ philosophiæ"; refers to the school of Pythagoras of Samos, whom Kepler associates with the idea of a sun-centered universe</note> have no <margin>It is much more valid in the Copernican [system].</margin> just cause to envy such people the communication of this most delightful speculation: for their joy will be many times more perfect, surely from the consummate perfection of the speculation, if they also accept the immobility of the Sun and the motion of the Earth.

# ON THE MOTIONS OF THE PLANETS

<margin>
**CHAPTER III.**
I. Which bodies' revolutions constitute the Harmonies.
</margin>
First, therefore, let readers keep this in mind: it is today a most certain fact among all astronomers that all the planets revolve around the Sun, with the exception of the Moon, which alone has the Earth for its center. The size of the Moon's orbit or course is not so great that it can be drawn on this page in proper proportion to the others. Therefore, a sixth body, the Earth, is added to the other five; whether it moves by its own motion while the Sun stands still, or is itself unmoved while the entire system of planets is turned around <note>Kepler is referring to the Tychonic system here as an alternative to the Copernican one</note>, the Earth describes a sixth circle around the Sun.

<margin>
II. What diversity exists in the intervals of those bodies.
</margin>
Second, it is also certain that all planets are eccentric; that is, they change their distances from the Sun, so that in one part of their circle they become farthest from the Sun, and in the opposite part they come nearest to it. In the attached diagram <note>original: "schemate"</note>, three circles are drawn for each planet. None of these indicates the actual eccentric path of the planet itself; rather, the middle one—as in the case of Mars, **BE**—is equal to the eccentric orbit in terms of its longer diameter. The orbit itself, however, such as **AD**, touches the upper of the three, **AF**, at one side **A**, and the lower, **CD**, at the opposite side **D**.

<margin>
Refer to the diagram here:
Saturn ♄, Jupiter ♃, Mars ♂, Sun ☉, Venus ♀, Mercury ☿.
</margin>
The circle **GH**, shaded with dots and described through the center of the Sun, indicates the path of the Sun according to **Tycho Brahe** <note>In the Tychonic system, the Sun orbits the Earth while the other planets orbit the Sun</note>. If the Sun moves along this path, then every single point of the entire planetary system depicted here travels an equal path, each according to its own nature. And when one of its points—namely the center of the Sun—stands in one part of its circle (as it does here at the lowest point), every single point of the system will stand in the lowest parts of their respective circles. Due to the narrowness of the space, the three circles of Venus have also run together into one, contrary to my intention.

<margin>
III. What cause determines the number of bodies making the Harmonies.
</margin>
Third, let the reader recall from my *Cosmographic Mystery* <note>original: "Mysterio meo Cosmographico," Kepler's first major work published in 1596</note>, which I published twenty-two years ago: that the number of planets, or orbits around the Sun, was derived by the most wise Creator from the **five regular solid figures**. <note>The "Platonic Solids": the cube, tetrahedron, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron.</note> **Euclid** wrote a book about these so many centuries ago called the *Elements*, so named because it is constructed from a series of propositions. However, that there cannot be more regular bodies—that is, that regular plane figures cannot fit together into a solid more often than five times—was made clear in the second book of this work.

<margin>
IV. The size of the spheres: what cause determines those through which the bodies pass?
</margin>
Fourth, as pertains to the proportion of the planetary orbits, the distance between any two neighboring orbits is always so great that it easily appears that each of them approaches the single proportion of the spheres of one of the five solid figures—namely, the proportion of the **Circumscribed Sphere** to the **Inscribed Sphere** of that figure. Yet, it is not perfectly equal, as I once dared to promise for a finally perfected astronomy. For after a complete demonstration of the intervals based on the observations of **Brahe**, I discovered this: that while the corners of the **Cube**, when applied to the innermost circle of Saturn, almost touch the middle circle of Jupiter with the centers of its planes; and the corners of the **Tetrahedron** resting on the innermost circle of Jupiter almost touch the outermost circle of Mars with the centers of its planes; so too the corners of the **Octahedron**, rising from any circle of Venus (for all three are reduced to a very narrow interval), the centers of the Octahedral planes penetrate and descend deeper, below the circle of Mercury...
