Finally, while the proportions of the Dodecahedral and Icosahedral Orbs <note>The 12-sided and 20-sided regular solids, respectively.</note> are equal to one another, the proportions or intervals between the circles of Mars and Earth, and between the circles of Earth and Venus, are the closest of all, and are similarly equal to each other; this is true if we calculate from the innermost part of Mars to the middle of Earth, and from the middle of Earth to the middle of Venus. For the middle interval of Earth is a Mean Proportional between the minimum of Mars and the middle of Venus. However, these two proportions between the circles of the Planets are still greater than they are in the orbs of those two figures; thus, the centers of the faces of the Dodecahedron do not touch the outermost circle of Earth, nor do the centers of the Icosahedral faces touch the outermost circle of Venus. Yet this gap is not filled by the radius of the Moon’s orbit—which is added above the Earth’s maximum interval and taken away below its minimum. Instead, I have discovered another figural proportion: 
<margin>Page 185</margin>
if indeed the augmented Dodecahedron, which I have named the "Hedgehog" <note>original: "Echino"; this refers to the "Stellated Dodecahedron," a star-like shape Kepler was the first to describe mathematically</note>—formed, that is, from twelve five-cornered stars and thus closest to the five Regular bodies—if this, I say, places its twelve points on the innermost circle of Mars, then the sides of the Pentagons, which are the bases of each of the rays or points, touch the middle circle of Venus. **Briefly**, the Cube and Octahedron, which are partners, penetrate their planetary orbs somewhat; the Dodecahedron and Icosahedron, which are also partners, do not quite reach theirs; the Tetrahedron precisely touches both. In the first case there is less, in the second more, and in the third it is equal in the intervals of the Planets.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;From this fact it is clear that the very proportions of the planetary intervals from the Sun are not taken from the Regular figures alone; for the Creator, the very source of Geometry, and—as Plato wrote—*exercising eternal geometry* <note>original: "æternam exercens Geometriam"</note>, does not wander from His own archetype. Indeed, this very thing could be gathered from the fact that all Planets change their intervals through certain periods of time: so that each one has two notable intervals from the Sun, a Maximum and a Minimum. Between any two Planets, there is a fourfold comparison of their intervals from the Sun: either of the maximums, the minimums, or the opposites (the furthest from each other or the closest). Thus, the comparisons of every two neighboring planets become twenty in number, whereas, on the contrary, there are only five solid figures. But it is surely consistent that the Creator, if He cared for the proportion of the Orbs in general, also cared for the proportion that exists between the varying intervals of each species; and that this care was the same for both, one being linked to the other. Having weighed this, we shall certainly obtain this result: that to establish both the diameters and the Eccentricities <note>The degree to which an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note> of the Orbs together, there is a need for more principles beyond the five regular bodies.

<margin>V. Astronomical axioms of true motions.</margin>

If we assume equal periods of time—say, one natural day on either side—the corresponding true daily arcs of a single eccentric orbit are in *inverse* proportion to their two distances from the Sun. I have also demonstrated that a planet’s orbit is elliptical, and the Sun, the source of motion, sits at one of the foci of this ellipse. <note>This is Kepler's First Law of Planetary Motion.</note> Thus, it happens that when a planet has completed a quarter of its full circuit from its aphelion <note>The point in an orbit furthest from the Sun.</note>, it is at a distance from the Sun that is exactly the mean <note>The average distance.</note> between the maximum distance at aphelion and the minimum at perihelion <note>The point in an orbit closest to the Sun.</note>. From these two axioms, it is established that the mean daily motion of a planet in its eccentric orbit is the same as its true daily arc at those moments when the planet is at the end of the quadrant measured from the aphelion, even though that true quadrant still appears slightly smaller than a "just" or perfect quadrant. It follows further that any two true daily eccentric arcs, equally distant from the aphelion and perihelion respectively, equal two mean daily arcs when joined together. Consequently, since the proportion of circles is the same as the proportion of their diameters, the proportion of one mean daily arc to the sum of all mean daily arcs (which are all equal throughout the circuit) is the same as the proportion of one mean daily arc to the sum of all true daily eccentric arcs, which are equal in number but unequal in size to one another. These facts regarding the true daily arcs of the eccentric orbit and the true motions must be understood beforehand so that we may now understand the apparent motions as seen by an eye positioned at the Sun.

<margin>
VI. Astronomical Axiom of movements as they appear from the Sun, or the angles formed at the center of the Sun by the lines encompassing the daily movements.
2.
</margin>
Sixth, as far as the apparent arcs from the perspective of the Sun are concerned, it has been known since ancient astronomy that among true motions—even if they are equal to one another—the one that is further from the center of the world (such as at the aphelion) appears smaller to a viewer at that center; the one that is closer (at the perihelion) appears larger. Since, in addition to this, the true daily arcs are actually larger when the planet is near the Sun because of its faster motion, and smaller at the remote aphelion because of its slower motion, I demonstrated in my work on Mars <note>original: "Martialibus"; referring to his book *Astronomia Nova*, which focused on the orbit of Mars.</note> that the *proportion of the apparent daily arcs of a single eccentric orbit is quite precisely the inverse square of the proportion of the distances from the Sun.* For example, if a planet on one of its days, when at aphelion, were 10 units away from the Sun, and on the opposite day, when at perihelion, it were 9 units away: it is certain that its apparent advancement from the Sun at aphelion will be to its apparent advancement at perihelion as 81 is to 100. <note>Kepler is explaining that apparent speed changes based on both actual speed and optical distance. If distance is $10:9$, the apparent speed ratio is $9^2:10^2$ or $81:100$.</note>

However, this is true with certain cautions. First, the eccentric arcs must not be too large, so that they do not span vastly different distances—that is, they must not cause a noticeable change in distance from the apsides <note>The two points, aphelion and perihelion, where the planet is furthest or closest to the Sun.</note> between their start and end points. Second, the eccentricity <note>The measurement of how much the elliptical orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note> must not be excessively large. For the greater the eccentricity (or the larger the arc), the more the angle of its appearance increases beyond the simple ratio of its approach to the Sun, *according to Theorem 8 of Euclid’s Optics.* However, in small arcs and at great distances, this is of no consequence, as I noted in Chapter XI of my own *Optics*. But there is another reason why I mention this: the eccentric arcs near the Mean Anomalies <note>The points in the orbit halfway between the closest and furthest points from the Sun.</note> are viewed obliquely from the center of the Sun, and this obliquity diminishes the size of their appearance; meanwhile, the arcs near the apsides are presented directly to the view of someone stationed at the Sun. Therefore, when the eccentricity is very large, the proportion of the movements is sensibly affected...

<margin>VII. Rejection of motions that appear to those looking from the Earth.</margin>
Seventhly, if anyone should happen to encounter those daily motions that do not appear as if from the Sun, but to those looking from the Earth—which are discussed in Book VI of the *Epitome of Copernican Astronomy*—let them know that no account of them is taken in this business. Indeed, it ought not be, since the Earth is not the source of their motion; nor can it be, since those motions degenerate not only into mere rest or apparent stationing, but clearly into retrogradation <note>The "apparent" backward motion of planets as seen from Earth, which Kepler explains as an optical illusion caused by the Earth's own movement.</note> as far as deceptive appearance is concerned. By this reasoning, an infinity of proportions is attributed to all planets simultaneously and equally. Therefore, so that we may hold as certain what kind of proper proportions the daily motions of each true eccentric orbit constitute (even though these are still "apparent" motions, as if to one looking from the Sun, the source of motion), we must first remove from these proper motions this "phantasm" of adventitious annual motion common to all five planets. This phantasm arises either from the motion of the Earth itself, according to Copernicus, or from the annual motion of the entire system, according to Tycho Brahe; then, the proper, clarified motions of each planet must be brought into view.

<margin>VIII. What is the proportion of periodic Times to the intervals of any two from the Sun? 2. 3. 4.</margin>
Eighthly, thus far we have dealt with the different motions or arcs of one and the same planet. Now we must also deal with the motions of two planets compared with each other. Here, note the definition of terms which will be necessary for us. We shall call the *nearest apsides* of two planets the perihelion <note>The point closest to the Sun.</note> of the higher [outer] planet and the aphelion <note>The point furthest from the Sun.</note> of the lower [inner] planet—notwithstanding the fact that they may tend toward parts of the world that are not the same, but different, and perhaps opposite. By *extreme motions*, understand the slowest and the swiftest of the entire planetary circuit. *Converging extreme motions* (or *conversed*) are those at the nearest apsides of two planets: namely, at the perihelion of the higher and the aphelion of the lower. *Diverging* (or *diverse*) motions are those at the opposite apsides: namely, the aphelion of the higher and the perihelion of the lower. Again, therefore, some part of my *Cosmographic Mystery*, suspended twenty-two years ago because it was not yet clear, must be completed here and introduced. For having found the true intervals of the orbits through the observations of Brahe <note>Tycho Brahe, the Danish astronomer whose precise data Kepler used.</note> by the continuous labor of a very long time, at last, at last, the genuine proportion of the periodic times to the proportion of the orbits—*late indeed, she looked upon the idle one* <note>Kepler is quoting Virgil’s *Eclogues*. He is personifying Truth or Discovery as a goddess who finally visited him after years of struggle.</note>—

> Yet she did look, and after a long time she came;

and if you ask for the exact moment, it was conceived in the mind on the 8th of March of this year, 1618, but brought to calculations unluckily, and therefore rejected as false. Finally, returning on the 15th of May with a new impulse, it overcame the darkness of my mind; with such great corroboration from both my seventeen years of labor on Brahe’s observations and this present meditation conspiring into one, that I first believed I was dreaming and assuming the very thing I sought among my first principles. But it is a thing most certain and most exact: **that the proportion which exists between the periodic times of any two planets is precisely the sesquialteral proportion of their mean distances** <note>This is Kepler's Third Law. "Sesquialteral" means a ratio of 3 to 2. In modern terms: the square of the orbital period ($P^2$) is proportional to the cube of the mean distance ($a^3$).</note>, that

For the cube root of 1 is 1, and its square is 1. And the cube root of 30 is greater than 3; therefore its square is greater than 9. And Saturn, at its average distance from the Sun, is a little higher than nine times the average distance of the Earth from the Sun. The use of this Theorem will be necessary below in Chapter IX for the demonstration of the <term>Eccentricities</term> <note>The measure of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note>.

<margin>
IX. How much space any planet traverses relative to another in any given time.
</margin>
Ninthly, if you now wish to measure the very true daily journeys of each planet through the ethereal air <note>original: *aura aetheria*</note> with the same ten-foot rod <note>original: *decempeda*, an ancient Roman measuring tool used here metaphorically as a standard unit of measure</note>, two proportions must be joined: one of the true (not apparent) daily arcs of the Eccentric, and the other of the mean distances of each from the Sun, because that is also the proportion of the size of the orbs. X. How the apparent motion from the Sun—the subject of Celestial Harmony—is obtained from the true journeys and the true distances of the planets from the Sun.
</margin>
Tenthly, so that you may truly have the measure of how much "appearance" <note>apparent speed</note> each of these daily journeys makes to an eye placed, as it were, in the Sun; although this same thing can be sought immediately from Astronomy, it will also be clear if you add to the proportion of the Journeys the inverse proportion of the distances—not the mean distances, but the true ones that exist at any place on the Eccentric orbits: *By multiplying the journey of the higher planet by the distance of the lower from the Sun, and conversely, the journey of the lower by the distance of the higher from the Sun.*

<margin>
XI. How the distances of the Planets from the Sun are elicited from the apparent daily motions (as seen from the Sun).
</margin>
Eleventhly, the proportions of the distances (specifically the <term>Aphelion</term> <note>the point furthest from the Sun</note> of one to the <term>Perihelion</term> <note>the point closest to the Sun</note> of the other, or vice versa) are elicited no less from the given apparent motions. However, in this case, the mean motions must be known beforehand—namely, the inverse proportion of the periodic Times, from which the proportion of the Orbs is elicited through *number VIII* mentioned above. Then, by taking the geometric mean <note>original: *medio proportionali*</note> between either apparent motion and its own mean motion, it happens that as this geometric mean is to the semi-diameter of the orb already revealed, so the mean motion is to the distance or interval sought. For example, let the periodic times of two planets be 27 and 8. Therefore, the ratio of the mean daily motion of the former to the latter is as 8 to 27. Wherefore the semi-diameters of the orbs will be as 9 to 4. For the cube root of 27 is 3, and of 8 is 2; the squares of these roots, 3 and 2, are 9 and 4. Now let the apparent motions be: the Aphelion of one is 2, and the Perihelion of the other is 33 and a third. The geometric means between the mean motions (8 and 27) and these apparent motions will be 4 and 30. If, therefore, the mean of 4 gives a mean distance of the planet of 9, then the mean motion of 8 gives an aphelion distance of 18 (corresponding to the apparent motion of 2). And if the other mean of 30 gives a mean distance of the other planet of 4, then the mean motion of 27 gives its perihelion distance as 3 and three-fifths. I say, therefore, that the Aphelion distance of the former is to the Perihelion distance of the latter as 18 is to 3 and three-fifths. From which it is clear that... <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "impe-"</note>

XII. What the ratio of the Mean Motion is to the extremes.

Twelfthly, it is also possible to find the **Mean Motion** from the different extreme motions of one and the same Planet; for this is not precisely the arithmetic mean <note>The simple average: (a+b)/2</note> between the extreme motions, nor precisely the geometric mean <note>The square root of the product: √(a*b)</note>; but it is as much smaller than the geometric Mean as the geometric Mean is smaller than the mean between both. <note>Kepler is describing a specific, non-linear way of calculating average orbital speed.</note> Let the two extreme motions be 8 and 10. XIII. The knowledge of the ratio of the intervals between two Planets and the Sun together with the ratio of the apparent motions of both of those intervals.

Thirteenthly, from the premises, this **PROPOSITION** is demonstrated (which will be very necessary for us): that just as the ratio of the mean motions in two planets is the **inverse sesquialterate** <note>original: "sesquialtera eversa"; This refers to the relationship where the square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the distance, now known as Kepler's Third Law.</note> of the ratio of the orbits; so the ratio of two **Apparent convergent extreme Motions** <note>The speeds of two different planets when they are at their closest approach to one another—the inner planet at its slowest (aphelion) and the outer at its fastest (perihelion).</note> always falls short of the sesquialterate ratio of the intervals corresponding to those Extreme motions. As long as the two ratios of the two corresponding intervals, joined to the two mean intervals (or to the semidiameters of the two orbits), make less than half of the ratio of the orbits, then the ratio of the two extreme convergent Motions is greater than the ratio of the corresponding intervals. If, however, that sum exceeds half of the ratio of the orbits, then the ratio of the convergent motions would become less than the ratio of their intervals.

Let the ratio of the Orbs be DH to AE, and the ratio of the mean Motions be HI to EM, the inverse sesquialterate of the former. Let the interval there be the minimum of its orb, namely CG, and here the maximum of its own, BF; and let the joined ratios DH to CG, and BF to AE be first smaller than half of the ratio DH to AE. And let the apparent perihelion motion <gloss>us</gloss> of the upper planet be GK, and the aphelion <gloss>us</gloss> of the lower be FL, so that they are the extreme converging motions. I say that the ratio of GK to FL is greater than the inverse ratio of CG to BF; yet smaller than its sesquialterate. For the ratio of HI to GK is double the ratio of CG to DH, and the ratio of FL to EM is double the ratio of AE to BF. Therefore, the two joined ratios, HI to GK and FL to EM, produce double the sum of the ratios CG to DH and AE to BF. But the joined ratios CG to DH and AE to BF are smaller than half the ratio AE to DH, by a certain deficiency, as is assumed; therefore, the joined ratios HI to GK and FL to EM are smaller than double that half—that is, smaller than the whole ratio AE to DH, by double the previous deficiency. But HI to EM is the sesquialterate ratio of AE to DH, by the eighth premise. Therefore, the ratios HI to GK and FL to EM, when subtracted from the sesquialterate ratio HI to EM, leave more than half of the ratio AE to DH, by a doubled excess; they leave, in fact, the ratio GK to FL. Therefore, the ratio GK to FL is more than half the ratio AE to DH, by a doubled excess. But the ratio AE to DH is composed of three: AE to BF, BF to CG, and CG to DH. And CG to DH together with AE to BF is...

And then indeed, the whole eccentrics, when compared with each other, have the same ratio as their semi-diameters, or mean intervals. However, the arcs of two eccentrics, though designated by the same number or name <note>For example, "one degree" on both orbits.</note>, nevertheless have unequal true lengths in proportion to the whole eccentrics. For example, one degree in the sphere of Saturn is nearly twice as large as one degree in the sphere of Jupiter. And conversely, the daily arcs of the eccentrics expressed in astronomical numbers do not show the ratio of the true journeys which the globes complete in one day through the <term>ethereal air</term> <note>original: "aura aetherea"; the subtle fluid once thought to fill space.</note>, because each unit denotes a larger portion of the journey in the wider circle of a superior planet, and a smaller portion in the narrower circle of an inferior planet. All these final values, as you see, shrink away from harmonic proportions and seem similar to <term>irrational numbers</term> <note>original: *ineffabilibus*; in a mathematical context, these are magnitudes that cannot be expressed as a ratio of whole numbers, like the square root of two.</note>. For let the number of days for Mars, 687, take the measure of 120, which is the standard for dividing a musical string; in this measure, for a sixteenth part, Saturn would be a little more than 117; for an eighth part, Jupiter would be less than 95; Earth would be less than 64; for a double part, Venus would be more than 78; and for a quadruple part, Mercury would be more than 61. And yet these numbers do not make any harmonic proportion with 120, though their neighbors—60, 75, 80, 96—do. Likewise, if Saturn is 120, Jupiter is nearly 97, the Earth is above 65, Venus is more than 80, and Mercury is less than 63. And if Jupiter is 120, the Earth is less than 81, Venus is less than 100, and Mercury is less than 78. Likewise, if Venus is 120, the Earth is less than 99 and Mercury is more than 94. Finally, if the Earth is 120, Mercury is less than 116. If a free choice of proportions had prevailed here, entirely perfect harmonies would have been taken, rather than these exceeding and falling short. It is not found, therefore, that God the Creator wished to introduce harmonic proportions among these sums of delays collected into periodic times.

<margin>The proportion of the planetary globes to one another.</margin>
And since it is a most probable conjecture (resting as it does on geometric demonstrations and the doctrine of the causes of planetary motions, handed down in the *Commentaries on Mars* <note>Kepler refers here to his 1609 work *Astronomia Nova*, where he first proposed that physical forces from the sun move the planets.</note>) that the masses of the planetary bodies are in the same proportion as their periodic times, so that the globe of Saturn is about thirty times larger than the globe of Earth, Jupiter twelve times larger, Mars less than double, the Earth one and a half times <note>original: *sesquialtero*</note> larger than the globe of Venus, and four times larger than the globe of Mercury: these proportions of the bodies will not be harmonic either.

Since, however, God has established nothing without geometric beauty, unless it is bound by some law of necessity to something else prior, we easily gather that their specific lengths come to the periodic times—and thus their specific masses to the moving bodies—from something that is prior in the <term>Archetype</term> <note>The divine blueprint or original model in the mind of God.</note>. To express this Archetype, these seemingly disproportionate masses and periods have been fitted into this small measure. But I have said that the periods are collected from "delays" <note>original: *moris*; refers to the time a planet "lingers" in a certain part of its orbit based on its speed.</note>, the longest, the intermediate, and the slowest; it is necessary, therefore, that geometric harmonies be found either in these delays or in something prior to them in the Mind of the Artisan. Indeed, the proportions of the delays are tied to the daily motion of the arcs.

</margin>

Even if, therefore, one interval departs slightly further from the Harmonies, this success was nonetheless an invitation to proceed further. These, then, were my reasonings. First, these intervals, insofar as they are lengths without motion, are not suitably examined for Harmonies, because motion is a subject more familiar to Harmonies, on account of speed and slowness. Next, in these same intervals, insofar as they are the diameters of the Orbs, it is believable that greater consideration was given to the five regular solids <note>Kepler refers to the "Platonic Solids" (cube, tetrahedron, etc.), which he believed defined the spacing between the planetary spheres</note>, by analogy: for whatever ratio exists between solid Geometric bodies and the celestial orbs—whether enclosed on all sides by celestial matter, as antiquity holds, or to be enclosed successively by the accumulation of many rotations—the same exists between the Plane figures inscribed in a circle (which figures produce Harmonies) and the celestial circles of motions, and the other spaces in which motions occur. Therefore, if we seek Harmonies, let us seek them not in these intervals as they are the radii of the Orbs, but in them as they are the measures of motions, that is, in the motions themselves. Truly, no other intervals can be accepted for the radii of the Orbs except the Mean <note>average</note> intervals; yet here we are dealing with the Extreme intervals <note>the furthest and closest points to the Sun</note>. We are not, therefore, dealing with the intervals in respect to their own orbs, but in respect to the motions.

For these reasons, therefore, when I had transitioned to the comparison of extreme motions, at first the proportions of the motions remained the same in magnitude as those of the intervals had been before, only inverted; for which reason some proportions were found among the motions, as before, that were discordant and alien to the Harmonies. I confessed that this happened to me deservedly: since I was comparing the arcs of the <term>Eccentric</term> <note>the off-center circular path used in older astronomy to approximate planetary orbits</note> among themselves, which were neither expressed nor numbered by a measure of the same magnitude, but were counted in degrees and minutes, which are of different magnitudes in different planets; nor do they even produce an appearance anywhere as great as the number of each says, except only at the center of each Eccentric. That center is supported by no physical body, and therefore it is also incredible that there is any sense or natural instinct in that place of the world capable of perceiving this appearance. Indeed, it is even impossible, since I was comparing the eccentric arcs of different planets based on their appearance in their own centers, which different planets hold in different locations. However, different apparent magnitudes, when compared, ought to appear thus in one place of the World, so that whatever has the faculty of comparing them is present in that place of common appearance. Either, therefore, I decided that the appearance of these eccentric arcs must be removed from the mind, or they must be shaped differently. But if I were to remove the appearance and turn my mind to the daily journeys of the Planets themselves, I saw that I must use that rule which I handed down in the previous chapter at Number IX. Therefore, having multiplied the daily arcs of the Eccentrics by the Mean intervals of the Orbs, these journeys were produced.

Therefore, as far as the daily journeys of each planet are concerned, the proportions contained within them must be of the same magnitude as those previously found in the intervals, but inverse in kind: because the arcs of the Eccentric <note>the non-circular path of the orbit</note>, as has been said, have an inverse proportion to their intervals from the Sun.

However, if we consider the extreme journeys of pairs of planets—whether diverging or converging—much less of anything harmonic appears than before, when we were considering the arcs themselves.

And indeed, if we weigh the matter more carefully, it will appear not very likely that the most wise Creator arranged Harmonies primarily between the planetary journeys themselves. For if the proportions of the journeys are Harmonic, then everything else the planets possess will be forced and bound to those journeys, so that there would be no room to arrange Harmonies elsewhere. But for whose good are the Harmonies between journeys; or who will perceive these harmonies? There are two things that reveal harmonies to us in natural things: either light or sound. The former is received through the eyes (or hidden senses analogous to the eyes), the latter through the ears. The mind, taking hold of these forms—either by instinct (of which I spoke abundantly in Book IV) or through Astronomical or Harmonic reasoning—distinguishes the concordant from the discordant. Now, no sounds exist in the heavens, nor is the motion so turbulent that a screech is drawn from the friction of the celestial air <note>original: *aurae coelestis*</note>. Light remains: if this is to teach us about the journeys of the Planets, it will teach either the Eyes, or a sensory organ analogous to them, situated in a certain place; and for light itself to teach immediately by itself, it seems necessary for a sense to be present. There would therefore be a sense in the whole World; specifically, so that one and the same sense may be present for the motions of all the Planets at once. For that path—led from observations through the longest winding ways of Geometry and Arithmetic, through the proportions of the orbits and other things to be learned beforehand, all the way to these very journeys—is too long for any natural instinct, for the sake of moving which it seems reasonable that harmonies were introduced.

Therefore, having brought all these things into a single view, I have correctly concluded that—setting aside the true journeys of the Planets through the ethereal air—we must turn our eyes to the **Apparent daily arcs**. These are the motions that appear from one specific and remarkable location in the World: namely, from the Solar body itself, the fount of motion for all the Planets. We must observe not how far any Planet is from the Sun, nor how great a distance it traverses in a single day (for that is a matter of calculation and astronomy, not something perceivable by the soul's instinct <note>Kepler uses the term *instinguibile* to describe something that can be sensed or felt directly, like a musical harmony, rather than just calculated</note>), but rather what angle the daily motion of each planet subtends at the solar body itself. We look for what arc it appears to complete on a single common circle described around the Sun, such as the Ecliptic, on any given day. In this way, this appearance—conveyed to the body of the Sun by the benefit of light—can flow directly with that light into the creatures who participate in this instinct, just as we said in the fourth book that the celestial configuration <note>original: *schema coeli*</note> flows into the fetus by the benefit of the Sun’s rays.

Therefore, Tychonic astronomy <note>Refers to the system of Tycho Brahe, whose precise observations Kepler used to derive his laws</note> teaches—once the parallaxes of the annual orbit are removed (which give planets the false appearance of standing still or moving backward)—that the daily motions of the Planets in their orbits, as they would appear to someone looking from the Sun, are as follows:

By this ratio, a **Fourth** <note>original: *Diatessaron*</note> is formed most exactly. For a third part of 26 minutes 26 seconds is 8 minutes 49 seconds, four times which is 35 minutes 15 seconds. And note that the harmony of the **Fourth** is found nowhere else among the apparent motions; note also the analogy of the **Fourth** in Harmonies with the **Quarter** <note>original: *Quadra*</note> in the lunar phases. These things, therefore, are found in the motions of individual planets.

These, therefore, are the Harmonies distributed among the planets; nor is there any of the principal comparisons (namely of the converging and diverging extreme motions) which does not come so close to some Harmony that, if strings were stretched in that way, the ears would hardly be able to discern the imperfection—excepting that one excess between **Jupiter** and **Mars**.

You will note, however, that where there is not a perfect Major Harmony, as between Jupiter and Mars, there alone is found a nearly perfect correspondence with the **solid figures** <note>Kepler's earlier theory that the distances between planetary spheres are determined by the five Platonic solids</note>, since the distance of the perihelion of Jupiter is nearly triple the aphelion of Mars; so that this pair affects a perfect Harmony in their intervals which they do not have in their motions. ### CHAPTER V.
## That the Places of the System, or the Keys of the Musical Scale, and the Musical Modes, *Hard* and *Soft*, are Expressed in the Proportions of the Apparent Planetary Motions (as seen from the Sun).

It has been proven so far, through numbers drawn here from Astronomy and there from Harmonics, that Harmonic proportions stand between these twelve terms or motions of the six planets running around the sun—up and down, and in every direction—or are closest to such proportions within an imperceptible part of the smallest Concord. Just as in the third book we first extracted each of the Harmonic proportions separately in the first chapter; then finally in the second chapter, we assembled all of them, as many as there were, into one common System or Musical Scale—or rather, we divided one of them, the Octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note>, which contains the others in power, through those others into its own degrees or Places, and brought it about that it should be a Scale—so now also, having found the Harmonies which God himself incorporated into the World, it follows that we see whether each stands separately so that they have no kinship with the rest, or whether they all agree among themselves? Although it is easy to conclude, even without further inquiry, that these Harmonies were fitted to each other with the highest design <note>original: "summo consilio"</note>, so that they might support each other within a single framework; and that one might not strike out another; since we see that in such a manifold comparison of the same terms, Harmonies occur everywhere. For unless they were all fitted to each other in one Scale, it could easily have happened (and has happened everywhere, necessity so urging) that more dissonances would exist. As if someone

### In the Proportions of the apparent planetary motions (as if seen from the Sun), the Places of the System, or the Keys of the Musical Scale, and the types of song, *Hard* and *Soft*, are expressed.

## CHAPTER VI.

### That the Musical Modes or Tones are in some way expressed in the Extremities of the Planetary Motions.

This follows from what has been said before, nor is there need for many words; for the individual planets mark individual locations of the system. By their perihelion motion, insofar as it is granted to each, they run through a certain interval in the Musical Scale, encompassed by certain Keys <note>original: "Clavibus," the specific notes or pitches</note> or locations of the System; the beginning of each being from that Key or location which happened to be its aphelion motion in the preceding chapter: for Saturn indeed at ♮ <note>B-natural, represented by the symbol ♄</note>, and for the Earth at G, but for Jupiter at B <note>original: "h", the German notation for B-natural</note>, which can be transposed higher into G; for Mars at f, for Venus at e; for Mercury at A, in a higher System. See each one in the customary musical notes. They do not, it is true, form the intermediate locations—which you see here filled with notes—in an articulate way as they do the extremes; because from one extreme, they strive toward the opposite not by leaps and intervals, but by a continuous tension <note>Kepler is explaining that planets don't "jump" from note to note, but slide through all frequencies like a trombone or a singer's glissando</note>, through all the intermediates,

Venus remains almost in a unison, not equaling even the smallest of the consonant intervals <note>intervals that sound pleasing to the ear, like a third or a fifth</note> in the range of its tension.

However, the signature of two keys in the common system, and the formation of the "skeleton" of the Octave through the inclusion of a certain consonant interval, is a sort of first step toward distinguishing the <term>Tones or Modes</term> <note>the precursors to modern major and minor scales, used in Renaissance music</note>; therefore, the Musical Modes are distributed among the planets. I know indeed that for the formation and definition of distinct Modes, more things are required which are proper to human singing (which moves by discrete intervals); and so I have used the word "voice" in a certain sense.

<margin>The Earth sings MI FA MI, so that we may observe from the symbol that even in our own home [original: *MImicilio*, a pun on *domicilio*] we obtain Misery [original: *MIsery*] and Famine [original: *FAmine*].</note>

It will be free, however, for the Harmonist to bring forth his own opinion: which Mode each planet expresses more closely, given the extremes assigned to it here. I would give to Saturn the Seventh or Eighth Mode from those commonly used, because if you place its fundamental key at G, its perihelion motion <note>fastest speed, closest to the sun</note> ascends to *b*. To Jupiter, I would give the First or Second Mode; because when its aphelion motion <note>slowest speed, farthest from the sun</note> is tuned to G, the perihelion reaches *b*. To Mars, the Fifth or Sixth Mode; not only because it nearly achieves a <term>Diapente</term> <note>a perfect fifth</note>, which is an interval common to all modes, but primarily because when it is brought into a common system with the others, its perihelion motion reaches *c* and its aphelion alludes to *f*: which is the root of the Fifth or Sixth Tone. To the Earth, I would give the Third or Fourth Mode: because its motions revolve within a semitone; and truly the first interval of those Tones is a semitone. To Mercury, however, on account of the vastness of its interval, all Modes or Tonics will suit it indiscriminately. To Venus, on account of the narrowness of its interval, clearly none; but in the common system, also the Third and Fourth, because she herself holds the position of *e* with respect to the others.

### ON THE MOTIONS OF THE PLANETS

<margin>
CHAPTER VII.

Would I be committing a crime if I were to demand from each of the modern **composers** a skillfully crafted **Motet** <note>a complex vocal composition popular in the Renaissance</note> for this Eulogy? The Royal Psalter and other Sacred books will be able to supply a suitable text for this. But look here! In the heavens, no more than six planets harmonize; for the **Moon** hums her own **Monody** <note>a solo song</note> separately. The **Earth**, sitting as if on a wedge <note>original: "ut cuneis assidens"</note>—contribute your shares!—I promise to be a diligent curator so that a six-part work may be made. To him who shall express and describe the celestial music more closely, described in this work, the Muse **Urania** promises **Venus** as his bride.
</margin>

The genuine Archetype <note>the original model or "blueprint" used by God</note> of the world’s framework is kept hidden away. Follow me, modern musicians, and judge the matter with your arts, unknown to antiquity: in these last ages, Nature—never anything but lavish with herself—has finally produced you, the first genuine examples of the universe, after a gestation of two thousand years. Through your harmonies of various voices, and through your ears, she has whispered her very self—as she exists in her innermost heart—to the human Mind, the most beloved daughter of God the Creator.

The harmonic proportions that two neighboring planets encompass with the extremes of their motions were explained above. But it happens very rarely that two planets, especially the slowest ones, fall into their extreme intervals at the same time: for example, the **apsides** <note>the points where a planet is closest to or farthest from the sun</note> of **Saturn** and **Jupiter** are distant by about 81 degrees. Therefore, while this distance between them measures out the whole **Zodiac** in certain leaps of twenty years, eight hundred years glide by; yet even the leap that closes the eighth century is not carried precisely to the very same apsides. And if it wanders a little further, another eight hundred years must be waited for, so that a luckier leap might be sought with better calculation; and this must be repeated as many times as the measure of the error is contained in the length of one halved leap. The other pairs also produce such Periods, although they are not as long. In the meantime, however, other harmonies of two planets occur: not between both extremes of motion, but between the intermediate speeds, or one or both of them, as if in different **tensions** <note>the range of pitch or speed a planet "sings" as it moves through its orbit</note>. For because Saturn is stretched from G to B and a little further, and Jupiter from B to D and more, these harmonies above the **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason"</note> can happen between Saturn and Jupiter: both types of **Thirds** and the **Fourth** <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>. One or the other of these occurs through the tension that holds the width of the remainder; this one truly through the width of a major tone. For a Fourth will exist not only from Saturn’s G to Jupiter’s C, but also from Saturn’s A to Jupiter’s D, and through all intermediates between his G and A and the other's C and D. However, the Octave and the **Fifth** <note>original: "Diapente"</note> occur only at the exact points of the apsides. But **Mars**, having obtained a larger internal interval, has achieved this: that it also makes an Octave with the higher planets through some width of tension. **Mercury** has obtained such a great interval that it generally forms all harmonies with all the others within its single period, which is no longer than the space of three months. The **Earth**, on the contrary, and **Venus** much more so, because of the narrowness of their own intervals, restrict their harmonies not only with the others, but especially their mutual harmonies with each other, to a remarkable fewness. <insert>...to this...</insert> But if three planets must agree in one harmony, many cycles must be waited for; yet there are many
<margin>Sign of the world's beginning.</margin>
harmonies, so that they happen all the more easily while each nearest one follows its neighbor. Triple harmonies seem to occur quite frequently among Mars, the Earth, and Mercury. But harmonies of four planets already begin to be scattered across centuries; those of five planets across tens of thousands of years. But that all six should harmonize: that is intercepted by the longest spaces of time, and I do not know if it is utterly impossible for it to happen twice through an exact revolution; rather, it perhaps demonstrates a certain **beginning of Time**, from which every age of the World has flowed.

But if only one single six-fold harmony could occur, or...

...among the many, one is uniquely distinguished; it can undoubtedly be held as the character of the Creation. We must therefore inquire whether, and in how many ways, the motions of all six planets may be reduced to a single common harmony. The method of inquiry is this: we begin with the Earth and Venus, because these two produce no more than two consonances, and (the reason for which is contained in this matter) they do so through very short ranges of motion <note>original: 'intensiones motuum brevissimas', referring to the small difference between their slowest and fastest speeds</note>.

Come then, let us set out two frameworks, like skeletons of the Harmonies, each contained within two extreme numbers (by which the boundaries of the tensions are marked), and let us seek what fits them from the variety of motions granted to each planet. Let the first skeleton have the ratio 3 to 5 between Earth and Venus. And here, with the aphelion of Jupiter and the perihelion of Saturn excluded, the aphelion of Mercury is admitted very nearly, besides the perihelion. The rest remains.

Therefore, astronomical experience testifies that universal harmonies of all motions can occur, and that they are of two genera, Hard and Soft <note>Major and Minor</note>; and in each genus, there are two forms or (if I may say so) Tones; and in any one of these, there are four cases, with some latitude of tension, and even with some variety of the particular harmonies of Saturn, Mars, and Mercury, each with the others. Nor is this achieved by intermediate motions alone, but entirely by all the extremes <note>the fastest and slowest points</note>, except for the aphelion of Mars and the perihelion of Jupiter. Because since the former [Mars] holds the note *f*, and the latter [Jupiter] holds *d*, and Venus perpetually holds the intermediate *e-flat* or *e*, she does not tolerate those dissonant neighbors in a universal harmony—which she would do if she had been granted the space to exceed beyond *e* or *e-flat*. This marriage of Earth and Venus, like that of a husband and wife, possesses this obstacle; these two planets distinguish the genera of Harmonies into the hard and masculine, and the soft and feminine.

Therefore, the motions of the heavens are nothing other than a certain perennial concert (**rational** <note>meaning perceived by the mind or through mathematics</note>, **not vocal** <note>meaning not audible to the human ear</note>) tending toward certain and prescribed musical endings [clausulae] through dissonant tensions, like certain **Syncopations** or **Cadences** (by which humans imitate those natural dissonances). # CHAPTER VIII.

->Who in the celestial concords performs the<-
->role of Soprano, who of Alto, who of Tenor, and<-
->who of Bass?<-

Even though these are names for human voices, and no actual voices or sounds exist in the heavens because of the absolute stillness of their motions; and even though the subjects in which we detect these Harmonies are not even categorized as true motion (since we only consider the motions as they appear from the Sun); and finally, even though there is no such cause in the heavens that would summon a specific number of voices to create Harmony, as occurs in human song; yet, there was first the number of six Planets circling the Sun, derived from the number of five intervals taken from the Regular Solids <note>Kepler refers to the five Platonic solids, which he believed determined the spacing between the six known planets</note>. Only later (in the order of Nature, not of time) was the congruence of their motions established. Nevertheless, I know not how it happens, but this wonderful agreement with human singing exerts such a force upon me that I feel compelled to pursue even this part of the comparison, even without a solid natural cause.

For those properties which common usage attributes to the Bass—and which nature claims for it—as described in Book III, Chapter XVI: these same properties are obtained in a certain way in the heavens by Saturn and Jupiter. Those of the Tenor we find in Mars; those of the Alto are present in the Earth and Venus; and Mercury has those of the Soprano <note>original: *Discanti*, or Treble</note>—if not in the equality of its intervals, then certainly in its proportion. For however much the eccentricities <note>the degree to which an orbit deviates from a perfect circle</note> of each planet are derived from their own specific causes in the following section, and through them, the specific intervals of their motions; yet an admirable result emerges from this—I know not whether it was not likewise arranged, rather than being a purely necessary adjustment:

I. Just as the Bass is set against the Alto, so there are two planets that have the nature of the Alto, and two of the Bass, as if there were one on each side in any kind of musical genre; of the other individual voices, there is one each.

II. Just as the Alto is nearly the highest voice and is constrained in narrow ranges for necessary and natural reasons explained in Book III, so the nearly innermost planets, the Earth and Venus, have the narrowest intervals of motion: the Earth not much more than a semitone, and Venus not even a <term>Diesis</term> <note>a very small musical interval, less than a semitone</note>.

III. And just as the Tenor is free but proceeds moderately, so Mars (with the exception of Mercury alone) can produce the greatest interval, namely a <term>Diapente</term> <note>a perfect fifth</note>.

IV. And just as the Bass makes harmonic leaps, so Saturn and Jupiter obtain harmonic intervals, and they themselves move between each other from a <term>Diapason</term> <note>an octave</note> all the way to a <term>Diapente</term> over a <term>Diapason</term> <note>a perfect twelfth, or an octave plus a fifth</note>.

V. And just as the Soprano <note>original: *Discantus*</note> is the freest, more than all the rest, and also the fastest, so too Mercury can travel through more than a <term>Diapason</term> <note>an octave</note> in a very short revolution.

But let this certainly be by accident; let us now hear the causes of the eccentricities.

## CHAPTER IX.

### The Origin of the Eccentricities in the Individual Planets from the Procurement of the Harmonies among their Motions.

Since we see, therefore, that the universal Harmonies of all six Planets could not occur by chance—especially through the extremes of their motions, which we have seen all converge toward universal Harmonies (except for two, which approached the nearest universal ones); and since it could much less happen by chance that all the locations of the system of the Octave (established in the third book through Harmonic sections) were fixed by the extremes of the planetary motions; and least of all that the most subtle business of distinguishing the celestial Harmonies into two types, major <note>original: *durum*, literally "hard"</note> and minor <note>original: *molle*, literally "soft"</note>, should arise by chance without the singular care of the Architect <note>original: *Opifex*, referring to God as the master craftsman or creator</note>: it follows, therefore, that the Creator—the source of all wisdom, the perpetual upholder of Order, the spring of Geometry and of eternal and super-essential Harmonics—that this very Architect of the heavens, I say, has joined the Harmonic proportions (arising from the regular plane figures) to the five regular solid figures. From both classes, He has formed one most perfect Archetype <note>The "Archetype" is Kepler's term for the original divine blueprint of the universe</note> of the heavens. In this blueprint, just as the Ideas of the orbits carrying the six stars shine forth through the five solid figures, so also through the offspring of the plane figures—the Harmonies deduced from them in the third book—the measures of the Eccentricities <term>Eccentricity: a measurement of how much a planet's elliptical orbit deviates from a perfect circle</term> in the individual orbits might be contained for the sake of proportioning the motions of the bodies. 

From these two things, a single tempering was made: the larger proportions of the Orbits would yield somewhat to the smaller ones of the Eccentricities necessary for procuring the Harmonies; and conversely, from the Harmonic proportions, those would be especially adapted to the Planets which had a greater kinship with each solid figure, insofar as that could be done through Harmonies. By that reasoning, both the proportions of the Orbits and the Eccentricities of each would spring together from the Archetype; and from the size of the Orbits and the mass of the bodies, the periodic Times of each would result.

While I strive to bring this method into the light of human Understanding through the standard geometric proof <note>original: *stœcheiosin*, a Greek-derived term for a systematic demonstration or fundamental arrangement</note> used by Geometers: may the Author of the Heavens himself be favorable, the Father of Understandings, the Giver of mortal senses, himself immortal and thrice-blessed; and may He prevent the darkness of our minds from bringing forth anything unworthy of His Majesty regarding this work of His; and may He bring it about that we, as imitators of God, may emulate the perfection of His works through holiness of life (for which He chose His Church on earth and cleansed it from sins by the blood of His Son) by the help of His Holy Spirit. May we keep far away all the dissonances of enmities, all contentions, rivalries, angers, quarrels, dissensions, sects, envy, provocations, irritations through taunts, and the other works of the flesh—which with me, all who [the spirit of]

->The Prior Reasons.<-

## I. Axiom

It is appropriate that, wherever it was at all possible, all various Harmonies should have been established between the extremes of the motions <note>original: *extrema motuum*; refers to the aphelion (slowest) and perihelion (fastest) points of a planet's orbit</note> as much of the individual planets as of pairs of planets, so that this variety might adorn the world.

## II. Axiom

It was necessary that the five intervals between the six Orbs <note>The "six orbs" refer to the six planets known to Kepler: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> should correspond in size to some degree to the proportions of the geometric spheres which are inscribed in and circumscribed around the five regular solid figures <note>These are the five Platonic solids: Cube, Tetrahedron, Dodecahedron, Icosahedron, and Octahedron.</note>: and this in the same order that is natural to the figures themselves.

->*On this, see Chapter I, the "Mysterium Cosmographicum," and Book IV of the "Epitome of Astronomy."*<-

## III. Proposition.

The intervals between Earth and Mars, and between Earth and Venus, ought to have been the smallest in proportion to their orbits, and nearly equal; those between Saturn and Jupiter, and between Venus and Mercury, should be middling and likewise nearly equal; and the interval between Jupiter and Mars should be the largest.

*For according to Axiom II, those figures which produce the smallest proportion between geometric spheres must likewise produce the smallest proportion for the planets corresponding to them in position; those which correspond to figures of middling proportion produce middling proportions; and those corresponding to the figure of largest proportion produce the largest. But the same order that exists between the Dodecahedron and the Icosahedron exists between the pairs of planets, one of Mars and Earth, the other of Earth and Venus. The same order that exists for the Cube and Octahedron exists for the pair of Saturn and Jupiter and the pair of Venus and Mercury. Finally, the same order that exists for the Tetrahedron exists for the pair of Jupiter and Mars (see Chapter III). Therefore, the proportion between the planetary orbits first mentioned will be the smallest; that between the orbits of Saturn and Jupiter will be nearly equal to that between Venus and Mercury; and finally, the largest will be between the orbits of Jupiter and Mars.*

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>

### IV. Axiom

**A**ll planets must have their own eccentricities <note>The degree to which an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note>, no less than a motion of latitude <note>The movement of a planet north or south of the ecliptic plane.</note>, and according to these, they must also have different distances from the Sun, the source of motion.

*Just as the essence of motion consists not in BEING <note>original: ESSE</note>, but in BECOMING <note>original: FIERI</note>, so also the species or shape of the region which any planet traverses in its motion is not made solid immediately from the beginning. Instead, with the passage of time, it finally acquires not only its length, but also its width and depth, perfecting the triad of dimensions. This happens gradually through the connection and accumulation of many revolutions, so that the shape of a hollow sphere is represented, having the same center as the Sun—just as the little house of a silkworm <note>original: edicula Bombyci</note> is constructed from many circles of silk thread connected and wound together.*

### V. Proposition.

**T**wo different harmonies must be attributed to each pair <note>original: bigæ, literally a two-horse chariot team</note> of neighboring planets.

*For according to Axiom IV, every planet has a longest and a shortest distance from the Sun; therefore, according to Chapter III of this book, it will also have a slowest and a fastest motion. There are, then, two primary comparisons of the extreme motions: one of the Divergent <note>The comparison between the fastest motion of the outer planet and the slowest motion of the inner planet.</note> motions in two planets, and the other of the Convergent <note>The comparison between the slowest motion of the outer planet and the fastest motion of the inner planet.</note> motions. It is necessary that these be different from each other, because the ratio of the divergent motions will be larger, and that of the convergent will be smaller. Furthermore, it was necessary that there be different harmonies for the different pairs of planets, so that this variety might serve to adorn the world (according to Axiom I); and also because there are different ratios of the intervals between pairs (according to Proposition III). To each ratio of the orbits, certain harmonic proportions correspond in quantitative knowledge, as was demonstrated in Chapter V of this book.*

### VI. Proposition.

**T**he two smallest harmonies, 4:5 <note>A Major Third.</note> and 5:6 <note>A Minor Third.</note>, have no place between pairs of planets.

*For 5 to 4 is as 1000 to 800, and 6 to 5 is as 1000 to 833 1/3. But the spheres circumscribed around the Dodecahedron and the Icosahedron have a larger ratio to the inscribed spheres—namely, the ratio of 1000 to 795, etc. These two ratios indicate the intervals between the nearest planetary orbits, or the minimum spaces; for in the other regular figures, the orbits are more distant from each other. Now, the ratio of the motions is even larger than the ratios of the intervals, unless the ratio of the eccentricities to the orbits is immense (according to Chapter III, Number 13). Therefore, the smallest ratio of motions is larger than 4:5 and 5:6. Thus, these harmonies, being hindered by the regular figures, find no place among the planets.*

## VII. Proposition.

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>

### The harmony of a Fourth <note>original: Diatessaron; the interval of 4:3</note> cannot have a place between the convergent motions <note>The closest approach of two planets' speeds: the slowest speed of the outer planet compared to the fastest speed of the inner planet.</note> of two planets, unless the sum of their own individual proportions of extremes <note>The ratio between a single planet's fastest and slowest speeds, caused by its eccentricity.</note> combined is greater than a Fifth <note>original: Diapente; the interval of 3:2</note>.

*For suppose the ratio of 3:4 exists between the convergent motions, and first, let there be no eccentricity—no individual proportion of motions for each planet—so that these same motions are both convergent and Mean <note>Average speed</note>. It then follows, through the logic of Chapter III, that the corresponding intervals (which in this supposition would be the semidiameters of the spheres) would constitute two-thirds <note>original: bessem</note> of this proportion, namely 4480 to 5424. However, this ratio is already smaller than the ratio of spheres for any Regular Solid. Thus, the entire inner sphere would be cut by the planes of the regular figure inscribed in any outer sphere. This, however, is contrary to Axiom II.*

*Secondly, let there be some sum of the individual proportions between the extreme motions. Let the ratio of convergent motions be 3:4 (or 75 to 100), and let the ratio of the corresponding intervals be 1000 to 795, since no regular figure produces a smaller ratio of spheres. Because that inverted ratio of motions exceeds this ratio of intervals by 750 to 795, let this excess also be subtracted from the ratio 1000 to 795 according to the teaching of Chapter III. There remains 9434 to 7950, which is half the ratio of the spheres. Therefore, the double of this—namely 8901 to 6320, or 10000 to 7100—is the ratio of the spheres. Subtract from this the ratio of the convergent intervals, 1000 to 795; there will remain approximately a Major Tone <note>The interval of 9:8</note>, 7100 to 795. This is the minimum required sum of the two proportions that the mean motions have to the convergent motions on both sides for a Fourth to exist between the convergent motions. Therefore, the extreme divergent intervals, compared to the extreme convergent ones, create a sum of proportions approximately double this, which is two Tones; and the convergent motions, in turn, double this again, which is four Tones—this is more than a Fifth. If, therefore, the sum of the individual proportions of two neighboring planets is less than a Fifth, a Fourth cannot exist between their convergent motions.*

## VIII. Proposition.

### To Saturn and Jupiter were owed the Harmonies 1:2 and 1:3, that is, the Octave <note>original: Diapason</note> and the Twelfth <note>original: Diapente epi Diapason; a Fifth above an Octave</note>.

*For these are the first and highest of the planets, and they have obtained the first figure, the Cube, according to Chapter I of this book. These harmonies are the first in the order of nature and are the heads of the primary families of figures: the Bisector or Tetragonal <note>Four-sided, like the cube</note> and the Trigonal <note>Three-sided</note>, as stated in Book I. That which is the head, the Octave (1:2), is nearly greater than the sesquialter <note>3/2 power</note> ratio of the spheres of the Cube; therefore, it is fit to become the smaller proportion of the cubic planets' motions according to Chapter III, Number 13. Consequently, 1:3 serves for the larger proportion. This same point can be shown thus: if any harmony relates to the ratio of the figural spheres as the ratio of motions apparent from the Sun relates to the ratio of the mean intervals, such a harmony is rightly assigned to the motions. But it is natural for the ratio of divergent motions to be much greater than the sesquialter of the ratio of the spheres (as per the end of Chapter III); that is, it approaches the square of the ratio of the spheres. And 1:3 is indeed the square of the ratio of the cubic spheres (which we say is the root of the triple ratio <note>original: Semitriplam</note>). Therefore, the Triple ratio (1:3) is owed to the divergent motions of Saturn and Jupiter. See Chapter II above for many other affinities between these proportions and the Cube.*

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>

## IX. Proposition.

**T**he proper proportions of the extreme motions of Saturn and Jupiter combined ought to have become approximately 2:3, a Fifth <note>original: Diapente</note>.
*This follows from the preceding proposition; for if Jupiter's perihelion <note>The point where a planet is closest to the sun and moving fastest</note> motion is triple the aphelion <note>The point where a planet is farthest from the sun and moving slowest</note> of Saturn, and conversely Jupiter's aphelion is double the perihelion of Saturn, then by removing 1:2 from 1:3, 2:3 remains.*

## X. Axiom.

**W**hen there is a free choice in other respects, the proportion of motions proper to a superior <note>Outer</note> planet is that which is prior by nature, or of a more excellent kind, or even larger.

## XI. Proposition.

**T**he proportion of the aphelion motion of Saturn to its perihelion ought to have become 4:5, a Major Third <note>original: Tertia major</note>; but for Jupiter’s, 5:6, a Minor Third <note>original: Tertia minor</note>.
*For because together they possess a 2:3 ratio, and this is not harmonically divided in any other way except into 4:5 and 5:6: the Harmonizer God <note>original: Harmonostes; Kepler’s term for God as the Architect of Harmony</note> divided the 2:3 harmony harmonically, according to Axiom I. He gave the larger harmonic part, of the more excellent "Hard" <note>original: generis Duri; the Major mode in music, considered "masculine" and more stable in the 17th century</note> genus, to the larger and higher planet Saturn, and the smaller 5:6 to the inferior Jupiter, according to Axiom X.*

## XII. Proposition.

**F**or Venus and Mercury, a Greater Harmony of 1:4 was owed, a Double Octave <note>original: Disdiapason</note>.

The Octahedron is positioned between the paths of the latter; see Chapter III. Therefore, some primary harmony related to the Octahedron is also owed to Venus and Mercury. Furthermore, among the harmonies after 1:2 and 1:3, 1:4 follows in the natural order; it is that cubic-related harmony of 1:2, because it arose from the same Tetragonal <note>Square-based</note> section of figures, and is commensurable with it, being its double. But this is also the reason why 1:4 is given here for the major, not for the minor. But even 1:3 is clearly double the Semi-triple, and thus larger than is proper; how much larger than proper will 1:4 be, since it is larger than 1:3? ->Harmonies were due to the extreme motions of Jupiter and Mars:<-

For because the Cube was allotted 1:2 and 1:3, and the ratio of the spheres of the Tetrahedron—which is situated between Jupiter <note>♃</note> and Mars <note>♂</note>—called Triple [1:3], is double the ratio of the Cube's spheres, called "Sub-triple" [1:$\sqrt{3}$]: therefore it was fitting that the proportions of the motions assigned to the Tetrahedron should also be doubles of the Cubic proportions. Now, the doubles of 1:2 and 1:3 are these proportions: 1:4 and 1:9. But 1:9 is not Harmonic, and 1:4 has already been used for the Octahedron. Therefore, harmonies near to these proportions had to be chosen, according to Axiom I. First, near to 1:9 are the smaller 1:8 and the larger 1:10. Between these, the choice is made by kinship with the Tetrahedron, which has nothing in common with the Pentagon <note>The shape associated with the Dodecahedron and Icosahedron</note>, whereas 1:10 is a division of the pentagonal type. But there is a greater kinship of the Tetrahedron with 1:8 on many accounts, which may be sought from Chapter I. Furthermore, this also supports 1:8: that just as 1:3 is the major harmony of the Cube, and 1:4 the major of the Octahedron, because they are multiples of the proportions between the figures' spheres; so also 1:8 ought to become the major harmony of the Tetrahedron. This is because, as the body of this figure is double that of the Octahedron inscribed within it (as stated in Chapter I), so also the term 8 of this Tetrahedral proportion is double the term 4 of the Octahedral proportion. Additionally, just as 1:2 (the minor of the Cube) is one Octave <note>original: Diapason</note>, and 1:4 (the major of the Octahedron) is two Octaves: so now 1:8 (the major of the Tetrahedron) ought to become three Octaves. More Octaves were due to this than to those, because while the minor Tetrahedral harmony is necessarily the smallest of all the others, the major ratio of the Tetrahedral spheres is the largest of all the figures. Thus, the major Tetrahedral harmony also ought to exceed the others in the number of its Octaves. Finally, the trinity of the Octave intervals has a familiarity with the trigonal <note>triangular</note> face of the Tetrahedron, and possesses a certain perfection, according to the saying, *Everything in threes is perfect* <note>original: Omne trinum perfectum</note>; especially since the number eight, its term, is the first of the cubic numbers of perfect quantity—that is, of three dimensions.

II. Near to 1:4 (or 6:24) are the Harmonies: the major 5:24 and the minor 6:20 (or 3:10). But again, 3:10 is a pentagonal division, which has nothing in common with the Tetrahedron. But 5:24, because of the numbers 3 and 4 (from which the numbers 12 and 24 are descended), has a familiarity with the Tetrahedron. For we neglect the other smaller terms, namely 5 and 3, because their degree of kinship with the figures is very slight, as can be seen in Chapter II. Moreover, the ratio of the Tetrahedron's spheres is Triple; and the ratio of the convergent intervals <note>The gap between the closest points of two planetary orbits</note> ought to be roughly the same, according to Axiom II. But according to Chapter III, the ratio of the convergent motions approaches the inverse of the 3/2 power <note>original: sesquialtera</note> of the intervals; and the 3/2 power of a Triple ratio is approximately between 1000 and 193. Therefore, in a scale where the aphelion motion of Jupiter is 1000, Jupiter's [convergent] motion will be a little more than 193, and much less than 333 (its third part). Therefore, it is not the Harmony 10:3 (which is 1000:333), but the Harmony 24:5 (which is 1000:208) that holds the place between the converging motions of Jupiter and Mars.

### XV. Proposition.

Among the converging motions <note>The "converging motions" refer to the ratio between the fastest speed (perihelion) of the inner planet and the slowest speed (aphelion) of the outer planet</note> of Mars and Earth, Earth and Venus, and Venus and Mercury, the following harmonies had to be distributed: the Fifth (2:3), the Minor Sixth (5:8), and the Major Sixth (3:5); and in that very order.

*For the Dodecahedron and the Icosahedron—the figures located between Mars, Earth, and Venus—have the smallest ratio between their circumscribed and inscribed spheres. Therefore, among the possible harmonies, the smallest ones are owed to them, being related for this reason, and so that Axiom II may hold true. But the very smallest of all harmonies, namely 5:6 <note>a minor third</note> and 4:5 <note>a major third</note>, are not possible according to Proposition VI. Therefore, the harmonies next largest to these are owed to the said figures: namely either 3:4, 2:3, 5:8, or 3:5.*

*Again, the figure located between Venus and Mercury, namely the Octahedron, has the same ratio of its spheres as the Cube. Now, for the Cube, an Octave (1:2) occurred as the minor harmony among the converging motions, as per Proposition VII. Therefore, by analogy, such a large ratio (1:2) would also be owed to the Octahedron for its minor harmony, if no difference were added. But this difference is added: the combined specific ratios of the "Cubic" planets—namely Saturn and Jupiter—produced a sum no greater than 2:3. Here, however, the combined specific ratios of the "Octahedral" planets—Venus and Mercury—will produce a sum greater than 2:3, which is easily seen as follows.*

*For suppose that you required an analogy between the Cube and the Octahedron as if it stood alone; let the Minor Octahedral harmony, I say, be greater than those prescribed here; and thus let it be exactly as large as the Cubic one was, namely 1:2. But the Major was 1:4 according to Proposition XII. Subtracting, therefore, the Minor 1:2 which we just proposed, there remains 1:2 for the sum of the specific ratios of Venus and Mercury. But 1:2 is more than the sum (2:3) of the specific ratios of Saturn and Jupiter. And indeed, from this greater sum, a greater eccentricity follows (according to Chapter III); and from a greater eccentricity, a smaller ratio of converging motions follows (by the same Chapter III). For this reason, by the addition of a greater eccentricity to the analogy between the Cube and the Octahedron, a smaller ratio of converging motions for Venus and Mercury is required than 1:2. It was also consistent with Axiom I that once the Octave harmony was used up by the Cubic planets, another nearby harmony should be assigned to the Octahedral ones—one that is smaller than 1:2, as shown by the previous demonstration. This left the Dodecahedron with either the remaining 2:3 or 3:4; but the former (2:3) is preferred, as it is closer to the Icosahedral 5:8, just as the figures themselves are similar.

# XVI. Proposition.

The proportions of the motions of Venus and Mercury, each their own, joined together ought to produce approximately 5:12.

For if you subtract the smaller harmony of 3:5 <note>a major sixth</note> (commonly attributed to this pair in Proposition XV) from their larger ratio of 1:4 <note>a double octave</note> or 3:12 (as per Proposition XII), there remains 5:12 for the sum of the specific motions of both. Therefore, the specific proportion of the extreme motions of Mercury alone is less than 5:12 by the amount of the specific proportion of Venus. Understand this concerning these first primary ratios. For later, through the secondary ratios, once a certain "leaven" <note>Kepler uses the term "fermento" to describe small adjustments or refinements to the perfect mathematical ratios</note> is added to the harmonies common to both, it will be brought about that the specific motion of Mercury alone perfectly obtains the 5:12 ratio.

# XVII. Proposition.

The harmony of the motions of Mars and Earth, when diverging, could not be less than 5:12.

The smaller harmony between them <note>the converging motions</note> is a Fifth (2:3) according to Proposition XV. Therefore, these two parts joined together make 12:25 <note>In musical math, adding 18:25 and 2:3 is (18/25) × (2/3) = 36/75, which simplifies to 12:25</note>. ## XVIII. Axiom.

Universal harmonies of motions had to be established by the blending of the six motions, especially through the extreme motions <note>The "extreme motions" are the minimum and maximum angular velocities of a planet as seen from the sun</note>.
->Proven by Axiom 1.<-

## XIX. Axiom.

Universal harmonies had to occur within a certain range of motion, so that they might happen more frequently.
> *For if they had been restricted to individual points of motion, it could have happened that they never occurred, or certainly only very rarely.*

## XX. Axiom.

Just as the distinction between the harmonic <term>genera</term>—Hard and Soft <note>In Kepler's time, "Hard" (Durum) and "Soft" (Molle) referred to what we now call Major and Minor scales</note>—is most natural, as proven in Book III; so universal harmonies of both kinds had to be provided between the extreme motions of the planets.

## XXI. Axiom.

Different species of harmonies of both Genera had to be established, so that the beauty of the World might be composed of all possible members of variety; and this was to be done through the extreme motions, or at least some of them.
->Through Axiom 1.<-

## XXII Proposition.

The extreme motions of the planets had to mark the places or strings of the system of the <term>Diapason</term> <note>The Diapason is the Greek term for an octave</note>, or the keys of the musical scale.
