For the origin and comparison of the harmonies starting from one common term generated the musical scale, or the division of the <term>Octave</term> <note>original: Diapason; the interval between two notes where the frequency of one is double the other</note> into its proper places or sounds, as proven in Book III. Since, therefore, various harmonies are required between the extremes of the motions—according to Axioms 1, 20, and 21—it follows that a real distinction of some celestial system or harmonic scale is required through the extremes of the motions.

## XXIII. Proposition.

**It was necessary** for there to be one pair of planets between whose motions no harmonies could exist except for two Sixths: the Major (3:5) and the Minor (5:8).

*For since the distinction of the types <note>original: generum; referring to the "Hard" (Major) and "Soft" (Minor) musical scales</note> of harmonies was necessary, according to Axiom 20, and this distinction is made through the extremes of the motions at the <term>apsides</term> <note>The points in an orbit where a planet is closest to (perihelion) or farthest from (aphelion) the Sun</note> according to Proposition 22; and because only the extremes—namely the slowest and the fastest—require the definition of a provider and an ordainer, the intermediate tensions occur naturally with the very passage of the planet from the slowest motion to the fastest, without special care. Therefore, this ordering could not happen otherwise than by designating a <term>Diesis</term> <note>original: Diesis; a very small musical interval (ratio 24:25) that separates a major scale from a minor one</note> (the ratio 24:25) between the extremes of two planetary motions; this is because the types of harmonies are distinguished by a Diesis, as explained in Book III. However, a Diesis is the difference either between two Thirds (a Major 4:5 and a Minor 5:6) or between two Sixths (a Major 3:5 and a Minor 5:8), or the same intervals increased by one or more Octaves. But two Thirds (4:5 and 5:6) found no place between any pair of planets according to Proposition 6; nor were a Third or a Sixth increased by an Octave found anywhere, except for the 5:12 ratio in the pair of Mars and Earth. Yet even that did not occur except in association with the <term>Perfect Fifth</term> <note>original: 2. 3. (Diapente)</note>; thus the intermediate ratios of 5:8, 3:5, and 1:2 <note>Minor Sixth, Major Sixth, and Octave</note> were likewise admitted. Therefore, it remains that two Sixths, 3:5 and 5:8, had to be given to one pair of planets. But only these Sixths were to be granted to the variation of those motions, so that they would neither expand their boundaries to reach the next larger interval of an Octave (1:2), nor contract to the narrowness of the next smaller interval, the Perfect Fifth (2:3). For even if it is true that two planets—producing a Perfect Fifth with their converging extreme motions and an Octave with their diverging motions—might also produce Sixths and thus pass through a Diesis, this would not reflect the singular providence of the Ordainer of motions. For the Diesis, the smallest of intervals, exists potentially within all larger intervals contained by the extremes of the motions; it is indeed passed through then by the intermediate motions varied by continuous tension; but it is not determined by their extremes, since a part is always smaller than the whole—namely, the Diesis is smaller than the larger interval of 3:4 <note>a Perfect Fourth</note>, which exists between the Perfect Fifth (2:3) and the Octave (1:2), and which whole interval would here be placed as determined by the extremes of the motions.*

## XXIV. Proposition.

**Two planets** that change the type of harmony must make the difference of their own proportions between the extremes of their motions equal to a Diesis; and the proper proportion of one must be greater than a Diesis. Furthermore, they must produce one of the Sixths with their <term>aphelion</term> <note>slowest</note> motions and the other with their <term>perihelion</term> <note>fastest</note> motions.

*For since the extremes of the motions produce two harmonies, differing by a single Diesis...*

...differing <note>Completing the word "differentes" from the previous page</note>, this can happen in three ways: either so that the motion of one planet remains constant while the other's motion varies by a <term>Diesis</term> <note>original: Dieſis; in the music theory of Kepler's time, this was a very small interval, often the difference between a major and minor semitone, with a ratio of about 24:25</note>; or so that both vary by half a Diesis and create a **Major Sixth** (3:5) when the superior planet is at <term>Aphelion</term> <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Sun, where the planet moves slowest</note> and the inferior is at <term>Perihelion</term> <note>The point in an orbit closest to the Sun, where the planet moves fastest</note>; so that once the journey through those spaces is made, meeting each other, with the superior moving toward Perihelion and the inferior toward Aphelion, they create a **Minor Sixth** (5:8). Or finally, that one planet varies its motion more than the other from Aphelion to Perihelion, and the excess is one Diesis; and thus a **Major Sixth** exists between both aphelia, and a **Minor Sixth** between both perihelia. 

The first way, however, is not legitimate; for one of these planets would then be without <term>Eccentricity</term> <note>A perfectly circular orbit</note>, which is against **Axiom IV**. The second way was less beautiful and less convenient; less beautiful because it was less harmonic. For the proportions of the proper motions of the two planets would have been "inconcinnous" <note>discordant or poorly fitted</note>; for anything smaller than a Diesis is inconcinnous. Indeed, it is better for only one planet to suffer from this inconcinnous smallness. Furthermore, it could not even happen; because in this way the extreme motions would have strayed from the "locations" of the system—the keys of the musical scale—against **Proposition XXII**. It would also have been less convenient because the Sixth would have occurred only at those moments when the planets were at opposite <term>apsides</term> <note>The extreme points of the orbit</note>: there would have been no "latitude" <note>a range or margin of error</note> through which these Sixths, and thus the universal harmonies according to them, could have occurred. Universal harmonies would therefore have been extremely rare, with the positions of all the planets reduced to the narrowness of certain and unique points in their orbits; this is against **Axiom XIX**. There remains, therefore, the third way: that each of the planets varies its own motion, but one varies more than the other by at least one perfect Diesis.

## XXV. Proposition.

For the planets that change the harmonic genus <note>meaning they switch the system between "Hard" (Major) and "Soft" (Minor) modes</note>, the superior planet must have a ratio of its own motions smaller than a **Small Tone** (9:10), and the inferior one smaller than a **Semitone** (15:16).

For they will create a 3:5 ratio either with their aphelion motions or their perihelion motions, according to what was stated before. Not with the perihelion motions: for then the ratio of the aphelion motions would be 5:8; the inferior would therefore have a ratio one Diesis greater than the superior, by that same premise. But that is against **Axiom X**. Therefore, they create a 3:5 ratio at aphelion and a 5:8 ratio at perihelion, which is less than the former by a ratio of 24:25 <note>the Diesis</note>. 

But if the aphelion motions create a **Major Sixth** (3:5), then the aphelion of the superior planet with the perihelion of the inferior will create more than a Major Sixth, for the inferior will add its entire proper ratio. In the same way, if the perihelion motions create a **Minor Sixth** (5:8), the perihelion of the superior and the aphelion of the inferior will create less than a Minor Sixth: for the inferior subtracts its entire proper ratio. But if the inferior's own ratio were equal to a **Semitone** (15:16), then in addition to the Sixths, a <term>Diapente</term> <note>A musical Fifth, with a ratio of 2:3</note> could also occur, because a Minor Sixth, when diminished by a semitone, becomes a Fifth; but this is against **Proposition XXIII**. Therefore, the inferior planet has less than a semitone in its own interval. And because the superior's proper ratio is larger than the inferior's proper ratio by one Diesis, and a Diesis added to a Semitone makes a **Minor Tone** (9:10), the superior's proper ratio is therefore less than a Minor Tone (9:10).

## XXVI. Proposition.

For the planets that change the genus of the Harmony <note>Kepler is referring to the shift between Major and Minor scales, which he believes is triggered by the relationship between Earth and Venus</note>, the superior planet <note>Earth</note> ought to have either a **double Diesis** <term>576:625</term> <note>original: Diesin duplicem; an interval approximately equal to two small semitones</note>, which is nearly **12:13**, for the interval between its extreme motions; or a **Semitone** <term>15:16</term>; or something intermediate, differing by a **Comma** <term>80:81</term> <note>The syntonic comma, a tiny interval representing the difference between a major and minor tone</note> from one or the other. The inferior planet <note>Venus</note>, however, ought to have either a **simple Diesis** <term>24:25</term>, or the difference between a Semitone and a Diesis, which is **125:128** (nearly **42:43**); or finally, something similar in the middle, differing by a Comma <term>80:81</term> from one or the other: namely, the former a double Diesis and the latter a simple Diesis, with both intervals diminished by a Comma.

For the proper interval of the superior planet ought to be greater than a Diesis, according to **Proposition XXV**, but smaller than a **Tone** <term>9:10</term> according to the preceding proposition. Furthermore, the superior ought to exceed the inferior by one Diesis, according to **Proposition XXIV**. Harmonic beauty suggests that the proper intervals of these planets—if they cannot be perfectly **Harmonic** due to their smallness—should at least be **Concinnous** <note>original: Concinnis; "fit" or "agreeable" intervals that, while not primary harmonies like an octave or fifth, are used to build scales</note>, if this can be done, according to **Axiom I**. Yet, there are only two concinnous intervals smaller than a Tone <term>9:10</term>: the **Semitone** and the **Diesis**. However, these two do not differ from each other by a Diesis, but by a smaller interval, **125:128**. Therefore, it is impossible for the superior to have a Semitone and the inferior a Diesis at the same time. Instead, either the superior will have a Semitone <term>15:16</term> and the inferior the interval **125:128** (that is, **42:43**), or the inferior will have a Diesis <term>24:25</term> and the superior a double Diesis (nearly **12:13**).

But since both planets have equal rights, if the nature of a Concinnous interval had to be violated in their proper motions, it should be violated equally in both; so that the difference between their proper intervals might remain an exact Diesis, which is necessary for distinguishing the genera of the Harmonies according to **Proposition XXIV**. Now, the nature of the Concinnous interval is violated equally in both if the amount by which the superior's proper proportion fell short of a double Diesis (or exceeded a Semitone) was the same amount by which the inferior's proper proportion fell short of a simple Diesis (or exceeded the interval **125:128**).

Furthermore, this excess or defect ought to be a **Comma** <term>80:81</term>, because once again no other interval was shown by the Harmonic proportions; and so that the Comma might be expressed among the celestial motions just as it is expressed in Harmonics: namely, only by the excess and defect between intervals. For in music, the Comma distinguishes between the Major and Minor Tones, and is known in no other way.

It remains for us to investigate which of the proposed intervals are preferable: whether the simple Diesis for the inferior planet and the double for the superior, or rather the Semitone for the superior and **125:128** for the inferior. The Diesis-based options win by several arguments. For although the Semitone is expressed in various ways in the Musical scale, the ratio **125:128** is not. Conversely, both the Diesis is expressed in various ways, and the double Diesis in a certain way: namely, in the resolution of Tones into Diesis, Semitones, and **Limmas** <note>Small melodic intervals in ancient Greek music theory</note>. For then, as stated in **Book III, Chapter VIII**, two Dieses follow each other very closely in two places. The other argument is that in the distinction of the genera, the rights belong to the Diesis, and none to the Semitone; therefore, greater respect had to be paid to the Diesis than to the Semitone. From all this, it is concluded: the proper interval of the superior <note>Earth</note> ought to be **2916:3125** (or nearly **14:15**); the proper interval of the inferior <note>Venus</note> ought to be **243:250** (or nearly **35:36**).

The question is asked: was the Supreme Creating Wisdom occupied in searching out these thin little reasonings? I respond: it is possible that many reasons escape me. But if the nature of Harmony did not allow for weightier ones,

## XXV. Proposition.

For those planets that change the genus of their harmony <note>shifting between Major and Minor scales</note>, the superior planet must have a ratio of proper motions smaller than a **Small Tone** (9:10), and the inferior planet a ratio smaller than a **Semitone** (15:16).

*For they will create a 3:5 ratio either with their aphelion motions or with their perihelion motions, according to the previous premise. Not with the perihelion motions: for then the ratio of the aphelion motions would be 5:8; therefore, the inferior planet would have a proper ratio one Diesis greater than the superior, by the same premise. But that is against Axiom X. They therefore create a 3:5 ratio at their aphelia, and at their perihelia a 5:8 ratio—which is less than the former by 24:25 <note>the Diesis</note>. Now, if the aphelion motions create a **Major Sixth** (3:5), then the aphelion of the superior planet with the perihelion of the inferior will create more than a Major Sixth, for the inferior will add its entire proper ratio. In the same way, if the perihelion motions create a **Minor Sixth** (5:8), the perihelion of the superior and the aphelion of the inferior will create less than a Minor Sixth, for the inferior takes away its entire proper ratio. But if the proper ratio of the inferior planet equaled a Semitone (15:16), then in addition to Sixths, a **Diapente** <term>3:2; a perfect fifth</term> could also occur, because a Minor Sixth diminished by a semitone becomes a Diapente; but this is against Proposition XXIII. Therefore, the inferior planet has less than a semitone in its own proper interval. And because the proper ratio of the superior is greater than the proper ratio of the inferior by one Diesis, and a Diesis added to a Semitone makes a **Minor Tone** (9:10), the proper ratio of the superior is therefore smaller than a Minor Tone (9:10).*

## XXVI. Proposition.

For the types of planets that change their scale of harmony, the higher planet <note>the one further from the Sun, in this case Earth</note> ought to have either a double **Diesis** <term>a small musical interval; here the ratio 576:625</term>—which is approximately the ratio 12:13—for the interval between its extreme motions, or a **Semitone** (15:16), or something in between, differing from one or the other by a **Comma** <term>the tiny mathematical difference between musical tones, 80:81</term>. The lower planet <note>Venus</note>, however, should have either a single Diesis (24:25), or the difference between a Semitone and a Diesis—which is 125:128 (roughly 42:43)—or finally, something intermediate, differing from these by a Comma. Specifically, the higher planet has a double Diesis and the lower a single Diesis, with both intervals diminished by a Comma.

*For the proper interval of the higher planet must be larger than a Diesis, according to Proposition XXV, but smaller than a Tone (9:10) according to the preceding proposition. Furthermore, the higher planet must exceed the lower by one Diesis, according to Proposition XXIV. The beauty of Harmony suggests that if these proper intervals cannot be perfectly Harmonic because of their smallness, they should at least be among the Concordant intervals, if possible, according to Axiom I. However, there are only two concordant intervals smaller than a Tone (9:10): the Semitone and the Diesis. But these two do not differ from each other by a Diesis, but by a smaller interval (125:128). Therefore, it is impossible for the higher planet to have a Semitone and the lower to have a Diesis at the same time. Instead, either the higher will have a Semitone (15:16) and the lower the ratio 125:128 (roughly 42:43), or the lower will have a Diesis (24:25) and the higher a double Diesis (roughly 12:13). Since both planets have equal rights, as it were: if the nature of Concordance had to be violated in their proper intervals, it had to be violated equally in both. This ensures that the difference between their proper intervals remains an exact Diesis, which is necessary to distinguish the types of harmonies, according to Proposition XXIV. Concordance is violated equally in both if the amount by which the higher planet’s proper ratio falls short of a double Diesis (or exceeds a Semitone) is the same amount by which the lower planet’s proper ratio falls short of a single Diesis (or exceeds the interval 125:128).*

Furthermore, this excess or defect had to be a Comma (80:81), because again, no other interval is demonstrated by Harmonic proportions; and so that the Comma might be expressed among the celestial motions just as it is expressed in Harmonics—namely, only by the excess and defect between intervals. For in music, the Comma distinguishes between the Major and Minor Tones, and is not known in any other way.

*It remains for us to investigate which of the proposed intervals are preferable: a single Diesis for the lower planet and a double for the higher; or rather a Semitone for the higher and 125:128 for the lower. The Diesis arguments win out. For although the Semitone is expressed in various ways in the musical scale, the ratio 125:128 is not. On the contrary, the Diesis is expressed in various ways, and the double Diesis in a certain way—namely, in the resolution of Tones into Diesis, Semitones, and **Limmas** <note>a small Greek interval</note>. For then, as stated in Book III, Chapter VIII, two Diesis follow each other closely in two places. The other argument is that in the distinction of musical scales, the rights belong to the Diesis, not the Semitone; therefore, greater regard had to be given to the Diesis than to the Semitone. From all this, it is concluded: the higher planet's proper interval should be 2916:3125 (nearly 14:15), and the lower planet's proper interval 243:250 (nearly 35:36).*

The question is asked: was the supreme creative wisdom occupied with seeking out these thin little reasonings? I answer that it is possible many reasons escape me. But if the weightier principles of Harmonic Nature did not allow...

### XXVII. Proposition.
The **Major proportion** of the motions of Earth and Venus ought to have been a **Major Sixth** <note>original: "Sexta dura"; a musical interval with the ratio 3:5</note> between their motions at aphelion <note>the point in orbit furthest from the Sun</note>; the **Minor proportion** ought to have been a **Minor Sixth** <note>original: "Sexta mollis"; a musical interval with the ratio 5:8</note> between their motions at perihelion <note>the point in orbit closest to the Sun</note>.

*For it was necessary that the types of Harmonies be distinguished, according to Axiom XX. This, however, could not happen in any other way than through Sixths, according to Proposition XXIII. Therefore, since Earth and Venus—the planets closest to the <image-desc>icosahedron symbol</image-desc> Icosahedral solid, according to Proposition XV—received one of these [Sixths], the 5/8 ratio, it was necessary that the other, the 3/5 ratio, also be distributed. This was not done between the extreme motions (whether converging or diverging), but between the extremes of the same region: one between the aphelia and the other between the perihelia, according to Proposition XXIV. Furthermore, the 3/5 Harmony is related to the Icosahedron, since both belong to the pentagonal division of geometry. See Chapter II.*
Here is the reason why precise Harmonies are found between the motions of these two planets specifically at their aphelia and perihelia, rather than between their "converging" motions <note>the speed of the outer planet at its slowest vs. the inner planet at its fastest</note>, as was the case with the planets discussed previously.

### XXVIII. Proposition.
A proportion of motions of approximately 14 to 15 was suitable for Earth's own motion; for Venus, approximately 35 to 36.

*For these two had to distinguish the different types of musical scales (the "genera" of harmonies), according to the previous proposition. Therefore, by Proposition XXVI, Earth, as the higher planet, ought to obtain the interval 2916 : 3125, which is almost 14 to 15. Venus, as the lower planet, ought to have the interval 243 : 250, which is very nearly 35 to 36.*
Here is the reason why these two planets have such small **Eccentricities** <term>the measure of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle</term>, and consequently small "proper intervals" (the difference between their own maximum and minimum speeds). This is notable because Mars, located just above Earth, and Mercury <note>represented by the symbol $\unicode{x263F}$</note>, located just below Venus, have significant eccentricities—the largest of all the planets. Astronomy confirms this to be true; for in Chapter IV, it was shown that Earth clearly had a ratio of 14 to 15, while Venus had 34 to 35, which astronomical observation can scarcely distinguish from 35 to 36 in the case of this planet.

### XXX. Proposition.

The proper proportion of the motions of Mercury ought to have been made greater than all other proper proportions.

For by Proposition XVI, the combined proper motions of Venus and Mercury had to be about 5 : 12. But the proper interval of Venus by itself is only 243 : 250, which is 1458 : 1500; when this is subtracted from 5 : 12—that is, from 625 : 1500—it leaves 625 : 1458. This is an interval for Mercury alone that is greater than an **Octave with a Major Tone**; meanwhile, the proper interval of Mars, which is the largest among the other planets, is less than a **Sesquialter** 2 : 3, that is, a **Fifth** <term>original: "Diapente"; a 3:2 ratio</term>.

The sum is 4 : 9—that is, 60 : 135; add the Earth’s 14 : 15—that is, 56 : 60; and the accumulation is 56 : 135, which is a little more than 5 : 12, just as the sum of the intervals of Venus and Mercury was. ### XXXI. Proposition.

The motion of the Earth at aphelion <note>the point in orbit furthest from the Sun</note> with the aphelion of Saturn ought to have agreed across some number of Octaves.

For there had to be universal Harmonies, according to Proposition XVIII: therefore, there had to be one between Saturn, Earth, and Venus. Therefore, Saturn ought to have harmonized at both its extremes: at aphelion with one of these two planets, and at perihelion <note>the point in orbit closest to the Sun</note> with the other—since it "grudges nothing" <note>Kepler personifies the planet as being generous with its harmonies</note>, being the first planet. These Harmonies will therefore be either identical in sound <note>original: "Identisonae"; in unison or octaves</note> or different in sound <note>original: "Diversisonae"</note>; that is, of a continuously doubled proportion <note>1:2, 1:4, 1:8, etc.</note> or another proportion. See Book III. Therefore, Saturn could not, by its two motions, make an Octave with the Harmonics falling between 3 and 5. However, since "Identical" harmonies <note>Kepler refers to octaves as "identical" because the notes have the same name in a scale</note> are more excellent, they must be established between the most excellent extremes of motion—namely, between the **aphelia** <term>aphelion: the point where a planet is furthest from the sun and moving at its slowest</term>. These hold the primary position because of the planets' high altitude, and they claim for themselves a certain prerogative over the **Harmony of 3 : 5** <note>a Major Sixth</note>, which we are now discussing as the greater harmony between the Earth and Venus. For although that harmony also fits the perihelion of Venus and a certain intermediate point of the Earth (according to Proposition XXII), the starting point must be from the extremes of motion; intermediate motions come after the principles. 

Now, since on one side we have the motion of Saturn (the highest planet) at its aphelion, we should pair it with the aphelion of the Earth rather than that of Venus. This is because, between these two planets that distinguish the types of harmony, the Earth is the higher one. There is also another, more immediate reason: although the later ratios we are now considering do slightly alter the earlier ones, they do so only by the smallest amounts—specifically, by intervals smaller than the smallest "concordant" interval <term>original: "concinnus"; a musically pleasing ratio</term>. According to those earlier ratios, it was the Earth’s aphelion, not Venus’, that approached several octaves when paired with Saturn’s aphelion. 

Consider the total sum:
1. First, the proper proportion of Saturn's own motions, 4 : 5 (from its aphelion to perihelion, per Prop. XI).
2. Second, the "convergent" ratio of Saturn and Jupiter, 1 : 2 (from Saturn's perihelion to Jupiter's aphelion, per Prop. VIII).
3. Third, the "divergent" ratio of Jupiter and Mars, 1 : 8 (from Jupiter's aphelion to Mars' perihelion, per Prop. XIV).
4. Fourth, the "convergent" ratio of Mars and the Earth, 2 : 3 (from Mars' perihelion to Earth's aphelion, per Prop. XV).

If you combine these, you will accumulate a total proportion of **1 : 30** between Saturn’s aphelion and the Earth’s aphelion. This is only a tiny bit short of **1 : 32**—which is a **Five-fold Octave** <term>original: "Pentakis Diapason"; a ratio of 2 to the power of 5</term>—by no more than the ratio 30 : 32 (which is 15 : 16, or a **semitone**). Therefore, if that semitone is divided into parts smaller than the smallest concordant interval and added to these four elements, the harmony between the aphelia of Saturn and the Earth would be a perfect Five-fold Octave. 

But if we tried to make that same aphelion of Saturn form an octave harmony with the aphelion of Venus, we would have had to tear away nearly an entire **Fourth** <term>original: "Diateſſaron"; a 4:3 ratio</term> from our previous calculations. For if we add the 3 : 5 ratio (the harmony between the aphelia of Earth and Venus) to the 1 : 30 sum produced by the four previous elements, the result between the aphelia of Saturn and Venus is **1 : 50**. This interval differs from the 1 : 32 Five-fold Octave by 32 : 50 (which is 16 : 25, a **Fifth plus a Diesis** <note>a "diesis" is a very small musical interval</note>). It also differs from a **Six-fold Octave** (1 : 64) by 50 : 64 (which is 25 : 32, or a **Fourth minus one Diesis**). Therefore, an "Identical" harmony (an octave) should not be placed between Venus and Saturn, but between the Earth and Saturn, so that a "divergent-sounding" harmony remains for Saturn and Venus.

### XXXII. Proposition.

**In the universal harmonies of the planets in the "Soft" genus, the aphelion motion of Saturn could not exactly agree with the other planets.**

For the Earth, by its aphelion motion, does not contribute to the universal harmony of the **Soft genus** <term>original: "generis Mollis"; equivalent to a Minor scale</term>, because the aphelia of the Earth and Venus create an interval of 3 : 5, which belongs to the **Hard genus** <term>original: "generis Duri"; equivalent to a Major scale</term>, according to Proposition XXVII. Saturn, however, creates an "Identical" harmony (an octave) with its aphelion and the Earth's aphelion, according to Proposition XXXI. Therefore, Saturn does not contribute with its aphelion motion either. Instead, a slightly faster motion of Saturn, very close to the aphelion, takes the place of the aphelion motion to fit the Soft genus, as appeared in Chapter VII.

## Proposition XXXIII.

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>
The **Hard** <note>original: "Durum"; in Renaissance music theory, this corresponds to the Major mode or scale</note> kind of harmonies and musical scale is associated with the **aphelial** motions; the **Soft** <note>original: "Molle"; this corresponds to the Minor mode or scale</note> kind is associated with the **perihelial** motions.

*For although a Hard harmony is established not only between the Earth’s aphelion <term>aphelion: the point where a planet is furthest from the sun and moves at its slowest speed</term> and the aphelion of Venus, but also between the Earth’s motions below its aphelion and the lower motions of Venus, all the way to its perihelion <term>perihelion: the point where a planet is closest to the sun and moves at its fastest speed</term>; and conversely, a Soft harmony is established not only between the perihelion of Venus and the perihelion of the Earth, but also between the higher motions of Venus up to its aphelion and the higher motions of the Earth (according to Proposition XXVII): nevertheless, the proper and evident designation of the musical kind is made only by the extremes of both planets, as shown in Propositions XX and XXIV. Therefore, the proper designation of the Hard kind belongs only to the aphelial motions, and the proper designation of the Soft kind belongs only to the perihelial.*

## Proposition XXXIV.

The Hard kind is more closely associated with the higher of two compared planets; the Soft kind is more associated with the lower planet.

*For because the Hard kind is proper to the aphelial motions and the Soft kind to the perihelial (according to the previous proposition), and since aphelial motions are slower and deeper <note>Kepler associates slower speed with lower musical pitch</note> than perihelial motions, the Hard kind therefore belongs to slower motions and the Soft kind to faster ones. Now, the higher of two planets is more closely associated with slow motions, and the lower planet with fast motions, because in the Universe, a slowness of proper motion always follows a greater height <note>meaning distance from the Sun</note>. Therefore, the higher planet also has a closer affinity to the Hard kind of scale, while the lower planet (both of which adapt themselves to either kind) has an affinity to the Soft kind. Furthermore, the Hard kind uses larger intervals, such as **4:5** <note>a Major Third</note> and **3:5** <note>a Major Sixth</note>, while the Soft kind uses smaller ones, such as **5:6** <note>a Minor Third</note> and **5:8** <note>a Minor Sixth</note>. Since the higher planet also has a larger orbit, slower (that is, larger) motions, and a longer circuit, these "large" characteristics on both sides combine more naturally.*

## Proposition XXXV.

Saturn and Earth embrace the Hard kind more naturally; Jupiter and Venus embrace the Soft kind.

*First, when the Earth is compared with Venus, and both designate each kind of scale, the Earth is the higher planet. Therefore, the Earth chiefly embraces the Hard kind, and Venus the Soft kind, according to the previous proposition. But Saturn, at its aphelion, harmonizes by an **Octave** <term>original: "Diapason"</term> with the aphelion of the Earth, according to Proposition XXXI. Therefore, Saturn also, according to Proposition XXXIII, embraces the Hard kind. Furthermore, Saturn in its aphelial motion favors the Hard kind more and rejects the Soft kind, according to Proposition XXXII. Thus, it has a closer affinity to the Hard kind than the Soft, because musical kinds are properly designated by the extreme motions.*

*Now, regarding Jupiter: in comparison with Saturn, it is the lower planet. Therefore, just as the Hard kind is assigned to Saturn, the Soft kind is assigned to Jupiter, according to the previous proposition.*

<summary>Kepler defines the "Hard" (Major) and "Soft" (Minor) musical modes of the planets, arguing that slower, higher planets (like Saturn and Earth) naturally express Major harmonies, while faster, lower planets (like Jupiter and Venus) express Minor harmonies.</summary>

### Proposition XXXVI

<margin>CHAPTER IX</margin>
The perihelial motion <term>perihelion: the point in a planet's orbit where it is closest to the sun and moves at its fastest speed</term> of Jupiter had to agree with the perihelial motion of Venus within one Musical Scale, but not also in the same Harmony; and this was even less possible with the perihelion of the Earth.

*For because Jupiter was chiefly assigned to the Soft genus <note>original: "generi Molli"; in Renaissance music, this corresponds to the Minor scale</note> according to the previous proposition, and because the perihelial motions are familiar to that genus (according to Proposition XXX), Jupiter therefore had to designate by its perihelion the Scale of the Soft genus—specifically, a certain position or pitch <note>original: "phthongum"; a Greek term for a distinct musical note</note>. But the perihelia of both Venus and the Earth also designate that same Scale (according to Proposition XXVII). Therefore, Jupiter’s perihelion had to be joined in the same pitch [tension] with their perihelia. However, it could not form a Harmony with the perihelion of Venus. For because (according to Proposition VIII) it had to make a ratio of about 1:3 with the aphelion <term>aphelion: the point where a planet is furthest from the sun and moves slowest</term> of Saturn—that is, the note **d** of that system in which Saturn’s aphelion made the note **G** and the aphelion of Venus made the note **e**—it therefore approached the note **e** within the space of the smallest Harmony <note>the "smallest Harmony" refers to a minor third, a ratio of 5:6</note>. This is because that harmony is 5:6, but between **d** and **e** there is a much smaller interval: specifically a 9:10 Tone. And although in the perihelial pitch Venus is raised from the aphelial pitch, this rise is less than a Diesis <note>a "diesis" is a very small musical interval, less than a semitone</note> (according to Proposition XXVIIII). A Diesis (and something even less than it) joined to a minor Tone does not yet equal the interval of the smallest Harmony, 5:6. Therefore, the perihelion of Jupiter could not maintain a ratio of approximately 1:3 with the aphelion of Saturn and simultaneously harmonize with Venus. Nor could it do so with the Earth. For if the perihelion of Jupiter were adjusted to the scale of Venus’s perihelion in the same pitch, so that it maintains an interval of less than the smallest concord with the aphelion of Saturn (distancing itself from Saturn's aphelion by 1:3), it would be distant from the perihelion of Venus by a minor Tone (9:10 or 36:40) toward the Bass. Indeed, the Earth’s perihelion is distant from that same perihelion of Venus by 5:8 (that is, by 25:40). Thus, the perihelia of the Earth and Jupiter would be distant by 25:36 (plus several octaves <note>original: "Diapason"</note>). That interval is not Harmonic: indeed, it is twice 5:6 [a minor third] or one-third of a Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note>, diminished by one Diesis.*

### Proposition XXXVII.

To the sum of the proper Harmonies of Saturn and Jupiter (2:3) and to their common greater harmony (1:3), an interval had to be added that is equal to the interval of Venus.

*For Venus, by its aphelial motion, properly assists the designation of the Hard genus <note>original: "generis Duri"; corresponding to the Major scale</note>, and by its perihelial motion, the Soft genus (according to Propositions XXVII and XXXIII). But Saturn, by its aphelion, also had to agree with the Hard genus, and thus with the aphelion of Venus (according to Proposition XXXV). Jupiter, however, by its perihelion, had to agree with the perihelion of Venus (according to the previous proposition). Therefore, whatever interval Venus makes from its aphelion to its perihelion, that much must also be added to that motion of Jupiter which makes a 1:3 ratio with the aphelion of Saturn, to reach the actual perihelion of Jupiter. But the Harmony of the converging motions of Jupiter and Saturn is exactly 1:2 (according to Proposition VIII). Therefore, when the interval of 1:2 is subtracted from that which is more than 1:3, something remains which is just as much more than 2:3 for the sum of the proper proportions of both planets.*

## XXXVIII. Proposition.

The addition of 243:250 to the sum of the proper motions of Saturn and Jupiter—which until now was established by the primary ratios as 2:3—had to be distributed between the Planets in such a way that a Comma (80:81) was added to Saturn, and the Remainder of 19683:20000 (roughly 62:63) was added to Jupiter.

>*That this had to be distributed between both Planets follows from Proposition XIX, so that both could concur with some latitude in the universal Harmonies of the musical genus familiar to them. However, the 243:250 interval is smaller than all Concinnous <note>original: "Concinnis"; refers to intervals that sound harmonious or "well-tuned"</note> intervals. Therefore, no Harmonic laws remain by which it might be divided into two Concinnous parts, except those used above in Proposition XXVI for the sectioning of the Diesis (24:25); namely, that it should depart into a Comma (80:81, which is one of the primary intervals serving the Concinnous sounds) and into a Remainder (19683:20000, which is slightly larger than a Comma, roughly 62:63). Not two, but one Comma had to be cut off, lest the parts become too unequal, since the proper motions of Saturn and Jupiter are nearly equal. This follows according to Axiom X, even extended to the Concinnous and their smaller parts. At the same time, it is because a Comma is defined by the intervals of the Major Tone and Minor Tone, whereas two Commas are not. Furthermore, to Saturn—the higher and more powerful Planet—was owed not the larger of these parts (even though it had a larger proper ratio of 4:5), but rather that part which is prior and more beautiful: that is, more Harmonic. For in Axiom X, the consideration of priority and Harmonic perfection takes precedence; the consideration of quantity holds the last place, because there is no beauty in quantity for its own sake. Thus, the motions of Saturn become 64:81, an "adulterine" Major Third <note>original: "Tertia major adulterina"; a slightly out-of-tune major third</note>, as we called it in Book III, Chapter XII; while Jupiter’s motions become 6561:8000.*

I do not know whether, among the causes for the Comma added to Saturn, it should be mentioned that the extreme intervals of Saturn could thereby constitute the ratio 8:9, the Major Tone; or whether that resulted spontaneously from the preceding causes of the Motions. You have here, therefore, as a Corollary, the reason why above in Chapter IV, page 195, the intervals of Saturn were found to encompass approximately the ratio of a Major Tone.

>*Since the aphelion of Saturn had to agree exactly with the aphelia of the Earth and Venus according to Proposition XXXI, that motion of Saturn which is more intense than its aphelion by one Major Third (4:5) will also agree with them. For the aphelia of the Earth...*

The motions of the Earth and *Venus* produce a Major Sixth <note>original: "Sextam duram"</note>, which, through the demonstrations in Book III, is divisible into a Perfect Fourth <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note> and a Major Third <note>original: "Tertia dura"</note>. Therefore, the motion of *Saturn*, which is even faster than what has already been agreed upon here, though still below the size of a "Concinnous" <note>An interval that fits naturally within a musical scale</note> interval, will not harmonize exactly. Therefore, the perihelion of *Saturn* does not harmonize exactly. Nor, for that matter, does the aphelion of *Jupiter* exactly: for it sounds with the perihelion of *Saturn*—which is already not harmonizing exactly—through a perfect Octave <note>original: "Diapason"; ratio 1:2</note>, and thus by the statements in Book III, it cannot harmonize exactly itself.

## XL. Proposition.

To the common Harmony of the divergent motions of *Jupiter* and *Mars*—the Triple Octave <note>original: "Trisdiapason"; ratio 1:8</note> established by previous reasoning—it was necessary to add the Platonic Limma.

For because between the aphelions of *Saturn* and the *Earth* there ought to be a ratio of 1:32 (which is 12:384) according to Proposition XXXI; and from the aphelion of the *Earth* to the perihelion of *Mars* there ought to be 3:2 (which is 384:256) according to Proposition XV; and from the aphelion of *Saturn* to its own perihelion 4:5 or 12:15, with the addition from Proposition XXXVIII; and finally, from the perihelion of *Saturn* to the aphelion of *Jupiter* 1:2 or 15:30 according to Proposition VIII: there remains, therefore, from the aphelion of *Jupiter* to the perihelion of *Mars* a ratio of 30:256, once *Saturn’s* addition is removed. Now, 30:256 is exceeded by 32:256 (which is 1:8) by the amount of 30:32, which is 15:16 or 240:256, a Semitone. Therefore, subtracting *Saturn's* addition—which according to Proposition XXXVIII ought to be 80:81 (or 240:243)—from this 240:256 leaves 243:256. That value is the Platonic Limma <note>A small mathematical interval used in Greek tuning, approximately 19:20</note>; see Book III. Thus, the Platonic Limma had to be added to the 1:8 ratio.

Consequently, the larger proportion of *Jupiter* and *Mars*—that is, of their divergent motions—must be 243:2048, which is somewhat in the middle between 243:2137 and 243:1944 (that is, between 1:9 and 1:8). The former was required by Analogy above, while the latter was closer to Harmonic suitability.

If [the interval of] Venus between the <term>aphelion: the point in an orbit farthest from the Sun</term> of Mars were a perfect <term>Minor Sixth: an interval of a sixth in a minor key</term> above a <term>Double Octave: an interval spanning two full octaves</term>, and not indeed deficient according to Proposition XIII, it follows that Mars marks a place with its aphelion motion which is one <term>comma: a very small musical interval, roughly 1/9th of a whole tone</term> higher than the genuine key. ->In the same way, it will be proven that the aphelion of Mars also disagrees with the motions of the Earth.<-

For because it makes a Semitone and a Comma with the perihelion of Venus, according to what has been said—that is, 14:15—but the perihelia of the Earth and Venus make a Minor Sixth, 5:8 or 15:24, according to Proposition XXVII; the aphelion of Mars with the perihelion of the Earth (adding octaves to it) will therefore make 14:24 or 7:12, a discordant interval, far from being Harmonic like 5:6 and 7:6. For it was said above that it makes a discordant 25:27 with the aphelion of the Earth (disregarding octaves); and now indeed, from 6:7 or 24:28 up to 25:27, all [intervals] are smaller than the smallest Harmonic interval.

### XLVI. Corollary.

It is evident, therefore, from this Proposition XLIII concerning Jupiter and Mars, and from XXXIX concerning Saturn and Jupiter, and from XXXVI concerning Jupiter and the Earth, and from XXXII concerning Saturn: why it was found above in Chapter V that the extreme motions of the planets were neither all perfectly accommodated to a single natural system or musical scale, nor did all those which were accommodated to the system of that same tuning divide those places by a natural ratio, or produce a purely natural succession of concordant intervals. For there are prior causes by which individual planets have obtained individual harmonies, by which all the planets also [attained] universal harmonies, and by which, finally, the universal harmonies have two genera, the Hard and the Soft. Once these are established, an all-encompassing accommodation to a single natural system is now prevented. But if those causes had not necessarily preceded, there is no doubt that either one system and one tuning of it would have embraced the extreme motions of all the planets; or if two systems were needed for the two types of song, the Hard and the Soft, the very same order of the natural scale would have been expressed not only in one of the Hard genus, but also in the remaining one of the Soft genus. You have here, therefore, the causes promised in the said Chapter V for the disagreements by the smallest [intervals], which are indeed smaller than all concordant ones.

# Proposition XLV.

<margin>CHAPTER IX</margin>
To the common <term>Major Double Octave: a musical interval spanning two octaves and a major third</term> of Venus and Mercury, as well as to Mercury’s own specific interval—both of which were established by previous arguments in Propositions XII and XVI—it was necessary to add an interval equal to the interval of Venus. This was done so that Mercury’s own interval would become a perfect 5:12 ratio, and so that <note>original: "☿"</note> Mercury might harmonize in both its motions with the single <term>perihelion: the point in an orbit closest to the Sun</term> of Venus.

*For because the <term>aphelion: the point in an orbit farthest from the Sun</term> of Saturn had to harmonize with the aphelion of the Earth—the outermost planet, circumscribed by its own figure and the highest, with the Earth, which distinguishes the classes of figures, at its highest—it follows by the laws of opposites that the perihelion of Mercury should harmonize with the perihelion of the Earth. Mercury is the innermost planet, inscribed within its own figure and the lowest, being closest to the Sun; it matches the lowest motion of the Earth, that common boundary. The former planets were intended to designate the <term>Hard: the Major musical key</term> genus of harmonies, while these latter designate the <term>Soft: the Minor musical key</term> genus, according to Propositions XXXIII and XXXIV. But the perihelion of Venus had to harmonize with the perihelion of the Earth in a 3:5 harmony <note>a Major Sixth</note> according to Proposition XXVII. Therefore, the perihelion of Mercury also had to be tuned into a single scale with the perihelion of Venus. Now, in Proposition XII, the harmony of Venus and Mercury when diverging <note>moving away from each other in pitch</note> was defined by earlier arguments as 3:4 <note>a perfect Fourth</note>. That harmony, therefore, had to be "leavened" <note>original: "fermentanda," meaning adjusted or tempered like dough rising</note> by these later arguments through the addition of the entire interval of Venus. Thus, there is no longer a perfect Double Octave from the aphelion of Venus, but rather from the perihelion of Venus to the perihelion of Mercury. Furthermore, the harmony of the planets when converging <note>moving toward each other in pitch</note> is a perfect 3:5, according to Proposition XV. When that is subtracted from the 1:4 <note>Double Octave</note>, there remains for Mercury alone a perfect 5:12 ratio, and it is no longer diminished by the specific proportion of Venus (as it was in Proposition XVI by the earlier arguments).*

Another reason: Just as the <term>Dodecahedron: a 12-sided Platonic solid</term> and <term>Icosahedron: a 20-sided Platonic solid</term>, being a pair, do not touch Saturn and Jupiter alone on the outside; so these same figures do not touch Mercury alone on the inside. For they touch Mars, the Earth, and Venus—the first on the inside, the last on the outside, and the middle one on both sides. Therefore, just as something equal to the specific interval of Venus was added separately to the specific proportions of the motions of Saturn and Jupiter (which are supported by the Cube and Tetrahedron), so now just as much had to be added to the specific interval of solitary Mercury. Mercury is contained by the <term>Octahedron: an 8-sided Platonic solid</term>, a figure that is the companion to the Cube and Tetrahedron. Indeed, just as the Octahedron, as the only figure among the Secondary class, takes the place of two figures (the Cube and Tetrahedron) among the Primary class—on which see Chapter I—so also among the lower planets, Mercury alone stands in the place of two of the upper planets, namely Saturn and Jupiter.

*Thirdly, just as Saturn, the highest, had to harmonize its aphelion motion through several octaves <note>original: "Diapaſon"</note>—that is, in a 1:32 ratio, a continuous doubling—with the aphelion motion of the two planets that change the harmonic genus (the Earth and Venus), being higher and nearer to itself, according to Proposition XXXI; so conversely, Mercury, the lowest, again through several octaves—that is, in a 1:4 ratio, also a continuous doubling—had to harmonize its perihelion motion with the perihelion motion of the two planets that change the harmonic genus, being lower and similarly nearer to itself. Fourthly, of the three upper planets (Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars), only one extreme <note>either aphelion or perihelion</note> of each conspires toward the universal harmonies; therefore, of the lower and solitary planet, Mercury, both extremes had to conspire toward them. For the middle planets, the Earth and Venus, had to change the genus of the harmonies, according to Propositions XXXIII and XXXIV. Finally, in the three pairs of upper planets, perfect harmonies were found between the converging motions, but "leavened" harmonies were found between the diverging ones and in the individual intervals. Therefore, in the two pairs of lower planets, the reverse should be true: perfect harmonies should be found not primarily between converging or diverging motions, but between motions of the same "side" <note>aphelion to aphelion, or perihelion to perihelion</note>. And because two perfect harmonies were owed to the Earth and Venus, two perfect harmonies were also owed to Venus and Mercury. And those two planets [Venus and Mercury] were more strongly required to have a perfect harmony between their aphelia as well as between their perihelia, because they had to change the genus of the harmony.*

For it was said above that it creates an unmusical 25:27 ratio with the aphelion of the Earth (ignoring Octaves); and truly, from 6:7 or 24:28 up to 25:27, all intervals are smaller than the smallest Harmonic interval.

# XLVI. Corollary.

It is clear therefore from this Proposition XLIII concerning Jupiter and Mars, and from XXXIX concerning Saturn and Jupiter, and from XXXVI concerning Jupiter and the Earth, and from XXXII concerning Saturn: why above in Chapter V it was found that the extreme motions of the planets were neither all most perfectly accommodated to a single natural System or musical scale, nor did all those who were accommodated to the system of that same tuning divide those places by a natural ratio, or produce a purely natural succession of <term>concinne: musically pleasing or harmonious</term> intervals. For the prior causes are those by which individual planets have obtained individual Harmonies, by which all planets also obtained universal Harmonies, and by which finally the universal Harmonies obtained two genera, the Hard and the Soft. Once these are established, a universal accommodation to a single natural system is now prevented. But if those causes had not necessarily preceded it, there is no doubt that either a single system and a single tuning would have encompassed the extreme motions of all the planets; or, if two systems were needed for the two types of song, the Hard and the Soft, the very order of the natural scale would have been expressed not only in the Hard genus, but also in the remaining Soft genus. You have here, therefore, the causes promised in the said Chapter V for the disagreements by the smallest intervals, which are indeed smaller than all harmonious ones.

<header>BOOK V ON HARMONY</header>

## Proposition XLV.

To the common major <term>Octave: a musical interval where the frequency of one note is double another (2:1 ratio)</term> of Venus and Mercury, as well as to Mercury's own [interval], established above by the previous reasonings of Propositions XII and XVI, it was necessary to add an interval equal to the interval of Venus, so that Mercury's own [interval] would become a perfect 5:12, and thus Mercury <note>original symbol: ☿</note> would harmonize at both its extremes of motion with the single perihelion of Venus.

*For because the aphelion of Saturn had to harmonize with the aphelion of the Earth—the outermost planet, circumscribed by its own figure and the highest, with the highest point of the Earth, which distinguishes the classes of the [geometric] figures—it follows by the laws of opposites that the perihelion of Mercury should coincide with the perihelion of the Earth. This is because Mercury is the innermost planet, inscribed within its figure, the lowest, and nearest to the Sun, [coinciding] with the lowest motion of the Earth, which acts as that common boundary. The former serves to designate the Hard <note>original: "Durum"; referring to the Major genus</note> and the latter the Soft <note>original: "Molle"; referring to the Minor genus</note> genus of harmonies, according to Propositions XXXIII and XXXIV. But the perihelion of Venus had to harmonize with the perihelion of the Earth in a 3:5 harmony according to Proposition XXVII. Therefore, the perihelion of Mercury also had to be adjusted into one scale with the perihelion of Venus. However, in Proposition XII, from those previous reasonings, the harmony of the diverging motions of Venus and Mercury was defined as a 3:4. That harmony, therefore, through these later reasonings, had to be "leavened" <note>original: "fermentanda"; Kepler's term for adjusting a musical interval to fit a scale</note> by the addition of the entire interval of Venus. Therefore, it is no longer from the aphelion, but from the perihelion of Venus to the perihelion of Mercury that there is a perfect <term>Double Octave: a musical interval of two octaves, or a 1:4 ratio</term>. And since the harmony of the converging motions is a perfect 3:5 according to Proposition XV, when that is subtracted from the 1:4 ratio, there remains for Mercury alone its own perfect 5:12 ratio, and it is no longer (as in Proposition XVI by the earlier reasonings) diminished by Venus's own proportion.*

<margin>CHAPTER IX</margin>
*Another reason: Just as the <term>Dodecahedron: a 12-sided Platonic solid</term> and the <term>Icosahedron: a 20-sided Platonic solid</term>, which are conjugates, do not touch Saturn and Jupiter at all on the outside, so too these same figures do not touch Mercury alone on the inside. They do, however, touch Mars, the Earth, and Venus—the former on the inside, the latter on the outside, and the middle one [Earth] on both sides. Therefore, just as something equal to the own proportion of Venus was added distributively to the own proportions of the motions of Saturn and Jupiter, which are supported by the <term>Cube: a 6-sided solid</term> and the <term>Tetrahedron: a 4-sided solid</term>, so now just as much had to be added to the own proportion of solitary Mercury, which is contained by the <term>Octahedron: an 8-sided solid</term>, the companion figure to the Cube and Tetrahedron. For just as the Octahedron, the only figure among the Secondary ones, takes the place of two—the Cube and the Tetrahedron—among the Primary ones (on which see Chapter I), so also among the lower planets, Mercury alone is in the place of two of the upper ones, namely Saturn and Jupiter.*

*Thirdly, just as Saturn, being the highest, had to harmonize through several Octaves—that is, in a 1:32 ratio of continuous doubling—by its aphelion motion with the aphelion motion of the one of the two planets that change the genus of harmony (the one higher and closer to itself), according to Prop. XXXI: so conversely, Mercury <note>original symbol: ☿</note>, being the lowest, again through several Octaves—that is, in a 1:4 ratio of continuous doubling—had to harmonize by its perihelion motion with the perihelion motion of the one of the two planets that change the genus of harmony (the one lower and closer to itself). Fourthly, of the three upper planets, Saturn <note>original symbol: ♄</note>, Jupiter <note>original symbol: ♃</note>, and Mars <note>original symbol: ♂</note>, only their individual extremes harmonize in universal harmonies; therefore, of the lower and only planet, namely Mercury, both extremes had to harmonize with the same. For the middle ones, the Earth and Venus <note>original symbol: ♀</note>, had to change the genus of harmonies, according to Propositions XXXIII and XXXIV. Finally, in the three pairs of the upper planets, perfect harmonies were found between the converging motions, but they were "leavened" between the diverging motions and the planets' own proportions. Consequently, in the two pairs of lower planets, conversely, perfect harmonies had to be found not primarily between the converging or diverging motions, but between the motions of the same region [i.e., aphelion to aphelion or perihelion to perihelion]. And because two perfect harmonies were owed to the Earth and Venus, therefore two perfect ones were also owed to Venus and Mercury. And those two, indeed, had to obtain a perfect harmony both between their aphelia and between their perihelia, because they had to change the genus of harmony:*

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>

*Venus and Mercury, however, as they do not change their musical genus <note>Kepler refers to the Major and Minor modes, or the Hard and Soft genera of harmony</note>, did not require perfect harmonies between both pairs of their aphelion <note>the point in an orbit farthest from the Sun</note> and perihelion <note>the point in an orbit closest to the Sun</note> motions. Instead, in place of a perfect harmony starting from the aphelia—which was already "fermented" <note>Kepler uses 'fermentata' to describe a ratio that has been slightly altered or adjusted to fit the cosmic system</note>—there followed a perfect harmony of the converging motions. Thus, just as Venus, the higher of the lower planets, possesses its own motion ratio that is the smallest of all (by 28), and Mercury, the lowest of the lower planets, has been allotted an individual ratio that is the greatest of all (by 30): so also the individual ratio of Venus would be the most imperfect of all, or the furthest removed from the Harmonies; while the individual ratio of Mercury would be the most perfect of all—that is, an absolute Harmony, without "ferment." In this way, the proportions would finally be opposed in every respect.*

For in this way, He who is before all ages and unto all eternity decorated the wonders of His wisdom: nothing is redundant, nothing is lacking, nor is there a place for anyone's criticism. How desirable are His works, etc. All things are twofold, one against another, and none lacks its opposite; He has confirmed (established with the best reasons) the good things (their Ornament and decency) of each one; and who shall be satisfied seeing their glory? <note>This passage paraphrases the Biblical Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 42:24-25, reflecting Kepler's view of astronomy as a form of worship.</note>

## Axiom XLVI.

The placement of the solid figures <note>the five Platonic solids: tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron</note> between the planetary Orbs, if it is free and not hindered by the necessities of preceding causes, ought to follow the analogy of geometric inscriptions and circumscriptions in its perfection; and thus it should also follow the conditions of the ratio of the inscribed [solids] to the circumscribed [solids].

For nothing is more reasonable than that a physical inscription should exactly represent the Geometric one, as a finished work represents its own archetype.

## Proposition XLVII.

If the inscription of the Figures between the Planets was free, the **Tetrahedron** <note>a four-sided pyramid</note> ought to have touched the perihelion orb of **Jupiter** exactly with its corners above, and the aphelion of **Mars** exactly with the centers of its planes below. The **Cube** and **Octahedron**, however, standing with their corners on the perihelion Orb of their respective Planet, ought to have penetrated the orb of their interior planet with the centers of their planes, so that those centers are moved between the Orbs of the aphelion and perihelion. The **Dodecahedron** <note>a twelve-sided solid</note> and **Icosahedron** <note>a twenty-sided solid</note>, conversely, brushing the perihelion Orbs of their Planets with their corners on the outside, ought not to have quite reached the aphelion orbs of their interior planets with the centers of their planes. Finally, the **Dodecahedral Urchin** <note>original: "Echinus Dodecaëdricus"; this refers to a stellated dodecahedron, a complex shape Kepler was the first to describe mathematically</note>, standing with its corners on the perihelion orb of Mars, ought to have come very near to the aphelion orb of Venus at the middle points of its inverted sides, which distinguish the two solid rays.

*For the Tetrahedron, the middle figure of the Primary ones <note>the "Primary" solids are the Cube, Tetrahedron, and Dodecahedron</note> in origin and position in the World, ought to have pushed apart both regions—Jupiter <note>original symbol: ♃</note> and Mars <note>original symbol: ♂</note>—equally if nothing hindered it. Because the Cube was above and outside it, and the Dodecahedron below and inside it, it was therefore fair that their inscription should also affect a contrary relationship to that of which the Tetrahedron held the middle; thus one of them would create an excess of inscription, the other a defect. That is, one would penetrate the interior orb to some extent, and the other would not reach it. And because the Octa-*

The *Octahedron* <note>A solid with 8 triangular faces</note> is related to the *Cube*, possessing an equal proportion of spheres; the *Icosahedron* <note>A solid with 20 triangular faces</note> is likewise related to the *Dodecahedron* <note>A solid with 12 pentagonal faces</note>. Therefore, whatever perfection of inscription <note>How a sphere fits inside or outside a solid</note> belongs to the *Cube*, the same was owed to the *Octahedron*; and whatever to the *Dodecahedron*, the same to the *Icosahedron*. Furthermore, the placement of the *Octahedron* is similar to the placement of the *Cube*, while that of the *Icosahedron* is similar to the *Dodecahedron*. This is because, just as the *Cube* holds the outer limit toward the exterior, so the *Octahedron* holds the remaining extreme toward the interior of the World; the *Dodecahedron* and *Icosahedron*, however, sit in the middle. Therefore, a similar inscription is appropriate: in the former case, it penetrates the interior planetary sphere; in the latter, it falls short of it.

But the *Echinus* <note>original: "Echinus" — Literally a "hedgehog" or "sea-urchin." Kepler is referring to a faceted solid, specifically the rhombic triacontahedron, which he discovered</note>, which represents the *Icosahedron* at the tips of its angles and the *Dodecahedron* at its bases, ought to fill, embrace, or arrange both regions: that between *Mars and the Earth* (allotted to the *Dodecahedron*) and that between the *Earth and Venus* (allotted to the *Icosahedron*). *Which of these opposites fits which partnership is made clear by the previously stated axiom. For the Tetrahedron <note>A pyramid with 4 triangular faces</note>, having an expressible <note>original: "effabilem" — referring to a rational mathematical ratio</note> inscribed sphere, was granted the middle place among the Primary solids, flanked on both sides by figures of incommensurable spheres, of which the exterior is the Cube and the interior the Dodecahedron, according to Chapter I of this book. This geometric quality—the "Expressibility" of the inscribed sphere—represents in Nature the perfect inscription of a planetary sphere.*

*The Cube and its partner therefore have inscribed spheres that are at least half-expressible (that is, only in power <note>referring to a ratio that is rational when squared</note>); they ought therefore to represent a semi-perfect inscription. In this case, although the very limit of the planetary sphere is not reached, at least something interior—specifically the midpoint between the spheres, the aphelion and perihelion <note>The farthest and closest points of an orbit to the Sun</note>—is touched by the centers of the figure's faces, if this can be achieved by other means. The Dodecahedron, by contrast, and its partner, have inscribed spheres that are plainly inexpressible <note>irrational</note> in both the length of the radius and in power. They must therefore represent a plainly imperfect inscription, touching absolutely nothing of the planetary sphere; that is, falling short and not quite reaching the aphelion of the planet's sphere with the centers of their faces.*

*Although the Echinus is related to the Dodecahedron's partnership, it nevertheless possesses something similar to the Tetrahedron. For the radius of the sphere inscribed by its inverted sides is indeed incommensurable with the radius of the circumscribed sphere, but it is meanwhile commensurable in length to the distance between two neighboring angles. Thus, the perfection of the commensuration of the radii is almost as great as the imperfection in the Tetrahedron on the other side, and as great as the Dodecahedron and its partner. It is therefore agreeable that a physical inscription should also belong to it, neither purely Tetrahedral nor purely Dodecahedral, but of an intermediate kind. Since the Tetrahedron's faces ought to reach the summit of the sphere, and the Dodecahedron's should not reach it by a certain space, this "spiny" figure <note>the Echinus</note>, with its inverted sides within the Icosahedral space and the summit of its inscribed sphere, nearly reaches this summit—provided that this figure too was to be admitted into the society of the other five, and that these laws could be tolerated alongside the laws of those others. Indeed, why do I say "could be tolerated"? They could not do without them. For if a loose, non-touching inscription was fitting for the Dodecahedron, what else could restrain that indefinite looseness within the boundaries of a certain quantity, other than this subsidiary figure? Related to the Dodecahedron and Icosahedron, it nearly touches with its inscription, failing no more (if indeed it fails) than the Tetrahedron exceeds and penetrates. We shall deal with this quantity in the following section.*

This cause of the *Echinus* being associated with the two related figures makes it very probable (specifically so that the proportion of the spheres of Mars and Venus, which those figures had left indefinite, might be determined) because the semidiameter of the Earth's sphere is found to be 1000, almost exactly in the middle proportional...

# XLVIII. Proposition.

The inscription of the regular solid figures <note>The five Platonic solids: cube, tetrahedron, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron</note> between the planetary orbits was not a matter of pure choice; rather, it was constrained in its smallest details by the Harmonies established between the Extreme motions <note>the fastest and slowest speeds of the planets</note>.

*For according to Axioms I and II, the proportion of the orbits for each Figure ought not to be expressed immediately by itself; instead, the Harmonies most closely related to those orbital proportions had to be sought out first and then adapted to the extreme motions.*

Then, as per Axioms XVIII and XX, since universal Harmonies of two kinds could exist, it was necessary to add a bit of "leaven" <note>original: "fermenti" — a metaphor for a small adjustment or tuning</note> to the Major Harmonies of each pair of planets, based on later principles. Therefore, so that these harmonies could stand firm and rely on their own specific principles, they required intervals that differ somewhat from those produced by a perfect inscription of the solid figures between the Orbits, according to the laws of motion explained in Chapter III. To prove this, and to show how much is taken away from each figure by the Harmonies established by their own principles: come, let us construct the intervals of the planets from the Sun from those harmonies, using a new method of calculation never before attempted by anyone.

<margin>
Calculation of the planetary intervals emerging from systematic harmony. <note>original: "Harmonicâ politicâ" — Kepler uses "political" to mean a well-ordered or governed system where different parts are balanced</note>
</margin>
There will be three headings for this inquiry: First, from the two extreme motions of each planet, we will seek its extreme intervals from the Sun, and from these, the Radius of the orbit in that dimension of extreme intervals specific to each planet. Second, from those same extreme motions, using a dimension common to all, we will seek the mean motions and their proportion. Third, from the proportion of the mean motions now revealed, the proportion of the Orbits (or the Mean intervals) will be investigated, along with the extreme ones; and these will be compared with the proportions of the figures.

Regarding the first point: we must recall from Chapter III, number VI, that the proportion of the extreme motions is the double <note>i.e., the square</note> of the inverse proportion of the corresponding intervals from the Sun. Since the proportion of squares is also double the proportion of their sides: therefore, the numbers by which the extreme motions of each planet are expressed will be considered as Squares, and their calculated roots will give the extreme intervals. From these, it is easy to take the arithmetic mean to find the semi-diameter <note>radius</note> of the Orbit and the Eccentricity <note>how much the orbit deviates from a circle</note>. Therefore, the Harmonies established so far have prescribed:

For the second part of our proposal, we must again refer to Chapter III, number XII, where it was shown that the number expressing the mean motion <note>The average speed of a planet in its orbit.</note> within the proportion of the extremes <note>The fastest (perihelion) and slowest (aphelion) speeds.</note> is smaller than their arithmetic mean <note>The simple average: (a+b)/2.</note>, and also smaller than their geometric mean <note>The square root of the product: √(ab).</note>, specifically by half the difference between the two means. Since we seek all mean motions within the same scale of measurement, let all the proportions established so far between pairs—as well as those specific to each individual planet—be expressed in the measure of a least common denominator <note>original: "communis minimi dividui"</note>. Then, let the means be sought: the arithmetic mean by halving the difference of the extremes of each motion, and the geometric mean by multiplying one extreme by the other and extracting the square root of the product. Then, by subtracting half of the difference between these means from the geometric mean, the number for the Mean Motion will be established in the dimension specific to each extreme motion; this is easily converted into a common dimension through the rule of proportions.

Therefore, from the prescribed Harmonies, the proportion of the Mean Daily Motions has been found—namely, the ratio between the numbers of degrees, minutes, etc., for each planet compared to one another. It is easy to explore how closely this approaches the findings of Astronomy.

The third part of the proposals requires Chapter III, number VIII. For once the proportion of the mean daily motions of each planet is found, it is possible to find the proportion of the Orbits <note>The distances of the planets from the Sun.</note> as well. Indeed, the proportion of the mean motions is the inverse sesquialter <note>original: "eversa sesquialtera" — this refers to the 3/2 power ratio. Kepler is using his Third Law: the square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the distance.</note> of the proportion of the Orbits. Furthermore, the proportion of Cubic numbers is sesquialter <note>The ratio of 3 to 2.</note> to the proportion of the Square numbers assigned to the same Roots in the Table of Clavius <note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612), a renowned Jesuit mathematician and astronomer who helped refine the Gregorian calendar. Kepler uses Clavius's published mathematical tables to speed up his calculations.</note>, which he appended to his *Practical Geometry*. Therefore, if our numbers for the mean motions are sought (truncated by an equal number of zeros where necessary) among the Cubes in that Table, they will reveal on the left, under the title of Squares, the numbers for the proportion of the Orbits. Then the Eccentricities <note>The amount by which an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note> assigned above to each in the dimension of its own semi-diameter can be easily transposed into a common dimension for all through the rule of proportions; thus, by adding these to and subtracting them from the semi-diameters of the orbits, the extreme intervals <note>The closest and farthest distances (perihelion and aphelion).</note> of each planet from the Sun are established. We shall assign to the semi-diameter of the Earth's orbit the round dimension of 100,000, as is customary in Astronomy. This is done for this reason: because this number, whether squared or cubed, always consists of pure zeros. Therefore, we shall also express the mean motion of the Earth by the number 1,000,000,000; proceeding by the rule of proportions, as the number of the mean motion of any planet is to the number of the mean motion of the Earth, so...

The Cubic planes descend a little below the middle of Jupiter; the Octahedral planes do not quite reach the very center of Mercury; the Tetrahedral planes fall a little below the highest point of Mars; the sides of the Echinus do not quite reach the highest point of Venus; but the planes of the Dodecahedron fall far short of the aphelion of Earth; and the planes of the Icosahedron also fall far, and almost proportionally, short of the aphelion of Venus. Finally, the square of the Octahedron is plainly unsuitable—and not without reason, for what place has a plane figure among the solids? You see, therefore, that if the planetary intervals are deduced from the Harmonic proportions of the motions demonstrated thus far, it is necessary that they turn out as large as they are allowed here, but not as large as the laws of free inscription <note>The theoretical nesting of solids within one another.</note> prescribed in proposition XLV would require. This is because here, a <term>geometrical world</term> <note>original: "κόσμῳ γεωμετρικὸς"</note> of perfect inscription was no longer <term>possible according to that other harmonic world</term> <note>original: "κόσμον ἁρμονικὸν ἐνδεχόμενος"</note>, to use the words of Galen taken from the frontispiece of this fifth book. This much had to be demonstrated by the calculation of numbers alone, for the clarification of the prescribed proposition.
