ON THE HARMONICS, BOOK V.

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>
...are presented by Astronomy. But first, I cannot defend that reduction by Harmonic ratios; for the aphelion <note>The point in an orbit furthest from the Sun.</note> of Mercury will not fit into any musical scale; nor is a full ratio of opposition for all conditions maintained in the Planets, which are positioned against each other in the World. Furthermore, the mean daily motion of Mercury becomes too great, and therefore the periodic time of Mercury <note>original: "☿"</note>—which is the most certain value in all of astronomy—is shortened too much. Therefore, I abide by the Harmonic policy of motions, employed here and confirmed throughout the whole of Chapter IX. <margin>A Challenge</margin> However, by this example, I challenge all of you who may happen to read this book—you who are steeped in the mathematical disciplines and the knowledge of the highest philosophy: come, be diligent, and tear away even one of the Harmonies applied throughout, or exchange it with some other; and try whether you will come as close to the astronomy prescribed in Chapter IV. Or, strive by reasoning whether you can build something better and more appropriate for the celestial motions, or destroy, in part or in whole, the arrangement employed by me. Whatever shall pertain to the glory of our Creator and Lord, let that be equally permitted to you through this book of mine; just as I myself have taken the liberty, even until this hour, of changing here and there those things which in previous days I could detect were conceived preposterously through drowsy care or hurried zeal.

## II. Concluding Summary <note>original: "Epiphonema"</note>.

It was good that the solid figures <note>The five Platonic solids: the cube, tetrahedron, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron.</note> in the generation of intervals should yield to Harmonic ratios, and the Major Harmonies of pairs should yield to the universal Harmonies of all, as much as was necessary for this purpose. *By a beautiful chance, we have arrived at the Square of Seven, 49; so that this may follow as a kind of Sabbath, after the six eightfold solid Divine Utterances concerning the work of the Heavens have been sent ahead. Justly, I have also made this Concluding Summary, which could have been placed among the Axioms at the start: because God, having now finished the work of Creation, saw all that He had made, and behold, they were very good.*

*There are two parts to this Concluding Summary: the first, concerning Harmonies in general, is demonstrated thus. For where a choice exists between diverse things that do not exactly match each other, there the more excellent things are to be preferred, and the lesser things are to be diminished as much as is necessary; the very word <term>kosmos<note>original Greek: κόσμος; meaning "order," "ornament," or "world-system."</note></term>, which signifies ornament, seems to prove this. And yet, by as much as life excels the body, or form excels matter, by so much does Harmonic ornament excel simple Geometry.*

<margin>see book IV, page 163.</margin>
*For just as life perfects the bodies of living things, because they were born to lead this life—which follows from the Archetype of the World, which is the divine essence itself—so the regions attributed to the Planets are measured by the motions of each of their stars; because in order for a star to be moved, its own region was assigned to it. And yet, the five solid figures, by the very force of the word, pertain to the spaces* <margin>see book IV.</margin> *of the regions, and to the number of those bodies; but Harmony pertains to the motions. Again, just as Matter is diffused and indefinite of itself, while Form is definite, united, and terminating that matter; so also the Geometric proportions are infinite, while Harmonies are few. For although even among the Geometric proportions there are certain degrees of definitions, formations, and restrictions, and no more than three can exist from the inscription of spheres into the regular figures; nevertheless, these also are followed by a common accident shared with all the rest: namely, that they presuppose an infinite possible division of quantities, which those whose boundaries they are also involve in a certain way in act.*

# ON THE MOTIONS OF THE PLANETS

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>
...are incommensurable with one another. But **Harmonic** proportions are all expressible, and the terms of all of them are commensurable; and these are taken from a certain and finite species of plane figures. Indeed, the infinity of division represents the matter; while commensurability, or the expressibility of terms, represents the form. Therefore, just as matter yearns for Form—like a rough stone of the correct mass yearns for the Idea of a human body—so the geometric proportions of figures yearn for Harmonies. They do so not so that they might create and form them, but because this Matter fits this Form, this quantity of stone fits this image, and likewise this figural proportion fits this Harmony more aptly; so that they might be further shaped and formed—the Matter by its Form, the stone by the sculptor <note>original: "Colapte"</note> into the likeness of a living creature—and the proportion of the figural orbits by its own Harmony, that is, a nearby and suitable one.

What has been said so far will become clearer from the history of my discoveries. When I happened upon this contemplation 24 years ago: first, I inquired whether the individual orbits of the planets were separated from each other by equal intervals (for in Copernicus, the orbits are distant and do not touch each other); I recognized nothing more beautiful, of course, than the principle of equality. But that principle lacked both head and tail: for this material equality provided no certain number of moving bodies, nor any certain quantity for the intervals. I therefore thought about the similarity of intervals to the orbits, that is, about Proportion. But the same complaint followed; for although intervals between the orbits did indeed emerge as unequal, they were neither "unequally unequal" as Copernicus requires, nor was the quantity of the proportion or the number of orbits established. I moved on to regular plane figures; intervals were formed from them by the inscription of circles: but still with no certain number. I came to the five solids <note>The five Platonic solids: tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron.</note>; here both the number of bodies and the magnitude of the intervals appeared nearly true; so much so that I appealed to the perfection of Astronomy concerning the remaining discrepancy. Astronomy was perfected in these last 20 years <note>Kepler refers here to the high-precision data gathered by Tycho Brahe</note>; and behold, the intervals still disagreed with the solid figures; nor were the causes of the eccentricities—distributed most unequally among the planets—yet apparent. Clearly, in this house of the World, I was seeking nothing but stones of a more elegant form, but of a kind that would suit stones; I was unaware that the Architect had shaped them into the most articulate likeness of a living body. Thus gradually, especially in these last three years, I came to the Harmonies, abandoning the solid figures regarding the smallest details: both because the Harmonies stood on the side of the Form which the final hand would impose, while the figures belonged to the Matter (which in the World is the number of bodies and the raw magnitude of spaces); and also because the Harmonies provided the eccentricities, which the figures did not even promise. The Harmonies, you see, reconciled the nose, eyes, and other limbs to the statue, for which the figures had prescribed only the external quantity of a raw mass.

Therefore, just as the bodies of living creatures are not made, nor is a mass of stone usually fashioned, according to the pure norm of some geometric figure—but the external round figure, however elegant, is modified (while the correct size of the mass remains) so that the body can obtain the organs necessary for life, or the stone the likeness of a living being—so also the proportion which the solid figures were to prescribe for the planetary orbits, being inferior and looking only to body and matter, had to yield to the Harmonies; as much of it as was necessary so that they might stand together and adorn the motions of the spheres.

For the final hand of perfection is due rather to that which more greatly perfects the World; conversely, something must be taken away (if it must be taken from either) from that which holds a secondary place here. But the universal Harmony of all things perfects the World more than the individual harmonies of pairs of neighbors...

# THE HARMONIES, BOOK V

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>
...the two pairs. For **Harmony** is a kind of ratio of unity; they are more united, therefore, if all [the planets] together conspire into one harmony, than if each pair separately conspire into two **Harmonies**. Therefore, in the conflict between the two, the singular harmonies of each of the two planets had to yield, so that the universal harmonies of all could stand. Moreover, the Greater harmonies, of the diverging motions, had to yield rather than the Smaller ones, of the converging motions. For if those motions diverge, they look toward planets that are not the proposed pair but other neighbors; but if these converge, the motion of one planet verges toward the motion of the other, interchangeably. For example, in the pair of **Jupiter** and **Mars**, the former's aphelion <term>aphelion: the point in an orbit furthest from the sun</term> verges toward **Saturn**, and the latter’s perihelion <term>perihelion: the point in an orbit closest to the sun</term> verges toward the **Earth**; but the former’s perihelion verges toward **Mars**, and the latter’s aphelion toward **Jupiter**. Therefore, the **Harmony** of these two, **Jupiter** and **Mars**, is more their own; whereas the harmony of those diverging motions is somewhat more foreign to **Jupiter** and **Mars**. Furthermore, the principle of unity, which binds pairs of neighbors together, was less harmed if a more foreign and remote **Harmony** were adjusted <note>original: "fermentaretur," literally "leavened" or "fermented," suggesting a subtle chemical-like blending or tuning</note> than if the proper one were, which exists between the closer motions of neighboring planets. Yet this adjustment was not very large: for a ratio was found by which both the universal **Harmonies** of all the planets could stand—and those of two distinct kinds—even with some breadth of tension that would at least equal a **Comma** <term>Comma: a very small musical interval resulting from the difference between two other ratios</term>; and also the two singular harmonies of neighboring pairs could be preserved. Of the converging motions in four pairs, they are perfect; of the aphelions in one, and of the perihelions in two, they are likewise perfect; but of the diverging motions in four pairs, they are within a discrepancy of less than one **Diesis** <term>Diesis: an extremely small interval, often the difference between a major and minor semitone</term>, the smallest interval, by which the human voice in figured song <note>original: "cantu figurato," referring to polyphonic music with complex rhythms</note> almost perpetually errs; but in the single pair of **Jupiter** and **Mars**, the discrepancy is between a **Diesis** and a **Semitone**. It appears, therefore, that this mutual yielding is in every respect very good.

***

Thus far have I proclaimed <note>original: "panephoneso" (Greek), meaning to cry out or speak with one voice</note> concerning the work of God the Creator. It remains now that, at last, having lifted my eyes and hands from the table of demonstrations and raised them to heaven, I should pray to the Father of lights with devotion and supplication: O You who by the light of Nature promote in us a longing for the light of Grace, so that through it You may transport us into the light of Glory; I give thanks to You, Lord Creator, because You have delighted me in Your creation, and I have exulted in the works of Your hands. Behold, I have now completed the work of my profession, having used as much strength of intellect as You have given me; I have manifested the glory of Your works to the men who will read these demonstrations, as much as the narrowness of my Mind could grasp of Your infinity; my soul has been ready to philosophize with the utmost correctness. If I, a little worm <note>original: "vermiculo"</note>, born and bred in the wallowing-place of sins, have uttered anything unworthy of Your counsel that You wish men to know, inspire me also to amend it; if I have been lured into rashness by the admirable beauty of Your works, or if I have loved my own glory among men while progressing in the work destined for Your glory, mild and merciful, forgive me; finally, may You deign to grant

ON THE MOTIONS OF THE PLANETS

# CHAPTER X.

## A conjectural epilogue concerning the Sun.

->From the celestial music to the listener; from the Muses to Apollo the leader of the choir; from the six circling planets making their Harmonies, to the Sun, who sits immobile in place at the center of all their courses, yet revolves upon himself.<- For since the most perfect **Harmony** exists among the extreme motions of the planets—not in terms of their true speeds through the ethereal air, but in terms of the angles formed by the ends of their daily arcs on their orbits when connected to the center of the Sun—it follows that **Harmony** does not merely decorate the ends (that is, the motions considered individually), but only insofar as they are joined and compared to one another, becoming the object of some **Mind**. And since no object is ever ordered in vain without some thing existing to be moved by it, those angles seem to presuppose some action similar to our sight, or certainly that sensation by which (as described in *Book IV*) **sublunary Nature** perceived the angles of the rays from the planets formed upon the Earth. Indeed, what kind of sight exists in the Sun, what eyes there may be, or what other instinct for perceiving these angles even without eyes and for esteeming the **Harmonies** of the motions entering through whatever gate to the vestibule of the mind—and finally, what that **Mind** in the Sun truly is—is not easy for us inhabitants of Earth to conjecture.

However these things may be, the arrangement of those six primary orbits around the Sun—honoring him with perpetual revolutions and, as it were, adoring him (just as separately **the globe of Jupiter is circled, honored, and served by four moons, Saturn by two, and the Earth and us its inhabitants by a single Moon**); and adding to that consideration this special business of **Harmony**, the most evident trace of the highest providence regarding Solar matters—these things extort from me this confession: Not only does **Light** go out into the whole world from the Sun, as from the hearth or eye of the World, and **Life** and **Heat** as from a heart, and all **Motion** as from a king and mover; but also, in turn, there are collected into the Sun from every province of the World, by royal right, these "returns," as it were, of the most desirable **Harmony**. Indeed, the <term>species: in Kepler's physics, the formal images or influences of things that travel through space</term> of the pairs of motions flowing together there are bound into a single **Harmony** by the work of some mind, and are stamped like coinage from raw silver and gold. Finally, in the Sun there is a **COURT, a Palace, and a Headquarters or Royal Residence** of the whole kingdom of Nature, whatever Chancellors, Palatines, or Governors the Creator has given to it, and for whomever He prepared those seats, whether created immediately at the beginning or to be transferred there one day. For even this earthly adornment was for a long time lacking the observers and users for whom it was destined, and the seats were empty.

There enters the mind, therefore, the thought of what the ancient **Pythagoreans** meant (according to **Aristotle**) when they used to call the center of the World (to which they referred, though they understood the Sun) **THE GUARD-POST OF JUPITER** <note>original: "Jovis EXCUBIAS," ΔΙΟΣ ΦΥΛΑΚΗΝ</note>; and likewise what the old translator was pondering in his mind when he wrote a verse from...

...from the Psalm, rendered it thus: IN THE SUN HE SET HIS TABERNACLE <note>original: "IN SOLE POSUIT TABERNACULUM"; from Psalm 19:4 (Vulgate 18:6)</note>. But I have also recently come across a hymn by the Platonic philosopher Proclus, written to the Sun and filled with venerable mysteries—if only you were to remove that one word <margin>CHAPTER X. Of whom much mention was made in the earlier books. He lived under Constantine, Maxentius, and Julian the Apostate.</margin> **Hearken** <note>original: "Κλῦθι" (*Klythi*), a standard pagan invocation to a deity</note>. Although even this was excused to some extent by the old translator I just cited: suggesting that he, in invoking the Sun, inwardly understands the One who set his tabernacle in the Sun. For Proclus lived at a time when to confess Jesus of Nazareth our Savior as God, and to despise the gods of the poets of the nations, was a crime which the monarchs of the world and the people themselves punished with every kind of torture. Therefore Proclus—who had perceived from afar the Son of God even from his own Platonic philosophy and the natural light of the mind, that true light which illuminates every man coming into this world—knew well that <margin>The judgment of the ancients concerning his book **On the Mother of the Gods** <note>original: "Μητρωακῆ" (*Mētrōakē*)</note> was this: that in it, not without divine rapture, the entire doctrine concerning God was explained; and since frequent tears of the author appeared in it, all suspicion was removed from those listening. Yet the same man wrote 18 **Arguments** <note>original: "Epichiremata"</note> against the Christians, which John Philoponus opposed, reproaching him for his ignorance of Greek matters which he had nevertheless undertaken to defend. Clearly Proclus had disguised those things which did not suit his philosophy.</margin> divinity was by no means to be sought in sensible things alongside the superstitious common people. Yet he preferred to appear to seek God in the Sun rather than in the sensible man Christ, so that he might simultaneously deceive the nations by honoring the Titan of the poets in word alone, and serve his own philosophy by drawing both the nations and the Christians away from sensible things—the former from the visible Sun, the latter from the Son of Mary. He did this because he rejected the Mystery of the Incarnation, trusting too much in the natural light of the Mind. Finally, he wished to adopt into his own philosophy that which the Christians held most divine and which was most in agreement with Platonic Philosophy, as if it were taken from them.

Therefore, the Gospel doctrine concerning Christ takes action to reclaim its own property against this Hymn of Proclus. Let that Titan keep his own things: the **Golden reins and the treasury of light, from the middle seat of the ether, the circling sun-bright wheel around the world** <note>original: "Χρυσήニア & ταμιεῖον φάος, μεσσατι’ αἰθερέω ἕδρης, κόσμῳ περιάϊον εἰλιφεγγέα κύκλον"</note>, an appearance which even Copernicus grants to him. Let him also have the **returning chariot-drivings** <note>original: "παλιννόσος διφρείας"</note>, although he does not possess them through the ancient Pythagoreans, but has in their place **the center, the guardhouse of Zeus** <note>original: "τὸ κέντρον, Διὸς φυλακὴν"</note> (a dogma of theirs which Proclus, as their successor, did not recognize, it having been deformed by the flood of forgotten centuries). Let him also have the **offspring budding forth from you** <note>original: "γενέθλην ἐκ σε βλαστήσασαν"</note> and whatever else is natural. 

In turn, let the philosophy of Proclus yield to Christian dogmas; let the sensible Sun yield to the Son of Mary. Let that Son of God, whom Proclus addresses under the name of Titan, yield: **Life-sustaining, O King, you yourself holding the key of the fountain** <note>original: "ζωαρκές, ὦ а̓́να, πηγῆς αὐτὸς ἔχων κληῖδα"</note>; and this: **you filled all things with your mind-awakening providence** <note>original: "πάντα τεῆς ἔπλησας ἐγερσινόοιο προνοίης"</note>; and that immense power **of the Fates** <note>original: "μοιρέων"</note>; and those things which were read in* no philosophy before the promulgation of the Gospel: the demons fearing his threatening whip, the demons lying in wait for souls, **so that they might forget the lofty hall of the ever-shining Father** <note>original: "ὄφρα ὑψιτενε͂ς λάθοιντο πατρὸς а̓ειφεγγέος αὐλῆς"</note>. And who but the Word of the Father is that **Image of the all-begetting God, who, appearing from the unutterable Begetter, stilled the roar of the elements rushing upon one another** <note>original: "εἰκὼν παγγενέταο θεοῦ, ὅς φανένθ’ а̓π’ ἀῤῥήτου γενετῆρος παύσατο στοιχείων ὀρυμαγδὸς ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισιν ἰόντων"</note>?

But let us see for what reason the Hymn was mentioned most especially. For this same Sun, who **from on high channels the rich stream of harmony** <note>original: "Ὑψοθεν ἁρμονίης ῥύμα πλούσιον ἐξοχετεύει" (*Hypsothen harmoniēs rhyma plousion exocheteuei*)</note>; the same one from whose lineage Phoebus is born, who **singing wondrous songs to the lyre, lulls the great wave of loud-roaring birth** <note>original: "κιθάρῃ ὑπὸ θέσκελα μέλπων Εὐνάζει μέγα κῦμα βαρυφλοίσβοιο γενέθλης" (*kitharē hypo theskela melpōn eunazei mega kyma baryphloisboio genethlēs*)</note>; and he whose choir is shared by Paean <note>A title for Apollo as a healer or singer</note>, **having filled the wide world with all-healing harmony** <note>original: "Πλήσας ἁρμονίης παναπήμονος εὐρέα κόσμον" (*Plēsas harmoniēs panapēmonos eyrea kosmon*)</note>—this same Sun, I say, he greets in the very first verse of the Hymn as the **King of intellectual fire** <note>original: "Πυρὸς νοεροῦ βασιλέα" (*Pyros noerou basilea*)</note>. By this opening, he indicates both what the Pythagoreans understood by the name of "Fire" (so that it is a wonder that the disciple should differ from his masters regarding the location of the Center, which they gave to the Sun itself); and at the same time, he transfers the whole Hymn from the body of the Sun and its sensible quality of light to intellectual things. To that "intellectual fire" of his (perhaps the **craftsman fire** <note>original: "igni... artifici"; a Stoic concept of a creative, rational fire</note> of the Stoics), to that "created God" of his Plato, the "Governing Mind" or **Self-governing one** <note>original: "Αὐτόνῳ" (*Autonō*) or "Principal Mind"</note>, he assigned a royal seat in the body of the Sun, confounding the Creature and the one through whom all things were created into one. 

But we Christians, taught to distinguish better, know that the eternal and uncreated **Word** <note>original: "Lógon"</note>, who was **with God** <note>original: "πρὸς τὸν θεόν" (*pros ton theon*)</note>, and who is contained by no dwelling—even though He is within all things and excluded by nothing, even though He is Himself outside all things—we know that He took on flesh from the womb of the most glorious Virgin Mary into the unity of His Person. And once the ministry of the flesh was completed, He occupied the royal seat of the heavens, where the heavenly Father is also recognized to dwell in a certain excellent way above the other parts of the world (namely, through glory and majesty). He also promised his faithful that there are mansions in that house of his Father. As for the rest, we consider it superfluous to inquire too curiously into that seat, or to summon our senses or natural reason to investigate that which "eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man." But the created Mind, of however great excellence it may be, we rightly subject to its Creator; nor do we, like the Magi, introduce innumerable armies of planetary spirits to be worshipped...

# HARMONIES, BOOK V. #

<margin>
CHAPTER 9.

<margin>

...or whether we propose that they are summoned by theurgic <note>original: "Theurgicis"; theurgy refers to rituals or magic intended to evoke the presence of divine spirits.</note> superstitions for mutual communication; being carefully on guard against this, we now further inquire freely, by natural reasoning, into what kind of Mind each one might be—especially if there is one in the heart of the World which, acting as the soul of the world, is bound more closely to the nature of things (or if perhaps some intelligent creatures, of a nature different from the human, inhabit or will inhabit such an animated globe). If one is permitted to thread through the labyrinths of Nature's mysteries by the lead of analogy, one would not argue foolishly, I think, that the relationship of the six orbits to their common center—and thus to the whole world—is the same as the relationship of **discursive thought** <note>original: "τῆς διανοίας" (*tēs dianoias*); the step-by-step process of reasoning.</note> to the **intellect** <note>original: "τὸν νοῦν" (*ton noun*); immediate, intuitive understanding.</note>, as these faculties are distinguished by Aristotle, Plato, Proclus, and others. And again, that the relationship of the local revolutions of the individual planets around the Sun to the **immovable** <note>original: "ἀμετάθετον" (*ametatheton*)</note> gyration of the Sun in the center of the whole system is the same as the relationship of the **discursive faculty** <note>original: "διανοητικῆς" (*dianoētikēs*)</note> to the **intellectual faculty** <note>original: "τὸ νοερὸν" (*to noeron*)</note>: that is, of the multiple paths of reasoning to the simplest mental understanding. 

For just as the Sun, rotated within itself, moves all the planets by the **species** <note>original: "speciem"; in Kepler’s physics, this is an immaterial power or force emitted by a body that acts upon others.</note> emitted from itself, so also the mind (as philosophers teach), in understanding itself and all things within itself, stirs up reasonings; and by extending and unfolding its own simplicity into them, it causes all things to be understood. So closely connected and bound together are the motions of the planets around the Sun at their center and the paths of reasoning, that unless the Earth, our dwelling place, moved in an annual circle in the middle of the other orbits—changing its position and its vantage point—human reasoning would never have struggled through to the truest distances of the planets and the other things depending on them, nor would it ever have established Astronomy.

Conversely, the simplicity of understanding follows the rest of the Sun in the center of the world in a beautiful correspondence; for up to this point, we have always maintained that those solar Harmonies of motions are defined neither by the diversity of regions nor by the vastness of the World’s spaces. Surely, if some mind looks out from the Sun, it lacks those aids of motion and different stations of its own seat, from which it might weave the reasonings and paths necessary for measuring the distances of the planets. It compares, therefore, the daily motions of each planet, not as they are in their orbits, but as they glide toward the center of the Sun through angles. Thus, if it has knowledge of the magnitude of the spheres, it must possess this *a priori* <note>meaning: known before experience or measurement.</note>, without the labor of reasoning—which indeed was shown above from Plato and Proclus to be true to some extent both of human minds and of sublunary <note>Earthly, or literally "below the moon."</note> nature.

<margin>
Let me be allowed to play the storyteller like Plato’s *Atlantis*, and the dreamer like Cicero’s *Scipio*.
</margin>
Since these things are so, it would certainly not be strange if someone, after taking a more generous draft from this **cup of Pythagoras**—which Proclus offers at the very first verse of his Hymn—and being warmed by it, and lulled into sleep by the most sweet Harmony of the planets' dance, should begin to dream: that the discursive or reasoning faculties are scattered throughout the other globes moving from place to place around the Sun (among which the most excellent and complete must be considered the one in the middle of those globes, namely, the human faculty on Earth); but that in the Sun dwells a simple Intellect, an **intellectual fire** <note>original: "πῦρ νοερὸν" (*pyr noeron*)</note> or **Mind** <note>original: "Νοῦν" (*Noun*)</note>, the source of all Harmony, whoever that might be.

# ON THE MOTIONS OF THE PLANETS #

<margin>
CHAPTER 10.
</margin>

For if, regarding the sheer vastness of those globes, it seemed to Tycho Brahe <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the Danish astronomer whose precise observations provided the foundation for Kepler's laws.</note> that they were not empty wastes in the world, but packed with inhabitants: how much more likely is it that we shall take a guess about the other globes from the variety of God's works and plans which we see on this globe of the Earth? For He who created species to inhabit the waters, beneath which there is no place for the air that living things breathe; He who sent birds supported by wings into the vastness of the air; He who gave **polar bears** and **white foxes** to the snowy regions of the north, and gave them the **whales** of the sea and the eggs of birds for food; He who gave **lions** to the solitudes of sweltering Libya, and **camels** to the vast plains of Syria, giving the former an endurance for hunger and the latter for thirst: would He have exhausted all His art on the globe of the Earth so that He *could not*, or all His goodness so that He *would not*, adorn the other globes with suitable creatures? These creatures would be suggested by the long or short durations of their revolutions, the proximity or distance of the Sun, the variety of their <term>eccentricities</term> <note>The degree to which an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note>, the brightness or darkness of their bodies, or the properties of the geometric figures upon which each region is supported. For behold: just as the races of living things on this globe of the Earth have the image of the male in the **Dodecahedron** <note>A 12-sided Platonic solid; Kepler associated these shapes with the structure of the universe.</note> and the female in the **Icosahedron** <note>A 20-sided Platonic solid.</note> (the former of which supports the Earth's orbit from the outside, the latter from the inside); and finally, they have the image of generation in the divine proportion and ineffability of that union: what shall we think the other globes have from the other figures? For what good do four Moons circle Jupiter, and two Moons Saturn <note>In 1618, the "two moons" of Saturn likely referred to the "ansae" or handles—the rings—which appeared as two blurry satellites in early telescopes.</note>, as this single Moon of ours circles our dwelling place? In the same way, we shall also reason about the globe of the Sun, and we shall, as it were, give a body to the conjectures taken from the **Harmonies** and other things (which are very weighty in themselves) by adding other conjectures that lean more toward physical bodies and are better suited to the grasp of the common people. Is that globe empty while the others are full, if everything else corresponds so closely? If, as the Earth breathes out clouds, the Sun breathes out dark soot? If, as the former is moistened by rain and turns green, the Sun glows with those burnt-out spots of his, while brighter little flames shine out on his body, which is entirely fiery. To what use is this preparation if the globe is empty? Do not the senses themselves cry out that fiery bodies dwell here, capable of simple Minds, and that the Sun is truly, if not the King, at least the Royal Palace of **intellectual fire**? <note>original: "πυρὸς νοεροῦ" (*pyros noerou*); a Neoplatonic term for a divine, thinking fire or spiritual light.</note>

I deliberately break off both this dream and this most vast speculation; only crying out this much with the Royal Psalmist:

# APPENDIX
## TO BOOK V OF THE HARMONIES.

Regarding the Appendix that I promised above in the Table of Contents of Book V: the reader should not expect it here.
> A wine jar began to be formed, but as the wheel turns, out comes a pitcher. <note>original: "Amphora coepit Institui, currente rotâ verùm urceus exit." Kepler quotes the Roman poet Horace’s *Ars Poetica* to explain that his grand plan for this section had to be scaled down due to circumstances.</note>

I will state the reasons briefly: I was about to navigate a great and overflowing river, when suddenly, as the volume of water subsided into a thin stream, a ford appeared that I could cross on foot, leaving the ship at its station for more necessary uses. This is what I mean: Ptolemy’s *Harmonics* <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the influential Greco-Egyptian astronomer and mathematician whose work Kepler is both building upon and critiquing.</note> in three books, which I possess in Greek manuscripts along with the commentaries of the most profound philosopher Porphyry <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a commentary on Ptolemy's *Harmonics*.</note> (likewise in Greek, from the beginning up to Book II, Chapter VII), always seemed to me worthy of being published in their entirety in a Greek-Latin edition. For that reason, ten years ago, I began to translate them into the Latin language; this version proceeded as far as the middle of Porphyry's manuscript. I was prevented from going further by a change of location, joined with many troubles, and, after I came to Linz, by a new beginning of astronomical studies.

But indeed, when I proposed a year ago to publish my five books of *Harmonics*, I saw that great importance lay in the comparison of my work with the Ptolemaic one, especially regarding my Book V and the final chapters of Ptolemy’s Book III—the last three of which contain nothing but "lemmas" or titles provided by Ptolemy. Therefore, though my spirit was reluctant, I proposed to pluck only one part from that mutilated work, which related most closely to my subject. To this end, I translated Book III of Ptolemy from Chapter III to the end; and to the three final empty titles, I added their own texts, composed with as much skill as possible from the principles of Ptolemaic astronomy and the mind of the author. Finally, I added commentaries or Notes, in which the defect of Porphyry’s commentary (which breaks off at Book II, Chapter VII) is supplied in this third book, and Ptolemy’s discoveries are compared with my own. The distinction is shown between Ptolemy’s **symbolisms** and my **legitimate demonstrations**. From this, the weakness and imperfection of those symbolisms, and the primary cause of this—namely, the falsity of the principles of Ptolemaic astronomy—becomes clear. 

However, when this appendix alone was set to occupy 30 pages of the book, behold: in the meantime, the neighboring Bohemian War <note>The Bohemian Revolt (1618–1620), the opening phase of the Thirty Years' War, which caused significant disruption across Central Europe during the printing of Kepler's work.</note> broke out; travel routes were blocked, and most of the workers have declared their names for military service. Thus, first the paper failed us, then the laborers who manage the press; finally, the time has been dragged out by the most tedious delays. Driven by these obstacles, I finally looked back at myself and cut short my plan; I would not expose—and almost destroy—the book of that excellent author Ptolemy and his commentator Porphyry by publishing only a mutilated fragment. Would it not be better, then, to spend the remaining half of the labor on a full translation of Porphyry’s exposition, write the Notes for the remaining chapters of Books II and III, and join them with those I have already written for almost all of Book III? In this way, the work would be made whole and published as a Greek-Latin edition in its own right. For such a publication, another time, another place, and a suitable printer are required.

Lest, however, anything I promised above be completely missed by the reader, or lest this final part lacks anything for the integrity or easier understanding of my work on *Harmonics*: come, I shall transcribe the titles of the chapters of Ptolemy’s Book III, and I will compare them with their places in my work; I will write a summary of what is contained in my Notes.

First, those things which Ptolemy handed down in Books I and II and at the beginning of the third regarding the discipline of *Harmonics*, I have embraced in my Book III by another method, quite different. While Ptolemy seeks the principles of harmonies from abstract numbers (following the ancients), I, on the contrary, denying that the power of number exists in them as they are counted, substitute for these num—

1 APPENDIX. 9
<sig>A</sig>
<meta>catchword: Pla-</meta>

counts of numbers—that is, the actual things subject to number, namely regular plane figures <note>Two-dimensional shapes like triangles and squares.</note> and the divisions of the circle to be managed by them—establishing the principles of Harmonies, I necessarily prefixed Books I and II concerning Harmonic figures to my Book III.

Now, in the third book, chapter 3 of his work, Ptolemy provided this title: *Under what category of things the nature or power of Harmony, and the knowledge of it, should be placed.* He shows that there is some causal, formal, mental, and even divine principle that reconciles Harmonies to things. In Chapter IV: *That the power of Harmonic blending exists in all things whose natures consist of a higher degree of perfection, and that this appears most clearly in human souls and in the celestial revolutions.* <note>Ptolemy is arguing that harmony is a fundamental law of the universe, found in both the spirit and the stars.</note> Here you see the division of what remained for Ptolemy to discuss; first, concerning Harmonies existing in Souls, and second, concerning Harmonies in the motions of the heavens. Regarding the first part, three chapters follow; regarding the second, the nine remaining chapters. In Chapter V, he compares individual consonances <note>Musical intervals that sound pleasing together.</note> with the individual faculties of the rational Soul, doing so concisely through subdivisions of both sets of things being compared. In Chapter VI, he compares the individual types of Harmonies with the individual types or classes of virtues. In Chapter VII, he compares the changes of Tones <note>Musical modes or scales.</note> with changes in public pursuits across different times, and thus also with the sudden changes of emotions in Souls.

In this section, I dispute many things against Ptolemy. Specifically, I argue that those symbolisms <note>Symbolic correspondences or analogies.</note> are for the most part not necessary, nor causal, nor natural, but rather poetic and oratorical. For those special faculties and virtues that exist in souls do not receive either their Form <note>Idea</note> or the numbers of their constitution from Harmonies as if from an Archetype <note>A primary model or pattern.</note>, but have other acknowledged or evident causes. Indeed, they do not even correspond to the number [of harmonies], but are far-fetched or poorly applied, so that they might be reconciled to them by some kind of multifaceted division. Many redundant things are included, or conversely, defects are ignored; certain things that do not quite fit are "dragged in by the hair" <note>original: "crinibus trahi." A Latin idiom meaning a point is forced or strained.</note>. Finally, even those things that respond to each other most aptly and skillfully are nonetheless not taken according to any proportion of quantity of the same kind—yet Harmonies cannot exist except in the comparison of quantities.

However, as for the fact that Musical Tones are compared to emotions and public character, I have shown that this is entirely natural and has the nature of a cause. On the occasion of Ptolemy's text, I have brought forward the opinions of various philosophers regarding the kinship of Souls, Numbers, and Harmonies among themselves, to which I have added the Epilogue of my Book V. And as specifically regards the effect of tones in moving souls in different ways: I have encompassed that material in the special Chapter XV of my Book III. Likewise regarding Commutative and Distributive Justice <note>Aristotelian concepts of justice: the former deals with fair exchange, the latter with fair distribution of honors or wealth.</note>, Friendship, and Economics and Politics: concerning this matter, and to what extent musical proportions prevail in them, I made a Digression at the end of my Book III. Finally, the subject matter of the aforementioned Chapters III and IV, and whatever true things could be said in general about V, VI, and VII: I have encompassed these in the first three chapters and again in the seventh chapter of my Book IV. There, having explained the nature of Souls, I showed that since a circle is geometrically divided by the inscription of plane figures, comparing the parts with the whole truly and properly defines Harmonic proportions. Therefore, by an essential reasoning, a circle exists in souls—formally and abstractly, not only apart from matter, but even in a certain way apart from quantity itself, considered materially. Therefore, since the circle is in souls, Harmonies are also in them, and this is the cause why Souls are moved by Harmonies. But all these things are only in general; no causation follows regarding the distribution of the Soul into special faculties. Such, therefore, is the case with human Souls.

Regarding celestial motions, Ptolemy in Book III, Chapter VIII of his work, compares the Zodiac with the musical system or scale; in Chapter IX, he compares the consonances themselves with the Emotions...

### APPENDIX
<sig>Ii 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: Physicians</meta>

Of the Planets. Here I have shown in which parts the doctrine of Aspects <note>original: "Aspectibus"; these are the significant astrological angles between planets, such as a square or a trine.</note> is lacking in Ptolemy’s work, and how, through the integration of number—on one hand of the Aspects, and on the other of the Consonances—the natural and causal connection of these things finally becomes apparent. This is the genuine material of my Book IV, especially chapters IV, V, and VI.

<margin>Planets. Chapter XI. Chapter XII. Chapter XIII.</margin>
In Chapter X, Ptolemy creates a kind of melody from the motion of a Planet from its rising to its setting; in Chapter XI, however, he creates genres of song from the motion of the Planets in height and depth <note>This refers to a planet's distance from the Earth, or its orbital eccentricity.</note>. In Chapter XII, from their motion to the sides of the equator <note>This refers to planetary latitude, or how far north or south of the ecliptic a planet moves.</note>, he creates a variety of Musical tones. In Chapter XIII, from the various configurations of the planets with the Sun, he creates the various Tetrachords <note>A series of four notes spanning a perfect fourth, the building block of ancient Greek music scales.</note> of the system. In these four chapters, I have shown that Ptolemy indulges in the exercise of poetic or oratorical comparison; for the things he compares are not real in the heavens, except for a small portion of Chapter XI, which I wish to be set aside for the last three chapters because of the kinship of the subject matter. <margin>Incomparable.</margin> I have also shown that here, in part, incomparable things are being compared—the very nature of the things compared crying out against it—and in part, things that correspond in every member do so at least accidentally, rather than cohering out of the necessity of some cause. Thus, up to this point, there is nothing or very little that agrees with my celestial Harmonies.

<margin>Inconsistent.</margin>
But indeed, the following Chapter XIV of Ptolemy proposes to inquire according to which prime numbers the sounds of the system or musical scale can be compared with the primary spheres in the Planetary system. Here I have shown that comparison was impossible for Ptolemy and the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, who believed the universe was built on numbers and the "Music of the Spheres."</note> in their usual Astronomy, although I attempted to devise something consistent with Ptolemaic principles so that his text might be supported by its own title. I also showed that since the primary spheres consist of their own quantities, no less than strings consist of their own lengths, the comparison ought to have been established according to those quantities; yet the proportion of the spheres differs greatly from the proportion of consonant musical strings. <margin>Archetype.</margin> However, the corrected and causal, or Archetypal <term>Archetype: A fundamental, original model or blueprint used by God to create the universe.</term> connection of the spheres of the World with the regular bodies <note>The five Platonic Solids.</note>, I have repeated from my earlier work, the *Mysterio Cosmographico* <note>The Secret of the Universe, Kepler’s first major work published in 1596.</note>, at the beginning of my Book V.

Chapter XV of Ptolemy seeks how the proportions of the proper motions can be taken through numbers; but the text is missing. I have therefore shown the same things as in the preceding chapter. For the rest, I have offered this for consideration: that here, 1500 years ago, Ptolemy set out to treat the specific material of my Book V, if only he had been able to do so through his own astronomy. I, therefore, in a repaired Astronomy—which retains the true and simple motions of the planets, having eliminated the appearances that consist of deceptions of the eyes—have shown that within the heavens, according to a true and genuine quantitative and measurable ratio, and not through mere light-weight symbolism, there exist all the Harmonic proportions: the genres of Harmonies, the system or Musical scale and most of its keys, the varieties of Tones, the planets as rivals of the voices in figured music <term>Figuralis musica: Polyphonic music where different voices move in independent rhythms, as opposed to simple plainchant.</term>, and finally the universal counterpoints of the 6 primary planets, varied by genres and tones. Chapter XVI and last: Ptolemy promises that he wants to investigate by what reason the familiarities of the Wanderers <note>original: "Erronum," a traditional term for the planets.</note> can be compared with the familiarities of sounds: that is, he busied himself with demonstrating astrological principles concerning beneficial and harmful planets, or those that are friends or enemies among themselves, through the celestial Harmonies. And because the text for this chapter is also missing, I have arranged it as best I could, especially from Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman author whose commentary on the "Dream of Scipio" preserved many Pythagorean musical and astronomical ideas.</note>. But at the same time, I have shown in the notes what is lacking in this business, so that it might succeed less according to ancient astronomy. In my own work, however, I have no part corresponding to Chapter XVI, except for a few things from the Epilogue of Book V. For astrology deals with the effects of the stars on the earth, but my celestial Harmonies are not formed for the sake of lands on the earth, but in the Sun. And here is the end of Ptolemy's work: with which I would also end the summary of the Appendix promised in the entrance of Book V, were I not invited by the affinity of these matters to satisfy also those who have entreated me, such as Dr. Robert Fludd <note>original: "D. Roberti de Fluctibus"; an English physician and mystic who argued for a different, more symbolic interpretation of cosmic harmony.</note>...

# 252 APPENDIX.

I should not omit mention in my work on Harmony of the Physician of Oxford <note>Robert Fludd (1574–1637), an English physician and mystical philosopher whose work often clashed with Kepler’s more mathematical approach.</note>, who a year ago published a book on the **Microcosm and Macrocosm** <note>The "Macrocosm" refers to the universe as a whole, while the "Microcosm" refers to the human being as a miniature reflection of that universe.</note> filled with harmonic contemplations. Rather, I should briefly show the reader in which matters he and I agree, and in which, conversely, we disagree.

<margin>On the **World Music** of Dr. Robert Fludd, Physician of Oxford.</margin>

Therefore, that author promised two volumes: one titled *On the Macrocosm* has already seen the light of day; the other, *On the Microcosm*, is still expected. The first volume, comprising two treatises, was also produced at distinct times. For I saw the first treatise, *On the Triple World*, after the Frankfurt autumn fair of the year 1617; the second, *On the Arts* (which he calls the **Ape of Worldly Nature** <note>original: "Naturæ Mundanæ Simius"; this refers to Fludd’s idea that human arts "ape" or imitate the processes of nature.</note>), I saw at the Easter fair of the following year, 1618. In the second treatise, he placed Music among the arts, covering the material of my third book to some extent. In the first treatise, however, which is completed in seven books, he destined the third book for **World Music** <note>original: "Musicæ Mundanæ"; the harmony of the spheres or the universe.</note>, using the same title that I prefixed to my entire work; indeed, he touched upon the material of my Books IV and V.

Let us therefore begin with his artificial Music. He treats it in seven books: in the first, he reviews authors, terminologies, and its power over the human soul. Regarding the authors or the history of the invention, I have said nothing, or certainly very little, because my intent is to reveal the causes of natural things. I have included necessary terminologies throughout my definitions; I have omitted the superfluous ones. Regarding the power of Music over souls, I deal with this in Book III, Chapter XV, and throughout Book IV. In the second book, the author approaches the subjects themselves, which he calls **Intervals and Times**. Again, I have said almost nothing about **Times** (or the length and brevity of sounds), for they are arbitrary and do not require an inquiry into their causes. He calls certain intervals "simple," which to me are the smallest dissonant concords—the major tone, minor tone, semitone, and **diesis** <note>A very small musical interval, smaller than a semitone.</note>. Others he wishes to be composed of these, which I call **Consonances**. Yet I expressly refuted this opinion of the ancients—that consonances are composed of smaller intervals as if they were prior by nature—in Chapter IV of my Book III, showing that, on the contrary, the smaller intervals arise from the larger consonances. 

In the third book, he explains the system or musical scale, which is the principal part of my Book III, from Chapter IV to IX. The remaining four books of the author contain practice, which I do not even touch upon. For in Book IV, he teaches about the measurement of the beat, its various modes, and the value of notes through them, about which I say very little in Book III, Chapter XV and Book IV, Chapter III. In Book V, he has the rules for composing **figured song** <note>original: "cantus figurati"; complex polyphonic music as opposed to simple chant.</note>, an art which I do not profess. In Book VI, he even digresses into various musical instruments, which I have not even thought about. Finally, in Book VII, he reveals a new instrument of his own. In these four latter books, therefore, he differs from me as a **Practitioner** from a **Theorist**. For while he presents instruments, I inquire into the causes of things or consonances; and while he teaches how to compose melody for several voices, I prepare mathematical demonstrations for most things that are naturally present in song, both **Choral** <note>Plainchant.</note> and **Figured**. For this reason also, there are many pictures in his work; in mine, there are mathematical diagrams labeled with letters. You may also see that he delights greatly in the dark enigmas of things, whereas I strive to bring things wrapped in obscurity into the light of the intellect. The former is familiar to the **Chemists** <note>original: "Chymicis"; likely referring to Alchemists.</note>, **Hermeticists**, and **Paracelsians**; the latter is the proper task of **Mathematicians**.

And so, even in Books II and III, where he treats the same material as I do, there is this difference between us: what he takes from the ancients, I dig out from the Nature of things and establish from the very foundations. What he received, he presented confusedly (on account of...

# APPENDIX 253

...uses the varying opinions of those handing down traditions, and incorrect ones at that; I proceed by a natural order, so that all things are corrected according to the laws of Nature, and confusion is avoided; thus, I do not even apply my findings to the decrees of the ancients, except where no confusion follows. So, where I expressly refute the ancients when discussing the causes of concordances, he follows the ancients without any risk of doubt; he does not even think about the truer causes. In a single word: in the <term>Harmonic</term> <note>The science of sounds and mathematical proportions.</note> discipline, one acts as a vocal and instrumental Musician; the other acts as a philosopher and Mathematician.

Now let us pass to the author's other section, where he introduces Music into the World. Here, indeed, there is a vast difference between us. First, those harmonies he intends to teach are mere **symbolisms**, about which I say the same as I did regarding the symbolisms of Ptolemy: they belong to the poet or the orator rather than to the philosopher or mathematician. This is the soul of that entire work, as is evident even from the title: **The Macrocosm and Microcosm**. For in the second volume, he undoubtedly intends to demonstrate that noble theme: that the Ideas of the whole great world and all its parts are found in man. This same "soul" is present in the first volume as well, because he distributes the whole world into three regions; where, according to that most celebrated **axiom of Hermes** <note>The Hermetic maxim "As above, so below," which suggests that the celestial and terrestrial realms reflect one another.</note>, he makes the higher things similar or analogous to the lower. But for this analogy to succeed in all things, the subjects being compared must often be **drawn by the hair** <note>A Latin idiom meaning the comparison is forced or strained.</note>. My own opinion on analogies is clear from the digression at the end of my third book: namely, that there is an analogy of proportions in geometric matters which is formal with respect to indefinite and indeterminate quantitative matter; yet, with respect to harmonic proportions, it can be considered a material affection. This is because, while harmonic proportions define a certain quantity, analogies, by contrast, are suited to run out into infinity by themselves, and thus they suppose a material state of infinity.

Even though I also treat some things similar to those "Macrocosmic" matters in my work—such as in Book IV, where I make the Earth a living animal—it is done for a far different reason. For I do not contend that there is a mere analogy between the Earth and animals, nor do I wish the archetype of the animal to be taken from the Earth itself; rather, I simply propose to demonstrate that those works seen on the globe of the Earth cannot arise from the motions of the elements or from the solitary properties of matter, but instead testify to the **presence of a Soul**. Now, for my arguments to be understood, it was necessary to cite various functions of the soul in the animal body. To come closer to the foundations upon which Robert Fludd builds his **World Music** <note>original: "musica Mundana"</note>: first, he occupies the whole world and all three of its parts—the **Empyrean**, the **Celestial**, and the **Elemental** <note>The Empyrean is the highest heaven of fire/light; the Celestial is the realm of the planets; the Elemental is the sublunary world of earth, water, air, and fire.</note>; I occupy only the celestial, and not all of that, but only the motions of the planets as if under the Zodiac. He, trusting in the ancients who believed the power of Harmonies resided in abstract numbers, is satisfied if he can demonstrate a concordance between parts by encompassing them in numbers in any way possible, with no care for what kind of units are accumulated in that number. I, however, nowhere teach the seeking of Harmonies where the things between which the Harmonies exist cannot be measured by the **same measure of quantity**; so that, by reason of quantity, there is the same proportion between them as there is between two strings of the same tension, by reason of length. Therefore, he divides the whole World into three equal parts by means of the semi-diameter, knowing well enough that those parts are not at all equal; he does so only because the first unit is the Elemental world, the second is the Ethereal world, and the third is the Empyrean; and indeed, units cannot be depicted otherwise than by the equality of lines. But I, unless astronomy testifies to that same quantitative measure of units, do not use them as units at all for counting...

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s direct critique of Robert Fludd's "macrocosm" model. Kepler is specifically addressing Fludd's geometric representations of the universe as interlocking pyramids of light and matter.</meta>

# APPENDIX 254

...[measuring] harmonic proportions. He, however, insisting on his own principles and raising a pyramid from a base—the great circle of the Earth—places its vertex at the very summit of the **empyrean heaven** <note>The highest part of heaven, thought in ancient cosmology to be the realm of pure fire or light and the dwelling place of God.</note>; and having divided its height into three equal parts (as if he truly possessed equal units), he counts how many parts go to the Empyrean, how many to the Celestial, and how many to the Elementary region. For in this way, the top of the Elementary region is twice as far from the top of the Celestial as it is from the top of the Empyrean. Furthermore, in the division of the Pyramid, with respect to the axis, three equal parts go to the three regions; but with respect to the triangle through the axis, one unit goes to the Empyrean, three to the Celestial, and five units to the Elementary. Finally, with respect to the space or the volume of the figure, one unit goes to the Empyrean, seven to the Celestial, and nineteen units go to the Elementary.

What shall I say now of the other, opposing **Pyramid of Light**, whose base he makes the adorable Trinity itself at the summit of the empyrean heaven, while he places its vertex on the Earth itself? When he mixes these two Pyramids together and draws forth musical proportions from that mixture, he attempts something entirely different from the purpose of my work. For he compares Light (the giver of form and Soul) and Matter—two things most different from each other, in which quantities do not exist in the same respect. I, however, for the terms of forming a **harmonic proportion** <note>original: "proportione Harmonica"; the mathematical ratio that produces a musical concord.</note> in the world, admit nothing except those things which receive quantities in the same respect; for example, the daily motion of Mars and the daily motion of Jupiter. 

No less a diversity exists between us in this: that he assigns four degrees of obscurity and darkness to the Elementary region because, he says, any thing has four quarters, surely no less than three thirds or five fifths; and now he says all four are in the Earth, three in the water (and thus it is already transparent), two in the air, and one in the fire. Again, elsewhere, he subdivides every region—whether of an Element or of Heaven—into three spaces: the highest, middle, and lowest, though not always following the probability of the senses. You see, his units are again arbitrary.

Yet because of this, he proceeds to establish a **perfect fourth** <note>original: "Diatessarôn"; a musical interval of a fourth.</note> between the Earth and water, and he applies its three intervals—tone, tone, and semitone—to the three spaces: highest, middle, and lowest; whereas those spaces have certain quantities derived from his own reasons, and these [musical] boundaries are not even set by nature. Indeed, the measurements according to these most general principles are plainly indeterminate. 

But for me, natural units are proposed in which I may seek Harmonies—namely, the two extreme motions of the planets (whether daily or hourly, it makes no difference) expressed by nature in their own certain quantities. He seeks harmonic proportions in the degrees of darkness and light, without regard for any motion; I seek Harmonies only in motions. He tastes a few small concordances and draws them out from the mixture of his Pyramids (by which he carries around the World privately pictured in his own mind), or he proves they are represented by it. I have demonstrated that the whole body of harmonic contemplation, with all its parts, exists in the extreme proper motions of the planets, according to certain measures demonstrated by **Astronomy**. Thus, his own concept of the World is the subject of harmony for him, but for me, it is the World itself, or the real motions of the planets within it.

From these few points, I believe it is clear: although to understand the mysteries crowded into the most profound philosophy which Robert [Fludd] delivers, a knowledge of harmonic proportions is altogether necessary; nevertheless, the man who has learned my entire work will still be quite far from those most perplexed mysteries—just as those mysteries have themselves withdrawn from the most accurate certainty of mathematical demonstrations.

And here, let this also be the END of the Appendix.

# THINGS TO BE CORRECTED IN THE WORK.

At the outset, you should know that the first two books, which were printed last, have a unique sequence of page numbers. Therefore, correct these numbers: Book I, folio 41. And Book III, folios 50, 63, 112, 150, 161, 200, 212, 228, 229, 236, 237. Correct the remaining errors as follows: Book I, folio 2, the third line from the bottom: "everywhere" <note>original: "undique"</note>. Page 17, the second line from the bottom: "then" <note>original: "tunc"</note>; between folios 52 and 55, two folios with copperplate illustrations should be inserted. Folio 66, in the margin for conclusion 29, let folio 150 be cited, and for conclusion 30, folio 82 of Book III.

In Book III, folios 23 and 24, the notes are to be corrected from the following folio 103. Folio 25, line 17: "into parts." Folio 29, in the first diagram, move the note at the number 6 from the space down into the line below; however, fill the deficiency from folio 86.

Folios 33, 34, and 35: The text was collected from sheets written at different times, and was not sufficiently well-organized; although everything in it is true, it has acquired a certain obscurity from the confusion of things that should be distinguished and from the repetition of propositions. The distinct questions are these:

*Question I.* Do **consonances** <note>Musical intervals that sound pleasant or "stable" to the ear, such as an octave or a fifth.</note> have parts which are themselves also consonances or at least **well-fitting intervals** <note>original: "concinna intervalla"; intervals that, while not perfect consonances, are musically useful.</note>?
*The response is this:* In consonances, these things are distinct: first, the proportion, which is a geometric matter; second, the quality of the proportion, which is the consonance itself. Insofar as they are proportions, one can be exceeded by another—the smaller by the larger—and thus one can be a part of the other. But insofar as each of them receives the quality of consonance from its own demonstrable geometric figure, no "composition" <note>The idea that one consonance is simply "built" by stacking others.</note> happens to them. The arguments are these:
1. A species, as a species, is indivisible and one.
2. A species is constituted by its cause: but the causes of the individual harmonies are distinct among themselves; therefore, the harmonies themselves are distinct in species from one another, nor can one (as a whole) be dissolved into others of its own species (as parts), though it can certainly be dissolved into smaller intervals of a different species.
3. If a consonance were like a quantity that increases when a part is multiplied, then a consonant or "well-fitting" part of a consonance would increase the consonance or the "fitness" of the whole; but instead, a dissonance or "unfit" sound is eventually produced from such accumulation.

*Question II.* Do consonances have one common measure, such as a **Tone**, a **Diesis**, or a **Comma** <note>Technical musical terms for small intervals used as units of measurement in tuning systems.</note>?
It is denied. They do not have one as proportions, because in that sense they are incommensurable (that is, lacking a shared measurable unit); nor do they have one as species, because they are mutually distinct from one another by the causes from which they arise and by which they are defined. For they have, in a way, the nature of geometric figures; just as a triangle and a pentagon in the same circle have side lengths that are incommensurable. Finally, a measure is prior to the things measured; but "well-fitting" intervals like the Tone or Diesis are posterior to the consonances <note>Meaning the small steps of a scale are derived from the larger harmonies, not the other way around.</note>. And note: these parts—the Major Tone, Minor Tone, semitone, etc.—are common to the consonances, but not all are common to all consonances, nor is there any one of them which alone can measure out the consonances.

Folio 35, in the first diagram, delete the mark after 8, and the number 3 next to 9; instead, place another mark above 9 in the space belonging to 8, followed by the number 3. In the second diagram, transfer the number 4 from the middle line to the nearest one. Folio 36, last line, delete the word "two." Folio 41, in the third diagram, for 66 in the middle line, write 96 in the second to last line. Folio 45, line 12: "Minor tone" instead of "hard." In the same place, in the diagram across from VI, express 10 transversely. Regarding folios 47 and 57, see folio 103. Folio 49, write h 7 9 5 6 2. Folio 60, fill the deficiency from folio 133 of the same Proposition XLIII. In the same place, line 9 from the end, read: "For 3, 4 is 60," etc. Folio 77, line 3: "the square of 3 units." Folio 80, <margin>in the margin let consequences 29 and 30 of Book II and proposition 44 of Book I be cited; and just below, proposition 47 of the same.</margin>

Folio 111, line 21: "for by work already"; line 22: "of the faculty of harmony, and common"; second to last line: "they set those aside." Folio 113, line 31: "principally." Folio 118, line 32: "most fortified." Folio 120, line 11: "let there be in the divine." Folio 127, line 33: "namely the species of motions." Folio 134, last line: "By the diagrams, which from here." Folio 141, second to last line: "the planets) the side first becomes known: correctly." Folio 143, lines 6 and 7 are these: "we previously used Proposition VI, center." Folio 147, <margin>the symbols for the Sun ☉ and Moon ☽ are missing in the margin.</margin> Folio 150, at proposition XV, <margin>let Book I, Prop. Folio 153, line 24, add these words: "it cannot be striven for." From the same foundation we shall also reason thus: An **aspect** <note>In astrology/astronomy, the specific angular distance between planets.</note> is an angle measured by an arc smaller than a semicircle. The remainder is larger than a semicircle; therefore, it measures no angle, no aspect. Wherefore the "remainder" is not considered in the constitution of aspects. But it *is* considered in the constitution of a harmonic division <note>Kepler is distinguishing between the physics of a vibrating string (where the leftover part of the string matters) and the geometry of planetary circles.</note>. Therefore, the division of a harmonic string (which uses the remainder) and the effective division of the **Zodiac** (which does not) do not cohere with one another. And thus, let it be rejected. THE FRENCH PERFUMER.

## "TREMBLING" SCENT.

There is another way to scent <term>Cyprus powder<note>original: "poudre de Chypre"; a popular 17th-century cosmetic powder made from oakmoss, often used for hair and skin.</note></term>, which is called *trembling in scent*, meaning that the odor is not as strong as the previous one, and that it only lasts as long as one wears it on themselves, and it does not immediately perfume a room as the other does; however, it is very pleasant, and a great deal of it is still consumed.

To make it, you must have Cyprus powder from the first or second preparation, which is not yet scented with any essence, and take whatever quantity you wish; for example, twelve pounds.

You will take two <term>drams<note>A historical unit of weight; one dram is approximately 3.9 grams.</note></term> of <term>ambergris<note>A rare, waxy substance produced by sperm whales, highly prized for its earthy scent and ability to make other perfumes last longer.</note></term>, one dram of <term>musk<note>A strong-smelling secretion from the musk deer, used as a base note in traditional perfumery.</note></term>, and half a dram of <term>civet<note>A pungent secretion from the civet cat, used sparingly in perfumes to add depth and warmth.</note></term>; you will grind them together with a little powdered sugar in a marble or porcelain mortar, with a <unclear>very clean</unclear> wooden pestle, <unclear>until the materials are well</unclear> <unclear>mixed</unclear>
